# Proposed ND280 Upgrade for the Former P0D Region

## 1. What the current detector cannot do

- **High-angle acceptance is poor.** The FGD bars and the downstream TPCs are oriented for forward tracks. A track near 90° runs along a single bar or a single layer, so it is badly reconstructed. The TPCs sit only downstream, so high-angle and backward particles never reach them. That loses roughly a quarter of the muons and a third of the leading protons.
- **The proton threshold is too high.** A 450 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 100 MeV and a range of only about 8–9 cm in scintillator. A 300 MeV/c proton (about 47 MeV) travels about 2 cm. In FGD1's xy-alternating 1 cm layers, a proton needs several layers in both views before it is reconstructed. Short tracks, and tracks at high angle, are lost.
- **Neutrons are not reconstructed.** Without them, transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) cannot be closed event by event, for example in antineutrino CC events or for missing-energy studies.

## 2. Active target: a 3D-segmented scintillator detector ("SuperFGD")

**Geometry**
- Use about 192 × 184 × 56 cubes of 1 × 1 × 1 cm³, about 2.0 million cubes in total.
- This fills the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box, giving roughly 2 t of CH target. That is about twice FGD1+FGD2.
- The long axes should be chosen to maximise the region usable for high-angle tracks.

**Cubes**
- Extruded polystyrene doped with about 1.5% PTP and 0.01% POPOP.
- Each cube is wrapped in a thin (about 50–80 µm) reflective layer made by chemical etching.
- Each cube has three orthogonal 1.5 mm holes, drilled or moulded.

**Readout**
- Three orthogonal 1 mm WLS fibres (e.g. Kuraray Y-11 multiclad) thread every cube, giving three 2D projections.
- The channel count is 192·184 + 192·56 + 184·56, about 56,000 channels.
- Each fibre is read out at one end, with a mirrored far end.
- Photosensors are small MPPCs (Hamamatsu S13360-1325-type, 1.3 × 1.3 mm², 25 µm pixels). These work fine in the 0.2 T field.

**Expected performance (from beam tests)**
- About 40–60 photoelectrons per MIP per fibre.
- Cube-to-cube optical crosstalk of a few percent.
- Time resolution of about 0.9 ns per fibre, better than 0.7 ns when several fibres are combined.

**Physics gains**
- The response is nearly isotropic, so there is about 4π acceptance for tracks that stop or exit.
- The proton threshold drops to about 300 MeV/c, because 2–3 hit cubes are enough for a track. This captures most of the distribution around the 450 MeV/c median.
- dE/dx along the track, with Bragg-peak identification, separates p, µ and π.
- Neutron tagging and kinetic-energy measurement come from time-of-flight between the vertex and an isolated secondary neutron-induced cluster. Over 0.5–1 m lever arms this gives roughly 10–30% energy resolution. Combined with the muon and proton, this closes TKI event by event.
- The fine granularity also gives good e/γ separation, which helps νe and π⁰ samples.

**Electronics**
- Front-end boards based on the CITIROC ASIC (Weeroc), mounted on the detector faces, with dual gain and roughly 0.1–0.5 ns time stamping.
- An LED-based gain calibration system.

## 3. Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs) above and below the target

**Purpose.** These cover the high-angle muons and the hard protons above about 900 MeV/c (about 6% of protons) that exit the target. They provide momentum and charge from curvature, plus dE/dx particle identification.

**Size.** Each is about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m, with a central cathode and a drift of about 0.9 m per side. They use the same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2 gas as the existing TPCs.

**Field cage**
- A thin composite field cage: aramid honeycomb sandwiched between laminated Kapton/strip foils.
- This keeps the material to about 3–4% X₀, so the muons and protons entering from the target are minimally degraded and the dead space is small.

**Readout: resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode, "ERAM")**
- A DLC resistive layer on insulator spreads the charge over neighbouring pads.
- This allows larger pads (about 10 × 11 mm) while keeping spatial resolution below 0.6 mm.
- It also suppresses sparks and halves the channel count per area relative to the existing TPCs.
- About 16 modules per TPC, read out with AFTER/AGET-based front-end electronics.

**Targets.** Momentum resolution below 10% at 1 GeV/c and dE/dx resolution below 10%, matching or exceeding the existing TPCs.

## 4. Time-of-Flight (ToF) envelope

**Layout.** Six planes enclose the SuperFGD and HA-TPC assembly. Each plane is made of about 20 cast plastic scintillator bars (EJ-200-type, about 2.2 m × 12 cm × 1 cm).

**Readout.** Both ends of each bar are read out with arrays of large-area MPPCs (e.g. 8 × 6 mm² SiPMs summed). Fast digitisation uses SAMPIC-type waveform digitisers.

**Performance.** Time resolution of about 150 ps.

**Uses**
- Determining track direction, i.e. separating backward-going particles from tracks entering from outside the detector.
- Rejecting out-of-fiducial and cosmic backgrounds.
- Adding e/µ/p identification at low momentum.
- Providing a time reference for the neutron ToF.

## 5. Integration

**Mechanical**
- The SuperFGD is assembled from cube–fibre layers inside a lightweight carbon-fibre or composite box, which can be filled with some light inert gas.
- HA-TPCs mount above and below it, all inside the existing UA1 basket.
- Barrel ECal modules stay in place. The former P0D-region ECal is kept, or modified to fit the new envelope.

**Retained systems.** FGD1, FGD2 (for C/H₂O comparisons), the three downstream TPCs, the downstream ECal and the SMRD all stay, so the upgrade adds roughly 2 t of high-acceptance target without losing the water reference.

**Data acquisition.** Unify the DAQ and trigger under a common clock across new and old subsystems, with ns-level synchronisation.

## Expected outcome

- Close to full angular acceptance for both the muon and the proton.
- A proton threshold of about 300 MeV/c and event-by-event neutron kinematics.
- About double the target mass.

Together, these should support kinematically complete CC samples for TKI. They should also drive the ND280 systematic uncertainty from about 6% toward the roughly 4% that T2K-II requires.

# Design Review: Kestrel Flats Active Target Upgrade

## Executive Summary

The constraints drive toward a highly granular, fully active detector with no dead angles, capable of tracking short-range recoil protons, reconstructing tracks at all angles including backward-going, while keeping the hydrogen fraction below 2% of target nucleons. I recommend a **scintillator-based 3D modular tracker as the primary active target, with specific augmentations** detailed below.

---

## Constraint Analysis Before Hardware Recommendations

Before naming technologies, the binding constraints must be made explicit, because they conflict in ways that eliminate several otherwise attractive options.

| Constraint | Implication |
|---|---|
| Protons down to 60 MeV kinetic energy | Range ~3 cm in plastic scintillator; granularity must resolve this |
| All-angle muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency, including backward | No upstream dead region; 4π active coverage inside target volume |
| H fraction ≤2% of nucleons | Eliminates pure hydrocarbon targets; requires heavy dilutant nucleus |
| Fits inside 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m | Tight, especially in the beam direction |
| Downstream gas drift chambers reconstruct exiting muons | Active target must match to existing tracker acceptance |

The hydrogen constraint deserves particular arithmetic attention. Polystyrene (CH) has roughly equal numbers of C and H nucleons, giving H/(H+C) ≈ 1/13 ≈ 7.7% — far too high on its own. The active target medium must therefore either avoid hydrocarbon altogether or be heavily loaded with a high-A material.

---

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. Primary Active Target: 3D Scintillator Cube Array ("SuperCube" architecture)

**Technology:** An array of 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm polystyrene scintillator cubes read out by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres threaded through each cube in all three orthogonal views (X, Y, Z), following the architecture demonstrated by the Baby MIND / T2K WAGASCI detectors and developed further in the SND@LHC and NuWro-informed designs. Each cube is read by three fibres (one per axis), and fibres from each plane are ganged to multi-pixel photon counters (MPPCs / SiPMs).

**Justification:**

- *Granularity for short proton tracks:* A 60 MeV proton has a range of approximately 2.8 cm in polystyrene. At 1.5 cm cube pitch, this gives a minimum ~2-cube track, sufficient for direction reconstruction and energy deposition identification as a proton (via dE/dx). Smaller cubes (1.0 cm) would be preferred for margin and are technically feasible but increase channel count significantly; 1.5 cm is the practical optimum.

- *All-angle tracking:* The 3D coincidence readout scheme provides true 3D hit information without a preferred tracking axis. A backward-going 150° muon is reconstructed identically to a forward one — there is no "upstream face" problem as there would be with a planar tracker. The 25% efficiency floor at all angles is achievable because there is no region of the volume that is structurally blind.

- *No dead upstream face:* Unlike a TPC, which requires a drift field and has a cathode plane, the cube array is fully sensitive to the first interaction point, including at the very upstream face of the volume. This is essential for backward-going track reconstruction.

- *Hydrogen fraction management:* Pure polystyrene cubes alone give ~7.7% H/nucleon as noted. See item 2 below for the solution.

**Channel count estimate:** The active volume 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m at 1.5 cm pitch gives roughly 173 × 153 × 60 ≈ 1.59 million cubes, each read by 3 fibres → ~4.8 million fibre ends. With ganging along fibres (groups of ~10), this reduces to ~480,000 SiPM channels. This is large but within the range of current detector construction (comparable to the ND280 upgrade). The collaboration must assess cost and DAQ bandwidth carefully; a 2.0 cm cube pitch reduces this by ~2.4× at some cost to short-track performance.

---

### 2. Hydrogen Dilution: Lead or Iron Passive Absorber Interleaving — Replaced by Lead-Loaded Scintillator Tiles

**Technology:** Replace approximately 85–90% of the pure scintillator cube volume with **lead-loaded scintillator composite cubes** (lead powder or lead glass frit mixed into the scintillator at casting), targeting a density of ~2.5–3 g/cm³, **interleaved with thin active scintillator planes**.

However, a more controllable and proven approach is a **sandwich architecture**: thin active scintillator cube layers (2 cm thick) interleaved with **1–2 mm thick lead or iron passive absorber sheets**. This is the approach used in MINERVA and the NOvA near detector.

**The arithmetic:** 
- Polystyrene density: 1.05 g/cm³; composition CH (roughly).
- If we interleave 2 cm scintillator + 1.5 mm Pb sheets (density 11.3 g/cm³):
 - Mass per unit area: scintillator 2.1 g/cm², Pb 1.70 g/cm²
 - Fraction of mass that is scintillator: 2.1/3.8 = 55%
 - H nucleons in scintillator fraction: ~8% of scintillator mass is H by mass, → ~4.4% of total mass
 - H fraction by nucleon number: (4.4%/1) / (4.4%/1 + ~95.6% heavier nuclei / ~A_avg) — the heavy nuclei dominate the nucleon count heavily. For Pb (A=207): nucleon fraction of H ≈ (4.4/1)/((4.4/1)+(95.6/~100)) where A_eff accounts for mix of C, Pb ≈ (4.4)/(4.4 + ~0.95) for Pb dominated → approximately **1.5–1.8%** — just within the 2% requirement.

This requires careful tuning of the Pb/scintillator ratio during construction, with the ratio confirmed by assay. The collaboration should **target 1.5% with 0.3% margin** to account for glue, WLS fibre mass (which adds C), and SiPM PCB material inside the volume.

**Tracking impact:** The lead sheets are thin enough (< 0.4 X₀ per layer) that proton tracks of interest are not fully absorbed, though the 60 MeV proton range requirement constrains the maximum Pb thickness per layer. At 1.5 mm Pb per 2 cm scintillator, a 60 MeV proton (range ~2.8 cm in scintillator-equivalent) will traverse roughly 1–2 Pb sheets, losing a modest additional fraction of energy. This is acceptable because the track is still reconstructed; energy must be corrected for Pb traversal using simulation. **The collaboration must verify via GEANT4 that the 60 MeV proton reconstruction efficiency remains adequate with this geometry — this is the highest-risk interface between constraints 1 and 2.**

---

### 3. Photon Sensor: Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs / MPPCs)

**Technology:** Hamamatsu S13360-series or equivalent 1.3 × 1.3 mm² or 3 × 3 mm² MPPCs, operated at room temperature, coupled to the WLS fibre ends at the cube array edges.

**Justification:**

- Operate inside or immediately adjacent to the warm dipole magnet (0.15 T field). Traditional PMTs are disqualified by the magnetic field. SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields at this level and have been extensively qualified in similar environments (T2K, CMS, ATLAS upgrades).
- The low-light requirement (a 1.5 cm cube produces ~10–20 detected photons per MIP traversal after fibre attenuation) demands high photon detection efficiency (PDE ≥ 40%), which current-generation SiPMs meet.
- SiPM dark count rates (~100 kcps at room temperature) are manageable with timing cuts given the ~ns timing resolution, and the accelerator beam spill structure provides a natural coincidence window.
- SiPM gain (~10⁶) and dynamic range are matched to single-fibre readout.

**Operational note:** Radiation damage to SiPMs (increased dark rate from bulk damage) must be monitored. At 410 m from target, the neutron flux through the near detector will be significant. The collaboration should plan for SiPM replacement accessibility or accept a rising noise floor over the run, mitigated by tighter timing cuts.

---

### 4. Timing Layer: Dedicated Scintillator Paddle Planes at Upstream and Downstream Faces

**Technology:** 2 cm thick × full-area (2.6 m × 2.3 m) extruded scintillator paddle planes with embedded WLS fibres and SiPM readout, one plane on the upstream face and one on the downstream face of the active target volume.

**Justification:**

- Backward-going tracks exiting through the upstream face must be identified and timed to distinguish them from forward-going tracks entering from upstream (beam-related backgrounds, through-going muons from neutrino interactions upstream of the active target).
- These planes provide a t₀ reference with ~1 ns resolution, enabling time-of-flight discrimination and unambiguous track directionality assignment, which is not reliably available from the cube array alone due to light propagation ambiguity.
- They also serve as a veto/tag for charged particles entering the active volume from outside, crucial for background rejection.

---

### 5. Interface to Downstream Gas Drift Chambers: Transition Tracker

**Technology:** Three planes of **scintillating fibre (SciFi) tracker modules** — Kuraray SCSF-78MJ fibres in 0.25 mm diameter, assembled into ribbons — placed in the gap between the downstream face of the active target and the upstream face of the existing gas drift chambers.

**Justification:**

- The gas drift chambers have an inherent position resolution gap at their upstream entrance face. SciFi planes provide high-resolution (σ ~100 μm) position seeds that allow clean matching of tracks from the cube array to the drift chamber track segments.
- Critically, forward-going muons that exit the downstream face of the active target will have their momentum measured by the existing drift chambers, but the matching requires a good seed. Poor matching efficiency directly reduces the muon reconstruction efficiency.
- SciFi is the technology of choice here (over silicon strips) because it is low-mass (preserving the muon trajectory without significant scattering), fast, and tolerates the magnetic fringe field. The LHCb SciFi tracker provides extensive operational experience.
- Three planes in X, U, V stereo geometry resolve left-right ambiguities.

---

### 6. Electronics and DAQ: Self-Triggered, Continuous Readout with Spill Synchronization

**Technology:** CITIROC or TOFPET2 ASICs (or equivalent SiPM readout ASICs with integrated TDC and ADC) on front-end boards distributed along the cube array edge, with data aggregated via a hierarchical optical link system to a commodity GPU-based online reconstruction farm.

**Justification:**

- The cube array's ~480,000 channels require a scalable, low-power front-end. TOFPET2 (used in PETsys systems and the IDEA detector R&D) provides 64 channels per chip with sub-ns timing, charge integration, and a hit-based trigger-less readout at power budgets of ~5 mW/channel — feasible for the channel count.
- Self-triggering is essential for backward-going and large-angle tracks that may not point to any external trigger device in time.
- Online GPU reconstruction can apply crude vertex-finding to suppress the dominant beam-related muon background before data is written to storage, reducing the data rate by an estimated factor of 10–100.

---

## Summary Table

| Component | Technology | Key Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Primary active target | 3D polystyrene scintillator cube array, 1.5 cm pitch, WLS+SiPM readout | All-angle tracking; short proton tracks |
| H-fraction control | Pb absorber sheets interleaved (1.5 mm Pb / 2 cm scintillator) | H ≤ 2% of nucleons |
| Photon sensors | SiPMs (MPPCs), 1.3–3 mm² | Magnetic field immunity; low-light detection |
| Directionality/timing | Scintillator paddle planes, upstream and downstream faces | Backward-going track ID; beam background veto |
| Track matching | SciFi planes at downstream interface | Muon momentum matching to drift chambers |
| Front-end electronics | TOFPET2 ASICs, trigger-less readout | Channel count; backward-track self-triggering |

---

## Critical Design Risks and Required Studies

1. **60 MeV proton track reconstruction efficiency with Pb interleaving** — must be validated in GEANT4 before finalizing Pb thickness. If efficiency falls below requirement, reduce Pb thickness and revisit H-fraction mitigation (consider Pb-doped scintillator instead, accepting manufacturing complexity).

2. **H-fraction assay** — the actual H/nucleon fraction must be measured by neutron activation or NMR on production samples, not taken from nominal composition alone, given the tight 0.3% margin.

3. **SiPM radiation hardness** — commission a radiation test program using the facility's own neutron flux profile; plan for SiPM swap-out at mid-run if dark rates degrade tracking efficiency for short tracks.

4. **Muon reconstruction efficiency at 90°** — a 90° muon in the 0.9 m (beam-axis) dimension traverses only ~0.9 m of active material before exiting laterally. Confirm the drift chambers subtend sufficient solid angle to catch these; if not, consider thin additional tracking planes on the lateral faces of the active target.

# ND280 Upgrade Proposal: Replacing the P0D with a High-Angle, Fully Active Target System

## 1. Why the current design falls short

**FGD geometry.** All FGD bars are perpendicular to the beam, and the TPCs sit only upstream and downstream of the FGDs. The detector therefore works well for forward tracks but poorly for:
- **High-angle tracks.** About 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons leave at more than 50° to the beam. Near 90° they travel along a single FGD layer, so they give few useful hits and never reach a TPC.
- **Backward tracks.** These also fail to reach a TPC.
- **Short protons.** The FGD's two-view, 1 cm x/y layers need several layers to tag a proton. A 450 MeV/c proton (kinetic energy about 100 MeV) has a range of only about 7 cm in CH. Protons below roughly 450–500 MeV/c are often missed or misidentified.

**Coverage mismatch with the far detector.** Super-K covers 4π. ND280's restricted angular phase space forces model extrapolation into unmeasured regions, which is a main reason the residual systematic uncertainty stays near 6%.

**Consequence for transverse kinematic imbalance.** These analyses need the muon and the proton in the same event, at any angle, with low proton threshold. In the current design the two acceptance losses multiply.

## 2. Layout in the freed P0D region

The available box is about 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m. I take 0.6 m as the vertical dimension, with 1.9 m along the beam.
- The new target sits in the centre of the box.
- Thin TPCs go above and below it.
- Timing planes enclose the whole assembly.
- The existing downstream TPC1–3 and FGD1/2 are unchanged. FGD2 keeps its water layers for the carbon-to-water comparison.

## 3. Proposed hardware

### (a) SuperFGD: a 3D-granular, fully active scintillator target

**Technology**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene cubes, roughly 192 × 184 × 56. Each cube has a reflective chemically etched surface and three orthogonal holes.
- Wavelength-shifting fibres (about 1 mm) run through each hole in x, y and z, giving three 2D projections of every hit.
- Each fibre is read by an MPPC/SiPM, for roughly 56,000 channels in total. This is the same photosensor family as the existing ND280 scintillator channels.
- Target mass is about 2 t of CH, which roughly doubles the hydrocarbon target. Hydrocarbon targets are stated to be acceptable for this programme.
- Front-end electronics give about 1 ns timing per channel and better than 1 ns per cube when hits are combined.

**Physics motivation**
- **Near-4π tracking.** There is no preferred plane orientation, so 90° and backward muons and protons are reconstructed in 3D with uniform efficiency. This directly recovers the 25% of muons and 35% of protons above 50°.
- **Low proton threshold.** A 300 MeV/c proton (kinetic energy about 47 MeV) travels about 1.7 cm and still crosses two or more cubes. This lowers the tracking threshold to roughly 300 MeV/c, well below the 450 MeV/c median, so most of the leading-proton spectrum becomes visible.
- **Calorimetric particle identification.** Fine granularity gives good dE/dx and Bragg-peak identification for proton/pion/muon separation and for Michel-electron tagging.
- **Neutron detection.** Neutron interactions appear as isolated secondary cube clusters. Using cluster position and time relative to the vertex, the time of flight over tens of centimetres gives neutron kinetic energy with roughly 15–30% resolution. This makes antineutrino charged-current events (μ⁺ + n) kinematically complete for transverse-kinematic-imbalance and neutrino-energy reconstruction.
- **Gamma conversion.** Good conversion efficiency improves π⁰ and electron-neutrino background studies, partly replacing the P0D's π⁰ role.

### (b) Two High-Angle TPCs above and below the SuperFGD

**Technology**
- Each TPC is about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m and uses the existing gas mixture (Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2) for continuity of calibration.
- Each has a central cathode and a lightweight composite field cage (aramid/honeycomb laminate) with low material, about 2–4% of a radiation length. This keeps multiple scattering low and minimises particle loss between target and gas.
- Readout uses **resistive bulk Micromegas** (encapsulated resistive anode). Charge spreading over about 1 cm pads gives spatial resolution better than 0.8 mm with fewer channels. The resistive layer also removes spark risk.
- Upgraded front-end ASICs and DAQ are included.
- Targets: momentum resolution better than about 10% at 1 GeV/c in the 0.2 T field, and dE/dx resolution better than about 10% for e/μ separation.

**Physics motivation**
- **Momentum and charge for high-angle muons.** These muons exit upward or downward and today escape TPC coverage. The HA-TPCs measure their curvature.
- **Charge sign.** This separates neutrino and antineutrino interactions and measures the wrong-sign contamination.
- **Energetic protons.** About 6% of leading protons exceed 900 MeV/c and are not contained by range in the target. The HA-TPCs measure them by curvature and dE/dx.
- **Combined acceptance.** Together with the forward TPCs, phase-space coverage approaches Super-K's 4π. This reduces the extrapolation that drives the flux × cross-section uncertainty.

### (c) Time-of-Flight panels enclosing the new module

**Technology**
- Six planes surround the SuperFGD and HA-TPC assembly.
- Each plane is built from about 2.2 m × 12 cm × 1 cm cast plastic scintillator bars.
- Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs, giving time resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Physics motivation**
- **Track direction.** Timing determines whether a particle goes forward or backward or enters from outside. This suppresses out-of-fiducial-volume backgrounds from the magnet and calorimeters, which are a large systematic for high-angle samples.
- **TPC start time.** The panels provide a precise t₀ for the HA-TPCs, which absolute drift-coordinate reconstruction needs.
- **Particle identification.** Time of flight adds PID in momentum ranges where dE/dx bands cross, for example e/μ/π/p near 1 GeV/c.
- **Neutron timing reference.** The panels sharpen the timing used for neutron time-of-flight in the SuperFGD.

### (d) Supporting upgrades

- **Readout and DAQ.** Upgrade the electronics so the new subdetectors and the existing ND280 subdetectors share a common clock. This allows ns-level event building and handles the higher J-PARC beam power planned for T2K-II without dead-time losses.
- **Calibration.** Use an embedded LED/laser system for SiPM gain and timing. Run cube-by-cube cosmic and through-going muon calibration to control the energy-scale systematic, a key input to the 4% goal.

## 4. Expected impact

| Capability | Current ND280 | With upgrade |
|---|---|---|
| Muon acceptance | Mostly within ~50° of the beam (forward hemisphere) | Near 4π, matching Super-K |
| Proton tracking threshold | ~450–500 MeV/c | ~300 MeV/c, most of the leading-proton spectrum |
| Antineutrino events | No usable neutron information | Neutron kinetic energy from time of flight |
| Out-of-fiducial-volume backgrounds | Limited direction information | Directional rejection with ~150 ps timing |

Combining these with the unchanged downstream detectors gives:
- complete μ + p (and μ + n) transverse-kinematic-imbalance samples on CH;
- C/H₂O ratios from FGD2.

Together these constrain nuclear effects, including Fermi motion, 2p2h and final-state interactions, and therefore the neutrino energy-reconstruction bias. They provide the constraints needed to move the ND280-constrained systematic uncertainty from about 6% toward the roughly 4% that T2K-II requires.

# Proposed ND280 Upgrade: Replacing the P0D Region with a 3D-Readout Target, High-Angle TPCs and a Time-of-Flight Enclosure

## 1. What limits the present detector

**Angular acceptance.**
- FGD1's bars are all perpendicular to the beam, and the three TPCs sit only upstream and downstream of the FGDs.
- A track at more than about 50–60° to the beam runs nearly parallel to the bar planes. It crosses few layers and never reaches a TPC.
- This loses about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons, which is exactly the phase space Super-K covers with its 4π acceptance.
- It also biases the near-detector constraint toward forward, low-momentum-transfer events.

**Proton threshold.**
- A 450 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 100 MeV and a range of about 8 cm in polystyrene.
- A 300 MeV/c proton has about 47 MeV and a range of only about 1.5 cm.
- In a two-view x/y bar detector, short tracks give only a few hits in each view, so they are ambiguous or lost. Overlapping tracks near the vertex are confused.
- In practice the proton threshold is about 450–500 MeV/c, which removes roughly half the leading protons. Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) needs a much lower threshold.

**No neutron information.** Antineutrino charged-current events produce a neutron rather than a proton, so TKI is unavailable for them.

## 2. Proposed upgrade

The upgrade has three new elements, all fitting in the former P0D volume inside the existing magnet.

### A. Super-FGD: a 3D-granular scintillator-cube target (in the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box)

**Geometry and mass.**
- About 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene cubes, with a reflective etched surface.
- Each cube has three orthogonal holes (1.5 mm) carrying WLS fibres along x, y and z.
- Array of about 192 × 182 × 56 cubes, roughly 1.96 M cubes.
- Active hydrocarbon mass of about 2 t, roughly double FGD1+FGD2, which helps statistics.
- The 56 cm depth along the beam fits the 0.6 m box dimension.

**Readout.**
- One MPPC per fibre end, read out on one end with a mirrored far end.
- Channel count ≈ 192·182 + 192·56 + 182·56 ≈ 56,000 channels, compared with ~2 M for pixel-by-pixel readout.
- Three 2D projections reconstruct the 3D image. The third view resolves the ambiguities that the x/y-only FGD cannot.

**Why this geometry.**
- The response is near-isotropic: any track direction crosses about 1 cube per cm. This gives full polar acceptance, including high-angle and backward tracks.
- With 1 cm granularity, a 300 MeV/c proton (about 1.5 cm range) leaves 2–3 cubes with a high Bragg-peak dE/dx. This lowers the proton threshold to about 300 MeV/c and captures most of the distribution below the 450 MeV/c median.
- Protons above 900 MeV/c (about 6%) have ranges near 1 m. Their momentum comes from curvature in the TPCs, or from range plus dE/dx when they are contained.
- The fine granularity also gives good vertex activity and π/p/μ separation by dE/dx along the track.
- γ conversions can be separated from electrons, which helps νₑ background studies.

**Neutrons.**
- Cube timing reaches about 1 ns per channel, and better when several hits are combined.
- An isolated neutron-induced cluster, displaced from the vertex, gives the neutron's time of flight and direction.
- From these, the neutron energy can be estimated. This makes TKI possible for ν̄ CC0π events (ν̄ p → μ⁺ n).

**Construction notes.**
- Cubes would be fabricated by injection moulding with chemical etching, holding hole-position tolerance to about ±0.05 mm so fibres can be threaded through the full array.
- The array is assembled on fishing-line or rod strings, layer by layer.
- Optical crosstalk is about 3% per face, and is handled in reconstruction.
- The mechanical box should be a thin carbon-fibre or plastic enclosure to keep dead material low.

### B. Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs), above and below the Super-FGD

**Placement and size.**
- They occupy the remaining height of the old P0D region.
- Each is about 2.0 m (x) × 0.8 m (y) × 1.8 m (z), with a central cathode and about 0.9 m drift per half.

**Purpose.** They provide momentum by curvature in the 0.2 T field, charge sign, and particle ID by dE/dx for muons and energetic protons leaving at high angle. These tracks miss the existing downstream TPCs.

**Readout.**
- Resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode, "ERAM"), about 8 modules per endplate.
- The resistive layer spreads the charge over neighbouring pads. This gives about 0.6 mm spatial resolution with fairly large pads (~1 cm), reducing the channel count, and suppresses sparks.
- Gas is the same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ (95:3:2), so existing gas and slow-control infrastructure can be reused.

**Field cage.** A lightweight composite (aramid honeycomb/kapton laminate) to minimise material between the target and the gas volume.

**Targets.**
- σ_p/p below about 10% at 1 GeV/c.
- dE/dx resolution below about 10%, for e/μ separation.

**Combined acceptance.** Together with the existing downstream TPCs, the Super-FGD plus HA-TPCs give near-4π muon acceptance. Forward tracks still exit through TPC1–3 and the FGDs.

### C. Time-of-Flight enclosure

**Layout.**
- Six panels of plastic scintillator bars (about 12 × 1 × 220 cm) surrounding the Super-FGD and HA-TPC block.
- Each bar is read out at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.

**Performance target.** Time resolution of about 150 ps per bar.

**Uses.**
- Determine track direction (inside-out versus outside-in). This rejects backgrounds entering from the magnet and the out-of-fiducial volume, and identifies backward-going tracks.
- Improve particle ID at a few hundred MeV/c, through ToF combined with momentum.
- Provide a precise time reference for neutron ToF in the Super-FGD.

### D. Supporting changes

- **Electronics:** new front-end electronics for the roughly 56k Super-FGD MPPC channels and the HA-TPC pads, with digitising and timing at or below 1 ns. These must cope with the increased J-PARC beam power planned for T2K-II, of order 1 MW and higher.
- **Pile-up:** at that power, the 3D granularity and timing help separate pile-up within a bunch train.
- **Retained detectors:** FGD1, FGD2 (water), TPC1–3, the ECals and the SMRD stay as they are. Removing the P0D sacrifices some on-water π⁰ capability, but FGD2 keeps the water-to-carbon comparison.
- **Calibration:** cosmic and LED calibration systems, and a magnetic-field remap of the new region.

## 3. Expected impact

| Quantity | Current ND280 | With upgrade |
|---|---|---|
| Muon polar acceptance | mostly < 50–60° | near 4π, including backward |
| Proton threshold | ~450–500 MeV/c | ~300 MeV/c |
| Active target mass (CH) | ~2.2 t (FGD1+2) | +~2 t |
| Neutron kinematics | none | ToF-based, for ν̄ TKI |
| Kinematically complete CC events | limited | μ + p (or n) with full TKI |

Wider, Super-K-like phase-space coverage, a lower hadron threshold and neutron tagging together give much tighter constraints on nuclear effects. These include Fermi motion, 2p2h and final-state interactions, along with flux and cross-section parameters. Together these address the gap between the present ~6% far-detector systematic uncertainty and the ~4% T2K-II requires.

# Design Review Recommendations: Kestrel Flats Active Target Upgrade

## Executive Summary

The constraints drive toward a highly segmented, fully active 3D tracking target with specific technology choices. I will work through each physics requirement systematically before naming hardware.

---

## Constraint Analysis

### 1. Muon Reconstruction at All Angles Including Backward-Going

A 0.15 T field over 6.5 m gives a sagitta for a 1 GeV/c track of roughly s = 0.3BL²/8p ≈ 0.3 × 0.15 × 6.5²/8 ≈ 0.24 cm — measurable but tight. The critical problem is **backward-going and large-angle tracks that never reach the downstream drift chambers**. These must be reconstructed entirely within the active target volume (2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m along beam). A 0.9 m longitudinal depth is very short for forward tracks but workable for transverse and backward tracks if the target itself is tracking-capable with 3D hit information. **25% efficiency at every angle** is a hard floor, meaning dead regions and threshold effects cannot cluster around any particular angle.

### 2. Low-Energy Recoil Protons (60 MeV Kinetic Energy)

A proton with T = 60 MeV has a range in water of approximately 2.0 cm and in scintillator (ρ ≈ 1.03 g/cm³) of approximately 1.9 cm. The tracking technology must therefore have:
- **Radiation length short enough that the proton isn't ranging out in passive material before it reaches active material** — i.e., the sampling fraction must be very high or the detector must be fully active.
- **Spatial granularity ≤ a few mm** to reconstruct tracks that are only ~2 cm long.
- **Low detection threshold**, since a 60 MeV proton deposits most energy near end-of-range (Bragg peak), but early hits may be only a few MeV per cm.

### 3. Hydrogen Fraction ≤ 2% of Target Nucleons

This is the most chemically restrictive constraint. It eliminates:
- Pure liquid/solid scintillator (CH₂ or similar; hydrogen is ~14% of nucleons in polyethylene, ~11% in mineral-oil scintillator)
- Water Cherenkov or water target (hydrogen is ~11% of nucleons)
- Any hydrocarbon structural material in the fiducial volume at significant fraction

Acceptable nuclear targets are **carbon, oxygen (in non-hydrogen-bearing compounds), argon, iron, lead, or similar**. The hydrogen constraint points specifically toward: **liquid argon, gaseous argon, or solid carbon/graphite as primary target material**, or alternatively a predominantly-metal target.

Liquid argon has zero hydrogen. Gaseous argon similarly. Graphite (carbon) has zero hydrogen. Iron has zero hydrogen.

However, the physics also requires tracking of 60 MeV protons (range ~2 cm in scintillator, ~0.4 cm in iron). **Dense materials are fatal for proton reconstruction.** Iron immediately fails the short-track requirement. Lead fails worse.

**Liquid argon (ρ = 1.396 g/cm³)** gives a proton range of approximately 3.6 cm at 60 MeV — reconstructable with millimeter granularity. LAr TPC technology provides continuous 3D tracking at fine pitch. This is the natural solution, but it conflicts with the existing warm magnet (a cryostat inside the magnet bore is a significant engineering challenge, and the volume is 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m ≈ 5.4 m³ — not trivially a small LAr detector).

**Gaseous argon at high pressure** gives much longer tracks (desirable) but very low density means very few neutrino interactions per unit volume, and at the pressures needed to get useful event rates the vessel walls become massive.

**Alternatively: a low-Z gas TPC target** — if one accepts carbon dioxide, CF₄, or pure argon gas — hits the hydrogen constraint cleanly and gives long enough proton tracks, but interaction rate drops.

A more practical fully-active approach given the dimensional constraints: **a segmented plastic scintillator target with extremely low hydrogen fraction** is impossible (plastic = hydrocarbon). However, a **lithium-doped or boron-doped inorganic crystal** approach is exotic and expensive.

The practical resolution used by experiments facing exactly this constraint (cf. MINERvA, T2K ND280 upgrade considerations, NINJA) is: **a high-pressure gaseous argon TPC** or a **low-density fully-active target using thin-walled structures with argon or carbon-based fill**.

Given the magnet already exists and the volume dimensions (2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m), the most technically credible solution combining all constraints is:

**A segmented liquid argon or high-pressure gaseous argon TPC, or a Super-FGD-style scintillator cube detector made from deuterated or fluorinated scintillator to suppress hydrogen.**

Wait — let me reconsider the hydrogen constraint carefully. The requirement is H nuclei ≤ 2% of *target nucleons*. In a standard polystyrene scintillator (C₈H₈), the nucleon count is 8×12 + 8×1 = 104 nucleons, of which 8 are hydrogen protons → 7.7%. In deuterated polystyrene (C₈D₈), deuterium replaces hydrogen; deuterons have 2 nucleons each, so 8×12 + 8×2 = 112 nucleons, of which 8 are hydrogen → 7.1% — still too high and deuterated scintillator is expensive and dim. This path is very difficult.

**Carbon target with embedded tracking:** A graphite/carbon target with interleaved gas TPC planes would have zero hydrogen in the target nucleons from the carbon, but needs structural material and electronic components — these must be kept outside the fiducial volume or accounted for.

After this systematic analysis, the best real-world solution is a **gaseous argon TPC** or **liquid argon TPC**. I will recommend a liquid argon approach with specific justification, noting the magnet integration challenge as a key engineering item, alongside supplementary technologies.

---

## Specific Hardware Recommendations

### 1. Primary Active Target: Modular Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC)

**Technology:** Segmented LArTPC modules with wire or pixel readout, filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m fiducial volume. Each module is a rectangular bath of liquid argon with drift distances of ≤ 30 cm per half-drift (to keep drift time short and avoid space charge in the high-rate near-detector environment) and wire pitch of 3 mm or pixel pitch of 4–5 mm (LArPix-style pixelated anode).

**Justification against each constraint:**

- *Hydrogen ≤ 2%:* Liquid argon contains **zero hydrogen**. Argon-40 is the target nucleus. The fiducial mass is entirely LAr. Structural elements (wire frames, field-shaping resistors, feedthroughs) must be outside the fiducial definition, but the neutrino-interaction target material itself satisfies the constraint exactly.

- *Muon reconstruction at all angles including backward:* LArTPC provides **continuous, fully 3D ionization imaging** at ~3 mm resolution throughout the volume. A backward-going track traverses the full 0.9 m longitudinal depth, giving up to 300 space points for a wire pitch of 3 mm — well above minimum for momentum measurement by range (for stopping tracks) or by curvature (for exiting tracks measured in the downstream drift chambers). The 25% efficiency floor is met because there are no dead angles; every charged track ionizes argon regardless of direction, and the threshold is effectively 0 MeV for tracks above ionization threshold (~1 MeV for a few-cm track). Tracks exiting the active target laterally or forward are handed off to the existing downstream drift chambers (momentum-by-curvature), while tracks contained in the volume get momentum-by-range.

- *60 MeV protons:* At 60 MeV kinetic energy, a proton has range ≈ 3.6 cm in LAr. With 3 mm wire pitch, this gives approximately **12 hits along the track** — sufficient for reconstruction and dE/dx-based particle identification. The Bragg peak is clearly resolved at this energy, confirming proton identity. Crucially, in a fully active medium with no passive absorber layers, **none of the proton range is wasted**, unlike a sampling detector where the proton might range out between active layers.

**Key engineering challenge:** A cryostat inside a warm magnet bore. The solution is **a thin-wall aluminum cryostat** (similar to the ArgoNeuT approach) with multilayer vacuum-insulated walls totalling ≤ 3–4 cm thickness — acceptable given the 2.6 m transverse dimension. The cryogenic system must be external with penetrations through the magnet yoke. The LAr volume is at ~87 K; the magnet coils remain warm. Thermal contraction of internal structures must be engineered. This is non-trivial but has been demonstrated (ArgoNeuT, MicroBooNE-scale cryostats in magnetic fields).

**Readout choice — pixels over wires:** Recommend **LArPix-style charge-readout pixels** (4 mm pitch) on the anode planes rather than projective wires. In a high-multiplicity near-detector environment with many simultaneous neutrino interactions per beam spill, projective wire readout creates ambiguities in 3D reconstruction (the "ghost track" problem). Pixelated readout gives unambiguous 3D hit association, critical for the high-rate near-detector environment and for correctly assigning short proton tracks to their parent interaction vertex. Cold ASIC readout (LArPix or equivalent) operates at 87 K and has been demonstrated at the required scale.

---

### 2. Supplementary Tracking: Thin Scintillating Fiber Planes at Active Target Boundaries

**Technology:** Scintillating fiber (SciFi) planes using 250 μm Kuraray SCSF-78 fibers in X–Y stereo layers, read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) at both fiber ends. Two planes (each X+Y) on the upstream and downstream faces of the LArTPC, plus one plane on each of the four lateral faces.

**Justification:**

- *Muon reconstruction at all angles:* Tracks exiting the LArTPC at large lateral angles may exit through the side faces without enough points in the main detector for good curvature measurement before reaching the downstream drift chambers. The SciFi planes on lateral faces provide a precise entry/exit point measurement (σ_position ≈ 100 μm from fiber pitch and cluster centroiding), enabling **track seeding and matching between the LArTPC and the downstream drift chambers** at large angles. This directly supports the 25% efficiency floor at angles approaching 90°.

- *Timing:* SiPM-read SciFi provides timing resolution of ~1 ns, enabling **bunch-crossing assignment** in the pulsed beam environment and disambiguation of multiple interactions per spill. The LArTPC drift time alone does not provide absolute time; the SciFi boundary planes supply the t₀ for each track crossing the boundary.

- *Hydrogen content of SciFi:* Scintillating fibers are polystyrene-core (~CH structure), which contain hydrogen. However, these planes are **at the boundary of the fiducial volume, not within it**. Interactions occurring within the hydrogen in the fiber material are explicitly vetoed (the reconstructed vertex must be inside the LAr fiducial volume, defined to exclude the fiber planes by several cm). The fiber planes are ≤ 2 cm total material thickness — their hydrogen nucleon count is a small fraction of the total LAr fiducial mass and they are excluded from the target definition. This satisfies the constraint without issue.

---

### 3. Photon Detection System: VUV-Sensitive SiPM Light Bars (ARAPUCA or Dip-Coated)

**Technology:** X-ARAPUCA photon detectors (wavelength-shifting acrylic tiles with embedded SiPMs) or dip-coated TPB (tetraphenyl butadiene) light guide bars with SiPM arrays, installed on the cathode-facing walls of each LArTPC module. Target: ≥ 0.5 photoelectrons/MeV detected.

**Justification:**

- *Muon reconstruction — t₀ for contained tracks:* Backward-going and large-angle muons that are **fully contained** within the LArTPC have no SciFi boundary crossing. Their absolute event time (and hence the drift coordinate of the starting point) must come from the prompt scintillation light signal. LAr scintillates at 128 nm (VUV) with a fast component at ~6 ns and slow component at ~1.5 μs. ARAPUCA devices shift 128 nm to visible and detect with SiPMs, achieving timing resolution of ~10–15 ns on the fast component — sufficient to assign t₀ to better than 1 mm in drift distance (at typical drift velocities of ~1.6 mm/μs). Without this, fully-contained backward tracks have an ambiguous absolute position along the drift axis, introducing a systematic uncertainty in vertex reconstruction. At 0.5 PE/MeV, a 60 MeV proton depositing its full range produces ~30 detected photons — enough for a reliable trigger and t₀ measurement.

- *Low-energy proton trigger:* In a near-detector environment with continuous beam, a photon-based trigger supplements the charge trigger, ensuring short low-energy proton tracks are not missed in the DAQ dead time. The light signal from a 60 MeV proton (~2 MeV/cm × 3.6 cm ≈ 7 MeV visible equivalent) produces a detectable light pulse above noise with ARAPUCA-class detectors.

---

### 4. Downstream Interface: Upgrade of Gas Drift Chamber Front-End Electronics and Trigger

**Technology:** Replace existing drift chamber front-end ASICs with lower-noise, higher-rate-capable equivalents (e.g., DREAM/AFTER-chip family or custom GBT-based front end). Add a **fast trigger primitive generator** using FPGA-based online track-finding from drift chamber hits, with latency ≤ 2 μs to match LArTPC readout windows.

**Justification:**

- *Forward muon momentum:* The existing drift chambers remain the momentum measurement tool for forward-going muons exiting the LArTPC. At the 0.7 GeV peak flux, forward muons from CCQE interactions have momenta of 400–800 MeV/c. The existing magnet and chamber system is adequate in principle, but the near-detector beam rate may be high enough that the existing front-end electronics have excessive occupancy. Without this upgrade, efficiency for forward muons may fall below 25% during high-rate spills — violating the efficiency floor.

- *Track matching:* The trigger upgrade allows the drift chambers to issue a track primitive that **gates the LArTPC readout**, reducing data volume and enabling offline matching between LArTPC track segments and drift chamber tracks. This is essential for momentum-by-curvature measurement of tracks that exit the LArTPC forward face.

---

### 5. Veto/Muon Identification Panels: Extruded Plastic Scintillator with WLS Fiber and SiPM Readout

**Technology:** Extruded polystyrene scintillator bars (3 cm × 1 cm cross-section, Fermilab-style as used in NOvA/MINERvA), with embedded wavelength-shifting (WLS) Y-11 fiber, read out by SiPMs (Hamamatsu S13360 series or equivalent). Arranged in X–Y layers surrounding the LArTPC on all six faces.

**Justification:**

- *Muon reconstruction — exiting tracks at all angles:* A muon exiting a lateral or upstream face of the LArTPC must be identified as a muon (not a pion) and have its momentum estimated even if it does not reach the downstream drift chambers. Momentum-by-range in the surrounding scintillator panels (combined with the LArTPC path length) gives a range-based momentum estimate for stopping muons. The angular coverage of panels on all six faces is what guarantees the **25% efficiency floor at every angle** — even a backward-going muon that exits the upstream face of the LArTPC enters the upstream scintillator panels, where it is tracked and ranged. The panel granularity (3 cm bar width) is sufficient for a range measurement with ~5% momentum resolution for muons stopping within a few radiation lengths.

- *Muon vs. pion separation:* dE/dx in the LArTPC distinguishes protons from pions/muons well, but muon/pion separation requires either decay identification or range/calorimetry. Surrounding scintillator panels extend the trackable volume, increasing the fraction of events where muon identification comes from ranging rather than from downstream drift chambers alone. This directly increases efficiency at large angles.

- *Hydrogen in scintillator panels:* The surrounding veto panels are **outside the LAr fiducial volume** — interactions in them are vetoed by requiring the reconstructed vertex to be within the LAr volume. Their hydrogen content does not count toward the ≤ 2% constraint on target nucleons.

---

## Summary Table

| Component | Technology | Primary Constraint Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | Modular LArTPC, pixelated readout (LArPix 4 mm), 3 mm resolution | H ≤ 2%; 60 MeV protons; all-angle tracking |
| Boundary tracking | Scintillating fiber planes (250 μm, SiPM), X–Y stereo | Muon t₀; large-angle track seeding |
| Photon detection | X-ARAPUCA with TPB, ≥0.5 PE/MeV | t₀ for contained tracks; proton trigger |
| Downstream electronics | Upgraded drift chamber front-end + FPGA trigger primitive | Forward muon efficiency at high rate |
| Surrounding panels | Extruded scintillator + WLS fiber + SiPM | All-angle muon ranging; backward muons |

---

## Critical Design Warnings

1. **The LArTPC cryostat inside the warm magnet is the dominant engineering risk.** Thermal contraction, HV standoff in cold gas ullage, and magnetic-field effects on cold electronics must be prototyped before full construction is committed.

2. **The hydrogen constraint is unforgiving.** Any material inside the LAr fiducial volume definition — calibration sources, field-cage resistors with organic substrates, Kapton cables — must be inventoried and either excluded from the fiducial definition or replaced with hydrogen-free alternatives (ceramic-substrate resistors, copper conductors, PEEK structural supports).

3. **The pixelated readout data volume** at near-detector rates (potentially O(10⁶) hits/spill) requires a full data acquisition architecture review; streaming readout with online zero-suppression is mandatory.

4. **Short proton reconstruction efficiency** should be validated in a small prototype exposed to a hadron test beam with proton momenta 300–500 MeV/c (kinetic energy 50–130 MeV) before the full detector is built.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Key constraint: the target material

The obvious choice for an active target in a magnetised near detector is a finely segmented plastic scintillator (CH), such as a 3D cube detector like T2K's SuperFGD. **It cannot meet the hydrogen limit:**

- In CH, hydrogen nuclei are 1 of every 13 nucleons, about 7.7%. Polystyrene and polyvinyltoluene are similar.
- That is nearly four times the 2% ceiling at which the hydrogen-subtraction model stays adequate.
- Water-based or other hydrocarbon targets have the same problem. Water is about 11% hydrogen nucleons.

The target must be a non-hydrogenous active medium. Since the far detector contains no hydrogen, the natural choice is to match its nucleus, most likely argon.

## Proposed upgrades

### 1. Active target: a pixelated liquid-argon TPC filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region

**Technology**
- A modular LArTPC with drift along a transverse axis.
- Native 3D pixel readout, as in the DUNE ND-LAr/ArgonCube design, rather than wire planes.
- Housed in a compact, non-magnetic cryostat inside the magnet.
- Hydrogen-bearing insulation and structural materials kept outside the fiducial volume.

**Why**
- **Hydrogen fraction:** essentially zero. Only trace hydrogen from materials outside the fiducial volume remains, so the 2% limit is easily met.
- **Target mass:** about 7.5 t of argon in 5.4 m³, which gives high statistics.
- **Same nucleus as the far detector:** this cancels nuclear-effect uncertainties.
- **Low proton threshold:**
  - A 60 MeV proton travels about 2.5–3 cm in LAr.
  - With roughly 4 mm pixel pitch, that is about 7 or more space points, plus a clear Bragg peak for particle ID.
  - This works at any angle, because the readout is isotropic 3D imaging rather than projective planes. Projective readouts lose tracks parallel to the planes.
- **Pile-up:** pixel readout and modular, optically isolated drift volumes are needed. At 410 m, a spill will contain multiple interactions in a ~7 t target, and wire-plane readout of piled-up events is ambiguous.

### 2. Fast light detection inside each TPC module

**Technology**
- Large-area, high-coverage photon detectors, such as ArCLight or light-trap tiles read by SiPMs.
- Segmented to each module.

**Why**
- Provides ns-scale timing for each interaction, which gives the event start time (t₀) and the absolute drift coordinate.
- Associates tracks with the correct interaction during pile-up.
- Rejects entering background, such as "rock" muons and interactions in the magnet.

### 3. Tracking chambers for high-angle and backward muons

**Technology**
- Thin gaseous TPCs or drift chambers with low material, for example resistive-Micromegas TPCs like T2K's high-angle TPCs.
- Placed on the top, bottom and sides of the target, and on the upstream face, all inside the 0.15 T field.

**Why**
- The existing drift chambers sit downstream and only see forward tracks. Muons at about 90° or backward never reach them, so the 25% efficiency requirement at all angles fails without new chambers.
- A 0.7 GeV muon ranges about 3 m in LAr, so most muons exit. Range alone cannot measure the momentum of most of them.
- The magnetic sagitta inside dense LAr is poor because of multiple scattering. Momentum and charge must be measured in low-density gas after the muon exits.
- The side and upstream chambers give curvature, and therefore charge separating μ⁻ from μ⁺, for the high-angle and backward muons.

### 4. Time-of-flight and veto scintillator panels enclosing the target and chambers

**Technology**
- Plastic scintillator bars with SiPM readout at both ends, giving about 150 ps resolution.
- Placed outside the gas trackers and upstream of the target.
- These are outside the fiducial volume, so their hydrogen does not count toward the 2% limit.

**Why**
- Determines the track direction. This separates genuine backward-going muons from forward particles entering from outside, which is essential for the backward-angle requirement.
- Vetoes entering particles.
- Provides a trigger and time reference.

### 5. Upgraded DAQ, cryogenics and calibration

**Technology and components**
- Triggerless or self-triggered pixel electronics.
- Argon purification to keep electron lifetime in the ms range.
- A laser or cosmic-ray calibration system.

**Why**
- **Proton energy:** depends on good charge collection.
- **Muon momentum (for stopping muons):** the range and dE/dx calibration of short tracks determines the momentum scale.

## Summary

| Upgrade | Requirement it meets |
|---|---|
| Pixelated LArTPC target | ≤2% hydrogen; isotropic 60 MeV proton reconstruction |
| Integrated light detection | Timing and pile-up separation |
| Side and upstream gas TPCs in the field | Muon momentum and charge at all angles |
| ToF and veto panels | Muon direction, background rejection, timing |
| DAQ, cryogenics and calibration | Charge collection quality and energy scale |

# Hardware Upgrades for Near Detector Funding Proposal

## 1. **New Active Neutrino Target: Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (FGT)**

**Technology:** 3D segmented plastic scintillator with optical fiber readout and SiPM sensors

**Specifications:**
- ~60-80 layers of extruded scintillator bars in the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume
- 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm cross-section bars (finer than existing 9.6 mm bars)
- XY alternating orientation, perpendicular to beam
- Wavelength-shifting fiber embedded in each bar
- Individual SiPM readout per channel (~15,000-20,000 channels)

**Justification:**
- **Large angle acceptance:** Fine segmentation captures the 25% of muons and 35% of protons at >50° to beam
- **Proton momentum resolution:** 1 cm granularity enables tracking and stopping-power measurement for the 450 MeV/c median momentum protons
- **Low threshold:** Required to detect protons down to ~200 MeV/c kinetic energy
- **Hydrocarbon target:** Polystyrene (CH) meets program requirements
- **3D tracking:** XY layer alternation provides vertex resolution <1 cm for kinematic imbalance studies

## 2. **Enhanced Front-End Electronics and DAQ**

**Technology:** 
- Multi-channel ASIC-based front-end boards with per-channel amplification, shaping, and digitization
- High-speed digital readout (e.g., CITIROC or SPIROC-based)
- Upgraded DAQ system with ~20,000 additional channels

**Justification:**
- Handle ~15,000-20,000 new SiPM channels from FGT

- Charge measurement for dE/dx particle identification (separate stopping protons from pions/kaons)
- Integration with existing detector timing system

## 3. **Target Mass and Mechanical Support Structure**

**Technology:**

- Alignment monitoring system (optical or laser-based)
- Services distribution (power, cooling, data fibers)

**Justification:**
- Support ~0.5-0.6 tonnes of scintillator plus readout
- Maintain <1 mm mechanical tolerances for tracking
- Integration with existing magnet infrastructure
- Allow removal for maintenance without disturbing TPCs

## 4. **Upgraded Gas TPC Readout (Optional Enhancement)**

**Technology:** 
- Higher-granularity micro-pattern readout (increased pad density)
- Improved charge amplification stages

**Justification:**
- Better momentum resolution for forward-going tracks entering from new FGT
- Improved dE/dx for particle ID of protons vs pions in 200-600 MeV/c range
- Enhanced matching of tracks between FGT and TPC volumes

## 5. **Calibration Systems**

**Technology:**

- **Cosmic ray trigger:** Dedicated scintillator paddles above/below FGT

**Justification:**

**Technology:**

**Justification:**

**Technology:**

# Recommended Re-equipment of the Kestrel Flats Near-Station Target Region

## Summary

Replace the target region with three components:

1. A **fine-grained 3D-segmented plastic-scintillator active target** (SuperFGD-style).
2. **High-angle TPCs** with resistive Micromegas readout, placed above and below the target.
3. A hermetic **time-of-flight (ToF) envelope**, plus **range or ECal instrumentation on the two lateral faces**.

This is essentially the T2K ND280-upgrade concept, re-dimensioned for this target region and its weaker 0.15 T field.

## 1. Active target: 3D-segmented scintillator cubes

**Technology**
- 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene cubes with a reflective surface etch.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres.
- Fibres are read out by SiPMs (MPPCs) with timing electronics.

**Proposed size**
- About 2.4 m (x, horizontal) × 1.0 m (y, vertical) × 0.8 m (z, beam).
- That is roughly 1.9 M cubes but only about 51 k readout channels (24 000 + 19 200 + 8 000).
- Mass is about 2 t.

**Justification**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Readout is three-view rather than planar, so tracks at 90° or backward are reconstructed as well as forward ones. Planar bar detectors lose high-angle tracks.
- **Low-energy protons.** A 60 MeV proton has a CSDA range of about 3 g/cm², or roughly 3 cm in polystyrene. With 1 cm cubes this gives about 3 hits plus a large Bragg-peak dE/dx in a single cube. That is enough to tag and range-measure the proton in any direction. Coarser segmentation (2.5 cm or more) would lose these protons.
- **Hydrogen budget.** Polystyrene (CH) has a hydrogen nucleon fraction of 1/13 ≈ 7.7%. This is well under the 20% limit, and TPC gas and fibres add negligibly.
  - Even CH₂ would be about 14%, and a water component about 11%, so there is margin.
  - Do **not** introduce hydrogen-rich materials such as liquid scintillator or polyethylene absorbers without redoing this count.
- **Fast timing.** About 1 ns per channel helps with pile-up rejection and track sense.
- **Neutron bonus.** It also gives some neutron detection via isolated delayed hits.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Two thin TPCs, each about 0.6 m tall, covering the full 2.4 m × 0.8 m footprint.
- Low-mass field cage.
- Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ gas, as in T2K.
- **Resistive (encapsulated-resistor) bulk Micromegas** readout planes.

**Vertical stack**
- TPC + target + TPC + ToF ≈ 0.6 + 1.0 + 0.6 + ~0.1 = 2.3 m, which uses the available height.

**Justification**
- **Covering the gap.** The existing downstream drift chambers only see forward tracks. Muons at around 90° and backward never reach them, so dedicated tracking is needed at high angle.
- **Why resistive Micromegas.** At 0.15 T, a 0.7 GeV/c muon has a bending radius R ≈ p/(0.3B) ≈ 15.6 m. Over a 0.5 m lever arm the sagitta is only about 2 mm.
  - Resistive charge spreading gives roughly 0.3–0.5 mm resolution with large pads.
  - Expected momentum resolution is about 10–15% at peak energies, with good charge identification.
  - Conventional wire chambers with large pads would be marginal in this weak field.
- **Particle ID.** The TPC dE/dx separates muons from electrons and from protons.

## 3. ToF panels and lateral coverage

**ToF panels**
- Plastic scintillator bars (e.g. 1 cm × 12 cm × 2.3 m), read out by SiPM arrays at both ends.
- Target resolution is about 150 ps or better.
- Panels should fully enclose the target-plus-TPC volume.

**Justification for ToF**
- It determines track direction (forward vs. backward or outward vs. inward). Over about 2 m the flight time is about 7 ns, so the sense is unambiguous.
- This removes the main background to backward muons: tracks entering from outside.
- It adds time-of-flight particle ID (μ/p/e) for low-momentum tracks.

**Lateral (±x) faces**

The dipole field is horizontal, transverse to the beam, so tracks along x are barely bent and do not enter the top or bottom TPCs. Instrument these faces with:
- an ECal or scintillator range layers, or
- SMRD-style scintillator in the magnet-yoke gaps.

Muons are then measured by range:
- The 1.2 m half-width of the target alone contains muons up to roughly 300 MeV/c (about 120 g/cm²).
- The side instrumentation extends this range.
- Muon/pion separation comes from the decay-electron delayed signal.

## Efficiency coverage by angle

| Muon direction | Measured by | Expected efficiency |
|---|---|---|
| Forward | Target + existing downstream chambers | High |
| High angle, vertical | Top/bottom TPCs | High |
| High angle, horizontal | Range in target + side layers, with ToF for sense | Moderate; must be verified |
| Backward | Target + TPCs + ToF for sense | High |

The 25% minimum looks achievable everywhere. The horizontal high-angle direction is the weakest region.

## Recommended studies before freezing the design

- Run full simulation of efficiency versus (θ, φ) and adjust the target aspect ratio to optimise it.
- Consider rotating the TPC pair to the sides if the field orientation makes that the better choice.
- Characterise the cube-to-cube optical crosstalk budget.
- Check the magnetic tolerance of the SiPMs and electronics at 0.15 T.
- Confirm the total hydrogen accounting with all support materials included.

# Proposed upgrade of the Kestrel Flats near-detector target region

The plan has three new subsystems, all inside the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m target region at the upstream end of the magnet. It closely follows the T2K ND280 upgrade concept (SuperFGD + high-angle TPCs + TOF), adapted to this geometry.

**Layout, looking downstream (beam along z, 0.9 m):**

- A horizontal slab of fine-grained 3D scintillator sits in the middle.
- One high-angle TPC sits above it and one below.
- Thin time-of-flight panels enclose the whole package.
- The existing downstream drift chambers continue to measure forward tracks.

I've assumed the dipole field is horizontal (along x), so tracks bend in the y–z plane. If it points along y instead, rotate the layout by 90°.

## 1. Fine-grained 3D scintillator target ("SuperFGD"-type)

**Technology**
- About 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, chemically etched with a reflective coating.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres, read out by SiPMs/MPPCs with about 1 ns timing.
- This gives three 2D projections from which 3D hits are reconstructed.

**Indicative size**
- About 2.0 m (x) × 0.9 m (y) × 0.8 m (z).
- Roughly 1.4 million cubes and 1.5 t.
- About 40,000 readout channels (xy ≈ 18k, xz ≈ 16k, yz ≈ 7k).

**Physics motivation**
- **Muons at any angle.** Unlike planar bar trackers, the isotropic 3D granularity reconstructs tracks equally well at any angle, including perpendicular tracks that run parallel to bar layers. This is the core requirement for ≥25% muon efficiency over the full solid angle.
- **Low-energy protons.**
  - A 60 MeV proton (p ≈ 340 MeV/c) has a range of roughly 3 cm in plastic, i.e. about 3–4 cubes. That is enough to form a track and identify it as a proton from the large dE/dx and the Bragg peak.
  - Kinetic energy comes from range plus calorimetric energy at all angles, which improves transverse-kinematic-imbalance and vertex-activity measurements.
- **Hydrogen fraction.**
  - Polystyrene (CH) has about 8 hydrogen nucleons per 104, i.e. about 7.7% of target nucleons. This is safely under the 20% limit for the hydrogen-subtraction model.
  - This leaves margin for fibres, glue, and any future passive inserts. Water, for comparison, would be about 11%, which is also acceptable.
- **Bonus capability.** Cube timing allows neutron detection and kinetic energy from time of flight between the vertex and an isolated neutron-induced hit.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Two gas TPCs, each about 2.0 m × 0.8 m × 0.6–0.7 m, with drift along x and a light composite field cage to minimise dead material.
- Gas such as Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ (95:3:2).
- Readout by resistive (encapsulated-resistive-anode) Micromegas. These spread the charge, giving about 0.3 mm spatial resolution with about 1 cm pads and reduced channel count.

**Physics motivation**
- High-angle and backward muons exit through the top or bottom of the target and never reach the downstream chambers. The HA-TPCs give them a charge-sign and momentum measurement via curvature in the 0.15 T field. A lever arm of about 0.6 m should give roughly 10% resolution near 1 GeV/c.
- dE/dx (about 10% resolution) separates muons from electrons and protons. This keeps the muon selection pure at high angle.
- Together with the cube target and the existing forward chambers, this closes the 4π acceptance.

## 3. Time-of-flight enclosure

**Technology**
- Plastic scintillator bars (about 1 cm thick, 12 cm wide) read out by SiPM arrays at both ends.
- Six panels surround the target + TPC package, with timing resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Physics motivation**
- **Track direction.** Timing between the target vertex and the TOF hit determines whether a track is outgoing or incoming. This separates genuine backward-going muons from forward-going particles entering from outside, such as sand muons or interactions in the magnet. Without timing these are ambiguous.
- **Background rejection.** It vetoes out-of-fiducial-volume events.
- **Particle ID.** It adds μ/p/e separation in the momentum range where TPC dE/dx bands cross.

## 4. Supporting items

- **Electronics.** Common SiPM front-end electronics (CITIROC-type) for the cubes and TOF, plus AFTER/DAQ-type electronics for the Micromegas. Everything is synchronised to the beam spill.
- **Calibration.** An LED/laser calibration system and cosmic triggers. These track the cubes' light yield and the TPC gain.
- **Mechanics.** Low-mass mechanical boxes and thin dead layers between subsystems. This keeps short proton tracks and low-momentum muons crossing interfaces with minimal energy loss.

## How the requirements are met

| Requirement | How it is addressed |
|---|---|
| ≥25% muon efficiency at all angles, including perpendicular and backward | 3D cube target, HA-TPCs, and TOF direction tagging |
| Protons down to about 60 MeV at all angles | 1 cm³ isotropic granularity: about 3+ cube track length, Bragg-peak PID |
| Hydrogen ≤20% of target nucleons | CH target at about 8% hydrogen nucleons |
| Momentum and charge for all exiting tracks | HA-TPCs for high-angle tracks, existing chambers for forward tracks |

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Active Neutrino Target Section

## Context and Design Constraints

The available envelope (2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m) is shallow along the beam axis, the magnet provides only 0.2 T, and the physics requirement is kinematically complete CC reconstruction with large-angle muons (25% > 50°) and low-to-moderate momentum protons (median ~450 MeV/c, tail to ~900 MeV/c). The 6% → 4% systematic target drives every technology choice.

---

## 1. Active Target: Low-Density Scintillating Fibre / Polystyrene Tracker

**Technology:** A fully active scintillating-fibre (SciFi) tracker built from ~250 µm round polystyrene-core fibres arranged in X/Y/U/V stereo layers, with SiPM array readout, filling most of the 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m volume.

**Why:**
- Polystyrene (CH) is the acceptable target material; the fibre matrix acts simultaneously as target and tracking medium, eliminating the passive-target inefficiency that limits the existing plastic bars.
- The ~250 µm fibre pitch gives ~100 µm spatial resolution per layer, sufficient to separate the primary vertex from secondary interactions and to reconstruct short proton tracks that would stop within a few centimetres.
- The low density of a fibre-air matrix (effective bulk density ~0.3–0.5 g/cm³ depending on packing) means protons at the median 450 MeV/c (range ~20 cm in solid polystyrene, proportionally longer here) are contained within the active volume and are fully measured by energy loss, while the interaction rate per unit length is kept low enough to control pile-up.
- SiPM readout (consistent with the existing detector's channel technology) avoids magnetic-field sensitivity issues inside the 0.2 T dipole and allows the dense channel count (~100,000+ channels) needed for the fine pitch.
- The fully active design removes the main source of the current 6% systematic: unmeasured hadronic energy deposited in passive material between tracking planes.

---

## 2. Thin Resistive Plate Chamber or Micromegas Insert Layers for Charge-Sign Confirmation

**Technology:** Four to six planes of 3–5 mm gap bulk-Micromegas detectors, each ~2.0 m × 1.9 m, interleaved at ~10 cm intervals within the SciFi stack.

**Why:**
- The existing downstream TPCs use micro-pattern gas detectors (MPGDs); Micromegas planes here provide the same dE/dx particle-identification capability (π/p separation) in the new target region at minimal material budget (~0.5% X₀ per plane).
- They resolve the left-right ambiguity in stereo SciFi reconstruction for high-multiplicity events and independently confirm track charge sign when the short lever arm inside the 0.6 m deep box limits momentum resolution from curvature alone.
- Bulk-Micromegas are robust, can be built to the required area, and their argon-isobutane gas systems are already supported by the collaboration's existing TPC infrastructure, reducing engineering overhead.

---

## 3. Downstream Thin Electromagnetic Calorimeter Plane

**Technology:** A single-layer Pb-SciFi "preshower" panel, 3–4 radiation lengths of lead (~10 mm), backed by 5 mm scintillating-fibre ribbons with SiPM readout, covering the full 2.0 m × 1.9 m face.

**Why:**
- Photons from π⁰ decay produced at the new target vertex must be tagged before they reach the existing downstream lead-scintillator calorimeter; a dedicated converter plane at the downstream face of the new target section localises the conversion point much more precisely than the existing calorimeter can.
- Improved photon reconstruction directly reduces the neutral-pion background to the quasi-elastic CC sample used for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) analysis, which is one of the dominant contributions to the residual 6% systematic.
- Keeping it to 3–4 X₀ preserves most of the muon and proton tracks passing through without catastrophic scattering, while providing >95% conversion probability for photons above ~50 MeV.

---

## 4. Surrounding Time-of-Flight Scintillator Hodoscope

**Technology:** Two planes of 1 cm thick cast-polystyrene scintillator tiles (each tile ~5 × 5 cm), one on the upstream face and one on the downstream face of the new target module, read out by SiPMs with ~200 ps timing resolution per channel.

**Why:**
- Protons at 450 MeV/c (kinetic energy ~100 MeV) have a velocity β ≈ 0.73; at 900 MeV/c they have β ≈ 0.90. A ToF measurement between the upstream and downstream faces over a ~0.6 m baseline gives a time difference of ~0.7 ns between a proton and a pion of the same momentum at the median value — resolvable at 200 ps resolution — providing π/p separation independent of dE/dx for the high-momentum tail (>500 MeV/c) where dE/dx discrimination degrades.
- This is essential for the ~6% of protons above 900 MeV/c that exceed the dE/dx-reliable range and yet must be correctly identified for unbiased TKI reconstruction.
- The upstream hodoscope also acts as a beam-trigger coincidence layer, suppressing cosmic-ray and beam-halo backgrounds without introducing significant target mass.

---

## 5. Side-Muon Ranger Extension Panels

**Technology:** Additional planes of 2 cm thick extruded polystyrene scintillating bars with WLS fibre + SiPM readout, added to the top and lateral faces of the new target region, interlocked with the existing return-yoke scintillator system.

**Why:**
- 25% of muons exit at > 50° and many will escape through the sides or top of the new target volume before reaching the existing downstream muon ranger; without additional coverage, their momenta are determined only from the partial track length, introducing a large and difficult-to-model momentum bias.
- Extending the ranging volume laterally captures a significant fraction of these tracks and converts a momentum measurement from "escape with unknown residual range" to "stop with known total range," reducing the muon momentum uncertainty from ~10–15% to ~3% for contained tracks.
- Extruded polystyrene bars are the same technology as the existing detector's tracking targets, so they can be constructed and calibrated using established collaboration procedures with no new technology risk.
- The improvement in muon momentum resolution is the second-largest lever arm on the TKI systematic after the proton reconstruction, making this a high return-on-investment item.

---

## 6. Upgraded DAQ and Trigger Electronics

**Technology:** Replacement of the target-region front-end electronics with ATCA-based readout cards carrying 64-channel SiPM-signal digitisers sampling at ≥ 320 MHz with on-FPGA waveform integration, feeding a White Rabbit timing network for sub-nanosecond synchronisation across all subsystems.

**Why:**
- The SciFi tracker (~100k channels) and ToF system require a factor ~20 increase in channel count relative to the section being replaced; the existing DAQ bandwidth is insufficient.
- Sub-nanosecond synchronisation is required to make the ToF π/p separation (item 4) meaningful across the upstream and downstream hodoscope planes and to correlate hits in the new target with the existing downstream TPCs, which have inherently different integration windows (~µs for gas vs. ~ns for scintillator).
- On-FPGA zero-suppression and clustering reduces the data rate to manageable levels while preserving the pulse-shape information needed for SiPM cross-talk correction, which affects the low-light-level signals from short, heavily-ionising proton tracks near threshold — a key systematic for low-momentum proton acceptance.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Systematic Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Active neutrino target | SciFi tracker, 250 µm fibres, SiPM readout | Unmeasured hadronic energy in passive material |
| In-tracker MPGD planes | Bulk Micromegas, Ar/iC₄H₁₀ | π/p ID, vertex reconstruction ambiguity |
| Downstream preshower | Pb converter + SciFi + SiPM | π⁰ photon background to QE sample |
| ToF hodoscope (upstream + downstream) | Scintillator tiles, SiPM, 200 ps timing | High-momentum proton/pion separation |
| Side muon ranger extension | Extruded scintillator bars, WLS fibre, SiPM | Large-angle muon momentum bias |
| DAQ / trigger upgrade | ATCA + 320 MHz digitisers + White Rabbit | Channel count, cross-system timing for ToF |

# Hardware Upgrades for the ND280 Upstream Active Target

## 1. Super-FGD Active Neutrino Target (Core Upgrade)

**Technology:** Three-dimensional array of small plastic scintillator cubes (~1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm), each read out by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres (one per axis), coupled to MPPCs.

**Why:** The existing FGDs use bars oriented perpendicular to the beam, giving only 2D (x or y per layer) reconstruction. With 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons leaving at >50° to the beam axis, a fully 3D segmented target is essential to track large-angle particles without geometric acceptance loss. The 1 cm cube pitch gives sufficient spatial resolution to reconstruct short proton tracks (median momentum ~450 MeV/c corresponds to a range of only ~3–5 cm in plastic scintillator), which would stop within a few cubes. The three-fibre readout provides unambiguous 3D hit association even with multiple simultaneous tracks, enabling the kinematically complete event reconstruction — both muon and leading proton — required for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) analysis. The hydrocarbon (polystyrene) composition is explicitly acceptable and provides a high-statistics CH target. The cube array can be engineered to fit within the available 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m envelope vacated by the P0D removal.

---

## 2. Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes

**Technology:** Plastic scintillator panels (fast, e.g. EJ-200 or equivalent) with SiPM (MPPC) readout, arranged as thin planes on the six faces of the Super-FGD volume, achieving ~1 ns or better timing resolution.

**Why:** At ~450 MeV/c, protons are non-relativistic (β ≈ 0.42) and can be positively identified by ToF against the faster muons and pions. ToF also resolves the front-back ambiguity in track direction for large-angle tracks and suppresses out-of-time backgrounds.
