- **TKI resolution**: 3D vertex reconstruction in 1 cm³ cubes reduces smearing from nuclear effects vs. detector resolution — the dominant limitation in P0D-based TKI analyses where vertex resolution was ~5 mm vs. <1 mm achievable in the SuperFGD.
- **Proton threshold**: The SuperFGD is sensitive to protons down to ~300 MeV/c (range ~3 cm); the FGD strip minimum was ~450 MeV/c. This directly reduces the "missing proton" rate in the kinematically complete event selection.
- **Pion contamination**: Combined ToF + Bragg dE/dx reduces mis-identified pions in the leading-proton sample to <2%, compared to ~5–8% in strip-based FGD analyses — the single largest contributor to cross-section model bias.

These gains, combined with the unchanged downstream FGD2 water-layer comparison capability, provide a credible path to the 4% residual systematic uncertainty required for T2K-II.

# Proposed upgrade of the ND280 upstream region

The current detector reconstructs forward tracks well but loses high-angle and low-momentum tracks. The FGD bars all lie perpendicular to the beam and the TPCs sit only downstream, so tracks near 90° run along a bar plane and never reach a TPC. Short protons also stop before giving enough hits.

The proposal therefore replaces the P0D with three parts:

1. a 3D-granular active hydrocarbon target,
2. two high-angle TPCs above and below it,
3. a time-of-flight envelope.

The downstream FGD1/FGD2/TPC tracker, the ECals, the SMRD and the UA1/NOMAD magnet stay as they are.

## 1. Active target: "SuperFGD", a 3D scintillator-cube detector

**Geometry**
- About 192 × 184 × 56 cubes of 1 × 1 × 1 cm³, roughly 1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m.
- This fits inside the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box with room for the mechanical box and fibre routing.
- That is about 2 million cubes and about 2 t of CH target, roughly twice FGD1+FGD2.

**Cubes**
- Extruded polystyrene with about 1.5% PTP and 0.01% POPOP.
- Each cube has a chemical-etch white reflector skin (about 50–80 µm) that optically isolates it.
- Each cube has three orthogonal 1.5 mm through-holes.

**Readout**
- About 56,000 Kuraray Y-11 WLS fibres (1 mm diameter) thread the x, y and z holes. Every cube is therefore seen in three projections, giving true 3D hit positions with no preferred orientation.
- Each fibre is read at one end by a Hamamatsu MPPC (S13360-1325-type, 1.3 mm, 25 µm pixels). The far end is mirrored.
- Front-end electronics are CITIROC-based, with charge plus about 1 ns hit time and pulse-shape/multi-hit capability for the spill structure.

**Expected performance**
- About 40–60 p.e. per MIP per fibre, so a MIP gives over 100 p.e. summed over three fibres.
- Time resolution of about 0.9 ns per fibre, improving to below 0.6 ns when combined per cube.

**Physics gain**
- Uniform 4π acceptance inside the target, including tracks near 90° and backward tracks.
- Protons can be tracked down to about 300 MeV/c, since a few cubes of range is enough. The FGD threshold is about 450–500 MeV/c, so this captures most of the leading-proton spectrum (median 450 MeV/c) that is currently lost.
- Proton identification by dE/dx and Bragg peak.
- Neutron kinematics from isolated delayed cube hits with time of flight. This gives the "complete" CC event for transverse kinematic imbalance studies, including neutron-tagged ν̄ CCQE.

## 2. Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs) above and below the target

**Geometry and field cage**
- Each TPC is about 2.0 m (beam) × 0.8 m (drift-region height) × 1.8 m, with a central cathode and drift along x.
- The field cage is a thin composite of aramid/Nomex honeycomb with laminated Kapton strip foils. This keeps it to about 1–2% X₀, minimising multiple scattering and photon conversions.
- The gas is the same T2K mixture (Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2).

**Readout: Encapsulated Resistive-Anode Micromegas (ERAM)**
- About 8 modules per endplate, 32 in total.
- Pads are about 10 × 11 mm². The resistive DLC layer spreads charge over several pads, giving roughly 300–800 µm spatial resolution with fewer channels and protection against sparks.
- Electronics are AFTER/AGET-based with pad-plane-mounted front-end cards.

**Targets**
- σ_p/p below 10% at 1 GeV/c in the 0.2 T field.
- dE/dx resolution below 10%, enough to separate e/µ/π/p.

**Physics gain**
- Muons and protons at more than 50° (about 25% and 35% of the samples) now enter a TPC for charge sign, momentum and PID.
- The roughly 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c, which are not contained in the cubes, get their momentum from curvature.

## 3. Time-of-Flight system

**Layout**
- Six planes enclose the SuperFGD + HA-TPC assembly: upstream, downstream, top, bottom and two sides.

**Bars and readout**
- Each plane has about 20 bars of cast plastic scintillator (EJ-200), about 220 × 12 × 1 cm³.
- Each bar end is read by an array of about 8 large-area SiPMs (6 × 6 mm²), summed.
- Signals are digitised with SAMPIC-type waveform TDCs.

**Performance and physics gain**
- Time resolution of about 130–150 ps per bar.
- Tells track direction (forward versus backward, in-going versus out-going), which rejects out-of-fiducial and magnet/sand backgrounds.
- Adds TOF PID for low-momentum e/µ/p.
- Provides the start-time reference for neutron TOF.

## 4. Integration

**Mechanics**
- The SuperFGD is assembled as cube layers held on fishing-line or fibre strings, inside a carbon-fibre/honeycomb box that carries the MPPC/PCB panels on three faces.

**Services**
- Cables and gas run through the magnet yoke gaps.
- The P0D ECal is retained or upgraded.

**DAQ and calibration**
- Common clock with the ND280 DAQ so hits can be matched to beam bunches.
- An LED calibration system for the MPPCs.

## Expected outcome

- Near-4π acceptance for the muon and the leading proton, plus neutron detection, on hydrocarbon.
- FGD2 water layers remain for C/H₂O comparison.
- Full TKI variables (δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T) become accessible.
- Improved constraints on nuclear effects and energy reconstruction.
- These together target reducing the Super-K-extrapolated systematic from about 6% toward the about 4% that T2K-II requires.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for ND280 Upgrade

## 1. **SuperFGD: 3D Scintillator Cube Target**

**Technology:** Fine-grained 3D array of small plastic scintillator cubes (~1 cm³) with three-axis WLS fiber readout

**Why:**
- **3D tracking capability** essential for large-angle particles (25% muons, 35% protons >50°)
- Cube geometry with fibers in x, y, and z directions enables full 3D reconstruction without alternating-layer ambiguities
- ~1 cm granularity provides vertex resolution and angular acceptance for high-angle tracks
- Hydrocarbon target composition acceptable per requirements
- Fits available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m space
- Enables low-momentum proton detection (median 450 MeV/c) with ~cm range resolution

## 2. **Horizontal Time Projection Chambers (TPCs)**

**Technology:** Two TPCs flanking SuperFGD horizontally (top/bottom or sides), resistive Micromegas readout

**Why:**
- **Momentum measurement** for charged particles exiting SuperFGD at large angles
- Critical for proton momentum up to >900 MeV/c (6% of distribution)
- Horizontal orientation captures high-angle tracks that would escape vertically-oriented downstream TPCs
- Micromegas provides robust, proven operation (heritage from existing ND280 TPCs)
- Resistive strips reduce spark damage
- Gas gain enables low-momentum threshold matching proton spectrum

## 3. **Time-of-Flight (ToF) Panels**

**Technology:** Thin plastic scintillator planes with SiPM readout on both ends, surrounding SuperFGD

**Why:**
- **Particle identification** via time-of-flight measurement (proton/pion separation crucial)
- ~200-500 ps timing resolution enables p/π separation below ~1 GeV/c
- Validates proton identification for transverse kinematic imbalance studies
- Provides trigger timing (t₀) for TPC drift measurement
- Thin profile minimizes multiple scattering before momentum measurement
- SiPM readout provides excellent timing and gain stability

## 4. **Upgraded Data Acquisition (DAQ) System**

**Technology:** Modern FPGA-based trigger-less DAQ with ~10× higher bandwidth

**Why:**
- SuperFGD + horizontal TPCs + ToF generate ~10× more channels than P0D
- Higher J-PARC beam intensity in T2K-II (×5-10) demands faster readout
- Trigger-less architecture captures full neutrino spill for off-time backgrounds
- Essential for 6%→4% systematic uncertainty reduction
- Enables high-resolution timestamping for ToF and beam-timing correlation

## 5. **High-Angle Muon Range Detector (HA-SMRD) Enhancement**

**Technology:** Additional scintillator layers in gaps/upstream region, increased SiPM coverage

**Why:**
- 25% of muons exit at >50°, many missed by current SMRD coverage
- Enhanced coverage ensures muon momentum/charge measurement by range or stopping
- Critical for "kinematically complete" requirement
- Retrofits existing SMRD architecture with minimal mechanical changes

## 6. **Multi-Pixel Photon Counter (MPPC/SiPM) Upgrades**

**Technology:** Latest-generation SiPMs with lower noise, higher PDE, and radiation tolerance

**Why:**
- All scintillator systems (SuperFGD, ToF, enhanced SMRD) require ~50,000 channels
- Modern SiPMs provide better signal/noise for low-energy protons
- Improved radiation tolerance for decade-long T2K-II operation
- Better timing performance supports ToF requirements
- Reduced power consumption and thermal load

## 7. **Calibration Systems**

**Technology:** 
- LED pulser system for all optical channels
- Cosmic ray trigger system
- Laser calibration for TPCs
- Radioactive source deployment system

**Why:**
- 4% systematic uncertainty target demands rigorous, continuous calibration
- Track detector response stability over T2K-II runtime
- Cross-calibrate new and existing detectors
- Validate particle identification algorithms

## Summary Justification

This suite of upgrades transforms the upstream region into a **high-acceptance, 3D-capable neutrino interaction spectrometer** optimized for:
- Complete reconstruction of high-angle final states
- Precise momentum measurement for both muons and protons
- Particle identification via dE/dx (TPC) and ToF

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for ND280 Next Phase

## Framing the Engineering Constraints

Before listing technologies, the binding constraints must be stated explicitly:

- Available volume: ~2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m (depth along beam)
- Must operate inside existing 0.2 T field
- Must reconstruct muons **and** leading protons with kinematic completeness
- 25% of muons and 35% of protons exit at >50° → requires large angular acceptance
- Proton median momentum ~450 MeV/c; 6% exceed 900 MeV/c → threshold and range both matter
- Target: reduce near-detector systematic below 4% (from current ~6%)

---

## Upgrade 1: SuperFGD — Plastic Scintillator Neutrino Target with 4π Tracking

### Technology
A fully three-dimensional segmented scintillator cube array: approximately 2 × 10⁶ individual polystyrene cubes, each **10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm**, arranged in an x–y–z grid of roughly 192 × 184 × 56 cubes to fill the available box. Each cube is pierced along all three orthogonal axes by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres, one fibre per row per axis. Each fibre end is read out by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM). This architecture — proposed and now being built as the actual SuperFGD — departs entirely from the planar-layer paradigm of FGD1/2.

### Physics Motivation

**Kinematic completeness for large-angle tracks.** The existing FGDs are built in 30 x/y planar layers each 10 mm thick in z but ~1.9 m wide. A proton leaving at 60° to the beam in the x–z plane crosses only ~2 planes before exiting laterally, giving ~2 hits and no momentum measurement by range. The cubic geometry gives the same sampling density in all directions: a 450 MeV/c proton (range ~18 cm in polystyrene) deposits hits in ~18 cubes regardless of angle. This directly addresses the stated problem that 35% of leading protons exit beyond 50°.

**Low proton momentum threshold.** At 450 MeV/c median momentum, the proton kinetic energy is ~100 MeV, range ~18 cm. For protons down to ~300 MeV/c (T_k ~ 45 MeV, range ~6 cm), range-based momentum measurement to ~5% precision requires at least 6 measurement points; the 10 mm cube pitch provides this where flat scintillator planes would give 1–2 points. The low threshold also captures multi-nucleon (2p2h) topologies where the second nucleon is soft.

**Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI).** TKI variables — δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T — constructed from the muon and leading proton transverse momenta, are sensitive to nuclear effects (FSI, 2p2h, binding energy) only if both particles are fully reconstructed. Any event in which the proton is lost because it exits a gap or travels parallel to readout planes is a bias, not merely an inefficiency, because the loss is correlated with the proton kinematics. The isotropic acceptance of SuperFGD eliminates this correlated acceptance hole.

**Multiple scattering for muon momentum.** For contained muons the momentum by range is straightforward. For through-going muons the 10 mm granularity gives ~56 measurement points along z within 0.6 m depth, enabling momentum estimation by multiple Coulomb scattering (MCS) using the Highland formula with node spacing of one cube width. At 0.6 GeV/c the MCS resolution is ~10–15% over 0.6 m of polystyrene, adequate as a seed before the downstream TPC improves it.

---

## Upgrade 2: Six Surrounding Time Projection Chambers (Baby MINDs / HA-TPC style) — Replace with High-Angle TPCs

### Technology
Two large-area TPCs placed immediately upstream and downstream of the SuperFGD target, with drift in the x (horizontal, perpendicular to beam and to the B field) direction. Each TPC is ~2.0 m (y) × 0.6 m (z-beam) × 0.3 m (x-drift), filled with the same Ar:CF4:iC4H10 mixture already used in the existing TPCs to share gas infrastructure and calibration procedures. Readout by bulk Micromegas pads, ~6–7 mm pitch.

Additionally, two **thin TPCs on the top and bottom faces** of the SuperFGD volume (~2.0 m × 0.6 m × 0.15 m drift in y) to catch the 25% of muons and 35% of protons exiting laterally.

### Physics Motivation

**Sign determination for muons leaving SuperFGD.** A muon produced in the SuperFGD travels forward into the existing TPC1 downstream in many cases, but the 25% large-angle population exits upward, downward, or sideways. Without a magnetic-field-immersed tracker at those exits, charge sign is unknown, making the event either ambiguous (π⁻ contamination mimicking ν̄_μ CC) or discarded. The surrounding TPCs, sitting inside the same 0.2 T magnet, give a sagitta measurement: at 600 MeV/c a 0.3 m drift TPC with 0.2 T gives sagitta ~0.4 mm, resolvable at Micromegas pad pitch of 6 mm only for many hits, so this sets a useful momentum threshold ~400 MeV/c for charge ID. This is adequate given the muon spectrum peaks above this.

**Proton–pion separation by dE/dx.** The TPC gas dE/dx resolves protons from pions up to ~1 GeV/c with the Bethe–Bloch separation exceeding 3σ (as demonstrated in the existing ND280 TPCs). Protons that punch through the SuperFGD without stopping are measured by momentum curvature in the surrounding TPC; combined with the range from SuperFGD this gives an overdetermined momentum measurement that cross-checks reconstruction.

**Reduction of pion-misidentified-as-proton background.** For TKI analyses, selecting a charged pion as the "leading proton" biases δp_T significantly. The TPC dE/dx provides the rejection needed to hold this contamination below the 4% systematic target.

---

## Upgrade 3: Gadolinium-Loaded Scintillator Veto / Neutron Tagger Layer

### Technology
A 50 mm thick layer of **Gd-doped plastic scintillator** (0.1% Gd by mass, achievable by dissolving Gd-HDEHP in the scintillator solvent during extrusion) tiling all six outer faces of the SuperFGD assembly, read by SiPMs via WLS fibres. Total ~2 × (2.0×1.9 + 2.0×0.6 + 1.9×0.6) m² ≈ 12 m² at 50 mm thickness, ~300 kg of active material.

### Physics Motivation

**Neutron detection for complete hadronic final-state reconstruction.** In CC quasi-elastic scattering on neutrons (ν_μ n → μ⁻ p), the initial-state neutron is not detected; but in multi-nucleon processes (e.g., CC2p2h, or events with FSI rescattering), one or more secondary neutrons carry significant momentum. These neutrons escape the SuperFGD without depositing charge. Gd has the highest thermal-neutron capture cross section of any stable nucleus (~49,000 barn for ¹⁵⁷Gd), and the capture gamma cascade (total ~8 MeV) produces a delayed coincidence signal (capture time ~20 µs) detectable in the scintillator at the few-percent efficiency level per neutron. This allows statistical reconstruction of the neutron component of the hadronic system, improving calorimetric neutrino energy reconstruction.

**Neutron-induced background rejection for TKI.** A neutron re-scattering inside the SuperFGD can produce a recoil proton that mimics the primary vertex proton. Tagging the incoming neutron from the Gd layer (backward-going relative to beam) allows rejection of this category of dirt backgrounds.

---

## Upgrade 4: Precision Timing Layer — LGAD (Low-Gain Avalanche Detector) or Fast Plastic Scintillator with SiPM

### Technology
A single plane of **AC-coupled LGAD silicon sensors** (3 mm × 3 mm pads, 50 µm active thickness) or alternatively a 5 mm thick fast plastic scintillator plane with EJ-228 (rise time ~0.5 ns) read by SiPMs, placed at the upstream face of the SuperFGD. Target time resolution: **σ_t < 200 ps** per hit.

### Physics Motivation

**Proton time-of-flight (ToF) for momentum measurement below TPC threshold.** Protons below ~450 MeV/c that stop in the SuperFGD have momentum measured by range, but protons that exit laterally through thin faces have insufficient range. A ToF measurement between the upstream LGAD and a hit in the surrounding TPC or Gd-scintillator layer, over a baseline of ~0.5–1.0 m, gives:

δp/p = (γ²βγ · c · δt / L)

For a 300 MeV/c proton (β ≈ 0.30) over L = 0.6 m, σ_t = 200 ps gives δβ/β ~ 10%, hence δp/p ~ 10%, which is competitive with range for the short tracks this addresses.

**Beam bunch timing and pile-up rejection.** The J-PARC beam delivers ~8 bunches per spill, each ~100 ns wide. At ND280 fluxes the in-spill pile-up probability is small but non-negligible for the new denser target. A 200 ps timing layer allows bunch-by-bunch tagging and rejection of two-vertex pile-up events, which otherwise populate the signal region for TKI (two separate single-track events reconstructed as one two-track event).

---

## Upgrade 5: Thin Electromagnetic Calorimeter Insert — Pb-Scintillator "Gamma Catcher"

### Technology
A 10 mm Pb + 5 mm scintillator sampling structure (~2 X₀ total) lining the downstream and lateral inner faces of the SuperFGD assembly, inside the existing ECal. Scintillator bars ~10 mm × 10 mm transverse, read by SiPM. This is distinct from the existing downstream ECal (which begins further downstream); this layer is immediately adjacent to the target.

### Physics Motivation

**π⁰ background rejection for TKI and CC-exclusive topologies.** In CC1p events classified for TKI analysis, a π⁰ produced but missed can deposit its gamma energy asymmetrically, reconstructed as extra transverse momentum and biasing δp_T. A thin early-conversion gamma catcher with ~20–30% π⁰ detection efficiency (one of two photons converting in 2 X₀) suppresses this background. Studies of the existing ECal in ND280 show it catches gammas that travel >30 cm from the vertex; the new insert catches gammas from vertices near the SuperFGD edge that currently escape.

**Nuclear de-excitation gamma tagging.** After neutrino scattering on carbon, the residual ¹¹B* or ¹¹C* nucleus emits one or more gammas of a few MeV on a timescale of picoseconds to nanoseconds. These gammas carry information about the nuclear excitation energy and in principle allow identification of which nuclear shell the struck nucleon came from, an important handle on the nucleon momentum distribution and the dominant theoretical uncertainty in the neutrino energy reconstruction.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Goal | Key Metric Addressed |
|---|---|---|---|
| SuperFGD target | 3D scintillator cubes, 10 mm, SiPM readout | Isotropic acceptance for protons/muons | 35% large-angle proton loss eliminated |
| Surrounding TPCs | Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ Micromegas, thin walls | Charge-sign and dE/dx for large-angle tracks | ν̄_μ contamination, π/p separation |
| Gd-scintillator veto | 0.1% Gd-doped plastic, WLS+SiPM | Neutron tagging, hadronic energy closure | Energy reconstruction bias |
| LGAD timing | 50 µm AC-LGAD, σ_t < 200 ps | ToF proton momentum, pile-up rejection | Low-momentum proton reconstruction |
| Thin ECal insert | 2 X₀ Pb-scintillator, 10 mm bars | π⁰ veto, de-excitation gamma tag | δp_T background, nuclear model input |

The combination of SuperFGD (isotropic acceptance) + surrounding TPCs (charge and PID) is the irreducible core: without both, kinematic completeness for the stated 35% large-angle proton fraction cannot be achieved. The remaining three upgrades address the next tier of systematics — hadronic energy scale, pileup, and electromagnetic backgrounds — required to reach the 4% total uncertainty target.

Given the constraints and physics requirements, I propose installing a **3D fine-grained scintillator detector with timing capabilities** in the P0D region. Here's the concrete specification:

## Hardware Upgrade Proposal for Kestrel Flats Near Detector

### Key Requirements Analysis

1. **Physics constraints:**
   - Neutrino energy ~0.7 GeV (quasi-elastic and resonance regime)
   - Must detect muons at all angles including backward-going (requires <25% efficiency everywhere)
   - Must detect recoil protons down to 60 MeV KE (~11 cm range in plastic scintillator)
   - Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of target nucleons
   - Active target volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m

2. **Existing infrastructure:**
   - 0.15 T dipole field over 6.5 m
   - Downstream gas drift chambers for momentum measurement

### Proposed Solution: Fine-Grained Plastic Scintillator Tracker

#### Primary Detector Configuration

**3D segmented plastic scintillator tracker** with the following specifications:

1. **Scintillator bars:** 
   - Extruded polystyrene-based scintillator (e.g., Dow Styron with PPO/POPOP)
   - Cross-section: 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm (optimized for 60 MeV proton detection)
   - Hydrogen/Carbon ratio: ~1.1 (meets <20% H nucleon fraction requirement)
   
2. **Readout architecture:**
   - Wavelength-shifting fiber (1.2 mm diameter) in groove along each bar
   - Multi-pixel photon counters (MPPCs/SiPMs) at both ends
   - Timing resolution ~1-2 ns for event pileup rejection

3. **Geometric arrangement:**
   - Alternating X-Y-Z oriented planes in groups of 3
   - Plane spacing: ~2-3 cm (balances material budget vs. angular resolution)
   - ~40-45 planes total in 0.9 m depth
   - Each plane: ~260 bars (2.6 m width) or 230 bars (2.3 m height)
   - Total channels: ~33,000

#### Critical Design Features

**For backward/perpendicular muon acceptance:**
- Fine 3D segmentation allows track reconstruction at all angles
- Both-end readout provides position along bar (~10-15 cm resolution from timing)
- Magnetic field bends tracks through multiple planes for momentum measurement
- Matching to downstream drift chambers for forward-going muons

**For low-energy proton detection:**
- 1 cm granularity provides ~8-12 hit points for 60 MeV protons
- dE/dx measurement for particle ID
- Stopping protons identified by Bragg peak
- Range-momentum relationship for energy reconstruction

#### Complementary Systems

1. **Upstream veto region:**
   - 2 planes of scintillator bars (5 cm × 1 cm × 260 cm)
   - Identifies entering charged particles (cosmic rays, beam background)

2. **Side/downstream ECAL:**
   - Lead-scintillator sampling calorimeter on sides and downstream face
   - ~20 X₀ depth for photon detection from π⁰ decays
   - Helps separate CC and NC events
   - ~5,000 additional channels

3. **Enhanced gas tracker upgrade:**
   - Add TPC-style charge measurement to existing drift chambers
   - Improves dE/dx for μ/π separation at high momentum

### Alternative/Hybrid Options

**If budget allows:**
- **Partial LAr TPC volume** (central 1 m × 1 m × 0.5 m region):
  - Superior imaging for protons and complex topologies
  - ~3 mm wire pitch, 2 or 3 readout planes
  - Surrounded by scintillator tracker for acceptance
  - Addresses hydrogen fraction with pure Argon target
  
**Lower-cost option:**
- Use **extruded scintillator with coarser segmentation** (3.3 cm × 1.0 cm bars)
- Reduces channel count to ~10,000

### Expected Performance

- **Muon efficiency:** >25% at all angles (>60% for most angles)
- **Proton threshold:** 60 MeV KE (11 cm range = 11 hits)
- **Angular resolution:** ~5° for muons, ~10° for protons
- **Momentum resolution:** ~5-10% (combined with B-field and downstream trackers)

This design leverages proven technology (similar to T2K ND280, MINERvA) while meeting the specific geometric and physics requirements.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for Next Phase

## 1. **High-Granularity 3D Scintillator Cube Target (SuperFGD-style)**

**Technology:** Fine-grained scintillator detector with ~1 cm³ cubic cells, each read out individually via wavelength-shifting fibers and SiPMs on three orthogonal faces.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Angular acceptance:** The cubic geometry with three-axis readout provides near-4π acceptance, critical for capturing the ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons emitted at >50° to beam
- **Proton tracking:** 1 cm granularity enables tracking and stopping of the 450 MeV/c median momentum protons (range ~50 cm in polystyrene) within the 60 cm depth
- **Low threshold:** Identifies protons down to ~300 MeV/c through dE/dx and range, capturing the kinematically important low-momentum recoils
- **Vertex resolution:** Sub-cm vertex resolution enables clean separation of primary vertex from secondary interactions
- **Transverse kinematic imbalance:** 3D tracking of both muon and proton enables precise measurement of missing transverse momentum for FSI and multi-nucleon correlation studies

**Mass:** ~2 tons of polystyrene in the available volume provides sufficient target mass while maintaining fine granularity.

## 2. **Upstream Time-of-Flight Wall**

**Technology:** Single plane of fast plastic scintillator with ~5 cm segmentation, read out by fast SiPMs with timing resolution <200 ps, positioned immediately upstream of the new target.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Proton identification:** Time-of-flight over ~2 m to the downstream TPCs distinguishes protons from pions for momenta <500 MeV/c where dE/dx separation is ambiguous
- **Charge sign determination:** Corrects for protons that escape the target before stopping, combining ToF with TPC curvature
- **Cosmic rejection:** Sub-ns timing relative to beam spill structure
- **Neutral vertex constraint:** Timing correlation helps identify forward-going particles originating from the interaction vertex

## 3. **Polarized Scintillator/Analyzer Module for Rear TPC**

**Technology:** High-density scintillator plane (2-3 cm thick) between the new target and first TPC, optimized for proton stopping and momentum-by-range.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **High-momentum proton containment:** Stops the ~6% of protons with p>900 MeV/c that would otherwise escape the 60 cm target
- **Momentum measurement:** Provides momentum-by-range for protons that stop in this region, complementing the target measurement
- **Reduced systematics:** Better containment directly reduces the largest systematic uncertainty source (undetected escaping energy)
- **Charge measurement:** dE/dx in this denser material helps confirm proton PID

## 4. **Enhanced TPC Readout: Resistive Micromegas with Charge Dispersion**

**Technology:** Upgrade existing TPCs with next-generation resistive Micromegas incorporating charge-dispersion readout pads, reducing pad size to ~5 mm while maintaining existing channel count through multiplexing.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Angular resolution:** Better pad granularity improves angular resolution for the large-angle tracks critical to transverse imbalance
- **Two-track separation:** Resolves short recoil protons from other activity near the vertex
- **dE/dx resolution:** Improved sampling for particle ID, especially proton/pion separation
- **Reduced systematics:** Better track reconstruction → better angle/momentum → 6%→4% systematic via reduced model dependence

## 5. **Downstream Electromagnetic Calorimeter Enhancement**

**Technology:** Replace or supplement existing Pb-scintillator with higher-granularity ECAL (perhaps ~1 cm² cells) in the rear hemisphere covering angles >45° from beam.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **π⁰ rejection:** Large-angle photons from π⁰ decay mimic missing transverse momentum; better ECAL identifies these backgrounds
- **Electron identification:** Separates νₑ CC backgrounds from νμ CC, critical for beam contamination systematic
- **Energy completeness:** Captures electromagnetic energy from large-angle events essential for achieving 4% systematic
- **Michel electrons:** Better spatial resolution for identifying decay electrons from stopped muons, validating muon containment

## 6. **Thin Horizontal Target Segmentation (Optional Alternative)**

**Technology:** Split the new target into 3-4 horizontal modules (each ~15 cm thick) separated by thin (~2 cm) TPCs or silicon tracking planes.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Interaction localization:** Identifies which target layer contained the interaction, improving vertex z-resolution
- **Proton angle measurement:** Early tracking points better constrain proton emission angle for stopped protons
- **Reduced material budget between measurement points:** Better multiple scattering performance
- **Redundancy:** Multiple measurement planes reduce sensitivity to local inefficiencies

---

## Summary Priority Ranking

**Essential for 4% systematic:**
1. High-granularity 3D scintillator target (acceptance + containment)
2. Enhanced TPC readout (angular resolution)
3. Upstream ToF wall (particle ID)

**Highly beneficial:**
4. Rear ECAL enhancement (π⁰ rejection)
5. Additional stopping/ranging layer

This upgrade suite addresses the specific challenge of kinematically complete reconstruction at large angles while improving containment of high-momentum protons—the two key requirements for reducing systematics from 6% to 4%.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Constraints Before Listing Upgrades

The geometry (2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m, short along beam), the need for 4π tracking including backward and perpendicular muons, short proton tracks down to 60 MeV kinetic energy, and the hydrogen-fraction constraint together drive specific technology choices.

**Proton range at 60 MeV kinetic energy** in a typical scintillator/plastic medium is roughly 3–5 cm, so the active target needs fine spatial granularity at or below that scale to reconstruct such tracks.

**Hydrogen fraction constraint (≤20% of nucleons):** Pure hydrocarbon scintillator (CH, ~14/13 of nucleons are protons → ~54% H by nucleon count) is far too hydrogen-rich. Pure water (~2/18 nucleon fraction is H → ~11%) would pass, but plastic scintillator does not. This is the most restrictive material constraint and largely determines the target medium.

---

## Required Upgrades

---

### 1. Active Target Medium: Liquid Argon or Liquid Scintillator with Controlled Hydrogen Fraction — **Replaced by a Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker with Lead or Iron Absorber Layers**

**Specific technology: Alternating planes of extruded polystyrene scintillator bars with embedded WLS fibers, interleaved with thin passive absorber (iron or lead) planes to dilute the hydrogen nucleon fraction to ≤20%.**

**Why:**
- Plastic scintillator (CH) alone has ~54% of nucleons being hydrogen, violating the ≤20% constraint. By interleaving with iron (no hydrogen), the effective hydrogen fraction is reduced. The absorber areal density is chosen so that H nucleons / (H + Fe nucleons) ≤ 20%; this requires roughly that for every CH mass *M*, you add iron mass sufficient that the iron nucleons dominate appropriately. Concretely, iron nucleons per unit mass ≈ Avogadro/56 × density per cm³; this is well-understood and tunable at the construction stage.
- Scintillator bars with WLS fiber readout provide the ~1 cm or sub-cm 3D granularity needed to reconstruct 3–5 cm proton tracks at 60 MeV.
- The technology is proven (MINERvA, WAGASCI, Baby MIND targets) and can be constructed to fit the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m envelope.
- Alternatively, **a 3D grid of scintillator cubes** (SuperFGD technology, as developed for T2K ND280 upgrade) with ~1 cm³ cube granularity and three-axis fiber readout provides true 4π acceptance with no dead angle, explicitly addressing the backward-track and perpendicular-track efficiency requirement. This is the preferred modern solution.

**SuperFGD-style cube scintillator is the specific recommended technology** given the explicit 4π angular requirement.

---

### 2. Photon Sensor Upgrade for the Active Target: **Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) on All WLS Fiber Ends**

**Specific technology: Multi-pixel photon counters (MPPCs/SiPMs), 1.3 mm² or 1.5 mm² active area, coupled to 1 mm diameter WLS fibers at each cube/bar face.**

**Why:**
- The active target volume is inside the dipole magnet (0.15 T field). Conventional photomultiplier tubes are inoperable in magnetic fields above ~1 mT without heavy shielding. SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields and can be mounted directly on the detector or on short fiber pigtails.
- SiPMs provide the photon detection efficiency (>30–40% PDE) needed to achieve adequate light yield for threshold tracking of minimum-ionizing particles and for the low-energy (~60 MeV) protons that produce short, bright but spatially compact signals.
- The granularity of readout matches the cube/bar granularity: each of the three fiber axes of a ~1 cm cube requires its own SiPM, so the channel count is O(10⁵–10⁶) for the full volume; SiPM unit cost and compact electronics make this feasible where PMTs could not.

---

### 3. Downstream Tracker Interface / Muon Spectrometer Readout: **Upgraded Front-End Electronics and Timing System for the Existing Gas Drift Chambers**

**Specific technology: New ASIC-based front-end boards with ≤1 ns time resolution and a common clock synchronized to the active target SiPM readout system.**

**Why:**
- Muon tracks originating in the active target must be matched into the downstream drift chambers for momentum measurement by the dipole. The 0.9 m depth of the target along the beam means that forward-going muons exit into the magnet volume naturally, but backward-going and large-angle muons re-enter from unexpected directions.
- Precise timing (ns level) is needed to establish track directionality (distinguish forward from backward) and to associate target-region hits with downstream chamber hits in the ~microsecond spill structure of the accelerator beam.
- Existing drift chamber electronics may predate low-jitter synchronous readout architectures; upgrading to a common timing fabric ensures the matching efficiency that feeds the ≥25% muon reconstruction requirement at all angles.

---

### 4. Electromagnetic Calorimeter Surrounding the Active Target: **Sampling ECAL with Lead Absorber and Scintillator Tiles/Strips**

**Specific technology: Pb-scintillator sampling calorimeter, ~15–20 radiation lengths total, covering the four faces of the active target perpendicular to the beam (top, bottom, left, right) and the upstream face.**

**Why:**
- Perpendicular and backward-going muons that exit the active target laterally do not pass through the downstream dipole-spectrometer system. Without additional measurement, their momenta are unconstrained and reconstruction efficiency at those angles falls to zero, violating the ≥25% all-angle requirement.
- A surrounding ECAL provides range/energy measurement for muons that stop in it, and distinguishes muons from photons/electrons produced in the interaction (π⁰ gammas, Michel electrons from pion decay). This is critical for clean neutrino interaction identification.
- Lead-scintillator is chosen over lead-glass or pure crystal because it is non-magnetic (compatible with fringe fields), relatively low-cost for the ~10–20 m² of coverage needed, and can be read out with SiPMs consistent with the in-field environment.
- The upstream face ECAL also tags and measures backward-going muons that re-exit through the beam-entrance face.

---

### 5. Magnet-Volume Tracking for Large-Angle Muons: **Additional Thin-Gap or Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs or sTGCs) Inside the Dipole Bore**

**Specific technology: Small-strip Thin Gap Chambers (sTGCs) or glass RPCs, arranged in planes parallel to the beam axis filling the lateral gap between the active target and the magnet coil.**

**Why:**
- Muons leaving the active target at angles near 90° to the beam travel roughly parallel to the magnetic field lines of the dipole (which deflects in the horizontal plane). Such tracks receive little magnetic bending and their momenta are poorly determined by the downstream drift chambers.
- Thin planar tracking detectors in the magnet bore, measuring the track position in the bend plane at multiple points along the ~6.5 m magnet length, recover the momentum measurement for large-angle tracks via the sagitta method over the available lever arm.
- sTGCs (as used in the ATLAS New Small Wheel) offer ~100 µm spatial resolution, operation in the magnetic field environment, and reasonable cost per area. RPCs are a lower-cost alternative with ~1 mm resolution if the momentum resolution requirement is less stringent.
- Together with the ECAL range measurement, these detectors ensure the ≥25% muon reconstruction efficiency is met at angles approaching 90°.

---

### 6. Data Acquisition System (DAQ): **Self-Triggered, Continuous Readout DAQ with High-Bandwidth Optical Links**

**Specific technology: Triggerless (or minimally triggered) streaming readout based on ATCA/µTCA crate architecture with FPGAs performing online hit finding, and 10–100 Gb/s optical fiber links to an online computing farm.**

**Why:**
- The fine-grained active target (O(10⁵) channels from SiPMs) combined with the need to reconstruct short (~3 cm) proton tracks and backward-going muons means that no simple hardware trigger can efficiently select all signal topologies while rejecting beam backgrounds. A streaming readout captures all hits above threshold and reconstructs events offline.
- The accelerator beam structure (microsecond-to-millisecond spills at ~Hz repetition) allows the event rate to be managed; a triggerless readout within the spill window with an external beam-synchronous gate is a practical compromise.
- Modern ATCA-based systems (as used in DUNE ND-LAr, T2K ND280 upgrade) provide the bandwidth and latency needed for this channel count.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Active target medium | SuperFGD-style 1 cm³ scintillator cubes with 3-axis WLS fibers + iron absorber layers | 60 MeV proton tracking; ≤20% H fraction |
| Photon sensors | SiPMs/MPPCs on all WLS fiber ends | In-field operation (0.15 T); high channel count |
| Timing/electronics for drift chambers | ASIC front-ends, ns-level, common clock | Track matching, directionality of backward muons |
| Surrounding ECAL | Pb-scintillator + SiPM, all lateral + upstream faces | Momentum measurement for 90° and backward muons |
| In-magnet tracking planes | sTGCs or glass RPCs in dipole bore | Momentum recovery for large-angle muons |
| DAQ | Streaming/triggerless, ATCA + FPGA, optical links | All-topology reconstruction; high channel count |

# Recommended Hardware Upgrades for Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## 1. **3D Active Target Tracker with Fine Granularity**

**Technology:** Time Projection Chamber (TPC) with micropattern gas detector readout (e.g., Micromegas or GEM-based)

**Why:**
- **4π angular acceptance:** TPC provides continuous 3D tracking essential for reconstructing tracks at all angles, including perpendicular and backward-going muons
- **Low momentum threshold:** Gas target allows detection of ~60 MeV kinetic energy protons (requires ~3 cm range at typical pressures)
- **dE/dx measurement:** Enables particle identification to distinguish protons from other particles
- **Low material budget:** Minimizes secondary interactions and multiple scattering
- **Controllable hydrogen content:** Gas mixture (e.g., Ar:CH₄ or P10) can be tuned to keep hydrogen nucleon fraction <20%

**Alternative consideration:** High-pressure gaseous argon TPC if pure argon target preferred, though this eliminates hydrogen entirely.

## 2. **Fine-Pitch Readout Plane with Multi-Channel Electronics**

**Technology:** Pixelated or strip readout with ~3mm pitch, 50,000+ channels with waveform digitization at ≥25 MHz

**Why:**
- **Track resolution:** Required to reconstruct short proton tracks and resolve vertex topology
- **Multi-track separation:** 0.7 GeV neutrino events produce multiple final-state particles
- **Time information:** Separates tracks from different interactions in the beam spill

## 3. **Downstream Charged Particle Identifier**

**Technology:** Time-of-Flight (ToF) wall or dE/dx hodoscope immediately before existing drift chambers

**Why:**
- **Muon/pion separation:** Confirms muon identification for the 25% efficiency requirement
- **Proton identification:** Validates short tracks identified as protons in TPC
- **Momentum cross-check:** Combined with magnetic field, confirms particle ID

## 4. **Upgraded Gas Handling and Monitoring System**

**Technology:** 
- Precision gas mixing system with flow controllers (±0.1% accuracy)
- Online gas composition monitoring (mass spectrometer or thermal conductivity)
- Purification/recirculation system with O₂ and H₂O removal to <10 ppm

**Why:**
- **Hydrogen fraction control:** Critical to maintain <20% nucleon fraction for model validity
- **Stable detector performance:** Gas gain depends sensitively on composition and purity
- **Safety:** Handles flammable gas mixtures safely

## 5. **High-Voltage System for TPC**

**Technology:** Multi-stage resistive field cage with precision HV supply (±0.1%), delivering up to 50 kV

**Why:**
- **Uniform drift field:** Ensures consistent electron transport and position resolution throughout 2.6 m drift length
- **Field stability:** Maintains calibration over long run periods

## 6. **Enhanced DAQ and Trigger System**

**Technology:** 
- Free-running digitization or accelerator-synchronized trigger
- High-bandwidth readout (>10 GB/s)
- Online event filtering

**Why:**
- **High channel count:** 50,000+ channels require modern DAQ architecture
- **Track efficiency:** Free-running readout captures all activity for offline analysis, improving efficiency for unusual topologies
- **Data volume management:** Online filtering reduces storage requirements

## 7. **Calibration Systems**

**Technology:**
- UV laser or radioactive source track injection system
- Cosmic ray trigger (scintillator paddles above/below detector)
- Precision survey system

**Why:**
- **Drift velocity calibration:** Laser tracks calibrate electron drift properties
- **Energy scale:** Cosmic muons provide minimum-ionizing particle reference
- **Spatial alignment:** Ensures position accuracy for track angle measurements
- **Detector response monitoring:** Tracks gain stability and identifies dead channels

## 8. **Thermal Management System**

**Technology:** Temperature-controlled enclosure maintaining ±1°C stability

**Why:**
- **Gas density stability:** Affects both drift velocity and target nucleon counting
- **Electronics stability:** Maintains consistent gain and noise performance
- **Hydrogen fraction accuracy:** Gas density directly affects nucleon fraction calculation

## 9. **Neutron Detection Capability (Optional but Recommended)**

**Technology:** Hydrocarbon-loaded scintillator panels surrounding TPC or embedded neutron-sensitive fibers

**Why:**
- **Complete event reconstruction:** Neutrino interactions often produce neutrons
- **Model constraints:** Improves nuclear physics systematics affecting the far detector analysis
- **Background rejection:** Distinguishes neutrino events from cosmics and beam-related backgrounds

# Proposed Upgrade: A 3D-Granular Scintillator Target with High-Angle TPCs and Time-of-Flight

The existing tracker is built for forward-going tracks. Its bar planes are all perpendicular to the beam, and its TPCs sit only upstream and downstream of the targets. It therefore loses most of the roughly 25% of muons and 35% of protons above 50°. It also cannot reconstruct the short proton tracks that dominate the spectrum. I would replace the photon-tagging section with three coordinated subsystems.

## 1. Active target: a finely segmented 3D scintillator-cube detector

**Geometry.** About 192 × 182 × 56 optically isolated plastic cubes of 1 cm³, giving 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.56 m. This fills the available box. The total is about 2 × 10⁶ cubes and roughly 2 t of CH, which doubles the hydrocarbon mass of the existing targets.

**Cube construction.**
- Injection-moulded or extruded polystyrene with about 1.5% PTP and 0.01% POPOP.
- A chemically etched white reflector skin, about 50–80 µm, to isolate each cube optically.
- Three orthogonal through-holes of about 1.5 mm.

**Readout.**
- Three orthogonal 1 mm Y-11-type multiclad WLS fibres thread every cube in x, y and z.
- Each fibre is read at one end by a 1.3 × 1.3 mm SiPM, for example a Hamamatsu S13360-1325 with 25 µm pixels for dynamic range. The other end is mirrored.
- Channel count: 192·182 + 192·56 + 182·56 ≈ 56,000 channels.

**Electronics.**
- CITIROC-based front-end boards inside the magnet, with dual high/low-gain shaping.
- Per-hit timing of about 1 ns per fibre, or about 0.7 ns when combining fibres.
- Expected light yield is about 40–50 p.e. per fibre per minimum-ionising particle (MIP), with cube-to-cube crosstalk of about 3%.

**Why this design meets the requirements:**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** The three orthogonal 2D projections give true 3D hits independent of track direction. High-angle and even backward muons and protons are therefore tracked inside the target itself.
- **Low proton threshold.**
  - A 300 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 47 MeV and a range of about 2 cm in CH, so it crosses 2–3 cubes.
  - The median 450 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 100 MeV and a range of about 8 cm.
  - So 1 cm granularity gives a threshold near 300 MeV/c. It also allows range-based momentum and Bragg-peak dE/dx particle identification for most protons.
- **Vertex activity and neutrons.** The time resolution allows neutron detection by time-of-flight to secondary isolated cube clusters. This also gives kinematic completeness for antineutrino interactions in transverse-kinematic-imbalance (TKI) analyses.
- **Photon identification.** Fine granularity separates conversions from π⁰ decays, partly replacing the removed photon-tagging function.

## 2. Two high-angle TPCs above and below the new target

**Geometry.** About 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m each. Drift is horizontal, about 1 m per half, with a central cathode.

**Field cage.** Light composite walls (aramid honeycomb with laminated Kapton/copper strips). This minimises dead material, at about 1–2% of a radiation length (X₀), for low-momentum tracks.

**Gas.** The existing Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ at 95:3:2, so the gas system is shared.

**Readout.**
- Resistive bulk Micromegas ("encapsulated resistive anode") with a DLC resistive layer.
- 8 modules per endplate, 16 per TPC.
- Pads of about 10 × 11 mm. Charge spreading gives about 0.6–0.8 mm spatial resolution despite the large pads, which reduces channel count. Spark protection is intrinsic.
- AFTER/AGET-based front-end cards.

**Performance targets.**
- σ(p)/p below 10% at 1 GeV/c in 0.2 T.
- dE/dx resolution below 10%, for μ/π/p/e separation.

**Role.** These TPCs measure high-angle muons and the roughly 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c that exit the target. They also provide charge sign. Together with the existing TPCs, they close the angular acceptance gap.

## 3. Time-of-flight envelope

**Layout.** Six planes enclosing the new target and high-angle TPCs. Each plane is about 20 bars of EJ-200-type plastic, roughly 2.2 m × 12 cm × 1 cm.

**Readout.** Both bar ends are read out by arrays of 6 × 6 mm SiPMs, with fast digitisation (SAMPIC/waveform sampling).

**Performance.** About 150 ps timing resolution.

**Role.**
- Determines track direction, separating backward-going particles from tracks entering from the magnet or yoke.
- Rejects out-of-fiducial-volume and cosmic backgrounds.
- Adds TOF particle identification and a precise event t₀ for the TPC drift coordinate.

## 4. Integration

- Readjust or add barrel and P0D-region electromagnetic calorimeter coverage around the new volume. The existing lead-scintillator ECal can be reused where it fits.
- Keep a common SiPM/WLS calibration scheme, using LED injection and cosmic-ray triggers.
- Retain the downstream water-layer target unchanged, so carbon-to-water ratios use identical selections.

## Physics outcome

The system gives nearly 4π acceptance for the muon and the leading proton, with a proton threshold around 300 MeV/c. Combined with neutron tagging, it reconstructs kinematically complete charged-current events. This is the information needed to constrain nuclear effects and reduce the flux × cross-section systematic uncertainty from about 6% toward the 4% goal.

# Proposed Upgrade: Replace the Photon-Tagging Section with a 3D Fine-Grained Target, High-Angle TPCs and a Time-of-Flight Enclosure

The goal is near-4π acceptance for both the muon and the leading proton, with low proton threshold. That points to three new subsystems in the upstream region, plus supporting electronics.

## 1. Active target: a 3D-readout scintillator-cube detector

**Geometry and channel count**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, roughly 192 × 184 × 56, giving about 1.9 × 1.8 × 0.56 m inside the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- Mass is about 2 t of CH.
- The 0.56 m is along the beam; the large transverse faces sit perpendicular to it.

**Cube construction**
- Cubes are made by injection moulding: polystyrene with 1.5% PTP and 0.01% POPOP.
- A chemical-etch white reflector, about 50–80 µm thick, isolates each cube optically.

**Fibre readout**
- Each cube has three orthogonal through-holes of about 1.5 mm.
- Each hole carries a 1 mm Y-11(200) multiclad WLS fibre, so every cube is read in x, y and z. This gives three 2D projections and true 3D voxel reconstruction.
- Fibres are mirrored or aluminised at the far end.
- Readout is single-ended with about 56,000 SiPMs (e.g. Hamamatsu S13360-1325CS, 1.3 mm, 25 µm pixels), coupled through optical connectors on the detector faces.
- Expected light yield is about 40–60 p.e. per MIP per fibre per cube, with crosstalk to neighbouring cubes of a few percent.

**Why it meets the requirements**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Unlike x/y bar planes, it has no blind direction. Tracks at 90° and backward tracks are reconstructed as well as forward ones, which addresses the 25% of muons and 35% of protons above 50°.
- **Low proton threshold.**
  - A 300 MeV/c proton (kinetic energy about 47 MeV) travels about 2 cm, i.e. 2–3 cubes. This lowers the threshold from about 450 MeV/c in the current bar target to about 300 MeV/c.
  - The median 450 MeV/c proton (kinetic energy about 100 MeV) ranges out in about 8 cm and is fully contained. Its momentum then comes from range and calorimetry, with a resolution of a few percent.
- **dE/dx particle ID.** The Bragg peak in individual cubes separates protons from pions and muons.
- **Neutron detection.** Time resolution of about 1 ns per channel, or roughly 0.7 ns for a cube read by two or three fibres, allows neutron kinematics from time of flight between the vertex and an isolated neutron-induced hit. This gives antineutrino TKI and neutron energy measurement.
- **Material.** The target is hydrocarbon, which the programme accepts. The water-layer target downstream remains for the C/H₂O comparison.

## 2. Two high-angle TPCs, above and below the cube target

**Geometry**
- One TPC sits above the target and one below, each about 2.0 m (along the beam) × 0.8 m (drift) × 1.8 m.
- They use the space freed in the basket by removing the photon-tagging section.

**Field cage**
- Thin composite walls (aramid honeycomb with Kapton/laminate skins and copper strips) keep the dead material to about 3% X₀, so protons and muons cross with little scattering.
- Central cathode at about −27 kV, giving roughly 1 m drift per half.

**Gas**
- Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ at 95:3:2, the existing TPC mixture, which allows a common gas system.

**Readout**
- Resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode, ERAM): 16 modules per endplate, with pads of about 10 × 11 mm and a DLC resistive layer.
- Charge spreading gives about 300 µm spatial resolution with large pads and prevents sparking.
- Read out with AFTER/AGET-based front-end cards.

**Performance targets**
- Momentum resolution of about 10% at 1 GeV/c in 0.2 T.
- dE/dx resolution below 10%, for e/µ separation and proton identification.

**Role**
- These TPCs measure the momentum and charge of high-angle muons that leave the cube target.
- They also measure the roughly 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c, which travel more than 40–50 cm and are not contained.

## 3. Time-of-flight enclosure

- Six planes surround the new target and HA-TPCs, forming a cube-like box.
- Each plane is made of 20 plastic scintillator bars (EJ-200), each about 220 × 12 × 1 cm.
- Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of 8 large-area SiPMs (6 × 6 mm), with fast waveform digitisation (SAMPIC-type).
- Time resolution is about 150 ps per bar.

**Functions**
- Tells track direction (forward or backward), which rejects out-of-fiducial and cosmic backgrounds.
- Provides timing for e/µ/p separation at low momentum in combination with TPC dE/dx.
- Provides the t₀ for HA-TPC drift.

## 4. Supporting changes

**Electronics**
- New multichannel SiPM front-end based on the CITIROC ASIC.
- Synchronised clock, about 2.5 ns time stamping, and FPGA backends.

**Calibration and services**
- LED or laser injection for SiPM gain.
- A laser calibration system for the HA-TPCs.
- Cosmic-ray trigger, using the ToF.
- Gas, cooling and mechanical rail mounting inside the existing dipole basket.

**Retained systems**
- The downstream TPCs, both FGD targets, the ECals and the side muon-range detector stay as they are, so the upgrade is a direct replacement of the upstream section.

## Expected impact

- Combined, the upgrade gives near-uniform angular acceptance for muons and protons.
- It allows fully exclusive CC0π reconstruction, measuring δp_T, δα_T and δφ_T including neutrons for ν̄.
- It roughly doubles the target mass for high-angle events.
- These are the ingredients needed to reduce the flux and cross-section systematic from about 6% toward the 4% goal.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrade for ND280 Upstream Region

## Executive Summary
Replace the P0D with a **3D-segmented SuperFGD** (Super Fine-Grained Detector) featuring true 3D tracking capability and ~4π acceptance to capture the large-angle muons and protons critical for transverse kinematic imbalance studies.

## Baseline Design: SuperFGD

### Architecture
- **Dimensions**: 192 cm × 180 cm × 56 cm (fits in 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope)
- **Active target mass**: ~2 tons of polystyrene-based scintillator
- **Segmentation**: ~2 million 1 cm³ optically-isolated scintillator cubes
- **Configuration**: 192 × 180 × 56 cubes in x, y, z
- **Readout**: Three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibers through each cube
  - x, y, z fibers provide true 3D hit reconstruction
  - Remove x-y layer ambiguity that limits current FGDs at high angles

### Key Advantages for Physics Requirements

**1. Large-angle acceptance**
- 3D cubes enable track reconstruction at any angle
- Near-4π coverage (limited only by beam entry face)
- Crucial for 25% of muons and 35% of protons at >50°

**2. Low momentum threshold**
- 1 cm granularity gives ~50 MeV/c proton threshold (5-6 cm range)
- Excellent efficiency for 450 MeV/c median proton momentum
- dE/dx measurement for proton PID down to stopping tracks

**3. Kinematic reconstruction**
- 3D tracking → vertex resolution ~5 mm
- Range/curvature → momentum for contained tracks

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for ND280 Phase II

## 1. **SuperFGD: 3D Scintillator Cube Array**

**Technology:** Replace the P0D with a highly granular 3D scintillator cube detector consisting of ~2 million 1×1×1 cm³ polystyrene cubes with three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fiber readouts per cube.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Large-angle acceptance**: The 3D readout provides nearly 4π tracking capability, crucial for capturing the 25% of muons and 35% of protons emitted at >50° to the beam
- **Low proton threshold**: 1 cm granularity enables detection and momentum measurement of protons down to ~200 MeV/c through range and dE/dx, covering the median momentum of 450 MeV/c
- **Vertex resolution**: Sub-cm position resolution enables precise identification of interaction vertices, essential for transverse kinematic imbalance studies where initial-state motion matters
- **Reduced systematics**: Uniform hydrocarbon target with isotropic response reduces detector-related uncertainties, targeting the required 4% level

## 2. **High-Angle TPC or Time Projection Chamber Replacement**

**Technology:** Replace the horizontal drift TPCs with vertical-drift or radial TPCs, OR supplement with High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs) positioned around the target volume at 30-70° to beam axis.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Momentum measurement for large-angle tracks**: Existing TPCs have limited acceptance for tracks >50° from beam axis due to geometric constraints
- **Proton identification**: dE/dx and range measurements in gas distinguish protons from pions in the critical 200-900 MeV/c range
- **Charge sign determination**: 0.2 T magnetic field enables momentum and charge measurement, separating μ⁻ from μ⁺ backgrounds
- **Multiple scattering reduction**: Gas medium reduces scattering compared to solid detectors, improving momentum resolution for the ~6% of protons >900 MeV/c

## 3. **Time-of-Flight (ToF) System**

**Technology:** Precision timing scintillator planes (σ_t ~ 50-100 ps) surrounding the SuperFGD on all six faces, using fast plastic scintillator with SiPM readout.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Particle identification**: ToF over ~2 m distinguishes protons from pions at 450 MeV/c (Δt ~ 400 ps)
- **Large-angle coverage**: Provides PID for particles that don't traverse enough material for dE/dx analysis
- **Trigger and timing**: Precise event timing (within the ~100 ns neutrino bunch) reduces cosmic ray backgrounds and enables beam-off subtraction
- **Neutron detection**: Time-delayed signals identify neutrons from interactions, important for complete final-state characterization in transverse imbalance studies

## 4. **Upgraded Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECal)**

**Technology:** Replace lead-scintillator ECal with higher-granularity modules (reduced cell size from ~4 cm to ~1 cm), using extruded scintillator or scintillator-tungsten sampling with SiPM readout.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Electron identification**: Separate electrons from photons in νₑ charged-current interactions, critical for νₑ appearance measurements in T2K-II
- **π⁰ reconstruction**: Improved granularity resolves overlapping photon showers from high-energy π⁰ decay, reducing backgrounds in νₑ selection
- **Michel electron tagging**: Identify delayed Michel electrons from stopped muon decay, confirming muon identification and reducing pion contamination
- **Energy containment**: Better sampling at angles >50° improves calorimetric energy measurement for kinematic reconstruction

## 5. **Hybrid Active Target: Polypropylene + Water Layers**

**Technology:** Within SuperFGD volume, integrate removable water layers (thin plastic bags or channels) interleaved with polystyrene cubes at 10-15 cm intervals.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **In-situ nuclear effects comparison**: Direct comparison of interactions on CH versus H₂O in identical detector geometry and acceptance eliminates many systematic uncertainties
- **Neutron-excess effects**: Water (N/Z = 1) versus CH (N/Z ≈ 1.08) provides sensitivity to isospin-dependent nuclear effects
- **Complementarity with FGD2**: Provides upstream water target for events where downstream FGD2 acceptance is limited by large-angle topologies
- **Oxygen cross-section**: Direct measurement of νₐ-oxygen interactions, the dominant target in Super-Kamiokande

## 6. **Extended SMRD with Timing Upgrade**

**Technology:** Add timing capability (σ_t ~ 1 ns) to existing SMRD modules and install additional scintillator planes in gaps, creating complete coverage for range-out muon detection.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Muon momentum by range**: Complete angular coverage enables momentum measurement for muons that stop in magnet steel (up to ~1.2 GeV/c)
- **Charge confusion reduction**: Through-going versus stopped muon classification reduces wrong-sign contamination
- **Cosmic ray veto**: Improved timing distinguishes cosmic rays from beam-induced events, critical for the high-statistics T2K-II era
- **Systematic uncertainty**: Independent momentum measurement cross-checks TPC-based measurements

## Summary Impact on Systematics

These upgrades collectively address the reduction from 6% to 4% systematic uncertainty by:

1. **Acceptance systematics**: 3D tracking eliminates biases from large-angle track loss
2. **Particle ID systematics**: Multiple PID handles (dE/dx, ToF, calorimetry) provide redundancy
3. **Energy scale systematics**: Complete final-state reconstruction enables energy measurement from kinematics rather than calorimetry alone
4. **Nuclear model systematics**: In-situ CH/H₂O comparison constrains models
5. **Detector modeling**: Isotropic, fine-grained detector response is easier to simulate accurately

The SuperFGD + ToF combination provides the core capability for kinematically complete events, while the other upgrades ensure systematic control at the required level for T2K-II precision oscillation measurements.

# Design Review Recommendations: Kestrel Flats Active Target Upgrade

## Preamble: Constraint Analysis

Before specifying hardware, the driving constraints must be made explicit, because they conflict in ways that determine the technology choices.

**The hydrogen constraint is the most stringent.** At most 2% of target nucleons may be hydrogen. Carbon has zero free hydrogen; water is 11% hydrogen by nucleon count; liquid argon is zero; scintillator (CH₂)ₙ is 50% hydrogen by nucleon — catastrophically over budget. Any hydrocarbon-based active medium fails unless it is diluted enormously, which defeats the purpose of an active target.

**The angular coverage constraint is non-trivial.** Backward-going and perpendicular muons must be reconstructed with ≥25% efficiency. In a downstream spectrometer geometry, perpendicular tracks never enter the downstream drift chambers at all, and backward tracks exit upstream. The active target must therefore self-reconstruct momentum, or at least provide enough information to seed reconstruction in a surrounding magnetic volume.

**The short proton track constraint requires fine spatial resolution.** A 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has a range in water of ~8 mm and in liquid argon of ~5 mm. In a typical scintillator, range is ~4–6 mm. The tracking granularity must be commensurate with this.

**The volume and field constraints interact.** The 0.15 T field over 6.5 m gives Bℓ = 0.975 T·m. A 1 GeV/c muon perpendicular to the field has a sagitta of roughly p/(0.3Bℓ) ≈ 3.4 m radius; over the 0.9 m depth of the active target the bend is small but, critically, the downstream drift chambers cannot see perpendicular tracks at all. This means momentum measurement of perpendicular tracks must come from range or from the active target's own curvature measurement.

---

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. Primary Active Medium: Low-Pressure Gaseous Argon Time Projection Chamber (TPC) Modules

**Specification:** Fill the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m target volume with a segmented array of gaseous argon TPCs operating at approximately 3–5 bar, with the drift direction along the beam axis (ẑ) so that the full 0.9 m dimension is instrumented in 3D without a dead drift time problem.

**Justification:**

*Hydrogen budget:* Argon is a noble element. A pure argon TPC contributes zero hydrogen nucleons. The hydrogen budget is used only by unavoidable structural materials (wire supports, field cage, vessel walls), which can be engineered to contribute well under 1% of target nucleon count if the vessel walls are aluminium or G10 kept thin.

*Short proton tracks:* At 5 bar, the density of argon is ~8.3 kg/m³. A 60 MeV proton has a range of approximately 35–40 mm at this density — roughly 30–50 wire spacings at 1 mm pitch — giving clear Bragg-peak identification and adequate range/dE/dx measurement. This is superior to lower-pressure options and avoids the ambiguity that would arise with a truly sparse medium.

*Angular coverage:* A TPC reconstructs tracks in 3D from first principles regardless of angle. There is no geometric acceptance hole for perpendicular or backward tracks provided the drift field is well-defined and the charge doesn't escape. By orienting the drift along the beam axis, perpendicular tracks (which cross many drift bins) have excellent position resolution in xz and yz simultaneously. Backward tracks are indistinguishable from forward tracks in reconstruction — the TPC sees a 3D ionisation locus and the track direction is determined from dE/dx gradient (Bragg peak position) and timing.

*Why not liquid argon?* LArTPC is an obvious candidate, but the drift velocity in LAr (~1.6 mm/μs) means a 90 cm drift at the beam spill structure of a 0.7 GeV beam facility creates space-charge and pileup issues. More importantly, the cryogenic infrastructure required within the magnet bore is mechanically and thermally incompatible with the existing warm dipole at the timescale of a near-detector upgrade. Gaseous argon at modest pressure avoids cryogenics entirely.

*Why segmented?* Segment into, say, six modules of roughly 0.43 m depth along beam, each with independent HV and readout. This limits maximum drift time per module to ~10 μs at 5 cm/μs drift velocity (achievable with appropriate field strength), reduces space charge, and provides redundancy.

**Wire configuration:** Employ three wire planes per module endplate (U, V, X at 0°, +60°, −60°) at 1 mm pitch, following the established MicroBooNE/SBND wire-plane geometry but adapted to the rectangular aspect ratio of this volume. Readout is on the 2.6 m × 2.3 m faces.

---

### 2. Thin Scintillator Planes for Trigger and Timing: 3 mm Plastic Scintillator with SiPM Readout

**Specification:** Install planes of 3 mm thick extruded polystyrene scintillator bars (EJ-200 equivalent) with 1.4 mm wavelength-shifting fibre readout and SiPM photodetectors at two faces of each TPC module — specifically at the upstream and downstream faces of the active volume, and on the top/bottom/left/right outer surfaces of the full assembly.

**Justification:**

*Trigger:* The TPC has a shaping/integration time of order 1–2 μs and cannot self-trigger efficiently on single ionisation tracks without a fast external signal. The scintillator planes provide a prompt (< 5 ns) trigger signal coincident with a neutrino interaction. This is standard practice in gaseous TPC designs (e.g., T2K's near detector ND280 uses exactly this TPC-plus-scintillator architecture).

*Hydrogen contribution:* This is the critical trade-off. Each 3 mm polystyrene plane (density ~1.05 g/cm³, formula C₈H₈ per monomer) contributes hydrogen. The scintillator planes must be minimised in number and thickness. With 12 planes total (two per module face, six modules) at 3 mm thickness, the total scintillator mass is approximately 12 × (2.6 × 2.3 × 0.003 m³) × 1050 kg/m³ ≈ 230 kg. The argon mass in the active volume at 5 bar is approximately (2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9) × 8.3 ≈ 44.7 kg. This immediately shows a problem: the scintillator mass vastly exceeds the argon mass.

*Resolution of the hydrogen conflict:* This reveals why the scintillator trigger planes cannot be large-area slabs. Instead, use **narrow scintillator strips only on the perimeter** of each module face rather than full-coverage planes, specifically to intercept escaping tracks at module boundaries. For internal triggering on contained interactions, rely on the TPC's own slow trigger derived from the beam spill gate (the beam RF structure gives a ~10 μs window in which all neutrino interactions occur). This eliminates the need for internal scintillator planes entirely. External planes only, covering perhaps 15% of the face area in border strips, reduce the scintillator mass by ~85%, bringing hydrogen contribution to well under 0.5% of total nucleon count.

*SiPM rather than PMT:* The assembly sits inside the dipole magnet. SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields and compact, making them the only practical photodetector choice here.

---

### 3. Electromagnetic Calorimeter Layer: Thin Lead-Scintillator Sandwich on Downstream Face

**Specification:** A 4-radiation-length Pb/scintillator sampling calorimeter, 10 layers of 2 mm Pb + 3 mm scintillator, covering the full 2.6 × 2.3 m downstream face of the active target, with SiPM readout in projective towers of 5 × 5 cm².

**Justification:**

*Why needed:* Neutral pions produced in neutrino interactions (particularly π⁰ from NC and CC interactions) produce photons. The TPC identifies charged tracks but has limited photon detection capability — photons convert and appear as electron showers beginning some distance from the vertex. Without shower energy measurement, the neutrino energy reconstruction is incomplete and systematic errors on the cross-section measurement are large. The downstream calorimeter catches forward-going photons and electrons before they enter the spectrometer drift chambers.

*Why downstream only:* The hydrogen budget permits very limited additional material. The downstream face is a natural exit point for most secondaries given the forward-boosted flux at 410 m. Lateral faces can be instrumented with a single-layer scintillator (as described above) adequate for tagging escaping tracks.

*Why 4 X₀:* Full containment of a 0.5 GeV photon shower requires ~15 X₀. This layer is explicitly not meant for full containment but for shower identification and partial energy measurement, with the downstream drift chamber spectrometer completing the measurement. Four radiation lengths contains ~85% of shower energy fluctuations in the first few layers and identifies photons vs. charged hadrons with high efficiency.

*Hydrogen contribution:* Ten 3 mm scintillator layers at density 1.05 g/cm³, area 2.6 × 2.3 m² = 5.98 m², mass ≈ 10 × 5.98 × 0.003 × 1050 ≈ 189 kg. Lead mass: 10 × 5.98 × 0.002 × 11340 ≈ 1356 kg. The hydrogen nucleon fraction relative to argon target mass: hydrogen in scintillator ≈ 189/9 ≈ 21 kg (mass fraction ~1/9 for polystyrene CH); argon target nucleon mass ≈ 44.7 kg. Ratio ≈ 21/44.7 ≈ 47%. **This massively violates the hydrogen constraint.**

*Revised specification:* The electromagnetic calorimeter must use a hydrogen-free scintillator substitute. Replace plastic scintillator with **liquid scintillator based on linear alkylbenzene (LAB) or, better, with inorganic scintillator tiles: specifically, LYSO or BGO tiles** (no hydrogen). Alternatively and more practically, use **silicon photomultiplier-read lead-glass** (SiO₂ — no hydrogen, Cherenkov-based, well-understood technology from OPAL, L3). Lead-glass tiles of 4 X₀ depth behind the downstream face provide shower energy measurement with ~5–8% energy resolution and contribute zero hydrogen. The main drawbacks are cost and the need for precise SiPM coupling, both of which are manageable engineering problems.

---

### 4. Tracking Resolution Enhancement: GEM-Based Inner Chamber Planes

**Specification:** At the upstream and downstream faces of the active target (the interfaces with beam entry and exit toward the spectrometer), install Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) foil detector planes with 100 µm spatial resolution, covering the full 2.6 × 2.3 m cross-section, using CF₄/Ar gas mixture.

**Justification:**

*Matching to downstream spectrometer:* The existing downstream drift chambers have spatial resolution of order 200–400 µm (typical for warm-gas drift chambers). The TPC has intrinsic 1 mm pitch and somewhat worse effective resolution due to diffusion over long drift distances (~0.9 m drift gives ~1–2 mm transverse diffusion in Ar at 5 bar and reasonable drift field). A GEM plane at the exit face provides a precise space point for the track as it enters the spectrometer, dramatically improving the momentum resolution of the combined fit. The position match reduces combinatorial background from multiple tracks.

*Backward track efficiency:* At the upstream face, a GEM plane provides a precise entry/exit point for backward-going tracks. Without it, backward tracks that re-enter the TPC from upstream leave only the TPC ionisation locus for reconstruction. With a GEM plane at the upstream face, a backward muon that exits through the upstream face creates a trigger coincidence, confirming the backward topology and providing a precise track exit point. This directly addresses the ≥25% efficiency requirement for backward tracks.

*Hydrogen budget:* GEM foils are made of kapton (C₂₂H₁₀N₂O₅), which does contain hydrogen. However, kapton foils are 50 µm thick with areal density ~70 mg/cm². Over 2.6 × 2.3 m² = 5.98 m², mass per foil = 0.007 kg/cm² × 59800 cm² ≈ 419 g per foil layer, with perhaps 4 layers per GEM stack (3 GEM foils + cathode), total ~1.7 kg per GEM plane. With two planes: ~3.4 kg total kapton. Hydrogen in kapton (10/382 mass fraction by formula) ≈ 0.09 kg. This is negligible against the argon target mass. The gas volume of the GEM detectors (a few mm gap) is small.

---

### 5. Upstream Muon Tagger: Scintillator Veto Panels

**Specification:** A set of four scintillator panels (each ~3 m × 2.5 m × 1 cm thick) arranged in a loose box around the upstream face and lateral sides, read out by SiPMs, providing a veto on charged particles entering the active target from upstream (beam halo muons, secondary particles from the target) and a tag for outgoing backward muons.

**Justification:**

*Background rejection:* At 410 m from the production target, the beam halo muon flux is not negligible. High-energy muons from pion/kaon decay can traverse the entire detector and mimic neutrino interaction topologies. A veto panel upstream tags these. This is a standard near-detector design element (used at T2K ND280, MINERvA, NOvA ND).

*Backward muon identification:* A backward-going muon (produced in a neutrino interaction in the active target, travelling upstream) will fire one of the upstream or lateral veto panels after the neutrino interaction is registered in the TPC. The timing sequence — TPC trigger first, then panel hit ~1–5 ns later (depending on distance) — clearly identifies backward topology. This is essential for the ≥25% efficiency requirement on backward tracks; without this tag, backward muons that exit upstream leave incomplete TPC tracks and their direction is ambiguous.

*Hydrogen budget:* 1 cm × 4 panels × (3 × 2.5 m²) = 0.3 m³ of scintillator, mass ≈ 315 kg. Hydrogen mass ≈ 35 kg. This is a very significant hydrogen contribution. **Solution:** Replace plastic scintillator with **EJ-204 scintillator sheets encapsulated in aluminium** but **reduce thickness to 5 mm** (sufficient for minimum-ionising particle detection; a MIP deposits ~2 MeV in 1 cm of plastic, so 5 mm gives 1 MeV — well above threshold) and **limit panel coverage to 60% active area** using strip geometry (10 cm wide strips with dead gaps) adequate for the tagging function. This reduces mass to ~80 kg and hydrogen contribution to ~9 kg. With the argon target at 44.7 kg nucleon mass, the fractional hydrogen contribution from these panels is 9/(44.7 × 40 + 9) ≈ 0.5% — within budget. (The factor of 40 accounts for Ar having 40 nucleons vs 1 for hydrogen per atom, so 44.7 kg Ar = 44.7 × (1/40⁻¹ × Nₐ) nucleons ≈ 44.7 × 40/40 × Nₐ nucleons... this requires a careful accounting below.)

---

## Hydrogen Budget: Consolidated Accounting

This is the critical check. Define "target nucleons" as nucleons in the active target volume (the gaseous argon). Then count all hydrogen nucleons in structural and detector material within or immediately surrounding the active volume.

| Component | Mass (kg) | H mass fraction | H mass (kg) | H nucleons (×10²⁷) |
|-----------|-----------|----------------|-------------|-------------------|
| Ar gas (5 bar, full volume) | 44.7 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| GEM kapton (2 planes) | 3.4 | 10/382 = 2.6% | 0.09 | 0.054 |
| Perimeter scintillator strips | 39 | 7.7% | 3.0 | 1.8 |
| Lead-glass calorimeter | ~0 (SiO₂/PbO) | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Upstream veto panels (strip, 5mm) | 80 | 7.7% | 6.2 | 3.7 |
| Field cage / vessel (Al) | — | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Wire supports (Al/W) | — | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Ar nucleons: 44.7 kg / (40 × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) = 6.72 × 10²⁶ nucleons
Total H nucleons: ~(0.054 + 1.8 + 3.7) × 10²⁶ / correction... 

Let me redo this carefully. All hydrogen nucleons vs. all target nucleons:

- Ar: 44.7 kg → 44700 g / 40 g/mol = 1118 mol → × Nₐ = 6.73 × 10²⁶ nucleons × 40 = **2.69 × 10²⁸ nucleon-equivalents** (each Ar nucleus = 40 nucleons)
- Actually the relevant quantity is simply: (number of H nuclei) / (total number of nucleons in target).
- H from all sources: 0.09 + 3.0 + 6.2 = 9.3 kg of hydrogen = 9300 g / 1 g/mol × Nₐ = **5.6 × 10²⁷ free hydrogen nucleons**
- Total nucleons: Ar contributes 44700/40 × Nₐ × 40 = 44700/1 × Nₐ / 1 ... (Ar: each gram = Nₐ/40 atoms × 40 nucleons = Nₐ nucleons/gram) → **44700 × Nₐ = 2.69 × 10²⁸ nucleons**
- H fraction: 5.6×10²⁷ / (2.69×10²⁸ + 5.6×10²⁷) = 5.6 / (26.9 + 5.6) = 5.6/32.5 = **17%**

This **violates the 2% constraint severely.** The veto panels and perimeter scintillator dominate.

**This reveals a fundamental problem: any plastic scintillator near a low-density gaseous target will violate the hydrogen constraint because the gas provides very few nucleons per unit volume.**

### Revised Strategy: Eliminate All Plastic Scintillator

The only way to satisfy the 2% hydrogen constraint with a low-density gas target is to eliminate essentially all hydrogenous material:

**Replace scintillator trigger planes with thin resistive plate chambers (RPCs) or thin-gap Cherenkov radiators:**

- **Timing RPCs** (2 mm gas gap, C₂H₂F₄/SF₆/iC₄H₁₀ gas, Bakelite or glass electrodes): Glass-electrode RPCs contain no hydrogen. The gas mixture contains hydrogen in isobutane, but isobutane is used at ~5% and the gas volume is minimal — a 2 mm gap over 5.98 m² = 11.96 litres per plane. At STP, 12 litres × 5% = 0.6 litres of isobutane, negligible mass. Standard RPCs use **glass** (SiO₂/Na₂O/CaO) or low-resistivity **bakelite** (phenol-formaldehyde — does contain H).
