| Track type | Old FGD (2D bars) | New cube target |
|---|---|---|
| Proton > 50° acceptance | ~40% | ~92% |
| Muon > 50° acceptance (with halo TPC + SMRD) | ~60% | ~88% |
| Fully kinematically complete CC events | ~25% | ~82% |

The improvement in complete-event fraction from ~25% to ~82% directly increases the statistical sample for TKI analyses by a factor ~3, and — more importantly — dramatically reduces the **kinematic acceptance correction** and its associated systematic uncertainty, which is currently one of the leading contributions to the 6% total systematic.

### 7.2 Proton Identification

Proton/pion separation using dE/dx measured by cube hit amplitude:

At 450 MeV/c, a proton (βγ ≈ 0.48) has dE/dx ≈ 5 MeV/(g/cm²) while a pion (βγ ≈ 3.2) has dE/dx ≈ 1.6 MeV/(g/cm²) — a factor of ~3. With 20–30 p.e./cm per fibre end, the signal-to-noise for single-cube hits is well above threshold, and the **Bragg peak identification** provides proton tagging efficiency > 95% with pion misidentification < 2% for tracks with more than 5 cm range.

### 7.3 Systematic Uncertainty Pathway to 4%

The current ~6% systematic breaks down approximately as:

| Source | Current contribution | Expected with upgrade |
|---|---|---|
| Flux uncertainty | ~3.5% | ~2.0% (more complete constraint) |
| Cross-section models | ~4.0% | ~2.5% (TKI with complete events) |
| Detector efficiency | ~2.0% | ~1.5% (better understood 3D detector) |
| Combined (approximate RSS) | ~6.0% | ~3.5% |

The quadrature combination reaches ~3.5%, satisfying the T2K-II requirement of ≤ 4%. The key lever is the cross-section model uncertainty reduction, which requires precisely the kinematically-complete events this detector is designed to provide.

---

## 8. Summary Table of Proposed Hardware

| Component | Quantity | Key technology | Channels | Cost driver |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 cm³ scintillator cubes | ~2×10⁶ | Injection-moulded PS + TiO₂ | — | Tooling + moulding |
| WLS fibres (Kuraray Y-11) | ~57,000 m | Multi-clad 1.0 mm | — | Fibre cost |
| SiPMs (1.3 mm², MPPC) | ~113,000 | Hamamatsu S13360 series | 113,000 | Dominant cost |
| CITIROC FEBs | ~1,770 | 64-ch ASIC boards | — | PCB production |
| Halo mini-TPCs (4 panels) | 4 | Ar:CF4:iC4H10, MicroMegas | ~12,000 | Mesh production |
| Upstream EM veto | 1 panel | Pb/scintillator tiles + SiPM | ~1,400 | Minimal |
| CFRP mechanics + rails | — | Structural frame | — | Machining |

---

## 9. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Optical cross-talk between adjacent cubes through fibres | Use black-painted fibre ends between cubes; demonstrated in SuperFGD prototype beam tests at CERN |
| SiPM dark count noise degrading hit finding | Require coincidence on both fibre ends (reduces rate by ×100); demonstrated viable in Baby-MIND |
| Assembly of 2×10⁶ cubes within schedule | Semi-automated assembly machine (conveyor + robotic fibre insertion); similar scale addressed in SuperFGD ND280 upgrade |
| Halo TPC space charge in high-occupancy spills | Low occupancy expected (<<1% of channels per spill); CF4 addition suppresses ion back-flow in MicroMegas |
| Integration with existing ND280 trigger | New detector issues independent trigger to ND280 master, combined offline; no hardware trigger change required |

---

## 10. Note on Relationship to Ongoing ND280 Upgrade

This proposal is consistent with and complementary to the ND280 upgrade (already approved and partially installed as of 2023–2024), which places a SuperFGD + HA-TPC + TOF configuration in the central region. The design described here **adopts the same SuperFGD cube technology** (reducing engineering risk and cost through shared tooling and expertise) while tailoring the surrounding detectors (halo TPCs rather than standalone HA-TPCs, given the available volume and the existing downstream tracker) to the specific geometric constraints of the upstream slot. It can be considered an extension module that further increases the neutrino-interaction fiducial mass and the solid-angle coverage for kinematically-complete events within the existing magnet.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Active Neutrino Target for the Upstream Section

## Executive Summary

The core problem is replacing a passive photon-tagger with an active target that reconstructs both the outgoing muon and the leading recoil proton in kinematically complete charged-current events, within a 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope, while reducing the residual systematic uncertainty from ~6% to ~4%. The box is shallow along the beam axis (0.6 m), which immediately constrains what can range out and what must be tracked. The solution proposed here is a **segmented scintillator tracker with embedded low-Z absorber, surrounded by a thin time-of-flight and veto shell, integrated with the existing downstream TPCs and return-yoke muon ranger**.

---

## 1. Physics-Driven Constraints That Shape the Design

### 1.1 Proton Reconstruction Challenge

| Quantity | Value | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Median proton momentum | ~450 MeV/c | Kinetic energy ~100 MeV; range in polystyrene ~18 cm |
| 35% of protons | >50° to beam | Must have large solid-angle acceptance; no forward-only spectrometer |
| 6% of protons | >900 MeV/c | Kinetic energy ~330 MeV; range ~90 cm in polystyrene—needs downstream handoff |
| Proton at 450 MeV/c, 90° | Fully contained? | Requires ~18 cm lateral tracker depth—tight but feasible within 1.9 m transverse |

### 1.2 Muon Reconstruction Challenge

| Quantity | Value | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| 25% of muons | >50° to beam | Side-going muons must reach the return-yoke ranger or be momentum-analysed by multiple Coulomb scattering (MCS) |
| Muon momentum at 0.6 GeV peak | ~300–500 MeV/c typical | Range ~1–3 m in scintillator; most forward muons exit into the downstream TPCs |
| Available depth | 0.6 m | Forward muons are not ranged here; they must be handed off downstream |

### 1.3 Systematic Target

The step from 6% → 4% requires improving the **flux × cross-section** product uncertainty. The key handles are:
- Neutrino-hydrogen separation (for nucleon-level cross-sections)
- Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) variables: δpT, δαT, δφT
- Carbon-to-water comparison with the existing downstream water target

Kinematic completeness means: vertex + muon track (momentum + charge sign) + leading proton track (momentum + direction) reconstructed simultaneously.

---

## 2. Proposed Detector Architecture

The 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume is divided into four functional sub-systems along the beam (z) axis.

```
Beam →   [Veto]  [SuperX Module]  [SuperX Module]  [ToF/Ecal shell]
           z~2cm    z~25cm           z~25cm            z~8cm
           
         ←————————————— 0.60 m total ————————————————→
         ←—————————————————————————————————————————————→
                     2.0 m (beam direction)
                  transverse: 1.9 m (y) × 2.0 m (x) [fit to magnet]
```

### 2.1 Upstream Veto Plane (~2 cm)

- Two planes of 1 cm thick extruded polystyrene scintillator bars (x and y), 1.5 cm × 1.0 cm cross-section
- Purpose: tag beam-entering charged particles; define fiducial interaction vertex
- SiPM readout on both ends for position resolution ~5 mm and timing ~1 ns
- This rejects muons and charged hadrons entering from upstream beam-related backgrounds

### 2.2 Two "SuperX" Scintillator Tracker Modules (~25 cm each, total ~50 cm)

Each module is a **finely segmented 3D scintillator block** constructed as follows:

#### 2.2.1 Scintillator Bar Geometry

- Extruded polystyrene bars, **triangular cross-section**, 1.5 cm height, 3.3 cm base, in the same style as the existing photon-tagger bars (leveraging existing tooling and WLS fibre + SiPM infrastructure)
- Bars arranged in alternating **X, Y, U (45°), V (−45°)** stereo layers, 4 views per 2-layer pair, to give 3D space-point reconstruction without ambiguities even with multi-track events
- Layer pitch: **1.5 cm** (one bar height per layer)
- Number of layers per module: 16 (4 view-pairs × 4 layers each), giving ~24 cm depth per module
- Bar length: 1.9 m (y-direction bars) or 2.0 m (x-direction bars)
- Number of bars per layer: ~130 (at 1.5 cm pitch across 1.9 m)
- **Total bars per module**: 16 layers × ~130 bars ≈ 2,080 bars
- Both modules: ~4,160 bars + 8,320 SiPM channels (dual-ended readout)

**Rationale for triangular bars**: Charge sharing between adjacent triangles gives sub-bar position resolution (~3 mm achieved in similar designs), essential for separating the proton track from the muon track near the vertex and for dE/dx-based particle identification.

#### 2.2.2 Passive Target Material Interspersed

The scintillator itself is the neutrino target (hydrocarbon, CH). No additional passive absorber is needed in the tracker volume—the scintillator density (~1.05 g/cm³) gives sufficient target mass while maintaining tracking capability.

**Target mass estimate**:
- Module volume: 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.25 m³ = 0.95 m³ per module
- Packing fraction ~0.85 (bars + gaps + WLS fibre)
- Mass per module: 0.95 × 0.85 × 1050 kg/m³ ≈ **850 kg**
- Both modules: **~1.7 t** of active hydrocarbon target

This compares favourably with the existing 1.1 t polystyrene targets downstream and gives roughly **1.5× more fiducial mass** in the upstream location where flux is higher (less upstream material to traverse).

#### 2.2.3 Readout

- WLS fibre (Y-11, 1 mm diameter) glued into groove, routed to SiPM at bar end
- SiPM: 1.3 mm × 1.3 mm Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS (or equivalent), chosen for low dark-count rate at room temperature given the underground-like environment
- Front-end ASIC: existing CITIROC-1A or equivalent 32-channel chip (already deployed in similar near detectors), zero-suppressed readout
- Single-ended readout for short bars (<1 m); dual-ended for bars >1 m to recover position from time difference
- Expected light yield: ~25 p.e./MIP/end, sufficient for >99% tracking efficiency per layer

#### 2.2.4 Why Not Liquid Argon or Water Cherenkov Here?

- **LArTPC**: Incompatible with the 0.6 m shallow depth; cathode-to-anode drift distance for a useful TPC would need to be along z (beam), giving only ~40 cm drift—insufficient for good electron lifetime-limited hit quality; also cryogenics infrastructure cannot be installed in the repurposed volume on the timescale of an upgrade. The downstream gas TPCs already provide precision tracking for forward tracks.
- **Water Cherenkov**: Low light yield for proton tracks below Cherenkov threshold (proton threshold ~1.07 GeV/c in water); would miss most of the 450 MeV/c median proton distribution entirely.
- **Emulsion**: Would provide superb spatial resolution but cannot do real-time event selection or give timing for beam-spill association; not suitable as primary active target.

---

## 3. Time-of-Flight and Thin Electromagnetic Calorimeter Shell (~8 cm)

Surrounding the two tracker modules on all four transverse faces (not upstream/downstream), a **thin TOF + ECal layer** serves multiple purposes:

### 3.1 Time-of-Flight Planes

- Two layers of 5 mm plastic scintillator paddles, each 5 × 5 cm² pixels, one on each of the four sides
- Timing resolution target: **σ_t < 300 ps** per plane
- Provides TOF between inner tracker hit and outer plane: at 1 GeV/c, Δt(π vs p) over 50 cm ≈ 1.5 ns—well-resolved at this resolution
- Critical for proton/pion separation for tracks that escape the tracker volume laterally but are stopped in the return yoke or ECal

### 3.2 Thin Lead-Scintillator Electromagnetic Calorimeter

- 4 radiation lengths of Pb + scintillator in 8 cm: approximately 8 layers of 5 mm Pb + 5 mm scintillator
- Purpose: tag photons from π⁰ decay that could fake the proton signal in TKI analyses; this partially recovers the photon-tagging function of the removed upstream section
- SiPM readout, same architecture as existing downstream ECal

---

## 4. Integration with Existing Downstream Detectors

The new module does not stand alone; it feeds into the existing detector chain.

### 4.1 Muon Momentum Measurement

| Muon trajectory | Measurement method | Expected resolution |
|---|---|---|
| Forward, θ < 30° | Range in downstream plastic targets + TPC tracking | δp/p ~ 3–5% |
| Forward, 30°–50° | MCS in scintillator + TPC + ECal | δp/p ~ 5–8% |
| Side-going, >50° | Range to return-yoke scintillator rangers | δp/p ~ 10–15% (range-based) |
| Side-going, >50°, 0.2 T field | Bend radius in existing dipole field | Supplements range, sign determination |

The existing 0.2 T dipole field gives a sagitta of ~2.5 cm for a 500 MeV/c muon over 2 m—measurable with ~3 mm position resolution per point, yielding charge sign determination for >90% of muons.

### 4.2 Proton Handoff to Downstream TPCs

For the ~6% of protons above 900 MeV/c, the proton exits the new target and enters the downstream gas TPCs. The gas TPC dE/dx can distinguish protons from pions at these momenta (proton Bethe-Bloch peak at ~900 MeV/c is well-separated from MIP pions). The combined tracker + TPC system thus provides proton identification across the full momentum range.

### 4.3 Vertex Matching

A reconstructed vertex in the new scintillator target is matched to the downstream track system using:
- Timing: bunch structure of the accelerator beam (typically 580 ns spill for T2K-like beams) provides ~ns-level bunch tagging
- Track direction: extrapolated upstream using hits in the first downstream TPC plane
- The 1.5 cm bar segmentation gives vertex resolution ~5 mm in z and ~3 mm transverse—sufficient to assign tracks to vertices in the multi-interaction-per-spill environment

---

## 5. Mechanical and Installation Design

### 5.1 Module Construction

- Each SuperX module built as a **self-supporting aluminium extrusion frame**, 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.25 m, with bars slotting into precision-machined grooves
- Frame wall thickness: 5 mm Al (0.054 X₀, minimising upstream material for photon conversions)
- Modules slide into the existing magnet yoke on rails, with electrical connectors at the downstream face
- Total new detector mass: ~1.7 t scintillator + ~0.3 t ECal/TOF shell + ~0.2 t frames = **~2.2 t**
- This is less than the 16.1 t photon-tagger section removed: **net mass reduction of ~14 t**, which may require mechanical support re-engineering of the magnet bore but reduces upstream material that attenuated the flux

### 5.2 Cabling and DAQ

- SiPM bias and signal routed along bar ends to patch panels on the module frame
- Front-end boards mounted on the frame outside the active volume
- Daisy-chained to existing detector DAQ backplane; the ~8,320 new SiPM channels represent a ~15% increase in channel count over the existing downstream targets—within headroom of the existing data acquisition system assuming it was designed with upgrade paths

### 5.3 Installation Sequence

1. Remove photon-tagger section (water bags, brass, Pb layers, scintillator planes): ~4 weeks
2. Install guide rails and downstream-face connector plate: ~1 week  
3. Insert veto plane: ~2 days
4. Insert SuperX Module 1, connect readout: ~1 week
5. Insert SuperX Module 2, connect readout: ~1 week
6. Install TOF/ECal shell on four sides: ~1 week
7. Commissioning with cosmic rays and then beam: ~4 weeks

**Estimated total installation downtime: ~10 weeks**, compatible with a scheduled accelerator maintenance period.

---

## 6. Expected Performance and Systematic Reduction

### 6.1 Reconstruction Efficiency

| Track type | Efficiency estimate | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Muons, all angles | >95% | >3 layers hit for tracks >150 MeV/c in 1.5 cm pitch |
| Protons, p > 200 MeV/c | >90% | Range > 2 layers at 200 MeV/c proton |
| Protons, p > 100 MeV/c | >70% | Low-p tracks stop in first few layers; recoverable by dE/dx cluster |
| Kinematically complete events | ~65–70% | Product of muon × proton × vertex efficiencies |

The 65–70% kinematically complete fraction compares with perhaps 30–40% achievable with the old photon-tagger geometry acting as a passive target read out only by the downstream TPCs (poor proton acceptance for large-angle tracks).

### 6.2 Particle Identification

**Proton vs. pion separation** using dE/dx in scintillator:

At 450 MeV/c:
- Proton: dE/dx ~ 3–4 MeV/cm (highly ionising, stopping Bragg peak visible)
- Pion: dE/dx ~ 2 MeV/cm (MIP-like)
- Separation > 3σ for tracks with ≥5 layers (7.5 cm), covering protons above ~300 MeV/c

For protons below 300 MeV/c, the Bragg peak is entirely contained within 3–4 layers; identification relies on the **range-momentum consistency** (measured range vs. expected range for proton hypothesis).

The TOF planes add a redundant p/π separation that is especially powerful for tracks exiting the sides of the module, where the in-tracker track length may be short.

### 6.3 TKI Variable Resolution

The transverse kinematic imbalance variables (δpT, δαT) require:
- Muon transverse momentum: **σ(pT,μ) ~ 20 MeV/c** (from MCS + downstream TPC, achievable)
- Proton transverse momentum: **σ(pT,p) ~ 25 MeV/c** (from range-momentum in tracker)
- Combined δpT resolution: **~35 MeV/c**, sufficient to resolve the FSI-induced broadening (~100–200 MeV/c width in δpT distributions)

### 6.4 Systematic Uncertainty Path to 4%

The dominant systematic sources and how this upgrade addresses them:

| Systematic source | Current contribution | Upgrade mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Flux shape uncertainty | ~3% | TKI near-detector constraint on spectral index improved by larger fiducial mass and better kinematic completeness |
| CC-QE vs CC-nonQE cross-section | ~2–3% | Proton multiplicity now measured; CC0π1p sample cleanly isolated |
| Nuclear FSI modelling | ~2% | TKI shape analysis directly constrains FSI; δpT distribution width is FSI-sensitive |
| Detector efficiency (p reconstruction) | ~1.5% | Reduced to <0.8% by in-situ efficiency measurement using stopping proton control samples |
| Photon backgrounds | ~1% | TOF/ECal shell partially recovers photon-tagging capability |

The combination of doubled target mass, 2× better kinematic completeness, and direct proton reconstruction enabling TKI constraints is expected to reduce the **flux × cross-section systematic product** from ~6% to **~3.5–4%**, meeting the programme target.

---

## 7. Optional Enhancement: Hydrogen-Subtraction Capability

If the downstream water-layer target permits carbon subtraction (C₈H₈ polystyrene minus CH₂ polyethylene on an event-rate basis), the new target could include **thin polyethylene inserts** (2–3 mm sheets of CH₂ between every 4 tracker layers) to give a statistical hydrogen-subtraction sample. The carbon background from the CH₂ itself is subtracted using the pure polystyrene layers. This is an established technique (used in MINERvA and proposed for NINJA) and could provide a quasi-free nucleon cross-section sample at the level of ~10% statistical precision per 10⁶ events, giving additional constraint on the absolute normalisation that reduces the correlated flux-cross-section uncertainty.

---

## 8. Summary Table of Proposed Hardware

| Component | Quantity | Key spec | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Upstream veto planes | 2 planes, 1 cm bars | σ_t ~ 1 ns, 5 mm position | Beam background rejection |
| SuperX scintillator module 1 | ~2,080 triangular bars, 16 layers | 1.5 cm pitch, x/y/u/v views | Active target + tracker |
| SuperX scintillator module 2 | ~2,080 triangular bars, 16 layers | identical | Active target + tracker |
| TOF planes (4 sides) | ~1,200 paddles, 5×5 cm² | σ_t < 300 ps | p/π separation for exiting tracks |
| Thin Pb-scintillator ECal (4 sides) | 8 layers, 5 mm Pb + 5 mm scint | 4 X₀ | Photon tagging, π⁰ rejection |
| WLS fibre + SiPM channels | ~8,320 channels (tracker) + ~2,400 (ECal/TOF) | 1 mm Y-11 fibre, 1.3 mm SiPM | Unified readout architecture with existing detector |
| Front-end ASICs | ~340 × 32-ch boards | CITIROC-1A or equivalent | Leverages existing DAQ |
| Al support frames | 2 | 5 mm wall, rail-mount | Rapid installation/removal |

---

## Conclusion

The proposed upgrade replaces the removed photon-tagger with two finely-segmented triangular-bar scintillator tracker modules providing ~1.7 t of active hydrocarbon target, supplemented by a thin TOF and ECal shell on the transverse faces. It is designed to fit within the available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope, integrate seamlessly with the existing downstream TPC and return-yoke ranging systems, leverage proven bar-and-SiPM technology already deployed in the detector, and deliver the kinematically complete CC event reconstruction—with both muon and leading proton measured—needed to push the residual systematic uncertainty below the 4% threshold through improved TKI-based flux and cross-section constraint.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Summary of Constraints Driving the Design

Before proposing hardware, let me be explicit about what the physics demands:

- **Muon reconstruction at all angles including 90° and backward**: requires tracking that is fully 3D and hermetic, not just forward-projective
- **Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy**: range ~3 cm in liquid argon, ~1.5 cm in scintillator, ~a few mm in iron — demands fine granularity and low threshold
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤ 2% of nucleons**: strongly constrains target material choice (rules out hydrocarbon-rich scintillator as the bulk target)
- **Volume ~2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m³** inside an existing warm dipole at 0.15 T
- **410 m from target, ~0.7 GeV peak flux**: moderate neutrino energy, so final states are mostly 1–3 track

---

## Proposed Active Target System

### 1. Bulk Target Material: Low-Density Straw Tube Tracker (STT)

**Technology**: Thin-wall (25 µm Mylar + 50 µm Cu-Be wire) straw tubes, 1 cm diameter, filled with Ar/CO₂ (70/30) at 1 atm.

**Rationale**:
- Straw tube trackers (as used in KLOE, NA62, ATLAS TRT) achieve ~150 µm spatial resolution per straw, adequate for short proton tracks
- The gas filling means hydrogen nuclei are negligible — Ar/CO₂ has effectively zero free hydrogen, satisfying the ≤2% hydrogen constraint comfortably
- Radiation length X₀ ~hundreds of meters, mean free path for hadronic interactions is long: minimal secondary interactions distorting the event topology
- Low density (~1.8 × 10⁻³ g/cm³ effective for the straw array) means even a 60 MeV proton (range ~3 cm in polystyrene) travels ~15–20 cm, giving ~15–20 straw hits — reconstructable
- Operates comfortably in the 0.15 T dipole field; gas gain unaffected

**Configuration**:
- Straws arranged in alternating X/Y/U/V stereo views (four orientations at 0°, 90°, +7°, −7°) to give full 3D reconstruction
- ~12,000 straws total filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m volume
- Straws run perpendicular to beam (along the 2.6 m or 2.3 m transverse dimensions) so that **backward-going and large-angle tracks cross multiple straws** regardless of direction
- Straw modules mounted in 10 cm thick planes along the beam axis (0.9 m / ~9 planes), with both longitudinal and transverse orientations interleaved

**What this buys**: 3D point resolution ~1 mm³ effective voxel; threshold for track reconstruction ~2 cm minimum length → ~40 MeV proton kinetic energy, meeting the 60 MeV requirement with margin.

---

### 2. Thin Radiator / Transition Radiation Detector (TRD) Layers for Particle ID

**Technology**: Interleave every second straw plane with a 2 cm thick foam radiator (Rohacell 71, density 71 kg/m³, essentially C/H/O but very thin — only ~8 planes × 2 cm = 16 cm total, contributing <0.1 nucleon-fraction of hydrogen).

Actually — given the hydrogen constraint, **replace foam radiators with carbon fiber honeycomb panels** (density ~50 kg/m³, pure carbon structure). These provide:
- Mechanical support for straw planes
- Some energy-loss contrast (dE/dx in carbon vs. gas) for PID
- Zero added hydrogen

**Primary PID** comes from dE/dx in the straws themselves: Ar/CO₂ gives good dE/dx sampling. At 0.7 GeV, separating muons from pions by range/dE/dx in the downstream tracker is adequate; the main need inside the target is separating protons from pions, which dE/dx handles well below ~1 GeV/c.

---

### 3. Downstream Muon Ranger / Range Stack

The existing gas drift chambers measure momentum magnetically for tracks that exit the target into the main magnet volume. However, **large-angle and backward muons will not reach those chambers**. 

**Proposed addition**: A thin active muon ranger surrounding the upstream and lateral faces of the target volume.

**Technology**: Extruded plastic scintillator bars (like MINERvA/NOvA technology), 3 × 3 cm² cross-section, with **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber** readout and **SiPM** (silicon photomultiplier) sensors.

**Configuration**:
- Upstream face: a plane of horizontal + vertical scintillator bars, ~2.6 × 2.3 m², 10 layers deep (30 cm total iron absorber interleaved) — acts as a muon range stack for backward-going tracks
- Two lateral walls (along beam, 0.9 m deep × 2.3 m tall and 0.9 m deep × 2.6 m wide): 5 layers each of scintillator + 2 cm iron, for large-angle containment
- Scintillator bars are read at both ends with **SiPMs (6 × 6 mm² Hamamatsu S13360 series or equivalent)** — SiPMs are robust in the modest field present at the target periphery and need no PMT shielding

**Why SiPMs over PMTs**: The 0.15 T fringe field at the edges of the warm dipole would require bulky shielding for PMTs. SiPMs operate in fields up to several Tesla with no degradation.

**What this buys**: Muons stopping in the range stack are measured by range (σ_p/p ~ 5% for 200–600 MeV muons). Combined with the magnetic spectrometer for forward tracks, this achieves the required ≥25% efficiency at all angles.

**Iron absorber specification**: 2 cm plates (not thicker) to maintain sensitivity to muons as low as ~150 MeV kinetic energy (range ~8 cm in iron) — this matters for near-threshold CC events.

---

### 4. Timing Layer for Event Separation and Direction Reconstruction

**Technology**: Upstream and downstream scintillator planes with fast timing — **LYSO or EJ-228 plastic scintillator tiles**, 5 mm thick, read by SiPMs, targeting **<300 ps single-hit time resolution**.

**Purpose**:
- Distinguish neutrino interactions from cosmics and beam-unrelated backgrounds
- Provide track direction for the STT (distinguishing forward from backward is otherwise ambiguous in a symmetric tracker without timing)
- At 410 m and 0.7 GeV, the beam spill structure (~10 µs for typical FNAL/BNL beams) already helps, but sub-ns timing resolves intra-spill pileup at higher intensities

**Configuration**: Two planes at the upstream and downstream faces of the STT volume, plus one mid-volume plane at z = 0.45 m.

---

### 5. Readout Electronics

**Technology**: 
- Straw tubes: **SAMPA chip** (developed for ALICE TPC upgrade, 32 channels/chip, 10 MHz sampling, ~1 mW/channel) or equivalent ASIC with continuous readout. This chip handles both the tracking pulse shape and charge integration.
- Scintillator bars and timing planes: **CITIROC 1A** or **FlexToT** ASICs for SiPM readout, with waveform digitization at 250 MHz to capture both timing and charge.
- Trigger: **triggerless streaming readout** preferred given the low rate at a near detector (beam neutrino rate ~few MHz during spill, mostly NC/beam gas), with software triggering offline. If a hardware trigger is needed, the scintillator timing planes form a fast coincidence trigger.

**Data volume estimate**: ~12,000 straw channels × 100 bytes/hit × ~5 hits/straw/spill × 10⁶ spills/year ~ manageable at ~few TB/year with zero-suppression.

---

### 6. Calibration Systems

- **UV laser system** injecting light into the STT via optical fibers to individual straws — standard drift time / gain calibration
- **Stopping muon sample** from cosmic rays (selected with the scintillator range stack) for dE/dx and momentum-by-range cross-calibration against the magnetic measurement
- **Michel electron** sample from stopped muons: gives absolute energy scale check at 52.8 MeV

---

## Summary Table

| Subsystem | Technology | Key Specification | Physics Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active target bulk | Straw tube tracker, Ar/CO₂, 1 cm Ø | ~150 µm/straw, ~12k channels | 3D track reconstruction, low-Z, zero free H |
| Structural support | Carbon fiber honeycomb panels | 50 kg/m³, pure carbon | Zero hydrogen addition |
| Backward/lateral muon ranger | Extruded scintillator + WLS fiber + SiPM + Fe absorbers | 2 cm Fe plates, 3×3 cm bars | ≥25% muon efficiency at all angles |
| Timing planes | LYSO/EJ-228 tiles + SiPMs | <300 ps resolution | Track direction, pileup rejection |
| Front-end electronics | SAMPA (straws), CITIROC (SiPMs) | Continuous/streaming readout | Low noise, in-spill efficiency |
| Calibration | UV laser + cosmic muon + Michel e | In-situ | Gain, dE/dx, energy scale |

---

## Critical Design Choices Justified Against Requirements

**Why not liquid argon?** LArTPC would give beautiful reconstruction but: (a) cryogenic infrastructure does not exist in the near hall and is expensive to retrofit, (b) argon's ~1.4 g/cm³ density means 60 MeV protons travel only ~3 mm — below practical threshold for wire-based reconstruction, and (c) hydrogen fraction would be zero, which is fine, but the marginal benefit doesn't justify the cost and infrastructure.

**Why not solid scintillator (NOvA-style)?** Polystyrene (CH) has a hydrogen-to-nucleon ratio of ~0.57 — catastrophically above the 2% limit. Even mineral oil based scintillator is CH₂-rich. This is the **decisive constraint** eliminating conventional scintillator as the bulk target.

**Why not emulsion?** Excellent for short tracks but offline and not suitable for the muon angular efficiency requirement or the continuous running needed.

**The straw tube tracker is the right answer** because it was essentially invented for this class of problem: low-mass, low-hydrogen, fine-grained 3D tracking in a magnetic field. The DRIFT experiment and the proposed NINJA-type near detectors validate this approach at similar scales.

# ND280 Upgrade: Hardware Proposal

The upgrade replaces the P0D with a new tracker built from three hardware elements and their readout. It is designed to fix two weaknesses of the current detector: poor acceptance at high angles and a high proton tracking threshold.

## The problem the upgrade must solve

- **Bar orientation:** The current FGD bars and the TPC drift volumes are arranged around the beam axis. Tracks at more than about 50° (roughly 25% of muons, 35% of protons) run nearly parallel to the FGD planes and often miss the TPCs, so their reconstruction efficiency is poor or zero. This high-angle acceptance loss contributes to the ~6% residual systematic.
- **Two-dimensional planes:** Alternating x/y bar layers give only two projections. Short tracks and multi-track vertices are ambiguous, so the proton threshold is high (about 450–500 MeV/c). That is near the median proton momentum, so about half the leading protons are lost.
- **Requirement:** Transverse kinematic imbalance needs both the muon and the proton over nearly the full solid angle, down to low proton momentum.

## 1. SuperFGD: a 3D-granular scintillator target in the P0D volume

**Technology:**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene cubes.
- The array is approximately 192 × 182 × 56 cubes, about 1.9 × 1.8 × 0.56 m. This fits the available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box, with room for the support box and readout.
- Target mass is about 2 t of CH, roughly double one existing FGD. Hydrocarbon is acceptable; FGD2 remains for the carbon/water comparison.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres (x, y, z), each read by an MPPC at one end. This gives about 56,000 channels.

**Why:**
- **Isotropic acceptance:** Three orthogonal views give the same response at every track angle, including high-angle and backward tracks.
- **Low proton threshold:** Fine 1 cm granularity lets protons be tracked down to about 300 MeV/c (2–3 cubes of range). This captures most of the leading-proton distribution, not just the upper half.
- **Particle identification:** Good dE/dx and range information separates protons from pions near the vertex.
- **Neutron tagging:** Nanosecond timing and fine segmentation allow time-of-flight between the vertex and a neutron's isolated secondary-interaction cluster. This adds neutron kinematics for antineutrino events.
- **Escaping protons:** The 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c, and higher-momentum muons, exit the cube volume. They are measured by the TPCs below.

## 2. Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs), above and below the SuperFGD

**Technology:**
- Each chamber is about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m, with the drift along the vertical (magnetic-field) direction.
- Same gas as the existing TPCs: Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2.
- The field cage is a thin, light composite laminate, which minimises dead material and multiple scattering.
- Readout uses resistive-anode ("encapsulated resistive") bulk Micromegas. Charge spreading through the resistive layer gives better spatial resolution with fewer, larger pads and suppresses sparks.

**Why:**
- They catch the high-angle tracks that leave the SuperFGD and would miss the downstream TPCs.
- Curvature in the 0.2 T field gives momentum and charge sign at high angles. The target is roughly 10% momentum resolution at 1 GeV/c.
- dE/dx gives particle identification, for example separating muons from electrons and identifying energetic protons.
- These measurements cover exactly the population of tracks that drives the acceptance systematic.

## 3. Time-of-Flight (TOF) system enclosing the new tracker

**Technology:**
- Six planes of about 2.2 m plastic scintillator bars around the SuperFGD and HA-TPC assembly.
- Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Time resolution is about 150 ps.

**Why:**
- It sets the track direction, rejecting backward-going particles and out-of-fiducial or outside-background entries.
- It gives a precise event time (t₀) for the TPC drift.
- It provides time-of-flight particle identification, complementing dE/dx in the energy region where dE/dx bands cross.

## 4. Readout and integration

- **Front-end electronics:** New MPPC front-end boards serve the ~56k SuperFGD channels and the TOF. They are compact enough to fit within the magnet gaps and preserve the nanosecond timing needed for neutron time-of-flight.
- **TPC electronics:** New DAQ for the HA-TPCs, compatible with the existing TPC system.
- **Integration:** A new support basket and services in the former P0D region, plus calibration systems such as LED and cosmic triggers.
- **Unchanged components:** The magnet, SMRD, ECals, the three existing TPCs, FGD1 and FGD2 stay in place. Combined with the new detectors, this gives near-4π coverage.

## Expected outcome

The upgrade provides:
- Full-solid-angle muon acceptance.
- A proton threshold of about 300 MeV/c.
- Neutron tagging.
- Charge, momentum and particle identification at high angles.

Together these enable transverse kinematic imbalance measurements. The tighter flux and cross-section constraints are what reduce the ND280 systematic from about 6% toward the ~4% T2K-II goal.

# Proposed upgrade for the Kestrel Flats target region

The aim is to fill the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m region with three systems:

1. A fine-grained, fully active 3D scintillator target.
2. Thin gas TPCs on the large-angle faces.
3. A hermetic time-of-flight (ToF) shell.

Together these provide 4π muon reconstruction and low-threshold proton tracking. This is essentially the ND280-upgrade concept adapted to this envelope and to a hydrogen-free far target.

## 1. Active target: 3D-segmented plastic scintillator (SuperFGD-type)

**Construction**
- About 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes with a reflective etched surface.
- Each cube is pierced by three orthogonal holes, each carrying a 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibre (e.g. Kuraray Y-11).
- Each fibre is read at one end by a silicon photomultiplier (e.g. Hamamatsu 1.3 mm MPPC), with a mirrored far end.

**Size**
- Roughly 1.9 m (x) × 1.6 m (y) × 0.8 m (z, along beam).
- That is about 190 × 160 × 80 ≈ 2.4 million cubes and about 2.4 t of target mass.
- Readout needs about 58,000 channels: 30.4k + 15.2k + 12.8k for the three views.

**Electronics**
- CITIROC-based front-end boards inside the magnet.
- Sub-nanosecond hit timing, giving about 0.9 ns resolution per cube when two views are combined.

**Why it meets the requirements**
- Isotropic 3D readout means there is no "dead" angle. Tracks perpendicular to the beam, or backward-going, are imaged as well as forward tracks. Planar bar detectors cannot do this at about 90°.
- A 60 MeV proton ranges about 2.5–3 cm in CH. That still crosses 3–4 cubes and is identified by its dE/dx Bragg peak.
- Higher-energy protons are measured by range in the cubes.

**Hydrogen fraction**
- In CH, hydrogen is 1 of 13 nucleons per CH unit, about 7.7% of nucleons.
- With fibres and coatings it stays well under 20%, so the hydrogen-subtraction model remains valid.
- Avoid water or other high-H additions; denser additives should not raise the H fraction.

## 2. High-angle TPCs

**Placement**
- Two TPCs on the faces of the target parallel to the beam, each about 1.9 m × 0.8 m × 0.3 m deep.
- Place them on the faces crossed by large-angle tracks that curve in the 0.15 T field, i.e. tracks moving perpendicular to B. These are top/bottom faces for a horizontal field, or left/right faces for a vertical field.
- The faces parallel to B, where large-angle tracks barely curve, get ToF and range measurement only.

**Gas, readout and field cage**
- T2K gas (Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀, 95:3:2).
- Resistive bulk-Micromegas readout with charge spreading, giving about 10 mm pads and about 0.3 mm resolution.
- Thin composite field cage (laminated aramid/honeycomb) to keep material and multiple scattering low.
- AFTER/DAQ-style electronics.

**Measurements**
- Momentum and charge of muons leaving at about 40–140°.
- dE/dx for μ/π/e/p separation.
- The existing downstream drift chambers still cover forward tracks.

## 3. Time-of-flight shell

**Construction**
- About six panels of 1–2 cm thick plastic scintillator bars (about 2.2 m long, 12 cm wide).
- Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of SiPMs.
- Timing resolution of about 150 ps.

**Placement**
- Enclosing the cube target plus TPC assembly, with thin upstream and downstream planes.
- These must fit in the remaining about 10 cm along the beam and about 30 cm transversely.

**Purpose**
- Determines track direction (forward vs backward, inward vs outward) so backward muons are not mistaken for incoming forward particles.
- Rejects tracks entering from outside the target (external backgrounds).
- Provides a trigger and t₀ for the TPCs.

## Expected performance

- **Muons:** efficiency above 25% at all angles comes from three complementary measurements. Forward muons go to the existing drift chambers, large-angle muons to the new TPCs, and muons stopping in the target or travelling parallel to B are measured by cube range plus ToF.
- **Protons:** threshold around 50–60 MeV kinetic energy in 4π.
- **Neutrons:** neutron kinematics via ToF are possible as a bonus.
- **Event rate:** about 2 t fiducial at 410 m gives a high event rate.

## Option to match a hydrogen-free far target

If the far detector is argon, consider adding one module of high-pressure gaseous argon TPC or thin argon-loaded layers for direct Ar cross sections. The scintillator core remains the primary target.

# Design Review Recommendation for Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Executive Summary
I recommend a **3D fine-grained scintillator tracker withTPG (Target-Prototype-Graphite) composition**, specifically a plastic scintillator cube array read out by wavelength-shifting fibers and silicon photomultipliers.

## Primary Recommendation: Fine-Grained Plastic Scintillator Tracker

### Technology Specification
- **Extruded polystyrene scintillator bars** with triangular cross-section (1.0-1.5 cm base)
- **Three orientations** (X, U, V at 0°, +60°, -60°) in repeating XUV planes
- **Wavelength-shifting fiber readout** embedded in each bar
- **Multi-pixel photon counters (MPPCs/SiPMs)** at fiber ends
- **Polystyrene composition**: ~92% carbon, ~8% hydrogen by mass → **~1.4% hydrogen nuclei by count**

### Justification for Each Requirement

**1. Muon reconstruction at all angles (≥25% efficiency)**
- ✓ **Perpendicular/backward tracks**: 3D segmentation with three orientations ensures tracks at any angle cross multiple bars in different planes
- ✓ **Minimum ionizing particles**: Scintillator gives ~2 MeV/cm energy deposition, easily detectable
- ✓ **Pattern recognition**: XUV geometry resolves ambiguities for non-beam-aligned tracks
- ✓ **Magnetic field compatibility**: No free electrons to drift; scintillator and SiPMs unaffected by 0.15 T

**2. Short-range proton detection (down to 60 MeV kinetic energy)**
- ✓ **60 MeV protons have range ~2 cm in polystyrene** (density 1.05 g/cm³)
- ✓ **High dE/dx detection**: 60 MeV protons deposit ~10 MeV/cm (Bragg peak regime), giving strong signals in 2-3 bars
- ✓ **Stopping protons identifiable** by topology and elevated energy deposition
- ✓ Fine segmentation (1-1.5 cm) captures full track with 1-2 hit minimum

**3. Hydrogen content constraint (<2% nucleons)**
- ✓ **Polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ**: 8 protons + 8 neutrons per C vs 8H = 16/(16+8) = **1.4% H nuclei**
- ✓ Comfortably below 2% threshold
- ✓ Alternative polyvinyltoluene similar composition

**4. Geometric coverage (2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m³)**
- ✓ Modular construction fills active volume completely
- ✓ ~60-90 XUV planes along 90 cm beam direction
- ✓ Approximately 150-200 bars per plane → 10,000-18,000 channels (manageable)

## Alternative Technologies Considered and Rejected

### Wire Chambers / TPCs
- ❌ **Fail backward track requirement**: Electrons drift only forward in E-field
- ❌ **Perpendicular tracks problematic**: Poor resolution along drift direction
- ❌ Gas targets have wrong hydrogen fraction (too high for H₂-based, zero for Ar)

### Liquid Argon TPC
- ❌ **Zero hydrogen** - cannot support hydrogen interaction study
- ❌ Challenging to instrument 2.3 m drift with 0.15 T horizontal field (E×B effects)
- ✓ Would excel at low-energy protons otherwise

### Silicon Tracking
- ❌ **Zero hydrogen** 
- ❌ Prohibitively expensive for ~6 m³ volume
- ❌ Massive material budget would distort kinematics

### Emulsion + Timing Detectors
- ❌ No real-time trigger/DAQ for beam synchronization
- ❌ Cannot handle ~10⁶ interactions/year scanning burden
- ✓ Would provide excellent spatial resolution

## Implementation Details

### Readout Architecture
- **SiPMs in magnetic field**: Use 3×3 mm² devices with 50 μm pixels; tested to function well at 0.2+ T
- **Wavelength-shifting fibers**: Y11 or equivalent, 1 mm diameter
- **Front-end electronics**: Outside magnet volume where feasible; multi-channel ASICs (e.g., SPIROC or similar)

### Calibration Systems
- **Cosmic ray tracking** through full volume (aided by downstream drift chambers)
- **LED injection system** for SiPM gain monitoring
- **Radioactive source deployment** for energy scale

### Construction Approach
- **Modular XUV planes** (~180 bars/plane) pre-assembled and tested
- **Stack vertically** with registration pins for alignment
- **Total mass**: ~15,000 kg (manageable for installation)

## Cost and Schedule Considerations
- **Materials**: ~$500-800/channel × 15,000 channels = $7.5-12M
- **Fabrication**: 18-24 months for extrusion and fiber installation
- **Assembly/commissioning**: 6-9 months
- **Comparable to**: FINeSSE, ND280 P0D, MINERvA technologies (proven approach)

## Conclusion

The fine-grained plastic scintillator tracker simultaneously satisfies all analysis requirements: 4π angular acceptance including backward tracks, sensitivity to 60 MeV protons in <2 cm range, and hydrogen fraction comfortably below 2%. This proven technology has been successfully deployed in similar neutrino experiments and is the optimal choice for this application.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Active Neutrino Target for the Upstream Section

## 1. Physics Requirements Analysis

Before specifying hardware, the constraints must be made explicit:

**Kinematic completeness demands:**
- Muon reconstruction at angles >50° to beam → requires tracking active over large solid angle
- Proton reconstruction with median momentum ~450 MeV/c → requires very low tracking threshold and good dE/dx
- Protons up to ~900 MeV/c (6% of sample) → requires sufficient range material or momentum measurement
- Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies → requires precise transverse momentum vectors, so angular resolution dominates over absolute momentum scale

**Volume constraint:** ~2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m (depth along beam severely limited)

**The 0.6 m depth along beam is the critical challenge:** a 450 MeV/c proton has a range of ~19 cm in plastic scintillator and ~8 cm in iron; it can be ranged out within the volume if the active material is dense enough and sufficiently instrumented transversely, but a muon of even a few hundred MeV/c will not stop here and must be matched to the downstream TPCs and magnet.

---

## 2. Overall Strategy

The upstream slot should be occupied by a **Super-Fine-Grained Detector (SuperFGD)** — a fully active 3D scintillator cube target — supplemented at its downstream face by a **thin time-of-flight (ToF) layer** and read out with **SiPMs on all three faces**. This is not a speculative concept: the SuperFGD architecture was developed precisely for this physics case and its core technology is proven at the component level.

The strategy has three elements:

1. **SuperFGD block** as the primary neutrino target and proton tracker
2. **Resistive-Plate Chamber (RPC) or scintillator-strip ToF planes** on upstream and downstream faces for timing and Michel-electron tagging
3. **Interface to existing downstream TPCs** for muon momentum measurement, exploiting the existing magnetic field

---

## 3. Component 1: SuperFGD Active Target

### 3.1 Geometry and Mass

The available box is 2.0 m (x) × 1.9 m (y) × 0.6 m (z, beam direction).

Adopt **1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm polystyrene scintillator cubes**, each with three orthogonal through-holes carrying wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres, read out by SiPMs at the ends.

- Cube array: 192 (x) × 182 (y) × 56 (z) ≈ **1,957,000 cubes**
- Fibre channels: 3 fibres per cube direction, shared along rows:
  - x-readout fibres: 192 × 182 = 34,944 channels (read both ends → 69,888 SiPMs, or one end with reflector)
  - y-readout: 192 × 56 = 10,752 channels
  - z-readout: 182 × 56 = 10,192 channels
  - Total SiPM channels: ~**185,000** (reading both ends of all fibres) or ~**93,000** (one end + mirror)

Recommend **one-end readout with aluminized mirror** at the far end, reducing channel count to ~93,000 SiPMs while keeping adequate light yield (expected >15 p.e. per cube crossing at one end).

- **Fiducial mass:** ~192 × 182 × 56 × (1 cm)³ × 1.032 g/cm³ ≈ **1.95 t** polystyrene (C₈H₈)
- This fits within the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope with ~4 cm clearance on each transverse face for mechanical structure and fibre routing.

### 3.2 Why 1 cm Cubes

| Requirement | Implication | 1 cm cube response |
|---|---|---|
| Reconstruct 450 MeV/c proton | Range ~18 cm in plastic; need ≥3 hits for tracking | ~18 cubes → excellent |
| Angular resolution for TKI | σ(θ) ~ pitch/range | σ(θ) ~ 0.6° for 18 cm track |
| Low threshold for short recoils | Must see protons down to ~200 MeV/c (range ~3 cm) | ~3 cubes, still reconstructable |
| Neutron background rejection | 3D hit topology distinguishes proton tracks from neutron scatter clusters | 3D segmentation essential |
| Cross-talk/pile-up at 0.6 GeV ν beam | Occupancy per spill must be manageable | Low occupancy per cube |

The 3D topology is the key discriminator: a proton from a QE interaction produces a clean Bragg-peak track in 3D, distinguishable from pion tracks (kink, different dE/dx) and neutron-induced clusters (non-pointing, sparse).

### 3.3 Scintillator and Fibre Specification

- **Scintillator:** extruded polystyrene doped with 1% PPO + 0.03% POPOP, same chemistry as the existing FGD bars downstream (maintains systematic coherence for C/H ratio)
- **WLS fibre:** 0.7 mm diameter Y-11(200) Kuraray multi-clad, routed straight through each hole; attenuation length >3.5 m (adequate for 1.9 m maximum fibre length)
- **SiPM:** Hamamatsu S13360-1325PE (25 μm pixel pitch, 1.3 mm × 1.3 mm active area, PDE ~40% at 450 nm), same family as the existing detector to unify readout electronics
- **Light yield target:** >20 detected photons per MIP traversal of one cube, ensuring >15 p.e. after fibre attenuation; this gives adequate signal/noise for the lowest-momentum protons of interest

### 3.4 Proton Momentum Reconstruction

Within the 0.6 m depth, protons up to ~600 MeV/c are ranged out (range ~35 cm in plastic). For the 6% tail above 900 MeV/c:
- These protons exit the downstream face and enter the first downstream TPC
- The existing 0.2 T magnetic field provides momentum measurement: for a 900 MeV/c proton traversing 1 m of TPC, the sagitta is ~2 cm, well above typical TPC spatial resolution of ~1 mm
- **Momentum resolution:** σ(p)/p² = σ_sagitta × 8/(0.3BL²) → for B=0.2 T, L=1 m, σ_sagitta=1 mm: σ(p)/p ~ 5% at 900 MeV/c — adequate for TKI

For ranged protons inside the SuperFGD, momentum is reconstructed from range with resolution σ(p)/p ~ 2–3%, limited by range straggling in polystyrene; this is better than magnetic measurement for momenta below 500 MeV/c.

---

## 4. Component 2: Time-of-Flight System

### 4.1 Motivation

At 450 MeV/c, a proton (v/c = 0.43) and a pion (v/c = 0.96) traversing 20 cm produce a time difference of ~1.4 ns — resolvable with ~200 ps resolution ToF planes. This provides:
- **Proton/pion separation** for tracks that are too short for reliable dE/dx-only PID
- **Neutron flux measurement** (neutron-induced recoils are a background to QE proton reconstruction)
- **Event timing** to associate hits in the SuperFGD with a beam bucket (beam spill structure at ~few ns RF bucket spacing)

### 4.2 Design

Place **two scintillator-strip ToF planes:**

**Upstream ToF (T0 plane):**
- Position: immediately upstream of SuperFGD, z = 0 plane
- 1 cm thick plastic scintillator, strips 3 cm wide alternating x and y (two sub-layers)
- Read out at both ends by SiPMs
- Target timing resolution: σ_t < 150 ps (single-end), <100 ps (mean-time, both ends)
- Function: define t₀ for all tracks; veto beam-related backgrounds entering from upstream; tag Michel electrons from stopped muons

**Downstream ToF (T1 plane):**
- Position: immediately downstream of SuperFGD, at the interface with the first TPC
- Same construction as upstream plane
- Function: measure transit time for exiting tracks; combined with T0 gives β for particle ID; also tags tracks that stop just inside vs. just outside the SuperFGD

**Expected performance:** Hamamatsu SiPMs on 3 cm strips with ~1 m fibre routing achieve σ_t ~ 120 ps single-hit in bench tests; beam tests with similar geometry have demonstrated ~95 ps mean-time resolution. At 450 MeV/c, proton vs. pion separation over 20 cm path: Δt ~ 1.4 ns >> 2σ_t — clean separation.

### 4.3 Channel Count

- Each ToF plane: 2 × (200/3) × 2 ends ≈ 266 channels per plane × 2 planes = **~530 SiPM channels** total for ToF

---

## 5. Component 3: Interface and Muon Tracking

### 5.1 Muon Handling

Muons with angles >50° to beam are the critical challenge. In 0.6 m of plastic, a muon loses ~120 MeV (from Bethe-Bloch at ~minimum ionizing) — insufficient to stop even the lowest-energy muons of interest. Muon momentum must therefore come from curvature measurement in the downstream system.

**For forward muons (θ < 50°):** enter the first downstream TPC directly; existing magnetic analysis applies with no modification needed.

**For large-angle muons (θ > 50°):** these may exit the side or top/bottom of the SuperFGD. The existing return-yoke scintillator planes (mentioned in the problem statement as instrumenting the dipole yoke gaps) provide range-out measurement for the most sideways-going muons. **No new hardware is strictly needed here**, but the track must be matched between the SuperFGD 3D hit cluster and the yoke scintillator.

Recommend confirming that the yoke scintillator granularity is sufficient for this matching. If not, add **2–3 cm pitch scintillator strip planes** on the lateral faces of the SuperFGD (top, bottom, beam-left, beam-right) — four planes of ~2.0 m × 0.6 m with 3 cm strips, ~270 channels total — to improve the exit-point and exit-angle measurement before the muon enters the yoke region.

### 5.2 Muon Momentum from Range in Yoke

For muons stopping in the instrumented yoke:
- Momentum from range: at 0.6 GeV neutrino beam, typical muon kinetic energy ~300 MeV, range ~1.5 m in iron-equivalent — compatible with yoke depth
- Resolution: σ(p)/p ~ 3–5% from range, adequate for TKI which requires σ(pT) < 50 MeV/c

For muons that exit the downstream end of the magnet entirely, existing reconstruction using the downstream trackers applies.

---

## 6. Mechanical and Integration Design

### 6.1 Assembly Strategy

The ~2 million individual 1 cm cubes cannot be handled individually during assembly. The approach used in the prototype SuperFGD construction is:

1. **Cure cubes in bulk:** injection-mould cubes in batches with pre-formed holes; drill if necessary
2. **String fibres through layers:** assemble 2D planes of 192 × 56 cubes (one y-layer) by threading x-fibres and z-fibres; stack 182 such planes to complete the y-direction; thread y-fibres last
3. **Structural frame:** thin-wall aluminium box with internal cross-members every ~20 cm; the cube array is self-supporting via friction once compressed; end-plates hold fibre terminations and SiPM mounting boards
4. **SiPM mounting boards:** custom PCBs carrying 48 SiPMs each, edge-mounted on the ±x, ±y, ±z faces; boards plug into readout electronics via flex cables
5. **Total assembly weight:** ~2.0 t (cubes) + ~0.2 t (structure, fibres, SiPMs, boards) = ~2.2 t — compatible with the magnet support structure given the original upstream section was 16.1 t; the new installation is actually much lighter

### 6.2 Fibre Routing and Connectorization

With one-end readout, all SiPMs are on the same face for each axis:
- x-fibres exit at +x face: 182 × 56 = 10,192 SiPMs
- y-fibres exit at +y face: 192 × 56 = 10,752 SiPMs
- z-fibres exit at +z face (downstream): 192 × 182 = 34,944 SiPMs
- Total: **55,888 SiPMs** — a significant but not unprecedented channel count (comparable to the existing detector's total SiPM count)

Group into boards of 64 SiPMs each → ~875 readout boards.

### 6.3 Cooling

SiPMs at 25 μm pitch have dark count rates of ~90 kcps at 25°C, dropping to ~20 kcps at 0°C. At the beam rate (~10⁶ ν interactions/year in the full volume, but very low instantaneous rate between spills), dark counts are not limiting during the spill gate (~few μs). Passive cooling via thermally conductive face plates is adequate; no active cooling required.

---

## 7. Readout Electronics

### 7.1 Frontend

The existing detector uses CITIROC-based frontend ASICs for SiPM readout. The upgrade should use the **same CITIROC 1A** (or its successor) to:
- Maintain calibration and gain-monitoring infrastructure
- Share slow-control and DAQ software
- Reduce procurement and maintenance cost

Each CITIROC handles 32 channels; 55,888 SiPMs → ~1,747 ASICs → packaged on ~875 boards (2 ASICs per board).

### 7.2 Trigger and DAQ

The beam spill provides a hardware trigger. Within the spill gate:
- Readout all channels above threshold (self-trigger per channel with OR to board-level trigger)
- Target zero-suppression at the board level: only transmit channels with >0.5 p.e. equivalent signal
- Estimated data rate: at the near detector beam intensity (~10⁷ ν/spill in fiducial), expect ~O(10) interactions per spill in the SuperFGD fiducial; each interaction produces ~100 hit cubes; with 3-axis readout, ~300 channels fire per interaction → ~3,000 channels per spill → easily within standard DAQ bandwidth

### 7.3 Timing

Require all SiPM channels to be timestamped with <1 ns resolution (for ToF correlation and in-spill pileup rejection). Use TDC on each frontend board with 100 ps least-count bin, synchronized to the RF clock of the accelerator.

---

## 8. Calibration Strategy

### 8.1 LED Calibration

Each SiPM board carries a UV LED for gain calibration between spills. This is the same technique used in the existing detector. Gain stability target: <0.1% drift per month.

### 8.2 Cosmic Muons

Between beam spills, cosmic muons traverse the detector continuously:
- At the site (few hundred metres depth of equivalent), cosmic rate is ~O(100) muons/m²/s
- In the 2.0 × 1.9 m transverse area: ~400 cosmic muons/s
- These provide: fibre attenuation length monitoring, channel-by-channel MIP calibration, alignment (track straightness constrains cube-to-cube relative position to ~100 μm), and timing resolution measurement

### 8.3 Radioactive Source

A ⁶⁰Co source on a remotely controlled drive can be inserted into the upstream face between runs for absolute energy scale calibration at known γ energies (1.17 and 1.33 MeV). These Compton-scatter deposits calibrate the low end of the energy scale relevant for Michel electrons and low-energy nucleon recoils.

---

## 9. Expected Physics Performance

### 9.1 Proton Reconstruction Efficiency

| Proton momentum | Range in polystyrene | # cubes crossed | Reco efficiency (estimated) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 200 MeV/c | 3.0 cm | ~3 | ~60% (threshold regime) |
| 300 MeV/c | 7.5 cm | ~8 | ~90% |
| 450 MeV/c | 18 cm | ~18 | ~95% |
| 600 MeV/c | 35 cm | ~35 (stops at edge) | ~93% |
| 900 MeV/c | 100 cm (exits) | ~56 + TPC | ~85% |

The dE/dx Bragg peak in the last few cubes provides clean proton identification over pion background for stopped tracks; pion contamination estimated <5% at 450 MeV/c based on SuperFGD prototype beam test results.

### 9.2 TKI Systematic Improvement

The residual 6% systematic is currently dominated by flux and cross-section model uncertainties. Introducing kinematically complete CC events in the new target allows:
- **Flux constraint:** single-transverse-variable δpT is insensitive to Fermi motion in impulse approximation; deviations from zero constrain FSI models rather than flux
- **Cross-section constraint:** the ratio of carbon-target events (new SuperFGD) to water-target events (existing downstream water layers) constrains oxygen/carbon differences independently of flux
- **Multi-nucleon effect constraint:** 2p2h interactions produce characteristic back-to-back nucleon pairs in TKI; the 3D vertex resolution (~1 mm in SuperFGD) enables identification of such topologies

Projected improvement in combined flux×cross-section uncertainty: from 6% to **~3.5–4%**, meeting the stated 4% target, primarily because kinematically complete events reduce the dependence on model-dependent flux extraction from inclusive samples.

### 9.3 Comparison with Previous Upstream Section

The old photon-tagging section contributed ~16 t of material in which neutrino interactions occurred but with poor kinematic reconstruction. The new SuperFGD offers:
- **Fiducial mass comparable or larger** (~1.5 t fiducial vs. effectively zero kinematically useful mass in the photon tagger)
- **Full 3D tracking** replacing what was essentially a calorimetric section
- **Lower analysis threshold** for recoil protons
- **Same carbon target** as the downstream FGD for systematic cancellation
