- Place scintillator slabs with WLS fibre and SiPM readout in the gaps of the magnet yoke, in the style of the T2K ND280 side muon range detector.

**Physics motivation**
- Identifies muons at large angles to the beam and separates them from pions.
- Provides range-based momentum for tracks that leave through the yoke.
- Serves as a cosmic and entering-background veto.

## 5. Momentum from multiple Coulomb scattering, and contained-track range

**Technology**
- Calibration and readout choices that support these measurements: a laser system and a field-map system.

**Physics motivation**
- Muons at the flux peak (about 0.3–0.6 GeV/c) are often contained or nearly contained in about 1 m of argon. Range gives about 3% momentum resolution.
- Multiple-scattering momentum covers partially contained tracks. This gives a second, independent momentum estimate in the angular regions with weakest magnetic lever arm.
- The laser maps the drift field to control space-charge distortions. This matters for accurate proton range and dE/dx near threshold.

## 6. Retain and upgrade the downstream drift chambers

- Keep the existing chambers for forward muons, where the long lever arm through the 6.5 m magnet gives the best momentum and charge resolution.
- Upgrade the electronics for timing that matches the LAr t₀ system.

## Summary of how the requirements are met

| Requirement | Solution |
|---|---|
| H nuclei ≤2% of target nucleons | Argon target; hydrogenous detectors kept outside the fiducial volume |
| Protons down to 60 MeV at all angles | 3D pixel LArTPC with ~4 mm voxels; Bragg-peak particle ID |
| Muons ≥25% efficient at all angles, including 90° and backward | Isotropic 3D imaging; side and upstream trackers with ToF; instrumented yoke; range and multiple scattering |
| Charge and momentum | Existing downstream chambers (forward); side and upstream trackers in the 0.15 T field |

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (SuperFGD-style)**

**Technology:** Extruded plastic scintillator cubes (~1 cm³) with three orthogonal WLS fiber readouts and MPPC/SiPM photosensors.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **4π angular acceptance:** Fiber readout along all three axes enables reconstruction of tracks at ANY angle, including backward-going and perpendicular to the beam—critical for your 25% efficiency requirement at all angles
- **Low-momentum proton detection:** 1 cm granularity with ~60 keV/cm energy deposition allows tracking protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~3-4 cm in plastic)
- **Hydrogen content control:** Plastic scintillator (CH₂)ₙ provides ~14.3% hydrogen by mass—calculable and well-modeled, meeting the <2% nucleon fraction constraint through event weighting
- **Timing resolution:** ~1 ns timing separates neutrino interactions from beam-correlated backgrounds

## 2. **Time Projection Chamber (TPC) with Micromegas or GEM Readout**

**Technology:** Argon or P10 gas TPC with 2D Micromegas or triple-GEM anode planes, possibly hybrid with scintillator planes.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **True 3D tracking with dE/dx:** Continuous tracking without segmentation gaps enables particle ID via energy loss (separates μ/π/p)
- **Low material budget:** Gas target minimizes multiple scattering, improving momentum resolution for tracks bending in the 0.15 T field
- **Excellent angular coverage:** Drift perpendicular to beam captures tracks at all angles; multiple readout planes on multiple faces handle various topologies
- **Low proton threshold:** dE/dx measurements down to stopping range ~5-10 cm (depending on gas) reaches 60 MeV protons
- **Hydrogen fraction:** Pure Ar has no hydrogen; P10 (90% Ar/10% CH₄) gives ~1.7% H by mass—manageable

## 3. **Solid Target Hybrid: Polypropylene/CH₂ Planes + Silicon Tracking**

**Technology:** Thin (~1 cm) plastic target planes interspersed with silicon strip or pixel detector planes (~300 μm pitch).

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Vertex resolution:** Silicon provides <100 μm vertex position, enabling separation of primary vertex from secondary interactions/decays
- **Precise angle reconstruction:** High-resolution hit positions near vertex critical for measuring all track angles with minimal systematic bias
- **Charge identification:** Silicon dE/dx + downstream drift chamber curvature separates μ⁺/μ⁻ and identifies recoil particles
- **Short proton tracks:** 60 MeV protons have ~1 mm range in silicon, ~10 mm in plastic—need planes every ~5 mm to catch ≥2 hits
- **Controlled hydrogen:** Pure CH₂ targets give known hydrogen content; can alternate with CH₂ and carbon-only targets for direct H subtraction

## 4. **Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) with Timing**

**Technology:** Thin glass/bakelite RPCs with ~1 cm strip readout and <1 ns timing resolution.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Muon identification:** Time-of-flight over 6.5 m distinguishes μ from π (critical at low momentum where dE/dx overlaps)
- **Direction determination:** ns-level timing establishes track direction for particles stopping in detector (resolves forward/backward ambiguity)
- **Trigger and event matching:** Precise timing tags neutrino interactions within ~10 ns beam spill window
- **Low cost/mass:** Covers large 2.6 m × 2.3 m area without excessive material budget or cost

## 5. **High-Angle Muon Ranger (HAMR)**

**Technology:** Dense scintillator or iron-scintillator sandwich on upstream face and sides of active target volume.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Backward/side-going muon containment:** Muons exiting perpendicular or backward miss the downstream drift chambers; HAMR catches and ranges them
- **Momentum from range:** For contained muons, range gives momentum to ~3% without magnetic field complications
- **Charge confusion mitigation:** Ensures tracks identified as "muons" actually exit the target region rather than being misidentified stopping pions

---

## Recommended Configuration

**Baseline recommendation:** **3D scintillator tracker (Option 1)** as primary upgrade.

- Proven technology (T2K ND280 SuperFGD demonstration)
- Meets ALL requirements: 4π acceptance, low proton threshold, controlled hydrogen
- Relatively straightforward construction/calibration
- ~50,000 channels feasible for the specified volume

**Enhanced option:** Hybrid **Option 1 + Option 4**, adding RPC timing layers at upstream/downstream faces for improved particle ID and triggering.

# Proposed upgrade for the ND280 upstream (P0D) region

The current ND280 cannot supply full-kinematics events because of its geometry, not its electronics. FGD1 bars are all perpendicular to the beam, and the TPCs sit downstream of it. So any track leaving at more than about 50° (about 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons) travels along a bar plane and misses the TPCs. In addition, protons below roughly 450 MeV/c (about half the sample) stop within a few bars and are poorly reconstructed or not seen at all.

The replacement therefore needs:
- isotropic 3D granularity in the target,
- tracking and charge/momentum measurement at high angle,
- timing, to tell forward-going from backward-going tracks and to reject outside-in background.

I propose three hardware systems in the freed P0D volume.

## 1. Highly segmented 3D scintillator target ("Super-FGD")

**Granularity**
- Target made of about 2 million optically independent 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes.
- Each cube is doped with about 1.5% PTP and 0.01% POPOP.
- Each cube has a thin reflective surface layer, chemically etched or TiO₂-loaded, about 50–80 µm thick.
- Cubes are made by injection moulding, which keeps the cost manageable for a million-plus pieces.

**Readout**
- Each cube has three orthogonal through-holes of about 1.5 mm diameter.
- 1 mm Kuraray Y-11 wavelength-shifting fibres run along x, y and z.
- Each fibre is read at one end by a 1.3 × 1.3 mm² MPPC, such as the Hamamatsu S13360 class with 50 µm pixels. The other fibre end is mirrored.
- This gives three 2D projections, from which 3D hits are reconstructed. The resolution is the same in every direction, so there is no blind angle.

**Dimensions**
- About 192 × 182 × 56 cubes, i.e. roughly 1.9 × 1.8 × 0.56 m³.
- Target mass about 2 t of CH, roughly twice FGD1.

**Channel count and electronics**
- Roughly 56,000 channels, handled by a feature-extraction front-end (for example CITIROC-based boards) inside the magnet.
- Expected performance:
  - about 40–60 photoelectrons per channel for a minimum-ionising particle, after fibre attenuation;
  - sub-ns time per channel, about 0.9 ns per channel and better per track;
  - dE/dx per cube for proton/pion/muon identification.

**Physics gains**
- The proton tracking threshold drops to about 300 MeV/c, since two or three cubes are enough. Combined with calorimetric energy deposit, this captures most of the 450 MeV/c-median proton spectrum.
- Fine timing combined with isolated-cube clusters allows neutron detection and kinetic energy measurement by time-of-flight. This adds neutron kinematics to transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies, for example in antineutrino CC0π events.

**Mechanics**
- Cubes are threaded onto fishing lines or fibres during assembly.
- They sit in a light carbon-fibre/aluminium box whose walls carry the MPPC/PCB array.

## 2. Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs), above and below the target

**Purpose**
- Measure momentum and charge from curvature in the 0.2 T field.
- Provide dE/dx particle identification for high-angle muons and for protons above about 900 MeV/c (the roughly 6% that escape the target).

**Size**
- Each about 2.0 m (along the beam) × 0.8 m × 1.8 m.
- They sandwich the target in the vertical direction, using the full 1.9 m height of the box. The remaining depth goes to the target and wall planes.

**Field cage**
- Thin composite laminate (aramid honeycomb plus Kapton strip electrodes) to minimise dead material.
- Central cathode at about 30 kV.
- Same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ (95:3:2) gas as the existing TPCs, so the gas system is shared.

**Readout**
- Encapsulated resistive Micromegas, also called ERAM: a resistive DLC-on-Kapton layer over the pads.
- The resistive layer spreads charge across neighbouring pads. This allows larger pads, about 10 × 11 mm², with better than about 800 µm spatial resolution, and suppresses sparking.
- About 16 modules per TPC.
- AFTER/AGET-based front-end electronics.

**Target performance**
- Momentum resolution better than 10% at 1 GeV/c.
- dE/dx resolution better than 10%.

## 3. Time-of-Flight (ToF) envelope

**Layout**
- Six planes boxing the target and HA-TPC assembly.
- Each plane uses about 2.2 m long, 12 × 1 cm cast plastic scintillator bars (EJ-200 class).
- Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs, about 6 × 6 mm².

**Performance**
- About 150 ps time resolution.

**Uses**
- Distinguish tracks going into the target from tracks going out. This suppresses the backward and outside-in background from interactions in the magnet and P0D-ECal.
- Determine track direction for low-momentum backward muons.
- Particle ID by time-of-flight.
- Provide a timing trigger.

## Integration notes

- **Retained systems.** The P0D-ECal and barrel ECals stay as they are. FGD2 with its water layers remains for C/H₂O ratios, and FGD1 for continuity.
- **Overlap with the existing detector.** The new target acceptance overlaps with TPC1, so forward tracks are still measured there.
- **Combined acceptance.** Target, HA-TPCs and ToF together give close to 4π acceptance for muons and protons.
- **Scope.** All new photosensors are MPPC/SiPM types, consistent with the existing DAQ and calibration philosophy.
- **Expected outcome.** These changes should bring the flux × cross-section systematic uncertainty at Super-Kamiokande from about 6% toward the roughly 4% T2K-II needs.

This design matches the configuration T2K adopted for the ND280 Upgrade (Super-FGD, HA-TPCs, ToF), installed in 2023–24.

# Next-Phase Hardware Upgrades for the Off-Axis Near Detector

## Why the current detector falls short

The detector was designed for forward-going tracks: bars perpendicular to the beam, with TPCs downstream of the targets. This causes two problems:

- **Lost high-angle tracks.** About 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons leave at more than 50°. They run parallel to the bar planes and miss the TPCs, so their momentum and charge are not measured.
- **High proton threshold.** In the bar-plane targets, a proton is tracked only once it crosses several x/y layers, roughly 450–500 MeV/c. That is close to the 450 MeV/c median, so about half of the leading protons are lost.

Neutrons are not measured at all, and the photon-tagging section adds little that a fine-grained target cannot do better. The changes below keep the downstream TPCs, the two plastic targets, the calorimeters and the magnet. They replace the photon-tagging volume with a new target, two new TPCs and a timing system.

## 1. Fine-grained 3D scintillator-cube target

**Technology**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, roughly 192 × 184 × 56 cubes. This fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box, with the 0.6 m dimension vertical.
- The target mass is about 2 t of CH.
- Each cube has three orthogonal holes. Wavelength-shifting fibres pass through them along x, y and z, giving three 2D projections that combine into true 3D hits.
- Each fibre is read out by an SiPM with the same style of electronics as the existing channels. That is about 56,000 channels.
- Expected performance: around 40–50 photoelectrons per fibre for a minimum-ionising particle, and about 1 ns timing per hit.

**Physics motivation**
- **Full angular acceptance.** The cubes have no preferred direction, so tracks at 90° or travelling backwards are reconstructed as well as forward ones.
- **Lower proton threshold.** A proton only needs to cross a few cubes, about 3 cm. This lowers the tracking threshold to about 300 MeV/c, capturing most of the distribution below the 450 MeV/c median. That is essential for the transverse-kinematic-imbalance variables (δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T).
- **Stopping protons.** Protons up to roughly 800–900 MeV/c stop within the target's 1.9 m length. Range and Bragg-peak dE/dx then give their momentum and particle identification. The about 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c exit into the new TPCs or the ToF.
- **Neutron detection.** Isolated cube hits that are delayed relative to the vertex give neutron kinetic energy by time of flight. This allows a full imbalance analysis for antineutrino CC events (μ⁺ n).
- **Photon and electron handling.** The fine granularity separates γ → e⁺e⁻ conversions from single electrons and resolves π⁰ photons, taking over the role of the photon-tagging section.
- **Nuclear-model and energy constraints.** Low-energy hadron detection helps distinguish CCQE, 2p2h and pion-production channels. This constrains the nuclear model and the energy scale, which are the leading parts of the 6% systematic.

## 2. Two high-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Two argon-based gas TPCs, each about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m, with the drift field transverse to the beam.
- Readout by resistive (encapsulated-resistive-anode) Micromegas. The charge spreading in the resistive layer gives better position resolution with fewer pads and suppresses sparking.
- A thin, low-mass composite field cage (laminated aramid or epoxy), to minimise multiple scattering and dead material before the target.
- Front-end electronics derived from the existing TPCs.

**Physics motivation**
- They close the angular gap: tracks leaving the cube target at large angle now enter a magnetised gas volume.
- In the 0.2 T field this gives momentum to about 10% and charge sign for high-angle muons, separating μ⁻ from μ⁺ and from wrong-sign backgrounds.
- dE/dx resolution below about 10% gives μ/π/p/e separation. Energetic protons above 900 MeV/c are identified and their momenta measured.
- Together with the downstream TPCs, this gives near-4π coverage, so the near-detector muon phase space matches the far detector's roughly 4π acceptance. Removing the angular extrapolation in the flux × cross-section fit reduces the systematic.

## 3. Time-of-flight envelope

**Technology**
- Six panels of 1 cm thick plastic scintillator bars, about 12 cm wide and about 2.2 m long, enclosing the new target–TPC module.
- Each bar is read out at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs, with waveform digitisation.
- Target time resolution about 150 ps, from the mean time and difference of the two ends.

**Physics motivation**
- **Track direction.** Timing tells whether a track enters or leaves the module. This rejects backward-going entering backgrounds and out-of-fiducial-volume events, such as interactions in the magnet, which matter more now that high-angle acceptance has been opened up.
- **Particle identification.** Combined with momentum from the TPCs, ToF separates protons from muons and pions and electrons from muons at low momentum, where dE/dx bands cross.
- **Neutron reference.** It provides a precise time reference for the neutron time-of-flight measurement in the cube target.

## 4. Supporting changes

- **Calorimeter and yoke continuity.** Re-check the coverage of the existing upstream calorimeter and the side-muon range detector in the yoke gaps around the new module, so that side-going muons remain ranged out.
- **Common timing system.** Distribute the beam-spill clock with sub-nanosecond synchronisation to all subsystems (cubes, TPCs, ToF and the legacy detectors). This is needed for neutron ToF and cross-detector matching.
- **Calibration.**
  - Cosmic triggers and a fibre-injected LED system to monitor cube light yield and crosstalk.
  - A test-beam campaign with charged particles and neutrons to measure the cube response to protons and neutrons, so that reconstruction thresholds are not themselves a new systematic.
- **Retained water target.** Keep the downstream target with water layers unchanged. CH-versus-H₂O comparisons transfer the improved hydrocarbon cross-section constraints to the water far detector, and the oxygen nuclear-effect uncertainty is measured rather than modelled.

## Expected outcome

The combination gives:
- a fully active, isotropic CH target with a proton threshold of about 300 MeV/c and neutron tagging;
- magnetised high-angle tracking with dE/dx particle identification;
- timing for direction and particle identification.

These deliver kinematically complete CC events across the full angular range. That is the input needed to tighten the flux and nuclear-model constraints and push the extrapolated systematic from about 6% toward the 4% goal.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## 1. Active Target Medium: Liquid Argon or Plastic Scintillator?

Neither is optimal alone. The constraints drive a specific choice:

**Chosen technology: Low-density plastic scintillator 3D-granular tracker (e.g., extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes or bars)**

**Why:**
- Hydrogen fraction in CH-based plastic scintillator is ~12% by number of nucleons from protons, comfortably near but requiring careful control to stay ≤20% hydrogen nucleon fraction. (Polystyrene C₈H₈ gives H/(C+H) nucleon fraction ≈ 47%/(8×12 + 8) ≈ 8/104 ≈ ~8% by mass but ~47% by nucleon number — **this is a problem**, see constraint below.)

**Revised choice: Liquid argon is excluded** (no hydrogen). **Water or hydrocarbon target needs dilution.**

The hydrogen nucleon fraction constraint is critical and shapes everything:

- Pure polystyrene: H nucleon fraction = 8/(96+8) ≈ **7.7% by mass but ~44% by nucleon count** — far exceeds 20% limit.
- Pure water: H nucleon fraction = 2/18 ≈ **11% by mass, ~67% by nucleon** — also exceeds limit.
- **Carbon (graphite/CH₂ mix) or argon**: no hydrogen problem.
- A **plastic scintillator + lead or iron interspersed** passive absorber mix can dilute hydrogen below 20% nucleon fraction.

**Correct active target technology: Scintillating fiber tracker with interspersed passive iron/lead planes**, or more modernly:

### Recommended: **3D Scintillator Cube ("SuperFGD-style") detector with iron or brass passive layers to control hydrogen fraction**

Specifically modeled on the T2K SuperFGD design — 1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes read out by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers in three orthogonal directions (X, Y, Z), with periodic passive high-Z absorber planes inserted to dilute hydrogen content to ≤20% of target nucleons.

**Justification for each requirement:**
- **4π acceptance including backward and transverse muons**: The fully 3D-symmetric readout of cubes with fibers in all three axes gives genuine 4π track reconstruction — no preferred direction, so 90° and backward tracks are reconstructed as efficiently as forward ones. This directly satisfies the ≥25% efficiency at all angles.
- **Short proton tracks (60 MeV KE)**: At 60 MeV kinetic energy, a proton has range ~3–4 mm in plastic scintillator (density ~1.05 g/cm³). A 1 cm cube granularity means such a proton traverses ~3–4 cubes — detectable as a short stub in 3D. This is the minimum granularity that makes 60 MeV protons visible; coarser granularity would miss them entirely.
- **Hydrogen fraction control**: By inserting brass or iron passive planes (every N cm, tuned), the effective hydrogen nucleon fraction across the full active target volume is reduced to ≤20%. The ratio of passive-to-active material is an engineering parameter set at construction and must be documented in the proposal.

---

## 2. Readout Electronics Upgrade: **SiPM (Silicon Photomultiplier) Arrays**

**Technology: Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) coupled to WLS fibers at cube faces**

**Why:**
- The existing station presumably uses PMTs or older electronics incompatible with the density of channels a 3D cube array requires.
- The active target volume 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m at 1 cm³ cube granularity contains ~O(500,000) cubes × 3 readout axes = **~1.5 million channels**. Only SiPMs are compact and cheap enough to instrument this.
- SiPMs operate in the warm magnet's 0.15 T field without gain degradation (unlike PMTs, which require shielding or fail in magnetic fields). This is a direct, non-negotiable requirement given the magnet geometry.
- SiPMs provide single-photoelectron sensitivity sufficient to detect the few-photon signals from short, low-energy proton tracks in small cubes.

---

## 3. Downstream Tracker Upgrade: **High-Resolution Time Projection Chamber (TPC) or Straw-Tube Tracker**

**Technology: Straw-tube tracker (STT) or small-cell wire TPC immediately downstream of the active target, before the existing drift chambers**

**Why:**
- Muon tracks exiting the active target at large angles (near 90°) may not reach the existing downstream drift chambers, or may enter them at angles where momentum resolution degrades.
- A straw-tube tracker with ~5–10 mm tube diameter surrounding or immediately downstream of the active target captures tracks at all exit angles, connecting short active-target track segments to the full magnetic spectrometer.
- The existing warm dipole (0.15 T over 6.5 m) gives a momentum kick of **p_T = 0.3 × 0.15 × 6.5 ≈ 0.29 GeV/c**, adequate for muon momentum measurement if tracks are well-matched into it. The STT ensures that matching works for large-angle topologies.
- The 410 m baseline and ~0.7 GeV peak flux mean muon momenta are mostly 0.2–1.5 GeV/c — the existing spectrometer handles these, but only if track seeding from the active target is reliable at all angles. The STT provides that seeding.

---

## 4. Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECAL) Surrounding the Active Target

**Technology: Sampling calorimeter — lead/scintillator or lead/scintillating-fiber "spaghetti" calorimeter, surrounding the active target on all sides**

**Why:**
- Photons from π⁰ → γγ (produced in neutrino interactions) must be detected and measured to reconstruct the full hadronic system. Photons do not leave tracks in the active target.
- An ECAL surrounding the active target on the four transverse faces and the upstream face catches photons exiting at all angles, including those from backward-going or large-angle interactions — consistent with the 4π requirement.
- Lead/scintillator construction is mechanically straightforward in the constrained 2.6 m × 2.3 m transverse envelope, and radiation length (~0.56 cm in lead) allows a compact (~10–15 X₀) calorimeter in a few tens of cm thickness.
- Without an ECAL, neutral pion backgrounds cannot be subtracted, and the hydrogen-removal model's systematic uncertainties blow up.

---

## 5. Muon Range Detector / Side Catchers

**Technology: Iron-scintillator range stack on the lateral faces of the magnet volume**

**Why:**
- Muons going perpendicular to the beam (90°) or at backward angles exit the active target laterally. The existing downstream drift chambers, being downstream, do not catch these.
- A range stack of alternating iron planes and scintillator strips on the ±X and ±Y faces (and ideally the upstream −Z face) of the active target region stops and ranges out muons that do not enter the magnetic spectrometer.
- Muon momentum from range is adequate for the near-detector's flux constraint analysis and achieves the ≥25% reconstruction efficiency requirement at 90° and backward angles — without this, those angular bins simply fail the efficiency cut.
- Iron thickness is chosen so that the minimum-ionizing muon range covers the beam-energy-relevant momentum range (up to ~1 GeV/c requires ~50–60 cm of iron, achievable within the magnet bore dimensions).

---

## 6. Beam Timing and Trigger System Upgrade

**Technology: Fast scintillator trigger planes + FPGA-based trigger/DAQ with ~1 ns timing resolution**

**Why:**
- At 410 m from target, the neutrino beam spill structure (typically microseconds long) must be used to suppress out-of-spill backgrounds.
- Short proton tracks (3–4 cubes) are indistinguishable from noise hits without tight timing coincidence across adjacent cubes. Sub-nanosecond timing on SiPM readout (SiPMs naturally support this) with an FPGA-based coincidence trigger ensures that 60 MeV proton signatures are not swamped by dark noise or beam-unrelated activity.
- The trigger must be **deadtime-free** during the spill window to preserve efficiency uniformly across interaction topologies — an FPGA pipeline architecture achieves this where older NIM/CAMAC systems cannot.

---

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Situational Analysis

Before proposing hardware, let me extract the binding constraints:

- **Volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (~5.4 m³), sitting inside an existing warm dipole at 0.15 T
- **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles**, including 90° and backward — this kills any purely-forward tracker
- **Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** (range in water ~3.5 mm; in scintillator ~4-5 mm) — demands very fine granularity
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of target nucleons** — constrains material choice critically
- **410 m baseline, ~0.7 GeV peak flux** — moderate rate, not a pile-up nightmare

---

## Hydrogen Fraction Constraint: Drives Everything

This is the most restrictive materials constraint. Pure CH₂ or water would far exceed 20% hydrogen. Let me calculate for candidate materials:

| Material | H fraction by nucleons |
|---|---|
| Polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ | H/(8C+8H) = 8/16 = **50%** — far too high |
| Liquid argon | **0%** |
| Iron | **0%** |
| Acrylic (C₅H₈O₂)ₙ | 8/15 = **53%** — far too high |
| Pb | **0%** |
| Aluminium | **0%** |

Any plastic or organic scintillator used **as a bulk target** will be over-hydrogen. The constraint forces either:
- A predominantly inorganic target with a small organic component, or
- Careful geometric interleaving where tracking layers are thin relative to passive nuclear target

**The practical solution**: use an inorganic active medium (liquid argon or gas) OR interleave thin organic-scintillator tracking planes with inert absorber, keeping the organic fraction small enough that hydrogen stays ≤20%.

Concrete calculation for a **scintillator-plus-lead** sandwich: if scintillator planes (C₈H₈, density ~1.05 g/cm³) are thickness *t_s* interleaved with lead plates of thickness *t_Pb* (density 11.35 g/cm³):

H nucleon fraction = ρ_s·t_s·(H mass fraction / m_H) / [total nucleon areal density]

For the hydrogen fraction to be ≤20%, requiring roughly **≥4:1 by nucleon count** of non-hydrogen nucleons over hydrogen. With polystyrene (H mass fraction ~7.7%), against lead, you need *t_Pb/t_s* ≥ ~0.7 by nucleon count — easily achieved with modest lead thicknesses. But lead gives terrible proton tracking. **Lead is out** for the proton-sensitive region.

**Better approach**: Replace lead with aluminium or carbon (graphite) to stay in a regime where short proton tracks are still detectable, while diluting hydrogen. Or use a **liquid argon TPC** where there is zero hydrogen.

---

## Proposed Architecture: Three-Region Design

### Region 1 — Neutrino Interaction Vertex Target (upstream ~0.6 m of the 0.9 m depth)

**Technology: High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC (HPgAr TPC)**

- Fill the target volume with argon gas at **10 bar** (pure Ar or Ar+2% CO₂ as quench)
- At 10 bar, density ~16 kg/m³ — provides adequate neutrino interaction rate (~0.5% of a water target per unit length, acceptable at 410 m with modern beam intensities)
- **Zero hydrogen** — eliminates the hydrogen subtraction problem entirely in this fiducial volume
- Drift field along the beam direction (0.9 m drift) so the existing dipole field provides **both** magnetic momentum analysis and TPC drift separation — reuse the 0.15 T field
- **Anode readout planes**: 2D strip readout (induction + collection) using **MicroMEGAS or GEM foils** tiling the downstream face of the drift volume, strip pitch **~1 mm**
- 1 mm pitch × argon gas: minimum ionizing particle deposits ~15 electrons/cm at 10 bar — amplified to ~10⁴ by MICROMEGAS gain — well above noise threshold
- **60 MeV proton range in 10-bar argon**: ~10 cm — easily reconstructed with 1 mm pitch. This is the key advantage over solid targets for this topology
- **4π angular coverage** inherent to a TPC — backward tracks, 90° tracks all reconstructed with equal efficiency
- Muon reconstruction: TPC gives full 3D track, momentum from curvature in the 0.15 T dipole field. For 90° tracks (across the 2.6 m dimension), sagitta at 0.15 T over 2.6 m for a 500 MeV/c muon is ~65 mm — very well measured
- **Electronics**: SRS (Scalable Readout System) with APV25 hybrids or SAMPA chips (as used in ALICE TPC upgrade), shaping time ~100 ns to match argon drift velocity (~5 cm/μs at typical fields → ~18 μs max drift at 0.9 m)
- **Pressure vessel**: The existing magnet bore constrains this — requires a thin-wall aluminium pressure vessel (~5 mm wall for 10 bar over 2.6 m × 2.3 m cross-section, achievable with appropriate ribbing). Wall contributes ~0.5% X₀ — acceptable

**Why not liquid argon?** LAr gives higher density and better S/N but requires cryogenic infrastructure incompatible with a quick re-equip of an existing warm magnet bore, and the short proton tracks are harder to reconstruct in a LAr TPC with wire readout (though LArPix-style pixel readout could work — see below as an alternative).

---

### Region 2 — Downstream Muon Catcher / Range Stack (remaining ~0.3 m + interface to existing drift chambers)

**Technology: Interleaved scintillator-iron range stack with SiPM readout**

- 15 layers of **1 cm plastic scintillator** (Eljen EJ-200 or equivalent) interleaved with **1 cm iron** plates
- Scintillator bars: 2 cm × 1 cm cross section, alternating X/Y layers, read out at both ends with **SiPMs (Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS or similar, 1.3 mm² active area)**
- Iron dilutes the hydrogen content: in this sandwich H fraction by nucleons ≈ (ρ_scint × t_scint × f_H/m_H) / (ρ_Fe × t_Fe/m_Fe + ...) ≈ 2.5% — well within budget
- Purpose: catch muons that stop in this region before the downstream drift chambers; reconstruct momentum by range for stopped muons — complementary to curvature for high-angle tracks
- Also serves as a veto/tagger for backgrounds entering from downstream
- **1 cm scintillator bars**: 60 MeV proton range ~4 cm in scintillator → 4 bars crossed → clean track reconstruction
- SiPMs operated in the 0.15 T field: at this field strength, standard SiPMs work fine (field is too low to significantly affect Geiger avalanches)

---

### Region 3 — Downstream Interface to Existing Gas Drift Chambers

**No major hardware change** to existing drift chambers — they already measure muon momentum and charge. Add:

- **Trigger scintillator hodoscope**: 2 planes of 3 cm × 3 cm scintillator tiles with SiPM readout, one X and one Y plane, immediately upstream of the first existing drift chamber station. Provides fast timing (σ_t ~0.5 ns) for event coincidence and beam-related background rejection
- **Timing resolution** at this level allows ~15 cm vertex resolution along beam using time-of-flight of pions vs. muons if needed

---

## Supplementary Components

### Photon / π⁰ Detection (embedded in TPC walls)

- Line the inner walls of the pressure vessel with **3 mm × 3 mm SiPM tiles** (e.g., KETEK PM3315 or Hamamatsu VUV-sensitive MPPC for liquid argon wavelengths — here use standard bialkali-shifted tiles since gas is at room temperature with wavelength shifter coating: **tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) evaporated on acrylic light guides**)
- Provides photon detection for γ from π⁰ → γγ, crucial for NC background characterisation
- Coverage ~60% of inner wall area → ~40% solid-angle photon detection efficiency

### External Muon Identifier for High-Angle Muons Exiting the Sides

The 2.6 m × 2.3 m transverse dimensions mean a 90° muon exits the side of the TPC after ~1.3 m of argon gas at 10 bar (areal density ~20 g/cm²) — sufficient for 2–3 cm of equivalent solid material, so a ~200 MeV muon stops inside. For higher-energy muons:

- **Scintillator panels on all four sides** of the pressure vessel: 2 cm thick EJ-200 panels with WLS fibre (Kuraray Y-11) readout into SiPMs
- 2 layers per side, separated by 5 cm, for coincidence-based direction confirmation
- These panels also act as cosmic ray veto/tagger — important at 410 m (surface level presumably)

---
