# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Active Neutrino Target Section

## Context and Constraints

The available volume (2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m) is shallow along the beam axis, the magnet provides only 0.2 T, and the physics requirement is kinematically complete CC reconstruction with large-angle muon and proton acceptance up to and beyond 50° and proton momenta peaking near 450 MeV/c. The residual systematic must fall from ~6% to ~4%.

---

## 1. Active Target: Scintillating Fibre Tracker (SciFi) on Hydrocarbon

**Technology:** Dense arrays of 0.25–0.35 mm diameter polystyrene scintillating fibres arranged in X/Y/U/V stereo layers, read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), following the approach demonstrated by the LHCb SciFi tracker and adapted for neutrino use as in the SND@LHC and proposed NINJA upgrades.

**Why:**
- Polystyrene fibres provide a hydrocarbon target (C:H ratio well defined) acceptable for the stated physics programme, with high and uniform density filling the shallow 0.6 m depth efficiently.
- Sub-millimetre spatial resolution per layer allows reconstruction of short proton tracks; a 450 MeV/c proton has a range of roughly 9 cm in polystyrene, giving ~25 measurable hits even in a compact volume.
- Fine granularity gives near-4π angular acceptance within the module itself, addressing the 35% of protons and 25% of muons that exit beyond 50°.
- No drift time means no ambiguity from out-of-time pile-up at the moderate beam intensity of a near detector.
- SiPM readout is compatible with the existing detector's readout architecture, reducing integration risk and cost.

---

## 2. Upstream Veto / Michel-Electron Tagger: Thin Scintillator Plane Array

**Technology:** Two layers of 3 mm thick extruded scintillator bars (the same triangular-profile polystyrene bars already used elsewhere in the detector) with SiPM readout, one layer in X and one in Y, placed immediately upstream of the SciFi volume.

**Why:**
- Provides an event-by-event charged-particle veto to reject interactions originating in the photon-tagging section material that was removed but whose upstream beamline material (horn, helium volume walls, etc.) still produces backgrounds.
- The thin profile (~6 mm total) adds negligible material and fits within the available box.
- The existing bar geometry and readout technology avoids new procurement and calibration procedures.
- Michel electrons from stopped pions and muons in the SciFi target can be tagged with ~ns timing resolution, constraining pion contamination in the CC-inclusive sample.

---

## 3. Time-of-Flight Layer: Fast Plastic Scintillator Paddles with SiPM Readout

**Technology:** A downstream face of large-area (2.0 m × 1.9 m) fast plastic scintillator paddles (~1 cm thick NE-102 / EJ-200 equivalent), read out at both ends by fast SiPMs (rise time < 1 ns), placed at the downstream boundary of the new target volume immediately in front of the first gas TPC.

**Why:**
- The leading proton momentum distribution has a median of ~450 MeV/c and 6% above 900 MeV/c. For protons below ~500 MeV/c that stop inside or just exit the SciFi volume, time-of-flight over even a ~20–30 cm baseline gives velocity resolution sufficient to separate protons from pions (Δβ/β ~ 5% at 450 MeV/c is resolvable with ~300 ps timing), which is critical for the transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) analysis where proton misidentification directly biases δp_T.
- The paddle sits at the natural boundary between the new target and the existing TPC section, adding no dead volume penalty.
- Fast timing also provides a relative T0 for the upstream SciFi, improving track-to-vertex matching when two interactions occur in the same beam spill.

---

## 4. Side-Exiting Track Ranger: Additional Scintillator Planes in Lateral Gaps

**Technology:** Stacks of extruded scintillator bar planes (the same 9.6 × 9.6 mm profile as the existing plastic tracking targets) inserted into the lateral gaps between the new target box and the inner face of the lead-scintillator calorimeter on the left and right sides of the magnet bore (the ±X faces, which have the most available clearance given the 3.5 m horizontal inner dimension).

**Why:**
- 25% of muons exit beyond 50°. At 0.6 GeV, a forward muon of moderate angle can range out in the existing return-yoke scintillator, but a muon exiting at 60–80° from a vertex in the new upstream location has a significantly shorter path through the existing downstream calorimeter. Additional ranging layers on the lateral faces extend momentum measurement by range for muons from ~200 MeV/c (which stop after ~15 cm in scintillator) up to ~600 MeV/c.
- The existing dipole return-yoke gap instrumentation already proves the concept; this extends it to the new interaction region.
- Using the same bar technology and SiPM readout as the rest of the detector keeps the calibration and DAQ overhead minimal.
- Improved muon momentum resolution directly reduces the uncertainty on the muon momentum component of δp_T, which is one of the two leading terms in the TKI systematic budget.

---

## 5. Readout Electronics Upgrade: Higher-Bandwidth SiPM Digitisers with Waveform Sampling

**Technology:** Replace the existing charge-integrating front-end ASICs on all SiPM channels in the new target (and optionally retrofit to the plastic tracking targets) with waveform-sampling ASICs (e.g., SPIROC2E or TARGET family), providing ~100 ps timing bins and pulse-shape digitisation.

**Why:**
- Pulse-shape discrimination in plastic scintillator is weak compared with liquid scintillator, but waveform sampling still provides: (a) improved single-photon timing for the ToF system; (b) better separation of overlapping hits from two nearby tracks (relevant for proton + pion ambiguity in the SciFi); (c) the ability to identify late-light components from proton recoil versus minimum-ionising tracks via the Birks-law-suppressed fast component.
- The existing readout was designed for the ~6% systematic era. Reaching 4% requires tighter control of energy scale and particle identification, which waveform information directly supports.
- The channel count in the new SciFi target is large (~50,000–100,000 channels depending on fibre pitch and layer count in the available volume), so a modern ASIC with high multiplicity and modest power budget is necessary to fit within the magnet volume power envelope.

---

## 6. Calibration System: UV LED Pulsers and Radioactive Source Deployment Tubes

**Technology:** Fibre-coupled UV LED pulsers (one per 64-channel SiPM tile) for gain monitoring, plus two thin-wall aluminium tubes running along the beam direction through the SciFi volume to allow periodic insertion of a 60Co or 137Cs wire source for absolute light-yield calibration.

**Why:**
- SiPM gain drifts with temperature and radiation dose at the ~1%/°C and ~1% per 10^10 n_eq/cm² level respectively; at the near-detector flux rates over a multi-year run this is non-negligible.
- The TKI analysis is sensitive to the proton energy scale at the few-percent level (a 5% shift in proton momentum shifts δp_T by a comparable fraction). Continuous gain monitoring and periodic absolute calibration keep the proton energy scale uncertainty below 1%, which is the budget available within the path from 6% to 4% total systematic after the other improvements.
- The LED and source-tube system adds negligible mass and cost relative to the main detector elements.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Active neutrino target | SciFi (0.25–0.35 mm polystyrene fibres, SiPM) | Short proton track reconstruction, large-angle acceptance |
| Upstream veto / Michel tagger | Thin extruded scintillator bars, SiPM | Background rejection, pion constraint |
| Downstream ToF layer | Fast EJ-200 paddles, fast SiPM, ~300 ps resolution | p/π separation at 450 MeV/c for TKI |
| Lateral track ranger | Extruded scintillator bar stacks, SiPM | Large-angle muon momentum by range |
| Waveform-sampling readout | SPIROC2E-type ASIC, ~100 ps bins | Energy scale, PID, hit disambiguation |
| LED + source calibration | UV LED per tile + 60Co/137Cs deployment tubes | Proton energy scale < 1%, SiPM gain stability |

# Hardware Upgrades for the ND280 Upstream Active Target

## 1. Active Neutrino Target Module (SuperFGD replacement for P0D volume)

**Technology: 3-D segmented plastic scintillator cube array**

Specifically, an array of 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each read out on three orthogonal axes by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres threaded through drilled channels, with MPPCs at each fibre end. The baseline geometry would fill approximately 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m with ~2 million cubes.

**Why:** The existing FGD architecture uses 1-D bar layers alternating in x and y, which reconstructs tracks well along the beam axis but is blind to steeply angled or backwards-going particles unless they cross many layers. With 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons leaving at >50° to the beam, a large fraction of kinematically interesting events produce short, steep tracks that stop within just a few x-layers and a few y-layers and are therefore poorly measured or lost entirely. The 3-D cube geometry provides true three-dimensional space points from the coincidence of three orthogonal fibre signals within a single cube, giving full angular acceptance down to very low momenta. This is the critical enabling technology for the transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) programme: both the muon and the leading proton must be reconstructed in the same fiducial volume to form the TKI variables δp_T, δα_T, and δφ_T. The hydrocarbon (polystyrene, CH) target is explicitly acceptable per the physics programme requirements, and the high-statistics CH sample can be compared against FGD2's water layers for carbon-to-water cross-section ratios.

---

## 2. Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes

**Technology: Fast plastic scintillator panels (e.g., EJ-200 or BC-408) with SiPM readout, targeting ~200–300 ps time resolution per plane, arranged as thin planes on each face of the new target volume**

**Why:** With a leading-proton median momentum of ~450 MeV/c, protons are non-relativistic (β ≈ 0.44 at 450 MeV/c) and are well separated from pions and muons by time of flight over even short baselines. The ~6% tail above 900 MeV/c approaches the region where ToF discrimination becomes harder but is still valuable. ToF planes on the upstream and downstream faces of the target, plus the lateral faces, serve three functions: (a) particle identification of the leading proton vs. charged pion vs. muon to suppress NC and wrong-sign backgrounds; (b) directionality tagging to identify backwards-going particles that would otherwise be misassigned in vertex reconstruction; (c) rejection of beam-unrelated backgrounds and cosmics by timing relative to the beam spill. SiPM readout is natural since MPPCs are already the standard technology across ND280, allowing shared infrastructure and expertise.

---

## 3. High-Angle TPC (HA-TPC) Modules

**Technology: Two or more compact gaseous TPCs with resistive Micromegas readout, using the same or similar gas mixture as the existing TPCs (Ar:CF4:iC4H10 95:3:2), positioned on the lateral (top/bottom and left/right) faces of the new target, inside the magnet yoke gap volume**

**Why:** The existing three TPCs are planar and downstream, so they efficiently reconstruct particles leaving within roughly ±30–40° of the beam direction. The 25% of muons and 35% of protons at >50° leave the target laterally and either enter the ECal or are lost. Lateral HA-TPCs intercept these high-angle tracks and provide: (a) momentum measurement by curvature in the 0.2 T dipole field (which is well-mapped across the inner volume), critically important because low-momentum protons stopping inside the SuperFGD are measured by range, but higher-momentum protons escaping laterally require curvature; (b) dE/dx particle identification, which at the momenta of interest cleanly separates protons from muons and pions; (c) extended lever arm for tracks that begin in the SuperFGD and exit laterally, improving angular and momentum resolution jointly. Resistive Micromegas is chosen over wire chambers for robustness against occasional high-occupancy events and because it is already the validated technology in ND280, reducing technical risk for a funding proposal.

---

## 4. Upgraded MPPC/SiPM Readout Electronics

**Technology: Updated front-end ASICs with higher dynamic range and finer time stamping (~1 ns or better), compatible with the WLS fibre + MPPC channels of both the SuperFGD and the ToF planes**

**Why:** The ~2 million channels of the SuperFGD cube array represent roughly a 100-fold increase over FGD1/FGD2 channel count. The existing ND280 AFTER-based front-end electronics were not designed for this occupancy or for the sub-nanosecond timing needed to support the ToF system. A new ASIC (such as the CITIROC family or a custom development as has been prototyped for the SuperFGD) must simultaneously handle: the relatively low light yield per cube (~15–20 photoelectrons for a minimum-ionising particle crossing 1 cm), the need to integrate charge for dE/dx-based proton identification, and the timing resolution requirement for ToF PID. Getting this right directly determines whether the leading-proton reconstruction efficiency achieves the level needed to reduce the systematic uncertainty from 6% to 4% as required by T2K-II, since mis-identified or missed protons bias the reconstructed neutrino energy and TKI distributions.

---

## 5. Upgraded Data Acquisition (DAQ) System

**Technology: A trigger-less, continuous-readout DAQ architecture based on commodity FPGAs and high-bandwidth optical links (e.g., GBT/lpGBT protocol), with online GPU-based hit clustering**

**Why:** The existing ND280 DAQ operates on a triggered readout matched to the ~5 µs beam spill. The SuperFGD's ~2 million channels producing three-axis coincidences require real-time hit association to suppress dark noise and cross-talk before data volume becomes unmanageable. A trigger-less architecture reads all channels continuously and uses FPGA pre-processing on the front-end boards to form 3-D cube hits from triple-axis coincidences, dramatically reducing data rate before transmission. GPU-based online reconstruction can then perform fast vertex finding to flag events with proton candidates, allowing prescaled readout of single-track events and full readout of multi-particle events. This architecture is also required to fully exploit the ToF timing information, since an offline trigger on muon candidates would bias the proton acceptance in exactly the high-angle region where the physics gain is largest.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Driver |
|---|---|---|
| 3-D scintillator cube target | 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, 3-axis WLS fibre + MPPC | Full acceptance for >50° muons and protons; TKI reconstruction |
| Time-of-Flight planes | Fast plastic scintillator, SiPM, ~200 ps resolution | Proton/pion/muon PID at 200–900 MeV/c; backwards-track tagging |
| High-angle TPCs | Resistive Micromegas, Ar:CF4:iC4H10, lateral placement | Momentum by curvature + dE/dx PID for escaping high-angle tracks |
| MPPC front-end ASICs | High channel-count, dual charge/time measurement | Channel scaling to ~2M; dE/dx and ToF from same readout |
| Trigger-less DAQ | FPGA + lpGBT + GPU online clustering | Manage data rate; unbiased high-angle proton acceptance |

Together these five upgrades form a coherent system: the SuperFGD provides the target mass and 3-D vertex reconstruction, ToF and HA-TPCs provide PID and momentum measurement for the particles the existing detector loses, and the electronics and DAQ provide the infrastructure to read the resulting factor-of-100 increase in channel count without deadtime or trigger bias. The combination is what enables the reduction of residual systematic uncertainty from 6% to 4% required by T2K-II.

# Proposed ND280 Upgrade: A 3D-Granular Active Target with High-Angle Tracking and Time-of-Flight

## 1. Why the current detector falls short

The goal is to reconstruct kinematically complete CC events, meaning the muon and the leading proton, for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies. Today's tracker does this poorly for three reasons.

**FGD bar geometry.**
- All FGD bars are perpendicular to the beam, and each layer gives only one coordinate (x or y).
- A track at high angle runs nearly parallel to the layers. It hits few layers and deposits light along whole bars, so it is badly reconstructed or lost.
- Short tracks crossing fewer than about 3–4 layers cannot be matched between the x and y views. This sets a proton momentum threshold of roughly 450–500 MeV/c.
- That threshold sits right at the 450 MeV/c median of the leading-proton spectrum, so about half the protons are lost.

**TPC placement.**
- The TPCs lie only downstream and upstream of the FGDs.
- A muon at more than about 50° (25% of muons) never reaches a TPC.
- Its momentum must then come from range in the ECal or SMRD, which is coarse, or it is not measured at all.
- The backward and high-angle phase space, where Super-K has full acceptance, is effectively missing. Extrapolating models into it is a large part of the residual ~6% systematic.

**No neutron or timing information.** There is no detection of the neutron in antineutrino interactions, and timing is poor, so the direction of high-angle tracks is often ambiguous. Backgrounds from interactions outside the fiducial volume are hard to reject.

## 2. Core proposal: a "Super-FGD" of optically isolated cubes

### Concept
Build the target from about 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes.
- Each cube is etched with a reflective chemical surface layer for optical isolation.
- Each cube is drilled with three orthogonal holes (~1.5 mm diameter).
- Three orthogonal WLS fibres (1 mm Y-11 type) pass through every cube, along x, y and z.

Every energy deposit is therefore seen in three 2D projections. This gives true 3D voxel reconstruction, with nearly isotropic response and no preferred track direction.

### Dimensions in the available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Cube array | ≈ 192 × 184 × 56 cubes (x × y × z, z = beam) |
| Number of cubes | ≈ 2.0 million |
| Active mass | ≈ 2.0 t of CH, about twice FGD1+FGD2 (and more fiducial) |
| Readout channels (3 views) | 192·184 + 192·56 + 184·56 ≈ 56,400 fibres/MPPCs, single-ended with the far end mirrored |

The thin dimension (0.6 m) lies along the beam. The large transverse faces then point toward the new high-angle TPCs (Section 3), and forward tracks reach the existing TPC2/TPC3.

### Readout
- Keep the proven ND280 fibre + MPPC technology. Use new-generation, low-crosstalk, low-dark-rate devices of about 1.3 × 1.3 mm² (e.g. a Hamamatsu S13360-class part).
- Use new front-end electronics based on a multichannel ASIC (CITIROC-type). These should provide:
  - high and low gain, giving dynamic range from 1 photoelectron up to stopping-proton Bragg peaks;
  - about 1 ns single-fibre timing, or about 0.7 ns for a cube read by several fibres;
  - triggerless or beam-gated operation.
- Expected performance:
  - Light yield: about 40–60 p.e. per fibre per MIP cube.
  - Cube-to-cube optical crosstalk: about 3%, which must be modelled.
  - dE/dx per cube gives good p/π/μ separation for stopping tracks.

### Physics gains for the stated requirements

**Proton threshold.**
- A proton crossing about 3 cubes (~3 cm) is reconstructible. That corresponds to a kinetic energy of about 50 MeV, or about 300 MeV/c, compared with about 450–500 MeV/c today.
- A 450 MeV/c proton (T ≈ 100 MeV) has a range of about 8 cm and is fully contained, so its momentum comes from range to a few percent.
- Most of the spectrum is therefore contained, and acceptance becomes flat in angle, covering the 35% of protons at more than 50°.

**High-momentum protons (6% above 900 MeV/c).**
- These have T ≳ 360 MeV and ranges approaching 1 m.
- Many exit the target. They are measured by curvature and dE/dx in the TPCs (forward or high-angle), with hadronic re-interaction tagged in the cubes.

**Muons.**
- Full 4π tracking at the vertex, including backward muons.
- Momentum is measured in whichever TPC the muon enters. Range or ECal/SMRD serves as a backup.

**Vertex activity and neutrons.**
- Fine granularity resolves low-energy vertex activity and π⁰ photon conversions.
- Neutron detection is a bonus: an isolated delayed or displaced cube cluster, with ns timing, gives neutron kinetic energy by time of flight. This extends TKI to antineutrino CC (μ⁺ + n).

**Material.** The target is fully active hydrocarbon, which is acceptable here. FGD2 with its water layers remains downstream for the C/H₂O comparison.

## 3. Two high-angle TPCs (HA-TPCs) above and below the target

### Purpose
Measure the charge, momentum (by curvature in the 0.2 T field) and dE/dx PID of high-angle muons and exiting protons. Today these tracks miss the TPCs.

### Geometry
- Place one TPC directly above and one directly below the cube target, inside the freed P0D volume.
- Each is about 2.0 m (along x) × 0.8 m (drift, vertical) × 1.8 m (z).
- The magnetic field is along x, so tracks going up or down bend in the y–z plane and are measured well.
- A dE/dx resolution better than 10% matches the existing TPCs.

### Technology
1. **Field cage.** A thin, light composite design (aramid honeycomb with Kapton/insulating laminate). This minimises dead material between the target and the gas, which matters for low-momentum protons.
2. **Readout.** Resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode, "ERAM"), about 8 modules per endplate.
   - Charge spreading over the resistive layer allows larger pads (about 1 cm × 1 cm) with better spatial resolution (≲ 0.6 mm).
   - It also suppresses sparks.
   - Fewer channels are needed for the same area.
3. **Gas and electronics.** The same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ (95:3:2) gas, sharing the existing gas system. Upgraded front-end electronics as an evolution of the AFTER/AGET ASIC.

## 4. Time-of-Flight (ToF) envelope

- Surround the target + HA-TPC assembly with six planes of plastic scintillator bars, about 1 cm thick and 12 cm wide. Read both bar ends with arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Target timing resolution is about 100–150 ps.
- Functions:
  - It distinguishes inward-going from outward-going tracks. This rejects backgrounds from interactions in the magnet, coil and ECal, which are critical for high-angle and backward samples.
  - It provides an extra trigger and cosmic calibration.
  - It adds particle ID through β for exiting tracks.

## 5. Supporting changes

- **Mechanics and integration.** Use a non-magnetic composite box with a carbon-fibre or plastic panel frame to hold the cubes. Fibre threading must proceed layer by layer. Route about 56k fibres to MPPC boards on the box faces. Keep cabling away from the HA-TPC acceptance where possible.
- **Calibration.** Use an LED/fibre light-injection system for MPPC gain. Use cosmic and through-going muons for cube-by-cube response and crosstalk tuning. Run a test-beam programme (charged particles and neutrons) on prototypes before construction.
- **Downstream ECal around the new region.** Reuse or retain the barrel ECal and SMRD. They will tag showers and range out high-angle muons that escape the HA-TPCs.
- **Unchanged parts.** Keep TPC1–3, FGD1 and FGD2 as the downstream tracker. The combined system then has forward, high-angle and backward acceptance.
- **Data acquisition.** Upgrade DAQ and trigger for the higher channel count and the higher beam power expected in T2K-II.

## 6. Expected impact

- **Angular acceptance.** Near-4π acceptance for muons and protons, matching Super-K's phase space instead of extrapolating into it.
- **Proton acceptance.** The threshold drops from about 450 to about 300 MeV/c, the high-angle loss is removed, and fiducial mass doubles. Together these give well-measured TKI variables (δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T). Those variables constrain nuclear effects such as Fermi motion, 2p2h and final-state interactions.
- **Neutron tagging.** This enables new antineutrino constraints.
- **Systematic reduction.** Better flux × cross-section constraints are the route from about 6% to the about 4% systematic needed for T2K-II. This path is consistent with sensitivity studies of this type, but the final number depends on the full analysis.

# Recommendations for Re-equipping the Kestrel Flats Near Station Target Region

## Summary

Replace the target region with three components:

1. A **3D-granular plastic-scintillator active target** of the SuperFGD type: optically isolated 1 cm cubes read out by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres and SiPMs.
2. Two **high-angle TPCs** above and below it, read out with resistive Micromegas.
3. A hermetic **time-of-flight (TOF) scintillator envelope** around the whole assembly.

The existing dipole and downstream drift chambers stay in place and continue to measure forward-going tracks.

This is essentially the architecture of the T2K ND280 upgrade, which faced the same three problems: 4π muon acceptance, low-threshold protons and a controlled hydrogen fraction.

## 1. Active target: SuperFGD-style 3D scintillator cube array

**What it is.** Polystyrene scintillator cubes, 1 × 1 × 1 cm³, each with a reflective (chemically etched) surface and three orthogonal holes. Each cube is threaded by three 1 mm WLS fibres, one per axis, and each fibre is read by an MPPC/SiPM at one end. Every cube therefore gives three orthogonal 2D projections, which can be combined into a true 3D image.

**Suggested envelope.** About 1.9 m (horizontal, transverse) × 0.6 m (vertical) × 0.85 m (along the beam). That is roughly 1.9 × 60 × 85 ≈ 1 million cubes and about 1 t of fiducial-quality target. The channel count is about 3 × 10⁴ to 6 × 10⁴, depending on whether some views are read at both ends. The remaining volume is reserved for the TPCs and TOF described below.

**Why this technology:**

- **Isotropic acceptance.**
  - Cubes have no preferred direction, unlike layered bar detectors. Bar planes lose tracks that run parallel to the planes, which is exactly the near-90° muons and protons the analysis requires.
  - In the cube array a track at any angle, including backward, produces hits in all three views.
- **Low proton threshold.**
  - A 60 MeV proton has a CSDA range of about 3 g/cm². That is roughly 3 cm in polystyrene, or about 3 cubes.
  - Three to four 3D-resolved cubes with Bragg-peak dE/dx are enough to reconstruct the track and identify it as a proton.
  - A conventional 2D-plane tracker typically needs several layers in each view, which pushes the threshold to about 300–400 MeV/c in momentum.
- **Hydrogen fraction.**
  - Polystyrene (C₈H₈) has 13 nucleons per CH unit, of which 1 is a hydrogen nucleus. That is about 7.7% of target nucleons.
  - Fibre cladding, TiO₂ reflector and support structure keep the total well under 10%, comfortably inside the 20% limit of the hydrogen-subtraction model.
  - **Do not use a water-based target.** Water gives about 11%, which is acceptable on its own, but it adds passive layers and loses the low threshold.
  - **Do not use hydrogen-rich materials** such as polyethylene absorbers.
- **Additional benefits.**
  - About 1 ns timing per channel allows neutron detection by time of flight within the cube volume.
  - Stopping muons and pions in the bulk can be measured by range. This is important for tracks running along the magnetic field direction, which barely bend.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**What they are.** Two TPCs, each about 2 m × 0.8 m × 0.85 m, sitting above and below the cube array and filling the rest of the 2.3 m height. Recommended features:

- **Lightweight composite field cages**, to minimise dead material between the target and the gas.
- **Resistive (encapsulated-resistive-anode) Micromegas readout.** The resistive layer spreads charge, which gives good spatial resolution with about 1 cm pads and fewer channels, and it suppresses sparking.
- **A proven T2K-style gas**, such as Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ at 95:3:2. Its hydrogen content is negligible.

**Why.** Muons emitted at large angles leave the cube array upward or downward and never reach the downstream drift chambers. Without this coverage the efficiency for perpendicular tracks would fall far below 25%. The TPCs:

- measure momentum from curvature in the existing 0.15 T field;
- measure charge sign;
- separate μ, e and p by dE/dx.

At 0.7 GeV beam energy, muon momenta at high angle are typically a few hundred MeV/c. With an 0.8 m lever arm at 0.15 T, the sagitta is several mm, which gives roughly 10% momentum resolution.

**Field orientation.** If the dipole field is horizontal and transverse, the field geometry is already aligned for tracks going up or down. Tracks exiting sideways, along the field, bend little, and their momenta come from range in the cube array or from the TOF plus range.

## 3. TOF envelope (about 6 panels)

**What it is.** Plastic scintillator bars, about 1 cm thick and 12 cm wide, read out at both ends by SiPM arrays. They surround the cube array and TPC assembly, and the target should achieve roughly 150 ps time resolution.

**Why:**

- **Direction.** Over a flight path of about 1–2 m, a time difference of a few ns between the cube array (about 1 ns resolution) and the TOF unambiguously tells whether a track is going forward or backward. This is mandatory for the backward-muon requirement. Without it, backward muons are confused with tracks from interactions outside the target, such as entering cosmics or particles produced in the magnet and surrounding material.
- **Particle ID.** Combined with momentum, the TOF provides mass discrimination, especially for e/μ and μ/p.
- **Vetoing and triggering.** It vetoes interactions occurring outside the target region and serves as a cosmic trigger for calibration.

## 4. Supporting changes

- **Keep the existing downstream drift chambers** for forward muons, which are the bulk of the sample. Match the downstream face of the cube array to their acceptance.
- **Front-end and DAQ.**
  - Use SiPM electronics with charge and roughly 1 ns timing, of the CITIROC/"FEB" class, for the cubes and TOF.
  - Use AFTER/DREAM-type readout for the TPCs.
  - Provide a common clock and add the system to the beam-spill trigger.
- **Calibration.**
  - A light-injection (LED) system for SiPM gain.
  - Cosmic runs using the TOF trigger.
  - Characterisation of a cube prototype in a hadron test beam to validate proton response down to 60 MeV. This calibrates the proton threshold and the Birks saturation effect.
- **Mechanics.**
  - Use a low-mass carbon-fibre box for the cube array. Dead material sitting between the target and the TPCs raises the momentum threshold for tracks to reach them.
  - Keep track of every hydrogen-bearing component in the material budget, so the 20% limit is verified rather than assumed. Expect a total around 8%.

## 5. How each requirement is met

| Requirement | Provided by |
|---|---|
| Muon efficiency ≥25% at all angles, forward | Cube array plus downstream drift chambers |
| Muon efficiency, high angle and perpendicular | Cube array plus high-angle TPCs |
| Muon efficiency, backward | TOF timing for direction, with TPCs or range for momentum |
| Muon efficiency, along the field | Range in the 1.9 m cube array plus TOF |
| Protons down to about 60 MeV kinetic energy at all angles | 1 cm isotropic 3D granularity (about 3 cubes) with dE/dx particle ID |
| Hydrogen at most 20% of target nucleons | Polystyrene target, about 8% hydrogen nucleons |

**Main risks** are the fibre-threading and assembly effort for about 10⁶ cubes, cube-to-cube optical crosstalk, and dead material between the target and the TPCs. Each has proven mitigations from the ND280 upgrade:

- **Assembly:** fishing-line pre-assembly with layer-by-layer fibre insertion.
- **Crosstalk:** chemical-etch reflector, with the remaining crosstalk calibrated in data.
- **Dead material:** composite field cages.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Active Neutrino Target for the Upstream Section

## 1. Physics Requirements Analysis

Before specifying hardware, I will translate the stated physics goals into concrete detector requirements.

**Kinematic completeness condition:** Both the muon and leading recoil proton must be reconstructed with sufficient momentum and angular resolution to form the transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) variables δp_T, δα_T, and δφ_T. These require:

- Muon momentum resolution ~few % (range or curvature)
- Proton momentum resolution ~5–10% (range is preferred over curvature at these momenta)
- Angular resolution ~1–2° for both tracks
- Vertex position resolution ~few mm to suppress pileup and correctly associate secondaries

**Angular acceptance challenge:** 25% of muons and 35% of protons emerge beyond 50°. This is a severe constraint. A conventional tracker with downstream-only readout would lose the majority of large-angle protons. The detector must therefore be **largely self-contained** in its angular acceptance, with active material surrounding the interaction region on most sides.

**Proton momentum challenge:** Median proton momentum ~450 MeV/c means range ~18 cm in polystyrene (using Bethe-Bloch, a 450 MeV/c proton has kinetic energy ~95 MeV, range in plastic ~8 cm). The 6% tail above 900 MeV/c (kinetic energy ~380 MeV, range ~35 cm in plastic) must also be ranged or tracked. The active volume plus surrounding calorimetry must provide sufficient material to stop or at least reconstruct these.

**Available envelope:** 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m (W × H × L, with beam along the 0.6 m axis). This is a shallow box — the longitudinal dimension is tight. This immediately drives the design toward a **highly granular, fully active 3D detector** rather than a conventional layered tracker.

---

## 2. Proposed Detector Architecture

### 2.1 Overall Concept: Segmented Scintillator Cube Array ("SuperCube")

The baseline proposal is a **fully active 3D scintillator target** constructed from optically isolated plastic scintillator cubes read out on three orthogonal faces, surrounded by a thin high-resolution tracker shell, enclosed in an electromagnetic calorimeter that reuses the existing downstream ECAL technology.

This architecture is motivated directly by the success of the SuperFGD concept, adapted here to the specific box dimensions and physics priorities of this programme.

---

### 2.2 Core: 3D Segmented Scintillator Cube Array

**Geometry and segmentation:**

The active cube array occupies approximately 1.8 m × 1.7 m × 0.4 m, leaving a ~10 cm clearance on all sides for structural support and the surrounding tracker shell.

Cube size: **1.0 cm × 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm** polystyrene scintillator.

This gives an array of approximately:
- 180 cubes × 170 cubes × 40 cubes = **1,224,000 cubes total**

Each cube is pierced by three wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres running along x, y, and z axes. Each fibre services an entire row of cubes along its axis and is read out at one end by a **silicon photomultiplier (SiPM)**. The other end is mirrored.

Total fibre channels:
- x-readout: 170 × 40 = 6,800 fibres (each 180 cm long)
- y-readout: 180 × 40 = 7,200 fibres (each 170 cm long)
- z-readout: 180 × 170 = 30,600 fibres (each 40 cm long)
- **Total: ~44,600 SiPM channels**

This is consistent in scale and technology with existing production experience and within the capacity of existing front-end ASIC families (e.g., CITIROC or FEBio-style chips).

**Material budget of active array:**

- Volume: 1.8 × 1.7 × 0.4 = 1.224 m³
- Polystyrene density: 1.05 g/cm³
- Mass: ~1.29 t (accounting for ~6% volume fraction of WLS fibres with similar density)
- Radiation length of polystyrene: X₀ ≈ 42 cm → array is ~0.95 X₀ deep longitudinally
- Nuclear interaction length λ_I ≈ 79 cm → array is ~0.51 λ_I deep

The 0.4 m depth means roughly half an interaction length of target, which is acceptable since the goal is vertex identification and short track reconstruction, not full containment of hadronic showers (the downstream detectors handle that).

**Why 1 cm cubes rather than bars:**

The existing downstream FGD uses 9.6 mm bars in x/y planes. The 3D cube geometry offers three critical improvements:
1. **Omnidirectional 3D tracking** — large-angle protons are reconstructed in 3D from the first cube, with no dead-zone orientation
2. **Hit disambiguation** — three-view coincidence eliminates the ghost-track problem endemic to 2D bar detectors at the high track multiplicities expected near 0.6 GeV
3. **Lower effective threshold** — a 1 cm cube provides ~2 MeV energy deposit threshold for a minimum-ionising particle, translating to a proton tracking threshold of roughly **~150 MeV/c** (kinetic energy ~10 MeV), well below the median recoil proton momentum

**Interaction rate estimate:**

Polystyrene (CH): carbon + hydrogen in roughly 12:1 mass ratio.
Neutrino interaction rate scales with mass and cross section. With ~1.3 t of hydrocarbon and a ~0.6 GeV flux, and assuming the existing targets at ~1.1 t each produce usable event rates for the current programme, the new target provides comparable or slightly better statistics. The shallower depth (0.4 m vs ~0.365 m for each existing FGD) is compensated by the larger transverse area.

---

### 2.3 Surrounding Thin Tracking Shell

A shell of **high-granularity silicon strip or scintillating fibre tracker planes** at ~5 mm pitch is mounted immediately outside all six faces of the cube array. This serves to:

1. Confirm tracks exiting the cube array
2. Provide a precise **exit-angle measurement** (~1 mrad) for tracks entering the downstream TPCs or the ECAL
3. Flag re-entering tracks (loopers in the magnetic field)
4. Distinguish forward-going from backward-going tracks without ambiguity

**Specification:** Six planes (±x, ±y, ±z faces), each two layers of **250 μm pitch scintillating fibres** with SiPM readout, staggered by half-pitch. Fibre ribbon technology (as in LHCb SciFi) is well-suited here. Each plane is ~3 mm thick (two layers + substrate), so the shell contributes <1% X₀ per face. Total additional channel count: ~O(10,000) channels, manageable.

The ±z faces (beam-entry and beam-exit) are most important for forward muon angle measurement; the ±x and ±y faces are most important for the large-angle proton programme.

---

### 2.4 Surrounding Electromagnetic Calorimeter

The existing detector already has lead-scintillator ECAL modules surrounding the inner detectors. The proposal is to **fabricate new ECAL panels** of identical technology (lead-scintillator with WLS fibre + SiPM) sized to fit the six faces of the new assembly within the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope.

Each ECAL panel: 11 radiation lengths of sampling calorimeter (~10 cm of lead-scintillator sandwich), giving:
- Photon conversion efficiency: >98%
- π⁰ reconstruction: identifies photon pairs from neutral-current background, critical for CC-exclusive selection purity
- Proton containment: a 900 MeV/c proton (range ~35 cm in plastic) that escapes the cube array and tracking shell enters the ECAL, where it ranges out in ~12 cm of effective plastic equivalent. The ECAL adds enough material to stop >95% of the protons in the momentum distribution

**On the beam-entry face (upstream ECAL):** Keep this panel thin (~3 X₀) to avoid pre-showering beam neutrinos. This is acceptable since photons entering from upstream are not part of the signal topology.

**Structural note:** The total assembly — cube array + tracking shell + ECAL panels — must fit within 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m. With 0.4 m for the active array, 0.006 m for the tracking shell on each z-face, and ~0.09 m for ECAL on each z-face, the longitudinal budget is: 0.09 + 0.006 + 0.4 + 0.006 + 0.09 = **0.59 m** — consistent with the available 0.6 m. Transversely, 0.09 m ECAL on each side leaves 2.0 − 0.18 = 1.82 m and 1.9 − 0.18 = 1.72 m for the active array, consistent with the specified 1.8 × 1.7 m.

---

### 2.5 Trigger and Timing

**Trigger:** The existing detector uses scintillator-based trigger planes. The cube array provides a self-triggering capability: any cluster of ≥3 coincident SiPM hits in a 100 ns window in the central array constitutes a neutrino interaction trigger. This is effectively dead-time free at the beam spill rates typical of this class of experiment (~few kHz peak during spill).

**Timing resolution:** The SiPM + WLS fibre system achieves ~1 ns resolution per channel. At 0.6 GeV, the beam spill structure is typically ~few μs with well-separated bunches in some machines, or ~100 μs flat-top. The 1 ns resolution is sufficient to suppress out-of-time cosmics and to separate multiple interactions within a spill at realistic pileup rates.

---

## 3. Detector Performance Projections

### 3.1 Proton Reconstruction Efficiency

| Proton momentum | Kinetic energy | Range in PS | Cubes traversed | Reconstructed? |
|----------------|---------------|-------------|-----------------|----------------|
| 200 MeV/c | 20 MeV | ~1.8 cm | ~18 | Yes (range) |
| 450 MeV/c | 95 MeV | ~8 cm | ~80 | Yes (range) |
| 700 MeV/c | 215 MeV | ~20 cm | ~200 | Yes (range or curvature) |
| 900 MeV/c | 380 MeV | ~35 cm | ~350 | Yes (range, partly in ECAL) |
| >900 MeV/c | >380 MeV | exits | — | Momentum from curvature in B-field |

The 0.2 T dipole field gives a sagitta of ~**1–2 cm** for a 900 MeV/c proton over 0.4 m, measurable at the 1 cm cube granularity (though marginally — a denser hit pattern from the 1 cm cubes gives 40 measurement points, allowing sagitta measurement at ~2–3 mm precision, hence ~15% momentum resolution by curvature for exiting protons). For contained tracks, range gives better resolution (~3–5%).

Estimated **proton reconstruction efficiency for the full momentum spectrum**: ~87%, limited primarily by protons below ~150 MeV/c (below threshold) and the ~6% above 900 MeV/c that exit sideways before the ECAL.

### 3.2 Muon Reconstruction

Forward-going muons (75% of events) exit through the z-face, through the downstream tracking shell, and into the existing TPC system where they are reconstructed with curvature in the magnetic field — no change to current performance.

Large-angle muons (25% beyond 50°): these exit through the ±x, ±y, or upstream z faces. The 3D cube array provides a track stub of ~5–15 cubes before the muon exits. The tracking shell gives a precise exit direction. The ECAL provides range measurement if the muon stops in it (~250 MeV/c muon has range ~20 cm in plastic, contained in ECAL). Higher-momentum large-angle muons exit the ECAL and reach the **return-yoke scintillator system**, which was already designed to range out side-going muons — this existing system is fully exploited. Momentum from curvature is available for all muons that cross at least two tracker planes in the magnetic volume.

Estimated **large-angle muon reconstruction efficiency**: ~70%, up from effectively ~30–40% with the previous bar-based upstream target (which had no active material on the ±x and ±y faces).

### 3.3 TKI Variable Resolution

The TKI variables δp_T and δα_T depend on transverse momentum components of muon and proton. For a typical 0.6 GeV CC-QE event:

- Muon p_T resolution: dominated by angular resolution at forward angles → ~25 MeV/c for forward muons, ~40 MeV/c for large-angle muons
- Proton p_T resolution: dominated by range straggling → ~15–20 MeV/c for contained tracks

Combined δp_T resolution: **~30–45 MeV/c**, compared to the QE signal width in δp_T of ~100–150 MeV/c. This is sufficient to resolve FSI-induced tails from the quasi-elastic peak.

### 3.4 Systematic Uncertainty Impact

The goal is to reduce the residual systematic uncertainty from ~6% to ~4%. The new target contributes through:

1. **Improved signal efficiency and purity:** The kinematically complete CC sample with both tracks reconstructed provides a cleaner neutrino energy estimator, reducing the smearing contribution to systematic uncertainty

2. **Carbon-to-water ratio with improved muon acceptance:** Since the downstream water-layer FGD remains, the ratio measurement (which constrains the water far-detector flux systematic) benefits from the improved muon acceptance in the upstream target

3. **Direct constraint on multinucleon (2p2h) processes:** TKI distributions in the hydrocarbon target are sensitive to 2p2h, which is a ~10–15% effect at 0.6 GeV and currently a dominant systematic. The new target provides a direct measurement of this process through the δp_T tail

Quantitatively, if the dominant remaining systematics are FSI (~2.5%), 2p2h (~2%), and flux shape (~1.5%), and the new target directly constrains the first two at the ~30% level (plausible from published TKI analyses with comparable statistics), the combined systematic reduces from ~√(2.5² + 2² + 1.5²) ≈ 3.4% (detector-corrected) toward ~2.5%, contributing to reaching the 4% total goal when combined with existing constraints.

---

## 4. Required Ancillary Upgrades

### 4.1 Front-End Electronics

The ~44,600 new SiPM channels require new front-end ASICs. The existing detector already uses SiPM+WLS readout on the ECAL and FGD — the same ASIC family can be used. Recommend deploying the **FEBio3** (or equivalent) chip: 64 channels per ASIC, so ~700 ASICs are needed. These are mounted on the ends of the fibre arrays outside the active volume on three faces.

Power budget: ~64 mW per ASIC × 700 = ~45 W total — negligible and well within the thermal budget of the existing magnet volume.

### 4.2 Data Acquisition

The existing DAQ must accept ~44,600 additional channels. The cube array will produce ~O(100) hit channels per neutrino interaction (a 450 MeV/c proton traverses ~80 cubes, each firing up to 3 fibres, plus muon track). At beam spill rates, the data rate increase is ~O(50 MB/s) per spill, manageable with a standard optical-fibre readout aggregation layer feeding into the existing DAQ farm.

### 4.3 Mechanical Integration

The existing upstream photon-tagger (40 planes, ~16 t, ~2.4 m long) must be removed. This is a significant civil/mechanical operation but is straightforward in principle — the detector is modular by construction. The new assembly (~1.5 t for cube array + ~0.3 t for ECAL panels + support structure, total ~2 t) is considerably lighter, reducing floor-load concerns.

Alignment: The cube array must be aligned to the existing TPC/FGD system to ~1 mm. This is achieved by survey during installation and cross-checked in situ using through-going muons from cosmic rays and beam halo, which provide straight tracks spanning the new and existing detector systems.

### 4.4 Calibration

**Energy calibration:** Through-going cosmic muons provide a minimum-ionising signal of ~2 MeV per cm of plastic per cube face (expected ~100 p.e. with 1 mm diameter WLS fibre and typical SiPM quantum efficiency of 40%), giving a >10:1 signal-to-noise ratio per cube per muon crossing. Full calibration of all ~44,600 channels can be accomplished with ~1 week of cosmic running between beam periods.

**Cross-calibration with downstream detectors:** Select CC events with a forward muon track that spans both the new cube array and the existing TPC. The muon momentum measured by curvature in the TPC provides an absolute momentum scale reference. Comparing the range of the same track in the cube array calibrates the energy-loss model, constraining the proton momentum scale at the ~1–2% level.

---

## 5. Summary and Prioritisation

| Subsystem | Technology | Channels | Mass | Purpose |
|-----------|-----------|---------|------|---------|
| 3D scintillator cube array | 1 cm³ PS cubes + WLS + SiPM | 44,600 | 1.3 t | Primary neutrino target + proton tracker |
| Thin tracking shell | Scintillating fibre, 250 μm pitch | ~10,000 | 0.05 t | Exit-angle measurement |
| New ECAL panels (5 faces) | Pb-scintillator + WLS + SiPM | ~5,000 | 0.5 t | Proton ranging + photon veto |
| New FEE | FEBio3 ASICs | 700 chips | — | Channel readout |
| DAQ extension | Optical aggregation + farm nodes | — | — | Data handling |

**The single most impactful element is the 3D scintillator cube array.** The omnidirectional tracking capability it provides is not achievable with any planar technology in the available 0.6 m longitudinal space, because a planar tracker with sufficient angular acceptance would require either an impractically large number of planes or an impractically large active transverse area. The cube geometry solves the angular acceptance problem intrinsically, at the cost of a moderately larger channel count relative to a 2D bar detector — a cost that is entirely manageable with current SiPM and ASIC technology.

The tracking shell and ECAL are important but secondary: the shell improves the muon angle measurement for the large-angle population, and the ECAL extends the proton momentum reach into the high-momentum tail. Both are strongly motivated by the 4% systematic target but could be deferred to a second installation phase if resources require prioritisation.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Constraints Before Listing Upgrades

The requirements drive the technology choices:
- **4π muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency**, including backward and transverse tracks → cannot rely on downstream spectrometer alone
- **Proton tracks down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** (range ~3 cm in plastic, ~1.3 cm in iron) → very low threshold, fine granularity
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤2% of target nucleons** → constrains material choice severely (polystyrene scintillator is ~7.7% H by nucleon count; liquid argon is 0%; aluminium is 0%)
- **Volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m** inside the warm dipole → must be non-magnetic material, fit the aperture
- **~0.7 GeV peak flux** → typical final states: 1 muon + 1–2 protons + few pions

---

## Upgrade 1: 3D Scintillator Cube Active Target

**Technology:** Fully-active plastic scintillator cube array — specifically **polystyrene scintillator cubes (~1.5–2.0 cm side)** assembled into an interlocking 3D grid with **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers** running in all three orthogonal directions, read out by **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)** at the cube faces.

**Why this technology:**

The fine granularity (cube side ~1.5 cm) gives a threshold track length of roughly one cube, corresponding to a proton kinetic energy of ~15–20 MeV — well below the 60 MeV requirement, with margin. The 3D fiber readout gives unambiguous three-dimensional space points on every cube that fires, enabling reconstruction of short, highly-ionizing, low-momentum proton tracks at any angle including transverse and backward-going. There is no preferred direction in the readout, satisfying the 4π geometric requirement for the hadronic vertex.

**However**, polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ has a hydrogen-to-carbon nucleon ratio of 8:8 per monomer → hydrogen is **50% of nucleons by count** — far exceeding the ≤2% limit. Therefore plain scintillator cubes alone **cannot serve as the bulk target material** without a technique to suppress the hydrogen content (see Upgrade 2 below). The cubes are nonetheless essential as the active sensing medium, and their hydrogen problem is addressed by making them thin relative to denser, low-hydrogen passive absorber layers.

---

## Upgrade 2: Passive High-Z, Low-Hydrogen Absorber Interleaved with Active Layers

**Technology:** Thin sheets of **carbon (graphite) or aluminium** passive absorber, interleaved with the scintillator layers at a pitch chosen to bring the hydrogen nucleon fraction below 2%.

**Why this technology:**

Carbon (graphite) contains **zero hydrogen**. Aluminium likewise. If scintillator slabs of thickness *t*_sc alternate with absorber slabs of thickness *t*_abs, the hydrogen fraction by nucleon number is:

f_H = (ρ_sc · t_sc · f_{H,sc}) / (ρ_sc · t_sc + ρ_abs · t_abs)

For polystyrene (ρ ≈ 1.05 g/cm³, f_{H,sc} ≈ 0.077 by mass fraction corresponding to ~0.50 by nucleon fraction after accounting for atomic mass) and graphite (ρ ≈ 1.8 g/cm³):

To reach f_H ≤ 2% by nucleon, the mass of absorber must be roughly 24× the mass of scintillator. This means absorber dominates the mass, while scintillator remains the active sensing medium. The absorber should be **carbon rather than a metal with large nuclear effects** because the neutrino cross-section model uncertainty on heavy nuclei is larger, and carbon is closest to the scintillator nucleus already in the interaction model, minimising systematic uncertainty introduced by the absorber material.

**Why not liquid argon or iron?** Iron would satisfy the hydrogen constraint and gives good density, but its large nuclear corrections and large radiation length make track reconstruction of low-energy protons harder, and it cannot be made granular at the centimeter scale inside this magnet bore cost-effectively. Liquid argon satisfies the constraint perfectly and gives excellent dE/dx for proton ID, but the cryogenic infrastructure would not fit within the existing 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m warm-magnet volume, and the proposal is an upgrade of an existing instrument.

---

## Upgrade 3: SiPM Readout Replacing Any Existing PMT-Based or Wire-Based Readout

**Technology:** **Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs, specifically multi-pixel photon counters, e.g., 1.3 mm × 1.3 mm to 3 mm × 3 mm active area)** mounted directly on the ends of WLS fibers at each cube face, with ASIC-based front-end electronics (e.g., CITIROC or MUSIC chip).

**Why this technology:**

SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields (unlike PMTs, which lose gain and can saturate in the 0.15 T dipole field that permeates the target region). They are compact enough to instrument individual 1.5–2 cm cubes — no PMT could physically fit at that pitch. Their single-photon sensitivity and high photon-detection efficiency (~40–50%) are necessary to detect the small light yield from the short WLS fiber segments serving each cube, ensuring adequate signal-to-noise for the low-energy proton tracks (which may traverse only 1–2 cubes). The low operating voltage (~25–70 V) simplifies power distribution inside the magnet volume, and the small form factor allows the full 3D array to be assembled without dead material from bulky photodetector housings.

---

## Upgrade 4: Time-of-Flight / Timing Layer at the Downstream Face of the Active Target

**Technology:** **Fast plastic scintillator panels (~5–10 mm thick, BC-420 or EJ-228 type) with SiPM readout**, achieving time resolution ~200–300 ps per plane, arranged as a planar wall at the downstream face (2.6 m × 2.3 m) of the active target volume.

**Why this technology:**

Tracks exiting the downstream face of the active target enter the existing dipole field volume and gas drift chambers. The timing layer provides: (a) a precise **t₀** for the event, needed to associate drift-chamber hits with the correct beam spill bucket; (b) **time-of-flight discrimination** between muons and pions exiting the target (at ~0.7 GeV beam energy, pion/muon separation by TOF over even a short baseline improves purity); and (c) a **veto/tag** for tracks that do exit downstream, complementing the 4π reconstruction requirement by flagging which tracks are handed off to the spectrometer versus which are fully contained in the active target.

A fast timing system also helps with **pile-up rejection** at high beam intensity — multiple interactions per spill can be separated in time if the near station sees high neutrino flux at 410 m from target.

---

## Upgrade 5: Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECAL) Surrounding the Active Target on Lateral and Upstream Faces

**Technology:** **Lead–scintillator sandwich calorimeter**, with ~2 mm lead sheets interleaved with 3–5 mm plastic scintillator strips, read out by SiPMs via WLS fibers, achieving ~10–15% / √E energy resolution, covering the four lateral faces and the upstream face (not the downstream face, which is covered by the TOF and spectrometer).

**Why this technology:**

The analysis requires muon reconstruction at **all angles including transverse and backward-going**. A muon track going transversely or backward exits through the lateral or upstream faces of the active target. Without instrumentation on those faces, such tracks are lost once they leave the scintillator cube array. The lateral ECAL serves multiple roles:

- **Range telescope for exiting muons:** A muon stopping in the ECAL has its momentum estimated by range; a muon punching through is tagged as high-momentum and handed to other reconstruction.
- **Photon/π⁰ containment:** Neutral pions produced at the vertex decay to photon pairs; containing and measuring these showers is essential for the neutrino energy reconstruction and for the cross-section model that underpins the hydrogen-subtraction procedure.
- **Muon–pion separation** via shower profile: pions begin hadronic showers in the lead, muons do not.

The lead–scintillator technology is chosen over pure scintillator because the high-Z lead provides short radiation length (~0.56 cm), containing electromagnetic showers within a physically thin layer that fits around the active target inside the magnet bore, while the scintillator strips provide the active sampling signal. Lead contains negligible hydrogen (lead has Z=82, A=207, zero hydrogen), so it does not worsen the hydrogen-fraction budget.

---

## Upgrade 6: Upstream Veto and Muon-Catcher Plane

**Technology:** **Plastic scintillator veto panels** (5–10 mm thick, full 2.6 m × 2.3 m cross-section) immediately upstream of the active target, plus a **steel–scintillator muon ranger** (alternating 2–5 cm steel plates with scintillator strips, ~1 m total depth) downstream of the TOF wall but upstream of the existing gas drift chambers.

**Why this technology:**

*Upstream veto:* Neutrino interactions occurring in the material upstream of the active target (beam line components, the magnet coil, structural material) can send charged particles into the active target mimicking a fiducial interaction. Scintillator panels with ~1 ns timing and high light yield efficiently tag charged particles entering from upstream, reducing this background. They must be thin to avoid introducing significant hydrogen or interaction probability; 5–10 mm polystyrene adds negligible mass.

*Muon ranger:* Muons from ~0.7 GeV CC interactions typically have momenta of 200–800 MeV/c. Many will exit the downstream face of the 0.9 m-deep active target (0.9 m of mixed scintillator/carbon is ~0.6–0.8 interaction lengths but only ~0.4 radiation lengths). These muons then travel through the dipole field and are measured by the existing gas chambers — but only if the existing spectrometer has sufficient angular acceptance. For **forward-going muons** (which is the majority), the existing downstream spectrometer already provides momentum measurement, so the muon ranger fills the gap for **intermediate-angle muons** that exit laterally from the active target's long (2.6 m or 2.3 m) faces but do not reach the lateral ECAL. A compact steel–scintillator ranger on two lateral sides, read out by SiPMs, allows momentum-by-range measurement for these tracks and ensures the ≥25% efficiency at every angle requirement is met. Steel is chosen over other absorbers because its high density (7.87 g/cm³) stops muons in the shortest physical depth, minimising the extra volume needed within the magnet bore.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| 1. 3D scintillator cube active target | ~1.5 cm polystyrene cubes, WLS fibers, SiPM readout | 60 MeV proton threshold; 4π reconstruction |
| 2. Carbon/graphite passive absorber | Interleaved graphite sheets, mass ratio ~24:1 absorber:scintillator | Hydrogen fraction ≤2% of nucleons |
| 3. SiPM photodetector replacement | 1.3–3 mm SiPMs, ASIC front-end | Operation in 0.15 T field; fine granularity readout |
| 4. Downstream timing/TOF layer | Fast plastic scintillator, SiPM, ~200 ps resolution | t₀ for spectrometer; particle ID; pile-up rejection |
| 5. Lateral + upstream ECAL | Pb–scintillator sandwich, SiPM | Transverse/backward muon reconstruction; photon containment |
| 6. Upstream veto + muon ranger | Thin scintillator veto; steel–scintillator ranger | Background rejection; intermediate-angle muon momentum |

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Summary of Constraints Driving Technology Choices

Before proposing hardware, let me be explicit about what the physics demands:

- **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles**, including 90° and backward — this kills passive absorber solutions and requires a fully active, 4π-sensitive volume
- **Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** (range in water ~13 mm, range in scintillator ~20 mm) — requires fine granularity, low threshold, and no dead material inside the fiducial volume
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤2% of nucleons** — this is the most chemically constraining requirement, essentially excluding water (11% H by nucleon count), liquid scintillator (~14% H), and pure plastic scintillator (~14% H)
- **Volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m** inside an existing warm dipole
- **Peak flux ~0.7 GeV** — typical hadronic final states have pions and short proton tracks

---

## The Hydrogen Fraction Problem: A Hard Constraint

For a nucleus with mass number A and atomic number Z, hydrogen nucleons as a fraction of total nucleons in a compound is:

**Polystyrene (CH):** ~7% H by nucleon → **fails**
**Water (H₂O):** ~11% H → **fails badly**
**Mineral oil:** ~12% H → **fails**
**Argon (pure):** 0% H → **passes, but no hydrogen signal for subtraction model**
**Carbon (graphite):** 0% H → **passes**

The requirement is ≤2%, which points toward materials that are predominantly heavy nuclei with minimal hydrogen. The practical solution space is narrow:

- **Liquid argon:** 0% H ✓ but argon has known complications (see below)
- **Solid-state high-Z scintillators:** e.g., inorganic crystals — typically no H ✓
- **Gaseous argon/neon tracking:** 0% H ✓, but very low density
- **Low-hydrogen plastic composites:** possible but difficult to get below 2%

The most viable solution combining tracking capability, low hydrogen, fine granularity, and operation inside a dipole field is a **modular liquid argon + fine-grained tracker hybrid**, described below.

---

## Proposed Upgrade: Modular High-Pressure Gas TPC + Thin Absorber Sandwich

After considering several architectures, I recommend a **two-component active target**:

### Component 1: High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC (HPgTPC)

**Technology:** A segmented high-pressure argon gas time projection chamber operating at ~10 bar.

**Rationale:**
- Pure argon → 0% hydrogen nucleons ✓
- At 10 bar, argon density ≈ 0.016 g/cm³ — low enough that short proton tracks (60 MeV KE → ~6 cm range at 10 bar) are fully contained and reconstructable
- TPC gives continuous 3D tracking with no dead zones → 4π muon reconstruction ✓
- Electric field is parallel to beam (or perpendicular — see below), drift electrons collected on segmented anode planes
- **Crucially:** a TPC inside a dipole magnet works well if drift direction is along the magnetic field (B along beam axis would be ideal, but the existing dipole is a warm dipole presumably with horizontal transverse field — drift direction must be chosen to avoid E×B distortions)

**Specific hardware:**
- Drift field: ~200 V/cm over ~45 cm drift cells (segment the 90 cm beam-direction depth into two back-to-back drift volumes of 45 cm each, with central cathode)
- **Anode readout:** Micro-Pattern Gas Detectors (MPGDs), specifically **MicroMegas** tiles, each ~10 cm × 10 cm, with 2D strip readout at ~1 mm pitch
- MicroMegas is preferred over GEM stacks here because: bulk MicroMegas has spark protection built in, they are robust against the relatively high ion flux from a neutrino beam spill, and the mesh-anode gap (~128 μm) gives excellent ion feedback suppression
- Strip pitch of 1 mm gives position resolution ~300 μm in both transverse directions
- Drift time resolution determines z-resolution: with ~8 cm/μs drift velocity at 200 V/cm in Ar at 10 bar, and ~10 ns electronics sampling, z-resolution ~800 μm — adequate for proton track reconstruction
- **Electronics:** SAMPA chip (developed for ALICE TPC upgrade) — 32 channels/chip, 10 MSPS ADC, shaping time tunable 160–300 ns; this is a proven solution for similar drift conditions
- **Pressure vessel:** The 2.6 m × 2.3 m cross-section at 10 bar requires a stainless steel pressure vessel with ~2 cm wall thickness; this is mechanically straightforward but adds dead material at the vessel walls — mitigate by locating vessel walls outside the fiducial volume

**E×B issue in existing dipole:** The existing warm dipole has B ≈ 0.15 T transverse (say, in x) over 6.5 m. If the TPC drifts in y (vertical), the E×B drift will bias tracks by approximately:

> δy/z ≈ (ωτ) where ωτ = μ_e · B ≈ (0.07 m²/V·s at 10 bar scaled appropriately) × 0.15 T

This is calculable and correctable with a detailed field map, but it must be mapped precisely. Alternatively, **orient the drift in the beam direction (z)**, making the central cathode transverse to the beam, with the E field anti-parallel to beam on each side. Then E is along z and B is along x; E×B force is along y and is uniform and large-scale — correctable. This orientation also means backward-going muons drift toward the upstream anode, giving natural efficiency for backward tracks.

---

### Component 2: Scintillator Planes for Triggering and dE/dx Anchoring

A pure HPgTPC has limited self-triggering capability because gas ionization signals are slow and the neutrino beam spill structure may require a faster trigger.

**Technology:** Thin planes of **gadolinium-doped lithium glass scintillator** or, more practically, **Saint-Gobain BC-408 plastic scintillator bars with WLS fiber readout**, placed at the upstream and downstream faces of the TPC pressure vessel.

Wait — plastic scintillator has ~14% H. These must be **outside** the fiducial volume and thin enough that they do not constitute significant target mass.

**Revised approach:** Use **SiPM-instrumented extruded plastic scintillator bars** (same technology as MINERvA's outer detector or NOvA cells) purely as a trigger and veto layer, 2 cm thick, positioned at the four lateral faces and both beam-direction faces of the TPC vessel. These are explicitly excluded from the fiducial volume by a geometric cut with margin. Total scintillator mass ≪ total argon mass, so the nucleon-weighted hydrogen fraction remains well below 2%.

**Specific hardware:**
- Extruded scintillator bars, 3 cm × 1.5 cm cross section, doped with 0.1% wavelength shifter, with 1.2 mm Kuraray Y-11 WLS fiber through central groove
- SiPMs: Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS (50 μm pixel pitch, 667 pixels, PDE ~40% at 450 nm), one per fiber end
- Trigger logic: coincidence of ≥3 adjacent bars in any plane within a 50 ns window, fed to a simple FPGA-based trigger board (e.g., using Xilinx Artix-7)

---

### Component 3: Downstream Muon Ranger

The existing gas drift chambers downstream already handle high-momentum muons. However, for **backward-going and large-angle muons**, a dedicated range stack is needed.

**Technology:** **Magnetized iron range stack** is tempting but the existing dipole already curves tracks — instead, use a **scintillator-only muon ranger** downstream that works with the existing drift chambers.

Actually, for backward-going tracks (the hardest case), the muon exits the upstream face of the TPC. The 410 m to the production target means there is no upstream detector. Therefore:

**Proposal:** Add an **upstream scintillator muon catcher**, a stack of 20 planes of 3 cm-thick iron absorber interleaved with scintillator strips (2 cm × 1 cm, SiPM readout, same technology as above), extending 60 cm upstream of the TPC pressure vessel. This provides ~3.3 nuclear interaction lengths — sufficient to range out muons up to ~400 MeV. Higher-momentum backward muons will exit this stack and their momentum is determined by the range + curvature in the main dipole field (which they traverse before exiting upstream).

For large-angle (near 90°) muons, they exit through the lateral walls of the TPC and enter the region of the main dipole magnet bore. The existing downstream drift chambers don't cover these. **Propose adding four planes of large-area scintillator strip detectors on the lateral walls of the magnet bore**, instrumented identically to the trigger planes, to catch 90° tracks and provide at least a range measurement.

---
