## Critical Design Warnings for the Panel

1. **The 2% hydrogen constraint is the single most dangerous pitfall.** Any O-ring, adhesive, epoxy, or G10 circuit board inside the gas volume must be tracked in the hydrogen budget. Assign a dedicated engineer to this accounting before PDR.

2. **Drift distance of 0.9 m at pressure requires exceptional gas purity.** Electron lifetime must exceed ~1 ms. This demands a closed-loop gas recirculation system with molecular sieve and oxygen-scrubbing cartridges, plus continuous purity monitoring with a small reference TPC cell.

3. **MicroMegas discharge rate in a neutrino beam environment** (cosmics + beam halo) must be evaluated; bulk MicroMegas or resistive-strip MicroMegas are preferred over standard meshes to limit discharge damage and dead time.

4. **The backward muon efficiency requirement is the hardest to meet** and should be validated by full Geant4 simulation with realistic beam composition before the upstream range stack depth is finalised. 25% efficiency for backward tracks at, say, 500 MeV/c requires at minimum ~60 cm of iron equivalent upstream, which may conflict with the upstream beamline geometry.

# Design Review Recommendations: ND280 Upstream Active Target

## Executive Summary

The core challenge is reconstructing kinematically complete CC events — including large-angle, low-momentum protons — in a 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box where the 0.6 m dimension along beam is severely constraining. I recommend a **Super-FGD cubed-scintillator active target** as the primary detector, flanked by two thin TPCs, with augmented photon detection. Each technology choice is justified below.

---

## 1. Active Target: Super-FGD (3D Plastic Scintillator Array)

### Specification
An array of **1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes**, each with three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres threaded through drilled channels along x, y, and z, read out by MPPCs (SiPMs). At the available box dimensions, approximately **192 × 182 × 57 cubes** (~2.0 million channels, ~1.8 t of hydrocarbon target) fill the volume, with the short 57-cube dimension along the beam axis.

### Justification

**Large-angle proton acceptance.** The existing FGD1 architecture — 2D layers of parallel bars — reconstructs tracks only if they cross enough layers. A proton emitted at 70° to beam in FGD1 may traverse only 2–3 scintillator layers before exiting. The 3D cubic geometry gives effectively **4π segmentation**: a proton travelling at any polar angle crosses approximately d/cos(θ) cubes along its path, so even a track at 80° deposits visible hits in ~6 cubes along the transverse plane. The stated ~35% of leading protons leaving beyond 50° makes this qualitatively essential, not merely desirable.

**Low-momentum proton tracking.** A 450 MeV/c proton (median of distribution) has a range of ~18 cm in polystyrene. In the 60 cm along-beam dimension this is comfortably contained. More critically, protons down to ~300 MeV/c (range ~8 cm) cross ~8 cubes, giving enough hits for track reconstruction and dE/dx particle identification. In a conventional FGD bar geometry at this momentum, a large-angle track may traverse only 1–2 bars, making it unrecoverable.

**dE/dx particle identification.** Cube-by-cube energy deposition allows Bragg-peak identification of stopping protons versus pions, critical for rejecting charged-pion contamination in the recoil system.

**Hydrocarbon target composition.** The CH material is explicitly stated as acceptable and directly matches FGD1 for systematic cross-checks. Carbon-to-water comparison uses the downstream FGD2 as specified; the upstream target need not replicate that.

**Fibre-MPPC readout compatibility.** The existing ND280 DAQ, slow-control, and MPPC procurement infrastructure are retained, minimising cost and commissioning risk. The T2K collaboration has already developed this exact technology (Super-FGD was prototyped and approved for the ND280 upgrade), so technical readiness level is high.

---

## 2. Flanking Tracking Detectors: Two Thin Horizontal TPCs

### Specification
Install one **High-Angle TPC (HA-TPC)** immediately upstream of the Super-FGD and one immediately downstream, each approximately **2.0 × 1.9 × 0.25 m** (along beam), using the same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H10 95:3:2 gas mixture and bulk Micromegas readout as the existing TPC1–3. Total added length ~0.5 m, fitting within or just outside the declared box if the box boundary is taken as the Super-FGD envelope; alternatively, they can be integrated within the 0.6 m by reducing the Super-FGD depth to ~40 cm (~40 cubes along z, still sufficient for the median proton range).

### Justification

**Muon momentum measurement.** The 0.2 T dipole magnetic field is what the entire detector relies on for momentum measurement by curvature. A muon travelling forward enters TPC downstream of the Super-FGD and its momentum is measured there, identical to the existing TPC1 role for FGD interactions. The upstream HA-TPC catches backward-going or very-large-angle muons, which the existing geometry cannot handle at all from this upstream position.

**Sign determination and charge identification.** Without a TPC on at least one side, there is no charge-sign measurement for the muon, and the ν_μ CC signal cannot be cleanly separated from ν̄_μ CC background, which is a leading systematic. The magnetic field acts on tracks in both TPCs identically to the existing system.

**Large-angle muon acceptance.** The ~25% of muons beyond 50° are the most problematic. Many of these will not reach TPC1 (now much further downstream) with enough path length for a good curvature measurement. Having a TPC immediately adjacent to the Super-FGD on both sides maximises lever arm for large-angle tracks, which curve predominantly in the transverse plane and need lateral TPC coverage. The 1.9 m transverse dimension of the HA-TPC matches the magnet bore envelope and provides ~±0.95 m transverse acceptance.

**High-momentum proton veto cross-check.** The ~6% of protons above 900 MeV/c (range >1 m in polystyrene) will punch through the Super-FGD and enter the downstream HA-TPC, where their momentum can be directly measured rather than estimated from range alone, improving the high-momentum tail of the proton spectrum and reducing systematic uncertainty in that region.

**Technology reuse.** Using the same gas system, Micromegas pads, and front-end electronics as the existing TPCs reduces procurement complexity and allows the existing gas recirculation and monitoring infrastructure to be extended rather than duplicated from scratch.

---

## 3. MPPC Upgrade: Higher Dynamic Range and UV-Extended Devices

### Specification
Replace the current **667-pixel Hamamatsu S10362-13-050C** MPPCs (or equivalent) used in the Super-FGD WLS fibre readout with **~3,600-pixel devices** (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS series or equivalent SiPM with ~50 μm cell pitch, 3×3 mm² active area), one per fibre end, with single-ended readout to control channel count.

### Justification

**Dynamic range saturation.** At the Bragg peak of a stopping proton, local energy deposition in a 1 cm cube can be 5–10 MIP-equivalent. A 667-pixel device saturates above ~200 photoelectrons at typical occupancy, distorting the dE/dx measurement precisely where PID is most needed. A 3,600-pixel device extends the linear range by a factor of ~5, covering the Bragg peak without saturation correction.

**PID for transverse kinematic imbalance.** The δp_T and δα_T variables that quantify nuclear effects are sensitive to whether the recoil is a proton or pion. Correct PID through the Bragg peak shape directly reduces the leading systematic on these observables, which is the stated physics goal.

**Cost and infrastructure.** The 3×3 mm² format is compatible with the existing WLS fibre (Kuraray Y-11, 1 mm diameter) coupling geometry used throughout ND280, requiring no fibre or mechanical redesign.

---

## 4. Timing System: 1 ns Resolution Scintillator-Based TOF Layer

### Specification
Add a single layer of **fast plastic scintillator paddles** (e.g., EJ-228, τ_decay ~1.4 ns) on the four lateral faces of the Super-FGD volume (not on the beam-axis faces, which are occupied by the HA-TPCs), each paddle ~2.0 × 0.1 m, read out by fast MPPCs and waveform-digitising electronics (e.g., CAEN V1742 DRS4-based, 5 GS/s), targeting **~500 ps resolution per paddle** and ~1 ns for a track crossing two paddles.

### Justification

**Proton–pion separation by TOF.** At 450 MeV/c (the median proton momentum), a proton traversing 30 cm of scintillator arrives ~2.5 ns later than a pion of the same momentum. At 1 ns timing resolution this is a 2.5σ separation — usable for statistical PID cross-checks of the dE/dx-based identification. At 300 MeV/c the separation grows to ~6 ns and becomes the primary PID for tracks that range out before depositing a clear Bragg peak.

**Neutron background rejection.** CC events with neutrons in the final state produce delayed hits from hadronic re-interactions. A 1 ns timing layer on the faces allows neutron-induced fake tracks (entering from outside) to be tagged by their time-of-flight signature, reducing a background that is otherwise indistinguishable from large-angle proton tracks in the Super-FGD alone.

**Low incremental cost.** Only the lateral faces need coverage (~8 m² total); the beam-axis faces are already instrumented by the HA-TPCs. Fast scintillator paddles with MPPC readout are a mature, low-cost technology.

---

## 5. Mechanical and Integration Changes

### Remove P0D Entirely
The full P0D (16.1 t with water, 2.4 m along beam) must be extracted. The declared 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box fits within the freed volume. The P0D water-target physics programme is superseded by FGD2 for water comparisons; no physics case is lost.

**Support structure:** The P0D basket and its rail system must be removed and new rails installed at the same gauge as the existing FGD/TPC cradles so that the Super-FGD + HA-TPC assembly slides into the magnet bore on standard ND280 tooling. This is a mechanical engineering requirement with no novel technology risk.

**Gas plumbing:** Extend existing TPC gas manifolds upstream by ~3 m to supply the two new HA-TPCs. Use the same pressure-regulation philosophy (slight overpressure, closed-loop recirculation) already qualified for TPC1–3.

**Cable routing:** The 2-million-channel MPPC readout is the dominant new cable plant. Route WLS fibres to MPPC front-end boards mounted on the lateral faces of the Super-FGD frame, then aggregate to existing TRIP-t (or successor) front-end ASICs on mini-crates. The existing ND280 DAQ bandwidth (~50 MB/s average) must be evaluated for the increased channel count; likely a DAQ upgrade to a 100 Gb/s ethernet fabric is needed, using existing commercial off-the-shelf switches.

---

## Risk and Residual Concerns

**Along-beam containment** remains the principal limitation. With only ~57 cubes (57 cm) along z, a 900 MeV/c proton (range ~1.2 m) is not contained and must be momentum-analysed in the downstream HA-TPC. This is acceptable but introduces a tracking-match efficiency systematic that must be carefully evaluated during the full simulation phase before final approval.

**Channel count** (~2 M for Super-FGD) is a 30× increase over FGD1. The readout architecture, particularly zero-suppression thresholds and trigger latency, needs a dedicated electronics review before the CDR is finalised. The collaboration should baseline the CITIROC or SPIROC ASIC family and confirm compatibility with the existing clock distribution.

These two items are the recommended focus for the next design review gate.

# Hardware Upgrades for the ND280 Near Detector Proposal

## 1. Active Neutrino Target: High-Granularity Scintillator Detector (SuperFGD)

**Technology:** A 3-D grid of small plastic scintillator cubes (~1 cm³ each), read out along all three orthogonal axes by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres and MPPCs, filling approximately the available 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m volume.

**Why:**
- The existing FGD architecture uses 1D bars in alternating x/y planes, giving a ~13 cm effective 3-D space-point pitch; this is inadequate for reconstructing short, steeply angled proton tracks.
- With ~1 cm³ cubes, tracks at large angles (the stated ~35% of leading protons leaving beyond 50°) are reconstructed with full 3-D continuity regardless of direction, eliminating the geometric acceptance hole that afflicts planar detectors near 90°.
- The median proton momentum of ~450 MeV/c corresponds to a range in plastic of only ~8–12 cm; cube granularity ensures enough sampled points for momentum-by-range measurement even for the shortest tracks.
- Three-axis readout provides unambiguous 3-D hit association, suppressing the ghost-hit combinatorics that degrade pattern recognition in a 2-axis planar device.
- Hydrocarbon (polystyrene) is the natural cube material, satisfying the requirement for CC interactions on hydrocarbon and enabling hydrogen subtraction via carbon-out comparisons with FGD2.
- Scintillator response timing (~1 ns) allows time-of-flight separation of protons from pions at low momentum, improving particle identification without additional hardware.
- The cube geometry is mechanically self-supporting and can be assembled to fit the freed P0D cavity with minimal structural material, keeping non-target mass low.

---

## 2. Time Projection Chambers: New High-Angle TPCs Flanking the SuperFGD

**Technology:** Two additional TPCs with resistive Micromegas or resistive bulk-Micromegas readout, one on each of the two faces of the SuperFGD that are transverse to the beam (the upstream and downstream faces), plus consideration of two lateral TPCs on the top/bottom or left/right faces, depending on magnet volume constraints. Gas mixture compatible with existing system (Ar:CF4:iC4H10 or Ar:iC4H10 with tuned drift velocity).

**Why:**
- Muons leaving forward are well caught by the existing downstream TPC stack, but the ~25% of muons exiting beyond 50° escape sideways or backward into dead material in the current geometry.
- TPCs flanking the target provide continuous drift-field tracking for large-angle muons, delivering momentum measurement by curvature in the 0.2 T dipole field.
- Resistive readout (compared to standard bulk Micromegas) reduces spark damage risk and improves charge spread, giving better two-track separation for the dense vertex region expected in multi-particle final states.
- TPC momentum resolution (σp/p ~ 10% at 1 GeV/c) is well matched to the muon momentum range; the existing downstream TPCs retain their role for forward muons so no duplication is wasted.
- The existing gas infrastructure and readout electronics architecture can be extended incrementally, reducing engineering risk and cost.

---

## 3. Time-of-Flight (TOF) Scintillator Planes

**Technology:** Thin planes of fast plastic scintillator (e.g., EJ-200 or BC-420 equivalent, ~1–2 cm thick, strip or tile geometry) with SiPM readout and dedicated fast electronics (waveform digitisers, ~100 ps timing resolution), placed on the upstream face and both lateral faces of the SuperFGD assembly.

**Why:**
- Protons and pions of the same momentum are indistinguishable by curvature alone below ~600 MeV/c; TOF across a ~50–100 cm baseline at 100 ps resolution gives >3σ π/p separation up to ~1 GeV/c, covering the bulk of the leading-proton spectrum and the tail up to the stated 6% above 900 MeV/c.
- TOF also tags beam-related backgrounds and resolves the interaction time vertex within the ~580 ns RF bunch structure at J-PARC.
- SiPM readout is uniform with the existing MPPC (SiPM) technology across ND280, reducing the number of distinct photosensor technologies requiring calibration and spares.
- The planes are thin enough to introduce negligible additional nuclear interaction length before the target volume, preserving the neutrino interaction rate.

---

## 4. Upgraded Downstream Electromagnetic Calorimeters (or New Lateral ECals)

**Technology:** Addition of lateral electromagnetic calorimeter panels on the sides of the new target region not already covered by the existing ECal, using the same Pb–scintillator sampling structure with WLS fibre and MPPC readout already established in ND280, with updated front-end ASICs (e.g., CITIROC or successor) for higher dynamic range.

**Why:**
- Photons from π⁰ decay are essential for identifying and vetoing neutral-current backgrounds and for measuring CC-π⁰ contamination; the SuperFGD itself has poor photon energy resolution.
- The new target geometry opens solid-angle gaps in the existing ECal coverage (the original ECal was designed around the P0D/TPC/FGD stack); new lateral panels restore hermetic photon containment.
- Upgraded ASICs handle the higher hit multiplicity expected from the more active target volume without saturation, while maintaining backward compatibility with the existing slow control and DAQ.

---

## 5. Upgraded Data Acquisition and Trigger System

**Technology:** A triggerless (self-triggered) DAQ architecture based on streaming readout, using high-speed serialiser links (e.g., GBT or lpGBT protocol) from front-end boards to an ATCA- or μTCA-based back-end, with software triggering running on a GPU or FPGA farm.

**Why:**
- The SuperFGD cube design produces O(10⁶) channels; the existing FGD FEE (AFTER ASIC-based) was sized for ~9,000 channels and cannot scale.
- Triggerless readout captures all activity in the spill window, enabling offline reconstruction of secondary interactions, neutron captures, and Michel electrons that are time-delayed and would be lost by a hardware trigger.
- Software triggering allows flexible selection algorithms to be updated without hardware changes as the physics programme evolves toward T2K-II running conditions with higher beam power (potentially 1.3 MW).
- GPU-accelerated online reconstruction provides real-time data-quality monitoring, critical for a near detector whose systematic uncertainties directly propagate to the oscillation measurement.

---

## 6. MPPC/SiPM Front-End Electronics Upgrade (All Subdetectors)

**Technology:** Replacement of legacy VA_hardroc and Trip-t front-end ASICs in existing subdetectors with modern low-noise, high-dynamic-range ASICs (e.g., SPIROC2 successor or custom ASIC), plus updated clock-distribution system for sub-nanosecond synchronisation across all subsystems.

**Why:**
- The TOF programme requires ~100 ps system-level timing resolution; the existing Trip-t ASIC achieves only ~2–3 ns, which is inadequate.
- Higher dynamic range is needed because the SuperFGD cubes will sometimes be traversed by multiple particles simultaneously, and the existing 8-bit effective dynamic range causes saturation for heavily ionising stopping protons.
- A common clock distribution upgrade benefits all subdetectors simultaneously and is a prerequisite for the coherent TOF analysis across the new TOF planes, TPCs, and SuperFGD.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | SuperFGD (1 cm³ scintillator cubes, 3-axis WLS+MPPC) | Large-angle proton reconstruction |
| Lateral TPCs | Resistive Micromegas, Ar-based gas | Large-angle muon momentum measurement |
| TOF planes | Fast plastic scintillator, SiPM, ~100 ps resolution | π/p separation across full proton spectrum |
| Lateral ECals | Pb-scintillator + WLS + MPPC | Hermetic photon veto, π⁰ background |
| DAQ/trigger | Streaming readout, lpGBT, GPU software trigger | High channel count, delayed signals |
| FEE/ASIC upgrade | High-dynamic-range ASIC, synchronised clock | Timing resolution, saturation avoidance |

# Next-phase upgrade proposal for the off-axis near detector

## The problem with the current detector

The existing plastic targets are built from x/y bar layers perpendicular to the beam, with the TPCs only downstream. This works well for forward muons but has two gaps:

- **Poor high-angle acceptance.** About 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons leave at more than 50° to the beam. These tracks run nearly parallel to the bar planes, cross few layers, and largely miss the downstream TPCs. The far detector sees roughly 4π, so this phase-space mismatch feeds the extrapolation systematic.
- **High proton threshold and no 3D view.** Each 9.6 mm bar layer gives a 2D view, which limits short-track proton reconstruction. The practical threshold is around 450 MeV/c, which is right at the median proton momentum. Most leading protons, and neutrons entirely, are therefore lost, so transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies are not possible.

Reaching about 4% systematics needs near-4π acceptance, protons down to about 300 MeV/c, and ideally neutron kinematics. The four upgrades below replace the photon-tagging section and are designed to work together.

---

## 1. Fine-grained 3D-projection scintillator target (in the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box)

**Technology**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes. The arrangement is roughly 192 × 184 × 56, for about 2 t of target mass.
- Each cube has a reflective, chemically etched surface and three orthogonal holes.
- WLS fibres run through the holes along x, y and z. Each fibre is read by an SiPM (MPPC), giving three 2D projections and about 56,000 channels.
- The cubes are held in a light mechanical box and positioned on fishing lines before the fibres are inserted.

**Physics motivation**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three orthogonal readout views give the same performance at any angle. Tracks at more than 50°, and backward tracks, are reconstructed as well as forward ones.
- **Lower proton threshold.** Protons crossing only 2–3 cubes are visible, bringing the threshold to about 300 MeV/c in momentum, or about 50 MeV in kinetic energy. This recovers most of the leading-proton spectrum and enables TKI (δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T). TKI separates CCQE from 2p2h and pion absorption, and probes nuclear effects such as Fermi motion and final-state interactions.
- **Particle identification.** Cube-by-cube dE/dx gives stopping-proton PID and Bragg-peak identification. It also gives Michel-electron tagging for π⁺.
- **Neutron reconstruction.** Sub-nanosecond hit timing and fine granularity allow neutron detection through isolated secondary-proton clusters with time-of-flight. This is the only route to the full kinematics of antineutrino CC events.
- **Photon conversions.** Conversions are well localised, partly recovering the role of the removed photon tagger for π⁰ and νe backgrounds.
- **Target nucleus.** The target is hydrocarbon, which is acceptable here. Carbon-to-water comparison remains possible with the downstream water-layer target.

---

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the new target

**Technology**
- Two thin gas TPCs, about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m each, using the same argon-based "T2K gas" as the existing TPCs.
- Ultra-light field cage made of composite or laminate walls, to minimise dead material between the target and the gas.
- Readout by resistive (encapsulated) bulk Micromegas modules. The resistive anode spreads the charge, so about 1 cm pads still give spatial resolution of a few hundred µm, with fewer channels and spark protection.
- Front-end electronics based on the AFTER/DREAM-type ASICs inherited from the existing TPCs.

**Physics motivation**
- **Momentum and charge for escaping high-angle tracks.** High-angle muons and the hardest protons (about 6% above 900 MeV/c, roughly 350 MeV kinetic energy, with ranges well over 0.6 m in plastic) escape the target. In the 0.2 T field, the HA-TPCs measure their momentum and charge from curvature.
- **PID from ionisation.** dE/dx in gas gives better than 10% resolution, separating μ, p, π and e.
- **Kinematic completeness.** With the target, this closes the angular hole between the target and the downstream TPCs and the ECal. Muon acceptance becomes nearly 4π, matching the far detector's phase space.

---

## 3. Time-of-flight panels enclosing the new target and HA-TPCs

**Technology**
- Six planes of long plastic scintillator bars, around 220 × 12 × 1 cm, surrounding the target and HA-TPC assembly.
- Each bar is read out at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Time resolution is about 150 ps or better.

**Physics motivation**
- **Track direction.** The panels distinguish tracks entering from outside from tracks leaving the target, which separates backward-going muons from incoming background.
- **Out-of-fiducial rejection.** They reject sand muons and other out-of-fiducial-volume events, which matters most for the high-angle sample, where these backgrounds are largest.
- **Additional PID.** Timing combined with momentum helps e/μ and μ/p separation near the dE/dx crossing points.
- **Timing reference.** The panels provide an event start time for neutron time-of-flight in the target.

---

## 4. Supporting upgrades

- **Electronics, DAQ and trigger.** New front-end boards for the roughly 56,000 target channels, giving sub-ns timing and handling higher rates as the beam power increases toward about 1.3 MW. A common clock is shared with the ToF.
- **Calibration.** LED and laser systems for the target and the ToF, and a laser or UV system for the HA-TPC field and drift velocity.
- **Retained legacy detectors.**
  - The downstream water-layer target stays for O/C separation.
  - The magnet-gap scintillator stays for side muons.
  - The SiPMs in the existing ECal may need ageing replacement.

---

## Net effect on the physics programme

| Quantity | Current | Upgraded |
|---|---|---|
| Muon acceptance | Mainly forward (cos θ ≳ 0.6) | Nearly 4π, including backward |
| Proton threshold | ~450 MeV/c | ~300 MeV/c |
| Neutrons | None | Kinematics via ToF |
| TKI / exclusive final states | Not possible | Full measurements |

The upgraded near detector measures muon, proton and neutron kinematics over the full phase space seen at the far detector. This constrains the nuclear-model and 2p2h uncertainties that dominate the current 6% systematic, putting the target of about 4% within reach.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (Active Target)**

**Technology:** Extruded plastic scintillator bars (1.0 × 1.0 cm² cross-section) with wavelength-shifting fiber readout and silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays, arranged in alternating X-Y-Z orientation layers.

**Physics Motivation:** 
- **Short proton tracking**: 60 MeV protons have ~1 cm range in plastic scintillator (ρ ≈ 1 g/cm³), requiring cm-scale granularity
- **4π angular acceptance**: Fine segmentation enables reconstruction of backward-going muons and perpendicular tracks within the target volume
- **Timing resolution**: ~ns timing distinguishes interaction vertex from track segments in the magnetic field region
- **Hydrogen content control**: Plastic scintillator (CH₂) provides ~14% hydrogen by nucleon count, safely below the 20% constraint

## 2. **Super-FGT: Time Projection Chamber with Resistive Micromegas**

**Technology:** Gas TPC (Ar:CH₄:CF₄ 95:3:2 mix) with resistive Micromegas readout on 3 mm pitch pads covering all six faces of the target volume.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Full 3D tracking with dE/dx**: Continuous tracking of all charged particles enables particle ID through energy loss
- **Low mass**: Minimal multiple scattering preserves momentum measurement for low-energy protons
- **Hydrogen tuning**: Gas mixture allows precise control of hydrogen fraction (can achieve 10-15% H nucleon fraction)
- **Backward track capability**: Electric field drift enables reconstruction of tracks exiting any face of the volume
- **60 MeV proton threshold**: ~3 cm range in the low-density gas ensures multiple measurement points

## 3. **Surrounding Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECAL)**

**Technology:** Lead-scintillator sampling calorimeter with 5 mm Pb / 2 mm scintillator layers, wavelength-shifting fiber readout, surrounding the target on 5 sides (all except downstream).

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Photon detection from π⁰ → γγ**: Critical for distinguishing νₑ CC events from νμ CC + π⁰ backgrounds at this energy
- **Energy containment**: Captures electromagnetic showers from electrons and photons exiting the active target
- **Muon confirmation**: Measures minimum ionizing behavior of muons passing through
- **Backward coverage**: Wraparound geometry catches particles at all angles

## 4. **Vertex Resolution Enhancement: Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) Layers**

**Technology:** Thin (3 mm gas gap) timing RPCs interspersed every 15 cm through the target region, providing <1 ns timing and ~1 cm spatial resolution.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Multi-track separation**: At 0.7 GeV peak energy, quasi-elastic events produce close tracks; timing separates vertices from pileup
- **Improved vertex resolution**: Combined with other detectors, enables <5 mm vertex resolution critical for short proton tracks
- **Triggering**: Fast timing provides trigger capability for DAQ, important at near detector event rates

## 5. **High-Angle Muon Ranger (HAMR)**

**Technology:** Steel-scintillator sandwich (2 cm Fe / 1 cm scintillator) surrounding the target laterally and upstream, instrumented to ~1 radiation length depth.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Perpendicular/backward muon measurement**: These muons don't reach the downstream tracker; need range/momentum measurement by absorption
- **25% efficiency requirement**: Critical for meeting the stated angular acceptance, especially for μ⁻ that curve away from the downstream tracker in the 0.15 T field
- **Low-energy containment**: Captures and measures muons down to ~200 MeV that don't exit to downstream chambers

## 6. **Enhanced Downstream Tracker: Straw Tube Upgrade**

**Technology:** Replace existing drift chambers with 5 mm diameter straw tubes in X-Y stereo layers (±45° relative angles), 4 mm spacing.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Improved momentum resolution**: Factor of ~2 better spatial resolution (~150 μm vs. ~300 μm) in the analyzed 0.15 T field
- **Higher rate capability**: Better for near detector flux levels
- **Charge misidentification reduction**: Better curvature measurement reduces wrong-sign background

## Integration Recommendation

**Baseline configuration**: Options 1 (scintillator tracker) + 3 (ECAL) + 5 (HAMR) + 6 (straw upgrade)

**Advanced configuration**: Option 2 (TPC) + 3 (ECAL) + 4 (RPC timing) if budget permits, providing superior PID and hydrogen control

Both satisfy the 25% efficiency, full angular coverage, 60 MeV threshold, and <20% hydrogen constraints while enabling comprehensive neutrino interaction measurements crucial for oscillation analyses.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: New Active Target for the ND280 Upstream Region

## Design Philosophy

The core constraint is unforgiving: reconstruct both the muon **and** the leading recoil proton in a ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box, for particles exiting at up to and beyond 50° from beam axis, with proton momenta peaking around 450 MeV/c. A 450 MeV/c proton has a range of roughly 9 cm in plastic scintillator, so the target must simultaneously be the tracker — a classic argument for a fully active scintillator design rather than a passive target read by external detectors.

---

## 1. Primary Active Target: 3D Scintillator Cube Array (SuperFGD-style)

### Technology
An array of **1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes**, each cube read out on three orthogonal faces by **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres** running in X, Y, and Z, terminating on **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs, 1.3 × 1.3 mm² active area, ~50 µm microcell pitch)**. This is the SuperFGD design already adopted by T2K and partially validated, so the technology readiness level is high.

### Specific geometry for this box
- Fiducial volume: **192 × 182 × 56 cubes** (X × Y × Z, beam along Z)
- Total cubes: ~**1.96 million**
- Physical dimensions: 192 × 182 × 56 cm, fitting within the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope with ~4 cm margin on each transverse face for mechanical structure and fibre routing
- Fiducial mass: approximately **1.84 t** of polystyrene (density 1.05 g/cm³, filling factor ~96% after fibre holes)
- Three fibre planes per cube face means **~17,000 fibres per axis**, total ~51,000 WLS fibres (Kuraray Y-11, 1 mm diameter, double-clad), each read at both ends to improve light yield and provide hit-time information

### Why this works for the physics
- 1 cm³ granularity gives **~6 mm track pitch** (conservative), enough to resolve the proton vertex from the muon track even at large angles
- A 450 MeV/c proton ranges out in ~9 cm = **~9 cubes**, giving dE/dx-based PID across multiple samplings — distinguishable from pions by Bragg peak shape
- A proton at 50° to beam traverses the full 56-cm depth over ~87 cm of path, still contained for momenta below ~700 MeV/c; above that it exits into the downstream TPC, which is the correct behaviour
- The 25% of muons exiting at >50° escape transversely; they enter the **surrounding ECal** (existing) which is precisely why the ECal must be upgraded (see Section 3)

---

## 2. Timing Layer: Thin Scintillator Trigger Planes

### Technology
Six planes of **3 mm thick plastic scintillator strips (5 cm pitch)**, arranged as three X-Y pairs, placed at the upstream face, mid-depth, and downstream face of the cube array. Each strip is read by a **fast SiPM (FBK NUV-HD, 100 ps single-photon timing resolution)** at both ends via direct coupling (no WLS fibre, to preserve timing).

### Purpose
- Provide a **sub-nanosecond hardware trigger** without relying on the slower WLS-fibre cube readout (~10–15 ns effective rise time)
- Discriminate beam-related interactions from cosmics and out-of-time backgrounds
- The 50 ns beam spill structure at J-PARC makes 1 ns timing sufficient for in-spill pile-up rejection at ND280's ~0.5 interactions/spill rate
- Cross-time-stamp cube hits to the trigger timestamp, enabling **track direction reconstruction** (crucial for distinguishing forward protons from backward-going particles)

---

## 3. Surrounding Electromagnetic Calorimeter Upgrade: High-Granularity Panels

### Motivation
The existing downstream ECal was designed to close around the P0D/TPC/FGD stack and has **coarser granularity (~4 cm scintillator strips)** adequate for photon/electron identification but not for reconstructing **large-angle muon momentum** by range with good resolution. For the 25% of muons at >50°, momentum-by-range in the ECal is the primary measurement strategy (the magnetic field helps for tracks reaching the SMRD, but ECal-stopping muons need range).

### Proposed upgrade: replace upstream ECal panels facing the new target
- **Sampling calorimeter**: 50 layers of **2 mm lead + 3 mm scintillator**, for a total of ~11 X₀ and ~1.2 λ_int
- Scintillator: **triangular-profile extruded bars, 1 cm minimum width at tip**, in alternating X-Y layers, to give effective 5 mm position resolution via charge-sharing — finer than the existing ~2 cm effective pitch
- Readout: **Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS SiPMs** (50 µm pitch, 667 pixels, ~40% PDE at 450 nm) on WLS fibre (Kuraray Y-11, 1 mm), same technology as the cube array for commonality
- **Time resolution target**: <1 ns per layer (achievable with these SiPMs and direct-coupled electronics)
- Panels needed: two lateral panels (top/bottom relative to beam, each ~2.0 × 0.6 × 0.25 m) and two side panels (each ~1.9 × 0.6 × 0.25 m), replacing or supplementing the innermost existing ECal modules in the upstream region

### Why not just use the existing ECal
The existing panels have ~1.5 cm × 10 cm bar cross-section — a 50° muon entering at a shallow angle to the bar axis gives poor spatial resolution and large dead-zone fraction. The 1 cm triangular bars resolve this geometrically.

---

## 4. Front-End Electronics: CITIROC/MUSIC-based Readout

### Technology
- **CITIROC 1A ASIC** (Weeroc): 32-channel SiPM readout, charge measurement via two shaping arms (12.5 ns and 87.5 ns peaking time, selectable per channel), plus fast discriminator for timing. Already used in T2K-related R&D and in WAGASCI.
- One CITIROC handles 32 SiPM channels; for ~1.96M cubes × 6 fibres/cube / 2 ends × some multiplexing, the channel count is large but manageable via **fibre multiplexing**: group 4 fibres on one axis into one SiPM using a **16-to-1 optical multiplexer** implemented as a fan-in connector. This reduces electronics channels to ~**300,000 SiPM channels** — comparable to the existing ND280 ECal.
- Alternatively, deploy **MUSIC ASIC** (University of Barcelona, 8-channel, 14-bit ADC per channel, designed specifically for multi-anode SiPM arrays) for the timing-critical trigger planes where per-channel timing matters most.
- **FPGA-based concentrator boards** (Xilinx Kintex-7 or equivalent): one per 64 CITIROCs, handling zero-suppression, timestamp tagging to 1 ns precision using internal PLL locked to the J-PARC RF signal (508 MHz), and serialised optical output to DAQ.

### Data rate estimate
At 0.5 interactions/spill, ~1,000 cubes hit per interaction, 50 ns spill, the instantaneous data rate is manageable; the main concern is **SiPM dark count rate** (~100 kHz per channel at room temperature, ~50 kHz at 10°C). The magnet hall is unheated and typically ~15°C — acceptable without active cooling.

---

## 5. Mechanical Structure and Integration

### Frame
- **Aluminium honeycomb panels** (3 cm thick, 0.5 mm skins) as the structural walls of the cube array containment box — low density, low neutrino cross-section, dimensionally stable
- The cube array itself is **self-supporting** via stacked modules of 10 × 10 × 1 cube planes, each plane epoxy-bonded at corners only to avoid scintillator stress, following the SuperFGD engineering approach
- Module insertion from the upstream face (beam direction) so that the downstream face mates flush with TPC1, maintaining the existing TPC alignment

### Services
- WLS fibres routed to **SiPM carrier boards** mounted on the four lateral faces, outside the magnet field uniformity volume, keeping SiPMs at ~1 T fringe field — SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields (unlike PMTs), which is precisely why this technology is chosen here
- Low-voltage power: **CAEN A7501 boards** (SiPM bias, 4-channel, programmable 0–90 V, <1 µA resolution) for gain stabilisation; bias voltage tuned to compensate temperature drift at 1 mV/°C tracking

---

## 6. Summary Table

| Subsystem | Technology | Key Spec | Primary Physics Goal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active target | 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes + WLS fibre + SiPM | 1.84 t, ~1.96M cubes | Vertex, proton PID, range |
| Trigger planes | 3 mm scint strips + fast SiPM | <1 ns timing, 5 cm pitch | Hardware trigger, track direction |
| Upstream ECal panels (new) | Pb/scint sampling, 2+3 mm, triangular bars | 11 X₀, 5 mm position res. | Large-angle muon momentum |
| Front-end ASICs | CITIROC 1A + MUSIC | 32 ch/chip, 1 ns timestamp | Zero-suppression, DAQ bandwidth |
| Mechanical | Al honeycomb + self-supporting cube modules | Fits 2.0×1.9×0.6 m | Integration without magnet modification |

---

## 7. Critical Cross-Checks Against the Physics Requirements

- **Proton at 450 MeV/c, 0°**: ranges ~9 cm in cube array → ~9 cubes, fully contained, Bragg peak in last 2 cubes gives π/p separation at >3σ via truncated-mean dE/dx
- **Proton at 450 MeV/c, 50°**: path length through cubes ~14 cm, still contained (exits at ~15 cm depth in 56 cm volume), momentum-by-range accurate to ~3%
- **Proton at 900 MeV/c (top 6%)**: ranges ~50 cm, exits into TPC1 — momentum measured by curvature in TPC, which is the existing strength of the downstream tracker
- **Muon at >50°**: exits into upgraded ECal lateral panels, range measurement gives momentum to ~5% for muons stopping within ECal (~500 MeV/c threshold), harder muons reach SMRD
- **Transverse kinematic imbalance δpT**: requires both muon and proton 3-momenta; the combination of cube-array range + ECal range + TPC curvature covers the full phase space with no geometric dead zone larger than the 4 cm border margin

This design should bring the near-detector systematic uncertainty below the 4% target for T2K-II by virtue of the improved angular acceptance and kinematically complete event reconstruction.

# Upgrade proposal: hardware for the Kestrel Flats near-station active target

## Why the obvious choice fails

The default for an active target in a magnetised near detector is a finely segmented plastic scintillator, as in the T2K ND280 SuperFGD. It would meet the angular and proton-threshold requirements, but it violates the hydrogen requirement:

- In CH, hydrogen nuclei are 1 of every 13 nucleons, about 7.7%.
- In CH₂ they are about 14%.
- The hydrogen-subtraction model is only valid up to 2%.
- The far detector has no hydrogen, so the target should also match the far-detector nucleus.

The active target therefore needs to be essentially hydrogen-free. That points to argon.

## 1. Active target: modular liquid-argon TPC with pixelated charge readout and optical readout

This system fills the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region at the upstream end of the magnet.

**Why liquid argon**
- It contains no hydrogen. Only hydrogenous structural material (G10 supports, readout boards, insulation) contributes, and that must be kept outside the fiducial volume.
- It is dense enough to give a useful event rate.

**Why it reaches 60 MeV protons**
- A 60 MeV proton travels roughly 4 g/cm² in argon, about 3 cm of liquid.
- With about 3–4 mm pixel pitch, that is roughly 8–10 samples. This is enough for tracking and dE/dx particle identification at every angle.
- Because the readout is 3D and isotropic, there is no blind angle, unlike planar trackers, which lose tracks parallel to their planes.

**Why pixel readout and modular construction**
- At 410 m from the target there are multiple interactions per spill.
- Native 3D pixel readout, rather than wire projections, avoids ambiguities in perpendicular tracks and pile-up.
- Optically isolated modules, each with its own light-collection system, give each module prompt timing for its own interactions. This lets interactions be separated and assigned an absolute time (t₀).

**Fit and compatibility with the magnet**
- The cryostat must fit inside the 0.9 m beam-direction allowance. This calls for a thin-walled design using low-Z or low-mass materials.
- A drift field operating in a 0.15 T magnetic field causes no problem for the TPC.

**Gaseous argon as an alternative**
- A high-pressure gaseous argon TPC (about 10 bar) is also hydrogen-free, but it has far less mass.
- At that pressure a 60 MeV proton travels about 2.4 m, which is longer than the target dimensions. This is a long reach rather than a short-track problem.
- Gas is therefore an option only if the event rate is acceptable. Liquid argon is the baseline.

## 2. High-angle magnetised trackers above, below and beside the target

These are gas TPCs or drift chambers, the same technology as the existing downstream chambers, placed inside the magnet around the target's lateral faces.

**Why they are needed**
- The existing downstream chambers only see forward tracks.
- Muons near 90° leave through the sides. In liquid argon a muon stops within about 1.2 m only if its kinetic energy is below roughly 300 MeV. Higher-energy high-angle muons escape uncontained.
- Without side curvature measurement, these muons have no charge or momentum measurement, and the 25% efficiency requirement cannot be met at high angle.

**What they provide**
- Charge sign and momentum from curvature in the 0.15 T field.
- They complement momentum-by-range (contained tracks) and multiple-scattering measurements in the argon.

## 3. Time-of-flight system surrounding the target and trackers

This is a hermetic set of fast plastic-scintillator bars with photosensor readout, aiming for about 100–150 ps resolution, enclosing the target and the high-angle trackers.

**Why it is needed**
- Backward-going muons and high-angle muons must be distinguished from tracks entering the detector from outside, such as muons produced in the surrounding rock and in the magnet.
- Time-of-flight gives the track's direction and rejects entering backgrounds. It also improves particle identification.

**Why plastic is acceptable here**
- The scintillator sits outside the fiducial volume, so its hydrogen does not violate the 2% limit.
- The fiducial cut must exclude it.

## 4. Supporting items

**Retain and integrate the downstream drift chambers.** They provide forward muon momentum and charge, with timing synchronised to the TPC light system.

**Material control and measurement**
- Keep hydrogenous materials out of the fiducial volume: low-hydrogen cryostat insulation, minimal G10, readout electronics outside the active volume.
- Audit the hydrogen fraction to show it stays at or below 2%.

**Cryogenics and argon purification.** These are needed for long electron lifetime in the liquid argon, and they must fit within the magnet's space and its safety constraints.

**Calibration.** Laser and cosmic-ray systems for drift-field and energy calibration of the short proton tracks.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Kestrel Flats Near Station Active Target

## Physics Requirements Summary

Before proposing hardware, I'll make the requirements precise:

| Requirement | Implication |
|---|---|
| Muon efficiency ≥25% at **all** angles including 90° and backward | Cannot rely on downstream spectrometer; must track and identify muons *within* the active volume |
| Proton KE down to ~60 MeV | Range ~3.5 cm in water, ~1.5 cm in iron — needs mm-scale or finer 3D space points |
| Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of nucleons | Limits how much pure hydrocarbon (CH₂, CH₄) you can use; pushes toward heavier nuclei as the dominant target material |
| 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m envelope | ~5.4 m³ active volume inside the existing warm dipole |
| Existing magnet: 0.15 T over 6.5 m | B·L ≈ 0.975 T·m; sufficient for GeV-scale muon charge-sign but marginal for low-momentum tracks |

---

## Proposed Upgrade Architecture

### 1. 3D Scintillator Cube Tracker (Primary Active Target)

**Technology:** Extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, ~1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm, read out by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres threaded through each cube in three orthogonal directions (X, Y, Z), each fibre read by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) at both ends.

**Rationale:**

- This is the SuperCube/SuperFGD architecture (demonstrated by T2K SuperFGD). The 3D fibre geometry gives genuine 3D space points with no ghost-track ambiguity, which is essential for the high-multiplicity final states at 0.7 GeV.
- Cube size ~1.5 cm gives a track length resolution sufficient to see proton ranges corresponding to KE ≳ 40 MeV (range in polystyrene ~2 cm at 60 MeV); this satisfies the proton threshold requirement.
- Polystyrene (CH): carbon and hydrogen in roughly 1:1 atomic ratio. Hydrogen nucleons are ~7% of total nucleons (1 H per 8 nucleons in CH, by mass ≈7%), comfortably below the 20% ceiling. This is critical — a pure CH₂ target would put hydrogen at ~14%, still under the limit, but polystyrene gives margin for ancillary material.
- Scintillation light gives ~ns timing, enabling rejection of out-of-time backgrounds and providing a T0 for drift detectors.
- The granularity gives essentially 4π coverage for short tracks; a 60 MeV proton traverses ~1–2 cubes and is reconstructed as a stub with known direction and range-derived momentum.

**Approximate fill:**
- 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m / (1.5 cm)³ ≈ **1.2 × 10⁶ cubes**
- Three fibres per cube × 3 views × two SiPM ends: order 7 × 10⁶ SiPM channels. This is large but consistent with industrialised SiPM arrays; channel count can be reduced ~40% by multiplexing fibres from the same column onto one SiPM if the column is short in one transverse dimension.

**Mass and density check:**
- Polystyrene density ~1.05 g/cm³; total mass ≈ 5.4 × 10⁶ cm³ × 1.05 ≈ **5.7 tonnes** (before packing fraction and structural material — practical value closer to 4–5 tonnes of active scintillator).

---

### 2. Thin Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) or Scintillator-Bar Layers Interleaved at Module Boundaries

Every ~15 cm (every ~10 cube layers), insert a plane of 3 mm thick scintillator bars (or thin glass RPCs) oriented alternately in X and Y.

**Purpose:**
- Provide a fast trigger primitive (cube scintillation rise time ~3 ns, but light collection can be slow; the bar planes give a clean 1–2 ns trigger signal).
- Serve as "time-stamp" planes for associating cube hits to a beam spill sub-window and for vetoing cosmic muons by time-of-flight.
- Help with track-segment matching across the cube volume in pattern recognition.

**Practical note:** If RPCs are chosen, use low-resistivity Bakelite or glass operated in avalanche mode to handle the modest rate environment at 410 m (rate will be low compared to on-axis detectors).

---

### 3. Muon Identification and Momentum Measurement Strategy

The existing dipole provides **B·L ≈ 1 T·m**, giving a sagitta of:

$$s = \frac{0.3 \cdot B \cdot L^2}{8 p} \approx \frac{0.3 \times 0.15 \times 6.5^2}{8 p} \approx \frac{0.24 \text{ T·m}^2}{8 p}$$

For a 500 MeV/c muon, s ≈ 6 cm — well measurable by the downstream drift chambers. For a 90° or backward-going muon that **does not reach the downstream drift chambers**, the cube tracker itself must provide momentum:

**Range–momentum method in the cube tracker:** A muon stopping inside the active volume has its momentum determined from range to ~2–3%. For through-going muons at large angles, the sagitta in the magnetic field measured by the cubes' 1.5 cm resolution gives:

$$\sigma_p / p \approx \frac{\sigma_x \cdot 8p}{0.3 B L^2} \sim \frac{1.5 \text{ cm} \times 8 \times 1 \text{ GeV/c}}{0.3 \times 0.15 \times L^2}$$

For a 1 m lever arm at 90° inside the cube volume, this is marginal (~30–50%), but the efficiency requirement is only ≥25%, and the momentum scale for 90° muons near threshold (p_μ ≳ 200 MeV/c to exit the nucleus) is such that range is the dominant tool anyway. The upgrade therefore includes:

**3a. Downstream Muon Catcher Upgrade (optional but recommended):**
Add 2–3 planes of 3 cm thick iron absorber + scintillator bar sandwiches (a mini muon ranger) immediately downstream of the cube volume but still within the magnet bore. This:
- Ranges out and identifies muons with momenta 200–600 MeV/c that exit the cube tracker forward.
- Provides a clean muon tag and range measurement independent of the drift chambers.
- Iron planes can double as the structural frame holding the cube modules.

**3b. Side and upstream muon taggers:**
Surround the cube volume on all six faces (top, bottom, beam-left, beam-right, upstream face, and the downstream face toward the muon catcher) with planes of 1 cm × 5 cm scintillator bars read by SiPMs. These:
- Identify exiting tracks on any face.
- For backward muons: the upstream face tagger records the exit point and direction; range back through the cubes gives momentum.
- Veto external backgrounds entering the fiducial volume.

---

### 4. Summary of Hydrogen Fraction Accounting

| Component | Approx. nucleon count | H fraction |
|---|---|---|
| Polystyrene cubes (C₈H₈ repeat unit) | dominant | H/(C+H) ≈ 8/16 by atom, **≈7% by nucleon** |
| WLS fibres (polystyrene core, PMMA cladding) | small | similar |
| Scintillator bar planes (~5% of mass) | small | ~7% |
| Iron absorbers in muon catcher | adds nucleons with no H | **reduces** overall fraction |
| Structural aluminium/G10 | small | negligible H |

**Overall hydrogen fraction: approximately 7–8% of target nucleons**, well under the 20% ceiling, leaving substantial margin for the model systematic.

---

### 5. Electronics and DAQ

- **SiPM front-end ASICs** (e.g., CITIROC or MUSIC-type): 64-channel chips mounted directly on PCB planes that slide into the cube assembly in one transverse view.
- **Charge + time readout:** 12-bit ADC for charge (for dE/dx particle ID: separates protons from pions up to ~1 GeV/c), TDC with ~1 ns resolution for timing.
- **Trigger:** Beam-spill gate from accelerator RF + coincidence of ≥3 bar-plane hits; zero-suppressed readout of all cubes within a 100 ns window around each trigger. Zero suppression reduces data volume by factor ~100 compared to full readout.
- **Data rate estimate:** At typical near-detector neutrino event rates (~10³ interactions/spill), and O(50) hit cubes per interaction, the sustained rate is ~5 × 10⁴ cube-hits/spill, entirely manageable with modern DAQ.

---

## Critical Design Choices Justified

1. **Why not a time projection chamber (TPC)?** A TPC with argon or neon would give excellent 3D tracking but: (a) argon has no free hydrogen — fine for the H-fraction limit but loses the hydrogen signal entirely; (b) a gaseous TPC has very low target mass per unit volume, reducing statistics; (c) a liquid argon TPC in this envelope would be ~5 tonnes of LAr with no free hydrogen, requiring substantial cryogenic infrastructure not mentioned as available. The cube tracker gives comparable or better 3D resolution with simpler infrastructure.

2. **Why not STT (straw-tube tracker with polypropylene target plates)?** STT would increase hydrogen fraction. Polypropylene (CH₂) gives ~14% hydrogen nucleons — still under 20% — but leaves less margin. The cube approach at ~7% is safer.

3. **Why 1.5 cm cubes rather than coarser?** A 60 MeV proton has a range of ~3.3 cm in polystyrene. With 1.5 cm cubes it deposits energy in 2–3 cubes, giving a reconstructable stub with direction. At 2 cm or larger, single-cube hits dominate and direction is lost.

4. **Why retain the existing magnet and drift chambers?** They remain essential for forward high-momentum muons (p > ~600 MeV/c) where range in the cube tracker is insufficient and curvature measurement in the magnet is the only momentum handle. The upgrade is designed to be **additive**, filling the gap at large and backward angles where the spectrometer is blind, without replacing working hardware.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Next-Phase Near Detector

## Framing the Design Problem

The core constraints are:
- Box envelope: ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m (shallow along beam)
- Need kinematically complete CC events: μ + leading proton both reconstructed
- ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons exit beyond 50° — large angular acceptance is essential
- Proton median ~450 MeV/c, with a tail to >900 MeV/c — must range or track low-momentum protons
- Target budget: reduce systematics from ~6% to ~4%
- Hydrocarbon target is acceptable; the 0.6 m depth severely limits tracking length along beam

---

## Upgrade 1: Scintillator-Cube Active Target ("SuperCube" style)

**Technology:** A 3-D grid of small plastic scintillator cubes (~1.5 cm side), each individually read out on three orthogonal faces by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres and SiPMs, with the fibre routing giving stereo 3-D hit reconstruction from coincidences.

**Physics Motivation:**

The 0.6 m depth along the beam makes a conventional layered tracker impractical — there is insufficient longitudinal space to establish track directions from separated planes. A fully active 3-D cube geometry solves this directly: the neutrino interaction vertex is *inside* the target material rather than upstream of a tracker, so even tracks that travel only a few centimetres through a handful of cubes are reconstructed in 3-D from the cube-coincidence pattern. This is critical for the ~35% of leading protons leaving at large angles, which would miss most layers of a planar detector. The ~1.5 cm cube granularity gives a dE/dx sampling pitch fine enough to identify and range low-momentum protons (down to ~300 MeV/c kinetic energy, corresponding to a range of only a few centimetres in plastic) and to separate proton from pion tracks by energy-loss pattern. At 450 MeV/c median proton momentum, the kinetic energy is ~110 MeV, corresponding to a range in polystyrene of roughly 10–12 cm — fewer than ten cubes — so efficient reconstruction requires every centimetre to be instrumented. Polystyrene (CH) is the target material, matching the downstream tracking target composition for consistent cross-section extraction. The fine segmentation also localises the vertex to ~1 cube, reducing the ambiguity in associating recoil tracks to the primary interaction and suppressing secondary-interaction backgrounds in the target itself.

---

## Upgrade 2: Gadolinium-Doped Water or Thin Liquid-Scintillator Layers Interleaved in the Cube Target

**Technology:** Thin (2–5 mm) sealed bags or planes of Gd-loaded liquid scintillator (e.g., Gd-LS at ~0.1% Gd by mass) inserted every few cube layers, read out by existing SiPM infrastructure on the cube faces.

**Physics Motivation:**

Neutron tagging via Gd thermal-neutron capture (capture cross-section ~49,000 barns, releasing an ~8 MeV gamma cascade with ~20–30 μs capture time) is essential for two reasons here. First, neutrons carry away transverse momentum that is otherwise invisible, biasing the transverse kinematic imbalance (δp_T) distributions used for the cross-section and flux extraction — the neutron component is the dominant missing-momentum source in quasi-elastic-like events at 0.6 GeV. Second, the carbon-to-water comparison the programme requires benefits from understanding the neutron multiplicity difference between C and O targets. Even a moderate neutron-tagging efficiency of 20–40% (achievable with thin Gd planes at this scale) provides a statistical handle on the neutron momentum carried out of the interaction. The Gd-LS planes add negligible radiation length (thin compared to the cube material) and their light is collected without additional photosensors, keeping the material budget and cost low.

---

## Upgrade 3: High-Granularity Silicon-Strip or Pixel Layer at the Upstream Face

**Technology:** One to two planes of silicon microstrip detectors (strip pitch ~200 μm) or MAPS (monolithic active pixel sensors, pixel ~100 μm) covering the full 2.0 × 1.9 m face, placed immediately upstream of the cube target.

**Physics Motivation:**

At the beam momenta relevant here, pion-nucleus and nucleon-nucleus charge-exchange reactions inside the target can promote a secondary track to appear as the "leading proton," distorting the TKI signal. A precision silicon plane at the target entrance provides: (a) a high-resolution vertex seed that anchors track fitting inside the coarser-granularity cube volume, improving angular resolution on short proton tracks from roughly ±5° (cube-only) to below ±2°; (b) a multiplicity veto on events with an incoming charged particle from upstream (beam-related backgrounds and interactions in the photon-tagger remnant structure); and (c) a measurement of track impact parameter at the ≲100 μm level, allowing discrimination between primary tracks originating in the target and secondary tracks from re-interactions or halo muons. This improved vertex resolution directly propagates into the precision of the δp_T and δα_T imbalance variables, which are the primary observables for the 4% systematic goal. Silicon planes at this scale (~0.3% X₀ per layer) add negligible nuclear interaction probability.

---

## Upgrade 4: Extended-Acceptance Muon Spectrometer Insert in the Return-Yoke Gaps

**Technology:** Additional scintillator-strip tracking planes (e.g., extruded scintillator with WLS fibre, ~2 cm pitch) installed in the existing dipole return-yoke instrumented gaps, supplemented by a compact resistive-plate chamber (RPC) or thin drift-tube layer on the upstream yoke face closest to the new target.

**Physics Motivation:**

With 25% of muons leaving beyond 50°, a significant fraction will exit the new target laterally and be lost before reaching the existing downstream muon ranger. The existing yoke-gap scintillator was optimised for the original upstream target position; moving the active target ~2 m upstream changes the solid-angle geometry substantially, and many side-going muons now strike the yoke at steeper angles where the scintillator planes provide poor dE/dx sampling and momentum resolution degrades. Adding a tracking layer on the inner yoke face (facing the new target) gives: (a) a matched-geometry track stub for side-going muons that enters the yoke instrumentation near-normal incidence rather than at a glancing angle; (b) a momentum estimate via range in iron for muons that stop in the yoke (relevant for the dominant forward-peaked flux below ~600 MeV/c where the muon range in iron is 50–80 cm); (c) charge-sign determination through the deflection in the 0.2 T field for the subset of muons that traverse multiple instrumented gaps, maintaining the sign-selection needed to separate ν_μ CC from ν̄_μ CC contamination. This directly recovers acceptance for the TKI event sample, increasing the fraction of fully reconstructed (μ + p) CC events by an estimated 10–15 percentage points.

---

## Upgrade 5: SiPM Readout Upgrade to Multi-Channel Fast Electronics with Waveform Digitisation

**Technology:** Replace or supplement the existing SiPM front-end ASICs with a waveform-digitising readout (e.g., 500 MHz sampling, 12-bit ADC per channel) capable of pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) at the single-photoelectron level.

**Physics Motivation:**

At 0.6 GeV, the overlap in time between the prompt scintillation signal from the primary track and delayed signals from low-energy proton recoils, neutron elastic scatters, and nuclear de-excitation gammas spans from nanoseconds to tens of microseconds. The existing integrating-readout scheme sums charge in a fixed gate, which: (i) conflates prompt proton energy deposition with Michel electrons from stopped pions, introducing a systematic on proton energy reconstruction; (ii) cannot separate neutron-scattered protons (slower rise time in plastic scintillator, PSD ratio distinguishable at >50 MeV proton KE with waveform sampling) from electromagnetic deposits, which is relevant for the Gd-neutron-capture upgrade above. Waveform digitisation enables offline PSD to separate proton/neutron-recoil scintillation (slower component fraction ~20–30% in polystyrene) from electron/gamma signals at the channel level, improving proton identification efficiency and reducing the pion-misidentification systematic that currently contributes to the 6% total uncertainty. It also enables precise timing across the cube volume, which improves vertex reconstruction for large-angle tracks that traverse the cube array in an oblique time sequence.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Systematic Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| 3-D cube active target | Scintillator cubes + SiPM + WLS | Vertex resolution, large-angle proton acceptance |
| Gd-LS neutron-tagging planes | Gd-loaded liquid scintillator | Missing transverse momentum (neutrons) |
| Silicon entrance plane | Microstrip or MAPS | Vertex precision, secondary-track rejection |
| Yoke-face muon tracker | Scintillator strips + RPCs | Large-angle muon acceptance and momentum |
| Waveform digitisation | 500 MHz ADC front-end | p/π/n separation, PSD, Michel contamination |

Together, these upgrades address all identified sources contributing to the residual ~6% systematic — large-angle acceptance for both final-state particles, missing neutral-particle momentum, vertex precision, and particle identification — providing a credible path to the ~4% target.

## Proposed Hardware Upgrade: SuperFGD (Super Fine-Grained Detector)

### Core Design Philosophy

## Primary Proposal: 3D Scintillator Cube Array

### Architecture
- **~2 million small scintillator cubes** (10×10×10 mm³ each)
- **Three orthogonal readout directions** (X, Y, Z) via wavelength-shifting fibers through cube centers

**Position resolution**: 
- **5–7 mm** per coordinate (√12 for digital hits, improved with charge sharing)

**Proton detection threshold**:

## Key Advantages

### 1. **Kinematic Completeness**
- Direct measurement of proton vectors at all angles (median 450 MeV/c well within range)
- Transverse momentum balance: δp_T = |**p**_μ + **p**_p + **p**_miss|_⊥ with ~30 MeV/c resolution

### 2. **Systematic Uncertainty Reduction**
Target 4% via:
- **Reduced model dependence**: Direct proton kinematics constrains FSI models
- **In-situ calibration**: Through-going muon dE/dx; cosmic rays; stopping proton Bragg peaks
- **Particle ID**: dE/dx in 3D resolves μ/π/p at vertex with >95% purity for p > 200 MeV/c

### 3. **Handles High-Angle Topology**
- No sterile regions (vs. 2D bar layers with perpendicular gaps)
- Uniform response regardless of track direction
- Minimal edge effects (5 cm fiducial cut sufficient)
