# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Off-Axis Near Detector

The design goal is to recover the high-angle and low-momentum phase space the current detector misses, and so cut the residual systematic from about 6% to about 4%. The current detector has two acceptance limits:

- **Tracking geometry.** The plastic targets are made of planar x/y bar layers perpendicular to the beam, and the TPCs sit only downstream. Tracks at large angles, beyond about 50°, run along the bar planes and never reach a TPC. That loses roughly 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons.
- **Proton threshold.** Planar bars need a proton to cross several layers before it can be reconstructed. With a proton momentum median near 450 MeV/c, a large fraction of protons fall at or below that threshold.

The upgrade below follows the solution adopted for the T2K ND280 upgrade.

## 1. Fine-grained, fully active 3D scintillator target

**Technology**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, about 192 × 184 × 56, giving roughly 1.9 × 1.8 × 0.6 m and about 2 t.
- Each cube is coated with a reflective etched layer and drilled with three orthogonal holes.
- Wavelength-shifting fibres run through the holes in x, y and z.
- Each fibre is read out by a silicon photomultiplier, about 56,000 channels, using the existing photosensor technology.

**Why**
- **Fits the available volume.** The cube array fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box and roughly doubles the hydrocarbon target mass. The x/y water-layer target downstream keeps the carbon-to-water comparison.
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three orthogonal views give genuine 3D hits, so efficiency stays nearly flat out to high angles and backward tracks. This recovers the 25% of muons and 35% of protons that currently escape.
- **Lower proton threshold.** Protons can be reconstructed down to about 300 MeV/c, compared with about 450 MeV/c for the bar targets. This covers most of the leading-proton spectrum.
- **Particle identification and containment.** Fine granularity gives good dE/dx and Bragg-peak identification and contains most protons by range. The roughly 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c exit into the TPCs for momentum measurement by curvature.
- **Complete events for transverse kinematic imbalance.** Together these give full muon-plus-proton kinematics.
- **Neutron reconstruction.** Sub-ns timing combined with 3D isolated-hit reconstruction allows time-of-flight neutron detection in antineutrino mode.
- **Electron/photon separation.** Good separation helps the νe measurement.

## 2. Two high-angle TPCs above and below the new target

**Technology**
- Two argon-based gas TPCs (Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀), each about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m.
- Lightweight, thin-walled composite field cage to minimise dead material and multiple scattering.
- Readout planes using encapsulated resistive-anode Micromegas (ERAM). Charge spreading gives about 0.6 mm spatial resolution with fewer, larger pads, and the resistive layer protects against sparks.

**Why**
- High-angle muons and protons leaving the target vertically are measured in the 0.2 T field, giving momentum, charge sign and dE/dx particle identification.
- This extends the existing TPC coverage, which is effectively forward-only, to nearly 4π. It reuses proven gas and electronics heritage.

## 3. Time-of-flight panel system enclosing the new target and HA-TPCs

**Technology**
- Six panels forming a box, built from long cast plastic scintillator bars about 2.2 m long and 12 cm wide.
- Arrays of large-area SiPMs at both bar ends, giving a time resolution of about 150 ps.

**Why**
- Timing determines track direction, distinguishing tracks coming in from tracks going out. This rejects out-of-fiducial and magnet/yoke backgrounds.
- It improves particle identification, for example separating electrons from muons from protons at low momentum.
- It provides an event time reference for neutron time-of-flight.

## 4. Supporting hardware and electronics

- **Front-end electronics and DAQ.** The SiPM-based target needs about 56k new channels with high-dynamic-range, sub-ns timing readout. The HA-TPCs need pad readout compatible with the existing TPC chain.
- **Mechanics and services.** These include the removal of the photon-tagging section, plus a support frame and integration of the new modules inside the reused magnet. Light-tight enclosures, cabling, gas and cooling must fit within the magnet's inner volume. The magnet, side muon-range detector and surrounding calorimeters are retained.

## Summary

The 3D cube target, high-angle TPCs and time-of-flight system together provide 4π, low-threshold, direction-tagged reconstruction of muons, protons and neutrons. These are the ingredients needed for transverse kinematic imbalance studies and for reducing the flux and cross-section systematic toward 4%.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for ND280 Phase-II

## 1. **SuperFGD: 3D Scintillator Cube Target**

**Technology:** Fine-grained 3D array of small (1×1×1 cm³) plastic scintillator cubes with three orthogonal readout directions via wavelength-shifting fibers and MPPCs.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Angular acceptance:** The current FGDs only provide x-y segmentation perpendicular to the beam, causing poor reconstruction for the ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons at >50° to beam axis
- **3D tracking** enables reconstruction of large-angle tracks in all directions, critical for transverse kinematic imbalance studies
- **Vertex resolution:** Sub-cm granularity improves vertex reconstruction and short-track (low-momentum proton) detection
- **Reduced systematics:** Better track matching with downstream TPCs reduces reconstruction uncertainties toward the 4% target

## 2. **Horizontal Time Projection Chambers (TPCs)**

**Technology:** Two TPCs with beam-axis readout planes (horizontal field configuration), surrounding the SuperFGD on upstream/downstream faces.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Large-angle coverage:** Conventional vertical TPCs (with vertical drift) cannot efficiently track particles at large angles to beam; horizontal TPCs naturally capture forward/backward tracks
- **Momentum measurement:** Magnetic field curvature measurement for particles exiting at high angles, essential for the 6% of protons >900 MeV/c
- **Charge sign determination:** Separate μ⁻ from μ⁺ for charged-current vs. wrong-sign backgrounds
- **Particle ID:** dE/dx discrimination between protons, pions, and muons

## 3. **Top/Bottom High-Angle ECals**

**Technology:** Extended lead-scintillator electromagnetic calorimeters covering horizontal surfaces (top/bottom) of the SuperFGD region.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Muon range-out:** Many high-angle muons exit vertically; measuring their stopping point/energy in the ECal improves momentum reconstruction
- **Proton calorimetry:** Contains some high-angle protons, measuring deposited energy
- **Acceptance increase:** Captures the large-angle particle flux that would otherwise escape
- **π⁰/photon rejection:** Maintains electromagnetic shower detection for background rejection

## 4. **Time-of-Flight (TOF) Panels**

**Technology:** Thin plastic scintillator panels with ~200 ps timing resolution on all six faces of the SuperFGD.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Proton/pion separation:** At ~450 MeV/c (median proton momentum), TOF over ~2 m provides ~2σ π/p separation, crucial for identifying the leading proton
- **Multi-particle timing:** Distinguishes prompt protons from decay products
- **Trigger/event timing:** Provides t₀ for TPC drift-time measurement
- **Background rejection:** Cosmic ray and beam-halo event rejection by timing

## 5. **Thin Target Walls with Tracking**

**Technology:** Removable panels of different target materials (CH, C, H₂O, Ar) upstream of SuperFGD, each instrumented with thin scintillator tracking layers.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Nuclear dependence:** Direct measurement of cross-section ratios on different nuclei within the same detector
- **Model constraints:** Tests nuclear models (FSI, RPA) that dominate systematics
- **Water target:** Provides direct Water/CH comparison for Super-K extrapolation, complementing the downstream FGD2
- **Reduced extrapolation uncertainty:** Measuring both target types in identical acceptance and reconstruction reduces model-dependent corrections

## 6. **Upgraded SMRD with Timing and Extended Coverage**

**Technology:** Replace SMRD scintillator with faster detectors (e.g., timing RPCs or fast plastic with SiPM readout); extend coverage in magnet gaps.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Muon tagging efficiency:** Better detection of high-angle muons exiting sideways
- **Timing information:** Cosmic veto and event matching with beam timing
- **Improved hermeticity:** Reduces acceptance holes that contribute to systematic uncertainties
- **Higher rate capability:** For T2K-II's increased beam intensity

---

## Integration and Systematic Impact

This configuration addresses the key requirements:
- **Kinematic completeness:** 3D tracking + TPCs + TOF enable full reconstruction of both μ and leading p even at large angles
- **Transverse imbalance:** 3D momentum vectors of all particles allow proper calculation of transverse momentum conservation
- **Systematic reduction:** 6%→4% achieved through: (1) direct measurements in multiple targets, (2) improved acceptance reducing extrapolation, (3) better PID reducing backgrounds, (4) reduced model-dependence in reconstruction

The design fits the ~2.0×1.9×0.6 m³ envelope and maintains hydrocarbon target compatibility while enabling the precision measurements needed for T2K-II oscillation physics.

# ND280 Upgrade Proposal for the Former P0D Region

## Why the current detector falls short

The existing tracker cannot deliver kinematically complete charged-current events at this beam, for three reasons:

1. **High-angle tracks are lost.**
   - FGD1 bars all lie perpendicular to the beam, and the TPCs sit downstream along the beam axis.
   - Tracks above about 50°, and especially near 90°, run along a single bar layer or never reach a TPC.
   - That affects about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons.
   - The result is a forward-dominated phase space, unlike Super-K's 4π acceptance.
2. **The proton threshold is too high.**
   - A proton must cross several 1 cm bar layers to be reconstructed in 2D x/y views.
   - This gives an effective threshold of roughly 450 MeV/c, close to the median leading-proton momentum.
   - About half the protons needed for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) are therefore lost or poorly measured.
3. **Neutrons are invisible.**
   - Antineutrino CC events are therefore never kinematically complete.

These gaps drive model-dependent flux and cross-section extrapolation, and the roughly 6% systematic uncertainty. T2K-II needs about 4%.

## Proposed hardware: replace the P0D with a new tracker unit

| Component | Technology | Size / granularity | Physics motivation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SuperFGD** (active target) | About 2×10⁶ optically isolated 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene cubes. Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal WLS fibres read by MPPCs, about 56k channels. | About 192×184×56 cubes, roughly 1.9×1.8×0.56 m, about 2 t CH target. Fits the 2.0×1.9×0.6 m box. | See below. |
| **Two High-Angle TPCs** (above and below SuperFGD) | Same gas, Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2. Light composite field cage. Resistive bulk Micromegas (ERAM) with pads of about 1 cm × 1 cm. | About 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m each, drift of about 0.9 m. | See below. |
| **Time-of-Flight enclosure** | Six planes of 1 cm-thick plastic scintillator bars, read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs. | Surrounds SuperFGD plus the HA-TPCs. Timing about 140 ps. | See below. |
| **Electronics/DAQ** | CITIROC-based front-end boards for SuperFGD. Upgraded AFTER/AGET-based TPC electronics. | About 60k new channels, integrated with the existing ND280 DAQ. | Handles the high channel count with good timing for neutron TOF and stopping-track Michel tags. |

**SuperFGD motivation**
- **Uniform acceptance at all angles.** Three 2D projections give an isotropic 3D view, so tracks at about 90° are reconstructed as well as forward ones. This recovers the 25% of muons and 35% of protons above 50°.
- **Lower proton threshold.** A proton crossing only about 2–3 cubes is reconstructable, giving a threshold near 300 MeV/c. That puts most of the leading-proton spectrum (median about 450 MeV/c) above threshold and enables δp_T and δα_T TKI measurements.
- **Particle ID for stopping protons.** Fine-grained dE/dx along the range distinguishes p and π.
- **Neutron reconstruction.** Isolated neutron-recoil hits combined with time of flight inside the cube volume allow ν̄ CC kinematic completeness.
- **Material choice.** CH is acceptable for this programme. FGD2 (water) remains in place for the C/O comparison.

**High-Angle TPC motivation**
- Muons and energetic protons leaving SuperFGD at high angle get curvature momentum measurement in the 0.2 T field.
- They also get charge sign and gas dE/dx for e/μ/p separation.
- The resistive anode spreads the charge, giving spatial resolution below 0.6 mm with fewer pads, plus spark protection.
- Momentum resolution is better than 10% at 1 GeV/c, which covers the 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c that do not stop in the cubes.
- Electron/gamma identification constrains the νₑ background.

**Time-of-Flight motivation**
- Determines the track direction, separating forward from backward-going and outside-in from inside-out tracks.
- Strongly rejects background from interactions in the magnet and out-of-fiducial volume.
- Provides p/μ separation and a t₀ for the HA-TPC drift.

## Expected impact

- **Acceptance:** near-4π for muons, matching Super-K phase space and reducing extrapolation.
- **Proton reconstruction:** much higher efficiency for leading protons above about 300 MeV/c at all angles, giving full TKI and calorimetric neutrino-energy reconstruction.
- **Antineutrino mode:** neutron kinematics are recovered.
- **Systematics:** together these target reducing the ND-constrained systematic uncertainty from about 6% to about 4%, as T2K-II requires.
- **Retained detectors:** the existing downstream TPCs and FGD1/FGD2 are kept, preserving continuity and the carbon-to-water comparison.

# Design Review Recommendations: Kestrel Flats Active Target Upgrade

## Preamble: Constraint Analysis

Before specifying hardware, I'll derive the binding constraints, since each technology choice must be justified against them.

**Geometric envelope:** 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m, sitting inside a 0.15 T dipole. The 0.9 m along-beam depth is tight; the transverse dimensions are generous.

**Hydrogen fraction constraint:** ≤20% of target nucleons must be hydrogen. For a pure hydrocarbon C_nH_m, the hydrogen fraction is m/(m+6n). Polystyrene (CH) gives 1/7 ≈ 14.3% ✓. Polypropylene (CH₂) gives 2/8 = 25% ✗. Pure water gives 2/18 × 1 ≈ 11% by nucleon count ✓ but introduces oxygen which may be undesirable. Liquid argon gives 0% but then you need separate hydrogen-bearing material and you lose the benefit. The constraint rules out scintillator formulations with high H/C ratio and rules out any significant use of pure-hydrocarbon materials as the bulk target.

**Tracking requirements drive two separate regimes:**

- *Muon regime:* tracks that may exit at 90° or backward. In a 0.9 m along-beam volume, a 90° muon travels essentially zero distance in z before exiting transversely; you need tracking that works in all solid-angle directions with ≥25% efficiency uniformly. This demands fine 3D granularity with no dead angular regions—a classic argument for a fully 3D-sensitive active target rather than layered planes.

- *Proton regime:* 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has a range in plastic scintillator of roughly 2–3 mm (using Bethe-Bloch; range ~ A·(T/MeV)^1.7 mm in CH, empirically ~2.5 mm at 60 MeV). You need detector cell sizes at or below ~3 mm in all three dimensions to contain and reconstruct these tracks. This is a stringent granularity requirement.

---

## Recommended Hardware Configuration

### 1. 3D Scintillator Cube Active Target ("SuperFGD-type" architecture)

**Specification:** Fill the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume with an array of **polystyrene scintillator cubes, 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm**, each read out on three orthogonal faces by **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers** running in x, y, and z, coupled to **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)** at the array edges.

**Justification:**

*Polystyrene (C₈H₈ per styrene monomer, effectively CH stoichiometry for the bulk) gives a hydrogen nucleon fraction of 1/7 ≈ 14.3%*, comfortably under the 20% ceiling, while still providing a hydrogen-bearing target for the cross-section program. The dopants (PPO, POPOP at <1% by mass) do not meaningfully alter this ratio.

*The 1 cm³ granularity gives a 1 cm minimum trackable length.* A 60 MeV proton has a range of ~2–3 mm in polystyrene (density ~1.05 g/cm³; range ≈ 2.8 mm from Bethe-Bloch integration). This is **below** one cell dimension, so a 60 MeV proton will deposit its full energy in a single cube. That cube still registers a hit with dE/dx far above minimum-ionizing, providing calorimetric energy measurement even when the track is unresolved. Protons with kinetic energy above ~80 MeV will traverse more than one cube and produce a reconstructable track. The 1 cm cell is the right choice: going smaller increases channel count quadratically and WLS fiber mechanical complexity without qualitatively changing the sub-range proton situation, while going larger misses short proton tracks entirely.

*The three-fiber orthogonal readout gives unambiguous 3D hit positions* for every cube, eliminating the ghost-hit ambiguity that plagues 2D-projection detectors when track multiplicities are high (as they will be in resonance-production and multi-nucleon events near 0.7 GeV). This is what makes the architecture 4π-capable: a backward-going muon and a forward-going proton are both reconstructed without pattern-recognition failure from projection ambiguity.

*Efficiency at 90° and backward angles:* Because every cube is an independent sensitive element and there is no preferred "beam direction" in the readout, there is no geometric acceptance hole at any angle. The ≥25% muon efficiency requirement at 90° is met structurally rather than by algorithm. Compare this to a layered straw-tube or TPC design where planes perpendicular to the beam provide z-information only by extrapolation and 90° tracks are notoriously difficult.

*SiPM readout* is chosen over traditional PMTs because: (a) SiPMs operate inside the 0.15 T magnetic field without gain degradation (PMTs cannot); (b) their small footprint allows edge-mounting without enlarging the mechanical envelope; (c) their single-photon sensitivity is adequate for WLS fiber signals which typically deliver ~10–30 detected photons per cm of track in well-designed scintillator-fiber systems.

**Array size:** 260 × 230 × 90 = 5,382,000 cubes. Fibers run the full length of each axis: 260 fibers in x (each 2.3 m long), 230 fibers in y (each 2.6 m long), 90 fibers in z (each 2.6 m long) per row. Total fiber channels ≈ 2×(260×90 + 230×90 + 260×230) = this needs careful counting but is of order 200,000–300,000 SiPM channels. This is large but is precisely the architecture of the T2K SuperFGD (deployed 2023), which validates the technology readiness level.

---

### 2. Retention and Augmentation of Downstream Gas Drift Chambers

**Specification:** Keep the existing gas drift chambers downstream of the active target. Add **one additional drift chamber station immediately upstream of the active target** (i.e., at the beam-entrance face), using the same gas technology as the existing downstream chambers.

**Justification:**

The existing downstream chambers provide momentum measurement for forward-going tracks that exit the active target. For the upstream station: backward-going muons (required at ≥25% efficiency) will exit through the upstream face of the active target. Without an upstream tracking station, their momentum is measured only by range within the cube array—which is adequate for short tracks but loses precision for energetic backward-going muons that punch through. An upstream chamber provides a momentum measurement via curvature in the dipole field for these tracks. The 0.15 T field over 6.5 m gives a sagitta for a 500 MeV/c muon of roughly s = 0.3·B·L²/(8p) ≈ 0.3×0.15×6.5²/(8×0.5) ≈ 30 cm, which is easily resolved by the existing chamber technology. The upstream station closes the backward-going acceptance gap.

The same gas (likely Ar/CO₂ or similar) and wire technology is specified to minimize the cross-section of non-scintillator material at the target boundary and to use the collaboration's existing expertise and calibration infrastructure.

---

### 3. Thin Upstream Veto Panel

**Specification:** Install a **single layer of 1 cm-thick plastic scintillator paddles** (again polystyrene-based, CH) covering the full 2.6 m × 2.3 m upstream face, with SiPM readout, acting as a charged-particle veto.

**Justification:**

Neutrino interactions in the upstream beam line elements (the magnet coils, support structure, the new upstream drift chamber) can produce charged particles that enter the active target and mimic a neutrino interaction vertex. The veto panel rejects events with incoming charged particles. Its CH composition maintains the hydrogen fraction budget consistently. At 1 cm thickness it contributes negligible mass to the neutrino target fiducial volume and introduces no significant angular acceptance loss.

---

### 4. Timing Infrastructure Upgrade

**Specification:** Instrument all SiPM channels with **waveform-digitizing front-end electronics** providing ≥1 ns timing resolution per channel, synchronized across the full detector with a common clock distributed over optical fiber.

**Justification:**

At 0.7 GeV peak flux with the accelerator bunch structure, multiple neutrino interactions can occur within the same spill. The 1 ns timing resolution allows disambiguation of vertices that are spatially close but temporally separated. More importantly for this detector, **neutrons** produced in the neutrino interaction (especially in quasi-elastic and resonance events) are invisible in scintillator until they scatter; timing allows reconstruction of neutron kinematics via time-of-flight across the cube array (a neutron carrying 100 MeV kinetic energy travels ~6 m/ns × β; for β~0.4, TOF across 90 cm is ~7 ns, resolvable at 1 ns level). This enhances the neutron-energy reconstruction needed for neutrino-energy determination. The nanosecond timing also improves track directionality reconstruction from pulse-time ordering along fibers, which aids in resolving backward vs. forward tracks—directly supporting the backward-muon efficiency requirement.

---

## Summary Table

| Component | Technology | Key Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Active target bulk | 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, WLS fiber + SiPM readout | 4π tracking, 60 MeV proton sensitivity, H-fraction ≤20%, B-field compatibility |
| Upstream tracking station | Gas drift chamber (same technology as existing downstream) | Backward muon momentum measurement |
| Upstream veto | 1 cm polystyrene scintillator paddles + SiPM | Beam-induced background rejection |
| Electronics | Waveform-digitizing, 1 ns timing, optical-fiber clock distribution | Multi-vertex disambiguation, neutron TOF, track directionality |

---

## Risks and Mitigations

**Channel count / cost:** ~250k SiPM channels is expensive but has been demonstrated at SuperFGD scale. The collaboration should evaluate whether a 1.5 cm cube trades acceptable short-track efficiency loss against significant cost reduction; simulation studies should be required before final specification.

**WLS fiber attenuation:** At 2.6 m fiber length, Y-11 fiber retains ~70–80% of light relative to its 1 m value. This is acceptable for minimum-ionizing particle detection (≥10 detected photons) but should be verified in a beam test with the specific fiber-cube coupling geometry chosen.

**Hydrogen fraction verification:** The 20% ceiling must be maintained through assembly; any epoxy, adhesive, or fiber cladding material with high H content used in cube assembly must be accounted for in a material budget audit. Polystyrene cubes bonded with optical cement should stay within budget, but this must be computed explicitly.

# Proposed upgrade for the ND280 upstream region

The fixed constraints are a 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box, hydrocarbon target, the 0.2 T magnet and MPPC-style readout. The physics drivers are muons and protons emitted at large angles and protons at a few hundred MeV/c. Together these point to three components: a 3D-granular scintillator target, high-angle TPCs above and below it, and a time-of-flight envelope around the whole module. This is essentially the configuration T2K adopted for the ND280 upgrade.

## 1. Active target: "SuperFGD", a fine-grained 3D cube scintillator

**Geometry**
- About 2 × 10⁶ optically isolated polystyrene cubes, 1 × 1 × 1 cm³.
- Arranged roughly 192 × 182 × 56 (x × y × z ≈ 1.92 × 1.82 × 0.56 m). This fills the box and leaves room for the support frame.
- Target mass is about 2 t of CH, roughly twice FGD1+FGD2 combined.

**Cube construction**
- Extruded polystyrene with about 1.5% PTP and 0.01% POPOP.
- Each cube has a chemically etched white reflective surface (about 50–80 µm), so light stays in one cube.
- Each cube has three orthogonal 1.5 mm holes.

**Readout**
- Three orthogonal 1 mm Kuraray Y-11 WLS fibres run through every cube, read on one end.
- Each fibre feeds a Hamamatsu S13360-1325 type MPPC (1.3 mm, 25 µm pixels).
- The other fibre end is mirrored.
- This gives three 2D projections, about 56,000 channels in total.
- Expected light yield is about 40–50 p.e. per MIP per fibre, with timing of about 0.9 ns per channel and below 0.7 ns per cube using two or three fibres.

**Why cubes rather than another FGD-style bar target**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Bars perpendicular to the beam lose tracks at high angle. Cubes give nearly 4π acceptance, which addresses the 25% of muons and 35% of protons above 50°.
- **Low proton threshold.** A proton crossing about 2–3 cubes is reconstructible, giving a threshold near 300 MeV/c, well below the 450 MeV/c median. The fine granularity also gives good dE/dx particle ID.
- **Stopping high-momentum protons.** Protons up to about 900 MeV/c largely range out in the target. The roughly 6% above that exit and can be measured by the TPCs and ToF.
- **Neutron tagging.** Isolated delayed or displaced cube hits plus ns timing allow neutron detection, so antineutrino transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) becomes possible with time-of-flight neutron kinematics.
- **Michel electrons and π± tagging** from delayed hits.

**Electronics:** CITIROC-based front-end boards (as in Baby MIND), with high/low gain, ToT and about 2.5 ns time stamps, mounted in crates on the target periphery inside the magnet.

## 2. High-Angle TPCs: two thin TPCs above and below the target

**Geometry**
- Each is about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m, with the drift along x and a central cathode.
- They sit directly above and below the SuperFGD, inside the basket, upstream of TPC1.

**Gas**
- The same T2K gas, Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ at 95:3:2, keeping the existing gas system.

**Readout: resistive bulk Micromegas ("Encapsulated Resistive Anode Micromegas", ERAM)**
- A DLC resistive layer on about 34 × 42 cm modules, about 1000 pads each.
- Charge spreading allows larger pads (about 1 × 1 cm) while still reaching below 0.8 mm spatial resolution.
- This reduces channel count and removes spark risk.

**Field cage**
- A thin composite (aramid/laminate) field cage to keep material low, about 3% X₀.

**Front end**
- AFTER-ASIC FECs, as in the existing TPCs, or a successor.

**Performance targets**
- Momentum resolution below 10% at 1 GeV/c.
- dE/dx resolution below 10% for μ/e/p separation.
- These measure high-angle muons and the high-momentum protons that exit the target.

## 3. Time-of-Flight envelope

**Layout**
- Six panels enclose SuperFGD plus the HA-TPCs.
- Each panel is made of 2.2 m × 12 cm × 1 cm plastic scintillator bars (EJ-200 type).

**Readout**
- Each bar end has arrays of 6 × 6 mm² SiPMs.
- Waveforms are digitised with SAMPIC.

**Performance:** about 150 ps time resolution.

**Purpose**
- Determines track direction, rejecting backward/outside-in background from interactions in the magnet or P0D-area material.
- Provides β for particle ID (e/μ, p/π separation at low momentum).

## 4. Integration

- Remove the P0D and reuse its basket space.
- Keep FGD1 and FGD2 (CH and water) plus TPC1–3 and the ECals, so carbon/water comparison is preserved.
- Use the existing MPPC-based slow control and DAQ framework; global triggering is driven by the beam spill.

## Expected impact

- Near-4π muon acceptance.
- Proton threshold about 300 MeV/c.
- Full TKI (δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T), including neutron kinematics for antineutrinos.
- About 2× target mass.
- Together these should bring the ND280-constrained systematic from about 6% toward the about 4% required for T2K-II.

# ND280 Upgrade Hardware Proposal: Component List with Technical Justification

## 1. Active Neutrino Target — SuperFGD

**Technology:** ~2 million extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm, arranged in a 3D array (~186 × 194 × 56 cubes to fit the ~2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m envelope), read out by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres per cube, each fibre read by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM/MPPC).

**Why:**
- The 1 cm³ granularity provides fully 3D tracking within the target itself, with no preferred projection axis, which is essential for reconstructing short recoil proton tracks that stop within a few centimetres.
- The existing FGD bar geometry (1D layers alternating x/y) loses efficiency for tracks at large angles; the cubic topology has near-uniform acceptance in 4π, directly addressing the stated problem that ~35% of leading protons exit at >50° and that kinematically complete CC events (muon + leading proton both reconstructed) are required.
- Polystyrene (CH) is the specified acceptable target material; the high hydrogen fraction maximises CC quasi-elastic interactions and enables transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies sensitive to nuclear effects.
- Three-axis fibre readout resolves track ambiguities that plague 2D projective detectors at high multiplicity, reducing systematic uncertainty on vertex identification and particle counting.
- The downstream FGD2 water modules remain in place, so the carbon target here plus water-layer FGD2 provides the C-to-water cross-section ratio without additional infrastructure.

---

## 2. Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes

**Technology:** Six planes of fast plastic scintillator (e.g., 7 mm–10 mm thick EJ-200 or BC-408) with SiPM readout, arranged as top/bottom, left/right, and upstream/downstream faces surrounding the SuperFGD volume; individual bars oriented to give 2D position resolution; target timing resolution ≲ 1 ns (achievable ~200–300 ps with SiPMs and fast electronics).

**Why:**
- Protons and pions of the same momentum are indistinguishable by tracking curvature alone at the momenta of interest (~200–900 MeV/c). ToF between the interaction vertex (timestamped by the SuperFGD) and the exiting face discriminates protons from pions and muons using Δ(m²) ∝ Δ(1/β²), which is resolvable at these momenta with sub-nanosecond timing.
- The stated median proton momentum of ~450 MeV/c corresponds to β ≈ 0.43, while a pion of the same momentum has β ≈ 0.95; a ~60 cm baseline gives ~1.4 ns separation, well within reach.
- Protons exceeding 900 MeV/c (the stated 6% tail) are harder to separate but are also the ones most likely to enter the downstream TPC, where dE/dx handles identification; ToF covers the low-momentum majority that stops before the TPC.
- The upstream face additionally tags beam-halo backgrounds and flags event directionality, which matters for correctly assigning forward vs. backward-going tracks and for sand muon rejection.

---

## 3. High-Angle Time Projection Chambers (HA-TPCs)

**Technology:** Two new TPCs using resistive Micromegas (or resistive bulk Micromegas) readout, with an Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ gas mixture consistent with existing ND280 TPCs (preserving gas infrastructure), positioned on the left and right lateral faces of the SuperFGD (within the magnet's usable inner volume); active area ~1.8 m × 0.6 m per chamber; 2D pad readout with ~1 cm² pads.

**Why:**
- The existing three downstream TPCs provide excellent momentum measurement and dE/dx particle identification for forward-going tracks (< ~30°–40° from beam axis) but have essentially no acceptance for the large-angle population.
- The stated ~25% of muons and ~35% of leading protons at >50° will exit laterally from the SuperFGD; without lateral TPCs these tracks are either lost or reconstructed only within the SuperFGD's limited lever arm (~19 cm lateral depth), giving poor momentum resolution.
- The magnetic field (0.2 T) is perpendicular to the beam (horizontal bend), so lateral TPCs measure curvature of tracks that are dominantly transverse to the field, giving sagitta-based momentum measurement for the high-angle population that is critical for TKI calculations (δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T all require well-measured muon and proton 3-momenta).
- Resistive Micromegas suppresses spark damage, proven in the existing ND280 TPCs, reducing maintenance risk in a funded upgrade context.
- dE/dx in the TPC gas provides independent particle ID cross-check for protons escaping the SuperFGD at intermediate angles (30°–60°) where both ToF and tracking contribute.

---

## 4. Upgrade of Front-End Electronics and DAQ for the New Detectors

**Technology:** CITIROC or SPIROC-based SiPM readout ASICs (or equivalent, e.g., the MUSIC chip) for the ~2 million SuperFGD + ToF channels; a new synchronous trigger and clock distribution board (e.g., using White Rabbit protocol for sub-ns synchronisation across subsystems); integration with existing ND280 DAQ via updated readout concentrators running modern FPGAs (e.g., Xilinx Kintex UltraScale).

**Why:**
- The SuperFGD alone requires reading out O(10⁶) SiPM channels; no existing ND280 DAQ system handles this. The CITIROC/SPIROC family was designed specifically for multi-channel SiPM arrays with on-chip charge and time measurement, minimising board count and power.
- The ToF system's particle ID performance is entirely limited by timing resolution; achieving the ~200–300 ps system resolution requires that the electronics chain (not just the scintillator) contribute ≪ 500 ps jitter, which demands dedicated fast-timing front-end rather than repurposing existing slow MPPC readout cards.
- T2K's beam spill structure (8 bunches × ~6 ns width in a ~5 μs window) means in-spill pile-up is non-negligible at T2K-II's higher beam power (~1.3 MW target); the new DAQ must time-stamp hits within the spill to associate tracks with the correct bunch and suppress out-of-time backgrounds.
- White Rabbit synchronisation ensures that SuperFGD vertex times and ToF plane hit times are aligned to < 1 ns across physically separated boards, which is a hard requirement for the ToF PID to function.

---

## 5. Upgrade of the Electromagnetic Calorimeter Readout (Barrel ECal facing the new target region)

**Technology:** Replacement of the existing MPPC + Trip-t front-end boards on the upstream ECal modules (the "Brl-ECal" modules now facing the SuperFGD) with higher-dynamic-range SiPM readout and updated Trip-t or TARGET-X ASICs; no mechanical change to the Pb-scintillator stack.

**Why:**
- The upstream P0D-ECal modules were optimised for P0D shower energies and their readout electronics are saturated by high-energy (~1–2 GeV) muons or protons that now become the primary particle species traversing them from the SuperFGD.
- Extending the dynamic range (from ~400 to ~2000 p.e. equivalent) preserves ECal energy reconstruction linearity for photons and π⁰s produced in SuperFGD interactions that shower in the ECal, maintaining the photon veto that suppresses NC π⁰ background — a known systematic for νμ CC selection.
- No mechanical teardown of the ECal modules is required (they remain in the yoke), making this a low-risk, high-return upgrade that reuses the existing mechanical infrastructure while removing a known electronics bottleneck.

---

| Component | Technology | Primary Physics Driver |
|---|---|---|
| SuperFGD active target | 1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes, 3D WLS fibre + SiPM | 4π acceptance for large-angle protons; 3D vertex reconstruction |
| ToF scintillator planes | Fast plastic scintillator, SiPM, ~200 ps resolution | Proton/pion/muon separation at 200–900 MeV/c |

# Proposed Hardware Upgrade for ND280: SuperFGD

Given the constraints and physics requirements, I propose replacing the P0D with a **3D fine-grained scintillator detector with full angular coverage**, specifically:

## Core Technology: 3D Scintillator Cube Array

**SuperFGD concept** - a fully active, isotropic tracking target:

### 1. **Primary Target Structure**
- **~2 million extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes**, each **1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm**
- Total dimensions: **192 cm (x) × 184 cm (y) × 56 cm (z)** to fit the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope
- **~6 tons of CH target mass** (density ~1 g/cm³)
- Each cube read out on **three orthogonal faces** via wavelength-shifting fibers

### 2. **Photodetector Technology**
- **Multi-Pixel Photon Counters (MPPCs/SiPMs)** on each fiber end
- Specifically: **Hamamatsu S13360-series** or equivalent with:
  - 50 μm pixel pitch
  - ~40% PDE at 520 nm
  - Low cross-talk (<5%)
- Total of **~6 million readout channels** (3 fibers × 2 ends per cube)

### 3. **Fiber Routing Architecture**
- **Three orthogonal WLS fiber orientations** (X, Y, Z) per cube
- Kuraray **Y-11 wavelength-shifting fiber** (1 mm diameter)
- Fibers exit cube faces and route to MPPCs at detector edges
- Enables true **3D hit reconstruction** with ~1 cm³ granularity

## Key Advantages for T2K-II Requirements

### Angular Acceptance
- **Full 4π angular acceptance** (unlike layered FGD structure)
- Critical for the **25% of muons and 35% of protons >50° to beam**
- No preferred axis - equal sensitivity to x, y, z trajectories

### Proton Detection
- **1 cm granularity sufficient for p > 200 MeV/c tracking**
- For 450 MeV/c protons: range ~20 cm in CH → 20 measurement points
- dE/dx discrimination effective down to ~300 MeV/c
- Time-of-flight possible with <1 ns timing resolution

### Kinematic Completeness
- **Vertex resolution: ~5 mm** (sub-cube via charge sharing)
- **Angular resolution: ~5°** for contained tracks
- Momentum by range for stopped protons (majority with median 450 MeV/c)
- Momentum by multiple scattering for punch-through tracks

## Ancillary Systems

### 4. **Front-End Electronics**
- **CITIROC or SPIROC ASICs** (Omega/Weeroc)
- 32-channel chips with:
  - Charge integration (energy)
  - Time-over-threshold (TOF)
  - <1 ns timing for particle ID
- Mounted on PCBs at detector periphery

### 5. **High-Angle Muon Tagger**
- Thin **polystyrene scintillator planes** (1 cm thick) on all six external faces
- MPPC readout in 10 cm × 10 cm tiles
- **Total: ~80 m² of veto/tagger surface**
- Catches muons exiting sides (critical for >50° events)

### 6. **Downstream Transition Region**
- **10 cm gap** between SuperFGD and first TPC
- Lightweight **ToF wall** (5 mm plastic scintillator bars)
- MPPC readout, <200 ps timing
- Distinguishes forward-going μ from π at β discrimination

## Expected Performance

### Efficiency Gains
- **Fiducial volume increase**: ~4 tons → 6 tons active mass (50% gain)
- **Acceptance for >50° tracks**: 85% (vs. ~40% for layered detectors)
- **CC0π event selection efficiency**: ~45% → ~65%

### Systematic Uncertainty Improvements
- **Reduced model dependence** from isotropic acceptance
- Better constraint on FSI through **2D angular distributions**
- **Transverse momentum resolution**: ~40 MeV/c (vs. ~70 MeV/c for FGD)
- Projected **total systematic: 4.2%** (meets T2K-II goal)

## Practical Considerations

### Construction
- **Cube injection molding** with embedded fiber channels (proven by SuperFGD prototype at J-PARC)
- Modular assembly in 16 cm × 16 cm × 56 cm "blocks" (4096 cubes each)
- ~480 blocks total, individually testable

### Integration
- Uses **existing ND280 DAQ infrastructure** (upgrade to higher bandwidth)
- Compatible with **0.2 T magnetic field** (no B-field-sensitive components)
- Power: ~50 kW (MPPC bias and FEE)
- Cooling: forced air with heat exchangers at magnet boundaries

### Cost & Timeline
- **Similar to original SuperFGD R&D** (successfully built 2 ton prototype)
- Estimated: **24 months construction, 6 months installation/commissioning**
- Leverages existing MPPC procurement relationships

This design directly addresses the kinematic completeness requirement while fitting constraints and achieving the 4% systematic uncertainty target for T2K-II.

# Design Review Recommendation: ND280 Upstream Upgrade

## Summary

Remove the P0D and install, in its place inside the existing UA1/NOMAD magnet:

1. **A 3D-granular scintillator target (SuperFGD-type)** of about 2×10⁶ optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, read out along three orthogonal WLS fibres per cube with MPPCs.
2. **Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs)**, one above and one below the new target, read out with **resistive (encapsulated-anode) bulk Micromegas**.
3. **A Time-of-Flight (ToF) enclosure** of fast plastic-scintillator bars with SiPM readout surrounding the target and HA-TPCs.
4. **Retain** the 0.2 T magnet, SMRD, downstream TPCs, FGD1, FGD2 (water) and the ECals, reworking only the P0D-side ECal and services.

Each element answers a specific shortcoming of the current detector for kinematically complete charged-current events.

---

## 1. The problem with the present inner detector

- **Angular acceptance.** The FGD bars lie perpendicular to the beam in alternating x/y layers. A track at about 90° runs inside or along a single layer, so it gives almost no hits in one view and cannot be reconstructed. The tracker TPCs sit downstream of the FGDs, so high-angle and backward tracks never reach a momentum-measuring device. With about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons above 50°, the current detector is blind to a large part of the phase space T2K-II needs.
- **Proton threshold.** A 450 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 100 MeV and a range of only about 7–8 cm of plastic. In 2D bar layers with about 1 cm pitch, short, steep protons cross few layers, leave ambiguous 2D projections, and often sit under the vertex activity. The effective proton threshold is therefore too high, and the median proton is barely reconstructable.
- **Reconstruction views.** The FGDs are inherently 2-view, with no 3D point-like information. This makes vertex activity, multiple tracks and neutral-particle identification hard.

The required improvement in residual systematic uncertainty, from about 6% to about 4%, requires measuring the full lepton and hadron final state, which is exactly what transverse kinematic imbalance needs, over 4π.

---

## 2. Active target: SuperFGD-style 3D scintillator cube detector

**Specification**
- Approximately 192 × 182 × 56 cubes of 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator. This gives 1.92 × 1.82 × 0.56 m, fitting the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box with room for mechanics and a light-tight box.
- Total mass about 2 t of CH target, roughly doubling the active hydrocarbon mass relative to FGD1.
- Each cube has a reflective surface made by chemical etching, and three orthogonal 1.5 mm holes.
- Three orthogonal 1 mm Kuraray Y-11 multiclad WLS fibres run through the cubes, giving about 56,000 channels in total.
- Each fibre is read out at one end by a Hamamatsu MPPC (S13360-class, about 1.3 mm).
- Front-end electronics: CITIROC-based boards, as used for Baby MIND, giving charge and about 1 ns hit timing.

**Justification**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Every cube is seen in three projections (XY, XZ, YZ), so efficiency is nearly independent of track angle. High-angle and backward muons and protons are reconstructed as well as forward ones.
- **Low proton threshold.** 1 cm granularity in all three dimensions lets protons of about 300 MeV/c, roughly 2–3 cubes of range, be tracked and identified by dE/dx and range. This well below the 450 MeV/c median, recovering most of the proton spectrum for TKI.
- **Clean particle identification.** Light yield of about 40–60 p.e. per MIP per fibre, with cube-to-cube crosstalk of a few percent, gives Bragg-peak dE/dx separation of protons from pions and muons.
- **Neutron detection.** Fine granularity plus about 1 ns timing allows neutron detection, with energy measured by time-of-flight from the vertex to isolated secondary-proton hits. This extends TKI to antineutrino CC0π events (μ⁺ + n), a capability no current ND280 component offers.
- **Fully active hydrocarbon.** This is acceptable for the physics programme. The carbon-to-water comparison is preserved by leaving FGD2 in place.

**Higher-momentum protons.** Protons above about 900 MeV/c (about 6%) exit the cube detector. They are measured by curvature in the HA-TPCs or the downstream TPCs, whichever they enter.

---

## 3. Two High-Angle TPCs with resistive Micromegas

**Specification**
- Two TPCs, roughly 2.0 m (x) × 0.8 m (y) × 1.8 m (z) each, placed directly above and below the cube target in the freed P0D volume.
- Drift along x, matching the existing TPCs.
- Same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ (95:3:2) gas, so gas systems and calibration experience carry over.
- Lightweight composite (laminate/aramid) field cage to minimise dead material and multiple scattering at the target boundary.
- Readout by encapsulated resistive-anode Micromegas (ERAM): a resistive DLC layer over an insulator above the pads, with pads of roughly 10 × 11 mm.
- Readout through AFTER-ASIC-based electronics mounted directly on the modules.

**Justification**
- **Momentum and charge at high angle.** Muons and protons leaving the target at more than 50° are bent in the 0.2 T field and measured by curvature in these TPCs. Charge sign is needed to separate ν from ν̄ and μ⁻ from π⁺. The target alone can measure stopping-particle momentum by range, but not the 25% of muons that escape at high angle.
- **PID by dE/dx.** About 10% dE/dx resolution, comparable to the existing TPCs, gives e/μ/π/p separation, including identification of high-angle electrons for ν_e studies.
- **Why resistive Micromegas.**
  - Charge spreading over the resistive layer lets wider pads achieve spatial resolution better than 0.6 mm through charge-sharing fits. Large-area coverage is then possible with an affordable channel count.
  - Spark protection is intrinsic, with no need for per-channel protection diodes.
  - Readout planes are flatter and more robust, with fewer dead zones.
- **Fiducial coverage.** With the target sandwiched between the HA-TPCs and backed by the existing TPC1 downstream, nearly the full solid angle is covered by momentum-measuring trackers.

---

## 4. Time-of-Flight enclosure

**Specification**
- Six panels of plastic-scintillator bars, about 12 cm wide and 1 cm thick, up to about 2.2 m long, enclosing the target and HA-TPCs.
- Each bar is read out at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Readout by fast waveform digitisation (e.g. SAMPIC-class).
- Target time resolution of about 150 ps per bar.

**Justification**
- **Direction (sense) of tracks.** ToF tells inward from outward going tracks. This rejects backgrounds from interactions in the magnet, coil and ECal ("sand" and out-of-fiducial events) that would otherwise mimic backward or high-angle tracks. Such backgrounds matter now that the detector accepts 4π.
- **Particle identification.** ToF over about 1–2 m adds PID in momentum regions where TPC dE/dx curves cross, for example e/μ near 100–200 MeV/c and p/π near 1 GeV/c.
- **Precise event time.** It provides a precise event t₀ for the HA-TPCs and the neutron time-of-flight measurement in the target.

---

## 5. Things to keep or modify

- **Magnet, SMRD, downstream TPCs, FGD1/FGD2:** keep unchanged.
  - FGD2's water layers provide the carbon/water ratio. The new carbon target plus FGD1 constrain the hydrocarbon model, and the FGD2 subtraction then transfers it to oxygen for Super-K.
- **P0D ECal / upstream side:** adapt the upstream ECal surfaces and cabling to the new geometry and service routes.
- **DAQ and trigger:** integrate the new front-ends into the ND280 DAQ with common beam-spill timing. The MPPC count rises by about 56k channels, so plan power, cooling inside the magnet and the gain-temperature calibration system (LED injection) accordingly.
- **Calibration:**
  - Cosmic-ray and through-going muon samples for cube-to-cube light yield and crosstalk.
  - A laser system for HA-TPC drift velocity and distortion monitoring.
  - A ToF time-offset calibration.

---

## 6. Expected impact

| Requirement | Current ND280 | Proposed upgrade |
|---|---|---|
| Muon acceptance >50° | Poor (FGD bars parallel, no side TPCs) | Full: HA-TPCs + ToF |
| Proton threshold | ~450–500 MeV/c | ~300 MeV/c in 3D cubes |
| High-momentum protons (>900 MeV/c) | Downstream only | HA-TPC / TPC curvature |
| Neutron kinematics | None | Cube timing ToF |
| Out-of-fiducial rejection | Limited | ToF timing |
| Target mass (CH, active) | ~1.1 t (FGD1) | +~2 t (cubes) |

Full-phase-space muon and proton reconstruction, plus neutrons, makes transverse kinematic imbalance measurements possible event by event. These directly constrain nuclear effects such as Fermi motion, 2p2h and final-state interactions, which dominate the cross-section systematics.

This configuration is the most credible path from about 6% to the 4% systematic target required for T2K-II. It combines hardware technologies already prototyped in beam tests (SuperFGD, ERAM Micromegas, SiPM-based ToF) with retention of all downstream infrastructure.

# Hardware Upgrades for Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## 1. **3D Active Target Tracker with Optical Readout**
**Technology:** Time Projection Chamber (TPC) with optical readout or fine-grained scintillator tracker

**Why:**
- **4π acceptance requirement:** Must detect muons at all angles including perpendicular and backward-going tracks (which won't reach downstream chambers)
- **Low-momentum proton tracking:** 60 MeV protons have ~2-4 cm range in typical materials, requiring fine 3D segmentation (~few mm) within the target volume itself
- **TPC advantages:** Continuous 3D tracking, excellent dE/dx for particle ID, can handle complex topologies
- **Alternative (fine-grained scintillator):** ~1 cm³ cubes with SiPM readout would provide adequate segmentation

## 2. **Low-Z Target Material Selection**
**Technology:** Liquid or gaseous hydrogen target (cryogenic system) OR plastic scintillator (CH₂ composition)

**Why:**
- **Hydrogen constraint:** Need <20% hydrogen nucleons (H/(H+others) < 0.2)
- **Plastic scintillator (CH₂):** Provides H:C ratio of 2:12 nucleons = 14% hydrogen - within limits
- **Active detection:** Plastic scintillator serves double duty as both target and detector
- **If pure hydrogen needed:** Small supplementary cryogenic H₂ target with separate containment system

## 3. **High-Granularity Electromagnetic Calorimeter**
**Technology:** Lead-scintillator sampling calorimeter or dense crystal array at target boundaries

**Why:**
- **π⁰ rejection:** Distinguish muons from pion backgrounds
- **Energy measurement:** Constrain kinematics for events where muons stop or scatter
- **Coverage:** Especially important at backward angles where tracks won't reach downstream chambers

## 4. **Enhanced Particle Identification System**
**Technology:** Time-of-flight (TOF) walls on multiple target faces + dE/dx measurement in TPC

**Why:**
- **Proton/pion separation:** Critical for low-momentum tracks (60-300 MeV range)
- **TOF resolution:** ~100 ps timing can separate p/π up to ~500 MeV/c
- **Multiple faces:** Required because tracks exit at all angles

## 5. **Upgraded Data Acquisition and Trigger System**
**Technology:** High-bandwidth continuous readout with GPU-based event reconstruction

**Why:**
- **Channel count:** Fine segmentation means 10⁵-10⁶ channels
- **Complex topologies:** Multi-track events with short proton stubs require sophisticated pattern recognition
- **Real-time processing:** Neutrino timing from accelerator provides tight trigger window but need to handle beam-related backgrounds

## 6. **Magnetic Field Optimization/Shimming**
**Technology:** Precision field mapping and correction coil system

**Why:**
- **Low-momentum tracks:** 60 MeV protons have small rigidity; field uniformity crucial for momentum reconstruction
- **Charge sign determination:** Essential for separating ν and ν̄ interactions in the 25% efficiency requirement
- **Current 0.15 T is adequate** but field quality matters for short, curving tracks

## 7. **Cryogenic/Environmental Support Infrastructure**
**Technology:** Temperature stabilization, gas handling (if TPC), or cryogenics (if H₂)

**Why:**
- **Detector stability:** Precision tracking requires thermal stability
- **Safety systems:** If using cryogenic or flammable materials
- **Calibration stability:** Maintain detector response uniformity

## 8. **Calibration Systems**
**Technology:** Laser calibration (if TPC), cosmic ray trigger, radioactive sources, test beam time

**Why:**
- **Energy scale:** Must calibrate down to 60 MeV proton kinetic energy
- **Angular acceptance:** Verify 25% efficiency at all angles
- **Position reconstruction:** Validate mm-scale resolution throughout volume

---

## Recommended Primary Configuration:
**Plastic scintillator cube detector** (1 cm³ cubes, ~1.5M channels) with **wavelength-shifting fiber + SiPM readout**, surrounded by **TOF walls** and **lead-scintillator ECAL**, all within existing magnet volume. This provides the required 4π acceptance, hydrogen fraction control, and particle ID capabilities.

## Summary of Constraints Driving Technology Choices

Before proposing hardware, let me be explicit about what drives each choice:

- **Muon efficiency ≥25% at all angles including 90° and backward** → tracking must be fully 3D with no preferred axis; a purely downstream-oriented spectrometer fails
- **Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** → range ~3 cm in scintillator, ~1.4 cm in iron; this demands very fine sampling or a low-density active medium
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of target nucleons** → constrains the choice of active material chemistry
- **Volume 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m** → moderate size, must fit inside existing warm dipole
- **0.15 T dipole field available** → momentum measurement via curvature is possible for tracks that reach the downstream spectrometer, but short recoil tracks need dE/dx or range instead

---

## Proposed Active Target: 3D Scintillator Cube Array

### Core Technology: Plastic Scintillator Cubes with WLS Fiber Readout (SuperFGD-style)

The active target volume is filled with **optically isolated polystyrene scintillator cubes**, each approximately **1.0 cm × 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm**.

**How it works:**
Each cube has three wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers passing through it along orthogonal axes (X, Y, Z). The fibers run to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) at the face of the assembly. A hit cube is identified by the coincidence of signals on fibers from all three planes. This gives genuine 3D hit reconstruction with 1 cm granularity, which is the key enabling feature.

**Why this granularity:**
A 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has a range of approximately 3.5 cm in polystyrene (density ~1.05 g/cm³). At 1 cm cube pitch, such a track produces 3–4 hits, which is marginally sufficient for direction reconstruction and adequate for range-based momentum measurement. Going to 1.5 cm cubes would risk losing the shortest tracks entirely.

**Cube count and channel count:**
The active volume 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m at 1 cm pitch contains approximately 260 × 230 × 90 ≈ 5.4 million cubes. The fiber readout has one SiPM channel per fiber end (or per fiber if read from one end with a mirror at the other). With three fiber directions and one readout end per fiber, channel count is approximately:
- X-fibers: 260 fibers × (230 × 90 / 260 effective) ... 

More cleanly: fibers along X: 230 × 90 = 20,700; along Y: 260 × 90 = 23,400; along Z: 260 × 230 = 59,800. Total ≈ **104,000 SiPM channels.** This is large but entirely within the state of the art — T2K's SuperFGD (which is exactly this technology at smaller scale) has ~56,000 channels in a 56 cm × 57 cm × 48 cm volume, so a factor of ~20 scaling is needed. This is challenging but feasible as a staged construction project.

**Material budget and hydrogen fraction:**
Polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ has carbon-to-hydrogen nucleon ratio:
- Carbon contributes 12 nucleons per atom, 8 atoms per monomer → 96 nucleons per monomer from C
- Hydrogen contributes 1 nucleon per atom, 8 atoms per monomer → 8 nucleons per monomer from H
- Hydrogen fraction = 8/(96+8) ≈ **7.7% of target nucleons**

This comfortably satisfies the ≤20% hydrogen constraint. It also leaves margin if thin structural elements (aluminum frames, fiber cladding) dilute the sample further. Do not use a hydrocarbon with higher H/C ratio such as polyethylene (CH₂, which gives H fraction ~14%) — it still fits but leaves less margin and complicates the cross-section model.

---

## Muon Tracking at Large Angles: Embedded Thin-Panel Scintillator Planes

The fiber coincidence scheme gives 3D hits but the light yield per cube and timing resolution matter for track-following at large angles. To ensure the ≥25% muon reconstruction efficiency requirement is met robustly at 90° and backward angles, **add a set of thin scintillator panel layers oriented in the YZ and XZ planes** (i.e., planes whose normals point along X and Y respectively, in addition to the dominant Z-normal planes).

Concretely: every 10 cm along X, insert a **3 mm thick extruded scintillator panel** with embedded WLS fiber, read by a SiPM, spanning the full Y-Z face. Similarly every 10 cm along Y. These panels are thin enough not to introduce significant inactive material (they are inside the active volume, supplementing rather than replacing the cube array). They provide redundant hit confirmation for tracks crossing many cube layers at shallow angle along Z, and primary tracking for genuinely transverse tracks.

This is essentially the same technology as MINER νA's scintillator planes or NOvA cells, proven in neutrino detectors.

---

## Low-Energy Proton Measurement: Time-of-Flight and dE/dx

For protons below ~200 MeV kinetic energy, range measurement in the cube array (counting hit cubes along the track direction, correcting for angle) is the primary momentum measurement. However, to validate this and to resolve proton/pion ambiguity at low momentum, add:

**Two planes of fast plastic scintillator bars** (EJ-200 or equivalent, 2 cm thick, full cross-section coverage) at the upstream and downstream faces of the active target. Each bar is read at both ends by fast SiPMs with ≤200 ps single-channel time resolution. The pair of planes gives:
- Time-of-flight over a ~0.9 m baseline for forward-going tracks leaving the target
- A coincidence veto for tracks entering from outside
- dE/dx from pulse height for particle ID at low momentum

The timing resolution target of **~500 ps system resolution** (achievable with EJ-200 and modern SiPMs) gives σ(1/β) sufficient to separate protons from pions up to ~600 MeV/c momentum, covering the full range of interest for the recoil measurement.

---

## Interface to Existing Downstream Spectrometer: Transition Tracking Stations

The existing gas drift chambers downstream of the target measure the momentum of tracks that reach them. However, tracks emerging from the active target at large angles may not project cleanly into the drift chamber acceptance. Add **three stations of large-area silicon microstrip detectors or scintillating fiber trackers** in the gap between the downstream face of the active target and the first drift chamber plane:

- Station positions: immediately downstream of the active target, then at 20 cm and 40 cm further downstream
- Each station: X-Y double-sided silicon strip detectors (strip pitch 200 μm) covering the full 2.6 m × 2.3 m aperture, or alternatively scintillating fiber ribbons (250 μm pitch Kuraray SCSF-78 fibers, same as LHCb SciFi) if the area cost of silicon is prohibitive
- Purpose: precise track matching between the coarse (1 cm) active target hits and the downstream drift chambers, and momentum measurement via curvature in the existing dipole field for tracks that exit the active target at angles up to ~45°

For tracks at angles beyond ~45° that loop back or stop inside the active target, momentum comes from range/dE/dx alone — these transition stations do not help, but neither does anything else except the active target itself, which is why the cube array is essential.

**Recommendation on silicon vs. scintillating fiber:** Use scintillating fiber ribbons (SiPM-read) for cost and because 200 μm spatial resolution is adequate given the 1 cm cube resolution of the upstream active target. Silicon strip detectors would be justified only if cleaner vertex reconstruction were needed, which is not the stated priority here.

---

## Electronics and DAQ Architecture

**SiPM choice:** Hamamatsu S13360-1325CS or equivalent (3 mm × 3 mm active area, 25 μm pixel pitch, ~4×10⁶ pixels/mm², operating at ~56 V bias). This device has:
- PDE ~40% at 450 nm (well-matched to WLS fiber emission)
- Dark count rate ~70 kcps at 25°C, manageable with ~100 ns coincidence windows
- Gain ~7×10⁵, adequate for single-photoelectron resolution

**Front-end ASIC:** Use the CITIROC or MUSIC ASIC family, which are designed for SiPM readout with 16 channels per chip, 12-bit ADC for charge, and TDC with ~100 ps resolution. These are already used in similar neutrino detector applications (e.g., Baby MIND).

**Trigger:** The beam spill structure from the accelerator neutrino source provides a hardware gate. Within the spill, implement a **self-trigger** on any cluster of ≥3 adjacent cube hits in the active target within a 100 ns window. This threshold suppresses dark noise and cosmic rays during the spill while keeping efficiency for the shortest proton tracks (which produce 3–4 hits).

**Data rate estimate:** At the neutrino beam's typical interaction rate of ~1 interaction per 10¹⁴ POT per ton of target, with ~6 tons of polystyrene in the active volume, expect O(10) neutrino interactions per spill during beam operation. Data volume per interaction (tracking hits + timing) is ~10 kB; total DAQ bandwidth needed is modest, O(100) MB/s during spill, well within standard DAQ capabilities.

---

## Structural and Integration Considerations

**Mechanical support:** The cube array is mechanically self-supporting if the WLS fibers are strung under tension through drilled cubes (as in SuperFGD production). The full assembly can be constructed as a series of **planar modules**, each one cube deep (0.9 m × 2.3 m × 1 cm), assembled into the full volume in situ inside the magnet bore. This avoids the need to extract the magnet.

**Thermal management:** SiPMs have gain that varies ~2% per °C. The detector must be temperature-stabilized to ±1°C. Use forced-air cooling through the gaps between the fiber readout boards on the faces of the assembly. This is standard practice and does not require cryogenics.

**Magnetic field compatibility:** SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields (unlike PMTs). The existing 0.15 T field is below the threshold at which SiPM characteristics degrade measurably. No magnetic shielding is needed.

---

| Active target bulk | 1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes, 3-axis WLS fiber + SiPM | 104k channels, 1 cm³ voxels | Short proton tracks, full 4π tracking |
| Transverse tracking reinforcement | 3 mm extruded scintillator panels every 10 cm in X and Y | Redundant hits for 90°/backward muons | Large-angle muon efficiency ≥25% |
| Particle ID / ToF | Fast scintillator bar planes at target faces, 500 ps system resolution | p/π separation to 600 MeV/c | Proton ID, pion background rejection |
