# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Context and Constraints

Before proposing upgrades, the driving requirements deserve explicit statement:

- **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles**, including 90° and backward tracks (these exit the target laterally or upstream, never reaching the downstream spectrometer)
- **Proton reconstruction down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** (range ~3 cm in water, ~1.5 cm in scintillator — extremely short tracks)
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤20%** of target nucleons (limits hydrogen-rich materials like pure plastic scintillator, which is ~67% H by nucleon count)
- **Active target volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (depth along beam), within a 0.15 T field
- **Existing asset**: downstream gas drift chambers provide momentum/charge measurement for tracks that *exit* the magnet volume

The hydrogen constraint is the most architecturally decisive: it rules out polystyrene (C₈H₈, ~47% H nucleons) and mineral oil as dominant materials, while still permitting small hydrogen fractions as a deliberate tool for transverse subtraction if controlled.

---

## Upgrade 1: Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC) Modules as the Primary Active Target

**Technology**: Modular LArTPC cells, each approximately 0.9 m × 0.9 m × 0.3 m (depth), tiled to fill the target volume, with cold electronics (ASIC-based charge amplification) on the anode wire planes and photon detection via ARAPUCA-style light traps embedded in the cathode panels.

**Physics motivation**:

Liquid argon (Z=18, A=40) has essentially zero hydrogen by nucleon count — argon nucleons are all neutrons or protons bound in a heavy nucleus, contributing negligible free hydrogen. It therefore trivially satisfies the ≤20% hydrogen constraint while providing very high density (1.39 g/cm³), giving a target mass of roughly 7–8 tonnes in the available volume.

The key capability is **millimeter-scale 3D spatial resolution** from drift-time measurement combined with wire pitch (~3–5 mm). This resolves proton tracks as short as ~1.5 cm corresponding to 60 MeV kinetic energy, satisfying the low-energy proton requirement. The dE/dx measured along each track provides particle identification through Bragg peak shape, distinguishing protons from pions and distinguishing short proton tracks from delta rays, which is essential when the recoil multiplicity is high.

For muons at large angles including perpendicular and backward tracks: a LArTPC records the full 3D trajectory within the volume regardless of exit direction. A backward-going muon is reconstructed from its ionization trail just as a forward one is; there is no geometric acceptance loss for tracks that do not point downstream. Combined with the existing downstream drift chambers for forward-exiting muons, this closes the angular acceptance gap that makes the ≥25% efficiency at all angles achievable.

The 0.15 T magnetic field presents a complication — the drift volume must be oriented so the electric field (typically 0.5 kV/cm) is not too severely distorted by the Lorentz force on drifting electrons. This is handled by orienting drift horizontally (perpendicular to beam and to the vertical magnetic field) with drift distances ≤30 cm per module to keep the Lorentz angle correction manageable (at 0.15 T and typical electron mobility, the Lorentz angle is ~1–2°, well within calibration tolerance).

---

## Upgrade 2: Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) or Scintillating-Fiber Tracker Planes Sandwiched Between LArTPC Modules — the "Side Muon Range Detector"

**Technology**: Thin (8–10 mm) scintillating-fiber hodoscope planes (SciFi, using 250 µm diameter Kuraray SCSF-78 fibers read by silicon photomultipliers) alternating with thin steel absorber plates (2 cm), forming a range-stack calorimeter on all four lateral faces and the upstream face of the active target volume.

**Physics motivation**:

Even with the LArTPC providing internal tracking, a muon that exits laterally from the target volume exits into the magnet bore, which provides bending but no measurement unless there is an active detector there. The existing gas drift chambers are only downstream. A lateral range detector on all four sides of the 2.6 m × 2.3 m cross-section serves two purposes simultaneously:

First, **muon momentum measurement by range** for tracks that stop within it. For a muon at 90° to the beam exiting the side of the target, the momentum is too low for precise curvature measurement in 0.15 T over a short path; range is more precise below ~600 MeV/c. The SciFi planes provide track-by-track range measurement with ~1 cm resolution sufficient for ~5–10% momentum resolution via the range-momentum relation.

Second, **charge-sign determination for lateral muons** using the residual field. The magnetic field deflects lateral tracks in the vertical plane; SciFi planes on top and bottom of the lateral range stack sample this deflection. With 0.15 T over ~1 m of lateral drift, the sagitta is small but measurable (~1 cm for 500 MeV/c), and the multi-plane SciFi tracker resolves it.

An **upstream face detector** (RPCs, chosen for cost-effectiveness in covering the full 2.6 m × 2.3 m upstream face) catches backward-going muons and measures their angle and, combined with their ionization length in the LArTPC, their momentum. This is the upgrade most directly addressing backward-going tracks, which are entirely invisible to the downstream spectrometer.

The SciFi technology specifically is chosen over RPC alone for the lateral range stack because SiPM-read fiber planes are immune to the magnetic field (no gas gain degradation), have sub-nanosecond timing (useful for pile-up rejection at the near detector's high rate environment), and their granularity (1 mm in one view) is sufficient to separate two nearby tracks — important when a muon and a recoiling proton happen to exit in similar directions.

---

## Upgrade 3: Thin High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC (HPgTPC) Liner Inside the LArTPC — or as an Alternative Sub-Volume

**Technology**: A central sub-volume (approximately 1.0 m × 1.0 m × 0.6 m) of high-pressure gaseous argon at ~10 atm, with MICROMEGAS or GEM readout at ~1 mm² pad size, surrounded by and read out separately from the main LArTPC modules.

**Physics motivation**:

This is motivated specifically by **very-low-energy proton reconstruction and neutron sensitivity**. At 10 atm, gaseous argon has ~1.6% of liquid argon density (~22 kg/m³), making the radiation length and nuclear interaction length proportionally longer. A 60 MeV proton that travels only ~1.5 cm in liquid argon travels ~90 cm in 10 atm gas — a long, beautifully reconstructed track with clear Bragg peak, with no ambiguity from diffusion (gas drift has lower diffusion per unit length than liquid at the same field).

Furthermore, in the gas volume, **neutrons occasionally scatter on argon nuclei**, producing short recoil protons that are now measurable. Neutron detection in the LArTPC is otherwise poor because the recoil argon nucleus is too short-ranged to reconstruct. In the gas volume, these recoil argon tracks are ~10 cm and reconstructable, providing a handle on the neutral hadronic energy not visible elsewhere. This matters because neutrino interaction models at 0.7 GeV have significant multinucleon (2p2h) components that produce neutrons rather than protons.

The hydrogen content of pure argon gas is zero, so this sub-volume contributes nothing problematic to the hydrogen budget.

The challenge is structural integration within the same magnetic volume and cryogenic environment — a pressure vessel inner liner with feedthroughs compatible with the surrounding liquid argon is non-trivial but precedented (the DUNE ND-GAr concept uses this architecture). A realistic implementation would place the HPgTPC as the upstream-most sub-volume since backward-going tracks from neutrino interactions in it must be caught by the upstream RPC face detector described in Upgrade 2.

---

## Upgrade 4: Precision Timing Layer (Low-Gain Avalanche Detectors, LGADs)

**Technology**: LGAD tiles (3 mm × 3 mm pixels) covering the downstream face of the active target where tracks exit into the existing spectrometer, plus a sparse layer on the upstream face. Target time resolution: ~100 ps per hit.

**Physics motivation**:

The near detector operates in a narrow beam spill at a facility where multiple neutrino interactions can occur within the same spill gate. At 0.7 GeV peak energy, the interaction rate in an 8-tonne argon target can be O(1–10) interactions per spill depending on beam intensity. Without timing, two interactions separated by 20 cm along beam but occurring within the drift time of the LArTPC (~250 µs for 30 cm drift at 0.5 kV/cm) are indistinguishable by position alone if the vertices are both in the fiducial volume.

The LGAD layer provides **100 ps timestamps on exiting tracks**. Combined with the LArTPC prompt scintillation light (~6 ns resolution from ARAPUCA photon detectors), this allows event-by-event disambiguation of overlapping interactions, which is essential for the hydrogen subtraction analysis: that analysis requires knowing with certainty that the reconstructed proton and muon came from the *same* vertex, because the kinematic constraint used to identify hydrogen interactions (zero transverse momentum of the neutrino-nucleus system) is completely invalidated if one track is stolen from an overlapping event.

Additionally, LGAD timing on exiting tracks improves the momentum resolution for tracks that re-enter the drift chamber spectrometer by constraining the track-matching between detector systems. The 0.15 T field gives modest bending (~100 mrad for a 500 MeV/c track over 6.5 m), and the lever arm to the drift chambers is long enough that timing can resolve left-right ambiguities in the drift chamber hits.

LGADs are specifically chosen over conventional scintillator hodoscopes because their granularity (3 mm pitch) handles the high track density near a neutrino vertex where several particles exit within a few cm of each other, and because they are thin (~300 µm silicon) so they contribute negligible material budget at the boundary between the active target and spectrometer magnet bore.

---

## Upgrade 5: Controlled Hydrogen-Doped Thin Target Planes ("H₂O sub-target") for Cross-Calibration

**Technology**: Thin (2 mm) polyethylene (CH₂) films interleaved at 5 cm spacing through the upstream quarter of the LArTPC volume, totaling ~15 kg of polyethylene in ~8 tonnes of argon. Each film is precisely surveyed and its position known to <1 mm.

**Physics motivation**:

This upgrade is in tension with the hydrogen constraint and must be carefully sized. Pure polyethylene is CH₂: 2 hydrogen per carbon, so by nucleon count it is 2/14 ≈ 14% hydrogen. Dispersed as thin films in a predominantly argon volume, the aggregate hydrogen fraction depends on the mass ratio: 15 kg CH₂ in (8000 + 15) kg total gives ~15 × 0.143 / 8015 ≈ 0.027% hydrogen by mass — far below the 20% nucleon limit. Even accounting for the fact that neutrino cross sections scale differently than mass (σ roughly per nucleon), the hydrogen nucleon fraction is well under 1% and completely negligible.

The purpose is to provide a **known, calculable hydrogen-interaction sample** using the well-established CH₂ minus C subtraction technique. Interactions in the CH₂ films produce a small but statistically significant excess of zero-transverse-momentum events identifiable by their vertex position (located at a film plane rather than uniformly distributed in argon). This sample, whose cross section on hydrogen can be compared against theory, provides an in-situ validation of the far-detector hydrogen subtraction model — specifically testing whether the kinematic selection criteria correctly isolate hydrogen events, and whether nuclear effects in argon are being modeled correctly by comparison with the cleaner CH₂ sample.

This is a physics-analysis upgrade rather than a pure instrumentation one, but it requires physical installation of the films and their precise survey, and it closes a potential systematic loophole: without it, the hydrogen-subtraction model is validated only against simulation, whereas with the CH₂ films the model is validated against real data from a structurally similar subtraction.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Driver |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Modular LArTPC | 3D tracking at all angles; proton down to 60 MeV; zero hydrogen |
| 2 | SciFi range stack + upstream RPC | Lateral and backward muon momentum/charge at all angles |
| 3 | HPgTPC sub-volume | 60 MeV proton long tracks; neutron detection via recoil |
| 4 | LGAD timing layer | Pile-up separation; hydrogen-subtraction vertex purity |
| 5 | CH₂ interleaved films | In-situ validation of hydrogen-subtraction model |

The combination addresses every stated requirement: Upgrades 1+2 jointly close the 4π muon acceptance gap; Upgrade 1+3 jointly cover the full proton kinetic energy range; Upgrade 4 protects the hydrogen-subtraction analysis from combinatoric backgrounds; and Upgrade 5 provides the experimental handle needed to trust that analysis at the level of precision required.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## 1. Active Target Medium: Liquid Argon or Plastic Scintillator?

Neither is optimal here. The hydrogen-fraction constraint (≤20% of nucleons) rules out hydrocarbon-rich materials as the *bulk* target. Let me work through this carefully.

**Hydrogen nucleon fraction by material:**
- Polystyrene (CH): H/(C+H) = 1/14 ≈ 7% by nucleon count ✓
- Mineral oil (CH₂): ~14% ✓ but barely
- Water: H/(O+H) = 2/18 ≈ 11% ✓
- Liquid argon: 0% ✓ (but no hydrogen signal to subtract)
- Pure scintillator (CH): ~7% ✓

The constraint is satisfiable with plastic scintillator but is a real operational bound on what fraction of the target can be structural hydrocarbon material.

---

## 2. Upgrade 1: Scintillator Tracker as Active Target

**Technology: Extruded plastic scintillator bars with WLS fiber readout and SiPM photodetectors**

Specifically, bars of dimensions ~1 cm × 1 cm × (spanning the 2.3 m or 2.6 m transverse dimensions), arranged in X-Y planes at ~1 cm pitch, filling the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m target volume. This is the architecture proven by MINERvA and proposed for NINJA/T2K upgrades.

**Why this technology:**

- **Short proton tracks:** 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has range ~1.3 cm in plastic scintillator (from Bethe-Bloch). With 1 cm bar pitch, such a track crosses ~1–2 bars, which is detectable via ionization signal (dE/dx for a stopping proton is large, ~several MeV/cm, giving easily detectable light yield). Thicker bars would miss these entirely.
- **Angular coverage including 90° and backward tracks:** An X-Y plane geometry with fine pitch gives full 4π solid angle reconstruction. Backward-going muons deposit hits in upstream planes; perpendicular tracks cross many bars in a single plane and are tagged by the pattern. No blind angles exist as long as planes tile the volume completely.
- **25% minimum muon efficiency at all angles:** The plane-to-plane spacing (~1 cm) ensures that even a track at 89° to the beam (nearly perpendicular) crosses at least one full bar and produces a detectable signal. The efficiency floor is set by the ratio of active scintillator to dead material (cladding, glue, fiber); with ~95% active fraction per bar this is achievable.
- **Hydrogen fraction compliance:** Polystyrene-based scintillator has nucleon hydrogen fraction ~7%, well under the 20% cap, leaving margin for structural materials and the WLS fibers.
- **SiPM photodetectors** replace PMTs because: (a) they operate inside or adjacent to the magnet's fringe field without gain degradation, (b) they are compact enough to mount directly on bar ends within the 2.6 m × 2.3 m cross-section without dead zones, (c) their single-photon sensitivity ensures adequate light yield even from the short (~1 cm) proton tracks at the edge of detection threshold.

---

## 3. Upgrade 2: Replacement of Front-End Electronics and Trigger

**Technology: Self-triggering, continuously sampling waveform digitizers (e.g., CITIROC or similar ASIC-based front-end) with a deadtime-free DAQ**

**Why:**

- Backward-going and large-angle tracks produce hit patterns that are topologically unlike the beam-forward signature used by a traditional hardware trigger. A conventional trigger that looks for a forward-going track will be systematically inefficient for exactly the backward and 90° events the analysis requires.
- Continuous sampling (at ~200 ns shaping time matched to scintillator decay) with a software trigger downstream allows arbitrary topological selection after the fact.
- The SiPM dark-count rate at room temperature (~100 kHz per SiPM) is manageable with coincidence requirements across neighboring bars in the software trigger without deadtime.
- Short proton tracks (1–2 bars) require low-threshold triggering; a hardware threshold set to suppress SiPM noise must not be so high it cuts the proton signal. The waveform digitizer approach allows offline threshold optimization.

---

## 4. Upgrade 3: Thin High-Pressure Gas TPC or Emulsion Cloud Chamber Insert (optional but strongly motivated)

**Technology: Either (a) an Emulsion Cloud Chamber (ECC) module or (b) a small-volume high-pressure gaseous TPC**

This addresses the residual gap: the scintillator bars at 1 cm pitch provide ~1 cm position resolution. For 60 MeV protons with ~1.3 cm range, the track length is at the resolution limit and angular reconstruction is poor (~30° uncertainty). A sub-millimeter resolution detector for a fraction of the fiducial volume dramatically improves the proton kinematics measurement.

**ECC (as used in NINJA):**
- Alternating nuclear emulsion sheets and thin iron or water plates, acting as both target and tracker at micron-level resolution.
- Proton tracks of even 30 MeV kinetic energy are reconstructed with sub-degree angular resolution.
- Hydrogen fraction in the water-layer ECC variant: water contributes 11% hydrogen by nucleon count, within the cap.
- Limitation: requires periodic emulsion development (film scanning), making it unsuitable for the full volume but excellent as a precision insert occupying e.g. 10–20% of the target volume.

**High-pressure gaseous TPC (alternative):**
- Argon/CF₄ mixture at 5–10 atm gives proton ranges of several cm for 60 MeV, with mm-scale track resolution from charge readout.
- Zero hydrogen nuclei in pure argon fill.
- Limitation: the existing dipole magnet field (0.15 T) is marginal for momentum measurement of short tracks within the TPC; it is more useful as a range-based energy measurement device.

**Recommendation:** ECC insert for the highest-priority interaction topology studies, gaseous TPC if online reconstruction is required.

---

## 5. Upgrade 4: Upstream Veto and Muon Catcher

**Technology: Additional scintillator planes upstream of the active target + downstream muon range stack of iron/scintillator**

**Why:**

- **Upstream veto:** Neutrino interactions occurring in the material upstream of the active target (beam pipe, shielding, magnet yoke) produce muons that enter the target from upstream and mimic backward-going signal tracks. Thin scintillator veto planes (2–3 planes of the same 1 cm bar technology) covering the upstream face tag these backgrounds.
- **Muon range stack:** The existing gas drift chambers downstream measure momentum of tracks exiting the magnet. However, low-momentum muons (produced by low-energy neutrino interactions near the beam flux peak at 0.7 GeV) may stop inside the active target or in the gap before the drift chambers. An iron/scintillator range stack immediately downstream of the active target, before the drift chambers, provides range-based momentum measurement for these tracks (σ_p/p ~ 5–10% from ranging vs. the drift chamber curvature measurement). This is the technology used in NOvA and MINERvA downstream hadron catchers. It also provides a second muon identification handle for the 25% efficiency floor requirement.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Motivation |
|---|---|---|
| Active target bulk | 1 cm × 1 cm extruded plastic scintillator bars, X-Y planes, WLS+SiPM | Detect 60 MeV protons; full angular coverage |
| Photodetectors | Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) on bar ends | Magnet field compatibility; single-photon sensitivity |
| Electronics/DAQ | Self-triggering waveform digitizers, software trigger | Efficiency for backward/perpendicular topologies |
| Precision insert | ECC modules (emulsion + water/iron) | Sub-mm proton track reconstruction |
| Upstream veto | 2–3 scintillator planes | Reject entering background tracks |
| Downstream muon catcher | Iron/scintillator range stack | Range-momentum for stopping muons; efficiency floor |

---

## Key Design Driver Summary

The 25% efficiency floor at *all* angles, including backward, combined with the need to see 60 MeV protons (range ~1 cm) and the hydrogen-fraction cap of 20%, jointly select **fine-grained plastic scintillator with SiPM readout and a deadtime-free DAQ** as the core technology, with emulsion inserts for precision kinematic reconstruction. The existing downstream drift chambers and dipole are retained; the upgrade is entirely within the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m target volume plus the upstream veto and downstream range stack interfaces.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near-Station Active Target

## Why the obvious choice fails

The usual way to build an active target for all angles is a finely segmented plastic scintillator, as in T2K's SuperFGD upgrade. The hydrogen limit rules this out. Polystyrene is roughly CH, so hydrogen supplies about 1 of every 13 nucleons, or about 7.7%. That is well above the 2% ceiling.

Water is also out (about 11% hydrogen), and so are hydrocarbon gas mixtures with much quencher. The target must therefore be essentially hydrogen-free. A noble-element TPC meets this, and argon is the natural choice.

## 1. Active target: modular liquid-argon TPC with pixelated charge readout

- **What:** a LAr TPC filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m volume, about 7.5 t of argon. It should be divided into several optically isolated modules with short drift lengths (about 0.5–1 m or less), on the ArgonCube / DUNE ND-LAr pattern. Charge would be read out by pixel tiles at roughly 4 mm pitch.
- **Hydrogen:** argon contains none, so the hydrogen fraction stays well below 2%. This also matches a hydrogen-free far detector, presumably also argon, which helps nuclear-effect systematics.
- **Muon acceptance at all angles:** a TPC images in 3D isotropically. There is no plane orientation that blinds it to tracks perpendicular to the beam, unlike stacked bars or the downstream chambers alone. This is what makes ≥25% efficiency at 90° and backward angles achievable.
- **60 MeV protons:** a 60 MeV proton travels about 2.3 cm in LAr (CSDA range ≈3.2 g/cm²). That gives roughly 6–8 hits at 3–4 mm pitch, enough for tracking and for dE/dx identification from the Bragg peak.
- **Why pixels rather than wires:**
  - Pixels give true 3D readout without the ambiguities of wire projections.
  - At 410 m from the target, the event rate per spill is high. Pixels, combined with short modular drifts, keep pile-up manageable.
- **Momentum for tracks that miss the downstream chambers:**
  - Range, for stopping muons and protons.
  - Multiple Coulomb scattering, for exiting high-angle tracks.

## 2. Cryostat and cryogenics fitted inside the warm magnet

- **What:** a thin-walled cryostat sized to the target region, with argon purification and recirculation.
- **Why:** the warm magnet accepts a cold insert. Minimising dead material at the downstream face preserves the matching of forward muons to the gas drift chambers.
- **Hydrogen in insulation:** hydrogenous insulation such as foam lies outside the active volume. A fiducial cut handles it, so it does not count toward the 2% target limit.

## 3. Segmented, fast light detection inside each module

- **What:** ArCLight / light-trap type detectors with SiPMs.
- **Why:**
  - It supplies the interaction time (t₀) for each event, which fixes the drift coordinate.
  - Segmentation ties each flash to the right module, which separates pile-up events within a spill.
  - It suppresses cosmic and out-of-time activity.

## 4. Time-of-flight / tracker panels surrounding the target region

- **What:** scintillator bars read by SiPMs, giving sub-ns timing. They would cover the top, bottom, sides and upstream face.
- **Why:**
  - Timing between the TPC flash and the panels gives the direction of exiting tracks, so backward muons are not confused with incoming ones.
  - The panels reject background entering from outside the detector, such as interactions in the magnet or surrounding rock.
  - They tag high-angle exiting muons that never reach the downstream drift chambers.

## 5. Instrumented magnet yoke (side muon range detector)

- **What:** scintillator in the yoke gaps.
- **Why:** perpendicular and backward muons exit sideways through the coil and yoke. These detectors confirm their identity as muons and constrain their momentum by range, which recovers efficiency at large angles.

## 6. Matching and integration with the existing downstream drift chambers

- **What:** a common trigger, timing and DAQ across the TPC, light system, panels and chambers.
- **Why:** forward muons can then be measured by curvature in the 0.15 T field to obtain momentum and charge, cross-checked against the TPC's own range or scattering estimate.

## 7. Calibration systems

- **What:**
  - A UV laser and/or cosmic-ray calibration, to map the electric field and account for space charge.
  - Purity monitors.
  - Light-yield calibration.
- **Why:** the 60 MeV proton threshold and the proton particle identification depend on accurate dE/dx and energy scale.

## Optional extension: high-pressure gaseous argon TPC

A high-pressure gaseous argon TPC could serve as a low-threshold sub-detector. At about 10 bar it would hold only about 0.1 t, so its statistics would be limited. In exchange it would reach proton thresholds well below 60 MeV.

Any hydrocarbon quencher must stay at the few-percent level. For example, about 3% CH₄ gives roughly 0.3% hydrogen nucleons. A hydrogen-free quencher such as CF₄ removes the issue entirely.

# Proposed upgrade: a magnetized liquid-argon active target with surrounding side and timing trackers

## 1. Why the target cannot be plastic

The obvious choice for an active target is a fine-grained plastic scintillator tracker, such as a SuperFGD-style cube detector. It fails the hydrogen requirement:

- Polystyrene (CH)ₙ has 1 hydrogen nucleon per 13 nucleons, which is **about 7.7%**.
- Water fails too, at 2/18, which is **about 11%**.
- Any hydrocarbon readout medium (scintillator, gas tracker with CH₄ or isobutane quencher) has the same problem if it sits in the fiducial volume.

The far detector contains no hydrogen, and the target must be at or below 2% hydrogen. A noble-liquid target therefore makes sense. **Argon** has zero hydrogen. I am assuming the far detector is an argon detector; if it uses a different hydrogen-free nucleus, the same design applies with that nucleus.

## 2. Core element: a modular LArTPC with pixel readout

**Cryostat**
- Use a thin-walled, vacuum-insulated cryostat (roughly 5–10 cm total wall), not a thick foam-insulated one. This preserves active volume in the 0.9 m beam dimension and keeps dead material between the argon and the trackers small.
- Approximate active volume: **2.3 × 2.0 × 0.65 m**, about 3 m³ or **4 t of LAr**.
- Event rate: a few-tonne target in a 0.7 GeV peak beam at 410 m should give a high event rate. Check this against the beam power before finalizing segmentation.

**Field cage**
- Use several optically isolated modules in an ArgonCube-like layout, with short drifts of about 30–50 cm.
- Short drifts keep pile-up, diffusion and purity requirements modest.

**Charge readout**
- Use pixelated 3D readout (LArPix-type, about 4 mm pitch) rather than wires. This gives unambiguous 3D reconstruction at high event rate.

**Light readout**
- Use ArCLight or SiPM-based photon detectors on the module walls.
- They give ns-scale t₀ for each interaction, which serves two purposes:
  - associating tracks with beam bunches;
  - determining track direction (forward versus backward) using external timing.

**Hydrogen budget**
- The fiducial volume is pure argon, so the hydrogen fraction there is 0%.
- Plastics in the field cage, PCBs and photon detectors lie outside the fiducial cut. They only need a background estimate, and a vertex-resolution cut handles that.

## 3. How the design meets the physics requirements

**Proton threshold**
- A 60 MeV proton has a CSDA range of about 4 g/cm², which is roughly **2.8 cm in LAr**, or about 7 pixels at 4 mm pitch.
- That is enough for dE/dx-based identification and range-based kinetic energy.
- The detector is isotropic, so acceptance is the same at all proton angles.
- Thresholds could go down to about 30–40 MeV.

**Forward muons**
- These exit downstream into the existing drift chambers in the 0.15 T field, which measure their charge and momentum.
- The thin cryostat downstream wall keeps the scattering contribution small.

**High-angle, perpendicular and backward muons** are the hard part, because the 0.9 m depth means many of them exit through the sides or the upstream face. Three measures address them:

1. **Side and upstream tracker planes.** Line the four lateral faces and the upstream face of the cryostat, inside the magnet, with thin tracker planes. These could be scintillating-fibre or small-cell scintillator bars; hydrogen there is irrelevant because they are outside the target. They:
   - provide exit points and timing, with about 0.5–1 ns resolution;
   - determine track direction by time-of-flight relative to the LAr light t₀, which rejects backward/forward ambiguity and out-of-volume (sand/magnet) muons.
2. **Momentum without the downstream chambers:**
   - range, for tracks contained in the LAr or in the side detectors;
   - multiple Coulomb scattering along the LAr segment (about 10–20% resolution);
   - curvature in the 0.15 T field, measured between the TPC track and the side tracker point. The bending radius is about 11 m at 0.5 GeV/c, giving a sagitta of about 1 cm over 1 m of track. This is enough to determine charge in most cases.
3. **Range-out layers (optional).** Interleave a few iron or brass layers in the side trackers so that sub-GeV muons stop there and their momentum comes from range.

With 4π LAr acceptance plus side and upstream tagging, **≥25% muon efficiency at every angle** is realistic. Efficiency is limited mainly by the fiducial cut and by exit-face geometry, not by intrinsic acceptance. Confirm this with a full simulation as part of the design study.

## 4. Supporting upgrades

- **Cryogenics and purification**
  - A compact recirculation and filtration system.
  - Purity monitors, needed for lifetime ≫ drift time; at 50 cm drift, a few ms is ample.
- **Magnet compatibility**
  - Use non-magnetic stainless or aluminium for the cryostat.
  - Check eddy currents and forces during magnet ramps.
  - Field maps must include the cryostat.
- **Downstream integration**
  - Upgrade the drift-chamber front-end timing so that downstream tracks can be matched to the LAr t₀ and the side-tracker hits.
- **Calibration**
  - Laser or UV ionization tracks to map drift-field distortions.
  - Cosmic-ray triggers to calibrate dE/dx and muon range.

## 5. Fallback option

A **high-pressure gaseous-argon TPC** (about 10 bar, ND-GAr-like) also contains no hydrogen in the target, provided the quencher is not a hydrocarbon (for example, use Ar–CF₄ or CO₂). It gives:

- excellent proton thresholds, below about 10 MeV;
- 4π acceptance and curvature-based charge measurement.

However, its target mass is only about 0.1 t, so it is suitable only if the beam intensity can deliver adequate statistics. The **LAr option is the baseline**.

# Next-Phase Upgrade Proposal for the Off-Axis Near Detector

This is effectively the ND280-upgrade problem. The aim is to replace the upstream photon-tagging section with a target-and-tracker system that has close to 4π acceptance and a low proton threshold. Only that upstream region changes. The downstream TPCs, the two tracking targets (including the one with water layers) and the calorimeters stay. Values below marked "~" are design estimates, not fixed specifications.

## 1. Fine-grained 3D-readout scintillator-cube target (replaces the photon-tagging section)

**Technology**
- Build the target from about 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, about 192 × 182 × 56 cubes. This fills the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box and gives about 2 t of target.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres (x, y, z).
- Every fibre is read out by its own silicon photomultiplier, about 56,000 channels in total. This extends the existing fibre-plus-SiPM readout scheme.

**Physics motivation**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** The existing target bars all lie perpendicular to the beam. Tracks at high angle, and especially near 90°, run along a single layer and are poorly reconstructed. About 25% of muons and 35% of protons go beyond 50°. Three orthogonal views give genuine 3D hits and roughly uniform efficiency at all angles, including backward tracks.
- **Lower proton threshold.**
  - With the current 1 cm bars in alternating layers, a proton must cross several layers to be tracked. In practice that means roughly 450 MeV/c or more, which sits at the median of the leading-proton spectrum.
  - With 1 cm cubes, a track of a few cubes can be reconstructed. This gives a threshold of about 300 MeV/c, so most leading protons are recovered.
  - Calorimetric dE/dx along the track and the Bragg peak at the stopping point give proton/pion separation and the proton momentum.
  - Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) needs exactly this: the full proton kinematics, not just a tag.
- **Neutron detection.** Hits that are isolated from the vertex, combined with timing (about 1 ns per channel, better with two-ended readout), allow neutron kinetic energy to be measured by time of flight. This adds antineutrino TKI and neutron-energy constraints.
- **Electromagnetic separation.** The fine granularity separates γ from e and helps select νₑ samples.
- **Material choice.** A hydrocarbon target is acceptable for this programme. The downstream water-layer target stays for carbon-to-water comparison.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the new target

**Technology**
- Two new argon-based TPCs, each roughly 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m, sit inside the 0.2 T magnet.
- They are read out by resistive-anode Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode, "ERAM"). The resistive layer spreads charge, giving better spatial resolution with larger pads and suppressing sparks.
- The field cage should be thin and lightweight to keep material low.

**Physics motivation**
- **Momentum for high-angle tracks.** The existing TPCs sit downstream and only measure forward-going tracks. High-angle and backward muons, which are about 25% of the sample, currently lack a curvature measurement and charge sign.
- **Particle identification.** The TPC dE/dx gives PID, separating μ from e and from protons.
- **Energetic protons.** Protons with momentum above about 900 MeV/c (about 6%) escape the cube target. They need a TPC momentum measurement rather than range.
- **Closer match to the far detector.** Restoring the high-angle region closes the phase-space gap with the 4π water far detector. This directly reduces the extrapolation systematic.

## 3. Time-of-flight system enclosing the new target and HA-TPCs

**Technology**
- Six planes of plastic scintillator bars surround the new target and the two high-angle TPCs.
- Each bar is read out by SiPM arrays at both ends.
- The target timing resolution is about 150 ps.

**Physics motivation**
- **Track direction.** Timing tells forward from backward tracks.
- **Background rejection.** It rejects out-of-fiducial-volume and sand-muon backgrounds, including events entering from the magnet.
- **Extra PID.** Combining time of flight with TPC momentum adds particle identification, for example e/μ separation at low momentum and help with p/π⁺.
- **Trigger.** The planes can also provide a cosmic trigger for calibration.

## 4. Supporting items

- Upgrade the front-end electronics and data acquisition to handle the roughly 56,000 new channels and the higher beam power expected in the next phase. This should include timing-capable digitisation for neutron time of flight.
- Plan a calibration programme, including a test-beam measurement of the cube response to protons and neutrons.
- Keep the side muon-range detectors and the calorimeters, which still serve the new layout.

## Expected impact

| Item | Current | Upgrade |
|---|---|---|
| Angular acceptance | Mostly forward | Near-4π for μ and p |
| Proton threshold | ~450 MeV/c | ~300 MeV/c |
| Neutron kinematics | None | Measured by time of flight |
| TKI samples | Limited | Full TKI samples |

Together these changes give the nuclear-model and flux constraints needed to bring the systematic uncertainty from about 6% toward the 4% goal.

# Proposed ND280 Upgrade: SuperFGD with 3D Scintillator Cube Array

## Primary Hardware: Super-Fine-Grained Detector (SuperFGD)

### Detector Concept
Replace the P0D with a **3D optically-segmented plastic scintillator cube array** providing ~1 cm³ voxel granularity:

**Dimensions:** 192 cm × 180 cm × 60 cm (fits in 200 × 190 × 60 cm envelope)

**Architecture:**
- ~2 million small polystyrene cubes (1.0 × 1.0 × 1.0 cm³)
- Three-orthogonal wavelength-shifting fiber readout (one fiber per cube face orientation)
- ~4 × 10⁶ readout channels via MPPCs
- Total scintillator mass: ~4 tons (hydrocarbon target)

### Key Advantages for T2K-II Requirements

**1. Large-angle acceptance:**
- Near-4π solid angle coverage (≥50° tracks remain contained or measured)
- 3D reconstruction eliminates the x/y layer ambiguity of bar detectors
- Fine granularity resolves vertex topology even for back-going tracks

**2. Low-momentum proton detection:**
- 450 MeV/c protons have ~15 cm range in polystyrene
- 1 cm granularity provides ~15 samples → dE/dx PID down to stopping threshold
- Range-momentum reconstruction for 200-800 MeV/c protons

**3. Kinematic completeness:**
- 3D vertex reconstruction to <5 mm
- Multiple Coulomb scattering momentum measurement for muons
- Proton angle and momentum from range + dE/dx
- All-angle calorimetric energy measurement

## Secondary Hardware Components

### 2. High-Angle Muon Tagger (HAMT)
**Six thin scintillator hodoscope planes** surrounding SuperFGD (outside magnet for upstream/downstream, inside magnet volume for sides):

- 1 cm thick planes with 5 cm strip granularity
- Top/bottom/sides coverage for muons exiting >50°
-Time-of-flight capability (σ ~1 ns) for direction determination
- Integrated into existing SMRD readout infrastructure

**Purpose:** Tag and measure exit angle for muons leaving SuperFGD without reaching TPC1

### 3. Time-of-Flight (ToF) Walls
**Two thin timing planes:**
- Upstream: 200 × 200 cm, immediately before SuperFGD
- Downstream: 200 × 200 cm, between SuperFGD and TPC1
- 2 cm thick scintillator, 6 cm strip width
- MPPC + fast digitization for σ_t < 150 ps

**Purpose:** 
- ToF over 60 cm baseline → π/p separation up to ~700 MeV/c
- Crossing muon veto (beam halo rejection)
- Trigger and timing reference (30-50 ps timestamp)

### 4. Target Region Tracker (optional enhancement)
**Two MicroMegas planes** inside the SuperFGD volume (at 20 cm and 40 cm depth):

- 40 × 40 cm² active area
- 400 μm strip pitch
- Minimal mass (~0.3% X₀ per plane)
- Resistive MM or μ-RWELL for robustness

**Purpose:** High-resolution angle measurement for muons (σ_θ ~1 mrad), improving momentum resolution via MCS when combined with TPC1

---

## Performance Expectations

| Requirement | Current ND280 | Proposed Upgrade |
|------------|---------------|------------------|
| **Proton threshold** | ~500 MeV/c (FGD) | ~200 MeV/c (stopping) |
| **Proton angular acceptance** | ~70% (>50° lost) | >95% (3D containment) |
| **Muon angular acceptance** | ~75% | >90% (with HAMT) |
| **Vertex resolution** | ~1 cm (bar size) | <5 mm (cube size) |
| **Target mass** | 1.1 t (FGD1) | ~4 t (SuperFGD) |
| **π/p separation** | TPC dE/dx only | dE/dx + ToF (up to 700 MeV/c) |

### Systematic Uncertainty Improvements
- **Cross-section model freedom:** 3D kinematics constrains all final-state particles → breaks degeneracies in FSI/RES/DIS models
- **Flux constraint:** Larger acceptance → higher statistics in transverse imbalance plane
- **Detector systemics:** Fine granularity reduces track-matching and PID ambiguities
- **Target mass uncertainty:** Polystyrene composition known to <0.5% vs. water bags

**Expected systematic:** ~4% (factor 1.5 improvement) from increased angular acceptance and kinematic constraint power

---

## Technical Readiness

**SuperFGD concept:** Validated by WAGASCI-BabyMIND (2017-2021) using 3 cm cubes; T2K has operated 1×1×1 cm prototypes. Mass production via injection molding is established.

**Timeline:** 3-year construction + installation during Long Shutdown 3 (2024-2027), matching T2K-II schedule.

**Cost drivers:** ~4M fibers + 4M MPPC channels require industrial partnerships (Hamamatsu, Kuraray); estimated ~$15M total including DAQ.

This configuration addresses all stated requirements while maintaining hydrocarbon target compatibility and integration with existing TPC/FGD2/SMRD systems.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Constraints Before Listing Upgrades

The requirements drive the technology choices:
- Muon reconstruction at **all angles including 90° and backward** in a magnetic field → needs 3D tracking with no dead regions
- **Short proton tracks down to 60 MeV KE** (range ~3.5 mm in water, ~1.5 cm in scintillator) → needs fine-grained, low-density active material
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤ 20% of nucleons** → constrains the target material chemistry
- Volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m inside a warm dipole

---

## Upgrade 1: Fine-Grained Scintillator Active Target

**Technology:** Extruded polystyrene scintillator bars with wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), arranged in alternating X–Y (and optionally U–V stereo) planes at ~1 cm pitch, filling the target volume.

**Why:**
- 1 cm pitch gives adequate resolution to reconstruct proton tracks stopping within a few centimeters, capturing kinetic energies down to ~60 MeV. A 60 MeV proton has a range of roughly 3.5–4 cm in polystyrene (density ~1.05 g/cm³), which spans ~3–4 bar widths — reconstructable but only just, so 1 cm pitch (not coarser) is necessary.
- Scintillator provides the energy deposition (dE/dx) information needed to identify and distinguish protons from pions and muons on short tracks.
- Polystyrene (CH formula unit) has a hydrogen-to-carbon nucleon ratio: each CH monomer has 1 H and 12 C nucleons, giving H fraction = 1/13 ≈ 7.7% by nucleon count. This is comfortably **below the 20% hydrogen-nucleon ceiling**, unlike water (H₂O: 2/18 ≈ 11%) or pure hydrocarbon liquids. Adding heavier dopants or using polystyrene with moderate TiO₂ coating (for optical isolation) does not appreciably shift this fraction.
- SiPM readout operates without issue inside or immediately adjacent to the dipole magnetic field (unlike traditional PMTs, which would require long light guides and suffer gain degradation in the 0.15 T field).
- The technology is well established at this scale (e.g., MINERvA, WAGASCI) and is compatible with the existing downstream drift chamber readout timing.

---

## Upgrade 2: Replacement or Augmentation of Upstream/Downstream End-Cap Tracking Planes with High-Efficiency Scintillating Fiber Trackers

**Technology:** Scintillating fiber (SciFi) modules — densely packed ~250 µm or 500 µm round plastic scintillating fibers arranged in multilayer X–Y–U–V stereo modules — at both the upstream face and downstream face of the active target volume, read out by SiPM arrays.

**Why:**
- Tracks exiting the target **perpendicular to the beam** (90°) leave the target through the lateral faces. These are the hardest tracks to reconstruct because they travel only 0.9 m (the short beam-axis dimension) or less inside the target before entering the magnet gap, and they may have very little lever arm for momentum measurement. Scintillating fiber planes on the lateral faces (the two 2.6 m × 2.3 m faces perpendicular to the beam, plus the top and bottom) provide the seed hit needed to match into the downstream drift chambers or confirm the track's exit point.
- For **backward-going tracks** (exiting the upstream face), the upstream SciFi endcap is essential — there is no existing upstream tracker — to initiate track reconstruction going in the minority direction and to prevent these tracks from being lost entirely. Without this, the stated ≥ 25% efficiency requirement at 180° (backward) cannot be met.
- SciFi offers sub-millimeter spatial resolution and fast timing (~1 ns) adequate to match to beam spill structure and suppress out-of-time backgrounds.
- The thin profile (~few cm per module) minimizes the passive material added to the edges of the fiducial volume.

---

## Upgrade 3: Low-Mass Lateral and Top/Bottom Support Panels with Embedded Thin Scintillator Veto/Tracker Planes

**Technology:** Thin (5–10 mm) scintillator panel planes (e.g., cast or extruded scintillator sheets with SiPM readout) lining the four lateral faces of the active target region (the faces parallel to the beam axis).

**Why:**
- Tracks leaving the target at large angles to the beam (approaching 90°) pass through these lateral faces before entering the magnet volume where the drift chambers can measure their momentum and sign.
- These planes serve as **track-matching surfaces**: the hit position and time allow the upstream active target track stub to be matched to the downstream drift chamber track, reconstructing the full trajectory and hence charge sign and momentum — both needed for the physics analysis.
- They also act as a **veto against entering backgrounds** (e.g., particles produced in the magnet coils or surrounding material that enter the active target laterally, which would fake neutrino interactions).
- SiPM readout again avoids the magnetic field incompatibility problem.

---

## Upgrade 4: Upgraded Readout Electronics with Waveform Digitization and Precision Timing

**Technology:** Self-triggering front-end ASICs (such as CITIROC or a custom ASIC similar to those used in NOvA/MINERvA upgrades) with ~10–12 bit ADC waveform sampling at ~125–250 MSamples/s per channel, combined with a White Rabbit or similar sub-nanosecond synchronization network, and an FPGA-based data concentrator with continuous readout buffering.

**Why:**
- The fine-grained scintillator target will have on the order of **~100,000 channels** (2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m at 1 cm pitch in X, Y, and Z planes). Existing readout (designed for the original, presumably sparser, detector) cannot handle this channel count.
- Waveform sampling (rather than simple charge integration) allows **pulse shape discrimination** to help separate proton signals (slower, higher dE/dx) from minimum-ionizing tracks — critical for identifying the short proton stubs.
- Precision timing (~1 ns or better) is needed to **disambiguate multiple neutrino interactions within the same beam spill** (the beam peaks near 0.7 GeV so spill structure can pile up interactions) and to match tracks across the target-to-drift-chamber boundary.
- Continuous or near-continuous buffering is required because backward-going tracks and large-angle tracks produce hit patterns in the target that are temporally spread, and a hardware trigger that looks for a downstream muon track would systematically veto exactly the events (backward muons, contained events) the upgrade is designed to recover.

---

## Upgrade 5: Passive Radiator / Interaction Target Mass Optimization Removal

**Technology:** This is a *removal* upgrade: any existing passive brass, iron, or lead interaction target planes currently in the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume must be **removed and replaced** entirely by the fine-grained scintillator of Upgrade 1.

**Why:**
- Passive high-Z/high-A material makes the hydrogen fraction problem worse only indirectly, but more importantly it creates **dead zones** where proton tracks (range ~3.5 cm at 60 MeV in CH) are absorbed invisibly before reaching the active material — destroying the efficiency for recoil proton reconstruction.
- The 25% minimum angular efficiency requirement for muons also fails if passive absorber creates regions where the muon track cannot be reconstructed before it exits the active target.
- The neutrino interaction point must be inside fully active material to allow the vertex and all outgoing tracks to be reconstructed, which is the whole premise of the active target upgrade.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Fine-grained active target | 1 cm pitch extruded scintillator bars + WLS fibers + SiPMs | 60 MeV proton reconstruction; H fraction ≤ 20% |
| Upstream & downstream endcap trackers | Scintillating fiber modules + SiPM arrays | Backward-going and forward muon tracking; ≥25% efficiency at all angles |
| Lateral face tracker/veto panels | Thin scintillator panels + SiPMs | 90° track matching to drift chambers; background veto |
| Waveform digitizing readout | High-channel-count ASIC + FPGA concentrator + precision timing | ~100k channel readout; proton PID; pile-up rejection; self-triggering |
| Removal of passive target material | — (prerequisite) | Full active volume; no dead zones for short tracks |
