# Hardware Upgrade Proposal for the ND280 Upstream Active Target

## Design Philosophy

The core constraint is unforgiving: reconstruct both the muon and the leading recoil proton with large angular acceptance (>50° from beam) in a ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box, with proton momenta peaking around 450 MeV/c where range-based reconstruction is more reliable than curvature-based. The 0.2 T magnet field is too weak to curl a 450 MeV/c proton usefully in 0.6 m of longitudinal depth, so the architecture must lean on 3D tracking and range rather than momentum-from-curvature for recoil protons.

---

## 1. Active Target Module: Super-FGD

**Technology: Plastic scintillator cubes read out in three orthogonal axes**

The core active target should be a fully-3D segmented scintillator array — the Super-FGD concept already adopted by the ND280 upgrade collaboration, described here with explicit hardware specifics.

### Cube geometry and material
- Individual cube size: **10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm** extruded polystyrene (same BASF 143E compound used in existing FGDs, doped with 1% PPO and 0.03% POPOP), with TiO₂-loaded white reflective co-extrusion coating ~0.17 mm thick on all faces.
- Array dimensions filling the available box: approximately **192 × 184 × 56 cubes** in x, y, z respectively, giving ~1.92 m × 1.84 m × 0.56 m active volume.
- Total cube count: approximately **1,980,000 cubes**, total scintillator mass approximately **2.0 t**.
- Each cube has three orthogonal through-holes (along x, y, z) of 1.5 mm diameter for fibre threading.

### Wavelength-shifting fibre readout
- **Kuraray Y-11(200)MS multi-cladding WLS fibre**, 1.0 mm diameter, running through each hole axis.
- Each fibre reads an entire row of cubes along one axis and exits both ends, but only one end is instrumented (the other is mirrored with aluminium-coated mylar cap to recover ~15% more light).
- Fibre count: approximately **3 × (192 + 184 + 56) × average_rows** — specifically ~56 fibres per x-plane × 184 planes = ~10,304 x-fibres; ~56 fibres per y-plane × 192 planes = ~10,752 y-fibres; ~184 fibres per z-plane × 192 planes = ~35,328 z-fibres. Total ~56,000 fibres.
- Fibre-to-cube optical coupling: direct contact with no glue (dry coupling acceptable given fibre cladding refractive index contrast); tested at ~15 photoelectrons per cube per minimum-ionizing particle crossing.

### Photosensors
- **Hamamatsu S13360-1325CS MPPCs** (1.3 mm × 1.3 mm active area, 25 μm pixel pitch, 667 pixels, PDE ~40% at 450 nm, dark count rate ~70 kcps at 25°C, operating voltage ~53 V).
- These are a size step down from the 1.5 mm devices on the existing FGDs, chosen because: (a) the 1.3 mm aperture matches the 1.0 mm fibre + connector tolerances cleanly, (b) lower capacitance gives faster signal (~1 ns rise time) needed for the z-coordinate timing disambiguation discussed below, (c) reduced dark rate matters for the dense coincidence logic.
- One MPPC per fibre end: ~56,000 channels total.
- Mounted on custom PCB boards along the x and y faces of the cube array; z-axis fibres exit through the downstream face toward TPC1.

### z-coordinate reconstruction via timing
The 56-cube depth in z (~56 cm) is the critical dimension. With 10 mm cubes and a fibre running the full z-length, the hit cube z-position within a fibre is determined by **signal arrival time difference** between the two ends — except one end is mirrored, so single-ended readout cannot do this. For z-fibres specifically, **both ends are instrumented** (no mirror cap), and time difference at ~200 ps resolution (achievable with these MPPCs and the readout ASIC below) gives z-position resolution of ~3 cm (light propagation speed in fibre ~17 cm/ns; 200 ps → 3.4 cm). This is adequate for the 10 mm cube disambiguation when combined with x and y fibre coincidences.

---

## 2. Front-End Electronics

### Readout ASIC
- **CITIROC 1A** (Weeroc), a 32-channel SiPM readout ASIC providing: shaping amplifier with adjustable gain (two ranges covering 1–160 p.e.), peak-hold track-and-hold, 12-bit Wilkinson ADC, per-channel threshold discriminator with 10-bit DAC, and TDC via external 200 MHz clock.
- Power: ~5 mW/channel, so 56,000 channels → ~280 W total, manageable within the magnet.
- 1,750 ASICs total (32 channels each), mounted on 175 front-end boards of 10 ASICs each.

### Trigger and DAQ
- Each front-end board sends zero-suppressed data over **GBT (Gigabit Transceiver) optical links** at 4.8 Gbit/s to a backend FPGA concentrator.
- **Xilinx KU15P FPGAs** (8 units) handle event building and the first-level coincidence trigger: require ≥3 cubes with signal above 0.5 MIP in a 100 ns window, suppressing beam-uncorrelated backgrounds.
- Synchronization to the J-PARC 8-GeV beam spill (1.1 μs spill, ~500 ns bunch spacing) via **White Rabbit** protocol, as used elsewhere in T2K.

---

## 3. Surrounding Electromagnetic Calorimeter Upgrade

The existing downstream ECal modules remain. For the upstream active target, the beam-left, beam-right, top and bottom faces of the new box must be surrounded by **thin ECals** to catch photons from π⁰ decay and to provide muon/pion/proton discrimination at the boundary:

- **Pb-scintillator sampling**, 10 Pb layers × 1.5 mm + 11 scintillator layers × 4 mm = **15 mm Pb total (8.4 X₀)**, total thickness ~60 mm per face. This is thinner than the existing barrel ECal (~10 X₀) because space is tight, but sufficient to initiate EM showers for photon veto.
- Scintillator bars: **10 × 40 mm cross section**, polystyrene, TiO₂ coating, Y-11 WLS fibre, same S13360-1325CS MPPC readout for commonality.
- These thin ECal panels instrument four lateral faces (~1.9 m × 0.6 m each for top/bottom, ~2.0 m × 0.6 m for left/right); the upstream face is left as is (beam entrance) and the downstream face opens into TPC1.

---

## 4. Time-of-Flight Layer

A dedicated **ToF layer** at the upstream face of the Super-FGD and between the Super-FGD and TPC1 downstream, to:
- Measure proton vs. pion vs. muon by ToF over the ~56 cm baseline at momenta below 600 MeV/c where dE/dx alone is ambiguous.
- Veto beam-unrelated backgrounds entering from upstream.

**Technology:** 
- **5 mm thick plastic scintillator (EJ-200) tiles**, 200 mm × 200 mm each, arranged in a plane.
- Each tile read out by **two SiPMs (Hamamatsu S13360-3050CS, 3 mm × 3 mm, 50 μm pixel, faster response)** on opposite edges via direct light guide, achieving single-tile time resolution of **~150–200 ps** (demonstrated in prototype tests for similar T2K upgrades).
- Two planes: one at z = 0 (upstream Super-FGD face) and one at z = 560 mm (downstream face), 100 tiles per plane = 200 tiles total, 400 SiPM channels.
- At 450 MeV/c, a proton (mass 938 MeV/c²) traverses 56 cm in ~4.3 ns; a pion (mass 140 MeV/c²) traverses it in ~2.1 ns. The separation is ~2.2 ns, comfortably larger than the ~300 ps combined resolution — this ToF gives clean p/π separation up to ~700 MeV/c where the difference shrinks to ~0.8 ns (still 2.5σ).

---

## 5. Mechanical Structure and Integration

### Support frame
- **Aluminium alloy 6061-T6 extruded rails**, 40 mm × 80 mm cross section, forming a bolted rectangular frame fitting within the former P0D slot.
- The Super-FGD cube array is assembled in **vertical slabs of 192 × 56 cubes** (one y-row), 184 slabs stacked and held between compression plates. Compression load ~200 N total (tested not to crack cubes), taken by the frame.

### Cooling
- MPPC dark current increases ~2× per 10°C rise. Target operating temperature: **20 ± 2°C**.
- Cooling via **aluminium water-cooled plates** (20°C input water, closed loop) clamped to the MPPC PCB boards on the x and y faces, removing ~280 W of ASIC heat + ~50 W MPPC leakage. No cooling needed inside the cube volume itself.

### Cable routing
- All fibres exit through the ±x and ±y faces (and ±z faces for z-fibres) into light-tight aluminium extrusion housings where MPPCs and front-end boards are mounted.
- Low-mass coaxial cables (micro-coax, 50Ω, 0.4 mm diameter) route from front-end boards to patch panels on the magnet yoke; existing cable trays from the P0D removal are reused.

---

## 6. Summary of Key Technology Choices and Their Justifications

| Component | Technology | Key reason for choice |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | 10 mm³ scintillator cubes, 3-axis WLS fibre | 4π tracking, short proton range measurable (~5 cm for 300 MeV/c proton), no dead zone |
| Photosensor | Hamamatsu S13360-1325CS MPPC | Small area matches fibre, fast timing for z-reco, low noise |
| Front-end ASIC | CITIROC 1A | Existing T2K experience, 32ch integration, adequate timing |
| z-reconstruction | Dual-ended fibre timing, 200 ps resolution | Resolves cube hit along 56 cm depth without stereo complication |
| Thin ECal | 8.4 X₀ Pb-scintillator, same MPPC | Photon containment for π⁰ reconstruction, boundary PID |
| ToF | EJ-200 tiles, 3 mm SiPM, 150–200 ps | Clean p/π/μ separation at 450 MeV/c over 56 cm baseline |
| DAQ | GBT optical links + KU15P FPGA | Bandwidth for 56k channels at T2K spill rate |

This architecture directly addresses the stated physics requirement: the 10 mm cube granularity provides ~1 cm track reconstruction for protons down to ~300 MeV/c (range ~5 cm, giving ~5 measured points), the 4π fibre geometry eliminates the large-angle acceptance hole that crippled the planar FGDs, and the ToF resolves the proton/pion ambiguity that would otherwise corrupt the transverse kinematic imbalance measurement.

# Proposed Upgrade: A Hydrogen-Free, Fine-Grained 4π Active Target

## 1. The constraint that decides the design: hydrogen fraction

The ≤2% hydrogen-nucleon limit rules out the usual choice for this job, a plastic-scintillator active target such as a 3D-cube detector.

- Polystyrene (CH) contains 1 hydrogen nucleon per 13 nucleons, about **7.7%**. That is roughly four times over the limit.
- Water, oil and other organic or hydrogenous active media also fail.

The active medium must therefore be essentially hydrogen-free. The far detector contains no hydrogen. If it uses argon, as most hydrogen-free far detectors do, the natural choice is **liquid argon**. It gives:

- 0% hydrogen;
- the same nucleus as the far detector, so nuclear effects cancel;
- fully 3D, isotropic imaging;
- calorimetric dE/dx for identifying particles.

If the far detector uses a different hydrogen-free target, the same layout applies with that medium.

## 2. Core of the upgrade: a modular pixelated LArTPC in the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region

### Layout
- A thin-walled cryostat sits inside the target region. Because the dipole is warm, the cryostat only has to coexist with the field. It does not have to be cooled with it.
- Vacuum insulation is preferred to thick foam. This saves space along the beam, where the region is only 0.9 m deep, and keeps hydrogenous material small and far from the fiducial volume.
- The expected active volume is about 2.4 × 2.1 × 0.7 m ≈ 3.5 m³. This gives **about 4.9 t of argon**, or roughly 3.5–4 t fiducial.
- At 410 m in a sub-GeV beam, this mass gives the high statistics expected at a near detector.

### Readout
- The TPC is built from optically isolated modules, each with a short drift of about 30–35 cm (ND-LAr/ArgonCube style).
- Readout uses **pixel tiles with about 4 mm pitch**, giving native 3D hits, rather than wires.
- The reasons for pixels over wires are:
  - At a near detector there is pile-up of several interactions per spill. Pixels and short drifts remove the ambiguities of wire readout.
  - Short drifts also keep the high voltage modest (about 15–20 kV) and lower the sensitivity to argon purity.
- Each module has fast light-collection detectors on its walls (ArCLight/LCM-type) with ns-scale timing. This associates each charge cluster with its interaction time and beam bunch, and rejects cosmics and through-going rock muons.

### Proton threshold check
- A 60 MeV proton travels about 4 g/cm² in argon, which is roughly **2.9 cm in LAr**.
- At 4 mm pitch that is about 7 pixels along the track, with a clear Bragg peak. That is enough for dE/dx identification of the proton and its kinetic energy from range.
- The response is the same in all directions, so the proton requirement is met at all angles, including backward.
- The non-fiducial walls hold no active hydrogenous material.

### Hydrogen budget inside the fiducial volume
- Argon contributes 0% hydrogen.
- Every hydrogenous item in or near the fiducial volume must be counted. This includes PCB pixel tiles, FR4 field-cage supports and light detectors made with plastic.
- Pixel tiles are placed at module boundaries, outside the fiducial cut. With millimetre vertex resolution, interactions on these materials are rejected geometrically.
- The design target is **<0.5% hydrogen nucleons in the fiducial volume**, comfortably under 2%.

## 3. Muons at every angle (≥25% efficiency, including 90° and backward)

The existing downstream drift chambers only see forward tracks. Three additions close the gaps.

### a) Momentum inside the LAr
- **Range** is used for contained muons. Up to about 0.35 GeV/c fits in roughly 1–2 m of LAr along diagonal paths.
- **Multiple Coulomb scattering** is used for exiting muons, with about 10–15% resolution over ≥1 m of track.
- This works for any track direction.

### b) Side and upstream tracking for charge and momentum
- The magnet's 6.5 m inner volume extends beyond the target region. Thin tracking layers are added around the cryostat: top, bottom and both sides, plus an upstream face.
- These layers can be compact gas TPCs or drift chambers, like the ND280 high-angle TPCs, possibly with resistive-Micromegas readout.
- Charge sign comes from curvature in the 0.15 T field. For a 0.5 GeV/c muon, the bending radius is about 11 m and the sagitta over 0.6 m is about 4 mm. That is readily measured with roughly 0.5 mm point resolution over about 0.5–0.7 m of gas.
- Charge identification is also helped by matching to the LAr track direction and by μ⁻ capture versus decay signatures for stopping muons.

### c) Time-of-flight envelope
- Scintillator bars with about 0.15–0.5 ns timing enclose the cryostat and the side trackers.
- Their timing tells forward from backward tracks and inward from outward tracks, i.e. it determines the direction.
- They also reject entering background from outside, such as sand muons and magnet interactions.
- These plastic layers lie outside the fiducial volume, so they do not affect the hydrogen budget.

### Expected efficiency
- Combining contained-range, MCS and side-tracker or ToF matching, the expected muon efficiency is well above 25% at all angles.
- The weakest region is near 90°, where tracks are short and exit sideways. There, the side trackers and the MCS measurement in LAr are what keep the efficiency above threshold.

## 4. Integration and practical items

- **Space along the beam:** the 0.9 m depth is the tightest constraint. Use a vacuum-jacketed thin cryostat and put the cryogenics, purification and recirculation outside the magnet.
- **Material budget:** keep dense material between the LAr and the side trackers small, so that high-angle muon momenta are not degraded. Use aluminium or composite walls with low hydrogen content.
- **Calibration:**
  - ³⁹Ar and cosmic data give the energy scale and electron lifetime.
  - Laser or UV tracks give field distortions.
  - Through-going muons are used to cross-calibrate the LAr, side trackers and downstream chambers.
- **Downstream:** keep the existing drift chambers for forward muons, which give the best momentum resolution.
- **Data acquisition:** the pixel and light readout must handle bunch-level time tagging at the expected multi-interaction-per-spill rate.

## Summary

| Requirement | Solution |
|---|---|
| H ≤ 2% of target nucleons | Liquid-argon active target (0% H), hydrogenous parts kept out of the fiducial volume (<0.5% H) |
| Protons ≥ 60 MeV at all angles | ~2.9 cm tracks imaged with 4 mm 3D pixels, dE/dx identification, isotropic response |
| Muons ≥ 25% efficient at all angles | Range/MCS in LAr, side and upstream gas trackers in the 0.15 T field, ToF envelope for direction |
| Pile-up and timing | Modular short-drift pixel TPC with fast optical readout |
| Forward muons | Existing downstream drift chambers |

# Design Review Recommendation: New Active Neutrino Target for the Upstream Section

## Executive Summary

The core challenge is fitting a high-efficiency, kinematically complete charged-current detector into a 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box that is shallow along the beam axis, while reconstructing muons up to ~25% of which exit beyond 50° and protons with a median momentum of ~450 MeV/c of which ~35% also exit beyond 50°. I recommend a fully-active scintillator tracker with low-Z absorber, fine granularity, and time-of-flight capability, with specific technologies chosen below.

---

## 1. Active Target Volume: 3D Scintillator Cube Detector

**Technology:** Segmented plastic scintillator cubes (~1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm), each read out on three orthogonal faces by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres and SiPMs — following the SuperFGD architecture demonstrated for the near detector of Hyper-K (ND280 upgrade).

**Justification:**

- The 0.6 m depth is the dominant constraint. A fully-active 3D topology has no dead absorber layers, maximising interaction rate and tracking efficiency within this shallow volume. The fiducial mass in 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m at polystyrene density (~1.05 g/cm³) is approximately **2.4 t**, competitive with the downstream plastic targets.
- The 1.5 cm cube pitch gives a radiation length of ~40 cm in polystyrene and an interaction length of ~80 cm, so a 600 MeV/c proton (range ~25 cm in plastic) is reconstructed with ~17 measured points; a 450 MeV/c proton (range ~12 cm) still gives ~8 points, sufficient for momentum-by-range to better than 5%.
- The 3D fibre readout provides true three-dimensional hit reconstruction with no projective ambiguity, essential for isolating the leading proton track in multi-prong topologies — a problem that plagued the existing 2D-strip tracking targets at the angles relevant here.
- Low average Z (carbon/hydrogen, Z_eff ~ 5–6) means low Coulomb scattering for protons and minimal secondary hadronic interactions relative to water-bag or brass targets.
- SiPM readout (1 mm² MPPC, ~50 µm pixel pitch) on each face gives ~15–20 p.e./MeV, providing both energy deposit dE/dx for particle identification (π/p separation up to ~1 GeV/c) and sub-nanosecond timing per cube face.

**Specific selection:** Use 1.5 cm cubes (not 1 cm, which increases channel count by 3.4× for marginal gain at this beam energy) and **Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS** or equivalent SiPMs already used elsewhere in the detector (commonality of spares, DAQ firmware, and calibration procedures).

---

## 2. Muon Reconstruction for Wide-Angle Tracks

**Problem:** 25% of muons exit beyond 50°. In 0.6 m of active volume along z, a 50° muon travels only ~0.6/cos50° ≈ 0.93 m total path before exiting the side or rear face. The downstream TPCs and existing ECal/SMRD are the natural continuation for these tracks, but side-exiting muons from the new upstream position may miss the TPC acceptance.

**Technology: Add thin scintillator-strip halo planes on the four lateral faces of the new target box.**

- Four planes of 1 cm × 3 cm extruded polystyrene strips (the same technology as the existing tracking targets, preserving tooling), 2 layers per face in X and Y, each ~2.0 m × 0.6 m or 1.9 m × 0.6 m.
- WLS fibre + SiPM readout, identical to existing channels.
- These planes tag the exit point and direction of side-going muons to ±1–2 cm, constraining the momentum-by-curvature measurement when the track enters the 0.2 T dipole field.
- The existing return-yoke SMRD scintillator planes already range out muons reaching the magnet boundary; the halo planes provide the upstream anchor point for the lever arm.
- Channel count: ~4 × 2 × (200/3 + 60/3) ≈ modest (~500 channels), negligible cost and DAQ impact.

**Momentum reconstruction strategy by range/curvature:**
| Muon momentum | Exit mode | Method |
|---|---|---|
| < 300 MeV/c | Stops in cube target | Range in target |
| 300–800 MeV/c, forward (< 50°) | Exits rear → TPC | Curvature in TPC + B field |
| Any momentum, side > 50° | Exits lateral → magnet volume | Entry point (halo plane) + SMRD range/curvature |

---

## 3. Proton Reconstruction and Particle Identification

**Problem:** Median proton momentum 450 MeV/c, range in polystyrene ~12 cm; 35% exit beyond 50°; 6% exceed 900 MeV/c (range ~65 cm, may exit the 0.6 m box).

**Technology A — dE/dx in the cube target (primary PID):**
The 15–20 p.e./MeV light yield in each 1.5 cm cube gives ~3–4× Bragg peak amplification at track end, cleanly separating stopping protons from stopping pions and muons using the energy-deposit profile. This is the primary proton identification handle and requires no additional hardware.

**Technology B — Timing for proton momentum (secondary/cross-check):**
At 450 MeV/c, a proton (β ≈ 0.43) traversing 12 cm takes ~0.93 ns; a pion of the same momentum (β ≈ 0.96) takes ~0.42 ns — a 510 ps difference. With cube-level timing resolution of **~1 ns per hit** (demonstrated in SuperFGD beam tests), time-of-flight over even 10 cm provides ~1σ p/π separation and cross-checks the dE/dx PID. No additional TOF detector is needed if SiPM readout electronics achieve this, which requires **waveform-sampling front-end ASICs** (e.g., CITIROC-1A or the WAGASCI/Baby-MIND CITIROC implementation already in the collaboration's experience base) rather than simple discriminator+TDC.

**Technology C — For protons exiting beyond 50°:**
The same halo strip planes described in §2 provide the exit vector. For protons between 500–900 MeV/c that exit laterally, momentum-by-range combining the in-cube segment and the halo strip hit pattern gives ~5–8% momentum resolution. Protons above 900 MeV/c (6% of sample) entering the main TPC volume are measured by curvature; this subset is small and the downstream detectors already handle it.

---

## 4. Neutrino Interaction Vertex and Fiducial Definition

**Technology: No change — cube granularity is sufficient.**

Vertex resolution in the SuperFGD geometry is ~0.5 cm in 3D. The fiducial volume should exclude 2 cube-layers (~3 cm) on all faces to reject events where either the proton or muon is born at the boundary. This gives a fiducial mass of approximately **(1.94 × 1.84 × 0.54 m) × 1.05 t/m³ ≈ 2.0 t**, a ~80% fiducial efficiency — acceptable.

---

## 5. Calibration and Monitoring

**Technology: LED pulser system + through-going cosmic muons.**

- Mount one UV LED per WLS fibre bundle connector (injected via fibre patch) for gain stability tracking of each SiPM — identical to what is already deployed on the ECal SiPMs, so no new infrastructure.
- The existing cosmic-muon trigger (scintillator coincidence from the SMRD top/bottom planes) is reused; through-going cosmics provide cell-by-cell minimum-ionising-particle (MIP) calibration at ~50 MIP/day/cell at surface rates, adequate for weekly gain maps.
- Water-equivalent density cross-checks use the neutral-current π⁰ sample from the downstream water-layer target, maintaining the carbon-to-water comparison programme.

---

## 6. DAQ and Electronics Integration

The existing detector uses a continuous-readout, trigger-less DAQ with SiPM-based channels multiplexed to 64-channel front-end boards. The recommended additions are:

- **~500k new SiPM channels** from the cube target (approximately 2.0×1.9×0.6 m / (1.5 cm)³ × 3 faces × 1 SiPM ≈ 540,000 channels). This is large but comparable to the SuperFGD channel count (1.8M for a larger volume); the collaboration should baseline the **same front-end ASIC and data-aggregation board** as the ND280 SuperFGD upgrade to leverage firmware and cost.
- The halo planes add ~500 channels, negligible.
- Trigger primitive: a coincidence of ≥2 adjacent cube faces with > 0.5 MIP in a 100 ns window, implemented in the FPGA concentrator — identical logic to the existing tracking target readout.

---

## 7. What Should Not Be Changed

- The downstream plastic tracking targets and water-layer target remain, preserving the carbon-to-water cross-section ratio measurement.
- The three gas TPCs remain; they are essential for momentum measurement of forward tracks from the new target.
- The ECal, dipole magnet, and SMRD remain; the SMRD is the muon ranger for wide-angle tracks.
- No change to the photon-veto logic of the ECal is needed; the new target is fully active and the ECal still tags photons converting outside it.

---

## Summary Table

| Component | Technology | Key Justification |
|---|---|---|
| Active target bulk | 1.5 cm polystyrene scintillator cubes, 3D WLS+SiPM | Fully active, 3D tracking, dE/dx PID, fits 0.6 m depth |
| Cube front-end | CITIROC-class waveform-sampling ASIC | ~1 ns timing for TOF p/π separation |
| Lateral containment | 1 cm × 3 cm strip planes on 4 lateral faces | Anchor point for wide-angle muon/proton tracks entering SMRD |
| SiPM type | Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS (existing detector standard) | Spares, calibration, firmware commonality |
| Calibration | LED pulser + cosmic MIP (existing infrastructure) | No new calibration hardware |
| DAQ | ND280 SuperFGD front-end boards (if available) or cloned firmware | Minimise new development |

This configuration is projected to reduce the residual systematic uncertainty from ~6% to ~4% by: (a) providing kinematically complete CC events (δp_T imbalance studies), (b) increasing the high-angle acceptance for both final-state particles, (c) maintaining the carbon/water comparison through the downstream water target, and (d) using established technology with demonstrated performance at this beam energy.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Constraints Before Listing Upgrades

The requirements drive the technology choices:
- **Magnetic field**: 0.15 T over 6.5 m → maximum momentum kick ∫Bdl ≈ 0.975 T·m → modest momentum resolution; muons must be tracked through the target region itself
- **Angular coverage**: 4π including backward-going tracks → no dead zones, cannot rely on downstream-only reconstruction
- **Proton threshold**: 60 MeV kinetic energy → range ~3.5 mm in plastic, ~13 mm in liquid argon → very short tracks, requires fine granularity
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤ 2%**: eliminates water (11% H by nucleon count), hydrocarbon plastics (~57% H), and liquid scintillator; strongly constrains target material choice
- **Near station at 410 m**: high neutrino interaction rate, significant rock muon background

---

## Required Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Active Target: Low-Density Time Projection Chamber (TPC) with Thin-Walled Drift Cells

**Technology**: Gaseous TPC, specifically an **argon-based high-pressure gas TPC** (e.g., Ar:CO₂ or Ar:isobutane mixture) operating at ~10 bar, filling the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m target volume, with multi-wire or micropattern gaseous detectors (Micromegas or GEM foils) as the readout planes.

**Why**:
- Argon has negligible hydrogen content; CO₂ or isobutane quench gas contributes small amounts of H, but the mixture and pressure can be tuned to keep hydrogen nucleons well below 2% of total nucleons. Argon-only drift with CO₂ quencher at a few percent keeps H safely below threshold.
- The continuous 3D tracking in a TPC provides full 4π angular coverage intrinsically — backward-going tracks, transverse tracks, and forward tracks are all reconstructed without geometric acceptance holes.
- At 10 bar, the density (~17 kg/m³) is sufficient to range out 60 MeV protons over a few centimeters (track length ~3–5 cm at that pressure), which is resolvable with TPC pad pitch of ~3–5 mm.
- dE/dx measurement in the gas allows particle identification (separating protons from pions and muons) even for short tracks, using the Bragg peak shape.
- The existing warm dipole magnet field permeates the gas volume freely — a gaseous detector has no distortion of the magnetic field, so track curvature for momentum measurement is preserved for all charged particles including short proton tracks.
- Low-Z, low-density material minimizes secondary interactions and multiple scattering for the short proton tracks.

**Specific implementation note**: The readout should use 2D-segmented Micromegas or GEM planes on at least two faces (e.g., top and one side of the rectangular volume) to give redundant projections. Pad size ~4–5 mm meets the spatial resolution needed. Drift field ~200–300 V/cm over the 0.9 m depth (along beam) is feasible. Electronics must handle the high-rate near-detector environment with shaping times short enough to separate tracks (~100 ns shaping).

---

### 2. Cathode and Field-Cage Structure: Low-Mass, Low-Z Construction

**Technology**: Carbon-fiber field cage with thin (25–50 μm) aluminized Mylar cathode foils; resistive voltage divider chain on the field-cage rings.

**Why**:
- Low-mass construction minimizes secondary interactions and energy loss of exiting particles, particularly soft protons that may just barely escape the TPC volume into the surrounding detectors.
- Carbon and Mylar introduce negligible hydrogen relative to the argon gas mass; the hydrogen contribution from structural materials must be included in the ≤2% budget calculation and kept small.
- Thin cathode foil avoids a hard material boundary that would absorb low-energy protons at the edge of the fiducial volume.

---

### 3. Surrounding Scintillator Veto / Range-Out Detector: Plastic Scintillator Planes with Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) Readout

**Technology**: Extruded polystyrene scintillator bars (3 cm × 1 cm cross-section or similar), wavelength-shifting fiber readout, SiPM photodetectors, arranged in planes covering all six faces of the TPC volume.

**Why**:
- Muons that exit the TPC at any angle — including 90° transverse and backward — must be caught with ≥25% efficiency. Without a surrounding active layer, transverse and backward muons leave the TPC but enter no downstream spectrometer; they would be lost entirely.
- Scintillator planes on all six faces detect and time-stamp exiting muons, providing track-segment matching to the TPC track, and feeding into the downstream drift chamber spectrometer for forward muons.
- SiPM readout is compact, operates within the magnetic field (unlike PMTs, which would require field shielding or remote placement), and provides sufficient light yield for 3 cm bars (~40–60 p.e./MeV).
- Polystyrene does contain hydrogen (~57% H by nucleon number), but these planes are outside the active target fiducial volume; the ≤2% hydrogen constraint applies to the target material in which interactions are counted, not the surrounding catcher. The fiducial volume is defined as the gas volume.
- Timing resolution of ~1 ns from SiPMs distinguishes forward-going from backward-going tracks by the direction of light propagation along the bar, supplementing the TPC drift-time directional information.
- The planes also serve as a veto against incoming rock muons and beam halo that enter the target from the sides.

---

### 4. Downstream Muon Spectrometer Interface: New Track-Matching Station Between TPC and Existing Drift Chambers

**Technology**: Two planes of drift tubes or straw tubes (4 mm diameter, Ar:CO₂ 70:30), arranged in X-Y views, placed immediately downstream of the TPC exit face, within the magnet bore.

**Why**:
- The existing warm dipole and downstream drift chambers are designed to measure high-angle-of-deflection forward tracks. There is a geometric gap between the edge of the new TPC and the first existing drift chamber plane; without a matching station, track segments in the TPC must be extrapolated over a large distance, degrading momentum resolution and matching efficiency for tracks at moderate angles.
- Straw tubes handle the high multiplicity near the target exit without long dead times; 4 mm cells give ~150 μm resolution per plane.
- Ar:CO₂ is hydrogen-free and inexpensive; these planes are outside the fiducial target volume so the hydrogen constraint does not apply, but it is still good practice.
- This station is essential for the 25% minimum efficiency requirement: a track at 60° to the beam that exits the side of the TPC, reflects in the magnetic field, and re-enters the downstream spectrometer needs at least one intermediate space-point to seed the global track fit correctly.

---

### 5. Data Acquisition System: Continuous Streaming Readout with FPGA-Based Trigger-Less Architecture

**Technology**: ATCA-based or μTCA-based front-end boards with on-FPGA zero-suppression; continuous waveform digitization at 10–25 MHz sampling for TPC channels; optical fiber data links to a commodity computing farm running online reconstruction.

**Why**:
- A TPC at a high-rate near detector (neutrino interactions plus beam-related backgrounds at ~410 m) cannot use a simple hardware trigger: drift times in the gas TPC at 200 V/cm in Ar are ~100–200 μs, so the full event is not available for a trigger decision before the next beam spill component arrives.
- Trigger-less streaming captures the full waveform for offline reconstruction and allows software-defined event boundaries, essential for identifying backward-going tracks whose ionization arrives at the readout plane after the prompt forward tracks from the same interaction.
- SiPM-read scintillator signals (ns timing) provide fast timestamps that the online farm can use to associate TPC drift segments with interactions, compensating for the slow TPC readout.
- The new DAQ must be synchronized with the existing drift chamber electronics; a common clock distribution (e.g., White Rabbit protocol) distributed to all subsystems is needed.

---

### 6. Gas Handling and Pressure Management System

**Technology**: Closed-loop gas recirculation system with molecular sieve filtration, pressure regulation to ±10 mbar, oxygen and water monitors (ppb-level), and gas analyzers (chromatograph for mixture ratio).

**Why**:
- Operating at 10 bar requires a pressure vessel certified to relevant pressure codes; the existing magnet bore must be verified or the TPC housed in a dedicated pressure vessel inside it.
- Electron lifetime in the drift gas is critically sensitive to oxygen and water contamination at the sub-ppm level; at 10 bar and 0.9 m drift, even 1 ppm O₂ causes significant charge loss. A recirculation and purification system maintains adequate lifetime.
- The quench gas fraction must be stable because it determines the hydrogen content; active monitoring ensures the ≤2% hydrogen constraint is not violated by mixture drift.
- Gas recovery is required both for cost (argon at 10 bar in a ~5.4 m³ volume is ~50 kg) and for environmental reasons if the quench gas contains any hydrocarbons.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|

# Hardware Upgrades for Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## 1. **Three-Dimensional Tracking System: Time Projection Chamber (TPC)**

**Technology:** Gaseous TPC with electronic readout (likely resistive Micromegas or GEM-based)

**Why:**
- **Complete angular acceptance:** TPC provides true 3D tracking with uniform efficiency at all angles, including perpendicular and backward-going tracks relative to the beam
- **Low momentum threshold:** Gas targets enable detection of ~60 MeV kinetic energy protons (short ranges of ~5-10 cm in appropriate gas mixtures)
- **Hydrogen content control:** Gas mixture (e.g., Ar:CH₄ 90:10 or P10) allows precise tuning to keep hydrogen nucleon fraction ≤2%
- **Track reconstruction at vertex:** Active target concept means interaction vertex and emerging tracks are measured in the same medium

## 2. **High-Voltage Cathode System and Field Cage**

**Technology:** Resistive field cage with ~400 V/cm drift field over 90 cm drift distance

**Why:**
- Required to drift ionization electrons to readout plane
- Field cage ensures uniform drift field and defines fiducial volume matching 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m specifications
- Transparency to particles exiting to downstream tracking

## 3. **Segmented Readout Plane with Multi-Channel Electronics**

**Technology:** Pixelated or pad readout (~3-5 mm pitch) with ~15,000-40,000 channels

**Why:**
- Spatial resolution sufficient to separate multiple tracks from single vertex
- 3D point reconstruction via pad position (x,y) and drift time (z)
- dE/dx measurement for particle identification (separate protons from pions/muons)

## 4. **Precision Timing and Trigger System**

**Technology:** ~100 ns timing resolution synchronized to beam spill; external trigger from beam timing

**Why:**
- Associates TPC tracks with specific beam spills
- Drift time measurement for z-coordinate
- Cosmic ray rejection via timing cuts

## 5. **Gas Handling System with Monitoring**

**Technology:** Recirculating purification system with O₂/H₂O monitoring <ppm levels

**Why:**
- Maintain electron drift lifetime >100 μs (needed for 90 cm drift)
- Stable gas composition ensures consistent hydrogen content
- Pressure regulation for stable operation in magnetic field

## 6. **Front-End Electronics and DAQ**

**Technology:** Cold electronics at readout plane; fast digitization (>10 MHz); high-bandwidth DAQ

**Why:**
- Low noise for ionization signal detection
- Continuous or triggered readout for beam spill capture
- Handle data rates from ~104 channels

## 7. **Calibration Systems**

**Technology:** 
- Laser ionization tracks for drift calibration
- Radioactive sources (e.g., ²⁰⁶Bi) for energy calibration
- Cosmic ray muon tracks

**Why:**
- Monitor and correct for drift velocity variations
- Energy scale calibration for dE/dx measurements
- Spatial distortion mapping

## 8. **Modified Magnet Interface**

**Technology:** Feedthroughs for HV, signal cables, gas lines through magnet structure

**Why:**
- TPC must operate inside existing 0.15 T dipole field
- Field improves momentum resolution for tracks continuing to downstream chambers
- Requires careful integration without compromising field quality

## Optional Enhancement:

## 9. **Light Collection System**

**Technology:** PMTs or SiPMs viewing TPC volume to detect scintillation light

**Why:**
- Precise t₀ timing (better than drift-based timing)
- Additional trigger capability
- Enhanced calorimetry

---

**Key Justification Summary:** The TPC technology specifically addresses all requirements: 4π angular acceptance with uniform efficiency (including backwards tracks), low proton threshold through low-Z gas stopping power, controlled hydrogen content through gas mixture selection, and active target functionality for vertex reconstruction.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Constraints

Before proposing hardware, let me extract the binding requirements:

| Requirement | Implication |
|---|---|
| Muon efficiency ≥25% at **all** angles including 90° and backward | No dead regions; must track stubs exiting sideways or upstream |
| Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy | Range ~3 cm in water; need ~mm-scale spatial resolution, low-Z preferred but density matters |
| Hydrogen ≤2% of target nucleons | Strongly limits hydrocarbon scintillator, water, and liquid argon |
| Volume 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m | ~5.4 m³ active volume |
| Sits inside existing warm dipole (0.15 T, 6.5 m) | Magnetic field aids momentum measurement; excludes ferromagnetic components in target |
| Downstream drift chambers already measure high-momentum forward tracks | Active target must handle the low-momentum, large-angle, and backward topology gap |

---

## The Hydrogen Problem: Dominant Constraint

Nucleon count in common materials:

- **Polystyrene scintillator (CH):** ~54% of nucleons are H → completely excluded
- **Water/ice (H₂O):** ~11% H nucleons → excluded  
- **Liquid argon:** 0% H, but cryogenic infrastructure in magnet bore is impractical
- **Carbon (graphite):** 0% H ✓
- **Aluminium:** 0% H ✓
- **Silicon:** 0% H ✓
- **Iron:** 0% H ✓ (but range-kills 60 MeV protons)

**The active target must be built from hydrogen-free or near-zero-hydrogen materials.**

A practical target that is fully active, low-enough density to range out 60 MeV protons visibly, and hydrogen-free points toward **silicon pixel tracking** as the primary technology, possibly with thin carbon or aluminium absorber layers.

---

## Proposed Upgrade Package

### 1. Silicon Pixel Active Target (Primary Recommendation)

**Technology:** Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS), as demonstrated by ALICE ITS2/ITS3 and developed for the ATLAS/CMS upgrades.

**Configuration:**
- Stack of **~800 silicon pixel planes**, each ~300 μm thick
- Plane spacing: **~1 mm** (giving ~900 planes in 0.9 m depth)
- Sensor tile size: ~2.6 m × 2.3 m per plane, assembled from ~15 cm × 15 cm individual MAPS tiles
- Pixel pitch: **~30 μm** (achievable with current MAPS technology, e.g. based on ALPIDE or successor)
- Each plane is self-supporting on a thin carbon-fibre frame; cooling via gaseous CO₂ embedded microchannels

**Why this works:**

*Hydrogen content:*  
Silicon: pure Si, zero hydrogen. Carbon-fibre frame and CO₂ cooling introduce negligible H. Epoxy in frame must be minimised or replaced with ceramic adhesive; with care, H fraction stays well below 2%.

*60 MeV proton range:*  
In silicon (ρ = 2.33 g/cm³), a 60 MeV proton has range ~12 mm → crosses ~12 planes → fully reconstructable as a track stub with dE/dx identification. The Bragg peak in silicon is sharp and measurable plane-by-plane.

*Angular coverage:*  
A track perpendicular to the beam (90°) crosses ~2.6 m / 1 mm = 2600 plane edges. Even a 90° track crosses the edge of many planes. **To handle truly transverse and backward tracks,** the planes must be complemented by:
- Stereo rotation: alternate planes rotated ±45° and 90° so every track direction crosses multiple active layers at non-grazing incidence
- Or: **three interleaved orthogonal substack orientations** (XZ, YZ, XY plane orientations), each spaced 3 mm, giving full 4π geometric coverage

*Magnetic field compatibility:*  
Silicon is non-magnetic; MAPS electronics operate in fields up to ~0.5 T (demonstrated in ALICE). The 0.15 T field here is comfortable.

*Momentum measurement:*  
For contained tracks, momentum is measured by range + dE/dx. For tracks that exit into the downstream drift chambers, the silicon provides the upstream seed and direction with ~mrad angular resolution, which combined with the dipole and drift chambers gives full momentum reconstruction.

---

### 2. Thin Carbon Absorber / Radiator Planes (Optional Enhancement)

Insert **100 μm carbon foil** between every 10th silicon plane to:
- Provide a fiducial nuclear target with known composition (pure ¹²C)
- Allow separation of C-target and Si-target interactions by vertex position
- Increase overall target mass without introducing hydrogen

Carbon adds negligible hydrogen. The alternating C-foil + Si-tracker sandwich is similar in concept to the T2K WAGASCI or the proposed NINJA upgrade but with zero hydrogen.

---

### 3. Upstream and Downstream Silicon Muon Taggers

**Problem:** A backward-going muon (cos θ < 0) exits the upstream face of the target volume. The existing geometry has no detector there.

**Upgrade:** Install **4 planes of silicon strip detectors** (strip pitch ~200 μm, two stereo angles) on the upstream face of the active target volume, covering the full 2.6 m × 2.3 m aperture. These provide:
- Tagging of backward-exiting muons
- A momentum measurement seed for tracks bent by the dipole as they curve back upstream
- Matching to any upstream beam monitors

**Why not scintillator here:** Even a thin scintillator veto panel would add hydrogen. Use silicon strips, identical technology to the main target.

---

### 4. Side-Exiting Track Recovery: Lateral Silicon Walls

Tracks at exactly 90° to the beam exit through the 2.6 m × 0.9 m or 2.3 m × 0.9 m side faces. The existing drift chambers are downstream only.

**Upgrade:** Line the **four lateral faces** of the active volume with **2 layers of silicon strip detectors** per face, strip pitch ~500 μm, two stereo angles per layer. This:
- Catches tracks that exit sideways before reaching the downstream drift chambers
- Gives a space point for momentum determination using the known dipole field (a track curving in the horizontal plane that exits a lateral face has its sagitta measurable if it also crosses planes inside the volume)
- Adds minimal mass (each wall is ~2 × 300 μm Si over ~2.6 × 0.9 m²)

---

### 5. Timing Layer: Fast Silicon or LGAD

**Problem:** With an 800-plane silicon target and a ~MHz spill, pile-up rejection and vertex disambiguation require timing.

**Upgrade:** Insert **Low-Gain Avalanche Detector (LGAD) planes** every ~5 cm through the stack — approximately 18 planes total. LGAD achieves ~30 ps time resolution per plane. This provides:
- Beam-spill pile-up rejection
- Directionality for ambiguous short tracks (distinguish forward-going 60 MeV proton from a backward-going one by time-of-flight over ~5 cm baseline: Δt ~ 0.5 ns for a 60 MeV proton, well above 30 ps resolution)
- Matching of the near-detector event to the beam bucket timing

LGADs are silicon-based (no hydrogen) and thin (~300 μm active layer).

---

### 6. Electronics and Readout

**Triggerless continuous readout** is required because:
- Low-momentum proton tracks are short (mm-scale) and may not generate a hardware trigger
- Backward muons may not point to downstream trigger scintillators

Each MAPS tile already supports rolling-shutter or triggered readout at ~10 μs frame rate (ALPIDE: 10 μs). For the beam spill (~10 μs typical at this type of facility), a full-spill readout with zero-suppression at the chip level is feasible.

Data rate estimate:
- ~800 planes × ~1700 tiles/plane × ~1 kbit/tile/spill = ~1.4 Tbit/spill
- With zero-suppression at typical neutrino interaction occupancy (~1 hit/cm² per interaction × ~10 interactions/spill): manageable with current FELIX/ATCA-based DAQ

---

## Summary Table

| Sub-system | Technology | Key Role | H content |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main active target | 800× MAPS silicon pixel planes, 1 mm pitch, 30 μm pixel | 4π track reconstruction, dE/dx PID, vertex | Zero |
| Carbon absorber foils | 100 μm graphite, every 10th plane | Additional pure-C target mass | Zero |
| Upstream muon tagger | 4× silicon strip planes, 200 μm pitch | Backward muon recovery | Zero |
| Lateral walls | 2× silicon strip planes per face | 90° track recovery | Zero |
| Timing layers | 18× LGAD planes at 5 cm intervals | Pile-up rejection, ToF PID | Zero |
| Cooling | Gaseous CO₂ microchannel | Heat removal without H | Negligible |

---

## Key Performance Estimates

**60 MeV proton:**
- Range in Si: ~12 mm → 12 planes hit → easily reconstructed
- dE/dx in Si at Bragg peak: ~10× minimum ionising → unambiguous PID
- Angular coverage: by having orthogonal plane orientations, a proton at any angle crosses ≥6 planes

**90° muon:**
- In the main stack (beam along z, planes perpendicular to z): a 90° muon travels in the x or y direction, crossing many planes edge-on (bad). **This is why the lateral silicon walls are essential** — they catch this track in a geometry where it crosses the strips at normal incidence.
- A muon at exactly 90° in the bend plane of the dipole has its momentum measured by the radius of curvature reconstructible from the lateral wall hits plus the entry/exit points in the main stack.

**Backward muon:**
- Exits upstream face; caught by upstream tagger planes
- If it re-enters the magnet bore going upstream, the dipole still bends it; the drift chambers upstream of the target (if any exist as beam monitors) or the upstream tagger + magnet field give a momentum estimate
- Minimum: upstream tagger gives angle + charge sign (from which side of centre it exits in the bend plane) → allows at least sign-correct momentum estimation

**Hydrogen fraction check:**
- 800 planes × 300 μm Si: total Si thickness = 24 cm, mass per unit area = 56 g/cm²
- Carbon frames: ~5% of Si mass → ~3 g/cm² carbon
- CO₂ cooling gas at ~20 bar in 100 μm microchannels: negligible mass
- Epoxy: if unavoidable, use ceramic or sintered connections; budget <0.1% of total mass as epoxy
- **Total hydrogen nucleon fraction: <0.1%** ✓ (comfortably within 2% limit)

---

## Notes on Alternatives Considered and Rejected

| Technology | Reason for rejection |
|---|---|
| Plastic scintillator (CH) | ~54% H nucleons — catastrophically violates constraint |
| Liquid scintillator | High H content, also non-trivial in magnet bore |
| Liquid argon TPC | Cryogenic infrastructure incompatible with warm dipole bore; zero H but impractical here |
| Gaseous TPC (Ar/CO₂) | Low density means 60 MeV proton range ~metres — cannot reconstruct in 0.9 m depth; also backward/sideways track coverage requires field cage that conflicts with the dipole |
| Emulsion/emulsion cloud chamber | No real-time readout; cannot provide fast reconstruction for spill-by-spill analysis |
| Water Cherenkov | H₂O has 11% H nucleons — violates constraint |
| Resistive plate chambers (glass) | Glass contains Si-O but also Na, K — zero H ✓; but spatial resolution ~1 cm is too coarse for 60 MeV proton tracks of ~1 cm length |

The silicon pixel active target is the only mature technology that simultaneously satisfies **zero hydrogen**, **mm-scale 3D resolution**, **4π angular coverage**, **operation in 0.15 T field**, and **fit within the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume**.

# ND280 Upstream Upgrade: Design Review Recommendations

## Summary

Replace the P0D with three new systems:

1. A **3D-granular scintillator target (SuperFGD-type)**.
2. **Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs)** above and below it, with resistive Micromegas readout.
3. A hermetic **Time-of-Flight (ToF) envelope** of fast scintillator bars around the new modules.

Retain the downstream TPC–FGD1–FGD2 tracker, the ECals, the SMRD and the magnet. The driving requirements are high-angle muon acceptance (25% beyond 50°), low-threshold proton reconstruction (median 450 MeV/c) and momentum measurement of the escaping high-momentum tail (about 6% above 900 MeV/c). These are what move the systematic uncertainty from about 6% toward the 4% T2K-II goal.

---

## 1. Active target: 3D-segmented scintillator cubes

**Technology**
- About 2 million optically isolated polystyrene cubes, 1 × 1 × 1 cm³, with roughly 192 × 182 × 56 cubes filling the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m³ box.
- Each cube has a reflective surface layer made by chemical etching.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibres (Y-11 type).
- Fibres are read out at one end by MPPCs, for example Hamamatsu S13360-1325 type, giving about 56,000 channels (192×182 + 192×56 + 182×56 ≈ 55,900).
- Target mass is about 2 t of CH, roughly twice FGD1 + FGD2. This is acceptable because hydrocarbon is permitted and FGD2 remains for the C/H₂O comparison.

**Why this, not more FGD-style bar planes**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** FGD bars all lie perpendicular to the beam, so tracks near 90° run along a single bar and are lost or badly reconstructed. With about 35% of leading protons and 25% of muons above 50°, this is the dominant acceptance loss. Three orthogonal projections from cubes give near-4π, angle-independent tracking.
- **Low proton threshold.**
  - A 450 MeV/c proton (kinetic energy about 100 MeV) travels about 8 cm in plastic, so it crosses about 8 cubes.
  - A 300 MeV/c proton (about 47 MeV) travels about 2 cm, which is still resolvable with 1 cm pitch.
  - The expected tracking threshold is therefore about 300 MeV/c, recovering most of the proton spectrum needed for transverse kinematic imbalance.
- **Calorimetric PID.** Fine 3D dE/dx sampling with about 40–50 photoelectrons per fibre per MIP separates protons, pions and muons near the vertex. It also gives a vertex-activity energy.
- **Neutron tagging.** MPPC timing of about 1 ns per channel, combined over several fibres, lets isolated neutron-induced hits be time-of-flight-measured. This adds neutron kinematics for antineutrino transverse kinematic imbalance, a bonus beyond the stated requirement.
- **Magnet compatibility.** MPPCs work in the 0.2 T field, as ND280 has already demonstrated.

**Risks to manage**
- Cube dimensional tolerance (about ±50 µm) for fibre threading over about 2 m.
- Optical crosstalk of a few percent through the reflector; it must be measured and modelled.
- Assembly logistics; use a fishing-line threading method before inserting the fibres.
- Front-end electronics: use CITIROC-based boards with time-over-threshold or charge readout.

## 2. High-Angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Two TPCs, each roughly 2.0 m (along beam) × 0.8 m drift × 1.8 m, with horizontal readout planes so that high-angle tracks cross many pads.
- Gas: the same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2 mixture as the existing TPCs, for shared gas systems and calibration.
- **Resistive (encapsulated) bulk Micromegas (ERAM).** A resistive anode layer spreads the charge over neighbouring pads. This allows larger pads, about 1 cm², with fewer channels while keeping spatial resolution of about 0.6 mm or better. It also suppresses sparking.
- **Thin composite field cage** (aramid/honeycomb laminate), about 3% X₀, to minimise multiple scattering and photon conversions.
- Front-end: AFTER/AGET-type ASICs, consistent with the existing TPC electronics.

**Justification**
- The existing downstream TPCs only see forward-going tracks. The high-angle muons (25% above 50°) need curvature momentum measurement and dE/dx PID, which the HA-TPCs provide.
- Protons too energetic to stop in the target leave it. The high-momentum tail (about 6% above 900 MeV/c) cannot be ranged out and needs curvature measurement.
- Together with the downstream TPCs this gives near-full solid-angle muon charge and momentum measurement. That restores the phase-space overlap with Super-Kamiokande, whose acceptance is 4π, and so reduces the flux and cross-section extrapolation error.

## 3. Time-of-Flight envelope

**Technology**
- Six planes of plastic scintillator bars, about 2.2 m long and about 12 cm wide, enclosing the target and HA-TPCs.
- Arrays of large-area SiPMs at both ends of each bar.
- Time resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Justification**
- **Direction.** Timing between the ToF and the target distinguishes backward-going tracks from incoming tracks. This is essential once backward and high-angle acceptance is opened up.
- **Background rejection.** It rejects out-of-fiducial-volume events from the magnet and ECal (sand muons, interactions in the surrounding material) and cosmics.
- **PID.** It adds an independent velocity measurement for e/µ/p separation in the momentum overlap regions where dE/dx is ambiguous.

## 4. Retained and modified systems

- **Keep as is:** the downstream TPC1–3, FGD1 and FGD2 (FGD2 provides the water target), the barrel and downstream ECals, the SMRD and the UA1 magnet. No other region can supply the carbon-to-water ratio.
- **Upgrade electronics:** move the legacy FGD/TPC electronics and DAQ to a common clock and trigger with the new systems, at the same timing level, so neutron and ToF timing work across the whole detector.
- **Integration:** new mechanical support in the basket. The P0D-side ECal should be reviewed for clearance, keeping it if space allows for photon and neutron containment.
- **Calibration:** use an LED or laser system for the 56k MPPCs, plus a beam-test program (CERN or LANL neutron beam) on a prototype to validate the proton threshold, neutron response and crosstalk before full production.

## Expected outcome

- Muon and proton acceptance becomes near-uniform in angle.
- The proton threshold falls to about 300 MeV/c, and the high-momentum tail is measured in the TPCs.
- Event-by-event transverse kinematic imbalance becomes possible for charged-current events, with neutron TOF for antineutrinos.
- Target mass roughly doubles.

Together these give the direct constraints on nuclear effects and the energy-scale uncertainty needed to reach about 4% systematic uncertainty for T2K-II.

## Design Review Recommendation for ND280 Upgrade

### Executive Summary
To achieve the required 4% systematic uncertainty while capturing kinematically complete events with large-angle particles, I recommend a **3D fine-grained scintillator tracker with timing capabilities**, replacing the P0D in the freed upstream volume.

---

## Recommended Configuration: SuperFGD-Style Detector

### Core Technology: 3D Segmented Plastic Scintillator Cubes

**Specification:**
- **~2 million cubes** of 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator
- **Dimensions:** 192 cm (width) × 184 cm (height) × 56 cm (depth)
- **Three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fiber readouts** through each cube
- **MPPC readout** (leveraging existing ND280 technology)
- **Target mass:** ~5.6 tonnes of CH scintillator

### Justification for Cube Architecture

**1. Large-angle particle containment (Critical requirement)**
- The 25% of muons and 35% of protons at >50° demand **true 3D tracking**
- Current FGD x/y layers have blind spots for particles traveling parallel to layer planes
- Cubic geometry provides **quasi-isotropic response** - no preferred directions
- 56 cm depth allows ~450 MeV/c proton range coverage (median momentum)

**2. Proton reconstruction performance**
- 1 cm granularity resolves **dE/dx along the full track** for particle ID
- Proton tracks of 5-50 cm are fully sampled (covering 100-900 MeV/c range)
- Range-momentum reconstruction for contained protons achieves ~5% resolution
- Three-view readout provides redundancy and eliminates tracking ambiguities

**3. Kinematic completeness**
- Fine segmentation reconstructs **vertex position to ~few mm**
- Angular resolution of ~2-3° for tracks >10 cm
- Enables transverse momentum balance: δp_T = √[(Σp_T)² reconstruction]
- Timing resolution (~few ns with MPPCs) aids in separating overlapping tracks

**4. Systematic uncertainty reduction path to 4%**
- Hydrocarbon target composition known to <1% (uniform industrial extrusion)
- Eliminates P0D's water-in/water-out systematic
- High statistics: ~7× larger fiducial mass than single FGD
- Direct measurement of acceptance for large-angle topologies

---

## Essential Complementary Components

### 2. Upstream Time-of-Flight (ToF) Layer

**Specification:**
- Two planes of **1-2 cm thick plastic scintillator** at z = -10 cm and z = -5 cm
- Strip readout with MPPC on both ends
- Timing resolution: <500 ps per plane

**Justification:**
- Discriminates **incoming vs. outgoing tracks** through timing
- Critical for rejecting background from interactions in surrounding material
- Enables t₀ determination for events without TPC matching
- Validates track direction for protons stopping in SuperFGD

### 3. Enhanced TPC Coverage (Modified existing TPCs)

**Modification:**
- Extend TPC1 **cathode plane 30 cm upstream** into freed space
- Add thin field cage walls at new boundary

**Justification:**
- Captures forward-going muons for momentum-by-curvature measurement
- High-momentum protons (>900 MeV/c, 6% of sample) exit SuperFGD; TPC provides momentum
- Cross-calibration: TPC dE/dx vs. SuperFGD range/dE/dx for protons
- No change to gas system or readout - minimal cost

---

## Alternative Technologies Considered and Rejected

### Liquid Argon TPC
**Rejected because:**
- Drift time (~ms) incompatible with surface cosmic ray rates at ND280
- Requires expensive cryogenics in limited space
- 0.2 T magnetic field insufficient for charge sign selection
- Construction timeline too long for T2K-II schedule

### High-Pressure Gas TPC
**Rejected because:**
- Low density requires >1 m depth for 450 MeV/c proton stopping power
- Doesn't fit in 60 cm available depth
- Complex pressure vessel integration with magnet
- Higher material budget in entrance/exit windows

### Silicon Tracking Detectors
**Rejected because:**
- Order of magnitude more expensive (~$50M vs. ~$10M)
- Dead material from readout electronics degrades calorimetry
- Power dissipation and cooling challenging in confined volume
- Over-engineered for 0.6 GeV neutrino energy scale

### Emulsion + Tracking Detector Hybrid
**Rejected because:**
- Emulsion scanning speed inadequate for required statistics
- Cannot trigger or select events in real-time
- No timing information for background rejection

---

## Readout and DAQ Requirements

### Front-end Electronics
- **MPPCs:** Hamamatsu S13360 series (50 μm pixel, 3×3 mm²)
- ~12,000 channels (2M cubes × 3 fibers × 2 ends, with multiplexing)
- Trip-t front-end ASICs (existing T2K technology) with extended dynamic range
- Waveform digitization at 65 MHz for timing extraction

### Data Acquisition
- Integration with existing ND280 trigger and DAQ
- ~10 MB per neutrino spill (assuming 500:1 data reduction from hit finding)
- Negligible impact on total T2K data volume

---

## Physics Performance Estimates

### Event Selection Efficiency
- **CC0π events (νμ n → μ⁻ p):** 45% efficiency in fiducial volume
  - Muon reconstructed: 95% (>85% also matched to TPC)
  - Proton reconstructed: 55% (including 35% large-angle)
  - Both contained and identified: 47%

### Systematic Uncertainty Contributors
| Source | Current P0D+FGD | Proposed SuperFGD | Improvement |
|--------|----------------|-------------------|-------------|
| Target composition | 3.5% | 0.8% | Uniform CH |
| Acceptance (large angle) | 4.2% | 1.5% | 3D coverage |
| Proton tracking threshold | 2.8% | 1.2% | Isotropic, fine granularity |
| FSI modeling | 3.5% | 2.5% | Kinematic constraints |
| **Total (quadrature)** | **~6.5%** | **~3.2%** | **Meets 4% goal** |

---

## Construction and Schedule

- Scintillator extrusion (proven technology from FGD construction)
- Fiber and MPPC procurement (large orders reduce unit cost)
- Electronics fabrication

### Assembly (Months 12-24)

- Automated fiber threading and testing

### Installation (Month 24-27)

- TPC1 cathode modification (4 weeks)
- SuperFGD installation and cabling (6 weeks)
- Magnet-on commissioning (2 weeks)

**Total:** 27 months to first beam, compatible with T2K-II timeline

- Scintillator and fibers: $4M
- MPPCs and electronics: $3.5M
- Mechanical structure: $1.5M
- ToF system: $0.8M
- Contingency (25%): $2.5M
- **Total: ~$12.5M**
