- About 2 million 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene cubes, roughly 192 × 184 × 56 cubes. This is about 1.9 × 1.8 × 0.56 m and fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- Total mass about 2 t of CH target, roughly twice FGD1+FGD2 combined.
- Each cube has a reflective chemical-etch coating and three orthogonal holes.
- Three orthogonal Kuraray Y-11 (1 mm) wavelength-shifting fibres run through the cube in x, y and z.
- Fibres are read out on one end by MPPCs of the Hamamatsu S13360 type, about 56,000 channels. The far end is mirrored.
- Target performance: about 40–60 p.e. per fibre for a MIP, sub-ns time resolution per fibre, and cube-to-cube optical crosstalk at the few-% level.

**Why this design**

- **Isotropic acceptance.** FGD bars all lie perpendicular to the beam. Tracks at large angle run along a single bar or layer and are lost or badly reconstructed. With about 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons above 50°, this is the dominant acceptance loss. Three orthogonal 2D projections from cubes give uniform 3D reconstruction at any angle, including backward.
- **Low proton threshold.** With 1 cm granularity seen in all three views, a proton needs only a few cubes, about 2–3 cm of range, to be tracked. The proton momentum threshold falls from roughly 450 MeV/c in the FGD to about 300 MeV/c. This matters because the leading-proton median is 450 MeV/c, so the current detector misses about half the protons. TKI variables (δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T) require that proton.
- **Fully active.** There are no passive layers, so vertex activity, short tracks and calorimetric dE/dx for particle identification are all measured. Stopping protons, π±, and Michel electrons from μ→e decay are all visible.
- **Neutron detection.** Neutrons are detected through isolated delayed hits plus timing. This gives access to antineutrino CC events and the full kinematic imbalance, which is an added physics bonus.
- **Acceptable target material.** The target is hydrocarbon, as the brief permits. FGD2 stays in place downstream to provide the C/H₂O comparison.

**Alternatives considered and rejected**

- *Finer x/y bars, or bars rotated in three views:* still blind to tracks along the bar direction, with an ambiguous 3D match for multi-track events.
- *Liquid-argon TPC:* wrong nucleus, cryogenics inside the magnet, and slow.
- *High-pressure gas TPC:* too little mass in 0.6 m.

## 2. High-Angle TPCs (two modules, above and below the target)

**What to build**

- TPC modules about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m, drifting vertically to the readout.
- The same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ (95:3:2) gas as the existing TPCs, for operational commonality.
- A thin, low-mass composite field cage (aramid/honeycomb laminate, a few % X₀) to minimise multiple scattering and conversions before the tracking volume.
- Readout by **resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode, "ERAM")** with pads of roughly 10 × 11 mm.

**Why the TPCs are needed**

- High-angle muons exit the target upward or downward and never reach the forward TPCs. Without these modules there is no magnetic momentum or charge-sign measurement for that quarter of the muons.
- Protons above about 900 MeV/c (about 6%) and energetic pions escape the target. The HA-TPCs measure them by curvature in the 0.2 T field. They also provide dE/dx particle ID (target resolution under 10%) to separate μ, π, p and e. The cube target cannot contain or reliably identify these particles alone.

**Why resistive Micromegas**

- The resistive layer spreads charge over neighbouring pads. Wider pads, and therefore fewer channels, then give *better* spatial resolution (below about 600 µm) through charge-sharing fits.
- The layer suppresses sparks, protecting the electronics without needing a protection network on every channel.
- Bulk Micromegas is already proven in ND280, which lowers technical risk.

## 3. Time-of-Flight envelope

**What to build**

- Six planes surrounding the target and HA-TPC assembly.
- Planes made of about 2.2 m long, 1 cm thick plastic scintillator bars.
- Each bar read out at both ends by arrays of large-area MPPCs.
- Target time resolution of about 150 ps or better per hit.

**Why it is needed**

- **Track direction.** The ToF identifies whether a track is entering or leaving. This rejects backgrounds from interactions in the magnet, the ECal or outside the fiducial volume, which become critical once backward and high-angle tracks are accepted.
- **Particle ID.** Velocity measurement improves PID, for example e/μ separation at low momentum and p/π⁺ separation where dE/dx bands cross.
- **Event timing.** It provides an event time reference for target-based neutron time-of-flight.

## 4. Readout and supporting changes

**Electronics**

- *Target:* new front-end electronics based on the CITIROC ASIC, giving charge and timing on about 56k channels with multiple-hit capability within a spill. Use the newest low-crosstalk, low-dark-rate MPPCs.
- *HA-TPC:* front ends based on the AFTER/AGET ASIC, mounted directly on the ERAM modules, compatible with the existing TPC DAQ.

**Integration**

- Mount the target, both HA-TPCs and the ToF on a common support in the former P0D basket.
- Keep the existing ECal and SMRD so the new region retains calorimetric and muon-range coverage.
- Recommission the upstream ECal envelope around the new volume where possible.

**Calibration**

- Plan for a cosmic-ray and test-beam programme on prototypes covering cube light yield, crosstalk and neutron response. Charged-particle and neutron test beams such as CERN and LANL are suitable.
- Provide an in-situ LED system for MPPC gain monitoring.

## Expected outcome

| Capability | Current FGD + TPC | Recommended upgrade |
|---|---|---|
| Muon acceptance | Forward hemisphere only | ~4π, including >50° and backward |
| Proton threshold | ~450 MeV/c | ~300 MeV/c |
| Protons above 900 MeV/c | Lost if not forward | Curvature measured in HA-TPC |
| Neutrons | No measurement | Detected by timing |
| CH target mass (new region) | — | ~2 t |

Together these allow TKI-based separation of nuclear effects (Fermi motion, 2p2h, final-state interactions). This directly reduces the flux × cross-section extrapolation uncertainty to Super-K toward the ~4% T2K-II goal.

The panel endorses this configuration and recommends prioritising cube production QA and early ERAM prototype validation, as these are the schedule-critical items.

# Recommendation: Active Target Upgrade for the Kestrel Flats Near Station

## Summary

Replace the target region with three systems:

1. **A fine-grained 3D plastic-scintillator target** of about 1 cm optically isolated cubes read out on three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibre axes, a "Super-FGD"-style design.
2. **Two thin high-angle TPCs** above and below the target, read out with resistive Micromegas.
3. **A hermetic time-of-flight (ToF) shell** of fast scintillator bars around the assembly.

Keep the existing downstream drift chambers for forward tracks. This is essentially the architecture of the T2K ND280 upgrade, which addresses a very similar problem at a similar beam energy. It is scaled here to your envelope and to the weaker 0.15 T field.

## 1. Active target: 3D-readout plastic scintillator cubes

**Technology**
- About 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene cubes with a reflective (TiO₂) etched surface.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal 1 mm WLS fibres.
- Each fibre is read out by an SiPM/MPPC at one end, with a mirror on the other.

**Why this, rather than the alternatives**

- **Isotropic acceptance.** Conventional 2D bar planes perpendicular to the beam lose efficiency for tracks near 90°, which run inside a single plane. Three orthogonal projections give roughly uniform hit efficiency at all polar and azimuthal angles, including backward-going tracks. This directly serves the muon requirement at every angle.
- **Low proton threshold.**
  - A 60 MeV kinetic-energy proton (p ≈ 340 MeV/c) has a range of about 3 g/cm², roughly 3 cm in polystyrene.
  - That gives about 3 cubes in any direction, which is enough for a reconstructed stub with a dE/dx Bragg-peak signature.
  - The Super-FGD prototypes demonstrated thresholds near 300 MeV/c (about 47 MeV kinetic energy), with margin below your goal.
  - Bar detectors with 1 cm × 4 cm granularity, or a scintillator-plus-water sandwich, cannot do this isotropically.
- **Hydrogen fraction.**
  - Polystyrene (CH)ₙ has a hydrogen nucleon fraction of 1/13 ≈ 7.7%.
  - This is well under the 20% ceiling, so the hydrogen-subtraction model stays valid with a large margin.
  - The choice also leaves room for any hydrogen in fibres, glue, or structural plastics.
  - For comparison, CH₂ liquid scintillator would give about 14% and water about 11%, both acceptable but with less margin.
- **Neutron and timing benefits.** The good timing (about 1 ns per channel, better when combined) allows ToF-based neutron detection and helps vertex-activity studies. This is a bonus for energy reconstruction.

**Sizing within the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m envelope**

I assume 2.6 m is horizontal-transverse, 2.3 m is vertical, and 0.9 m is along the beam.

- **Target:** a horizontal slab of about 2.4 m (horizontal) × 0.5 m (vertical) × 0.85 m (beam), giving about 240 × 50 × 85 cubes.
  - This is roughly 1 m³, or about 1 tonne of CH, which is ample statistics at 410 m.
  - It needs about 12k + 20k + 4k ≈ 37k readout channels.
- **Space for the TPCs:** this leaves about 0.85–0.9 m above and below the slab.
- **Pile-up:** event rates should be checked against the spill intensity. At a near detector, cube-level 3D reconstruction tolerates overlapping activity better than bars.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Gas TPCs with T2K-type gas (Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀).
- Light composite (aramid/honeycomb) field cages, to keep material between the target and gas low.
- Readout by **resistive (encapsulated-resistor) Micromegas**.

**Justification**

- **Covering muons near 90°.** Muons near 90° exit up or down and never reach the downstream chambers. The HA-TPCs measure their momentum, charge, and dE/dx (μ/e/π separation), restoring high-angle muon efficiency. Backward muons that exit upward or downward are measured the same way.
- **Momentum resolution in a 0.15 T field.** The field is weaker than ND280's 0.2 T, so spatial resolution matters.
  - The sagitta at 1 GeV/c over about 0.8 m is s = 0.3·B·L²/(8p) ≈ 3.6 mm.
  - Resistive Micromegas spread charge over neighbouring pads. They reach about 0.3–0.6 mm resolution with ~1 cm pads and far fewer channels than fine pads.
  - With ~70–80 samples, this gives roughly 10% at 1 GeV/c and better at the typical 0.3–0.7 GeV/c muon momenta.
  - It also gives clean charge identification.
- **Spark protection.** The resistive layer protects the electronics from sparks without needing sector-level HV trips.

**Muons exiting sideways.** Muons that leave horizontally in the transverse direction cross up to about 1.2 m of scintillator. Many range out, so their momentum comes from range. The rest are measured by curvature in the cubes plus the ToF exit timing. This still meets the 25% floor.

## 3. Time-of-flight shell

**Technology**
- Plastic scintillator bars (about 12 cm wide, 1 cm thick).
- Double-ended SiPM-array readout, giving about 150 ps resolution.
- Panels on all six faces of the target-plus-TPC assembly, including an upstream wall.

**Justification**
- **Direction of travel.** Light takes about 3 ns per metre. At 150 ps resolution the shell unambiguously separates backward-going muons from forward-going particles entering from outside. Without this, backward tracks are a large ambiguity.
- **Out-of-detector background.** The upstream and side panels veto particles produced in the magnet and surrounding material.
- **Particle ID.** Combined with the cube timing, the shell adds e/μ/p separation in the crossover regions where dE/dx alone is weak.

## 4. Retained and supporting items

- **Downstream drift chambers:** keep them unchanged for forward tracks. Align their trigger and timing to the new systems.
- **Readout:** use common front-end electronics (SiPM ASICs for cubes and ToF; AFTER/DREAM-type electronics for the TPCs) with a beam-spill-synchronised trigger.
- **Calibration:**
  - Cosmic-ray running, which is valuable precisely for high-angle and backward tracks.
  - LED injection for the SiPMs.
  - A TPC laser or ⁵⁵Fe gain system.
- **Validation:** before construction, run a beam-test prototype (about 10³–10⁴ cubes) to confirm proton-stub reconstruction at about 60 MeV and timing at your fibre lengths. Up to about 2.4 m, fibre attenuation should be checked.

## Requirement traceability

| Requirement | Satisfied by |
|---|---|
| Muon ≥25% efficiency at all angles, including 90° and backward | 3D cubes (isotropic tracking); HA-TPCs (up/down momentum and charge); ToF (direction) |
| Protons at all angles down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy | 1 cm cubes with three-view readout: ~3 cm range gives ≥3 hits isotropically |
| Hydrogen ≤20% of target nucleons | Polystyrene: 7.7% |
| Fits the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m envelope and the 0.15 T magnet | ~2.4 × 0.5 × 0.85 m target plus two ~0.85 m HA-TPCs; resistive Micromegas compensate for the low field |

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Constraints Before Listing Upgrades

The requirements drive the technology choices:
- Full 4π muon reconstruction including backward and transverse tracks → needs tracking that works in all directions, not just downstream
- Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~3 cm in water, ~1.5 mm in scintillator) → needs fine-grained, high-density active material
- Hydrogen fraction ≤ 2% of nucleons → essentially **no free hydrogen**, ruling out water, plastic scintillator (CH ratio too high), and hydrocarbon-based materials
- Volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (depth along beam only 0.9 m, so shallow along beam)
- Must sit inside existing warm dipole, working with existing downstream drift chambers for through-going muon momentum

---

## Upgrade 1: Active Target Tracking Medium — Liquid Argon or Gaseous Argon TPC

**Technology: High-pressure Argon gas TPC, or more practically, a fine-grained plastic scintillator replaced by a liquid argon TPC with imaging capability**

Wait — plastic scintillator is ruled out by the hydrogen constraint. Let me be precise.

**Technology: High-Pressure Gaseous Argon Time Projection Chamber (HPgAr TPC)**

**Why:**
- Argon is a pure noble element — **zero hydrogen**, so the hydrogen fraction constraint is trivially satisfied
- A gas TPC provides continuous, fully 3D tracking of all charged particles in the active volume, with no preferred direction — satisfying the 4π reconstruction requirement for both muons and protons
- The pressure can be tuned to optimize the density/range tradeoff: higher pressure shortens the range of 60 MeV protons (kinetic energy range in Ar gas at 10 atm is a few cm, which is detectable), while still allowing track reconstruction
- Gas TPCs have demonstrated reconstruction of tracks at all angles including 90° and backward-going in experiments such as ALICE and in prototype near detectors (e.g., ND-GAr concept for DUNE)
- The existing dipole field permeates the gas volume and provides momentum measurement for contained tracks via curvature, **supplementing** the downstream drift chambers for tracks that do exit
- No preferred readout axis means transverse and backward muons curve in the magnetic field and can be reconstructed from their helical trajectories entirely within the volume
- Spatial resolution of ~1 mm or better (achievable with pad or pixel readout) is needed to resolve the short ~2–5 cm proton tracks from 60 MeV protons at higher pressure

**Specific implementation:** Cylindrical or rectangular field cage with the drift direction along the beam axis (taking advantage of the 0.9 m shallow dimension as a manageable drift length); cathode at the upstream face, anode readout planes at the downstream face. Pad or pixel-based anode plane readout (e.g., Micromegas or GEM detectors) at ~3–5 mm pitch.

**Concern addressed:** At 10 atm, 60 MeV proton range ≈ several cm → reconstructible. Muon tracks traverse the volume and either stop (reconstructed by range + curvature) or exit into the downstream drift chambers (reconstructed by combined fit).

---

## Upgrade 2: Anode Readout Planes — Pixel or Fine-Pad Micromegas/GEM Arrays

**Technology: Resistive Micromegas or GEM-based pad readout with ~3 mm pitch, tiled across the 2.6 m × 2.3 m anode face**

**Why:**
- Required to achieve ~1 mm 3D point resolution needed for short proton tracks
- Micromegas and GEMs are well-established, robust, and can be tiled to cover the large anode area
- Resistive Micromegas suppress ion feedback and discharge damage, critical for longevity in a high-rate near-detector environment
- Fine pitch ensures two-track separation for events with multiple protons or pion-proton overlap in the vertex region
- Must be compatible with operation inside the magnetic field — standard issue for Micromegas/GEM detectors, which are non-ferromagnetic

---

## Upgrade 3: Downstream Muon Identifier / Range Stack — Magnetized Iron or Instrumented Return Yoke

**Technology: Instrumented iron range stack with scintillator planes interleaved, placed immediately downstream of the TPC exit**

**Why:**
- Muons that exit the TPC must be identified as muons (not pions) and have their momentum measured
- The existing downstream drift chambers measure curvature but do not provide muon/pion separation or range measurement for stopping muons
- An iron range stack with scintillator planes provides:
  - **Muon identification** via penetration depth (pions interact hadronically and stop earlier)
  - **Momentum by range** for muons that stop in the stack, cross-calibrating with the curvature measurement
  - Partial containment of Michel electrons from stopping muons → purity cross-check
- 25% minimum efficiency at **all angles** means some muons exit sideways through the 2.6 m × 2.3 m lateral faces; the range stack cannot catch these
- Therefore: **lateral muon taggers** (see Upgrade 4) are also needed

---

## Upgrade 4: Lateral and Upstream Muon Taggers — Scintillator Panels with SiPM Readout

**Technology: Large-area plastic scintillator panels (e.g., extruded scintillator bars with WLS fiber + SiPM readout), covering the four lateral faces and upstream face of the TPC volume**

**Why:**
- Transverse muons (90° to beam) and backward muons exit through the lateral and upstream faces
- The ≥25% efficiency at **every** angle, explicitly including perpendicular and backward tracks, cannot be met by downstream instrumentation alone
- Scintillator panels on all five non-anode faces (the four sides and the upstream cathode face) tag exiting muons and provide:
  - A hit time and position for the exiting track
  - A seed for momentum reconstruction using curvature within the TPC gas volume (even a partial arc in the magnetic field gives momentum)
  - Charge sign from the direction of curvature
- Plastic scintillator is acceptable here because these panels are **outside** the active target volume — they do not contribute hydrogen to the interaction target
- SiPM readout is preferred over PMTs: operates in the magnetic field without gain degradation, compact, and reliable
- The 0.15 T dipole field means muon track bending radius for a 500 MeV/c muon is ~11 m, so only modest curvature is visible in the 0.9 m depth; the lateral taggers are essential to constrain the exit angle and thus the full momentum vector for such tracks

---

## Upgrade 5: High-Speed, Low-Deadtime Data Acquisition System

**Technology: Continuous waveform digitization with streaming readout (e.g., 65 MSPS or faster ADCs per channel, FPGA-based trigger-free readout, similar to the DUNE ND-LAr or ALICE TPC upgrade DAQ architecture)**

**Why:**
- A gas TPC at the near detector position (410 m from target) sees very high neutrino interaction rates during beam spills; a triggered DAQ would have deadtime that disproportionately cuts efficiency for the specific topologies of interest (backward/transverse tracks are slower to form triggers)
- Streaming readout with online hit-finding eliminates deadtime and allows offline reconstruction of all track topologies without trigger bias
- The 2.6 m × 2.3 m anode with ~3 mm pitch Micromegas implies O(10⁵) channels; this requires a scalable DAQ architecture with on-detector zero-suppression and optical fiber readout to surface electronics
- Synchronized timing with the beam spill structure at the sub-microsecond level is needed to associate interactions with the correct beam bucket

---

## Upgrade 6: Slow Control and Gas Purity / Pressure Management System

**Technology: Closed-loop gas recirculation system with inline purity monitors (using UV laser or alpha-source electron lifetime monitors), pressure regulation to ±0.1% stability, and O₂/H₂O filtration to <1 ppb levels**

**Why:**
- Electron lifetime in the gas directly determines whether tracks near the cathode (up to 0.9 m drift) produce detectable signals; impurity levels above ~1 ppb O₂-equivalent cause unacceptable attenuation
- Pressure stability is critical: density fluctuations change the range of 60 MeV protons and would smear the energy reconstruction needed for the hydrogen-subtraction model
- The hydrogen-subtraction analysis requires that systematic uncertainties on target composition remain small; gas purity and density are direct inputs to this, so instrumented monitoring is not optional
- A closed recirculation system with charcoal and molecular sieve filters is standard for noble gas TPCs (ArgoNeuT, MicroBooNE, ND-GAr prototypes) and is well-understood technically

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Active target medium | High-pressure gaseous Ar TPC | Zero hydrogen; 4π tracking; short proton tracks |
| Anode readout | Resistive Micromegas / GEM, ~3 mm pitch | mm-scale resolution for 60 MeV protons |
| Downstream muon ID | Instrumented iron range stack + scintillator | Muon ID and momentum for forward-going tracks |
| Lateral/upstream taggers | Extruded scintillator + WLS + SiPM panels | ≥25% muon efficiency at transverse and backward angles |
| DAQ | Streaming waveform digitization, FPGA readout | No trigger bias against non-forward topologies |
| Gas system | Recirculating purifier + purity and pressure monitors | Hydrogen model validity; track reconstruction quality |

# ND280-Style Near Detector Upgrade: Proposed Hardware

The current detector is built around forward-going tracks. Its targets are planar x/y bar layers perpendicular to the beam, and its TPCs sit downstream. That geometry fails for the roughly 25% of muons and 35% of protons that leave at more than 50°. It also loses short, low-momentum proton tracks, which cross only a few planes and have no 3D view.

The box left by removing the photon-tagging section should hold a highly granular, isotropic 3D target with tracking and timing wrapped around it. Each upgrade below gives the technology and the reason for it.

## 1. Fine-grained 3D scintillator target in the central volume

**Technology:**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes. Their surfaces are chemically etched to form a reflector.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres along x, y and z.
- Each fibre is read at one end by an SiPM (MPPC), consistent with the existing readout.
- An array of about 192 × 182 × 56 cubes fills the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box, giving about 2 t of hydrocarbon.
- The order of magnitude is ~56,000 channels, rather than one per cube.
- Front-end electronics with good timing (sub-ns per channel) are needed, for example Citiroc-class ASICs.

**Why:**
- **Near-4π acceptance.** Three orthogonal 2D projections give true 3D reconstruction. Tracks at high angle, and even perpendicular to the beam, are reconstructed as well as forward ones. This directly recovers the large high-angle muon and proton fractions.
- **Low proton threshold.** A proton near the 450 MeV/c median has about 100 MeV kinetic energy and ranges roughly 8 cm in plastic, or about 8 cubes. A 1 cm pitch keeps the tracking threshold near 300 MeV/c. The current 9.6 mm bars in alternating 2D layers lose these short tracks.
- **Proton identification and momentum by range and dE/dx.** Most protons stop inside the target. Their momenta come from range and calorimetric energy, and the Bragg peak gives particle ID. Transverse kinematic imbalance needs exactly this proton vector.
- **Fully active hydrocarbon target.** It adds about 2 t of target mass. This is acceptable because the programme accepts carbon, and the water-layer target stays for carbon-to-water comparison.
- **Neutron tagging.** Fine granularity plus timing lets isolated neutron-induced hits be associated with the vertex. Their time of flight gives the neutron energy, which extends kinematic imbalance analysis to antineutrino events.

## 2. Two high-angle gas TPCs, above and below the new target

**Technology:**
- Two thin TPCs of about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m each, sharing the magnet's 0.2 T field.
- An argon-based gas like the existing chambers, for example Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀.
- A lightweight composite field cage (laminated aramid/honeycomb panels) to minimise dead material between the target and the TPC gas.
- Readout by **resistive (encapsulated-resistive-anode) Micromegas**. Charge spreading through the resistive layer gives better spatial resolution with fewer, larger pads (about 1 × 1 cm). It also suppresses sparking.
- Upgraded front-end electronics (AFTER/AGET-class ASICs) mounted directly on the modules.

**Why:**
- The existing TPCs sit downstream and see only forward tracks. High-angle muons, and the protons that escape the target, exit vertically. The new TPCs catch them.
- They provide magnetic momentum and charge-sign measurement from curvature for escaping tracks, which range cannot provide. This covers the most energetic muons and the roughly 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c, which often leave the 0.6 m target.
- dE/dx in gas gives particle ID to separate μ/π/p/e. Electron identification also supports νe and photon-background studies after the photon-tagging section is removed.
- Resistive Micromegas keeps spatial resolution good while limiting channel count and cost.

## 3. Time-of-flight panels enclosing the new module

**Technology:**
- Six planes surrounding the target-plus-TPC assembly.
- Each plane is made of long plastic scintillator bars (about 1 cm thick, 12 cm wide, ~2 m long).
- Bars are read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs, giving a timing resolution of about 100–150 ps.

**Why:**
- They measure track direction, distinguishing inward- from outward-going tracks. This rejects backgrounds entering from outside the magnet and from the yoke, and resolves backward and high-angle tracks, which can be ambiguous without timing.
- Time of flight adds particle ID, such as μ/e separation at low momentum where TPC dE/dx bands cross.
- They give a precise global timing reference (t₀) for the TPCs and for neutron time of flight in the target.

## 4. Supporting infrastructure

- **DAQ and global trigger/clock upgrade.** New subdetectors must integrate synchronously with the existing TPCs, calorimeters and side-muon detectors. This needs common timing distribution and higher bandwidth for about 100k extra channels.
- **Mechanics.** A support structure in the old photon-tagging basket keeps dead material low, especially between the target and the high-angle TPCs. It must fit inside the 7.0 × 3.5 × 3.6 m magnet volume.
- **Calibration systems.** Cube-by-cube light-yield and timing calibration, using cosmic-ray tracks plus LED/laser injection. A laser photoelectron-generation system for TPC drift-velocity monitoring.
- **Gas system expansion** for the two additional TPCs.

## How this meets the 6% → 4% goal

- **Full phase space.** Near-4π muon and proton acceptance makes the near-detector selection match the far detector's nearly isotropic acceptance. This reduces extrapolation model dependence.
- **Kinematically complete events.** A low proton threshold and good proton momentum resolution enable transverse kinematic imbalance measurements, plus neutron-tagged antineutrino events. These constrain nuclear effects (Fermi motion, final-state interactions, 2p2h) and improve neutrino energy reconstruction.
- **More statistics.** The added ~2 t of active target increases event counts.
- **Carbon-to-water comparison retained** through the existing downstream water-layer target, so the far detector's water target is still constrained.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Summary of Constraints Driving the Design

Before proposing hardware, let me be explicit about what the physics demands:

- **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles** including 90° and backward tracks — rules out any purely downstream-projective tracking
- **Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** — range ~3 cm in liquid argon, ~1.5 cm in plastic scintillator; requires fine-grained tracking with low-Z material to keep range long enough to measure
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤2% of nucleons** — this is the most severe constraint and effectively **rules out hydrocarbon scintillator (CH₂, polystyrene) as the primary target material**
- **Volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m** within an existing warm dipole at 0.15 T
- **Flux peaks ~0.7 GeV, 410 m baseline** — moderate event rate, not a pile-up nightmare

---

## Proposed Active Target: Optically-Segmented Liquid Argon STT Sandwich

I propose a **segmented liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC) with an embedded straw-tube tracker (STT)**, deliberately avoiding hydrogen-rich materials in the fiducial volume.

Actually, let me reconsider more carefully and propose what genuinely fits the constraints.

---

## Revised Proposal: Segmented Scintillator Cube Tracker with Liquid Argon Absorber Panels (No — hydrogen problem)

After working through the hydrogen constraint more carefully:

**Polystyrene**: C₈H₈ per monomer → H nucleons/(H+C nucleons) = 8/16 = **50%** — completely excluded  
**Liquid argon**: no hydrogen → 0% — allowed  
**Water (H₂O)**: H/(H+O) = 2/18 nucleons = **11%** — excluded  
**Liquid helium**: no hydrogen — allowed but impractical  
**Carbon (graphite/diamond-like)**: no hydrogen — allowed  
**Silicon**: no hydrogen — allowed  
**Iron**: no hydrogen — allowed  
**Aluminum**: no hydrogen — allowed  

The ≤2% hydrogen constraint means the target must be either **hydrogen-free entirely**, or use a material where the hydrogen fraction is naturally ≤2% by nucleon count. 

**Example**: Aluminium has no hydrogen → 0%. Iron → 0%. Liquid argon → 0%.

The target material itself must therefore be a **non-hydrogenous medium** such as liquid argon, aluminum, or iron, with tracking embedded within it.

---

## Final Concrete Proposal

### 1. Primary Target Medium: Liquid Argon Modules

Fill the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume with **modular liquid argon mini-TPC cells**, each approximately **30 cm × 30 cm × 30 cm** (a 3D cubic array of roughly 8 × 7 × 3 = ~168 modules).

**Why modular rather than monolithic LArTPC:**
- A single-volume LArTPC of this size (~5.4 tonnes) in a magnet bore is feasible but the drift direction must be chosen; with 0.9 m along beam, drift along beam axis gives 0.9 m maximum drift (~180 µs at 1 kV/cm), acceptable
- However, 90° and backward tracks in a single-volume TPC are reconstructible — LArTPC already handles 4π by nature
- Modular design allows the existing magnet bore dimensions and permits maintenance

**Specific LArTPC parameters:**
- Electric field: 500 V/cm (standard), giving ~1.6 mm/µs drift velocity
- Wire pitch: **3 mm** on collection and two induction planes (U, V, Y at 0°, ±60°)
- Maximum drift in 30 cm module: ~190 µs — no space charge issue at near-detector rates
- Each module: 3 wire planes on the anode end, cathode at opposite face
- Front-end ASICs: **LArASIC** (already developed for SBND/MicroBooNE/DUNE) cold inside the LAr
- Readout: cold multiplexing via **ColdADC + COLDATA** chips (DUNE FD technology, adapted)

**Why this handles the angular coverage requirement:**
LArTPC is inherently a 3D imaging device. A backward-going muon or a 90° proton leaves a track in the LAr image regardless of direction. The 3mm wire pitch gives ~3 mm position resolution, sufficient to reconstruct proton tracks down to ~3 cm length (60 MeV proton range in LAr).

**Hydrogen content check:**  
Liquid argon (Ar, Z=18, A=40): **zero hydrogen nucleons**. ✓

---

### 2. Muon Momentum Measurement: Existing Downstream Drift Chambers + Range Supplement

The existing gas drift chambers downstream already measure momentum for forward-going muons via magnetic rigidity in the 0.15 T field. These are retained.

However, 90° and backward muons **do not reach the downstream spectrometer**. For these:

#### 2a. Embedded Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) Between LAr Modules

Install **2 mm-gap glass RPC planes** between columns of LAr modules, with **1 cm strip pitch** in both transverse dimensions.

- Spacing: every ~10 cm along beam axis → ~9 RPC planes across the 0.9 m depth
- Strip pitch 1 cm provides adequate position resolution for muon tracking in the magnet field
- RPCs are thin (< 5 mm total with gas gap + electrodes), minimally invasive
- Operating gas: standard RPC mixture (C₂H₂F₄/iso-C₄H₁₀/SF₆)
- These provide **timing** (∼1 ns resolution) for drift time reference in LAr modules and **muon identification** via minimum-ionizing signature

**Hydrogen in RPC gas**: negligible — the gas volume is tiny compared to LAr target mass, and C₂H₂F₄ has some F, H but the mass fraction in the total detector is well below 2% nucleon fraction.

**Momentum from curvature for 90° muons:**  
A 90° muon (traveling transverse to beam, within the 2.6 m × 2.3 m transverse plane) traverses the full 2.6 m or 2.3 m width. At 0.15 T, the sagitta for a 1 GeV/c muon over 2 m is:

s = L²qB/(8p) = (4 m²)(1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C)(0.15 T)/(8 × (1 GeV/c / c))

Converting: p = 1 GeV/c = 5.34 × 10⁻¹⁹ kg·m/s

s = (4)(1.6×10⁻¹⁹)(0.15) / (8 × 5.34×10⁻¹⁹) = (9.6×10⁻²⁰)/(4.27×10⁻¹⁸) ≈ **2.2 cm**

With 1 cm RPC strip pitch and multiple samplings, this sagitta is **measurable** at ~2σ per point, adequate for ≥25% reconstruction efficiency requirement (which is an efficiency floor, not a resolution requirement per se).

#### 2b. Backward-Going Muon Handling

Backward muons re-enter the upstream face of the target volume. The LArTPC imaging reconstructs the track within the volume. If the muon exits upstream, it enters a region outside the active target.

**Add an upstream muon tagger**: a plane of **scintillating fiber tracker** (SciFi, as used in LHCb UT or T2K's SFGD) immediately upstream of the LAr target volume.

- 2 planes of **250 µm diameter Kuraray SCSF-78 scintillating fibers**, arranged in X-Y grid
- Silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readout: **Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS** (1.3 mm pitch, 50 µm cells)
- 2 cm total thickness — minimal nuclear interaction length (~0.1 X₀ in polystyrene fibers)
- This provides a **hit** when a backward muon exits, plus a momentum constraint from range in LArTPC + field integral

**Hydrogen in upstream SciFi plane**: polystyrene fibers — yes, this contains hydrogen. However, this is **upstream of the fiducial volume** and not part of the target definition. The fiducial volume is the LArTPC region only.

---

### 3. Proton Reconstruction at Low Kinetic Energy (down to 60 MeV)

A 60 MeV proton has range ~3.5 cm in liquid argon (from Bethe-Bloch, stopping power ~1.7 MeV·cm²/g × 1.4 g/cm³ ≈ 2.4 MeV/cm, range ≈ 60/2.4 × (Bragg peak correction factor) ≈ **~2.8 cm**).

With 3 mm wire pitch in the LArTPC, a 2.8 cm track spans **~9 wires** — this is **reconstructible** in a 3D LArTPC image with modern pattern recognition (e.g., Pandora, wire-cell tomography).

The critical issue is **noise and threshold**:
- Required: sensitive to ~10-20 ionization electrons/wire for short tracks
- LArASIC equivalent noise charge: ~400 e⁻ ENC cold, giving S/N ~ 15:1 for a minimum track segment — adequate
- **No additional hardware needed for proton tracking beyond the LArTPC itself** provided wire pitch is ≤3 mm

For protons at all angles including 90°: same argument as muons — LArTPC is 4π by nature.

**What about proton momentum?** Range-momentum is determined from the LArTPC image. For a 60 MeV proton:
- Range measurement uncertainty: ~±1 wire = ±3 mm → ±few MeV in kinetic energy — sufficient
- For higher-energy protons that exit the LArTPC module, they enter adjacent modules or hit RPC planes; range can still be summed across modules

---

### 4. Light Detection System for LArTPC Triggering and t₀

Each LAr module needs a **t₀ reference** for the drift coordinate.

**Install X-ARAPUCA light traps** on the cathode face of each module:
- X-ARAPUCA: wavelength-shifting plates (pTP + tetracene) + dichroic filter + SiPM array
- Sensitive to 128 nm LAr scintillation light after shifting to ~430 nm
- Each 30 cm × 30 cm cathode: **4 × X-ARAPUCA cells** (7.5 cm × 7.5 cm each)
- SiPM: **Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) NUV-HD-SF** 6 mm² cells, operated cold at 87K
- Expected light yield: ~20-50 detected photons per MeV deposited → easily triggered on muon tracks and proton tracks ≥10 MeV visible energy
- Timing resolution: **~10 ns** (sufficient for 3 mm spatial resolution along drift: 1.6 mm/µs × 10 ns = 0.016 mm — drift resolution is actually wire-pitch limited, not timing limited)

---

### 5. Summary of Proposed Hardware Stack

| Component | Technology | Purpose |
|-----------|------------|---------|
| Primary active target | Modular LArTPC cells, 30 cm³, 3 mm wire pitch, LArASIC+ColdADC FEE | Neutrino interaction vertex, 4π tracking, proton down to 60 MeV |
| Inter-module tracking planes | Glass RPC, 2 mm gap, 1 cm strips, C₂H₂F₄ gas | Muon tracking in B field for 90° tracks, timing reference |
| Upstream backward-muon tagger | SciFi planes, 250 µm Kuraray SCSF-78, SiPM readout | Tag/veto backward-exiting muons |
| Light detection | X-ARAPUCA + FBK NUV-HD-SF SiPMs, 4/module | t₀ for drift, trigger, Michel electron tagging |
| Downstream spectrometer | **Retain existing gas drift chambers** | Forward muon momentum from magnetic rigidity |

---

### 6. Why This Satisfies the Hydrogen Constraint

| Component | H nucleon fraction |
|-----------|-------------------|
| Liquid argon (bulk target) | 0% |
| RPC gas (by volume, tiny) | Trace; by nucleon fraction of total target mass: <<0.1% |
| X-ARAPUCA wavelength shifter plates | ~grams total vs. ~5 tonnes LAr: negligible |
| Wire insulation, cryostat walls | Outside fiducial volume |
| **Total fiducial H fraction** | **≪ 2%** ✓ |

---

### 7. Critical Engineering Considerations

**Operating LArTPC inside a warm magnet** is non-standard but feasible:
- The cryostat for each module must be non-magnetic: **304 stainless steel** walls (weakly paramagnetic, acceptable at 0.15 T)
- The 0.15 T field does **not significantly affect** electron drift in LAr (drift velocity perturbation < 0.1% at 500 V/cm for B⊥E configuration) for drift lengths < 30 cm
- If drift direction is parallel to B (along beam), magnetic effect is zero by symmetry

**Wire tension in cold LAr modules**: standard MicroBooNE/SBND wire materials (CuBe alloy, 150 µm diameter) handle thermal contraction; already validated.

**Data rate**: ~168 modules × ~3 wire planes × ~100 wires/plane × 2 MHz sampling × 12 bits = ~120 GB/s raw; zero-suppression to ~1% occupancy → ~1.2 GB/s, manageable with modern DAQ (e.g., FELIX readout boards as used in ATLAS/DUNE).

---

This design gives you a **genuine 4π active target** with sub-centimeter 3D imaging, built from demonstrated LArTPC technology, sitting entirely within the hydrogen constraint, and compatible with the existing downstream magnetic spectrometer.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Near Detector Active Target Module

## Core Design Philosophy

The fundamental constraint is the available volume (~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m), the need for kinematic completeness at large angles (>50°), and proton tracking down through the momentum distribution with a median near 450 MeV/c. The 0.6 m depth along beam is tight, so the active target must simultaneously serve as both the neutrino interaction medium and the tracker, with minimal passive material internal to the fiducial volume.

---

## 1. Primary Active Target: Scintillating Fibre Time Projection — SuperFGD

**Technology: Super Fine-Grained Detector (SuperFGD) architecture**

Concretely, an array of **1 × 1 × 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes**, each penetrated along all three orthogonal axes by **1 mm diameter Y-11 wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres** read out at both ends by **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs, e.g. Hamamatsu S13360-1325PE or equivalent 1.3 mm pitch MPPC)**.

### Why this addresses the specific problems:

- **Large-angle proton tracking**: The fully 3D-symmetric cube geometry has no preferred projection axis. A proton leaving at 70° to beam is tracked with identical granularity as one leaving forward. The existing downstream FGD has 2D x/y layer structure that degrades badly for tracks beyond ~40–45° in the z–transverse plane because layer spacing limits dE/dx sampling rate and introduces ambiguities. The cube structure eliminates this.

- **Proton momentum measurement by range**: A 450 MeV/c proton has a range of approximately 9–10 cm in polystyrene (density ~1.05 g/cm³). At 1 cm cube pitch this gives ~9–10 hit cubes along the track, sufficient for range-momentum reconstruction to roughly 2–3% precision. The 900 MeV/c protons (the 6% tail) have ranges of ~40–45 cm, well within the 60 cm depth even for near-axial tracks, and within the 190–200 cm transverse dimensions for the large-angle population.

- **Low threshold for recoil protons**: The fine granularity gives a practical kinetic energy threshold around 40–50 MeV (range ~2 cm), capturing the bulk of the proton momentum spectrum.

### Specific dimensions and count:

Fill the available box to roughly **192 × 184 × 56 cm**, giving approximately **192 × 184 × 56 ≈ 1,978,368 cubes**. Rounding to production units, target ~2 million cubes. Each cube is threaded by fibres in x, y, and z; fibre readout is at the cube-array faces. Total SiPM channel count: for a 192 × 184 × 56 array, the three face-projection counts are:
- x-faces (y–z plane): 184 × 56 × 2 ends = 20,608 channels
- y-faces (x–z plane): 192 × 56 × 2 ends = 21,504 channels  
- z-faces (x–y plane): 192 × 184 × 2 ends = 70,656 channels  
- **Total: ~113,000 SiPM channels**

This is large but comparable to detectors already built (the T2K SuperFGD for ND280 upgrade is 1.8 M cubes, ~56,000 channels at single-ended readout — double-ended readout here is chosen to recover the z-coordinate from timing on the ≤56 cm short fibres).

### Mass and interaction rate:

Volume ≈ 1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m³ ≈ 1.98 m³, mass ≈ 2.08 tonnes of polystyrene (CH). Neutrino interaction rate scales with the downstream FGD1 (1.1 t) so approximately 1.9× the FGD1 rate per unit time, providing useful statistics within the constrained depth.

---

## 2. Timing Layer: Scintillator Time-of-Flight Planes

**Technology: Plastic scintillator planes with SiPM readout, ~200 ps timing resolution**

Place **two scintillator hodoscope planes** immediately upstream and downstream of the SuperFGD cube volume:

- Each plane: array of **2 cm thick × 2 cm wide extruded scintillator bars** (e.g. Eljen EJ-200) running alternately horizontal and vertical, with WLS fibre (Saint-Gobain BCF-92) read at both ends by fast SiPMs (e.g. FBK NUV-HD, 50 µm cell pitch for good photon statistics at this bar size).
- Target single-bar timing resolution: **≤200 ps**, achievable with this technology.
- Purpose: **proton–pion separation** below the momentum range where dE/dx in the cube array alone is unambiguous. At 300 MeV/c, the ToF difference between a proton and a pion over a 60 cm baseline is ~1.3 ns, comfortably resolved at 200 ps. This directly addresses the recoil particle identification needed for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) where misidentified pions fake the signal.
- These planes also provide a fast trigger primitive and help reject beam-unrelated backgrounds (sand muons, cosmic rays) by coincidence timing with beam spill.

---

## 3. Surrounding High-Angle Muon Catcher: Magnetised Iron-Scintillator Sandwich

**Technology: Mini-iron/scintillator range stack on the four transverse faces of the SuperFGD**

The existing dipole magnet yoke instrumentation handles muons that reach it, but the problem stated explicitly is that **~25% of muons leave at >50°**. For a 0.6 GeV peak beam, typical muon momenta are 200–500 MeV/c. A 500 MeV/c muon has a range of ~100 cm in iron or ~170 cm in scintillator. The SuperFGD alone (max ~96 cm diagonal transverse) will not range out the harder muons going sideways before they exit.

Proposal: on the upstream-facing and the four lateral faces of the SuperFGD box, install **thin iron–scintillator sandwich range-stack modules**:

- **10 layers of 2 cm iron + 1 cm plastic scintillator bar plane** per face
- Each scintillator plane: same 2 cm bar technology as the ToF planes above
- Total depth per face: ~30 cm (fits within the magnet aperture given the cube array is set ~15 cm inboard of the magnet bore boundary)
- Magnetic field (0.2 T already present) curves muon tracks through these layers, allowing **sign determination and momentum measurement by curvature** for muons that stop within the range stack
- For muons that punch through, the existing downstream TPCs and ECal take over — these are already in the beam path

This explicitly recovers kinematic completeness for the large-angle muon fraction by instrumented ranging rather than relying on extrapolation.

---

## 4. Upstream Veto and γ-Tagger Replacement

**Technology: 2-layer scintillator veto + thin lead converter**

Since the photon-tagging section is being removed, its γ-rejection function must be partially recovered:

- **Two planes of 1 cm thick scintillator bars** (same SiPM-read WLS-fibre technology) immediately upstream of the SuperFGD, acting as a charged-particle veto to tag beam-related charged backgrounds entering from upstream (e.g. muons from neutrino interactions in upstream material).
- A **1 radiation length (X₀) lead converter plane** (1.76 cm Pb) sandwiched between the two veto planes: photons converting here produce e⁺e⁻ pairs that are vetoed, partially recovering photon-tagging capability for NC π⁰ background rejection relevant to the νe appearance contamination studies.
- Total material: <0.5 cm equivalent active depth, negligible fiducial volume loss.

---

## 5. Front-End Electronics and DAQ

**Technology: Triggered waveform digitisation with ~1 ns sampling**

- Each SiPM channel read by an ASIC (e.g. CITIROC-2A or TARGET-C variant) providing:
  - Charge integration (50 ns gate) for dE/dx
  - Time-over-threshold or peak-time stamp at **~1 ns precision** for 3D hit reconstruction by fibre-light propagation timing
- The double-ended readout on z-fibres (the short 56 cm fibres) enables z-position reconstruction from **timing difference** at ~1 ns → position resolution ~10 cm along fibre, adequate since x/y fibres give the transverse coordinates precisely
- Data concentrator boards (e.g. FPGA-based, Xilinx Kintex UltraScale) aggregating 8×8 SiPM arrays per board, with White Rabbit timing synchronisation to the beam spill signal for <1 ns absolute time alignment

---

## 6. Calibration Hardware

- **LED pulsers** embedded at cube-array face edges, one per 16-fibre group, for SiPM gain monitoring at the ~0.1% level needed to keep dE/dx calibration stable
- **Cosmic-muon reconstruction**: the SuperFGD running in self-triggered mode between beam spills provides ~10⁴ through-going cosmics per day for continuous gain and alignment calibration; the 1 cm cube pitch gives enough hits per cosmic track to perform cell-by-cell gain equalisation
- **Radioactive source channels**: one ⁵⁵Fe source per ToF-plane quadrant for SiPM operating-point verification

---

## Summary Table

| Subsystem | Technology | Key parameter | Physics purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active target | 1 cm³ PS scintillator cubes + WLS fibre + SiPM, double-ended | ~2M cubes, ~113k channels | 4π proton tracking, range-momentum |
| Timing planes | 2 cm EJ-200 bars + BCF-92 WLS + fast SiPM | ≤200 ps per bar | p/π separation below 400 MeV/c |
| Lateral range stack | 10× (2 cm Fe + 1 cm scintillator) per face | ~30 cm depth, 4 faces | Large-angle muon ranging and sign |
| Upstream veto + converter | 2× scintillator + 1 X₀ Pb | <2 cm total depth | Charged veto, partial γ-tagging |
| FEE/DAQ | CITIROC-2A ASICs + FPGA concentrators + White Rabbit | 1 ns timing, 50 ns charge gate | dE/dx + 3D timing reconstruction |
| Calibration | LED pulsers + cosmic self-trigger + ⁵⁵Fe | Continuous, between spills | Gain stability <0.1% |

---

## Expected Performance Gain

The combination of the SuperFGD 4π geometry with the lateral range stack and ToF planes should:

- Raise proton reconstruction efficiency at >50° from roughly 30–40% (FGD1-like) to **>85%**, directly addressing the kinematic completeness requirement for TKI
- Provide proton–pion separation to below 300 MeV/c kinetic energy via combined dE/dx + ToF, reducing the dominant background to TKI signal selection
- With the increased mass (~1.9× FGD1) and improved efficiency, the statistical+systematic combination should approach the **~4% flux×cross-section uncertainty target** for the upgrade phase, particularly because the more complete event reconstruction constrains the multi-nucleon interaction backgrounds that currently dominate the residual systematic

# Proposed Upgrade for the Kestrel Flats Near Station Target Region

## What the requirements imply

- **Muon efficiency of at least 25% at every angle.** Any target built from planes perpendicular to the beam loses tracks near 90°, because they run inside a single plane. The target needs isotropic 3D granularity. The region around it must also catch tracks leaving sideways, up, down and backward, not only forward toward the existing drift chambers.
- **Protons down to about 60 MeV kinetic energy.** The CSDA range of a 60 MeV proton in polystyrene is about 3 g/cm², roughly 3 cm. Seeing such a proton as a track, with dE/dx and a Bragg peak, needs about 1 cm granularity in all three dimensions.
- **Hydrogen at most 20% of target nucleons.** For CH, hydrogen is 1 of 13 nucleons, about 7.7%. For water it is about 11%. Plastic scintillator meets the requirement with margin.
- **Weak field and modest flux energy.** The field is 0.15 T and the flux peaks near 0.7 GeV, so most muons are below about 1 GeV/c. Range and gas-TPC curvature can both measure them.

## Upgrade 1: Fine-grained 3D scintillator-cube active target

**Technology**
- About 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each with a reflective surface (chemical etch).
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibers, read by SiPMs/MPPCs. This follows the SuperFGD approach.
- A suggested footprint is about 2.4 m (x) × 0.8 m (y, vertical) × 0.9 m (z, beam). That gives roughly 1.7 million cubes and about 56,000 channels (sum of the three projection planes, 240×80 + 240×90 + 80×90).
- Front-end electronics with about 1 ns timing.
- The remaining vertical space is reserved for Upgrade 2.

**Physics motivation**
- The three 2D views resolve tracks at any angle. Short protons and high-angle muons are no longer confined to a single plane.
- Protons above about 60 MeV cross at least 3 cubes and are identified through dE/dx.
- Timing information supports:
  - neutron detection via time of flight from the vertex to a secondary hit (transverse kinematic imbalance);
  - Michel electron tagging, which identifies stopping muons and pions.
- The target is fully active, about 1.7 t of CH. Hydrogen makes up about 7.7% of nucleons, well under the 20% limit.
- Horizontal high-angle muons travel along the 2.4 m x-dimension. They can be ranged out in the scintillator, and the range gives their momentum.

## Upgrade 2: High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Two thin gas TPCs, each about 0.7 m tall, filling the remaining height of the 2.3 m region.
- Readout by resistive (encapsulated-resistor) Micromegas, using the T2K-style "ERAM" modules.
- Field cage built from a lightweight composite to minimize dead material.

**Physics motivation**
- Muons near 90° in the vertical plane leave the target and would miss the downstream chambers.
- The TPCs measure their momentum and charge from curvature in the 0.15 T field. They also provide dE/dx to separate muons from pions, protons and electrons.
- This recovers the 60–120° region, where neutrino energy reconstruction and nuclear effects are most sensitive.

## Upgrade 3: Time-of-flight envelope

**Technology**
- Plastic scintillator bars with SiPM readout at both ends, giving about 150 ps resolution.
- The bars enclose the target and TPC package on all six faces.

**Physics motivation**
- The ToF determines track direction, separating backward-going muons from incoming entering tracks.
- It vetoes particles from interactions in the magnet and surrounding material.
- It adds particle ID by velocity.
- Together with the cube target, it makes backward-going muons reconstructable with at least 25% efficiency.

## Integration notes

- **Calibration and monitoring:** an LED or laser light-injection system to track SiPM gain over time.
- **Stability:** temperature control for the SiPMs.
- **Space:** keep cabling and services at the edges of the region to preserve active volume.
- **Downstream use:** the existing drift chambers continue to measure forward tracks that exit the region, giving combined 4π acceptance.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## Context and Constraints

Before proposing upgrades, the key physics requirements drive everything:
- **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles** including 90° and backward tracks (≥90°)
- **Proton tracking down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** (range ~3 cm in water, ~1.4 cm in iron)
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤2% of target nucleons** to keep the hydrogen-subtraction model valid
- **Active target** in a 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume inside a 0.15 T dipole
- Downstream drift chambers already handle forward, high-momentum tracks

The 0.9 m depth along the beam is the tight dimension. Tracks perpendicular to the beam are entirely contained within the transverse envelope (2.6 × 2.3 m) but exit the 0.9 m depth immediately if at all forward or backward, which is why a fully active, fine-grained target is needed rather than a passive target followed by a tracker.

---

## Upgrade 1: Scintillator-Based Fine-Grained Detector (FGD-style)

**Technology:** Extruded polystyrene scintillator bars (e.g. 1 cm × 1 cm cross-section), arranged in alternating X–Y planes, with wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs).

**Physics motivation:**

The 60 MeV kinetic energy threshold for protons corresponds to a range of roughly 3 cm in polystyrene (density ~1.06 g/cm³). With 1 cm bars, a 60 MeV proton traverses approximately 3 bars in a plane pair, giving 3–4 hit coordinates and a usable track. Finer bars (0.5 cm) would improve this but worsen the hydrogen fraction (see below).

Plastic scintillator is composed of roughly (CH)_n, giving a hydrogen-to-carbon ratio near 1:1 by atom count. The hydrogen fraction by nucleon count is approximately:

> H nucleons / total nucleons = 1 / (1 + 12) ≈ 7.7%

This **exceeds** the 2% requirement by a large factor. Therefore plain plastic scintillator cannot serve as the bulk target material in this configuration. However, a water-layer interleaving or a denser fill (see Upgrade 2) can reduce the effective hydrogen fraction while retaining scintillator for active readout. Alternatively, a thin layer of pure scintillator bars can serve as a tracking/veto layer surrounding a denser target, keeping its mass fraction small.

A practical hybrid: scintillator planes every ~2 radiation lengths of denser material keep tracking while the hydrogen fraction from scintillator itself stays below 2% of total nucleon count. If scintillator constitutes ~25% of the mass and the dense material has negligible hydrogen, the effective H fraction ≈ 0.25 × 7.7% ≈ 1.9% — just within budget.

**Benefit for angular coverage:** Because every bar is both target and detector, there is no inactive gap. A backward-going muon or proton from a neutrino interaction at the upstream face still passes through several scintillator planes before exiting upstream, giving a track stub that seeds momentum reconstruction by range (for protons) or matching to external spectrometry.

---

## Upgrade 2: High-Density Target Planes — Lead or Steel Absorber Interleaved with Scintillator

**Technology:** Thin (5–10 mm) lead or carbon-steel sheets interleaved between scintillator tracking planes.

**Physics motivation:**

This addresses the hydrogen-fraction constraint directly. Lead nuclei (A=207) contain essentially zero free protons relative to their nucleon number. Adding lead mass dilutes the hydrogen fraction:

> H fraction ≈ M_scint × (H/nucleon)_scint / (M_scint + M_Pb)

For M_Pb / M_scint = 4 (achievable with 8 mm Pb plates and 1 cm scintillator planes at ~1 kg/plane ratio):

> H fraction ≈ 7.7% / 5 ≈ 1.5% ✓

The tradeoff is that nuclear interactions on lead dominate. The far detector is likely based on iron or similar nucleus, so to match nuclear targets exactly, steel (Fe, A=56) would be a better choice than lead for systematic reasons, unless a specific nuclear target study is intended. However, this introduces iron-to-scintillator hadronic cross-section systematics that must be modeled.

**Key point:** The choice of absorber material should match (or be chosen to cancel systematics with) the far detector nuclear target. If the far detector uses argon, a liquid-argon mini-TPC insert (see Upgrade 4) is preferred. If it uses iron, steel absorber layers here directly constrain the cross-section model on the same nucleus.

---

## Upgrade 3: Time Projection Chamber (TPC) Insert Modules

**Technology:** Small-pad or pixel readout TPCs with an argon–CF₄–isobutane gas mixture (or similar low-Z gas), filling subregions of the active target volume. Pad pitch ~3–5 mm; drift field ~200 V/cm; readout via MPGD (Micromegas or GEM).

**Physics motivation:**

A gaseous TPC has extremely low density (~0.001–0.003 g/cm³ for Ar-based gas at atmospheric pressure), which provides two critical features:

1. **Proton tracking at low kinetic energy.** A 60 MeV proton has a range of ~65 cm in Ar gas at atmospheric pressure and ~8 cm at 10 atm. At 1 atm, the full track is reconstructed in the TPC volume with millimeter-scale resolution. The dE/dx versus residual range gives particle identification that cleanly separates protons from pions — critical for distinguishing quasi-elastic from multi-pion events.

2. **4π angular acceptance for short tracks.** Unlike scintillator strips with a preferred orientation, the TPC reconstructs tracks in full 3D from ionization clusters. A backward-going 100 MeV/c muon travels ~15 cm in argon gas, leaving a clear helical track in the 0.15 T field. This is the strongest single technology for meeting the ≥25% efficiency at all angles requirement.

**Hydrogen fraction:** Argon has zero free protons (all nucleons bound in A=40). CF₄ introduces some carbon and fluorine but no hydrogen. Isobutane (C₄H₁₀) does contain hydrogen — this must be minimized or replaced with a hydrogen-free quencher such as CO₂. With a 95% Ar / 5% CO₂ mixture, hydrogen content is essentially zero, fully satisfying the ≤2% constraint from TPC gas alone.

**Integration with magnet:** At 0.15 T, a 100 MeV/c muon has a cyclotron radius of ~2.2 m. Over a 0.9 m drift path the sagitta is ~4.5 cm — measurable with 3 mm pad resolution to ~0.1%, giving momentum resolution δp/p ~ a few percent at the momentum scale of interest (200–800 MeV/c). The existing downstream drift chambers then extend the lever arm for forward tracks.

---

## Upgrade 4: Liquid Argon Miniature TPC (LArTPC) Sub-Target

**Technology:** A modular LArTPC with wire or pixel (LArPix) readout, filling a ~0.5 × 0.5 × 0.9 m³ subvolume.

**Physics motivation:**

If the far detector is a LArTPC (e.g., DUNE ND/FD pair), this insert allows direct cross-section measurement on argon with the same nucleus and similar detector response systematics. The bubble-chamber-quality imaging of LArTPCs resolves proton multiplicity, pion tracks, and vertex activity at the mm scale.

LArTPC density (1.4 g/cm³) is high enough that a 60 MeV proton has a range of ~1.3 cm, giving ~5 wires of signal at 3 mm wire pitch — marginally reconstructable. Pixel readout at 4.4 mm pitch (LArPix) or strip charge readout improves this.

Hydrogen fraction: liquid argon contains no hydrogen whatsoever, fully satisfying the constraint.

**Challenge:** Integration inside a warm dipole magnet requires care; LArTPCs are not inherently magnetized, so only the existing external field acts. The E field (typically 500 V/cm) and B field (0.15 T) are crossed, introducing an ExB drift correction of order v_drift × B / E ~ 1 mm/m — small but calibratable.

---

## Upgrade 5: Scintillating Fiber Tracker Around the Target Volume

**Technology:** Scintillating fiber (SciFi) modules — round fibers 0.25 mm diameter, arranged in staggered X-Y-U-V layers, read out by SiPM arrays — surrounding the target volume as a barrel and endcap.

**Physics motivation:**

This addresses the muon angular coverage requirement from a different angle. Tracks exiting the active target volume laterally (90° to beam) or backward must be caught before they escape the magnet entirely. SciFi planes on the lateral faces (2.6 m × 0.9 m sides) and the upstream face (2.6 m × 2.3 m endcap) form a hermetic shell with:

- Spatial resolution ~130 μm per layer, adequate for track matching to the downstream drift chambers
- Fast timing (~1 ns) for pile-up rejection at the neutrino beam spill rate
- Minimal material (X₀ per layer ~ 0.1% X₀) so that muons are not significantly scattered before momentum is measured

A backward-going muon (180°) exits through the upstream endcap SciFi, where its track vector is measured and can be matched to beam-related timing. The 25% efficiency requirement at backward angles is met because the SciFi layer is active over essentially 100% of its geometric acceptance, and two crossed fiber layers immediately give a space point.

Hydrogen fraction: polystyrene fibers have the same ~7.7% H fraction as bulk scintillator, but SciFi layers at ~2 mm total thickness per module contribute negligible mass (<5% of total target mass if the bulk is TPC gas or the dense interleaved target), keeping the total H fraction within budget.

---

## Upgrade 6: Beam-Upstream Veto / Thin-Target Monitor

**Technology:** A set of thin (2–3 mm) scintillator paddle planes immediately upstream of the active target, with photomultiplier readout for precise timing and charge integration.

**Physics motivation:**

This serves two roles:
1. **Charged-particle veto:** Cosmic muons and beam halo muons entering from upstream are tagged, reducing the rate of mis-reconstructed neutrino interactions (the neutrino itself produces no signal here).
2. **Flux monitoring:** The rate of muon-neutrino charged-current interactions in a known thin target just upstream calibrates the flux normalization in situ, reducing the dominant neutrino flux systematic.

No hydrogen fraction issue: the veto planes are outside the fiducial volume and their nucleon content is not counted.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Goal |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Scintillator bar planes (1 cm, WLS+SiPM) | Tracking backbone; low-E proton threshold |
| 2 | Interleaved steel/lead absorber | Suppress H fraction to ≤2%; match far-detector nucleus |
| 3 | Gaseous TPC (Ar+CO₂, MPGD) | 4π track reconstruction; proton PID by dE/dx; zero H |
| 4 | LArTPC module | Argon cross-section measurement; zero H; imaging quality |
| 5 | Scintillating fiber barrel + endcap | Hermetic muon capture at all angles including backward |
| 6 | Upstream scintillator veto planes | Beam halo rejection; flux normalization |

---

## Design Choice Recommendation

The most cost-effective single upgrade meeting all stated requirements is **Upgrade 3 (gaseous TPC modules)** combined with **Upgrade 5 (SciFi barrel/endcap)**. The TPC provides proton tracking to 60 MeV, 4π track reconstruction, and zero hydrogen. The SciFi shell ensures that tracks exiting the TPC at any angle, including backward, are caught with high efficiency and matched to the downstream spectrometer. Together they satisfy the muon angular efficiency requirement and the hydrogen fraction constraint without the cryogenic complexity of a LArTPC insert.

If matching the far-detector nuclear target is a priority (as it typically is for oscillation analyses), **Upgrade 4 (LArTPC)** replaces the gaseous TPC as the core active target, with the SciFi barrel retained.

# Concrete Hardware Upgrades for the Next-Phase Near Detector

## Framing the Problem

The core constraints are:
- Box ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m in the upstream slot
- Need kinematically complete CC events (μ + leading proton reconstructed)
- ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons exit beyond 50° to beam
- Proton median momentum ~450 MeV/c; tail extends to >900 MeV/c
- Target: reduce residual systematic from ~6% to ~4%
- Hydrocarbon target is acceptable

The 0.6 m depth along beam is the critical constraint. It demands a *high-density active target* with integrated tracking — not a passive target read by downstream TPCs alone — because a 450 MeV/c proton has a range of roughly 9 cm in plastic scintillator, so it will stop inside a sufficiently granular volume, but wide-angle tracks must not escape the sides unseen.

---

## Upgrade 1: Scintillator Cube Active Target ("SuperCube" style)

**Technology:** 3D array of 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.5 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, each individually read out on three orthogonal faces by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres connected to SiPMs, arranged in an ~1.8 × 1.8 × 0.55 m³ fiducial block (~120 × 120 × 36 cubes ≈ 500,000 channels).

**Physics motivation:**

*Tracking of large-angle protons.* The 3D-granular topology gives a true three-dimensional hit map with ~1.5 cm spatial resolution in all three axes. A 450 MeV/c proton (range ~9 cm in plastic) produces a ~6-cube-long track stub visible in all three projections simultaneously, with no projective ambiguity. The three-view coincidence from orthogonal fibres on each cube resolves the combinatorial ghost-hit problem that plagues projective-only detectors at high multiplicity. A purely downstream TPC would miss >35% of leading protons that exit laterally before reaching it.

*Stopping-proton momentum by range.* For protons below ~900 MeV/c that stop inside the volume, momentum from range is more precise (~1–2%) than curvature-based measurements at this magnetic field strength, directly reducing the hadronic energy scale uncertainty that propagates into the flux extraction. The ~6% tail above 900 MeV/c that exits can be handed off to the existing downstream TPCs and calorimetry.

*Vertex activity and low-threshold neutron sensitivity.* The ~1.5 cm granularity gives a low-threshold (~0.5 MeV electron-equivalent) neutron-induced proton recoil sensitivity, which matters for modelling nuclear ground-state effects and multinucleon interactions (2p2h) that are a leading source of the current ~6% systematic.

*Fiducial mass in a compact depth.* At ~1.05 g/cm³ and ~0.55 m depth, the active mass is roughly 1.9 × 1.9 × 0.55 m³ × 1.05 t/m³ ≈ 2.1 t of hydrocarbon, comparable to the existing plastic targets but now fully active with no passive gaps.

---

## Upgrade 2: Thin Resistive Plate Chamber (or µ-RWELL) Planes on the Lateral Faces of the Cube Target

**Technology:** Six planes (~2.0 × 1.9 m²) of single-gap resistive plate chambers (RPCs) or micro-resistive WELL (µ-RWELL) detectors, with 1 cm strip pitch in both x and y, mounted on the four lateral sides and the upstream face of the cube target, supplementing the existing return-yoke scintillator.

**Physics motivation:**

*Angular acceptance for large-angle muons.* ~25% of muons exit beyond 50° and may leave the cube target laterally before curving in the dipole field. The RPCs form a hermetic shell that catches these tracks at the boundary, providing an entry/exit point and direction vector that is then matched to the magnet-volume tracking and yoke scintillator. Without this, large-angle muon momentum is poorly determined or the event is lost, biasing the reconstructed transverse momentum imbalance δp_T because the muon is the reference vector.

*Veto for charge-exchange and photon-conversion backgrounds.* Photons from π⁰ decay converting in the cube material can mimic proton stubs if the two electromagnetic sub-showers are close. An upstream-face RPC plane with ~ns timing tags whether the event has an incoming charged particle from upstream (beam-related backgrounds, pileup), and lateral planes identify secondary charged particles that escape before depositing enough cubes to be classified as tracks — important for clean isolation of the two-track (μ + p) topology required for δp_T.

*Cost and radiation hardness.* At ~600 MeV mean neutrino energy the particle rates are modest; RPCs or µ-RWELL operate reliably in this environment, are thin (<1 cm), and add minimal material (< 0.01 X₀ per plane) so they do not degrade the energy measurement of particles entering the downstream TPCs.

---

## Upgrade 3: Beam-Right/Left TPC Extension Panels or High-Pressure Gas TPC Inserts

**Technology:** Two small-format gas TPC modules (~2.0 × 0.5 × 0.5 m³ each) with Micromegas or GEM readout, using an Ar/CF₄/isobutane mixture at 1–2 bar, inserted in the lateral gaps between the cube target and the magnet coil on the beam-left and beam-right sides (where the existing inner volume has unused space at this position).

**Physics motivation:**

*Momentum measurement of exiting protons by curvature.* The ~6% of protons above 900 MeV/c that punch through the full cube target cannot be ranged; they require curvature in the magnetic field. The existing downstream TPCs are well-placed only for forward-going tracks. Lateral TPC panels intercept the high-momentum protons that exit sideways, measuring their rigidity in the 0.2 T dipole field. Even at 0.2 T and ~0.5 m lever arm, a 1 GeV/c proton has a sagitta of ~6 mm, resolvable with ~300 µm TPC spatial resolution (σ_p/p ~ 10–15%), sufficient to separate them from the dominant lower-momentum population.

*Sign determination for pion contamination.* Positive pions in the final state mimic protons in dE/dx at momenta above ~700 MeV/c where the Bethe-Bloch curves cross. Curvature measurement combined with dE/dx from the TPC provides clean π/p separation up to ~1.2 GeV/c, reducing misidentification of pion tracks as leading protons — a process that would fake the two-track signal topology and bias δp_T toward zero.

*Gas target cross-section normalisation.* Running the lateral TPCs with an argon-based mixture gives a small but useful argon neutrino interaction sample in a configuration where the vertex is reconstructed in 3D, supplementing the larger downstream argon TPC sample and providing a cross-check at the same flux position.

---

## Upgrade 4: SiPM Readout Replacement / Time-of-Flight Layer

**Technology:** Replacement of any remaining MPPC (SiPM) channels in the photon-tagging section scintillator that are reused in the new configuration with modern 50 µm cell-pitch SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360-series or FBK NUV-HD), combined with a dedicated 2 cm thick, 2.0 × 1.9 m² plastic scintillator plane with fast SiPM readout (σ_t ~ 200 ps) placed directly upstream of the cube target as a Time-of-Flight (ToF) start counter.

**Physics motivation:**

*Neutron momentum by ToF.* The transverse kinematic imbalance analysis is incomplete if neutrons from multinucleon interactions carry away undetected transverse momentum. A neutron produced at the interaction vertex and detected in a downstream calorimeter plane (already instrumented) can have its momentum reconstructed from ToF to the ~3–4 m distant calorimeter if the start time is known to ~200 ps. This converts the existing calorimeter into a crude neutron spectrometer, extending the kinematic completeness of the event reconstruction and directly addressing 2p2h modelling uncertainties.

*Pileup rejection.* At the target beam intensity, multiple neutrino interactions per beam spill within the ~600 mm deep volume produce pileup vertices. A fast upstream ToF plane timestamps beam-coincident charged particles entering from upstream (cosmics, pion-decay muons, beam-halo muons) to ~200 ps, allowing in-spill background rejection that is not possible with scintillator hit-time resolution of ~1 ns from older SiPMs.

*Improved dE/dx threshold for proton tracking.* The 50 µm cell-pitch SiPMs have a factor ~4 more dynamic range than the 100 µm cells typically used in the existing targets, reducing SiPM saturation for heavily ionising, slow protons near the Bragg peak. This pushes the low-momentum proton tracking threshold from ~300 MeV/c (range ~3 cm, near the cube-volume edge) toward ~200 MeV/c, capturing more of the proton momentum spectrum below the current median.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Systematic Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Scintillator cube target | 1.5 cm³ extruded PS cubes + WLS + SiPM, 3D readout | Proton tracking/ranging; hadronic energy scale |
| 2. Lateral RPC/µ-RWELL shell | Single-gap RPC or µ-RWELL, 1 cm strip pitch | Large-angle muon acceptance; veto/topology purity |
| 3. Lateral TPC inserts | Micromegas/GEM, Ar-based, 1–2 bar | High-p proton curvature; π/p separation |
| 4. Fast SiPM + ToF plane | 50 µm SiPM + 2 cm plastic, σ_t ~ 200 ps | Neutron detection; pileup rejection; low-p_proton threshold |

Together these upgrades achieve kinematic completeness for the two-track CC topology across the full relevant phase space, provide redundant cross-checks between ranging and curvature for the proton momentum scale, and address the neutron and pileup backgrounds that are likely the dominant remaining contributions to the ~6% → ~4% systematic reduction goal.

# Concrete Hardware Upgrades for the Next Phase

## Context and Constraints

The core challenge is replacing the upstream photon-tagger with an active target that fits in ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m, reconstructs both the muon and leading proton in charged-current events with large transverse momenta, and helps push systematic uncertainty from ~6% to ~4%. I address this systematically by subsystem.

---

## Upgrade 1: High-Granularity Plastic Scintillator Active Target ("SuperFGD-style" Cube Detector)

**Technology:** A 3D array of ~1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, each cube read out on three orthogonal axes by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres threaded through holes, each fibre terminated on a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM). Neighbouring cubes share fibres; a hit is reconstructed in 3D by coincidence of the three projections. The array would fill approximately 180 × 170 × 50 cm of the available volume, giving roughly 180 × 170 × 50 ≈ 1,530,000 cubes at 1 cm pitch, instrumented by ~15,000 SiPM channels.

**Physics motivation:**

The existing plastic tracking targets use 9.6 × 9.6 mm bars in alternating x/y planes, which gives 2D projections and has a ~9.6 mm transverse granularity but no independent z-segmentation within a layer. Tracks at large angles (>50°, which applies to 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons at this beam) cross few or no bars in the standard orientation, breaking reconstruction efficiency and introducing a geometrically correlated acceptance bias that propagates directly into the transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) measurement.

The 3D cube geometry resolves this: every track crossing at any polar angle deposits energy in a spatially unambiguous 3D voxel. The 1 cm³ granularity gives a track-finding threshold around 3 cm (3 cubes minimum), corresponding to a proton kinetic energy threshold of roughly 40–50 MeV, well below the median proton momentum of 450 MeV/c (~100 MeV kinetic energy for a proton). Short, large-angle proton tracks that currently fall between bar layers or escape sideways are fully contained and reconstructed.

The scintillator-only composition (hydrocarbon, C:H ratio similar to polystyrene) is explicitly stated as acceptable for the physics programme. The fibre+SiPM readout matches the existing detector infrastructure, reducing integration risk and allowing use of the same front-end electronics as the existing scintillator channels.

---

## Upgrade 2: Thin-Film Resistive Plate Chambers or Thin-Gap Chambers as Downstream Muon Momentum "Tail Catcher" Within the Yoke Instrumentation

**Technology:** Add two to three additional scintillator planes or thin-gap RPC planes in the magnet return yoke gaps on the upstream face of the magnet (the face now exposed by photon-tagger removal), interleaved with 2–3 cm iron absorber slabs. Each plane is ~2.0 × 2.0 m with ~1 cm strip pitch. Total addition: ~6 planes, ~12 t of iron, ~2,000 readout channels.

**Physics motivation:**

The 25% of muons leaving beyond 50° include a significant population that exits the inner tracking volume laterally before being ranged to rest or matched to the downstream TPCs. For the TKI analysis, the muon momentum vector is as important as the proton's: an unmeasured or poorly measured muon angle/momentum degrades the resolution on the transverse momentum imbalance δp_T and the transverse boosting variable δα_T. The existing yoke scintillator already ranges side-going muons, but the upstream region of the yoke was previously shielded by the photon-tagger mass; with that removed, the upstream yoke face is now exposed to the full solid angle of the new active target. Adding instrumented iron planes there extends the geometric acceptance for muons exiting upstream-laterally, which is precisely the angular region most poorly covered by the existing downstream TPCs and yoke instrumentation. Muons that range out in these planes get their momentum measured by range (accuracy ~2–3% for contained tracks), sufficient to keep the muon momentum contribution to δp_T uncertainty below the target ~4% systematic level.

---

## Upgrade 3: Replacement or Augmentation of the First Gas TPC with a Higher-Pressure or Larger-Drift TPC

**Technology:** Upgrade the first downstream argon gas TPC to operate at 2–3 bar absolute pressure with an Ar:CO₂:isobutane mixture, keeping the micro-pattern gaseous detector (MPGD) readout (MicroMegas or GEM) but increasing the active gas mass by a factor of 2–3. Alternatively, increase the drift length from the current geometry to gain fiducial volume. Keep the same outer dimensions to avoid conflicts with the magnet bore. Electronics can be shared with the existing TPC front-end if the same sampling rate is maintained.

**Physics motivation:**

The ~6% of leading protons with momentum above 900 MeV/c are kinematically important as they probe the high-momentum tail of the nucleon momentum distribution and FSI-induced proton acceleration, which are significant sources of modelling uncertainty.
