With 3D cubic segmentation, every cube contributes a signal regardless of track direction, giving near-uniform geometric efficiency for the stated 25% of muons and 35% of protons beyond 50°. This is not an incremental improvement — it is qualitatively different from the downstream planar targets.

**Short-range proton tracking.** The median leading-proton momentum of 450 MeV/c corresponds to a range in polystyrene of roughly 8–9 cm. At 1 cm cube pitch, this gives 8–9 hit cubes along the track, which is sufficient for momentum-by-range determination with ~3–5% resolution. The 6% tail above 900 MeV/c (range ~50 cm) is comfortably contained within the 55 cm depth. Crucially, protons down to roughly 300 MeV/c (range ~4 cm, ~4 cubes) remain reconstructible — well below the threshold achievable with any wire-based TPC at this gas pressure and drift distance.

**dE/dx particle identification.** Proton/pion separation relies on dE/dx measured cube-by-cube along the track. The Bragg peak in a stopping proton at 450 MeV/c is clearly visible at 1 cm sampling; pions of the same momentum produce a flatter, lower dE/dx profile. This is essential for identifying the *leading proton* specifically rather than any charged hadron.

**Neutrino target composition.** Polystyrene (CH) is explicitly stated as acceptable. The mass achievable in this envelope at ~1.0 g/cm³ packing fraction is approximately 1.8 × 1.7 × 0.55 × 1.0 × (packing efficiency ~0.85) ≈ 1.4 t, comparable to the existing downstream plastic target but in a configuration delivering kinematic completeness. This gives adequate statistics for the systematic reduction goal.

**3D topology for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI).** TKI variables (δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T) require the full 3D momentum vectors of both the muon and leading proton. The 3D cube readout provides three independent 2D projections per track, enabling unambiguous 3D reconstruction even for short, steep tracks — something the existing x/y planar design cannot do reliably for large-angle protons in the 55 cm depth.

**Compatibility with existing magnet and readout infrastructure.** The SiPM-on-fibre readout scheme is already deployed throughout this detector. The collaboration has the expertise, vendor relationships, and DAQ firmware to integrate additional SiPM channels. The cube target's flat, modular construction fits within the rigid dimensional envelope without structural modification to the magnet bore.

---

## 2. Surrounding Thin-Wall Mini-TPC Layer

### Technology
Two thin (approximately 3–4 cm active depth) small-pad resistive Micromegas or μRWELL modules, one on each of the two large lateral faces of the cube target (the faces perpendicular to the x-axis, i.e., the faces that intercept the dominant fraction of wide-angle tracks). Gas: Ar/CO₂ (70/30) at atmospheric pressure, chosen for its maturity, non-flammability and compatibility with the existing downstream TPC gas systems. Pad pitch ~3 mm.

### Justification

**Muon momentum measurement for forward-going tracks.** Muons exiting the front or rear face of the 55 cm deep cube target along or near the beam axis do not range out within the target. These muons (~75% of the sample, forward-going) must be matched to the downstream gas TPCs which provide curvature-based momentum measurement in the 0.2 T field. No change is required for this population — the existing TPCs handle it.

**Muon momentum measurement for wide-angle tracks.** A muon leaving at >50° through a lateral face enters the mini-TPC layer. Even 3–4 cm of drift in 0.2 T gives a sagitta of order 100 μm for a 500 MeV/c muon at 60° — marginally insufficient for standalone momentum measurement, but the layer provides a precise entry angle and dE/dx confirmation that the track is a muon rather than a proton, complementing range-based momentum from the cube target.

**Charge-sign for wide-angle muons.** For TKI studies, muon charge sign matters. The mini-TPC provides a short lever arm but sufficient to confirm the bend direction when combined with the known field orientation, reducing the mis-assignment rate.

**Why not a full TPC in this space?** The 0.6 m constraint is fatal to any conventional TPC with useful drift length and fiducial mass in the beam direction. A full TPC here would sacrifice neutrino target mass for drift volume. The cube target provides superior proton tracking; the mini-TPC layer is explicitly a supplement, not a replacement.

---

## 3. SiPM Upgrade: Higher PDE Devices with On-Detector Digitisation

### Technology
Replace or supplement existing SiPMs on the new target with current-generation devices offering >50% photon detection efficiency (PDE) at the WLS fibre emission peak (~490 nm), e.g., the SiPM families now commercially available from Hamamatsu (S13360 series or successor) or KETEK. Pair with CITIROC-2A or similar 32-channel ASIC for on-detector charge integration and time-stamping, with digital output over low-mass cables.

### Justification

**Low-light hits from short proton tracks.** A proton traversing a single 1 cm cube deposits roughly 2 MeV, generating ~200 photons after scintillation and fibre attenuation losses reaching the SiPM. At <40% PDE (older devices), borderline single-cube hits may fall below threshold, introducing a reconstruction inefficiency that is momentum-dependent and therefore a systematic effect on TKI distributions. At >50% PDE this margin is recovered.

**Timing for in-time pile-up rejection.** At the beam intensity required for the statistical goals of the next phase, multiple neutrino interactions per spill within the 55 cm deep target are non-negligible. SiPM timing resolution of <1 ns (achievable with the cited devices and ASIC readout) allows in-spill interaction separation, which is not possible with fibre-to-external-SiPM runs of the existing detector's longer optical paths.

**Cable mass reduction.** On-detector ASICs replace individual analogue coaxial runs per channel, dramatically reducing the cable plant within the already-crowded magnet bore. The existing downstream targets have acceptable cable routing because they are further from the magnet entrance; the new upstream location has tighter clearance.

---

## 4. Thin Upstream Veto Plane

### Technology
Two planes of 5 mm thick plastic scintillator strips (3 cm pitch, x and y), read out by SiPM, immediately upstream of the cube target. Total material: ~0.5% X₀.

### Justification

**Charged-particle veto.** Interactions upstream of the new target (in remaining structural material or the magnet entrance) produce charged particles that enter the cube volume and can be misidentified as interaction products. The veto plane tags these at >99% efficiency with negligible material addition.

**Beam-related background tagging.** The upstream photon-tagger being removed eliminates one source of background rejection. This thin plane partially recovers charged-particle tagging without adding significant target material within the fiducial volume.

**Why not a full veto sandwich?** Additional material upstream raises the interaction probability before the fiducial volume and introduces secondary particles that are harder to reject than primary beam tracks. The single two-plane veto is the minimum necessary.

---

## 5. No Change to Downstream Systems

The downstream gas TPCs, plastic tracking target (with water layers), lead-scintillator calorimeters, and yoke scintillator remain unchanged. This is a deliberate recommendation:

- The carbon-to-water comparison programme explicitly depends on the downstream water-layer target remaining in place.
- Forward-going muons from the new upstream target are measured by the existing downstream TPCs — the lever arm in the 0.2 T field is longer there, giving better momentum resolution than any new device in the tight upstream space.
- Disrupting the downstream calorimetry would require re-calibration campaigns that absorb the schedule margin needed to reach 4% systematics before the far detector's statistical power demands it.

---

## Summary Table

| Component | Technology | Key Motivation |
|---|---|---|
| Primary active target | 3D scintillator cubes, 1 cm³, WLS fibre + SiPM × 3 axes | 4π proton acceptance, low-momentum tracking, dE/dx PID |
| Lateral TPC supplement | Thin μRWELL or Micromegas, Ar/CO₂, 3 mm pads | Charge-sign and angle for wide-angle muons |
| SiPM generation | >50% PDE devices + CITIROC ASIC on-detector | Single-cube efficiency, timing, cable reduction |
| Upstream veto | 2 × scintillator strip planes, 5 mm, 3 cm pitch | Beam-halo and upstream-interaction rejection |
| Downstream systems | **Unchanged** | Forward-muon momentum, water comparison, schedule |

---

## Risk Register

**Dominant risk:** WLS fibre routing density in a 1 cm³ cube array with three fibres per cube generates ~5.5 million fibre-SiPM channels in this volume. Channel count is manageable (comparable to the SuperFGD prototype demonstrated at ~2M channels in a smaller volume) but requires aggressive ASIC multiplexing and careful optical connector design. The collaboration should commission a 10 × 10 × 10 cm³ mechanical prototype within six months to validate fibre insertion yield and uniformity before committing to full production.

**Secondary risk:** The 0.2 T field causes SiPM gain variation of 1–2% when devices are oriented perpendicular to field lines. This is known from the existing detector but should be re-characterised for the new higher-PDE devices, whose internal carrier dynamics may respond differently. A bench measurement programme during prototype phase is mandatory.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Constraints Before Listing Upgrades

The requirements drive the technology choices:
- Muon reconstruction at **all angles including 90° and backward** in a dipole field means tracks must be measured *within* the target volume, not just downstream
- **Short proton tracks** (60 MeV KE → range ~3 cm in liquid argon, ~1-2 cm in scintillator) require fine granularity
- **Hydrogen ≤ 2% of nucleons** severely restricts material choice (rules out water, plastic scintillator as primary target)
- The **0.15 T field** is warm (accessible) and the existing downstream trackers are retained

---

## Required Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Active Target: Low-Density Straw-Tube Tracker (STT) or similar gaseous tracker

**Technology:** Thin-walled aluminized Mylar straw tubes (~1 cm diameter) filled with an Ar/CO₂ or similar gas mixture, arranged in stereoscopic layers, filling the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m target volume.

**Why:**
- A gas target is overwhelmingly hydrogen-free nucleons from argon or carbon (from the Mylar walls), keeping hydrogen fraction easily below 2% while still providing a hydrogen-containing component that can be used for the hydrogen subtraction analysis — but crucially the hydrogen fraction is *controllable and known*
- Fine granularity (~1 cm cell size) gives track-finding capability for short recoil protons; a 60 MeV proton has a range of roughly 3–4 cm in typical detector gas, crossing several straw layers, making it reconstructable
- Stereo layer arrangement measures 3D track directions without ambiguity
- Crucially, the straw tubes provide **hit information throughout the volume**, so a muon going perpendicular to the beam crosses straw layers and is measured; a backward-going muon is similarly detected without having to exit downstream
- Low density means minimal multiple scattering, preserving angular resolution for soft protons
- The existing downstream drift chambers and dipole provide momentum measurement for forward-going tracks; the STT handles the vertex region

**Specific note:** The NOMAD and T2K ND280 fine-grained detectors and especially the proposed NINJA/NuPRISM-style detectors and the Baby MIND concept inform this. The closest realized example is the MINERvA-style scintillator, but here the hydrogen constraint *rules out* scintillator as the primary active target material.

---

### 2. Thin Radiator / Transition Radiation Detector (TRD) Layers Interspersed in Target

**Technology:** Thin polypropylene foam or fiber radiator layers (~2 cm thick) interleaved with proportional tube arrays (Xe/CO₂ gas), several modules through the target depth.

**Why:**
- Provides electron/pion separation to tag Michel electrons from stopped pions and to identify the rare cases where the "muon" candidate is actually an electron neutrino CC event
- Also contributes tracking layers at negligible radiation length per module, aiding the all-angle reconstruction
- Low mass per module keeps the hydrogen fraction in check (polypropylene CH₂ contributes hydrogen, so the number and thickness of radiator layers must be engineered to stay within the 2% hydrogen nucleon budget — this is a design constraint, not a reason to omit TRD, but the radiator material and thickness must be optimized accordingly)

*Note: If the hydrogen budget is too tight, TRD layers may need to use carbon-foam radiators instead of polypropylene.*

---

### 3. Time Projection Chamber (TPC) Modules at Upstream and Side Faces of Target Volume

**Technology:** Small-drift-distance TPCs (drift distance ~10–15 cm, to keep drift time short and ion buildup manageable) with GEM (Gas Electron Multiplier) or Micromegas readout planes, using an Ar/isobutane or Ar/CO₂ fill, positioned at the upstream face and both lateral faces of the target volume (the faces perpendicular to and parallel to the beam).

**Why:**
- Backward-going muons (traveling upstream, away from the downstream drift chambers) will exit through the upstream face; a TPC there measures their momentum via curvature in the dipole field and their angle precisely
- Sideways-going muons exit through the lateral faces; TPCs there catch these tracks
- The 0.15 T field that fills the warm magnet bore permeates the TPC volumes, so curvature is measured continuously
- GEM/Micromegas readout gives 2D hit positions on the readout plane; combined with drift time this gives full 3D reconstruction
- Short recoil protons that stop within the STT but whose tracks reach a TPC boundary get a redundant momentum measurement
- The T2K near detector ND280 TPC modules (using similar technology) have demonstrated this works at the relevant energy scale

---

### 4. Scintillator Veto / Muon Catcher Planes on All Six Faces of the Target Volume

**Technology:** Extruded polystyrene scintillator bars (~3 cm × 1 cm cross section) with wavelength-shifting fiber readout and silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readout, assembled into X–Y planes on each of the six faces.

**Why:**
- Muon tracks at all angles, including 90° and backward, must be identified when they exit any face; scintillator planes provide a trigger signal and a precise entry/exit point measurement
- SiPM readout is preferred over traditional PMTs because the detector is inside the warm magnet bore where even a 0.15 T field would affect conventional PMTs operating near the gap
- The fine bar width (~1 cm in the bending plane) ensures the exit position is well measured, constraining the track fit from the STT and TPC
- The planes also serve as a veto against entering cosmic ray muons and beam-associated muons that originate outside the target volume
- Scintillator bars do contain hydrogen (CH ratio ~1:1 by atom), but as *face planes* rather than bulk target material, their mass is small relative to the total target mass; the hydrogen fraction contribution must be verified to stay within budget — bar thickness should be minimized accordingly, or replaced with thin aluminum-strip hodoscopes if the hydrogen budget is violated

---

### 5. Upgrade of Readout Electronics: High-Speed, Triggerless DAQ with Waveform Digitization

**Technology:** Self-triggered front-end ASICs (e.g., AFTER-chip or DREAM/AFTER family as used in T2K TPCs, or custom developments) with ~100 ns shaping time, digitizing at 25–50 MHz, feeding into an FPGA-based data concentrator and a triggerless streaming readout architecture.

**Why:**
- At 410 m from the target, the near detector sees a high neutrino interaction rate; pile-up within a single beam spill is significant at a high-intensity machine
- Triggerless readout allows offline reconstruction of all activity in the beam spill window, enabling proper pile-up rejection and spill-by-spill efficiency measurement
- Waveform digitization (rather than simple threshold triggering) is essential for the STT and TPC channels to separate the prompt ionization signal from later-arriving ions, improving position resolution along the drift direction and enabling dE/dx measurement for particle identification
- dE/dx from waveform integration distinguishes protons from pions from muons in the momentum range of interest (protons at 60 MeV KE are very heavily ionizing), which is critical for the recoil proton requirement
- The SiPM readout of the scintillator planes also benefits from waveform digitization for improved timing (sub-nanosecond timing is achievable) and for distinguishing single photons from afterpulsing

---

### 6. Magnetic Field Mapping System and Temperature/Pressure Monitoring for Gas Detectors

**Technology:** NMR probes or Hall probes on a motorized mapping stage inside the magnet bore (deployed during commissioning and periodically thereafter); temperature and pressure sensors (PT100 RTDs, barometric sensors) on each gas volume feeding into the slow-control database.

**Why:**
- Momentum reconstruction for all-angle tracks depends on knowing the field integral along the full curved track path; the warm dipole will have fringe fields at the upstream and lateral faces where the new TPC modules sit, and these must be mapped to better than ~0.1% to achieve the required momentum resolution
- Gas gain in the STT and TPC proportional counters is exponentially sensitive to temperature and pressure; a 1°C change shifts gain by ~1–2%; for dE/dx-based proton identification, gain stability of better than a few percent is needed, requiring continuous monitoring and software correction
- These are low-cost additions but are essential for systematic error control in the cross-section analysis the proposal is targeting

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Active target bulk | Straw tube tracker (Mylar/Ar:CO₂) | All-angle tracking; hydrogen < 2%; short proton tracks |
| Side/upstream tracking | TPC with GEM/Micromegas readout | Backward and 90° muon momentum measurement |
| Face hodoscopes | Scintillator bars + SiPM | Track exit point; trigger; entering-particle veto |
| Particle ID layers | TRD (Xe tubes + low-H radiator) | e/π/μ separation; purity of muon sample |
| Readout electronics | Triggerless waveform DAQ (AFTER-type ASICs) | Pile-up rejection; dE/dx for proton ID |
| Field & environment monitoring | NMR/Hall probes; RTD/pressure sensors | Momentum scale and dE/dx systematic control |

Based on the detector description and physics requirements, here are concrete hardware upgrades for the next phase:

## 1. **SuperFGD-style 3D Scintillator Cube Target**

**Technology:** Fine-grained plastic scintillator detector with 1 cm³ optically-segmented cubes, three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fiber readouts per cube, SiPM readout at all cube faces.

**Physics Motivation:** 
- **3D tracking capability** essential for the ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons at >50° to beam—conventional x/y alternating planes have poor resolution for particles between planes
- **Low tracking threshold** (~300 MeV/c for protons) captures the 450 MeV/c median proton momentum
- **Stop/range-out capability** for contained protons enables kinematic reconstruction via range
- **Time resolution** (~few ns) provides event timing for TPC matching
- Fits within 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m³ constraint with ~2 tonnes hydrocarbon target mass

## 2. **High-Angle Muon Ranger (HAMR) Panels**

**Technology:** Additional scintillator planes installed on magnet upstream and downstream faces, with coarser segmentation (~5 cm bars) but full geometric coverage.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Current geometry poorly constrains **high-angle muons** (>50° to beam)
- Muons at large angles to magnetic field have degraded momentum resolution from curvature
- Improved **angular acceptance** directly reduces systematic uncertainty from model-dependent extrapolations
- **Range-based momentum** for stopping muons (up to ~1 GeV/c in magnet + steel) complements curvature measurement
- Targets the 6%→4% systematic reduction goal

## 3. **Upgraded TPCs with Resistive Micromegas and Higher Gas Pressure**

**Technology:** Replace existing TPCs with 10 bar argon-based gas mixture, resistive-anode Micromegas with charge dispersion readout, 2 mm pad pitch.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Higher gas pressure** increases proton range and dE/dx sampling for better particle ID
- 900 MeV/c protons (top 6%) have ~40 cm range at 10 bar vs escaping at 1 bar
- **Improved position resolution** (sub-mm) enhances vertex reconstruction for transverse imbalance
- **Better dE/dx resolution** separates protons from pions at low momentum (crucial for "leading proton" definition)
- Argon provides additional heavy-target nuclear physics

## 4. **Neutron-Tagging Calorimeter Panels**

**Technology:** Plastic scintillator with ⁶Li-loading or boron-loading (10-20 cm thick) on magnet exterior surfaces, large-area SiPM readout, 100-200 ns timing window.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Transverse kinematic imbalance** critically depends on detecting neutrons from FSI
- Missing transverse momentum indicates neutrons; detecting them validates reconstruction
- ~5 MeV γ from neutron capture (100-200 ns delayed) tags neutron presence
- Reduces systematic from **undetected hadronic activity**
- Low cost/mass upgrade with direct impact on systematic uncertainty

## 5. **Precision Muon Momentum Spectrometer Cavity**

**Technology:** Field-cage region (50 cm upstream of TPCs) with ultra-low-mass drift chamber or fiber tracker (100-200 μm position resolution), calibrated uniform field region.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Muon momentum uncertainty dominates** neutrino energy reconstruction error
- Multiple Coulomb scattering limits momentum resolution for through-going muons
- Dedicated **low-mass tracking region** minimizes scattering material
- **Improved momentum resolution** (δp/p from ~10% to ~3-5% at 1 GeV/c) directly improves neutrino energy scale
- Critical for distinguishing quasi-elastic from resonance events

## 6. **ToF Hodoscope System**

**Technology:** Two thin (1 cm) scintillator hodoscope planes with ~5 cm segmentation, 150 ps timing resolution, one just downstream of new target, one upstream of first TPC.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Time-of-flight measurement** over ~1 m baseline separates protons from pions at high momentum
- Proton β = 0.67 at 450 MeV/c; 500 ps time difference vs pions
- Validates **"leading proton" identification** which is model-dependent
- Provides **event t₀ reference** for TPC drift time
- Low cost, addresses key systematic from hadron misidentification

---

## Recommended Priority Ranking:
1. **SuperFGD target** (essential for kinematic completeness)
2. **High-angle muon rangers** (directly addresses acceptance)
3. **Neutron tagging** (cost-effective systematic reduction)
4. **ToF system** (hadron ID systematic)
5. **Upgraded TPCs** (if budget allows)
6. **Precision spectrometer** (longer-term, highest cost)

This combination addresses the 6%→4% systematic goal through improved acceptance, particle identification, and kinematic reconstruction.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for ND280 Phase II

## 1. **SuperFGD: 3D Segmented Plastic Scintillator Cube**

**Technology:** Fine-grained (~1 cm³) plastic scintillator cubes with three-orthogonal readout via wavelength-shifting fibers and MPPCs, creating a fully active 3D tracker.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Large-angle track reconstruction**: The 25% of muons and 35% of protons at >50° require true 3D tracking capability. The current FGD's 2D x-y alternating layers cannot efficiently reconstruct tracks that travel significantly along z (beam direction).
- **Low-momentum proton detection**: With median proton momentum ~450 MeV/c, range-based particle ID is crucial. 3D cube geometry provides ~1 cm³ granularity for precise dE/dx measurements and range determination for protons stopping within the detector.
- **Reduced dependency on TPCs**: Large-angle tracks may miss downstream TPCs. A fully active target enables standalone vertex reconstruction and particle identification.
- **Transverse kinematics**: Complete 3D vector reconstruction of both muon and proton enables accurate transverse momentum imbalance studies (δp_T) essential for constraining nuclear effects.

---

## 2. **High-Angle TPC (HA-TPC) or Time Projection Chamber with Horizontal Drift**

**Technology:** TPC modules surrounding the target with drift directions optimized for large-angle particle trajectories (potentially horizontal drift perpendicular to beam, or multiple small TPCs with various orientations).

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Large-angle momentum measurement**: Current TPCs are optimized for near-beam-axis tracks. 35% of leading protons exit at >50°, requiring momentum measurement via curvature in the 0.2 T field.
- **High-momentum proton tagging**: The 6% of protons with p>900 MeV/c punch through the target. TPCs provide crucial momentum measurement for these non-stopping particles.
- **Particle ID**: TPC dE/dx discriminates protons from pions, critical for identifying the "leading proton" in multi-hadron final states.
- **Systematic reduction**: Independent momentum measurement cross-checks against range-based measurements, reducing systematic uncertainties toward the 4% goal.

---

## 3. **Time-of-Flight (ToF) System**

**Technology:** High-precision timing scintillator panels (~50-100 ps resolution) positioned downstream/around the target volume, potentially integrated with electromagnetic calorimeters.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Low-momentum proton/pion separation**: At 450 MeV/c, ToF over ~1-2 m provides π/p separation where dE/dx alone may be ambiguous.
- **Neutron detection**: ToF enables detection of recoiling neutrons via their interaction time in downstream detectors, crucial for understanding nuclear final states.
- **Directionality confirmation**: Combined with 3D position, ToF validates track direction (particularly important for low-momentum particles where multiple scattering dominates).
- **Background rejection**: Timing cuts against cosmic rays and out-of-time beam backgrounds reduce systematic uncertainties.

---

## 4. **Target Mass Enhancement: Water-Hydrocarbon Hybrid Target**

**Technology:** Alternating modules or compartments with water and plastic scintillator within the SuperFGD volume, maintaining active readout throughout.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Direct water comparison**: While FGD2 downstream provides some comparison, in-situ water targets in the same acceptance and reconstruction framework reduce detector systematics.
- **Carbon vs. Oxygen nuclear effects**: The nuclear model systematic uncertainty dominates at ~6%. Direct comparison of CH versus H₂O in identical geometry constrains nuclear effects (Fermi motion, final-state interactions).
- **Hydrogen target**: Water provides increased hydrogen content for quasi-elastic scattering studies where nuclear effects are minimal.
- **Redundant measurements**: Multiple target materials enable cross-validation of reconstruction and systematic uncertainty estimates.

---

## 5. **Enhanced Electromagnetic Calorimeter with Finer Segmentation**

**Technology:** Upgrade ECAL modules with finer transverse and longitudinal segmentation (potentially 5×5×5 mm³ vs. current ~10 mm bars), maintaining lead-scintillator sandwich structure.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **π⁰ rejection**: Neutral pion production is a critical background for quasi-elastic selections. Finer segmentation improves π⁰→γγ reconstruction and rejection.
- **Electron identification**: Charged-current electron neutrino events are backgrounds but also carry physics information. Better e/π separation reduces systematics.
- **High-angle electromagnetic shower containment**: Large-angle muons may produce δ-rays or bremsstrahlung photons at steep angles.
- **Energy resolution**: Improved ECAL performance reduces uncertainties in total energy reconstruction, crucial for transverse imbalance studies where missing energy matters.

---

## 6. **Improved SMRD or Additional Muon Range Detector**

**Technology:** Enhanced scintillator coverage in magnet yoke gaps, potentially with finer segmentation or additional layers for better position resolution.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **High-angle muon containment**: 25% of muons at >50° are more likely to reach the SMRD. Better range measurement in magnetized iron provides momentum information for these escaping muons.
- **Momentum resolution**: For muons that don't traverse TPCs, range in magnetized iron is the only momentum constraint.
- **Charge identification**: Muon charge sign from curvature in the magnet confirms νμ vs. ν̄μ interactions, reducing wrong-sign backgrounds.

---

## Summary: Integrated Approach

The combination of **SuperFGD** (3D active target), **HA-TPC** (large-angle tracking), and **ToF** (particle ID) addresses the core requirement: kinematically complete reconstruction of both muon and proton at all angles. The water-hybrid target directly attacks the dominant nuclear systematic uncertainties, while ECAL and SMRD upgrades ensure no signal is lost at the edges. This integrated upgrade path targets the reduction from 6% to 4% systematic uncertainty required for T2K-II physics goals.

# Recommended Hardware Upgrades for T2K ND280 Upgrade Proposal

## 1. **SuperFGD: 3D Scintillator Cube Target**

**Technology:** ~2 million small plastic scintillator cubes (~1 cm³), each read out on three orthogonal faces via wavelength-shifting fibers and MPPCs

**Why:**
- **True 3D tracking** with ~1 cm granularity enables reconstruction of tracks at all angles, critical for the 25% of muons and 35% of protons emitted >50° to beam
- The FGD bars (oriented only perpendicular to beam) have poor angular coverage for large-angle tracks
- Fine granularity provides excellent vertex resolution and proton identification via dE/dx
- Hydrocarbon target (CH) is acceptable per requirements
- Fits in ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m³ available volume with ~1-2 ton active mass

## 2. **Horizontal Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) Around SuperFGD**

**Technology:** Two "HA-TPC" (Horizontal Arrangement) modules upstream and downstream of SuperFGD, with resistive Micromegas readout, vertical drift field

**Why:**
- Current TPCs only cover tracks exiting downstream; no coverage for upstream/sideways emission
- Provides momentum measurement and particle ID (dE/dx) for particles exiting at large angles
- Resistive Micromegas more robust to sparking than bulk Micromegas
- Vertical drift allows side placement within magnet constraints
- Essential for measuring the 6% of protons >900 MeV/c that would otherwise escape

## 3. **Time-of-Flight (ToF) Panels**

**Technology:** Thin plastic scintillator panels (~5 cm thick) on six faces around the TPC/SuperFGD system, with ~150 ps timing resolution

**Why:**
- **Critical for proton ID** at forward angles where particles reach the ToF before stopping
- Discriminates protons from pions in 450 MeV/c momentum range (median of leading-proton spectrum)
- Timing information helps match tracks to beam bunch structure
- Complements dE/dx for kinematically complete event selection
- Improves particle flow reconstruction

## 4. **Upgraded Data Acquisition System (DAQ)**

**Technology:** Modern FPGA-based electronics with higher bandwidth, larger buffers, and improved timing synchronization

**Why:**
- SuperFGD has ~6 million channels (vs. 15,000 in FGD1)
- 100× increase in data rate requires complete DAQ replacement
- Must handle T2K-II beam intensity increase (×2-5 from current)
- Needs <10 ns timing resolution for ToF and cosmic rejection
- Self-triggering capability reduces dead-time

## 5. **Enhanced ECAL Coverage (Optional but Recommended)**

**Technology:** Additional lead-scintillator modules filling gaps in upstream acceptance

**Why:**
- Current ECAL has limited upstream coverage (P0D region)
- Needed to contain electrons from νₑ CC events for beam νₑ constraint
- Improves photon detection from π⁰ backgrounds
- Helps contain electromagnetic showers from high-angle muons

## 6. **Improved Calibration Systems**

**Technology:** 
- LED/laser light injection system for all photodetectors
- Cosmic ray trigger hodoscopes around detector
- Automated water target system with precision filling/draining

**Why:**
- Factor-of-100 increase in channels demands automated calibration
- Need <2% energy scale uncertainty to achieve 4% systematic goal
- Cosmic rays provide continuous momentum calibration for TPCs
- Water target movements must be precisely controlled for C/H₂O comparison

---

## Summary Justification

This upgrade transforms ND280 from a forward-focused detector into a **near-4π acceptance** apparatus optimized for neutrino energies around 0.6 GeV. The combination of:
- 3D granular target (vertex + angles)
- Surrounding TPCs (momentum + PID)  
- ToF panels (low-momentum proton ID)

enables the **kinematically complete reconstruction** required for transverse kinematic imbalance methods, which can break degeneracies in neutrino interaction models and reduce systematic uncertainties from ~6% to the required ~4% for T2K-II precision oscillation physics.

# Proposed Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

The re-equipped target region should become a three-part system:

1. A finely segmented 3D scintillator active target.
2. High-angle gas TPCs above and below it, inside the magnet.
3. A time-of-flight envelope around the whole assembly.

The existing downstream drift chambers continue to handle forward tracks.

---

## 1. Active target: 3D-segmented plastic scintillator (SuperFGD-style)

**Technology**
- About 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, each with a reflective (chemically etched) surface.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres.
- Fibres are read out at one end by silicon photomultipliers (MPPC/SiPM) with nanosecond-level timing.

**Size and channel count**
- Filling 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m gives 260 × 230 × 90 ≈ 5.4 million cubes.
- That is roughly 5.6 t of target.
- The three projections need 260·230 + 260·90 + 230·90 ≈ 104,000 readout channels.

**Hydrogen constraint**
- Polystyrene is (C₈H₈)ₙ, so hydrogen supplies 8 of 104 nucleons, about 7.7%.
- This is well under the 20% limit, so the hydrogen-subtraction model stays valid.
- Adding about 1–2% of non-scintillating support material does not change this.
- It also passes a more conservative design. A water-based target would be about 11% hydrogen and would still pass.
- Hydrogen-rich alternatives such as liquid scintillator or pure CH₂ are less favourable: CH₂ alone is about 14% hydrogen and would leave little margin.

**Physics motivation**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three orthogonal fibre views give real 3D reconstruction with no dead projection angle. Tracks perpendicular to the beam or going backward are reconstructed as well as forward ones. Bar trackers with planes facing the beam lose these tracks, so this directly addresses the ≥25% efficiency requirement at all muon angles.
- **Low-energy protons.** A 60 MeV kinetic-energy proton travels only about 3 cm in plastic. With 1 cm cubes it crosses at least 3 cubes in any direction, which is enough for a track direction and a dE/dx Bragg-peak signature to separate protons from pions and muons. Coarser segmentation, such as 2.5 cm, would turn these protons into single-hit blobs.
- **Vertex activity, range and calorimetry.** Stopping muons and pions get momentum from range. This matters most for high-angle muons that never reach the downstream drift chambers.
- **Neutrons.** Cube-level timing of about 1 ns lets isolated neutron-induced hits be measured by time of flight from the vertex. That gives the neutron kinetic energy, adding transverse-kinematic-imbalance and calorimetric information.
- **Pile-up rejection.** Fine timing separates multiple interactions within one beam spill.

---

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Two thin-walled gas TPCs inside the magnet, flanking the target region transverse to the beam.
- A low-material composite field cage, for example a laminate of aramid honeycomb and Kapton strips.
- A T2K-like Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ gas mixture.
- Readout by resistive Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode). The charge spreading gives sub-millimetre resolution with pads about 1 cm wide, which keeps channel count and cost down.

**Physics motivation**
- The target is only 0.9 m deep along the beam. High-angle and backward tracks therefore leave through the sides, out of the downstream chambers' acceptance.
- The TPCs restore magnetic momentum measurement and charge sign for these tracks. Charge sign separates μ⁻ from μ⁺, which is the wrong-sign background.
- They also add dE/dx particle identification (μ/π/p/e) for exiting tracks.

**Momentum resolution at 0.15 T**
- For a 0.5 GeV/c muon over about 0.7 m of track, the sagitta is s = 0.3·B·L²/(8p) ≈ 5.5 mm.
- With roughly 0.5 mm point resolution and tens of points, this gives momentum resolution near 10%.
- That is adequate for a beam peaking at 0.7 GeV.

---

## 3. Time-of-flight envelope

**Technology**
- Panels of long plastic scintillator bars surrounding the target and TPCs.
- Read out at both ends with arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Target timing resolution of 0.15 ns or better.

**Physics motivation**
- **Direction of travel.** Timing between the target and the ToF planes separates backward-going tracks from inward-going tracks entering from outside. Without this, a backward muon is indistinguishable from an entering one.
- **Background rejection.** This removes interactions in the magnet and surrounding material that would otherwise fake target vertices.
- **Particle ID.** It adds ToF-based particle identification in the momentum range where dE/dx bands cross, such as electron versus muon near 100–200 MeV/c.
- **Event timing.** It provides a common time reference for neutron ToF measured in the cubes.

---

## 4. Supporting upgrades

- **Electronics.** Shared front-end and DAQ for the scintillator, TPCs and ToF, with synchronised clock distribution to well below 1 ns and trigger-less readout gated on the beam spill.
- **Calibration.** A cosmic-muon trigger and LED or light-injection system to equalise roughly 10⁵ SiPM gains. Light-yield monitoring across the large cube volume.
- **Mechanics.** A thin-walled support box for the target, keeping inactive mass and non-target nuclei minimal to preserve the CH composition and protect low-energy proton tracks near the edges.

---

## How the system meets each requirement

- **Muon at all angles:** 3D cubes, plus high-angle TPCs for momentum and charge, plus ToF for direction.
- **Protons down to 60 MeV:** 1 cm segmentation, giving at least 3 hits and a Bragg peak.
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤ 20%:** polystyrene target at about 8% hydrogen.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## 1. Active Target Medium: Liquid Argon or Plastic Scintillator?

Neither is optimal here. The hydrogen-fraction constraint (≤2% of nucleons) rules out hydrocarbon-rich scintillator as the **primary** target material, since plastic scintillator (CH) has hydrogen making up roughly 1 in 13 nucleons (~7.7%), far exceeding the 2% limit. Liquid argon has essentially zero free hydrogen. However, the analysis specifically **needs** the hydrogen signal (to then subtract it), so a moderate hydrogen content is acceptable if it stays ≤2%.

The 2% nucleon limit means: for a material of mass number A with H fraction by nucleon count ≤ 0.02, one could use a **low-Z, low-hydrogen-density medium**.

**Recommended primary active target: Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC)**

- Argon (A=40) has negligible free hydrogen; hydrogen nucleons are ~0% of total → comfortably within the 2% constraint
- Provides true 3D tracking with ~mm spatial resolution, enabling reconstruction of very short proton tracks (60 MeV kinetic energy in LAr gives a range of ~3–4 mm, which is resolvable)
- Uniform, dense, fully sensitive volume with no dead material
- dE/dx particle identification distinguishes protons from pions and muons over a wide momentum range
- Well-established technology (MicroBooNE, SBND, ICARUS, DUNE ND prototypes)

**Why not plastic scintillator (e.g., SuperFGD-style)?**
A polystyrene-based scintillator cube detector has ~7.7% hydrogen by nucleon count — exceeding the 2% limit by a factor of ~4. Unless one uses a predominantly non-hydrogenous scintillator matrix (e.g., inorganic scintillator), this is problematic. However, see item 4 below for a hybrid role.

---

## 2. Muon Reconstruction at All Angles Including Perpendicular and Backward-Going: Surrounding Muon Detector

**Technology: Plastic scintillator tracker planes or resistive plate chambers (RPCs) surrounding all six faces of the active target volume**

- The existing downstream gas drift chambers only capture forward-going tracks exiting the downstream face; they provide zero efficiency for transverse (90°) or backward-going muons
- Scintillator planes (e.g., 1–2 cm thick X–Y paddle layers) or RPCs on the **upstream, top, bottom, and side faces** of the active volume capture muons exiting in all directions
- These must be placed **inside** the warm dipole magnet bore (the volume is 2.6 m × 2.3 m in cross-section, fitting within the stated inner volume)
- The 0.15 T dipole field, while modest, provides momentum measurement for tracks long enough to curve measurably; the surrounding scintillator planes provide additional track segments for momentum-by-range for shorter tracks
- For backward-going muons, a dedicated **upstream scintillator/RPC wall** is essential — without it, no geometric acceptance exists for tracks heading toward the target station wall
- RPCs offer good spatial resolution (~1 mm) and timing, while scintillator paddles provide fast triggering and energy deposition information

**Specific addition: Upstream muon catcher**
- A steel-scintillator sandwich (mini-muon-range-stack) of ~0.5 m depth upstream of the active volume
- Allows momentum-by-range for backward muons that stop within it, and provides a veto/tag for muons that punch through

---

## 3. Short Proton Track Reconstruction (60 MeV Kinetic Energy): High-Resolution 3D Tracking Within the Active Volume

**60 MeV proton range in LAr ≈ 3–4 mm; in denser materials it is shorter.**

The LArTPC (item 1) addresses this if the wire pitch and electronics are chosen appropriately:

**Technology: Fine-pitch LArTPC with wire pitch ≤ 3 mm and low-noise cold electronics**

- Standard LArTPC wire pitches of 3–5 mm are marginal for 3–4 mm tracks; a **3 mm pitch** in both induction and collection planes is needed
- Cold ASIC front-end electronics (e.g., LArASIC or COLDATA-generation chips) operated inside the cryostat reduce noise to ≤ 500 e⁻ ENC, enabling detection of the small ionization signal from a short, slow proton
- A **photon detection system** (e.g., ARAPUCA or dip-coated light guide bars) provides the t₀ for each interaction, essential for drift-direction position reconstruction; without t₀, the drift coordinate is unknown and the 3D track cannot be reconstructed
- Alternatively or additionally, a **pixel-based LArTPC** (e.g., LArPix architecture) provides true 3D charge readout without the left-right ambiguity of wire planes, at the cost of higher channel count; this is preferred if the collaboration can manage the O(10⁵) channels needed for this volume

**If cost forces a non-LAr solution:** A **3D scintillator cube detector** (SuperFGD-type, but with the hydrogen constraint in mind) using 1 cm³ cubes of **non-hydrogenous scintillator** (e.g., inorganic GAGG:Ce or LaBr₃-based, though these are expensive) would provide the necessary granularity. More practically, a **high-pressure gaseous TPC** (see below) is an alternative.

---

## 4. Alternative/Complementary Active Target: High-Pressure Gas TPC

**Technology: High-pressure (≥ 5–10 bar) gaseous argon TPC with GEM or Micromegas readout**

- At ~10 bar, argon gas density is ~0.018 g/cm³ — lower than LAr but sufficient for neutrino interactions while providing extremely good angular resolution
- Hydrogen content is zero (pure Ar) or negligible (Ar+CO₂ or Ar+CF₄ admixtures keep H well below 2%)
- Excellent dE/dx resolution for proton identification
- Very low detection threshold: a 60 MeV proton has range ~15 cm at 10 bar Ar, easily reconstructed with mm-pitch GEM readout
- Full 4π track reconstruction is natural in a TPC — backward and transverse tracks are recorded with equal efficiency as forward ones, directly satisfying the ≥25% efficiency requirement at all angles
- GEM or Micromegas planes at both ends (or cylindrical geometry) provide redundant readout
- T2K's ND280 high-pressure TPC demonstrator and ALICE TPC provide the technology baseline

**Trade-off vs. LArTPC:** Gas TPC has lower target mass (fewer neutrino interactions per unit time), but the near detector at 410 m from an accelerator beam has very high flux, so rate is not the primary concern. The gas TPC more naturally handles the all-angle tracking requirement and avoids the cryogenic infrastructure of LAr.

**Recommendation: Hybrid** — gas TPC modules interleaved with thin passive/active LAr or liquid-scintillator panels to increase target mass while maintaining tracking quality.

---

## 5. Charge-Sign Determination for Backward and Transverse Muons: Magnet Instrumentation Upgrade

The existing warm dipole at 0.15 T provides ∫Bdl ≈ 0.15 × 6.5 = 0.975 T·m — adequate for forward tracks of moderate momentum but marginal for short or transverse tracks.

**Technology: Instrumented magnet yoke with scintillator or RPC tracking layers embedded in the return yoke**

- Embedding tracking detectors (scintillator strips or RPCs with ~1 cm pitch) in the iron return yoke of the dipole allows measurement of muon tracks **after they exit the active volume in any direction**, including through the yoke walls
- This extends the effective spectrometer to larger angles
- The yoke instrumentation also acts as a **muon identification system**, distinguishing muons from pions by penetration depth (iron equivalent)
- Existing examples: T2K ND280 SMRD (Side Muon Range Detector), NOvA near detector muon tagger

**Additionally:** If the magnet field cannot be increased (warm magnet, power/cooling constraints), consider **magnetic field mapping** and an upgraded field-uniformity correction to the existing spectrometer to improve momentum resolution for the existing downstream chambers.

---

## 6. Timing System Upgrade: High-Precision Trigger and Event Timing

**Technology: Waveform digitizers with ≤1 ns timing resolution distributed across all subdetectors, synchronized to the beam spill structure**

- The accelerator beam delivers bunched spills; pile-up of multiple neutrino interactions in one spill is a concern at 410 m
- A **GPS-disciplined or white-rabbit timing system** synchronizes all subdetectors to <1 ns
- Fast plastic scintillator trigger planes (upstream and downstream of the active volume) provide a prompt trigger signal with ~0.3 ns resolution to associate tracks across subdetectors and reject cosmic ray backgrounds
- This is essential for correctly associating the recoiling proton (possibly a very short stub inside the active volume) with the muon that exits into the surrounding tracker

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Key Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Active target medium | Fine-pitch LArTPC (3 mm wire pitch, cold electronics + photon detection) **or** high-pressure gaseous Ar TPC (GEM/Micromegas) | Short proton tracks (60 MeV), H ≤ 2%, 3D vertex reconstruction |
| All-angle muon tracker | Scintillator/RPC planes on all 6 faces of active volume | ≥25% muon efficiency at all angles including 90° and backward |
| Upstream muon catcher | Steel–scintillator range stack (~0.5 m) upstream of active volume | Momentum-by-range for backward muons |
| Instrumented magnet yoke | Scintillator strips or RPCs embedded in dipole return yoke | Muon ID and tracking for large-angle exit tracks |
| Photon/light detection | ARAPUCA bars or dip-coated light guides (in LAr option) | t₀ for drift coordinate reconstruction |
| Timing and trigger | Waveform digitizers, white-rabbit sync, fast scintillator trigger | Pile-up rejection, cross-subdetector track matching |

The single most critical upgrade is the **active target itself** (LArTPC or HPgTPC) combined with the **surrounding all-angle tracker**, since the existing configuration has no sensitivity to backward or transverse muons and cannot reconstruct the short proton stubs required by the analysis.

# ND280 Upgrade Proposal: Upstream High-Acceptance Tracking Target

## 1. What limits the present detector

| Limitation | Cause | Consequence for the 4% goal |
|---|---|---|
| Poor high-angle acceptance | FGD bars and TPC readout planes are all perpendicular or parallel to the beam. Tracks at more than ~50–60° run along a single bar layer and never reach a TPC. | About 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons are badly reconstructed. The far detector covers 4π, so the near and far phase spaces differ and the cross-section model must be relied on to extrapolate. |
| High proton threshold | A proton must cross at least 2–3 one-centimetre bar layers in both views before it is seen. | The threshold is about 450–500 MeV/c, which is near the median of the leading-proton distribution. Half the protons are lost. |
| Only 2D views | x/y bars give two projections. | Short, overlapping vertex tracks are ambiguous. Kinematic imbalance (δp_T, δα_T) needs both the muon and the proton fully reconstructed. |
| No neutron information | — | Antineutrino events have unconstrained missing momentum. |

The P0D's role (π⁰ on water) is no longer essential, because water-versus-carbon comparisons can be made with FGD2. Its volume is therefore best used for an isotropic tracking target.

## 2. Proposed configuration (upstream region, inside the existing magnet)

```
          [ TOF panel ]
   [   High-Angle TPC (top)    ]
 T [       Super-FGD           ] T  → beam → TPC1 | FGD1 | TPC2 | FGD2 | TPC3
 O [   ~1.9 x 1.8 x 0.56 m     ] O
 F [ High-Angle TPC (bottom)   ] F
          [ TOF panel ]
   (existing barrel / downstream ECal, SMRD retained)
```

### 2.1 Super-FGD: 3D-granular scintillator target

**Geometry**
- About 2×10⁶ optically isolated plastic cubes, each 1 × 1 × 1 cm³.
- Polystyrene with 1.5% PTP and 0.01% POPOP, with a chemically etched reflective skin.
- Layout of about 192 × 184 × 56 cubes, giving roughly 1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m. This fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box with room for the support frame.
- Target mass about 2 t of CH, roughly twice FGD1+FGD2's hydrocarbon mass.

**Readout**
- Each cube has three orthogonal through-holes of about 1.5 mm.
- Three 1 mm Kuraray Y-11 WLS fibres pass through each cube, along x, y and z.
- Each fibre is read at one end by a MPPC with about 1.3 mm sensitive area and a mirrored far end.
- This gives about 56,000 channels and three orthogonal 2D projections, which are combined into 3D voxels.

**Expected performance**
- Light yield of roughly 40–60 p.e. per fibre per MIP.
- Time resolution of about 1 ns per channel, improving to about 0.5 ns per cube with two or three fibres.

**Physics gains**
- *Isotropic acceptance.* No orientation of track is degenerate, so high-angle and even backward muons and protons are reconstructed.
- *Low proton threshold.* About 300 MeV/c, where the kinetic energy is about 47 MeV and the range is roughly 2 cm, or 2–3 cubes. This recovers most of the proton spectrum below the 450 MeV/c median.
- *Particle identification.* Range and dE/dx distinguish protons, pions and muons. Bragg-peak shape helps p/π separation.
- *Neutrons.* Isolated delayed hits, time-of-flight against the vertex, and the lever arm give neutron kinetic energy. This allows full kinematic closure in ν̄ charged-current events.
- *Michel electrons* identify π⁺.

**Contained and exiting tracks**
- Protons up to about 600–700 MeV/c stop inside the detector and are measured by range.
- The roughly 6% above 900 MeV/c, and most muons, exit into a TPC where momentum is measured by curvature at 0.2 T.

### 2.2 Two High-Angle TPCs (above and below the Super-FGD)

- **Size:** each about 2.0 m (along the beam) × 0.8 m (drift region) × 1.8 m. They give momentum and dE/dx for tracks leaving the Super-FGD at large angles, which ND280's forward TPCs cannot see.
- **Gas:** the same T2K gas, Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2, for continuity.
- **Field cage:** light composite (aramid honeycomb with laminated copper strips) to minimise dead material and thickness. This preserves acceptance and reduces proton re-interactions in the walls.
- **Readout:** resistive bulk Micromegas, an evolution of the existing bulk Micromegas.
  - A resistive anode spreads the charge, so pads can be larger (about 1 × 1 cm) with fewer channels and no loss of resolution.
  - The resistive layer also gives intrinsic spark protection.
  - Eight modules per endplate.
- **Targets:**
  - Space-point resolution below 800 µm.
  - Momentum resolution below 10% at 1 GeV/c.
  - dE/dx resolution below 10%, giving e/µ separation for ν_e studies.

### 2.3 Time-of-Flight envelope

- Six planes of about 1 cm thick plastic scintillator bars enclose the Super-FGD and the HA-TPCs.
- Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Target time resolution about 150 ps.

**Uses**
- Identify track direction (forward or backward), which suppresses out-of-fiducial background such as interactions in the magnet or ECal entering the target.
- Add e/µ/p ToF particle identification at low momentum.
- Provide a cosmic trigger.

### 2.4 Integration and services

**Electronics**
- Super-FGD: front-end based on a CITIROC ASIC, to match the high channel density and timing needs.
- HA-TPCs: AFTER/AGET-type electronics, adapted from the existing TPCs.
- Common clock with the beam spill, giving sub-ns timing for the neutron ToF.

**Mechanics**
- Super-FGD built as a self-supporting light box (carbon-fibre or plastic-composite panels), assembled layer by layer with fibres threaded afterwards.
- MPPCs are insensitive to the 0.2 T field, so the existing magnet and the read-through feedthroughs are compatible.

**Retained systems**
- Barrel ECal, downstream ECal, SMRD, and the downstream tracker (TPC1–3, FGD1, FGD2).
- The water target in FGD2 continues the C/H₂O comparison.
- The existing P0D ECal is replaced or reduced so the new modules fit.

**Calibration**
- Cosmic and through-going muons for cube-by-cube gain and light-yield equalisation.
- An LED or laser system for the MPPCs.
- The TPC laser and photoelectron calibration systems are reused.

## 3. Expected impact

- Muon and proton acceptance near 4π, matched to Super-Kamiokande phase space.
- Proton threshold lowered from about 450 MeV/c to about 300 MeV/c, so most leading protons are measured.
- Event-by-event transverse kinematic imbalance (δp_T, δα_T) and neutron momentum reconstruction. These constrain nuclear effects (Fermi motion, 2p2h, final-state interactions) and the energy-reconstruction bias.
- Roughly double the upstream CH target mass, giving more statistics with the same beam.
- Combined with the retained FGD2 water data, this reduces the flux × cross-section systematic on the far-detector prediction from about 6% to the roughly 4% required for T2K-II.

## 4. Risks and R&D items

- **Cube mass production and assembly:** dimensional tolerance of about ±30 µm, plus light crosstalk through the reflector, which must stay below a few percent.
- **Fibre threading** across about 2 m and roughly 56,000 holes.
- **Resistive Micromegas:** uniformity of the resistive layer and long-term stability at J-PARC rates.
- **Neutron reconstruction:** needs validation in a test beam with a tagged neutron source.
- **Schedule:** installation must fit within an accelerator long shutdown. The P0D removal and the new detectors' installation should be planned as one campaign.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for ND280

## 1. **SuperFGD (Super Fine-Grained Detector) - 3D Scintillator Cube Array**

**Technology:** ~2 million small (1 cm³) plastic scintillator cubes in a 3D lattice structure, each read out by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibers connected to MPPCs.

**Why:** 
- **3D tracking capability**: Essential for reconstructing tracks at large angles (>50°) where current 2D x/y layers have blind spots
- **Isotropic acceptance**: Handles the ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons emerging >50° from beam axis
- **Fine granularity**: 1 cm resolution enables precise vertex reconstruction and separation of multi-particle final states
- **Low threshold**: Detects protons down to ~200 MeV/c kinetic energy, covering the median of 450 MeV/c
- **Hydrocarbon target**: Provides CH target mass while serving as active detector

## 2. **High-Angle TPC (HA-TPC) - Horizontal Gas TPCs**

**Technology:** Thin gas TPCs with resistive Micromegas readout, positioned horizontally (perpendicular to beam) on top and bottom of SuperFGD, potentially also on sides.

**Why:**
- **Momentum measurement**: Provides momentum-by-range and dE/dx for particles exiting SuperFGD at high angles
- **Charge identification**: Distinguishes protons from charged pions via dE/dx
- **Large acceptance**: Horizontal orientation captures forward-going and high-angle particles
- **Particle ID at stopping**: Critical for ~450 MeV/c protons that stop in the detector volume
- **Complements existing TPCs**: Existing TPCs primarily measure forward-going tracks

## 3. **Time-of-Flight Detector (TOF) - Timing Planes**

**Technology:** Planes of thin plastic scintillator with very fast timing (σ ~150-200 ps), placed around SuperFGD faces.

**Why:**
- **Proton/pion separation**: TOF measurement over ~0.5-2 m distinguishes protons from pions at momenta 400-900 MeV/c where dE/dx overlaps
- **Direction determination**: t0 reference enables track direction determination in SuperFGD
- **High-momentum protons**: Particularly valuable for the 6% of protons >900 MeV/c that are minimum-ionizing
- **Reduces systematics**: Direct particle ID reduces model-dependence in event selection

## 4. **Enhanced SMRD or Target Surrounding ECal**

**Technology:** Additional compact lead-scintillator ECal layers or improved SMRD coverage with timing capability.

**Why:**
- **Muon containment**: Contains and measures high-angle muons that miss downstream TPCs
- **Energy measurement**: Calorimetric measurement for muons exiting active tracker
- **Photon detection**: Maintains π⁰ rejection capability for charged-current event selection
- **Reduce escapes**: Increases acceptance for kinematically complete events

## 5. **Upgraded DAQ and Readout Electronics**

**Technology:** Modern FPGA-based readout with increased bandwidth, higher sampling rates, and extended readout windows.

**Why:**
- **Channel count**: SuperFGD alone requires ~6 million channels (2M cubes × 3 fibers)
- **Timing precision**: Needed for TOF (sub-ns) and three-dimensional charge matching
- **Trigger flexibility**: Must handle increased complexity of multi-detector coincidences
- **T2K-II rate**: 8× beam power increase requires higher throughput and pile-up rejection

## 6. **Magnetic Field Considerations**

**Technology:** Either maintain 0.2 T dipole field OR upgrade to stronger field if mechanically feasible.

**Why:**
- **Charge sign selection**: Separates ν and ν̄ events via muon charge
- **Momentum measurement**: Improves momentum resolution for through-going particles
- **Sub-GeV tracking**: Even 0.2 T provides useful curvature for ~600 MeV/c muons
- **Systematic reduction**: Direct charge measurement reduces wrong-sign backgrounds

## 7. **Calibration Systems**

**Technology:** 
- Laser calibration system for photodetector gains
- Cosmic ray trigger system
- Potentially a movable radioactive source system

**Why:**
- **Channel equalization**: Essential for 2M+ channel detector
- **Stability monitoring**: Long-term gain stability over T2K-II run
- **Absolute energy scale**: Cosmic muons provide known dE/dx reference
- **Systematic control**: Calibration precision must match 4% systematic target

---

## Summary

This upgrade transforms ND280 from a primarily forward-oriented detector to one with **4π-like acceptance**, enabling kinematically complete reconstruction of events with high-angle particles. The combination of 3D tracking (SuperFGD), momentum measurement (HA-TPC), particle ID (TOF + dE/dx), and containment (enhanced ECal/SMRD) addresses all requirements for transverse kinematic imbalance studies while reducing systematics from 6% to the T2K-II target of 4%.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal for the Kestrel Flats Near Station

The 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m region would be filled with three systems:

1. A fine-grained, fully active 3D-segmented scintillator target at the centre.
2. Thin gaseous TPCs above and below it, inside the same 0.15 T field.
3. A hermetic shell of fast time-of-flight (TOF) panels around everything.

Each choice follows from one of the stated requirements.

## 1. Active target: 3D-segmented plastic scintillator ("SuperFGD-type")

**Technology**
- About 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes. Each cube is surface-etched with a reflector and threaded by three orthogonal 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibres.
- Fibres are read out at one end by magnetic-field-tolerant SiPMs (MPPCs), with time-stamping electronics giving about 1 ns resolution.
- Suggested envelope: about 2.4 m (x) × 1.3 m (y) × 0.8 m (z, along the beam).
  - This is about 2.5 million cubes and about 2.5 t of target.
  - Only about 6×10⁴ readout channels are needed, from the three orthogonal projections (240×130 + 240×80 + 130×80).

**Physics motivation**
- **Isotropic acceptance.**
  - Conventional bar-layer trackers lose tracks that run parallel to the layers, i.e. near 90° to the beam. Three orthogonal readout views make the response essentially angle-independent.
  - Backward and high-angle muons start and are tracked in the same granularity as forward ones.
  - Muons exiting sideways (along the field direction, where they barely bend) can still be identified and measured. Momentum comes from range: a 300 MeV/c muon ranges out in about 1 m of plastic. Direction comes from dE/dx growth toward the stopping point and from timing.
- **Low-energy protons.**
  - A 60 MeV proton has a range of about 3 g/cm², i.e. about 3 cm, or 3 cubes.
  - With 1 cm pitch and no dead material, this gives a reconstructable track with a clear Bragg peak. That is enough for proton identification and calorimetric kinetic energy at all angles.
  - The detection threshold falls well below that of the previous detector. This gives access to the hadronic final state and to transverse-kinematic-imbalance variables.
- **Hydrogen fraction.**
  - In polystyrene (CH)ₙ, hydrogen nuclei make up 1/13 ≈ 7.7% of target nucleons. This is comfortably under the 20% limit.
  - This leaves margin for fibres, glue, and any later inserts, so the hydrogen-subtraction model remains valid.
  - Carbon is also a reasonable bridge to the hydrogen-free far-detector nucleus.
- **Neutrons (bonus).** Isolated, delayed cube hits combined with ns timing allow neutron detection and time-of-flight energy measurement. This helps close the energy budget in antineutrino interactions.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Two thin TPCs, each about 2.6 m × 0.4 m × 0.9 m, with a central cathode and drift along x.
- Light field cage (composite laminate), to minimise material between the target and the gas.
- Gas: argon-based (e.g. Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀).
- Readout: resistive-anode (encapsulated-resistor) Micromegas. Charge spreading lets ~1 cm pads achieve sub-mm resolution with modest channel count.

**Physics motivation**
- **Charge and momentum for high-angle tracks.**
  - The existing downstream drift chambers only see forward tracks. These TPCs give charge sign and momentum for muons emitted upward or downward, including at about 90° and backward.
  - Example: a 0.4 GeV/c muon in 0.15 T has a radius of curvature of about 9 m. Over 0.8 m that is a sagitta of about 9 mm, which is easily measured, giving roughly 10% momentum resolution.
  - Charge sign is needed to separate ν from ν̄ in the wrong-sign beam component.
- **Particle identification.** dE/dx in gas separates μ, e, p and π.
- **Efficiency coverage.**
  - Tracks bending in the y–z plane go to these TPCs.
  - Tracks escaping along x are covered by range in the target.
  - Together these keep muon efficiency above 25% for every polar angle.

## 3. Time-of-flight shell

**Technology**
- Plastic scintillator bars about 2 cm thick enclosing the target and TPCs, read at both ends by SiPM arrays.
- Timing resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Physics motivation**
- **Direction of travel.** TOF between the target and the shell unambiguously distinguishes a backward-going muon from a forward-going particle entering from outside. Without this, backward tracks are swamped by out-of-fiducial-volume background, such as muons from interactions in the magnet and surrounding sand.
- **Particle identification** for tracks that exit, complementing dE/dx.
- **Triggering and background rejection.** The shell acts as a cosmic and entering-particle veto, and gives timing to separate beam bunches.

## 4. Integration notes

- **Space budget.** The vertical stack (1.3 m target + 2 × 0.4 m TPCs + TOF layers) fits the 2.3 m height. The 0.8 m target depth leaves room in the 0.9 m beam dimension for TOF panels at the upstream and downstream faces.
- **Downstream matching.** Forward muons pass into the existing drift chambers, so forward tracks keep the established high-resolution momentum measurement.
- **Field compatibility.** SiPMs and Micromegas both tolerate the 0.15 T field. Electronics should sit at the periphery to keep dead material out of the active volume.
- **Calibration.**
  - Cosmic muons and an LED/laser system provide cube-by-cube light-yield calibration.
  - Test-beam characterisation of proton response near the 60 MeV threshold underpins the proton efficiency model.

## Summary

| Requirement | Hardware answer |
|---|---|
| Muon ≥25% at all angles, incl. 90° and backward | 3D-segmented scintillator + high-angle TPCs + TOF direction tagging |
| Protons down to ~60 MeV at all angles | 1 cm cube granularity, fully active (3+ cube tracks, Bragg peak) |
| H nuclei ≤20% of target nucleons | Polystyrene target (≈7.7% H by nucleon) |
| Charge/momentum of exiting tracks | Resistive-Micromegas TPCs + existing downstream drift chambers in the 0.15 T dipole |

Based on the detector description and physics requirements, here are concrete hardware upgrades for the next phase:

## 1. **SuperFGD-style 3D Scintillator Cube Target**

**Technology:** Fine-grained scintillator detector with 1 cm³ optically-isolated cubes, each read out on three orthogonal faces with wavelength-shifting fibers and SiPMs.

**Physics Motivation:** 
- Provides true 3D tracking with ~1 cm granularity for complete event reconstruction
- The 4π acceptance captures the ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons leaving at >50° to beam
- Fine segmentation enables proton identification and momentum measurement down to ~300 MeV/c via range and dE/dx
- Hydrocarbon (polystyrene) target acceptable for the physics program
- Mass: ~1.9 t fills available volume (2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m), providing sufficient statistics
- Three-view readout resolves ambiguities in transverse kinematics critical for imbalance studies

## 2. **Time-of-Flight System**

**Technology:** Thin plastic scintillator planes with ~200 ps timing resolution at entrance and exit of new target volume.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Discriminates forward-going protons from backwards-going muons in ambiguous topologies
- With 60 cm flight path, provides π/p separation up to ~500 MeV/c
- Reduces backgrounds from through-going tracks that fake contained vertices
- Improves trigger efficiency and event-time definition for TPC readout downstream
- Critical for identifying the "leading" proton among multiple candidates

## 3. **High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC Module**

**Technology:** 10 bar argon gas TPC with 2 mm pitch micromegas readout, ~0.6 m drift, replacing one plastic target module downstream.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Provides independent argon target for cross-section measurements (complements hydrocarbon and water)
- Excellent dE/dx resolution (5-7%) for particle ID, especially proton/pion separation
- Measures proton kinetic energy directly for the ~6% of protons >900 MeV/c that punch through scintillator
- Low threshold (~250 MeV/c for protons) captures recoil proton spectrum at median of 450 MeV/c
- At 10 bar, provides 2.2 t fiducial mass in available TPC volume
- Argon is increasingly important target nucleus for DUNE far detector

## 4. **Electromagnetic Calorimeter Upgrade**

**Technology:** Replace brass/lead layers in side ECals with sampling calorimeter: 3 mm lead + 5 mm scintillator, reducing Molière radius and improving sampling fraction.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Better photon/electron reconstruction for identifying π⁰ backgrounds to CCQE candidates
- Improved energy resolution for transverse momentum balance: need <15% energy resolution for final-state electromagnetic energy
- Captures photons from π⁰ decay where one or both photons exit target at large angles
- Better shower separation reduces neutral-current backgrounds that contaminate the sample
- Critical for systematic uncertainty reduction from 6% to 4%

## 5. **Horizontal Drift TPCs**

**Technology:** Reorient new TPC modules with horizontal drift (perpendicular to beam) rather than vertical.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Minimizes track projection effects for large-angle tracks in the horizontal plane
- Gravity-driven positive-ion removal is more effective with horizontal field
- Better momentum resolution for side-going tracks via multiple scattering in longer drift projections
- Reduces systematic uncertainties in angular reconstruction for transverse kinematics
- Optimal for measuring transverse momentum imbalance Δp_T where most activity is perpendicular to beam

## Summary Physics Impact:

These upgrades collectively address the 6%→4% systematic uncertainty reduction requirement by:
- Increasing acceptance for large-angle tracks (particularly protons)
- Providing complete kinematic reconstruction for transverse imbalance studies
- Enabling multiple target nuclei comparisons (CH, H₂O, Ar)
- Improving particle identification and energy measurement across the relevant momentum range
- Reducing backgrounds through better particle ID and containment

The SuperFGD and ToF systems are highest priority for the stated kinematic completeness requirement.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## The key constraint: what the target can be made of

The hydrogen limit decides the choice of target technology.

- **Plastic scintillator is ruled out.** Polystyrene (C₈H₈) has 8 hydrogen nucleons out of 104, which is about 7.7% hydrogen. That is far above the 2% limit. So a T2K-style finely segmented scintillator cube detector (SuperFGD-type) cannot be used, despite its good 4π acceptance.
- **Water is ruled out.** Water is about 11% hydrogen by nucleon count.
- **Argon is the natural choice.** It contains no hydrogen, it is likely the far-detector nucleus (or close to it), and it can serve as both target and tracking medium.

The core upgrade is therefore a noble-liquid active target.

## 1. Pixelated liquid-argon TPC as the active target

**Technology**
- A modular LArTPC fills the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region, similar in style to ArgonCube / DUNE ND-LAr.
- The volume is split into several optically isolated modules, each with:
  - short drift lengths of about 30–50 cm (perpendicular to the beam);
  - a cathode at the centre;
  - native 3D pixel readout (LArPix-type, roughly 4 mm pitch) rather than wire planes.
- The cryostat is a thin-walled design inside the warm dipole. It leaves roughly 4–5 m³ of active liquid, about 5–6 t of argon.

**Physics motivation**

*Hydrogen fraction*
- The argon itself contains no hydrogen.
- The only hydrogen sources are the pixel PCBs, the field-cage insulators, and the cryostat insulation.
- These sit at the boundaries of the volume. Millimetre-scale vertex resolution allows a fiducial cut that keeps the hydrogen fraction of fiducial-volume interactions well below 2%.

*Low-threshold protons*
- A 60 MeV proton travels about 2.5–3 cm in liquid argon. That spans several pixels, with a clear Bragg peak.
- This gives particle ID and kinetic energy by range down to the required threshold, and well below it.
- Because the readout is fully 3D, there is no angular dependence. Protons perpendicular to the beam or going backward are reconstructed as well as forward ones.

*Muons at all angles*
- An isotropic 3D imaging detector has no blind spot for tracks at 90°. Planar trackers, by contrast, lose such tracks.
- Track direction (forward versus backward) is established from:
  - the vertex topology;
  - dE/dx growing toward the stopping end of contained tracks;
  - the timing of the scintillation light.

*Pile-up*
- At 410 m, a tonne-scale target sees multiple interactions per spill.
- Pixel readout avoids the ambiguities of projective wire readout.
- Optical segmentation lets prompt light assign each charge cluster to the correct interaction.

## 2. Scintillation-light detection inside each module

**Technology**
- Large-area light traps line the field-cage walls, of the ArCLight or light-guide type.
- They are read out by SiPMs, with nanosecond-level timing.

**Physics motivation**
- Light provides the interaction time (t₀) for absolute drift-coordinate reconstruction.
- It separates pile-up events within a spill.
- It determines the time ordering along tracks, which helps tag backward-going muons.

## 3. Muon detectors surrounding the target

High-angle and backward muons do not reach the downstream drift chambers. The target is only 0.9 m deep along the beam, and its transverse half-widths are about 1.2–1.3 m, so many muons at large angles will exit sideways.

**Technology**
- Thin tracking and timing planes cover the upstream face, top, bottom and sides of the target region. Two options:
  - scintillator bars with WLS-fibre/SiPM readout; or
  - small resistive-micromegas or drift-tube planes.
- They are placed outside the cryostat but inside the magnet.
- They act as time-of-flight walls with a resolution better than 0.5 ns.
- Their hydrogen content does not matter because interactions in them fall outside the fiducial volume.

**Physics motivation**
- They identify exiting muons and measure their entry and exit positions.
- Time of flight between these planes and the light system sets track direction. This cleanly distinguishes a backward-going muon from an incoming particle (for example, one from an upstream rock or magnet interaction).
- This identification helps hold the reconstruction efficiency above 25% at every angle.

## 4. Momentum for muons that do not reach the downstream chambers

**Technique and hardware**
- Measure the curvature of the exiting track in the 0.15 T field. The lever arm is the TPC track segment plus the outer planes from item 3.
- Add multiple-Coulomb-scattering momentum estimates from the fine-grained LAr track. This works well at sub-GeV momenta.
- Use range for muons that stop in the target.
- Extend the outer muon/tracking planes along the sides of the magnet yoke (an SMRD-like system) to measure range or curvature for high-angle muons.

## 5. Supporting changes

**Thin, low-mass cryostat walls**
- Use a vacuum-insulated, low-Z wall design, avoiding thick hydrogenous foam inside the acceptance.
- This minimises energy loss for tracks heading to the downstream chambers.
- It also keeps the hydrogen near the target small and confined to a well-measured region outside the fiducial volume.

**Optional high-pressure gas-argon TPC section**
- A downstream gaseous argon TPC at about 10 bar could replace part of the volume, or be added in front of the drift chambers.
- It would provide a cross-check sample with very low proton thresholds (a few MeV) on the same nucleus.

**Calibration and material accounting**
- Deploy cosmic-ray and laser calibration of electron lifetime and drift field.
- Make a precise material-assay inventory of the PCBs and insulators. This demonstrates that the hydrogen fraction in the fiducial volume stays below 2%.

## Summary

| Requirement | How it is met |
|---|---|
| No more than 2% hydrogen nucleons | Argon target with a fiducial cut away from the PCBs and insulators |
| Protons down to 60 MeV at all angles | 3D pixel readout; LAr range of a few cm with a clear Bragg peak |
| At least 25% muon efficiency at all angles, including 90° and backward | Isotropic 3D imaging, plus surrounding timing and tracking planes |
| Muon momentum and charge | Downstream chambers for forward muons; field curvature, multiple scattering and range for others |
| Pile-up at 410 m | Modular, optically segmented pixel LArTPC with SiPM light timing |

# Recommendation: ND280 Upstream Upgrade

## Summary

Remove the P0D. In the space it frees, install:

1. A **3D-granular plastic-scintillator target ("SuperFGD")** made of 1 cm optically isolated cubes with three-view fibre readout, filling the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
2. **Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs)**, one above and one below the new target, read out by **resistive (encapsulated-resistor) bulk Micromegas, "ERAM"**.
3. **Time-of-Flight (ToF) panels**, six planes of fast plastic-scintillator bars with SiPM readout at both ends, enclosing the target-plus-HA-TPC volume.

Keep the downstream tracker (TPC1–3, FGD1, and FGD2 with its water layers), the barrel and downstream ECals, the magnet and the SMRD. FGD2 remains the water target for the carbon-to-water comparison.

## Why the current geometry cannot meet the goal

- **Bar orientation.** FGD bars, and the P0D's triangular bars, all lie perpendicular to the beam. A track at more than about 50–60° travels along a bar or crosses very few planes, so it is poorly reconstructed or lost. The muons (25% beyond 50°) and protons (35% beyond 50°) that matter for transverse kinematic imbalance are exactly these tracks.
- **TPC placement.** The existing TPCs sit downstream with their drift planes oriented for forward tracks. High-angle and backward particles from an upstream target never reach them.
- **Proton threshold.** In 1 cm bars, a proton needs to cross several layers to be identified. This makes the threshold high, roughly 450 MeV/c, which is the median of the proton momentum distribution. Half the leading protons are therefore unusable.
- **Timing.** There is no fast timing to distinguish forward from backward tracks or to reject particles entering from outside the target.

Closing the gap from about 6% to about 4% systematics needs near-4π acceptance and a low proton threshold, matching Super-K's acceptance.

## Recommended hardware

### 1. SuperFGD active target (about 2 t of CH)

**Design**
