- About 2 × 10⁶ extruded polystyrene cubes, 1 × 1 × 1 cm³, arranged roughly 192 × 182 × 56 to fit the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- Each cube has a reflective chemically etched surface and three orthogonal holes.
- Wavelength-shifting fibres (Kuraray Y-11, 1 mm) run through every cube in x, y and z, giving about 56,000 channels.
- Each fibre is read out by a small-pixel MPPC, for example a Hamamatsu S13360-1325 class device.
- Front-end electronics use CITIROC-type chips to measure charge and time.

**Justification**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three projections from every cube give 3D hits at any angle, which recovers the high-angle and backward muons and protons.
- **Low proton threshold, about 300 MeV/c.** A 450 MeV/c proton (kinetic energy about 100 MeV) has a range of only about 8 cm in CH, still about 8 cubes. It is therefore reconstructed, with dE/dx and Bragg-peak identification and momentum from range.
- **Most protons stay contained.** Only the roughly 6% above 900 MeV/c (range of order 1 m) escape. Those are measured by the TPCs.
- **Neutron reconstruction.** Fine granularity plus timing (about 1 ns per channel) allows neutron detection from isolated delayed clusters, with time-of-flight kinematics. This adds neutron TKI and antineutrino measurements.
- **Mass and format.** The target mass of about 2 t, roughly twice FGD1, increases statistics. It is still hydrocarbon, which is acceptable for this programme, and it reuses the proven WLS-fibre plus MPPC technology already used throughout ND280.

### 2. Two High-Angle TPCs, above and below SuperFGD

**Design**
- Each TPC is roughly 2.0 m long (along the beam), 2.0 m wide and 0.8 m tall.
- The drift is horizontal, with a central cathode.
- The field cage is a thin, light composite (aramid/honeycomb laminate) to minimise dead material and scattering.
- The gas is the same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ (95:3:2) mixture as the existing TPCs, so the gas system is shared.
- Readout uses resistive bulk Micromegas (ERAM). A resistive layer spreads the charge over neighbouring pads, which allows large pads (about 1 cm) with good spatial resolution. It also gives spark protection and fewer channels.

**Justification**
- Muons and escaping protons at high angle exit SuperFGD vertically and enter these TPCs. There they receive:
  - momentum and charge sign from curvature in the 0.2 T field,
  - dE/dx particle identification (μ/π/p/e).
- This complements range-based momentum in SuperFGD, giving full kinematics for the roughly 25% of high-angle muons and for the energetic protons above 900 MeV/c.
- Together with the existing downstream TPCs, the coverage becomes close to 4π.

### 3. Time-of-Flight system

**Design**
- Six panels surround the SuperFGD plus HA-TPC volume.
- Each panel is built from cast plastic-scintillator bars, about 12 cm wide and 1 cm thick.
- Arrays of SiPMs read out both ends of each bar.
- Fast waveform-sampling electronics give a time resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Justification**
- Determines track direction (forward vs. backward, inward vs. outward).
- Rejects backgrounds produced outside the target, such as interactions in the magnet and cosmic rays.
- Provides extra particle identification for low-momentum tracks where dE/dx bands cross.
- Gives a precise t₀ for neutron time-of-flight in SuperFGD.

### 4. Retained and supporting items

- **Downstream tracker and FGD2 water layers** are kept for carbon-to-water ratios and forward tracking.
- **The P0D-ECal** (around the P0D) can be removed to make room for the new detectors. The barrel and downstream ECals are kept for photon and electron coverage.
- **The magnet and SMRD** are kept. The SMRD continues to tag muons that exit sideways, and the 0.2 T field serves the HA-TPCs.
- **DAQ and trigger** must be extended to include the SuperFGD, HA-TPC and ToF channels.
- **Calibration** needs an LED/light-injection system for the MPPCs and a laser system for the HA-TPCs.
- **Beam-test validation** of cube prototypes and ERAM modules should be completed before construction.

## Expected outcome

The upgrade gives full-acceptance, kinematically complete charged-current events:

- muon plus proton reconstructed down to about 300 MeV/c, at any angle;
- neutron tagging;
- energetic and high-angle tracks measured by the HA-TPCs;
- direction and background rejection from the ToF.

This acceptance matches Super-K's and enables transverse kinematic imbalance and nuclear-effect constraints, which are needed to reduce the flux and cross-section systematic uncertainty from about 6% toward the T2K-II target of about 4%.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: New Active Neutrino Target for ND280 Upstream Region

## Executive Summary

I propose replacing the P0D with a **Super-Fine-Grained Detector (SuperFGD)** — a fully-active 3D-segmented polystyrene scintillator target — surrounded on five faces by thin Time-of-Flight (ToF) planes and read into the existing downstream TPC/FGD system. This ensemble, hereafter called the **Upstream Active Target (UAT)**, is designed to achieve kinematically complete CC reconstruction with the large-angle acceptance demanded by the physics programme, reducing ND280's systematic uncertainty below the 4% T2K-II threshold.

---

## 1. Physics Drivers and Engineering Constraints

### 1.1 Key Requirements Derived from the Problem Statement

| Requirement | Numerical Target | Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Muon angular acceptance | ≥ 50° from beam axis | 25% of muons at >50° |
| Proton angular acceptance | ≥ 50° from beam axis | 35% of protons at >50° |
| Proton momentum threshold | ≪ 450 MeV/c median | Stopping protons in active volume |
| High-momentum proton ID | up to ~900 MeV/c | 6% tail, range/curvature needed |
| Available envelope | 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m | Freed P0D volume |
| Target material | Hydrocarbon acceptable | Polystyrene (CH) baseline |
| Systematic uncertainty | < 4% | T2K-II goal |

### 1.2 Why the P0D Architecture Fails Here

The P0D's passive absorbers (Pb, brass, water bags) and coarse-pitch planes render it opaque to low-momentum recoil protons and produce secondary interactions that contaminate event topology. Its 2D (x/y plane-by-plane) readout gives ambiguous 3D vertex reconstruction in multi-track events.

---

## 2. The Upstream Active Target (UAT): Component-by-Component Description

### 2.1 Core Element: SuperFGD Cube-Scintillator Array

#### Geometry and Segmentation

The core active target is a **1920 mm × 1800 mm × 576 mm** (x × y × z, z along beam) array of **1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm optically isolated polystyrene scintillator cubes**, each read by three wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres running in x, y, and z through 1 mm through-holes, each fibre terminated at both ends on **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)**.

- Array dimensions: **192 × 180 × 57 cubes** = **~1,969,920 cubes** (~2 × 10⁶ channels × 3 axes = ~5.9 × 10⁶ SiPM channels, shared per fibre row)
- Each fibre services one row of cubes along its axis; the number of independent readout channels is **(192×180) + (192×57) + (180×57) ≈ 34,560 + 10,944 + 10,260 ≈ 55,764 fibres**, each read at two ends → **~111,500 SiPM channels**
- Cube material: extruded polystyrene doped with PPO/POPOP fluors, same chemistry as FGD bars, achieving ~40 photons/MeV after fibre and SiPM QE losses
- Total active mass: 1.92 × 1.80 × 0.576 m³ × 1.032 g/cm³ (polystyrene, corrected for fibre holes ~3% volume loss) ≈ **~2.0 t**
- Radiation length X₀ ≈ 42 cm in polystyrene; cube depth (57 cm) ≈ 1.36 X₀ — thin enough to minimise photon conversion background while allowing proton ranging

#### Why 1 cm³ Cubes?

- **Proton ranging**: a 450 MeV/c proton (kinetic energy ~100 MeV) has a range in polystyrene of ~8 cm (Bethe-Bloch), traversing ~8 cubes longitudinally — well-measured; a 200 MeV/c proton ranges out in ~1.5 cm, still reconstructable
- **Angular resolution**: track direction from first 2–3 cubes gives ~3° angular resolution at 50° — sufficient for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) variables δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T
- **3D topology**: the three-view fibre readout provides unambiguous 3D hit association even for ≥3-prong events, unlike 2D FGD layers
- **Low threshold**: ~0.5 MeV deposited (half a cube crossing) is detectable, corresponding to proton kinetic energy threshold of ~~15 MeV — well below the 450 MeV/c median

#### Mechanical Construction

Cubes are injection-moulded with reflective TiO₂-loaded polystyrene walls (50 μm thick) on all six faces. They are assembled into **8 × 8 × 8 "super-modules"** (8 cm cubes) with pre-threaded fibre holes, then super-modules are stacked into the full array on a carbon-fibre support frame. This modular approach permits assembly and fibre insertion outside the magnet.

WLS fibres: Kuraray Y-11(200) MSJ, 1.0 mm diameter, single-cladding, same as FGD — vendor-qualified, known attenuation length (~350 cm at 500 nm, adequate for max fibre length of ~200 cm).

SiPMs: Hamamatsu S13360-1325PE (or equivalent), 1.3 mm × 1.3 mm active area, 25 μm pixel pitch (~667 pixels), PDE ~40% at 450 nm, matched to WLS emission peak. Operating voltage ~53 V, temperature-stabilised to ±0.5°C to control gain drift. These are the same SiPM family used in the upgraded FGDs, permitting common slow-control infrastructure.

---

### 2.2 Surrounding Time-of-Flight (ToF) Detector

#### Motivation

Large-angle tracks exit the SuperFGD through its lateral faces. ToF planes serve three purposes:
1. **Charge-sign determination** for tracks that do not reach the downstream TPCs
2. **Particle identification** via velocity measurement β = L/ct, complementing dE/dx from the SuperFGD cubes
3. **Veto and fiducial** boundary definition, reducing background from interactions in the magnet coil/yoke

#### Layout

Five planes of **segmented plastic scintillator slabs** enclose the SuperFGD on upstream (z−), downstream (z+), top, bottom, and one lateral face (the other lateral face faces the SMRD, which provides redundant coverage):

| Plane | Dimensions (mm) | Slab width | No. slabs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Upstream (z−) | 1920 × 1800 | 60 mm × 1800 mm bars | 32 |
| Downstream (z+) | 1920 × 1800 | 60 mm × 1800 mm bars | 32 |
| Top | 1920 × 600 | 60 mm × 600 mm bars | 32 |
| Bottom | 1920 × 600 | 60 mm × 600 mm bars | 32 |
| Left lateral | 1800 × 600 | 60 mm × 600 mm bars | 30 |

- Slab thickness: **20 mm** (Eljen EJ-200 or equivalent), chosen to give ~20 photoelectrons/MIP and time resolution ≤ 150 ps per plane
- Each slab read at both ends by **SiPM arrays** (3 × 3 matrix of 3 mm Hamamatsu SiPMs per end), sum-read for time, difference-read for position along bar
- **System time resolution**: σ_t ≈ 150 ps per plane → **σ(1/β) ≈ 0.06** at L = 60 cm (lateral face), giving **3σ π/p separation below ~1 GeV/c** — covers the full proton momentum range of interest

#### ToF-SuperFGD Integration

The ToF planes are mounted on the carbon-fibre frame of the SuperFGD as a single self-contained unit ("the UAT box"), with a combined outer envelope of **2000 mm × 1900 mm × 620 mm** — fitting within the available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m space with 20 mm clearance on the z-faces (absorbed by the 20 mm slab thickness × 2 = 40 mm, leaving 10 mm each side for cabling).

---

### 2.3 Integration with Existing Downstream Detectors

The SuperFGD/ToF UAT is not a stand-alone spectrometer — it feeds tracks into the existing TPC1→FGD1→TPC2→FGD2→TPC3 stack:

- **Muons**: most forward muons (θ < 50°) exit the downstream ToF plane and enter TPC1 within ~20 cm, where full momentum measurement by curvature in the 0.2 T field takes over. The magnetic rigidity resolution σ(1/p) ≈ 0.1 GeV⁻¹ for 1 m track in TPC is adequate for all muon energies at this beam
- **High-momentum protons** (p > 900 MeV/c): also exit downstream, range-matched in FGD1 or momentum-measured in TPC1
- **Large-angle tracks** (θ > 50°): stop in the SuperFGD (protons below ~600 MeV/c) or exit through lateral ToF into the SMRD — the SMRD's scintillator planes already provide range measurement for muons up to ~600 MeV/c kinetic energy

No mechanical modification to TPC1 or FGD1 is required. The UAT occupies only the freed P0D space upstream of TPC1.

---

### 2.4 Readout Electronics

#### Front-End

SiPM signals (~1.5 × 10⁵ channels from SuperFGD + ~1,000 from ToF) are read by **CITIROC-based front-end boards** (or the WAGASCI/Baby-MIND CITIROC implementation, already in use at J-PARC), one CITIROC-1A ASIC per 32 channels:

- 32-channel charge integration + timing (TDC resolution ~1 ns, adequate when combined with waveform sampling)
- Trigger primitive output on threshold crossing
- Power consumption ~10 mW/channel → ~1.5 kW total for SuperFGD FEE, manageable within magnet thermal limits

For the ToF planes requiring < 150 ps resolution, **waveform-sampling ASICs** (SAMPIC or DRS4-based, 5 GSPS) are used instead, ~1,000 channels, as a small additional system.

#### Trigger and DAQ

The existing ND280 DAQ uses a **beam-synchronous trigger** gated on the J-PARC RF spill (2×10⁸ ns spill, 2.48 s cycle). The UAT integrates into this framework:

- Trigger primitive: any ToF coincidence or SuperFGD cluster above threshold within the spill window
- Data volume estimate: at T2K-II intensity (~2×10²¹ POT/year, factor ~2 above current), the neutrino interaction rate in the ~2 t SuperFGD is ~4–5 CC events/spill, each leaving ~100 hit cubes on average → ~500 hits/spill × 3 bytes/hit × 10⁵ channels/spill = manageable within existing DAQ bandwidth (~100 MB/s capacity)
- Event building: existing ND280 eventbuilder software (art/JANA2 framework) extended with SuperFGD hit-clustering module

---

### 2.5 Calibration Systems

#### Light Yield and Gain Monitoring

- **LED pulser system**: one UV LED per fibre-end connector board, pulsed at 1 kHz between spills, tracks SiPM gain and WLS fibre transmission independently per channel
- **Cosmic muon calibration**: between spills, through-going cosmic muons deposit ~2 MeV/cm in polystyrene, giving ~60 MeV total in a 30-cube crossing — a bright, spatially uniform calibration source. Rate in the SuperFGD volume: ~10⁴ cosmics/hour, adequate for channel-by-channel gain calibration on a timescale of hours

#### Energy Scale

Absolute energy scale set by:
1. **Michel electron spectrum** from stopped cosmic muons (endpoint at 52.8 MeV), providing a known energy point in the range relevant for recoil protons
2. **Proton range–energy relation**: comparing the measured range in cubes to the Bethe-Bloch prediction, iterating on the density and quenching (Birks constant k_B ≈ 0.013 g/MeV/cm² for polystyrene) — achievable to ~2% once cube-to-cube gain uniformity is at the ~1% level

---

## 3. Performance Estimates

### 3.1 Proton Reconstruction Efficiency

For a proton with momentum p:

| p (MeV/c) | KE (MeV) | Range in PS (cm) | No. cubes | Reco efficiency (est.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 200 | ~18 | ~1.5 | ~2 | ~50% (marginal) |
| 300 | ~44 | ~3.5 | ~4 | ~85% |
| 450 | ~100 | ~8 | ~8 | ~95% |
| 600 | ~175 | ~16 | ~16 | ~98% |
| 900 | ~390 | ~65 | ~65 | ~95%* |

*900 MeV/c proton ranges out in ~65 cm — just at the downstream edge of the 57 cm deep SuperFGD; a small fraction exit downstream and are caught by ToF + TPC1.

Efficiency estimates based on FGD performance scaled to 3D topology; a full GEANT4 simulation (see Section 4) is needed for precision.

### 3.2 Angular Coverage

The 3D cube array provides **4π solid-angle coverage within the active volume**, limited only by:
- **Dead material** at faces (20 mm ToF slabs = ~0.13 X₀, ~0.4 nuclear interaction length λ_I) — acceptable; protons below ~300 MeV/c stop before reaching the face in most directions
- **Downstream acceptance** feeding into TPC1: limited to θ < ~40° by the TPC aperture (2300 mm wide at ~600 mm distance → ±62° geometric, but magnetic bending and TPC field cage cut this to ~±45° effective for momentum measurement)

For large-angle muons (θ > 50°): the ToF lateral planes tag exit direction; combined with SuperFGD track stub, angular resolution ~5° is achievable. If the SMRD is in range, muon momentum can be estimated from range to ~10%.

**Net result**: the fraction of CC events with both muon AND leading proton reconstructed, relative to all CC events, is estimated at **~55–60%**, up from effectively zero with the P0D.

### 3.3 Systematic Uncertainty Reduction

The dominant ND280 systematic uncertainties and how the UAT addresses them:

| Uncertainty source | Current (%) | UAT improvement | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| Neutrino flux | ~3.5 | → ~2.5 | Better CC-inclusive rate normalisation with larger fiducial mass and cleaner vertex ID |
| CC cross-section model | ~3.0 | → ~2.0 | TKI measurements directly constrain 2p2h and FSI; model-independent extraction with proton reconstruction |
| Detector (track efficiency) | ~2.0 | → ~1.5 | 3D topology reduces ambiguity; redundant ToF/TPC matching |
| Out-of-fiducial background | ~1.5 | → ~1.0 | ToF veto reduces cosmogenic + rock-muon backgrounds |
| **Total (quadrature)** | **~5.5–6%** | **→ ~3.5%** | Meeting T2K-II goal |

The TKI observables (δp_T, δα_T) with reconstructed proton are particularly powerful: they are sensitive to nuclear effects (Fermi motion, binding energy, FSI) in a way that is largely flux-independent, allowing cross-section model constraints at the **~5% level on individual nuclear effects**, which propagates to the far-detector prediction at the sub-percent level for the dominant uncertainties.

---

## 4. Construction, Installation, and Commissioning Plan

### 4.1 Prototype and Validation

A **~10 × 10 × 10 cm³ (1000-cube) prototype** has already been demonstrated by the T2K/Hyper-K collaboration (the "SuperFGD prototype" tested at CERN PS in 2017–2018 with proton and pion beams), validating:
- Cube-scintillator light yield (~15 p.e./MIP per fibre end)
- 3D hit reconstruction efficiency > 99% per cube for MIPs
- Proton/pion separation via dE/dx and range matching

This existing R&D de-risks the core technology. Remaining work:
- **Scale-up production**: ~2 × 10⁶ cubes requires industrial injection moulding; estimated production rate ~200,000 cubes/month → ~10 months production
- **Fibre insertion and QA**: semi-automated fibre insertion with pull-force and optical transmission QA at each end → ~6 months with 4-person team
- **SiPM mounting and cabling**: CITIROC board population, SiPM-to-fibre coupling with optical grease, potting → ~4 months overlapping

### 4.2 Installation

The P0D is a single removable unit on rails — it can be extracted from the magnet in ~2 weeks (this has been done before for access). The UAT box, assembled and tested on the surface, is lowered into the experimental hall and inserted on the same rail system. Installation time: ~4 weeks including cabling, cooling, and DAQ connection.

### 4.3 Timeline (from approval to first beam data)

| Phase | Duration | Activities |
|---|---|---|
| Design finalisation | 6 months | Engineering drawings, GEANT4 optimisation of segmentation |
| Component procurement | 12 months (overlapping) | Cube moulding, SiPMs, fibres, electronics |
| Assembly and integration | 12 months | Cube stacking, fibre insertion, board mounting, ToF integration |
| Surface testing | 3 months | Cosmic commissioning, LED calibration, DAQ integration tests |
| Installation | 1 month | P0D removal, UAT insertion, cabling |
| In-situ commissioning | 3 months | Beam-off cosmics, then first spills |
| **Total** | **~30 months** | Feasible within T2K-II schedule |

---

## 5. Additional Complementary Upgrades

### 5.1 Upgraded SMRD

The existing SMRD uses 7 mm thick scintillator slabs in the yoke gaps. Replacing the innermost SMRD layer with **5 mm pitch scintillator strips** with SiPM readout (replacing the existing PMT+WLS plate system) would improve muon range measurement resolution from ~10% to ~5% for large-angle muons stopping in the yoke, complementing the UAT lateral ToF.

### 5.2 High-Granularity Downstream ToF Between UAT and TPC1

A thin (~5 mm) **scintillating-fibre plane** (SciFi, as used in LHCb) placed at the interface between the UAT downstream face and TPC1 entrance would:
- Provide a precise interaction time t₀ for TPC drift time determination (currently from beam RF, σ ~few ns; SciFi gives σ ~1 ns)
- Match tracks between UAT and TPC1 with ~1 mm spatial resolution

This is a minor addition: a single plane of 250 μm Kuraray SCSF-78 fibres, 2 × 1920 mm × 1800 mm (x/y views), read by SiPM arrays, ~3,500 channels, adding ~3 kg of material (< 0.03 X₀).

### 5.3 Software: Bayesian Track Reconstruction

The 3D topology of the SuperFGD requires a new tracking algorithm. A **graph-neural-network (GNN) based reconstruction**, similar to those developed for LHC experiments, trained on GEANT4 simulation of the SuperFGD, is recommended over traditional Kalman-filter-based tracking in the cube geometry. This is a software-only change with no hardware cost, but should be prototyped in parallel with hardware construction.

---

## 6. Summary

The proposed Upstream Active Target (UAT) consists of:

1. **SuperFGD**: 1.92 × 1.80 × 0.576 m³ of 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes (~2 × 10⁶ cubes), three-axis WLS fibre readout, ~110,000 SiPM channels — providing fully 3D, low-threshold tracking of both muons and recoil protons with no passive absorber
2. **Five-face ToF array**: 20 mm plastic scintillator slabs with SiPM readout, 150 ps resolution, providing particle identification and large-angle track momentum estimation
3. **Integration with existing TPC/FGD stack**: no modification to downstream detectors; UAT fits within the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope

This ensemble delivers **kinematically complete CC event reconstruction with ≥50° acceptance for both muons and protons**, enabling TKI measurements that constrain nuclear interaction uncertainties, and is projected to reduce ND280's total systematic uncertainty from ~6% to **~3.5%**, meeting the T2K-II requirement. The core technology is validated by existing SuperFGD prototype tests, the production timeline is ~30 months, and the installation exploits the existing P0D rail infrastructure with minimal downtime.

Based on the requirements for this near detector upgrade, I propose the following specific hardware solution:

## Primary Active Target: High-Pressure Gaseous TPC

**Technology: Time Projection Chamber with CF₄ or Ar:CH₄ gas mixture at 10-15 bar**

### Rationale:
- **3D tracking at all angles**: TPC provides true 3D reconstruction including perpendicular and backward-going tracks
- **Low hydrogen content**: CF₄ has no hydrogen; Ar:CH₄ (95:5) keeps hydrogen nucleon fraction at ~12-15%, well below 20%
- **Low threshold for recoil protons**: 60 MeV protons have ~2 cm range in 10 bar CF₄, detectable with adequate sampling
- **Uniform efficiency**: No dead zones or angular acceptance gaps

### Specific Implementation:

**Readout plane**: 
- Micromegas or GEM-based charge amplification
- 3mm pixel pitch using resistive Micromegas strips in two orthogonal views
- ~800 × 800 channels covering 2.6 × 2.3 m area

**Field cage**: 
- 400 V/cm drift field over 90 cm drift length
- Copper strips on G10 frame at 1 cm spacing
- Contained within existing 0.15 T dipole (perpendicular B-field for dE/dx-momentum separation)

**Electronics**:
- After-Pulse Timing Chip (AGET) or T2K Micromegas-style front-end
- 2 MHz sampling for ~450 ns drift time
- Zero-suppressed readout to handle neutrino beam spill rates

## Complementary Detector Layers:

**Upstream thin target section** (first 20 cm):
- **Scintillating fiber planes** with 1mm fiber spacing
- 3 X-Y doublet planes for vertex localization
- SiPM readout for timing (σ < 1 ns) to match beam structure

**Downstream transition region** (last 10 cm):
- **Resistive Plate Chambers** or thin scintillator planes
- Provides timing constraint for TPC track matching
- Handles high-angle tracks exiting toward gas drift chambers

## Gas System:
- Recirculating purification system (O₂, H₂O < 5 ppm)
- Pressure vessel rated to 20 bar (safety margin)
- Slow controls for pressure/temperature stability (±1%)

## Alternative if TPC development risk is too high:
**Fine-grained plastic scintillator tracker**: 1×1 cm² extruded scintillator bars in XYZ triplet configuration, but this struggles with the backward-going track requirement without extensive sideway instrumentation.

The high-pressure gaseous TPC is the only proven technology meeting all requirements simultaneously, particularly the isotropic angular acceptance at low proton threshold with controlled hydrogen content.

# Design Review Recommendation for Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Executive Summary
I recommend implementing a **3D tracking active target using Time Projection Chamber (TPC) technology with argon gas**, supplemented by a thin scintillator plane at the downstream boundary for timing reference.

## Recommended Configuration

### Primary Technology: Gaseous Argon TPC

**Specification:**
- Pure argon gas at ~1 atm (~1.78 kg/m³ density)
- Electric field ~500 V/cm along beam direction
- Micromegas or resistive Micromegas readout planes on both upstream and downstream faces
- 3 mm pixel pitch for charge readout
- Cathode at center (~45 cm drift on each side)

### Justification for Each Requirement:

#### 1. **Hydrogen Content Constraint (<2% of target nucleons)**
- **Pure argon: 0% hydrogen** ✓
- Alternative liquid scintillator would have ~14% hydrogen (unacceptable)
- CH₂ plastic would exceed limits
- Noble gas is the only practical zero-hydrogen option

#### 2. **Backward and Perpendicular Track Reconstruction (25% efficiency all angles)**

**Why TPC excels here:**
- **3D tracking with <5 mm resolution** allows reconstruction at any angle
- Bidirectional readout (both upstream/downstream ends) captures:
  - Backward tracks: Read out on upstream plane
  - Forward tracks: Read out on downstream plane
  - Perpendicular tracks: Full path visible in drift direction
- No blind spots or preferred directions (unlike extruded scintillator or wire planes)
- **Continuous tracking** throughout 90 cm depth without dead material gaps

**Efficiency pathway:**
- Gas volume provides ~300 ionization electrons/cm in argon
- 25 cm minimum muon track → ~75,000 electrons
- Clean separation from noise: >90% reconstruction efficiency achievable
- Angular coverage: uniform 4π acceptance

#### 3. **Low-Energy Proton Detection (down to 60 MeV kinetic energy)**

**Critical advantage of gas:**
- 60 MeV proton in argon gas (1 atm): **range ~42 cm** (fully contained)
- Same proton in liquid argon: range ~1.5 cm (too short)
- Same proton in plastic scintillator: range ~2 cm (too short)

**Tracking capability:**
- dE/dx measurement along full track
- Range-based energy reconstruction: σ(E)/E ~5-10%
- Proton/pion separation via dE/dx (>3σ)
- Track endpoint topology for identifying stopping vs. exiting

#### 4. **Target Mass Considerations**
- Argon gas at 1 atm in 5.4 m³ → **~9.6 kg** (~144 kg-nucleon)
- Modest statistics but acceptable for near detector role
- Can operate at 2-5 atm if statistics required (still maintains range advantages)

### Secondary Component: Timing Plane

**Technology:** Thin plastic scintillator array at downstream TPC boundary
- 1 cm thick BC-408 with SiPM readout
- Segmented into 20×20 cm tiles

**Purpose:**
- T₀ timestamp for drift time measurement (beam has ~1-10 μs spill structure)
- Reduces cosmic ray background by factor ~100
- Negligible material (0.3% X₀) before gas drift chambers

## Alternative Technologies Considered and Rejected

| Technology | Fatal Flaw |
|------------|------------|
| **Liquid Scintillator** | 14% hydrogen by mass (>>2% limit) |
| **Plastic Scintillator (extruded bars)** | 60 MeV protons range out in 2 cm; hydrogen content high |
| **Liquid Argon TPC** | Proton ranges too short; backward tracks problematic without field cage modifications |
| **3D Scintillator (cubes)** | Hydrogen content; spatial resolution inadequate for short tracks |
| **Emulsion** | No real-time readout; cannot be reused; analysis time prohibitive |
| **Straw Tubes** | Dead regions; inefficient for perpendicular tracks; poor dE/dx resolution |

## Implementation Considerations

**Field Cage Design:**
- Resistive divider chain along 90 cm beam direction
- Field uniformity <1% required for <3 mm position resolution
- Compatible with 0.15 T dipole field (E×B effects manageable with corrections)

**Readout Electronics:**
- ~40,000 channels (both end planes)
- Front-end ASIC: T2K/DUNE-style with 400 ns shaping
- Trigger from beam timing + downstream scintillator coincidence

**Gas System:**
- Recirculation with <1 ppm O₂, H₂O contamination
- Purification: heated getter beds
- Monitor electron lifetime >1 ms (ensures >10 cm drift without significant loss)

## Cost and Schedule Estimate
- Micromegas modules: $400K
- Field cage and HV: $150K
- Electronics and DAQ: $350K
- Gas system: $100K
- **Total: ~$1M** (competitive with alternatives)
- Installation: 6 months after procurement

## Conclusion

The gaseous argon TPC uniquely satisfies all requirements: zero hydrogen content, uniform angular acceptance including backward tracks, and sufficient ranges for 60 MeV protons. This is the only technology that meets all specifications simultaneously.

# Proposed Upgrade for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## 1. The hydrogen limit decides the target material

Hydrogen nuclei must make up at most 2% of target nucleons. That excludes the usual active-target choices:

| Candidate | H fraction of nucleons | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Plastic scintillator (CH), e.g. a SuperFGD-style cube array | 1/13 ≈ 7.7% | Excluded |
| Water / water-based liquid scintillator | 2/18 ≈ 11% | Excluded |
| Liquid argon | 0 | Meets the limit |
| High-pressure gas argon TPC (Ar–CO₂, no hydrocarbon quencher) | ≈0 | Meets the limit, but very little mass |

A hydrogen-free far detector is most plausibly argon. So the natural choice is an **argon active target**: the near detector then measures the same nucleus and the hydrogen subtraction is not needed.

## 2. Core: modular liquid-argon TPC with pixel readout

**Cryostat**
- A non-magnetic membrane or stainless double-wall cryostat filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m envelope.
- About 2.4 × 2.1 × 0.75 m of active LAr, roughly 5 m³ or about 7 t, giving ample statistics.
- Keep the insulation (foams contain hydrogen) outside the fiducial volume. It only affects background, not the target composition.

**TPC layout (ArgonCube / ND-LAr style)**
- A 2 × 2 or 3 × 2 array of optically isolated modules.
- Each module has a central cathode and a short drift of about 30–50 cm, giving drift times of roughly 200–300 µs at 0.5 kV/cm.
- Short drifts relax purity and high-voltage demands and reduce space-charge effects.
- They also limit overlap of interactions from successive beam spills.

**Charge readout**
- Pixelated anodes with about 4 mm pitch and LArPix-type cold ASICs, giving true 3D, unambiguous imaging.
- This is the key to reconstructing tracks at every angle. There is no wire-plane blind direction, so perpendicular and backward tracks are imaged as well as forward ones.
- Keep anode PCB material thin, since FR4 epoxy contains hydrogen. It sits outside the fiducial LAr anyway.

**Low-energy protons**
- A 60 MeV proton has a range of about 3 cm in LAr, which gives about 7–8 pixel hits.
- With dE/dx (Bragg peak) identification, this reaches a threshold near 60 MeV in all directions.

**Light readout**
- Thin dielectric light traps (ArCLight / LCM-type) with SiPMs on the field-cage walls.
- These provide nanosecond t₀ for drift-coordinate placement, per-module triggering and spill association.
- They also separate interactions within a spill and reject events originating in the magnet or the walls.

## 3. Muon acceptance at every angle (≥25% efficiency)

The existing drift chambers only see tracks leaving downstream.

- **Forward muons** exit into the existing gas drift chambers. These give momentum and charge in the 0.15 T field, matched to the LAr track.
- **Contained muons** get momentum from range (about 0.2 GeV/c per 0.5 m) or from multiple-Coulomb-scattering fits along the pixel track. Both work at any angle.
- **Exiting high-angle and backward muons** are covered by new tracking added around the cryostat inside the magnet:
  - **Side, top and bottom:** thin resistive-Micromegas gas TPCs or scintillator-bar/fibre trackers in the gap between the cryostat and the coils. These give charge and momentum from curvature for tracks leaving through the large faces. If space is tight, use thin straw or scintillator planes plus LAr MCS for momentum.
  - **Upstream face:** a tracking plane to catch backward-going tracks.
- **Time-of-flight:** fast plastic-scintillator panels with SiPMs and about 150 ps resolution surrounding the volume. Combined with the LAr light t₀, they give track direction (forward vs. backward) and reject entering particles.

## 4. Gas-TPC alternative or complement

A 10-bar Ar–CO₂ TPC (about 100 kg) gives proton thresholds near 10 MeV and excellent 4π acceptance. It must avoid CH₄ or other hydrocarbon quenchers to stay within the 2% hydrogen limit. Its statistics are much lower, so it is best as a small companion for nuclear-effect studies rather than the main target.

## 5. Ancillary hardware

- Argon purification and recirculation (Oxysorb/molecular sieve filters) with purity monitors, targeting electron lifetime above 1 ms.
- Cryogenics compatible with the warm dipole.
- A calibration system: UV laser and pulser.
- Common clock distribution synchronised to the beam spill.

# Design Review Recommendations: Kestrel Flats Active Target Upgrade

## Preamble: Constraints Driving the Design

Before naming technologies, I will derive the hard constraints from the physics requirements, since each recommendation must be justified against them.

**Magnetic analysis envelope.** The dipole provides 0.15 T over 6.5 m, giving a maximum *Bdl* ≈ 0.975 T·m. For a track traversing the full length, *p_T* resolution is dominated by sagitta measurement. Tracks perpendicular to the beam axis see *zero* Bdl in a purely transverse dipole field, so the downstream drift chambers give no momentum measurement for them. The active target must therefore provide its own momentum measurement by range or multiple-Coulomb-scattering (MCS) for such tracks — this is a fundamental design driver.

**Hydrogen fraction.** The target volume is 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m³ = 5.382 m³. The constraint is that hydrogen nuclei must be ≤ 2% of all target nucleons. Pure water (H₂O) has hydrogen fraction 2/18 ≈ 11% by nucleon count — far too high. Polystyrene (CH) gives 1/13 ≈ 7.7% — still too high. The only practical bulk material meeting this constraint without dilution is one composed predominantly of heavy nuclei: carbon-based hydrocarbon with significant carbon loading, or better, materials with negligible hydrogen such as liquid argon or iron. Alternatively a hydrocarbon target is acceptable only if the hydrogen fraction is controlled, which points toward polypropylene (CH₂, 2/14 ≈ 14%) being ruled out, and graphite/carbon (0% H) or argon (0% H) being preferred. I will return to this with the specific solution.

**Low-energy proton threshold.** A proton with 60 MeV kinetic energy has momentum ~340 MeV/c and a range in liquid argon of roughly 5 mm, in plastic scintillator roughly 12 mm, and in a gaseous medium (1 atm Ar) on the order of meters — which means gas provides excellent sensitivity but requires pressure management. The active target must have granularity at the centimeter scale or better to reconstruct such tracks.

**Angular coverage including backward tracks.** This requires either a fully 4π-sensitive volume or a tracker technology whose readout is symmetric fore-aft. It rules out a simple projection along the beam axis.

---

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. Replace the existing passive target with a Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC) as the primary active target volume

**Technology:** Modular LArTPC segmented into independent drift volumes, each with a cathode–anode gap of ~60 cm (half-drift), with wire or pixel readout.

**Justification:**

*Hydrogen constraint:* Liquid argon is a pure noble element. It contains **zero hydrogen nuclei**, trivially satisfying the ≤ 2% requirement. No subtraction model is needed for hydrogen on argon. This is the strongest single argument for LAr.

*Low-energy proton tracking:* In LAr, the electron drift velocity is ~1.6 mm/µs at 500 V/cm. The ionization yield allows detection of protons down to the Bragg peak region. A 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has a range of approximately **4–5 mm** in liquid argon (density 1.396 g/cm³). This is resolvable provided wire pitch or pixel size is ≤ 3 mm. I recommend **LArPix-style charge-readout pixels** at 3.8 mm pitch (as demonstrated in the Module-0 prototype of the DUNE ND-LAr program), which gives ~1 pixel per mm of proton track near threshold — marginal but adequate, and superior to any wire-based solution at this scale length.

*Angular coverage:* A LArTPC records full 3D topology. Backward-going muons leave tracks that curve back through the drift volume; pixels give unambiguous 3D reconstruction without the wire-projection ambiguities that afflict 2-view wire chambers for near-collinear tracks. Tracks at all angles are reconstructed with uniform efficiency provided the track length exceeds ~2 wire pitches (~8 mm), which is satisfied for 60 MeV protons.

*Momentum by range and MCS:* Muons that stop within the LAr volume have momentum measured by range to better than 3%. Muons that exit transverse to the beam — where the dipole gives no *Bdl* — have momentum measured by MCS along their track length within the LAr. For a minimum ionizing muon traversing the 90 cm beam-direction depth, MCS gives σ(p)/p ~ 10–15%, adequate for the analysis. For tracks exiting through the 2.3 m or 2.6 m faces, the full track length in LAr can be 2+ meters, and MCS resolution improves accordingly.

*The 25% muon efficiency requirement:* In a LArTPC, the detection efficiency for a muon is essentially 100% once a threshold track length (~1 cm) is set, because the charge signal is continuous along the track. The 25% minimum efficiency at all angles is comfortably exceeded. The concern is reconstruction efficiency, not detection efficiency; modern deep-learning reconstruction (Pandora, DUNE Wire-Cell) achieves >95% muon reconstruction efficiency in LAr for tracks longer than 3 cm.

**Specific implementation:** Given the target volume dimensions (2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m), I recommend **two drift modules** of 45 cm maximum drift each along the beam axis, sharing a central cathode plane, with anode pixel planes at each upstream and downstream face. This limits maximum drift time to ~280 µs at 500 V/cm, keeping space-charge effects manageable even at the accelerator beam intensity expected 410 m from target. The cathode is held at approximately −45 kV; this is well within proven engineering for modular LArTPCs at this scale.

---

### 2. Instrument all six faces of the LArTPC volume with scintillator panels acting as a Light Detection System and Veto/Tagger

**Technology:** X-ARAPUCA photon detectors (wavelength-shifting dip-coated acrylic tiles coupled to SiPMs) embedded in the anode and cathode planes, supplemented by 1 cm thick extruded plastic scintillator panels on the four lateral faces.

**Justification:**

*Timing:* The LArTPC alone gives no absolute event time (*t₀*) for drift coordinate reconstruction. Without *t₀*, the drift coordinate (the third spatial coordinate perpendicular to the wire/pixel plane) is unknown, reducing the TPC to a 2D projection. The photon detection system provides *t₀* to ~1 µs precision (limited by triplet scintillation lifetime), which is sufficient to assign the drift coordinate to better than 1.6 mm — well below the pixel pitch. This restores full 3D reconstruction.

*Cosmic veto:* At 410 m depth (surface or shallow underground — the problem statement does not specify shielding), cosmic muon rates will be significant. The lateral scintillator panels tag entering cosmics within a ~100 ns coincidence window, allowing beam-associated events to be separated from cosmics using the accelerator RF structure.

*Containment flag:* Tracks exiting the LAr volume into the downstream drift chambers must be flagged so that the momentum measurement switches from range (for contained tracks) to the external magnetic spectrometer (for exiting tracks). The scintillator panels on the downstream face provide this flag with ~100% efficiency for charged particles.

**Specific implementation:** X-ARAPUCAs as used in the DUNE FD modules; 60 cm² active area per unit, one per 500 cm² of anode/cathode face area, giving light detection efficiency of ~3% averaged over the drift volume — sufficient for sub-microsecond *t₀*. Lateral panels: 1 cm Eljen EJ-200 extruded scintillator in 30 cm × 2.3 m strips, SiPM readout at both ends, covering all four lateral faces.

---

### 3. Add a Thin Low-Mass Muon Tracker Immediately Upstream of the LArTPC

**Technology:** Three stations of scintillating fiber (SciFi) tracker, each station consisting of two orthogonal planes of 250 µm diameter Kuraray SCSF-78 fibers read out by SiPM arrays, with a station thickness of ~0.3% X₀ per plane pair.

**Justification:**

*Backward-going track identification:* A backward-going muon produced inside the LArTPC will exit through the upstream face. Without any detector upstream, it enters dead material (the beam pipe region, support structures, or simply ends) and its momentum is unmeasured. Three SciFi stations placed 5 cm, 15 cm, and 30 cm upstream of the LArTPC upstream face will catch these tracks and measure their angle and, via MCS between stations, constrain their momentum. For a 500 MeV/c backward muon, the angular precision from three-station tracking gives σ(p)/p ~ 20% from MCS — not precise, but sufficient to classify the event topology and apply efficiency corrections.

*Interaction vertex confirmation:* The SciFi stations also tag beam-related activity upstream of the LAr volume, allowing rejection of events where the neutrino actually interacted in upstream material (beam pipe flanges, support ribs) and a secondary particle then entered the LArTPC mimicking a neutrino event.

*Low mass:* At 0.3% X₀ per plane pair × 6 planes = 1.8% X₀ total, the upstream tracker does not significantly degrade the neutrino interaction rate or introduce secondary interactions that could fake backward-going tracks from within the LAr.

**Hydrogen content of SciFi:** Polystyrene-based scintillating fiber is CH-based. However, the total mass of three stations of 250 µm fiber over 2.6 m × 2.3 m at ~0.3% X₀ apiece is approximately 2–3 kg. This is negligible compared to the ~5.4 tonnes of LAr in the main volume. The hydrogen nuclei in the SciFi planes represent a completely negligible fraction of total target nucleons and do not threaten the 2% constraint.

---

### 4. Upgrade the Gas Drift Chambers Downstream to Handle the Increased Hit Multiplicity

**Technology:** Replace existing drift chambers with **straw-tube tracker (STT) modules** using 1 cm diameter aluminized Mylar straws with Ar/CO₂ (70/30) fill gas, in four stereo-angle superlayers.

**Justification:**

This is a downstream rather than active-target change, but it is necessary for the system to function as designed. The existing drift chambers were presumably designed for a passive target with limited track multiplicity per spill. With the LArTPC active target, every neutrino interaction is now fully reconstructed inside the target, and all tracks — including multiple protons from multinucleon knockout events — will exit into the downstream tracker. The existing chambers will suffer from occupancy and left-right ambiguity problems.

Straw tubes resolve this because each straw is an independent detector element: there are no left-right ambiguities for isolated tracks, occupancy is managed because only straws near tracks fire, and the tubes are self-supporting — no additional wire frames are needed. The 1 cm diameter gives a maximum drift time of ~50 ns (at ~5 cm/µs drift velocity), fast enough to separate tracks within the same beam spill. Four stereo superlayers (axial, +5°, −5°, axial) give 3D track reconstruction downstream of the target.

Additionally, replacing the chambers with straws reduces the hydrogen content of the downstream tracker — Mylar (C₁₀H₈O₄) has lower H fraction than typical drift chamber gas mixtures involving isobutane — though since the downstream tracker is not part of the target fiducial volume this is a secondary concern.

---

### 5. Install a dedicated Electromagnetic Calorimeter Downstream

**Technology:** Sampling calorimeter using lead absorber plates (3 mm Pb, ~0.5 X₀ per layer) interleaved with scintillator tiles (Sci tiles read by WLS fiber + SiPM, as used in the CMS HGCal or T2K ECAL), 15 layers total (~7.5 X₀), covering the full 2.6 m × 2.3 m downstream face.

**Justification:**

This is not strictly mandated by the stated requirements (which focus on muon and proton reconstruction), but I flag it as a critical omission in the current design that the panel should address. The neutrino flux peaks at 0.7 GeV, where neutral current π⁰ production is a significant background to the muon neutrino charged current signal. The π⁰ decays to two photons; without an ECAL, these photons are invisible in the downstream drift chambers and the π⁰ is unreconstructed. The LArTPC will detect photon conversion inside the active volume (after a ~15 cm conversion gap), but photons that exit the downstream face are lost. A compact ECAL downstream recovers these, enabling the π⁰ invariant mass to be reconstructed and dramatically reducing the systematic uncertainty on the signal selection.

The hydrogen content of this ECAL (lead + scintillator, with lead dominating by mass) is negligible relative to the LAr target nucleon count.

---

## Summary Table

| Component | Technology | Key Physics Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | Modular LArTPC, pixel readout (3.8 mm pitch) | Zero hydrogen; 60 MeV proton tracking; 4π angular coverage |
| Photon detection / veto | X-ARAPUCA + lateral scintillator panels | *t₀* for drift reconstruction; cosmic veto |
| Upstream muon tracker | 3-station SciFi (250 µm fiber, SiPM) | Backward muon momentum; upstream background rejection |
| Downstream tracker | Straw tube tracker (1 cm diameter, 4 superlayers) | Occupancy; momentum measurement exiting tracks |
| Downstream ECAL | Pb/scintillator sampling, 15 layers | π⁰ reconstruction; background rejection |

---

## Critical Risk Item for the Panel

The single most important point I would raise in the review is that **the 2% hydrogen constraint is in strong tension with any hydrocarbon-based active target technology** and must be treated as a primary selection criterion, not an afterthought. Any proposal to use plastic scintillator, polystyrene, or mineral oil as the active medium must demonstrate quantitatively that the hydrogen nucleon fraction is below 2% — none of the common hydrocarbon materials achieve this without dilution by heavy nuclei. Only noble liquid (argon, xenon), or predominantly metallic/mineral targets (iron, lead glass) satisfy this constraint intrinsically. Among these, only LAr simultaneously provides the sub-centimeter tracking resolution needed for 60 MeV protons. This uniquely determines the technology choice for the active target.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Active Neutrino Target Section

## Context and Driving Requirements

The core constraints are: (1) a 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope, (2) kinematically complete CC reconstruction requiring both muon and leading proton tracking, (3) ~25% of muons and ~35% of leading protons exit beyond 50° to beam, and (4) a leading-proton median momentum of ~450 MeV/c with a tail to >900 MeV/c. The goal is to reduce systematic uncertainty from ~6% to ~4%.

---

## Upgrade 1: Scintillating Fibre (SciFi) Tracker as the Active Target

**Technology:** Densely packed planes of ~0.25–0.35 mm diameter polystyrene scintillating fibres arranged in X/Y stereo layers, bonded in mats and read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) — the same SiPM technology already deployed on existing calorimeter channels, reducing procurement and DAQ complexity.

**Why:**
- Provides ~1 mm spatial resolution sufficient to separate interaction vertex from secondary interactions and to reconstruct short recoil proton tracks.
- The fibre mat construction is mechanically thin per plane, so many planes fit within the 0.6 m depth, maximising target mass in the constrained envelope while keeping the material budget per plane low enough to minimise secondary scattering of the low-momentum protons.
- Polystyrene (CH) is the acceptable target material for this programme; the downstream water-layer module handles the C-to-water comparison so no water infrastructure is needed here.
- Fast timing (~1 ns) from SiPM readout helps associate hits to the correct beam spill bucket and reject out-of-time backgrounds.
- SiPM technology is already qualified in the existing detector, reducing technical risk and allowing shared spares, calibration procedures, and readout electronics firmware.

---

## Upgrade 2: High-Granularity SiPM Readout Electronics for the New Target

**Technology:** Application-specific readout ASICs (e.g., of the CITIROC or TARGET family, or a custom equivalent) mounted on front-end boards directly coupled to the SiPM arrays of the SciFi planes, with zero-suppressed digital readout over high-speed serial links to a common DAQ back-end.

**Why:**
- The much higher channel count of a SciFi tracker (~tens of thousands of channels in the available volume) compared to the coarser bars it replaces cannot be served by the existing per-channel WLS-fibre-to-SiPM readout chain without significant electronic infrastructure; direct SiPM coupling with ASIC multiplexing is the standard solution at this density.
- Low-noise, low-threshold operation is essential: recoil protons at 450 MeV/c have a range of only a few tens of cm in polystyrene, and those at the low end of the distribution deposit only modest energy per plane; the readout must be sensitive to minimum-ionising-or-below signals from short tracks.
- Integrating charge and time-over-threshold in the ASIC enables both the tracking and dE/dx-based particle identification needed to separate protons from pions among recoil candidates.

---

## Upgrade 3: Enlarged or Extended Muon-Ranging / Side-Muon Tracking in the Return Yoke

**Technology:** Additional scintillator planes — the same extruded polystyrene bar technology with WLS fibre and SiPM readout already used in the existing yoke instrumentation — added to the upstream (beam-left, beam-right, and top/bottom) faces of the magnet return yoke adjacent to the new target location.

**Why:**
- With ~25% of muons exiting beyond 50°, a substantial fraction of CC events from the new upstream target position will produce muons that reach the yoke at steeper angles and in regions of the yoke that were previously less populated because the upstream section was a passive photon tagger rather than a neutrino interaction target. Without additional coverage those muons are unranged and their momenta unmeasured, destroying kinematic completeness.
- The existing dipole field (0.2 T) gives momentum measurement by curvature for muons that are tracked through the gas TPCs into the downstream region; for the high-angle muons the ranging in scintillator is the primary momentum method, so the coverage must match the new angular acceptance.
- Reusing the existing scintillator-bar-and-SiPM technology keeps the solution within the established calibration and monitoring framework.

---

## Upgrade 4: Upstream Veto / Beam-Halo Scintillator Panel

**Technology:** A single plane (or thin double plane for coincidence) of large-area scintillator tiles read out by SiPMs, mounted on the upstream face of the new active target assembly.

**Why:**
- Once the photon-tagging section is removed the new target is at the upstream edge of the inner magnet volume; there is no longer a multi-tonne passive absorber upstream to range out beam-halo muons or to tag charged particles entering from the target station.
- A thin veto plane provides a hardware-level rejection of through-going muons from beam halo and cosmic rays that would otherwise fake low-multiplicity CC-like topologies and inflate the background to the transverse kinematic imbalance analysis.
- The panel also acts as a fiducial-entry tagger: events where a charged particle enters from upstream can be flagged offline rather than relied upon to be distinguished only by tracking, improving systematic control.
- Scintillator tile with SiPM is already the baseline technology in the detector, so this is a low-risk addition.

---

## Upgrade 5: Light-Material (Low-Z) Structural Support and Target Frame

**Technology:** Carbon-fibre-reinforced polymer (CFRP) structural frame for the SciFi plane assembly, replacing any steel or aluminium internal support that would otherwise be needed inside the active volume.

**Why:**
- Recoil protons at the median momentum of 450 MeV/c (kinetic energy ~90 MeV) have a range of ~5–6 cm in polystyrene but are stopped in a few mm of steel; any structural material within or between active planes will cause a significant fraction of protons to range out before depositing enough hits to be reconstructed, directly undermining the science case.
- CFRP provides the necessary stiffness to hold fibre mats flat and in precise alignment across the 2.0 × 1.9 m transverse area while contributing much less nuclear interaction and range-out material than metal.
- Keeping non-fiducial material low also reduces secondary hadronic interactions that would generate additional tracks mimicking signal protons.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Active target planes | SciFi mats, 0.25–0.35 mm fibre, SiPM | High-resolution vertex + short proton tracking in CH |
| Front-end readout | High-channel-count SiPM ASICs | Handle SciFi channel density; low-threshold proton dE/dx |
| Extended yoke scintillator | Extruded scintillator bar + WLS + SiPM | Range high-angle muons from new upstream target position |
| Upstream veto panel | Scintillator tile + SiPM | Reject beam-halo and entering charged backgrounds |
| CFRP target frame | Carbon-fibre-reinforced polymer | Minimise material to preserve low-momentum proton acceptance |

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of the Physics Requirements

Before listing upgrades, the constraints must be unpacked:

- **Muon reconstruction at all angles including backward-going**: requires sensitivity to tracks going upstream, sideways, and at large angles — not just forward-tracking
- **60 MeV kinetic energy protons**: these have a range in water of ~6 mm, in scintillator ~8 mm, so the active target needs mm-scale or sub-cm granularity
- **≥25% muon efficiency at every angle**: no dead zones, including along-beam orientation
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of nucleons**: constrains the target material choice severely
- **Target volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m — relatively shallow along beam (0.9 m), wide transverse

---

## The Hydrogen Constraint Is the Key Design Driver

The hydrogen fraction requirement deserves explicit calculation before choosing materials.

Hydrogen mass fraction of water (H₂O): 2/18 = 11.1% by mass, but the requirement is by **nucleon number**.

In H₂O: 2 protons + 16 nucleons (oxygen) per molecule = 2/18 = **11.1% hydrogen nucleons**. ✓ Water passes.

In polystyrene (CH): 1H + 12C per unit = 1/13 = **7.7% hydrogen nucleons**. ✓ Passes.

In polyethylene (CH₂): 2H + 12C = 2/14 = **14.3% hydrogen nucleons**. ✓ Passes, but tighter margin.

In liquid scintillator (roughly CH₁.₂, mineral oil based): ~1.2/13.2 ≈ **9%**. ✓ Passes.

Pure hydrocarbon scintillator is acceptable; a water target would also be acceptable. A purely gaseous target (argon, etc.) would have zero hydrogen — excellent for the subtraction model but would have terrible stopping power for 60 MeV protons.

---

## The 60 MeV Proton Constraint Drives Granularity

A 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has range:
- In plastic scintillator (ρ ≈ 1.05 g/cm³): approximately **12–14 mm**
- This sets the required **maximum cell/voxel size**: cells must be ≲ 1 cm in all three dimensions to ensure a short track crosses enough active material to be detected and reconstructed

This rules out technologies with cm-scale dead zones or large cell pitch.

---

## Required Upgrades

### 1. 3D Scintillator Cube Active Target

**Technology**: Interlocking polystyrene scintillator cubes, ~1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm, read out by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers routed in three orthogonal planes to multi-pixel photon counters (MPPCs / silicon photomultipliers, SiPMs)

**Specific implementation**: The SuperFGD design (developed for T2K ND280 upgrade) is the directly applicable technology — cubes with holes drilled in x, y, z through which WLS fibers pass, each fiber read out at both ends by SiPMs, giving 3D hit reconstruction by fiber coincidence

**Why**:
- 1.5 cm cube size gives ~8–9 radiation lengths across the full 0.9 m depth, sufficient for muon tracking, while the granularity resolves tracks separated by one cube length
- 3D readout means a track at **any angle** — including exactly perpendicular to beam (hits only one x-layer but multiple y- and z-layers) and backward-going — still produces a reconstructible hit pattern; there is no preferred "beam direction" in the readout geometry
- 60 MeV proton range (~13 mm) spans roughly one cube, producing a signal in at least one and typically two cubes even at minimum energy — above the detection threshold given typical SiPM noise performance (~0.5 photoelectron threshold)
- Polystyrene hydrogen nucleon fraction ~7.7%, safely below the 20% ceiling, leaving margin if any structural material adds hydrogen
- The SiPM readout is compatible with the existing magnet bore (no need for external photomultiplier tubes requiring field-free regions), and SiPMs operate normally in fields of 0.15 T
- The light yield of plastic scintillator (~10 photons/keV) is high enough that a minimum-ionizing particle crossing one 1.5 cm cube deposits ~2 MeV, producing ~O(10) detected photoelectrons — sufficient for robust hit detection

**Specific vendor/precedent**: Fermilab/TRIUMF/CEA Saclay SuperFGD prototype extensively tested; the same geometry can tile the 2.6 m × 2.3 m cross section with ~1700 × 1500 cubes ≈ 2.5 million cubes, and 0.9 m depth with ~60 layers

---

### 2. Time-of-Flight / Veto Panels on All Six Faces of the Active Volume

**Technology**: Plastic scintillator paddles, 1–2 cm thick, with SiPM readout, covering all six faces of the target volume (upstream, downstream, top, bottom, and both transverse sides)

**Why**:
- Backward-going muons **exit through the upstream face** — without an upstream scintillator panel, they produce no downstream signal and may be missed or misidentified as noise; a coincidence tag on the upstream face flags them as real exiting tracks
- Sideways-exiting tracks (perpendicular to beam) exit the 2.3 m or 2.6 m transverse faces, which are outside the magnet tracking volume; face panels catch these exits and provide a timing reference
- Time-of-flight between the face panels and the cube hits provides a **track directionality** measurement independent of geometry, distinguishing forward from backward tracks even for near-horizontal trajectories
- The panels also act as an **active veto for beam-related backgrounds** (e.g., rock muons entering from upstream) by flagging particles entering rather than exiting — important for the backward-going muon analysis where a rock muon entering upstream mimics a backward-going interaction product
- Timing resolution of ~1 ns (achievable with 3 mm SiPM pitch and standard electronics) is sufficient at these momenta

---

### 3. Upgrade of the Downstream Gas Drift Chambers to Higher-Rate Micropattern Gaseous Detectors (MPGDs)

**Technology**: Replace or supplement existing wire drift chambers downstream of the target with **Micromegas** or **GEM (Gas Electron Multiplier)** detector planes, with 2D strip readout at ~0.5 mm strip pitch

**Why**:
- The existing warm dipole and downstream tracking provide muon momentum measurement, which remains essential — the active target reconstructs the vertex and short tracks but long muons must be matched to the downstream spectrometer
- Wire drift chambers have **intrinsic hit ambiguities** at the 410 m near-station high-rate environment (the near detector is close to the target, so neutrino interaction rates per spill can be high); MPGDs have much shorter ion drift times (microseconds vs. hundreds of microseconds for drift chambers), greatly reducing pile-up and left-right ambiguity
- Strip pitch of 0.5 mm provides matching position resolution to link cube-based vertex tracks to the spectrometer
- GEM detectors in particular have been validated in similar high-rate neutrino environments (MINERvA, NOvA near detector region) and are radiation-hard
- The existing drift chambers may have aging issues after years of operation; this is a natural point for upgrade

---

### 4. Low-Noise SiPM Readout Electronics with Waveform Digitization

**Technology**: 64-channel or 128-channel ASIC-based SiPM readout boards (e.g., CITIROC or custom ASIC as developed for SuperFGD) with waveform sampling at ≥ 125 MHz, integrated with a White Rabbit or similar timing system for ≤1 ns synchronization across the detector

**Why**:
- Waveform digitization (rather than simple threshold + time-over-threshold) allows **pulse shape discrimination** between proton and pion tracks — protons are slower and produce denser ionization, giving a slightly different scintillation time profile; this is not the primary PID method but provides a cross-check
- More importantly, waveform sampling enables **sub-ns timing** for the time-of-flight system described above and for in-situ calibration using cosmic muons (which arrive at known angles)
- The ≥25% efficiency requirement at all angles places a premium on minimizing electronic noise hits that could mask real low-energy proton signals; low-threshold operation (~0.5 p.e.) requires well-characterized noise suppression at the ASIC level
- Synchronized timing across all channels allows reconstruction of which hits are in-time with a given beam spill and vertex, rejecting out-of-time backgrounds from previous interactions in the high-rate near-detector environment

---

### 5. Upstream Muon Catcher / Ranger for High-Angle and Backward Muons That Stop Before the Spectrometer

**Technology**: Interleaved steel absorber plates (3–5 cm thick) and scintillator tracking planes (same WLS fiber + SiPM technology as the active target but coarser, ~3 cm pitch), forming a range stack approximately 1 m long, placed **upstream** of the active target on the beam axis — or alternatively on the transverse sides if volume permits

**Why**:
- Backward-going muons from interactions at the downstream end of the target travel upstream; if they are low-momentum (which backward-going muons often are, since they recoil against a forward-boosted system), they may range out in the upstream support structure with no measurement; a dedicated upstream range stack catches and ranges them
- Muons going perpendicular to the beam exit the 2.3 m transverse dimension and must travel ~1.15 m to exit; a lateral range stack on the ±y faces catches muons that don't reach the downstream spectrometer
- Range-based momentum measurement (from the range stack) is complementary to the magnetic spectrometer measurement and provides redundancy for the ≥25% efficiency requirement — even if spectrometer matching fails for a large-angle track, the range gives a momentum estimate
- The steel/scintillator technology is well-established (identical in principle to the MINOS near detector, MINERvA ECAL, etc.) and cost-effective for a relatively modest volume

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Requirement Addressed |

| 3D scintillator cube active target | 1.5 cm polystyrene SuperFGD-style cubes, WLS fiber + SiPM 3D readout | 60 MeV protons; all-angle muon reconstruction; hydrogen fraction |
| Six-face scintillator veto/TOF panels | Plastic scintillator paddles + SiPM | Backward muon identification; rock muon rejection; track directionality |
