## What the Proposal Should Explicitly Justify

The proposal should include a table showing that the chosen scintillator composition keeps the hydrogen nucleon fraction below 20% after accounting for the WLS fiber material (typically polystyrene or PMMA, both of which have similar or lower H fractions than the cube material itself) and any epoxy or structural resin used in assembly — the margin is comfortable for polystyrene (~7.7%) but should be explicitly verified rather than assumed.

# Proposed Active-Target Upgrade: Modular Pixelated Liquid-Argon TPC

## 1. Why the usual answer does not work

The obvious modern choice is a finely segmented plastic-scintillator target (a SuperFGD-style 3D cube array) plus high-angle TPCs. It fails the hydrogen requirement:

- In polystyrene (CH)ₙ, hydrogen is 1 of every 13 nucleons, about **7.7%**.
- Water, other plastics and hydrocarbon gases are similar or worse.

The 2% limit therefore forces a hydrogen-free *target medium*. Hydrogen may appear only in thin structural and readout materials. Since the far detector contains no hydrogen, argon is the natural match. It removes the hydrogen problem and matches the far-detector nucleus, so most nuclear-model systematics cancel.

## 2. Core proposal: ArgonCube-style modular LArTPC

**Geometry and mass**
- About 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m ≈ 5.4 m³ of liquid argon, roughly **7.5 t**.
- Built from a 2 × 2 or 3 × 2 array of optically isolated TPC modules.
- Each module has a central cathode and two short drift regions of about 30–50 cm. The drift runs horizontally, transverse to the beam.
- Short drifts limit the drift field needed, high voltage, diffusion and space-charge effects, and pile-up in drift time.

**Charge readout**
- Pixelated anode tiles with about 4 mm pitch, read out by LArPix-type cryogenic ASICs.
- These give true 3D imaging with no wire ambiguities.
- Readout is isotropic, which is the key property here. Tracks perpendicular to the beam and backward-going tracks are reconstructed as well as forward ones. This easily exceeds 25% muon efficiency at every angle.

**Light readout**
- Large-area, segmented dielectric light traps (ArCLight / LCM type) on the module walls, read by SiPMs.
- Nanosecond timing tags each interaction to its beam bunch, separates pile-up and cosmics, and supplies t₀ for absolute drift position.

**Field cage**
- Resistive-film (e.g. carbon-loaded Kapton) or other low-mass field shells instead of thick G10 and copper strips.
- This minimizes both dead material and hydrogen.

**Cryostat and purification**
- Thin-walled, low-mass inner vessel: aluminium or stainless steel, vacuum-insulated rather than foam-insulated on the sides that face other detectors.
- The cryostat must fit inside the warm 0.15 T dipole. Plan the magnet interface (non-magnetic supports, heat load, flange penetrations) early.
- Argon recirculation and purification with filters, plus purity monitors, targeting electron lifetime above a few ms.
- N₂ and O₂ contamination control.

## 3. Meeting each physics requirement

**Low-energy protons (KE ≈ 60 MeV)**
- Range in liquid argon is about 2.5 cm, which gives about 6 or more pixel hits at 4 mm pitch.
- dE/dx and Bragg-peak identification separate protons from pions and muons.
- Expect a proton threshold of about 40–50 MeV in KE, with full angular coverage.
- This is far better than gas-chamber-only or coarse-bar designs.

**Muons at all angles, momentum and charge**
- *Contained muons:* momentum from range (a few % resolution).
- *Exiting muons:* momentum from multiple Coulomb scattering in the TPC (roughly 10–15%).
- *Forward muons:* matched to the existing downstream drift chambers for precise momentum and charge sign.
- *Charge sign for high-angle and backward exiting muons:* curvature in 0.15 T inside liquid argon is marginal, because multiple scattering dominates. So add:
  - **Thin outer trackers on the cryostat sides, top and bottom, inside the magnet.** These can be gas TPCs with resistive Micromegas readout (high-angle TPC style) or straw/scintillator-strip planes. They measure exit-point curvature and charge.
  - **A thin scintillator time-of-flight shell around the target.** It gives track direction (forward vs. backward), which removes sign ambiguity, and acts as a veto for external entering backgrounds.

These plastic elements lie outside the fiducial volume. Interactions in them are rejected by vertex position, so they do not count against the hydrogen budget.

**Hydrogen budget check**
- Liquid argon itself contributes 0% hydrogen.
- 2% of about 7.5 t of target nucleons is about 150 kg of hydrogen-nucleon mass.
- The internal plastics (anode PCBs, light detectors, field-cage films, cable insulation) amount to well under 1% hydrogen fraction inside the fiducial volume, provided materials are chosen carefully.
- Keep a material inventory so the hydrogen fraction is known, and so the residual hydrogen subtraction uses a small, well-measured correction.

## 4. Supporting upgrades

- **DAQ and triggering:** beam-spill gated, with light-based triggering. Beam timing synchronized to the bunch structure.
- **Calibration:** UV laser tracks for field and E×B distortions, cosmic-ray muons, purity monitors, and possibly a ³⁹Ar / pulsed-neutron program.
- **Readout integration:** a common clock with the downstream drift chambers for track matching across the TPC exit window. Make the downstream cryostat wall a thin window to minimize scattering before the chambers.

## 5. Fallback option if cryogenics inside the magnet is impractical

Use a **high-pressure gaseous argon TPC** (about 10 bar, with Micromegas or GEM readout).

- It is hydrogen-free if a non-hydrocarbon quencher is used, or if the quencher amount is small enough to stay under 2%.
- It has excellent proton thresholds (tens of MeV or less), 4π acceptance and good curvature measurement in 0.15 T.
- The cost is target mass: only about 90 kg, roughly 80 times fewer interactions.

It is valuable as a supplement but is statistics-limited as the primary target.

## Recommendation

Install a modular, pixel-readout LArTPC with fast SiPM light detection, surrounded by thin side and top trackers and a ToF shell inside the existing dipole, and keep the downstream drift chambers for forward muon spectrometry. This satisfies the angular coverage, the 60 MeV proton threshold and the 2% hydrogen limit.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for ND280 Next Phase

## Framing the Engineering Constraints

Before listing technologies, the binding constraints must be stated explicitly, since they discipline every choice:

- Available volume: ~2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m (depth along beam)
- Must reconstruct both the outgoing muon **and** the leading recoil proton
- ~35% of leading protons and ~25% of muons exit at >50° — demanding large angular acceptance
- Median proton momentum ~450 MeV/c; proton range at that momentum in polystyrene is roughly 20 cm, so the active target must also be a tracker with fine enough granularity to contain and measure these tracks
- Residual systematic target: reduce from ~6% to ~4%, which means better constraint on nuclear effects, flux, and cross-sections simultaneously
- The downstream FGD2 (with water) stays; the new detector provides the hydrocarbon sample for C/H₂O comparison

---

## Upgrade 1: Highly Granular Plastic-Scintillator Neutrino Target (SuperFGD)

**Technology:** A three-dimensional array of small plastic-scintillator cubes, each approximately 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm, with three wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres running through each cube along orthogonal x, y, z axes, each fibre read out by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM/MPPC). The full array for the available volume would be approximately 192 × 184 × 56 cubes (~2.0 million cubes), giving a mass of roughly 2 t of polystyrene.

**Why this geometry works mechanically:** The cubes are injection-moulded with through-holes for fibres and are held in a self-supporting matrix. The technology was prototyped and validated by the Baby MIND and WAGASCI groups and later adopted as the baseline SuperFGD for the T2K upgrade, so production tooling and SiPM multiplexing schemes are already established.

**Physics motivation:**

*4π tracking of short recoil protons.* Because every 1 cm³ voxel is independently active in three views simultaneously, there is no dead region or fibre-shadow. A proton stopping after even 2–3 cm leaves a resolvable track, giving a momentum threshold by range of roughly 300 MeV/c (compared to ~450 MeV/c in the planar FGDs). This directly captures more of the leading-proton distribution: moving the threshold from ~450 MeV/c down to ~300 MeV/c recovers roughly 25–30% more proton tracks, which is essential for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) analysis. TKI variables such as δp_T and δα_T are only calculable when both final-state particles are reconstructed; incomplete reconstruction biases the inferred cross-section shape.

*Large angular acceptance for wide-angle tracks.* The planar FGD architecture loses tracking efficiency for tracks beyond ~40–45° because they exit through the layer edges after crossing only one or two XY modules. The isotropic 3D cube geometry provides equal path length in every direction; a 50° proton traverses approximately 7–8 cubes even if it exits the short (z) dimension, still giving a measurable track. This directly addresses the 35% of leading protons at >50°.

*Neutron tagging.* The fine-grained active volume enables time-of-flight reconstruction of neutron-induced proton recoils within the target itself. At T2K energies, a non-negligible fraction of events include neutrons in the final state (from np-nh and pion absorption); measuring their multiplicity reduces the model uncertainty on multinucleon knockout, which is currently a leading systematic in the oscillation fit.

*Reduced cross-section systematic.* The cube target is essentially pure polystyrene (CH), giving a well-known nuclear target with a precisely calculable hydrogen fraction. By subtracting carbon interactions (measured on the downstream carbon FGD1 and from the cube data itself using carbon-only event topologies) the hydrogen quasi-free cross section can be isolated, providing an almost model-independent flux constraint.

---

## Upgrade 2: Replacement Time Projection Chambers with Resistive Micromegas or Pixel Readout

**Technology:** The three existing TPCs use bulk Micromegas pads (~10 mm × 7 mm pitch). The proposed upgrade replaces the anode readout planes with **resistive Micromegas** (or, more ambitiously, a pixel-pad readout based on the AFTER/AGET ASIC chain already used in T2K but with pads reduced to ~3 mm × 3 mm), combined with an updated gas mixture optimised for lower drift velocity to extend the effective time window and improve z-resolution.

**Physics motivation:**

*Improved dE/dx particle identification for low-momentum protons.* At 300–500 MeV/c, protons and pions are separated by dE/dx in a TPC, but the separation power scales with the number of independent samples. Reducing pad pitch from ~10 mm to ~3 mm triples the number of charge samples along a typical track, improving the truncated-mean dE/dx resolution from ~8% to ~5%. This directly reduces misidentification of pion-contaminated proton samples, which currently contributes to the interaction-model systematic.

*Space-charge mitigation.* The existing Micromegas suffer from ion back-flow building space charge at high beam intensity. T2K-II plans to increase beam power from 500 kW toward 1.3 MW, which increases interaction rates in ND280 by a factor of roughly 2.5. Resistive Micromegas suppress ion back-flow by roughly two orders of magnitude compared to standard bulk Micromegas because the resistive layer spreads and quenches the ion current before it enters the drift volume. Without this upgrade, track distortions at high intensity would degrade momentum resolution and increase systematic uncertainty on the neutrino energy reconstruction.

*Photon-conversion vertex resolution.* For π⁰ reconstruction (relevant to the νe appearance background), the displaced conversion vertex must be resolved from the primary interaction vertex. Finer pad pitch improves transverse position resolution from ~700 μm to ~300 μm (scaling roughly with pitch/√12 for charge centroid methods), reducing π⁰ background uncertainty in the νe sample.

---

## Upgrade 3: Thin Electromagnetic Calorimeter Panels on the Inner Faces of the New Target Volume

**Technology:** Ultra-thin lead–scintillator sampling calorimeters using **3 mm scintillator bars interleaved with 1 mm lead sheets** (approximately 2–3 radiation lengths total), read out with the same WLS-fibre + SiPM technology as the existing ECal but in a segmented panel geometry that lines the upstream and lateral faces of the SuperFGD box. Each panel is roughly 15–20 mm thick, so the radiation length budget is kept small and the panels fit within the available 0.6 m depth without consuming target mass.

**Physics motivation:**

*Photon and π⁰ detection from the SuperFGD.* The 3D cube target has no electromagnetic shower containment by itself; photons from π⁰ decay produced in neutrino interactions will escape the cube volume before depositing significant energy. Without a surrounding ECal, neutral-current π⁰ events would be misclassified as charged-current quasi-elastic events (the signal) because the shower looks like nothing while the low-angle muon candidate is selected. Thin ECal panels on all six faces of the cube volume capture the leading photon of the π⁰ at the ~100–200 MeV scale, enabling the NC π⁰ veto that is critical for maintaining a clean CCQE-enriched sample for TKI analysis.

*Measurement of photon-going events at large angles.* The existing downstream ECal (Ds-ECal) has good acceptance only for forward-going particles. Lateral panels specifically recover photon detection efficiency at 60–90°, which is exactly the region most poorly covered by the downstream geometry and also the region most populated by decay photons from forward-pion production in resonance events.

*Energy scale cross-check.* An independent ECal with known lead/scintillator ratio at the target allows the energy scale of electron neutrino candidates to be calibrated in situ using Michel electrons from stopping muons. The existing ECal calibration is done remotely; a local calibration source in the target region reduces the ECal energy-scale systematic from ~5% to ~2%, which matters for the νe appearance analysis at the far detector.

---

## Upgrade 4: Beam-Timing Upgrade — SiPM Readout Replacement with Fast Silicon and Waveform Digitisers

**Technology:** Replace the existing 667 MHz AFTER-chip ADC readout on SiPMs with **1 GSa/s waveform digitisers** (such as the DRS4 chip or a custom ASIC) on every SiPM channel in the new target and the surrounding ECal, achieving single-channel timing resolution of ~1 ns and system-level timing resolution of ~200 ps after offline corrections.

**Physics motivation:**

*Neutron momentum measurement by time-of-flight.* A neutron of kinetic energy 50 MeV travels ~27 cm in 2 ns; at 200 ps timing resolution and typical distances of 30–80 cm between the interaction vertex and a neutron scatter point in the cube target or the ECal, this gives a velocity resolution of ~5–8%, sufficient to reconstruct neutron kinetic energy in the 30–200 MeV range that dominates the T2K spectrum. This is a qualitatively new capability: existing ND280 is completely blind to neutrons. Neutrino interaction models (NEUT, GENIE) differ by 15–30% in predicted neutron multiplicity in this energy range, and constraining that directly at ND280 propagates to a reduction in the nucleon-knockout model uncertainty at Super-K, addressing part of the gap between 6% and 4% systematic.

*Separation of beam bunches from out-of-time backgrounds.* The J-PARC beam arrives in eight 58 ns-wide bunches spaced by ~582 ns within a 1.17 μs spill, repeated at 2.48 s intervals. With 200 ps resolution, tracks and energy depositions can be assigned to individual bunches, reducing cosmic-ray and beam-halo backgrounds by a factor of roughly 50 compared to accepting the full 1.17 μs spill window. This is increasingly important at T2K-II intensity where event pile-up within a spill becomes non-negligible.

---

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Gain | Systematic Addressed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3D scintillator target (SuperFGD) | 1 cm³ plastic cubes + WLS fibre + SiPM | Reconstruct low-momentum, wide-angle protons; complete TKI events | Nuclear model, signal efficiency |
| Resistive Micromegas TPCs | Resistive anode + fine pad pitch | dE/dx PID at high rate; space-charge immunity at 1.3 MW | Flux × cross-section degeneracy |

The combined effect of Upgrades 1 and 4 is particularly significant: the SuperFGD provides the interaction vertex and the charged tracks for TKI, while fast timing adds the neutral-recoil information that makes the hadronic final-state measurement genuinely complete — which is the physics case that motivates the entire ND280 upgrade programme.

## Proposed Hardware Upgrade: SuperFGD (3D Fine-Grained Detector)

Given the constraints and physics requirements, I propose replacing the P0D with a **3D scintillator cube detector with optical readout on three axes**.

### Core Design: SuperFGD

**Architecture:**
- ~2 million small scintillator cubes (1 cm³ each), arranged in a ~200 × 190 × 60 cm³ array
- Three orthogonal WLS fiber readouts through each cube (X, Y, Z directions)
- Total active mass: ~2 tons of polystyrene (CH)
- Fiber routing to MPPCs at the six faces of the detector volume

**Key advantages for T2K-II requirements:**

1. **True 3D tracking** eliminates the x-y layer ambiguities of the current FGD design, crucial for large-angle tracks (>50°)

2. **Fine granularity (1 cm³)** enables:
   - Low-momentum proton tracking down to ~200 MeV/c (range ~5 cm in scintillator)
   - Vertex resolution <1 cm for transverse kinematic studies
   - dE/dx particle identification throughout the track

3. **4π acceptance within fiducial volume** captures the large-angle population without reliance on downstream detectors

4. **High efficiency for CC𝜈μ with proton:**
   - Muons: range out to ~1 GeV/c in detector; higher momenta measured by downstream TPC1
   - Protons 200-900 MeV/c: fully contained and reconstructed
   - Time resolution ~few ns distinguishes muon/proton timing

### Complementary Upgrades

**Enhanced TPC readout:**
- Increase TPC1 readout channels near the upstream face to better match high-multiplicity events from SuperFGD
- Implement improved track-matching algorithms for SuperFGD→TPC transitions

**Target downstream ToF detector (optional):**
- Thin (2-3 cm) timing layer between SuperFGD and TPC1
- ~200 ps resolution to tag particle species and reduce combinatorics
- Reuses MPPC technology; ~4 m² coverage

**SMRD timing upgrade:**
- Add timing calibration to existing SMRD for through-going muon angle constraints
- Improves acceptance recovery for events with muons exiting sideways

### Expected Performance

**Systematic uncertainty improvements:**
- **Acceptance systematics:** <2% (vs. ~4% current) due to 4π coverage and 3D reconstruction
- **FSI modeling:** <3% improvement from proton angular coverage
- **Energy scale:** <1.5% from contained-track calorimetry
- **Combined:** ~3.5-4% total systematic uncertainty ✓

**Physics capabilities:**
- ~60% of CC events with reconstructed proton (vs. ~30% current)
- Transverse momentum balance: δp_T ~50 MeV/c resolution
- Enables 2p2h validation and nuclear model constraints

### Technical Readiness

This design is based on demonstrated technology:
- Wagasci detector (J-PARC) validated 3D cube concept
- T2K already operates 215k MPPC channels; scaling factor ~3× manageable
- Construction: 2-3 years; integration: 6 months
- Cost estimate: ~$8-10M (dominated by MPPCs and cubes)

**Alternative considered:** High-pressure TPC in P0D region offers better momentum resolution but has inferior low-momentum proton threshold and higher technical risk.

This upgrade directly addresses T2K-II's systematic uncertainty goals while maintaining compatibility with the existing ND280 infrastructure.

# Design Review Recommendation: New Active Neutrino Target for the Upstream Section

## Executive Summary

The core problem is converting ~6% systematic uncertainty to ~4% by replacing the passive photon-tagger with an active target that reconstructs kinematically complete CC events, enabling transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) analysis. The constrained box (2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m) and the demanding angular acceptance (25% of muons and 35% of protons beyond 50°) drive nearly every technology choice. I recommend a **SuperFGD-style scintillator cube active target** as the primary detector element, surrounded by a thin time-projection-chamber layer for charge-sign determination and high-angle track reconstruction, with the existing magnet providing momentum measurement. Below I justify each element and flag the trades the collaboration must make.

---

## 1. Primary Active Target: 3D Segmented Scintillator Cube Array ("SuperFGD-type")

### Recommendation
Fill the majority of the available volume (~1.8 × 1.7 × 0.55 m fiducial) with an array of 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm polystyrene scintillator cubes, each penetrated along all three orthogonal axes by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres read out at the faces by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs).

### Justification

**Angular acceptance.** A conventional fine-grained detector built from extruded bars oriented perpendicular to the beam reconstructs tracks well along the beam direction but degrades severely for tracks beyond ~45°. The existing plastic tracking targets (9.6 mm bars, 30 x/y layers) illustrate exactly this limitation. The cube geometry eliminates the preferred-axis problem: a proton travelling at 60° or 80° crosses roughly the same number of cubes regardless of azimuth, giving uniform dE/dx sampling. This directly addresses the stated requirement that 35% of leading protons leave beyond 50°.

**Proton threshold and ranging.** The median leading-proton momentum is ~450 MeV/c (kinetic energy ~95 MeV). A 450 MeV/c proton ranges out in ~24 cm of polystyrene (density ~1.05 g/cm³). In 1 cm cubes this gives ~24 sampled points, providing clean dE/dx-based particle identification and momentum-by-range, which is more precise than curvature measurement at these momenta given the 0.2 T field. The 6% of protons exceeding 900 MeV/c (~370 MeV kinetic energy, ~110 cm range) will often exit the target volume but are handed off to the downstream TPCs — this is acceptable since those events are a small minority and the TPCs provide coverage.

**Neutron sensitivity.** TKI analyses benefit from neutron tagging. The ~15 cm mean free path of ~300 MeV neutrons in polystyrene means a non-negligible fraction of neutrons will scatter in the cube array, producing visible recoil protons. This is a capability the old photon tagger had in a different form; the cube target preserves it without dedicated passive absorbers.

**Target mass and statistics.** At 1 cm³ per cube and 1.05 g/cm³, filling the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box with cubes gives a mass of ~2.3 t. With the existing downstream targets (~2.2 t hydrocarbon plus water layers) the total active hydrocarbon mass exceeds 4 t, comfortably maintaining interaction rate while improving reconstruction quality. The neutrino interaction rate scales with mass, so the ~2.3 t cube volume roughly matches the mass of the removed photon-tagger section (~16 t with water removed → passive absorbers gone, so net active hydrocarbon mass is now comparable).

**Established technology readiness.** The SuperFGD for ND280 (T2K near detector upgrade) has validated this architecture at scale, demonstrated cube-by-cube light yield uniformity, SiPM dark-noise management, and the multi-axis fibre readout scheme. The collaboration can adopt the same 1 mm diameter Kuraray Y-11 WLS fibre, Hamamatsu S13360-1325PE SiPM specification, and the CITIROC or similar front-end ASIC chain with minimal R&D risk. This is critical for a phase upgrade on an experiment timescale.

### Key numbers
- Cube count: ~(180)(170)(55) ≈ 1.68 million cubes
- Readout channels: 3 faces × (180+170+55) directions × ~average 180 fibres per face side ≈ of order 12,000–15,000 SiPM channels (fibres grouped per row/column, not per cube)
- Spatial resolution: effectively 1 cm³ voxel, comfortably above the ~3 mm Molière radius concern for EM showers at these energies
- Vertex resolution: < 1 cm, sufficient to separate primary vertex from secondary interactions

---

## 2. Surrounding Thin-Wall Gas TPC Layer: Short-Drift Resistive Micromegas or µRWELL

### Recommendation
Instrument the four long faces of the cube-array box (two in x, two in y, leaving beam-entrance and beam-exit faces open to the upstream void and the existing TPCs respectively) with thin-gap (~5–8 cm drift) gas TPC modules using resistive Micromegas or µRWELL readout, operated in an Ar:CO₂:isobutane mixture.

### Justification

**High-angle muon momentum measurement.** A muon exiting the cube target at 60° with 500 MeV/c has a sagitta of only ~4 mm over 1 m in a 0.2 T field — marginal for momentum measurement by curvature alone using only the cube hit pattern. A thin TPC surrounding the cube volume provides a precise space-point just outside the target. Combined with the downstream main TPCs (which have already demonstrated sub-mm space-point resolution with micropattern readout), a track segment in the outer TPC constrains the exit angle to better than 1 mrad and gives an additional rigidity measurement lever arm. For muons that enter the return-yoke scintillator and are ranged out, this outer TPC provides the intermediate segment needed for clean track matching.

**Charge-sign determination for high-angle tracks.** For tracks that do not reach the main TPCs (exiting sideways into the return-yoke scintillator), charge sign must be determined from curvature within the available path length. The outer TPC layer, even with 5 cm drift, provides ~20 space points over the ~30–40 cm path in the magnet gap, giving σ(q/p)/(q/p) ≈ 15–20% at 500 MeV/c — adequate to discriminate µ⁻ from µ⁺ and reject the NC background at the level needed.

**Low material budget.** Resistive Micromegas or µRWELL detectors can be built with a total material budget of ~0.3–0.5% X₀ per module, which is essential here: the upstream face of the new target must not degrade photon conversion tagging for events whose photons enter from the interaction region, and additional scattering of the low-momentum protons (median 450 MeV/c, range ~24 cm in plastic) must be minimised.

**Why not a full additional TPC?** The 0.6 m depth of the available box is the binding constraint. A full-volume gas TPC with ~30 cm drift on each side plus field cage plus cathode would consume essentially the entire depth with no room for the active target mass needed for statistics. The thin-layer approach preserves target mass while adding tracking coverage.

---

## 3. SiPM Readout Upgrade: Common Tile Format with On-Detector Digitisation

### Recommendation
Adopt a common SiPM tile carrying 4 × 4 or 8 × 8 SiPMs with on-tile waveform discrimination (threshold + time-over-threshold) and serialised digital output over low-mass flex cable, replacing the current approach of routing analogue signals to off-detector electronics.

### Justification

**Channel count.** ~12,000–15,000 channels cannot be routed as individual analogue coaxial or twisted-pair lines without unacceptable cable mass and heat load inside the magnet volume. On-tile digitisation (as demonstrated by the WAGASCI and T2K SuperFGD collaborations using the CITIROC-1A ASIC or the TARGET ASIC family) reduces the cable plant to serial digital links, manageable within the magnet bore.

**Timing for neutron rejection and pile-up.** At a few-hundred-metre baseline with the beam spill structure typical of these experiments (spill width ~5 µs, bunch spacing ~O(100) ns), time-of-flight separation of neutron-induced recoils from primary vertex protons requires ~1 ns resolution at the channel level. Modern SiPM tiles with on-ASIC TDC achieve 500–800 ps timing resolution, sufficient for a ~30 cm spatial separation of a 300 MeV/c neutron scatter from the primary vertex.

**Dark-noise management.** At room temperature the SiPMs will have dark count rates of ~100–200 kcps per channel. The on-tile coincidence logic (requiring 2-of-N fired in a tile within a short window) reduces effective noise rates by >100×, which is essential to avoid fake hits contaminating the dE/dx measurement used for proton ranging.

---

## 4. Thin Lead-Converter Layer on the Upstream Face

### Recommendation
Instrument the upstream face of the new cube-array module with a single layer of 3 mm Pb converter (0.53 X₀) backed by a double-layer of scintillator strips (1 cm pitch), serving as a residual photon pre-tagger.

### Justification

The old photon-tagger section's primary physics function was identifying π⁰ → γγ events for NC background estimation. Removing it entirely would degrade NC π⁰ rejection. A single thin converter layer recovers the leading photon conversion signature (γ → e⁺e⁻ in Pb, detected as a pair of ionising tracks in the scintillator strips) with minimal material. At 0.53 X₀ the conversion probability per photon is ~40%, compared to the ~95% conversion provided by the full multi-layer tagger — but the cube array itself provides additional conversion probability for photons that enter the fiducial volume, since photons with energies above ~100 MeV have ~15–20 cm conversion length in polystyrene, meaning the 55 cm deep cube array provides ~30% additional conversion probability. The combined system retains ~55–60% photon tagging efficiency, which the analysis group must assess against their NC background requirements.

The scintillator strips in this layer should be oriented orthogonally (x and y) at 1 cm pitch and read out by the same SiPM+WLS fibre technology as the rest of the detector for channel uniformity and to avoid introducing a new technology.

---

## 5. Retain and Extend the Return-Yoke Scintillator for High-Angle Muon Ranging

### Recommendation
Add two additional scintillator planes to the return-yoke instrumentation on the upstream half of the magnet (covering the new target's z-position), increasing plane spacing from the current configuration to match the radiation length needed to range muons from the new target position.

### Justification

The new target is ~1.5–2 m further upstream than the existing tracking targets. Muons produced there at high angles (25% beyond 50°) that exit sideways now encounter a longer path through the return yoke before reaching the existing scintillator planes, but also a larger transverse displacement, potentially missing the instrumented region. Adding two planes on each side (four planes total, ~1.2 × 3.5 m each, 2 cm thick polystyrene scintillator with SiPM readout matching the existing system) at the upstream end of the return yoke closes this acceptance gap. The cost is modest (of order a few scintillator planes is straightforward), the technology is identical to what is already installed, and the alignment with existing reconstruction software is trivial.

---

## 6. What the Collaboration Should Not Do

**Do not deploy a liquid argon TPC in this space.** Despite superior performance, the cryogenic infrastructure, 0.6 m depth constraint making a drift volume too shallow for practical readout, and the commissioning risk on an upgrade timescale all argue against it.

**Do not use a water-target configuration as the primary new target.** The downstream target already provides carbon-to-water comparison. Duplicating it upstream adds no new information for the TKI programme, which needs clean CC reconstruction rather than nuclear target comparison at this stage. Hydrocarbon (polystyrene) is explicitly stated as acceptable.

**Do not increase the magnetic field.** Modifying the existing reused dipole to increase from 0.2 T would require a magnet rewind or replacement, incompatible with an upgrade schedule. Momentum measurement by ranging (which the cube geometry enables down to ~200 MeV/c protons) is superior to curvature measurement at the relevant momenta in this field.

---

|---|---|---|
| Primary active target | 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cube array, 3-axis WLS fibre + SiPM readout | Full angular acceptance; proton ranging; established technology |

Replace the P0D with a **3D-segmented plastic scintillator cube detector** optimized for large-angle tracking and low-momentum threshold.

**2. Readout Technology**

# Hardware Upgrades for Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## 1. **3D Tracking Active Target System**

**Technology: Time Projection Chamber (TPC) with resistive or pixelated readout**

**Why:**
- **4π angular acceptance**: TPC provides continuous 3D tracking essential for reconstructing muons at all angles, including backward-going and perpendicular tracks (required for ≥25% efficiency at all angles)
- **Low material budget**: Gas target minimizes multiple scattering, crucial for short, low-energy proton tracks
- **Vertex resolution**: Excellent spatial resolution (~1 mm) needed to distinguish interaction vertices from secondary interactions
- **dE/dx measurement**: Particle identification capability to separate protons from pions/other particles at all angles

**Alternative consideration:** Fine-grained plastic scintillator tracker (e.g., 1 cm³ cubes with fiber readout), but inferior momentum resolution and higher hydrogen content

## 2. **Hydrogen-Lean Target Gas Mixture**

**Technology: Argon-based gas (e.g., Ar:CO₂:CF₄ 90:5:5 or pure Ar with small quench gas)**

**Why:**
- **Hydrogen constraint**: Must keep H nucleons <20% of total target nucleons to maintain model validity
- CH₄ additions would provide hydrogen but violate this constraint
- Argon provides: adequate drift properties, sufficient density, known cross-sections
- **Trade-off management**: Some CH₄ could be added (up to ~3-4%) if proton detection efficiency gains outweigh hydrogen fraction concerns

## 3. **High-Granularity Electronic Readout System**

**Technology: Micropattern gas detector readout (MicroMegas or GEM foils) with fine-pitch pad/strip structure (3-5 mm pitch)**

**Why:**
- **Short track detection**: 60 MeV protons have ranges of only ~3-5 cm in atmospheric pressure argon; need mm-scale position resolution
- **Hit density**: At 0.7 GeV neutrino energy, expect complex multi-track final states requiring excellent pattern recognition
- **Timing resolution**: ~100 ns timing separates beam-related events from cosmics
- **Low-Z materials**: Minimize interactions before downstream tracker

## 4. **Enhanced Downstream Gas Tracker Modules**

**Technology: Additional drift chamber or straw tube planes with closer spacing (10-15 cm between planes instead of typical 30-50 cm)**

**Why:**
- **Forward proton tracking**: Many recoil protons go forward but stop before exiting the magnet
- **Momentum resolution**: Better lever arm for tracks that don't traverse full tracker length
- **Charge-sign determination**: Critical for separating μ⁺ from μ⁻ in the 0.15 T field

## 5. **Active Target Outer Electromagnetic Calorimeter Shell**

**Technology: Lead-scintillator sampling calorimeter or resistive plate chambers (RPC) with lead absorbers surrounding target volume**

**Why:**
- **π⁰ detection**: Essential for separating charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) from CC-resonant events
- **Photon energy measurement**: Constrain event kinematics and reduce backgrounds
- **Containment**: Identify events where particles escape active target before stopping
- **Thickness**: ~10 radiation lengths (5-6 cm Pb equivalent)

## 6. **Precision Monitoring and Calibration Systems**

**Technology:**
- UV laser tracks or radioactive wire sources for TPC calibration
- Temperature/pressure sensors (0.1°C, 0.1 mbar precision)
- Gas circulation and purification system with O₂/H₂O monitoring (<10 ppm)

**Why:**
- **Drift velocity stability**: 0.1% drift velocity changes alter momentum scale
- **Low-energy threshold**: 60 MeV proton detection requires stable gain and minimal electron attachment
- **Long-term operation**: Maintain calibration over multi-year run

## 7. **Upgraded Data Acquisition and Trigger System**

**Technology: Streaming readout with software triggering, ~1 GB/s sustained rate**

**Why:**
- **Triggerless operation**: Beam spill (~10 μs) contains multiple interactions; read everything
- **Cosmic ray calibration**: Continuous readout enables in-situ tracker alignment and dE/dx calibration
- **Efficiency**: Avoid hardware trigger biases against unusual topologies (e.g., backward tracks)

## 8. **Target Region Support Infrastructure**

**Technology: Low-mass carbon-fiber support structure and thin field cage**

**Why:**
- **Material budget**: Minimize interactions outside active volume
- **Magnetic field compatibility**: Non-magnetic materials in 0.15 T field
- **Structural integrity**: Support ~1000 L gas volume with minimal deflection

## Budget Priority Ranking:
1. TPC with MicroMegas/GEM readout (core requirement)
2. DAQ and readout electronics (enables TPC operation)
3. Gas system and monitoring (maintains performance)
4. Outer calorimeter (critical for physics)
5. Enhanced downstream tracking (improves forward acceptance)

This upgrade transforms a passive target region into a comprehensive near detector meeting all stated physics requirements.

# ND280 Upgrade: Hardware Components for the Proposal

The current inner detector cannot deliver kinematically complete events, for three reasons:

- **FGD bars all lie perpendicular to the beam.** Tracks at large angles run along a single bar or within one layer, so they are poorly reconstructed.
- **The TPCs sit only downstream.** Particles leaving at more than about 50° never reach them, so they get no momentum or charge measurement.
- **Low-momentum protons are lost.** A proton of a few hundred MeV/c crosses only a few 1 cm layers and is often missed.

With about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons above 50°, these losses are large. They are a major part of the gap between the present ~6% systematic uncertainty and the ~4% that T2K-II needs.

The proposal should include the four items below, placed in the region freed by removing the P0D.

## 1. Super Fine-Grained Detector (SuperFGD): fully active 3D-segmented scintillator target

**Technology**
- Plastic scintillator (polystyrene) cubes, 1 × 1 × 1 cm³, with a reflective surface etch.
- Each cube has three orthogonal holes, threaded by wavelength-shifting fibres along x, y and z.
- Each fibre is read out by an MPPC, consistent with the rest of ND280.
- For the ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box, this is roughly 192 × 182 × 56 cubes, about 2 million cubes and about 2 t of target.
- The three-view readout needs only about 56,000 channels (192·182 + 192·56 + 182·56), not 2 million.

**Why**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three orthogonal projections give true 3D reconstruction at any angle, including high-angle and backward tracks.
- **Low proton threshold.** Fine segmentation and a fully active volume, with no passive material, allow protons down to about 300 MeV/c to be tracked and identified. That threshold sits well below the ~450 MeV/c median, which matters for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI).
- **Momentum by range for most protons.** A 900 MeV/c proton (about 360 MeV kinetic energy) ranges roughly 1 m in plastic, so the ~94% below that value mostly stop in the target. Range and dE/dx then give their momentum and PID. The ~6% above 900 MeV/c, and the muons, exit into the TPCs.
- **Hydrocarbon target.** CH is acceptable here, and FGD2 keeps the carbon/water comparison.
- **Neutron tagging.** Fast timing, together with the ToF detectors, also allows neutron detection by time of flight. This adds to TKI and energy-reconstruction studies.

## 2. Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs): one above and one below the SuperFGD

**Technology**
- Gas TPCs inside the 0.2 T field, using the same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ (95:3:2) mixture.
- Readout by **resistive (encapsulated) bulk Micromegas**. A resistive layer spreads the charge, which gives:
  - good spatial resolution with larger pads, so fewer channels;
  - intrinsic spark protection.
- Lightweight field cage made of thin composite or laminate walls, to minimise dead material between the SuperFGD and the gas volume.
- Updated front-end electronics, such as AFTER/AGET-type ASIC readout.

**Why**
- High-angle muons and the energetic protons that exit the SuperFGD need curvature-based momentum, charge sign and dE/dx PID.
- The existing downstream TPCs cannot see these tracks.
- Together, the SuperFGD and HA-TPCs give near-4π coverage of the muon and the leading proton.

## 3. Time-of-Flight (ToF) system enclosing the new target and TPCs

**Technology**
- Six planes of long plastic scintillator bars, read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Target time resolution of about 100–150 ps.

**Why**
- **Track direction.** Timing separates forward-going from backward-going tracks, which is important now that high-angle and backward particles are accepted.
- **Background rejection.** It rejects particles entering from interactions in the magnet, the ECals or outside the detector, which reduces out-of-fiducial-volume background.
- **PID.** It adds particle identification, such as proton/pion/muon separation at low momentum and electron/muon separation.
- **Neutrons.** It supports neutron time-of-flight measurements.

## 4. Readout, trigger and integration upgrades

**Technology**
- New front-end boards for the ~56k SuperFGD MPPCs, CITIROC-type, with sub-ns timing and wide dynamic range.
- Integration with the existing ND280 DAQ, clock and trigger.
- A new support and mechanical frame in the P0D region.
- Calibration systems, such as LED light injection and cosmic triggers.

**Why**
- The new subdetectors need timing precision and channel counts beyond the legacy electronics.
- Good timing is essential for direction finding, PID and neutron tagging.
- Mechanical integration is needed to keep dead material low in the magnet volume.

## Retained detectors

The following stay in place: the downstream FGD1, FGD2 and their three TPCs, the ECals, and the SMRD. FGD2 in particular provides the water target for carbon-to-water comparison.

## Combined effect

Together, the upgrades give:
- full polar-angle acceptance for muons and protons;
- a lower proton threshold;
- neutron tagging;
- better background rejection.

This is what TKI-based, kinematically complete CC measurements require. It is the route to cutting flux and cross-section systematic uncertainties from ~6% to the ~4% that T2K-II needs.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## Context and Constraints

Before proposing upgrades, the key physics requirements can be summarised:

- **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles** (including 90° and backward), within a ~6.5 m long magnet with only 0.15 T field
- **Proton reconstruction down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** (range ~3 cm in plastic, ~1 cm in iron)
- **Hydrogen content ≤2% of target nucleons** (rules out hydrocarbon-dominant materials as primary target)
- **Peak flux ~0.7 GeV** means typical final states: one muon, one or two protons, a few pions; quasi-elastic and resonance production dominate

---

## Upgrade 1: Straw-Tube Tracker (STT) as Active Target

**Technology:** Thin-walled aluminised-Mylar straw tubes (~1 cm diameter, ~0.3 mm wall) filled with Ar/CO₂ or Ar/CO₂/CF₄, arranged in alternating X-Y-U stereo layers, interspersed with passive radiator/target panels.

**Physics motivation:**

The requirement that hydrogen nucleons be ≤2% of target nucleons is the dominant constraint on material choice. A pure polystyrene or CH₂ slab would be ~15% hydrogen by nucleon count — roughly seven times too high. An STT with graphite or aluminium passive plates can tune the hydrogen fraction precisely. The straw gas itself (argon-based) contributes negligible hydrogen. Passive panels of graphite (density ~1.7 g/cm³) dominate the nucleon count; graphite contains zero hydrogen. By adjusting the ratio of graphite-to-gas volume one can hold the hydrogen fraction comfortably below 2% while maintaining a low-Z, low-density active volume.

Low density (~0.1–0.15 g/cm³ effective) also means that a 60 MeV kinetic energy proton (range ~35 mm in water-equivalent material) travels several centimetres of active detector before stopping, giving enough hits (~4–6 straws) for a reconstructed stub. Single straw position resolution of ~150–200 μm provides good angular and dE/dx measurement; dE/dx from the Bragg-peak region distinguishes stopping protons from pions at low momentum. The fine granularity also recovers backward-going and large-angle tracks because there is no dead region between radiator slabs: hits appear in both upstream and downstream straw layers surrounding each graphite panel, and the track-finding algorithm has no intrinsic directionality requirement.

---

## Upgrade 2: Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) or Scintillator-Strip Muon Catcher Inserted into the Downstream Iron Return Yoke

**Technology:** 2 cm-thick iron absorber plates alternating with 1 cm plastic scintillator strips (or glass-electrode RPCs, 2 mm gap) in X-Y configuration, filling the downstream and lateral yoke regions of the existing dipole. Scintillator strips read out with SiPMs via wavelength-shifting fibres.

**Physics motivation:**

With only 0.15 T and a 6.5 m long field volume, a muon perpendicular to the beam (p_T = p) exits the upstream or downstream face with almost no bending (sagitta ≈ 0 for a purely transverse track). Such tracks cannot be momentum-measured by the downstream gas drift chambers, which see only the projected forward angle. A muon catcher embedded in the lateral yoke captures side-exiting tracks: the iron provides range measurement (a 200 MeV/c muon has a range ~15 cm in iron, well within a 30–40 cm thick lateral catcher), and strip readout gives the position for a range-momentum conversion. For backward-going muons the same catcher on the upstream face serves analogously.

The 25% minimum efficiency requirement at all angles means the solid angle coverage must be nearly 4π. The downstream drift chambers alone subtend perhaps ±15° from the beam axis with good efficiency; without the lateral catcher the efficiency at 60–90° may be near zero. Even a relatively crude range measurement (10% momentum resolution from range) is adequate for the cross-section analyses anticipated from a neutrino beam peaked at 0.7 GeV, where the neutrino energy reconstruction from muon kinematics alone requires only ~10–15% muon momentum resolution.

The scintillator-strip option (3 cm × 1 cm strips) rather than RPCs is preferred if there is a modest rate from cosmic rays and beam-related backgrounds because it offers intrinsic timing (~1 ns) that can suppress out-of-spill backgrounds and provide a trigger.

---

## Upgrade 3: High-Granularity Plastic Scintillator Cube Array ("SuperCube") in a Thin-Wall Inner Region

**Technology:** 1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes individually read out by three orthogonal WLS fibres per cube (X, Y, Z), each fibre read by a SiPM. Cubes are assembled into modules of ~10 × 10 × 10 cm³ to ~25 × 25 × 25 cm³.

**Physics motivation:**

This addresses the short-track proton requirement most directly. A 60 MeV kinetic energy proton stops in roughly 1.3 cm of plastic scintillator (density ~1.03 g/cm³). With 1 cm³ cubes a stopping proton deposits energy in 1–3 cubes, which is enough for a 3D position measurement (from the three-fibre readout scheme) and a rough direction from the energy deposition pattern and Bragg peak. This is fundamentally impossible in a gas tracker for such short ranges.

However, plastic scintillator is CH material (C₈H₈ for polystyrene), contributing roughly 7.7% hydrogen by nucleon count — far above the 2% cap. Therefore the scintillator cube array **cannot** be the primary target mass. Instead it is deployed as a thin active layer (~1–2 radiation lengths, perhaps 10–15 cm deep along the beam) lining the inner walls of each STT module, acting as a vertex detector and short-track catcher. Its fractional contribution to total target nucleons is kept small: if 90% of the target mass is graphite STT panels and 10% is scintillator, the blended hydrogen fraction is approximately 0.10 × 7.7% ≈ 0.77%, safely below 2%.

The 3D cube readout eliminates the left-right ambiguity intrinsic to wire-based tracking, which is especially important for low-multiplicity events where pattern recognition is hardest. The timing resolution (~1 ns per cube) allows time-of-flight separation of protons from pions at low momentum (at 300 MeV/c, Δt over 20 cm is ~0.5 ns between p and π), complementing the dE/dx from the STT.

---

## Upgrade 4: Upstream Veto and Beam-Muon Tagger

**Technology:** Two planes of 2 cm × 2 cm plastic scintillator bars with SiPM readout, one plane immediately upstream of the active target, one surrounding it laterally, with ~1 ns time resolution.

**Physics motivation:**

At a near detector 410 m from the target, the neutrino beam is accompanied by a substantial flux of beam-related muons (from pion decay before the absorber) and by neutrino interactions in the upstream material (shielding, cryogenics, structural steel) that can send charged particles into the active volume. Any such particle entering from outside mimics a neutrino interaction vertex in the active target.

The veto planes tag entering charged tracks. Combined with the cube and STT timing, they also reject events where a slow (out-of-time) cosmic ray overlaps with a beam spill. For the hydrogen-subtraction analysis in particular, a contamination of "external" events that fake a vertex in the hydrogen-rich scintillator region would bias the cross-section ratio between hydrogen and heavier nuclei, undermining the entire physics case.

The beam-muon tagger on the upstream face additionally allows the detector to trigger on beam muons for alignment and calibration, providing a data-driven intercalibration of STT channel gains and drift velocities from a source that illuminates the whole detector uniformly.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Goal |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Straw-tube tracker with graphite panels | Low-H active target; proton stubs ≥60 MeV; 4π track finding |
| 2 | Scintillator-strip/RPC muon catcher in yoke | Muon efficiency at 90° and backward angles |
| 3 | 1 cm³ scintillator cube vertex detector | 3D short-track proton reconstruction; Δt p/π separation |
| 4 | Scintillator veto planes | Reject entering tracks; protect hydrogen-subtraction analysis |

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades: Replacing the Upstream Photon-Tagging Section

## The problem the upgrade must fix

The current tracking targets have two built-in limits.

**Limited angular acceptance**
- The target bars all lie perpendicular to the beam, and the gas TPCs sit only upstream and downstream of them.
- A track at more than about 50° crosses few bar layers. It also misses the TPCs or crosses them nearly parallel to the drift and readout planes.
- At this beam that is about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons.
- Backward-going tracks can be confused with forward ones without timing information.

**High proton threshold**
- With 9.6 mm bars read in alternating 2D x/y views, short proton tracks are hard to reconstruct.
- The proton-tracking threshold is around 450 MeV/c, which is the median of the leading-proton spectrum. Roughly half the protons are therefore lost, so transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) measurements are statistics- and acceptance-limited.

**The goal**
- Near-4π acceptance for both muons and protons.
- A proton threshold of about 300 MeV/c (kinetic energy of order 50 MeV).
- Unambiguous track direction.

Together these support reducing the systematic uncertainty from about 6% to about 4%.

## 1. Highly segmented 3D scintillator target ("SuperFGD"-type) — the new active target

**Technology**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, roughly 192 × 184 × 56, filling the ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- About 2 t of CH, roughly double one existing target.
- Each cube has a reflective chemical-etch coating and three orthogonal holes.
- Wavelength-shifting fibres run along x, y and z, about 56,000 channels in total.
- Each fibre is read at one end by an SiPM (MPPC), matching the existing photosensor technology.

**Why this choice**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Every track is seen in three orthogonal 2D projections, so the 3D reconstruction is isotropic. High-angle and backward muons and protons are reconstructed as well as forward ones.
- **Lower proton threshold.**
  - Fine 1 cm granularity resolves short tracks: a 300 MeV/c proton travels only a few centimetres.
  - This brings the threshold down to about 300 MeV/c, capturing most of the 450 MeV/c-median spectrum.
  - Good dE/dx per cube gives proton/pion separation and resolves the vertex region.
- **Fully active hydrocarbon.**
  - The large active mass adds statistics.
  - Hydrocarbon is acceptable for this programme, and the downstream water-layer target remains for the C/water comparison.
- **Neutron detection.** Sub-ns timing plus fine granularity allows neutron detection by time-of-flight to isolated hits. This can complete the kinematics of antineutrino events.

## 2. Two High-Angle TPCs (above and below the new target)

**Technology**
- Gas TPCs filled with the same argon-based "T2K gas" mixture, sharing the existing gas system.
- Lightweight composite field cages (thin laminate with a solid insulator) to minimise dead material and cracks.
- Readout planes tiled with encapsulated **resistive Micromegas** (resistive anode, ERAM type).
  - Charge spreading across pads gives good spatial resolution with fewer, larger pads.
  - The resistive layer protects against sparks.
- Low-noise front-end electronics derived from the existing TPC ones.

**Why this choice**
- **Momentum and charge for high-angle tracks.** High-angle muons, and the proton tail above about 900 MeV/c (about 6%), escape the scintillator cube target. The 0.2 T field in the HA-TPCs measures their momentum and charge by curvature.
- **Particle identification.** dE/dx in the gas gives PID for these tracks.
- **Closing the acceptance gap.** Together with the existing downstream TPCs, this gives momentum and charge measurement over nearly the full solid angle. That is essential for TKI and for the angular phase space the far detector samples.

## 3. Time-of-Flight panels enclosing the new target and HA-TPCs

**Technology**
- Six planes of long plastic scintillator bars, read out at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Time resolution of about 100–150 ps.

**Why this choice**
- **Track direction.** Timing separates forward from backward tracks, rejecting out-of-fiducial and backward-entering backgrounds such as muons from interactions in the magnet.
- **Extra PID.** Timing adds particle identification, for example e/μ/p separation at low momentum.
- **Cosmic-ray trigger.** The panels provide a cosmic trigger for calibration.

## 4. Supporting systems

- **Electronics and DAQ.** Front-end boards (CITIROC-type ASICs) are needed for the ~56k new SiPM channels, with good timing and dynamic range. They must be integrated into the existing DAQ and clock distribution.
- **Calibration and monitoring.** LED or light-injection systems for the SiPMs, and laser or cathode calibration for the HA-TPCs.
- **Mechanical integration.** A support frame for the cube target plus HA-TPCs and ToF in the former photon-tagging space, inside the reused magnet. Cabling must not compromise the surrounding lead-scintillator calorimeters or the yoke scintillator planes.

## Summary

| Upgrade | Technology | Main physics gain |
|---|---|---|
| 3D target | 1 cm³ scintillator cubes, 3-axis WLS fibres + SiPM | Isotropic tracking; proton threshold about 300 MeV/c; neutron timing |
| HA-TPCs ×2 | Argon gas, composite field cage, resistive Micromegas | p/charge/PID for high-angle μ and high-momentum p |
| ToF | Scintillator bars, double-ended SiPM, ~100–150 ps | Track direction, background rejection, PID |
| Electronics/DAQ | New SiPM front-ends | Read out ~56k+ channels with timing |

Together these make charged-current events kinematically complete over nearly 4π. That is the route from about 6% to about 4% systematic uncertainty.
