# Design Review Recommendation: New Active Target for the Upstream Section

## Executive Summary

The 6%→4% systematic goal requires kinematically complete CC event reconstruction (muon + leading proton) in a constrained ~2.0×1.9×0.6 m envelope. The core challenge is threefold: (1) reconstructing large-angle tracks (>50° for 25% of muons, 35% of protons) within a shallow longitudinal depth; (2) tracking low-momentum protons that will range out in centimetres of dense material; and (3) maintaining sufficient fiducial mass on a hydrocarbon target to accumulate statistics. I recommend a **SuperFGD-style 3D segmented scintillator cube active target** as the primary detector element, surrounded by a thin time-of-flight layer, with no change to the downstream TPCs or magnet.

---

## 1. Primary Active Target: 3D Segmented Scintillator Cube Array

### Technology
Extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, **1.0 cm × 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm**, each pierced by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres (X, Y, Z axes), read out by **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)** at the fibre ends. This is the SuperFGD architecture, now technically proven.

### Geometry
- Fill the available box to approximately **190 cm × 185 cm × 56 cm**
- Instrumented volume: ~190×185×56 layers = approximately **190 × 185 × 56 ≈ 1,970,200 cubes**, call it ~2.0 million cubes at ~1 g/cm³ effective density
- Fiducial mass: with 2 cm dead-edge exclusion on all faces, approximately **186×181×52 cm fiducial volume ≈ 1.75 × 10⁶ cm³ ≈ 1.75 t** of active polystyrene (C₈H₈), a usable hydrocarbon target mass

### Justification

**Large-angle track containment.** The 0.6 m longitudinal dimension is the binding constraint. A track leaving at 70° to the beam travels only ~0.6/cos70° ≈ 1.75 m of path before exiting longitudinally, but in a fully 3D-sensitive volume every cube it crosses generates a hit. With 1 cm granularity, a 90° transverse proton at 450 MeV/c (range in polystyrene ~18 cm) traverses ~18 cubes and is fully contained laterally within the 190 cm transverse width. The conventional planar x/y scintillator bar architecture used downstream (9.6×9.6 mm bars in 30 alternating layers) has a ~2-layer stereo ambiguity and cannot reconstruct large-angle tracks without long longitudinal lever arms; the 3D cube geometry eliminates this entirely because each cube is a space point.

**Low-momentum proton tracking.** The leading proton momentum median of 450 MeV/c corresponds to a kinetic energy of ~100 MeV, range in polystyrene ~18 cm: fully contained. Even the 94th-percentile protons at 900 MeV/c (T_p ≈ 430 MeV, range ~160 cm) are largely contained within the 185 cm transverse dimension if they exit sideways, or will enter the downstream TPC if forward. The 1 cm cube size means dE/dx can be measured cube-by-cube: Bragg peak identification distinguishes protons from pions at low momentum, directly reducing the systematic uncertainty on proton identification that currently feeds into the 6% total. This capability is absent in the existing planar bar targets.

**Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI).** TKI variables (δpT, δαT, δφT) require both the muon and leading proton 3-momenta. The 3D reconstruction from three orthogonal fibre views gives a genuine 3D track rather than the 2-view projective reconstruction of the planar system; this is essential when both final-state particles can exit at large angles in uncorrelated azimuthal directions.

**SiPM readout continuity.** The existing detector already uses WLS-fibre + SiPM readout universally; the collaboration retains identical photodetector procurement, QC procedures, and front-end electronics (e.g., CITIROC or equivalent ASIC). This is a practical cost and risk control argument.

---

## 2. Thin Time-of-Flight Boundary Layer

### Technology
A single layer of **fast plastic scintillator paddles** (e.g., EJ-228 or BC-418, ~2 ns rise time), 5 mm thick, tiling all six faces of the cube array, read out by SiPMs at both ends for time and longitudinal position.

### Geometry
- ~24 paddles per face at manageable size (e.g., 20 cm × full face length per paddle)
- Total added material: 5 mm polystyrene, radiation length ~86 cm, so X₀ contribution < 0.6%—negligible

### Justification

**Muon–pion separation.** At 0.6 GeV beam energy, forward muons exiting the cube array and entering the first downstream TPC are well tracked there. However, large-angle muons that exit the cube array sideways or backward (25% at >50°) may not reach the TPC. A TOF boundary layer with ~200–300 ps resolution (achievable with EJ-228 + SiPM + waveform digitiser) provides a cross-check on particle velocity. Combined with the range from cube-counting, this gives an independent β measurement: for a 300 MeV/c pion vs. muon, Δβ ≈ 0.013, corresponding to ~40 ps difference over a 30 cm path—marginal but nonzero. More importantly, the TOF layer flags whether a track **exits** the active volume (through-going) versus **stops** inside (contained), which is the first-order decision for momentum reconstruction strategy (range vs. curvature).

**Veto for external backgrounds.** Sand muons and secondary neutrons entering from outside are tagged by the TOF layer firing without an associated cube-array vertex, allowing clean rejection without relying on upstream detectors that are being removed.

---

## 3. Retention of the Existing Downstream TPC–Target System

### No hardware change recommended here.

The three argon gas TPCs with micro-pattern readout (likely Micromegas or GEM) provide the highest-resolution tracking for forward muons above ~200 MeV/c, and the downstream water-layer plastic target is explicitly retained for C/water comparisons. The new cube array feeds muons forward into TPC1 exactly as the previous plastic targets did; the interface geometry is unchanged.

---

## 4. Magnet Return-Yoke Scintillator: Minor Addition

### Technology
No structural change, but **extend the existing yoke scintillator trigger logic** to form a dedicated large-angle muon "range stack" trigger that is coincident with a cube-array vertex. This is firmware/DAQ work, not hardware procurement, but should be on the construction scope list.

### Justification
The 25% of muons at >50° that do not enter the TPC will range into the return yoke scintillator. These tracks are currently available but may not be efficiently triggered and reconstructed for TKI analyses. At 0.6 GeV, a 50° muon has ~350 MeV/c transverse momentum; it will traverse roughly 50–80 cm of return-yoke iron before stopping, well within the existing scintillator coverage. Including these muons directly increases the kinematically complete event sample by a potentially significant fraction, reducing the statistical component of the systematic extrapolation.

---

## 5. What Is Explicitly Not Recommended

| Option | Reason Rejected |
|---|---|
| Liquid argon TPC in the upstream slot | 0.6 m longitudinal depth is too shallow for LAr drift; HV, cryogenics, and purification infrastructure cannot fit; and the existing gaseous TPCs downstream already provide LAr-class resolution for forward tracks |
| Water Cherenkov target | Below ~200 MeV/c proton threshold, Cherenkov light is absent; the leading proton median of 450 MeV/c is near threshold and the 35% large-angle fraction would exit without sufficient photon yield for vector reconstruction |
| High-pressure gaseous TPC filling the box | Technically viable but: pressure vessel in the existing magnet geometry, large X₀, and poor performance for the sub-100 MeV/c short-range protons; also the existing downstream TPCs are already argon-based and adding a third gas species introduces cross-calibration uncertainty |
| Emulsion cloud chamber | Excellent spatial resolution but offline analysis is too slow for the statistical programme required at this beam intensity; also incompatible with real-time trigger requirements |

---

## 6. Summary Table

| Component | Technology | Key Specification | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary active target | 3D scintillator cubes | 1 cm³, polystyrene, 3-axis WLS fibre + SiPM | Kinematically complete CC, large-angle & low-p proton tracking |
| Boundary layer | Fast plastic scintillator paddles | 5 mm EJ-228, SiPM both ends, ~250 ps resolution | TOF, containment tagging, external veto |
| Downstream system | No change | — | Forward muon tracking, C/water comparison |
| Yoke scintillator trigger | Firmware update | Coincidence with cube-array vertex | Large-angle muon recovery |

---

## 7. Expected Systematic Impact

The 6%→4% target requires roughly halving the dominant flux×cross-section correlated uncertainties. The cube-array target contributes through three mechanisms: (i) TKI measurements on hydrocarbon directly constrain nuclear momentum smearing, the dominant shape uncertainty; (ii) dE/dx Bragg-peak proton ID reduces the charged-pion background contamination in the leading-proton sample, currently a ~1–2% effect; (iii) improved large-angle muon acceptance reduces the angular acceptance correction, which currently relies on extrapolation from the planar-bar detector's limited solid-angle coverage. Together these are consistent with the collaboration's internal sensitivity studies on SuperFGD-class detectors, and the choice of a proven, productionised technology (the SuperFGD for ND280 is a direct precedent) substantially reduces schedule risk relative to novel alternatives.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Kestrel Flats Near-Detector Active Target

## 1. The hydrogen limit rules out a scintillator target

The obvious choice for a 4π active target is a finely segmented plastic-scintillator detector, such as a cube-based design. However, polystyrene (CH)ₙ has 1 hydrogen nucleon out of 13 per CH unit, which is about **7.7% hydrogen**. That is nearly four times the 2% limit. Any hydrocarbon-based target (scintillator, CH₄-rich gas, water) fails for the same reason.

The far detector has no hydrogen, and argon is the likely far-detector nucleus. Matching the nucleus would also remove most nuclear-model extrapolation, so the target should be **argon**. Its hydrogen fraction is essentially 0%, as long as any quencher gas or plastic structures inside the fiducial volume are negligible.

## 2. Recommended active target: a modular, pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC

**Geometry.** The cryostat must fit within the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region.
- Use a thin-walled, vacuum-insulated aluminium or stainless cryostat, with about 10–15 cm of insulation and walls.
- This leaves an active volume of roughly **2.3 × 2.0 × 0.7 m ≈ 3.2 m³**, about **4.5 t of LAr**.
- The fiducial mass is about 3 t.

**Event rate.** At 410 m from a sub-GeV beam, this mass gives a high event rate, so pile-up is the main design driver. Two mitigations follow:
- Split the volume into about 4–6 optically isolated modules, each with a short drift (≤ 50 cm, so drift time is ≈ 300 µs).
- Use 3D **pixel readout** (about 4 mm pitch) instead of wire planes. This removes wire ambiguities for tracks at any angle, which matters for tracks perpendicular to the beam and for tracks parallel to a wire plane.
- Add fast light detection, with ns timing, per module. This assigns each track to its interaction and time, gives t₀, and provides the direction (forward or backward) of exiting tracks.

**Proton threshold check.** The CSDA range of a 60 MeV proton in argon is about 3.9 g/cm², or roughly **2.8 cm** in LAr. With 4 mm pixels that is about 7 space points, plus a strong Bragg peak. This is enough for identification by dE/dx versus range, and to measure kinetic energy by range at any angle. Protons down to about 40 MeV remain usable.

**Muon direction coverage.** The LAr images tracks isotropically, so efficiency does not collapse at 90° or backward, unlike planar trackers. Momentum is measured three ways:
- **Contained muons:** by range.
- **Partially contained muons:** by multiple Coulomb scattering, with about 10–15% resolution over 0.5–1 m of track.
- **Exiting muons:** by the external trackers below, which also give charge.

## 3. Surrounding tracking for exiting muons and charge sign

A 0.7 GeV muon has a range of about 3 m in LAr, so most muons exit. A muon at 90° exits through the side faces after about 1 m. The 0.15 T field cannot give a useful sagitta over 1 m of LAr, so charge and momentum need gas tracking outside the cryostat:

- **Downstream:** keep the existing drift chambers for forward tracks.
- **Lateral (top, bottom, left, right):** add thin gas TPCs or drift-chamber modules between the cryostat and the magnet, along the length of the target region and extending downstream. These measure the curvature, and hence charge and momentum, of high-angle tracks.
- **Upstream face:** add a tracker plane so backward-going muons are measured.

Lightweight construction for these trackers is acceptable: hydrogen outside the fiducial volume does not enter the target-nucleon budget.

**Timing.** Fit the outer surfaces of the target region with thin scintillator time-of-flight panels, with about 100–150 ps resolution. Combined with the LAr light t₀, these give unambiguous forward versus backward direction. They also veto entering backgrounds: muons from interactions in the magnet, the cryostat or upstream rock.

The goal is at least 25% muon efficiency at every angle. A full-geometry simulation should confirm this, especially for tracks near 90° that exit through gaps between trackers.

## 4. Control of hydrogen and dead material

- Keep plastics (light guides, cable insulation, field-cage supports) out of the fiducial volume. Budget their mass explicitly against the 2%.
- Use pure argon with no organic dopant.
- Reject interactions in the cryostat walls with a fiducial cut of a few cm. The 3D vertex resolution of a few mm makes this efficient.
- Measure out-of-fiducial backgrounds with an argon-filled versus empty-volume comparison, or with sidebands.

## 5. Fallback option: a high-pressure gaseous argon TPC

A high-pressure gas TPC (about 10 bar, Ar with a few % CH₄ or CO₂-based quencher) would give the lowest proton thresholds (≪ 60 MeV) and excellent charge and momentum measurement in the 0.15 T field.

Its drawbacks are mass and hydrogen. The target mass would be only about 80–100 kg. Hydrogen stays below 2% of nucleons only if the CH₄ fraction is kept to a few % at most, or if a CO₂-based quencher is used instead. It could serve as a complementary low-threshold sample, but LAr is the primary recommendation for statistics.

## 6. Summary of upgrades

1. Replace the target region with a **modular pixel-readout LArTPC** (about 4.5 t) in a thin cryostat. This gives 0% hydrogen and the same nucleus as an argon far detector.
2. Add **fast light detection** per module for timing and pile-up separation.
3. Add **lateral and upstream gas trackers** inside the magnet for charge and momentum of high-angle and backward muons.
4. Add **ToF panels** enclosing the target for direction and background vetoes.
5. Integrate cryogenics compatible with the warm magnet, and keep a strict hydrogenous-material budget.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Summary of Constraints Driving Technology Choices

Before specifying hardware, let me be explicit about what constrains the choices:

- **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles including 90° and backward** → requires a fully 3D-sensitive volume with no dead angular regions; a purely downstream-instrumented target fails
- **Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** → range ~3 cm in water, ~1.4 cm in iron; requires fine granularity and low-Z material to keep tracks measurable
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of nucleons** → limits how much CH₂, water, or hydrocarbon scintillator you can use; pushes toward heavier admixtures
- **Volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m** → roughly 5.4 m³, manageable but not trivial
- **Sits inside existing warm dipole at 0.15 T** → rules out technologies with performance strongly degraded by magnetic fields (some photosensors); favors tracking technologies that benefit from the field for sign determination

---

## Proposed Active Target Architecture: Modular Liquid Argon + Scintillator Sandwich

I propose a **segmented sandwich design** rather than a monolithic detector, for reasons explained below.

---

## Module 1: Upstream 60% of Target Volume — High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC with Resistive Micromegas Readout

**Dimensions:** 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.54 m along beam

### Technology: High-Pressure Gaseous Argon Time Projection Chamber (HPGAr-TPC)

**Why this specific choice:**

A gaseous TPC at ~10 bar argon gives you:
- **Low density (~18 kg/m³)** so a 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has a range of roughly 25 cm — easily reconstructed in 3D
- **Full 4π angular acceptance** — the drift field is along one axis but ionization is collected from tracks at all angles; a 90° or backward muon still leaves a continuous ionization trail
- **dE/dx particle identification** at the few-percent level, distinguishing protons from pions from muons on a track-by-track basis
- **Sub-mm spatial resolution** achievable with Micromegas pads

**Specific readout: Resistive Micromegas**

The Micromegas (Micro-MEsh Gaseous Structure) planes use a resistive anode to spread charge and suppress discharge, crucial in an argon environment with potential for high-gain operation. Use a **2D strip readout** with:
- Strip pitch: **1.0 mm** in both x and y projections on each readout plane
- Readout planes at both ends of the drift volume (upstream and downstream faces) to handle tracks parallel to the drift direction
- Drift field: ~200 V/cm, drift velocity ~6 cm/µs in Ar:CO₂ (90:10) at 10 bar
- Maximum drift length: 54 cm → maximum drift time ~90 µs, manageable with the beam spill structure of a neutrino beam

**Structural:** The gas volume is a stainless steel pressure vessel, 25 mm wall, with thin (3 mm) aluminum entrance/exit windows on the beam faces to minimize interactions outside the fiducial gas. Field cage made from kapton-copper PCB rings on PEEK supports.

**Hydrogen content check:** Argon-CO₂ at 10 bar: negligible hydrogen. CO₂ contributes some carbon and oxygen but no hydrogen. ✓

---

## Module 2: Downstream 40% of Target Volume — Plastic Scintillator + Lead Absorber Sampling Calorimeter with SiPM Readout

**Dimensions:** 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.36 m along beam

### Why a separate downstream module:

The 0.15 T dipole field is essential for charge-sign determination of the muon, but the muon typically exits downstream. A denser downstream module serves two purposes:
1. **Range-out short muons** that stop within the target, measuring their momentum by range rather than curvature
2. **Measure electromagnetic activity** (π⁰ → γγ) to tag NC background

### Technology: Scintillator-Lead Sampling Stack (ECAL-style)

**Specific design:**
- **36 layers**, each consisting of:
  - 2 mm lead sheet (absorber)
  - 3 mm extruded polystyrene scintillator bar (Bicron BC-408 or equivalent), **bars running alternately in x and y** for 2D position measurement
  - Each bar: 1 cm × 3 mm cross-section, read out at both ends
- Total radiation lengths: ~20 X₀ — sufficient to fully contain EM showers from π⁰ decay photons up to ~1 GeV
- Total interaction lengths: ~1.5 λ_int — not a full hadronic calorimeter, but enough to initiate showers and measure energy via sampling

**Photosensors: Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)**

SiPMs are the right choice here because:
- They operate in the 0.15 T magnetic field without degradation (unlike PMTs, which would require careful shielding)
- Small form factor allows dense instrumentation
- **Specific device:** Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS or equivalent (3 mm × 3 mm active area, 50 µm pixel pitch, ~40% PDE at 450 nm)
- One SiPM per bar end → ~2 × 2 × (2.6/0.01) × (2.3/0.01) × 36 ≈ order 10⁵ channels — use **SiPM-on-tile** MPPC arrays to reduce channelcount by ganging bars in groups of 4 along z within one layer, reducing to ~25,000 readout channels

**Hydrogen content:** Polystyrene (CH) is hydrocarbon. Need to account for this carefully. With lead fraction by mass ~85%, hydrogen nucleon fraction is well below 20%. Explicit calculation: polystyrene C₈H₈ has 8 H per 104 amu monomer = 7.7% by mass hydrogen atoms. But the lead dominates the nucleon count — hydrogen nucleons are <2% of total. ✓

---

## Module 3: Lateral and Upstream Veto/Tagger Planes

### Technology: Plastic Scintillator Paddle Arrays with WLS Fiber + SiPM Readout

The ≥25% muon efficiency at all angles, including **backward-going tracks**, requires instrumentation on the upstream face and all four lateral faces of the target volume.

**Design:**
- **Upstream face (2.6 m × 2.3 m):** 2 planes of 2 cm × 2 cm × 230 cm scintillator bars, one plane with bars vertical, one with bars horizontal, read out with 1 mm diameter Y-11 WLS fiber embedded in a groove, coupled to a single SiPM (Hamamatsu S13360-3050PE) at each end. This gives ~2 cm position resolution transverse to the bar.
- **Four lateral faces:** Same bar-fiber-SiPM technology, bars oriented to give position along the beam axis.
- These planes serve triple duty: (a) tag and veto muons entering from outside, (b) catch backward-going muons from neutrino interactions, (c) provide a rough position measurement for tracks leaving the gas TPC laterally

**Channel count:** ~4 × (2.6 × 0.9 / 0.02) × 2 planes + upstream face ≈ order 1,500 channels total — modest.

---

## Interface to Existing Downstream Gas Drift Chambers

The existing gas drift chambers downstream of the target measure high-momentum muon tracks. The active target upgrade must **match track segments** between the new upstream modules and the existing downstream trackers.

**Required addition:** A **transition tracker** — 4 planes of large-area straws (4 mm diameter Mylar drift tubes, as used in e.g. the MINERvA outer detector or T2K ECal) installed in the ~20 cm gap between the downstream face of the new active target and the entrance of the existing drift chambers. These straws:
- Are field-transparent enough for the dipole fringe field not to cause problems
- Provide 2–3 mm position resolution to seed tracks into the existing chambers
- Operate in Ar:CO₂ (70:30) at 1 bar — simple, robust, well-understood

---

## Electronics and DAQ

**Front-end ASICs:**
- For the Micromegas TPC: **SAMPA chip** (developed for ALICE TPC upgrade) — continuous shaping and digitization at 10 MSPS, 10-bit ADC, 32 channels/chip. Already proven in multi-bar magnetic field environments.
- For SiPMs on scintillator modules: **CITIROC** (Omega/IN2P3) or **MUSIC** ASIC — 8-channel or 16-channel SiPM readout with adjustable shaping time, charge integration, and trigger output.
- Both ASICs are radiation-tolerant to the levels expected 410 m from the target.

**Trigger:** The neutrino beam delivers a narrow spill (typically ~10 µs for a fast-extracted beam). Use a **global spill trigger** from the accelerator to open readout windows. Within the window, the scintillator modules provide a fast coincidence trigger (< 50 ns) to flag candidate neutrino interactions; the TPC reads out continuously within the spill window and uses offline track-finding.

**Data volume:** TPC at 10 bar in a ~1 m drift volume: ionization from one neutrino interaction is ~10³ electrons per cm of track, spread over ~10⁴ channels. With ~1 interaction per spill on average, data volume per spill is manageable at O(10 MB) before zero-suppression; after zero-suppression, ~100 kB/spill. At 1 Hz spill rate, ~100 kB/s — trivially within modern DAQ bandwidth.

---

## Calibration Systems

1. **UV laser system for the TPC:** A 266 nm UV laser (Nd:YAG 4th harmonic) fed via fiber through fused-silica windows creates straight ionization tracks in the gas at known positions, calibrating drift velocity, field uniformity, and spatial distortions. This is the same approach used in ALICE and NA61.

2. **LED pulsers for SiPMs:** Each SiPM channel gets an optical fiber from a blue LED (450 nm) pulsed by a precision DAC, providing single-photon calibration of gain and dark rate at O(1 Hz) between beam spills.

3. **Cosmic ray muons:** At surface or shallow depth, cosmic muons provide straight through-going tracks at known angles for alignment of all sub-modules relative to each other and to the downstream drift chambers. A dedicated cosmic trigger (top scintillator paddle OR bottom scintillator paddle, in anti-coincidence with beam spill) collects these continuously.

4. **Radiative capture on hydrogen:** As a physics-based calibration, the 2.2 MeV γ from thermal neutron capture on hydrogen in the scintillator material provides a known energy deposition point for the EM calorimeter module.

---

| Upstream active target | HPGAr-TPC at 10 bar, resistive Micromegas, SAMPA readout | 1 mm strip pitch, 25 cm proton range at 60 MeV | Proton tracking, 4π acceptance |
| Downstream EM section | Pb-scintillator sampling, SiPM+WLS | 20 X₀, 1 cm bar pitch | π⁰ rejection, muon ranging |

## What This Design Does Not Include and Why

- **No liquid argon TPC:** LAr gives excellent performance but the 87 K operating temperature is incompatible with the warm dipole magnet and would require a cryostat that eats fiducial volume and complicates the interface to downstream trackers. The gas TPC at 10 bar gives adequate density while staying at room temperature.
- **No water Cherenkov target modules:** The hydrogen fraction in water (2 H per 18 amu = 11% by mass, translating to a large fraction of nucleons) makes it very difficult to stay below the 20% hydrogen nucleon limit while using a large water volume. The argon-based TPC gas is essentially hydrogen-free.
- **No resistive plate chambers for the active target core:** RPCs have 2–3 mm position resolution and dead time issues that would hurt the short proton track reconstruction.

## Design Review Recommendation for ND280 Upgrade

### Executive Summary
To achieve the required 4% systematic uncertainty for T2K-II through kinematically complete event reconstruction, I recommend a **3D fine-grained scintillator detector with timing capabilities**, replacing the P0D in the available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume.

---

## Primary Recommendation: SuperFGD-style Detector

### Core Technology: Extruded Plastic Scintillator Cubes

**Specification:**
- **1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes** arranged in a 3D array (~200 × 190 × 60 = 2.28 million cubes)
- Three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fiber readouts per cube
- Multi-Pixel Photon Counter (MPPC/SiPM) readout matching existing ND280 infrastructure
- Total target mass: ~2.4 tonnes of hydrocarbon (CH)

**Critical Justification:**

1. **Large-angle particle detection (≥50°)**: 
   - True 3D tracking with ~1 cm³ granularity captures particles at any angle, unlike the existing FGD's beam-perpendicular layers
   - Three-view readout provides unambiguous 3D reconstruction without projective ambiguities
   - Essential for the 25% of muons and 35% of protons exiting at >50°

2. **Low-momentum proton detection**:
   - 450 MeV/c median proton momentum → range ~30 cm in CH
   - 1 cm granularity provides ~30 samples for dE/dx measurement
   - Stopping protons give superior particle ID through Bragg peak measurement
   - Range-momentum reconstruction achieves ~5% resolution for contained tracks

3. **Proton/pion separation**:
   - Combining dE/dx with track topology separates protons from pions (critical contaminant)
   - Time-of-flight capability (see below) adds additional separation

### Technology: Fast timing readout (σ < 1 ns)

**Implementation:**
- Modern MPPCs with <100 ps intrinsic resolution
- Fast digitization electronics (~GHz sampling or leading-edge discrimination)
- Reference time from beam structure or TPCs

**Justification:**

1. **Time-of-Flight particle ID**:
   - 60 cm flight path with 1 ns timing → Δt(π-p) ≈ 2-3 ns at 450 MeV/c
   - Resolves proton/pion ambiguity for through-going tracks
   - Critical for non-stopping protons (6% exceed 900 MeV/c)

2. **Multi-track separation**:
   - Resolves overlapping tracks from multi-nucleon emission
   - Separates backward-going protons from forward muons in dense regions
   - Essential for transverse kinematic imbalance requiring all final-state particles

3. **Background rejection**:
   - Michel electron tagging via delayed coincidence
   - Sand muon and out-of-time cosmic rejection

# Concrete Hardware Upgrades for the Next Phase

## Context and Constraints

The core challenge is replacing the upstream photon-tagger with an active target that fits in ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m, reconstructs both the outgoing muon and leading proton in charged-current events, handles large-angle tracks (25% of muons and 35% of protons beyond 50°), and must push the systematic uncertainty from ~6% to ~4%. Each upgrade must earn its volume.

---

## Upgrade 1: Scintillator-Based High-Granularity Active Target

**Technology:** 3D-granular plastic scintillator cube detector — an array of ~1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes read out on three orthogonal faces by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres and SiPMs, following the SuperFGD architecture.

**Dimensions and mass:** A cube array of approximately 192 × 182 × 56 cm (fitting the available box with margins) filled with ~1 cm³ cubes gives of order 2 million channels if read on three faces with 1 cm pitch fibres. A practical implementation uses a subset: e.g., ~185 × 185 × 57 cm active volume, ~1.7 t of plastic scintillator, giving a hydrocarbon target of known composition.

**Physics motivation:**

- *Large-angle proton reconstruction:* The 3D-granular topology has no dead directions. A proton leaving at 70° to the beam crosses ~56/cos(70°) ≈ 164 layers of 1 cm cubes — sufficient for ranging. By contrast, a planar tracking detector with planes perpendicular to the beam loses acceptance for tracks beyond ~60° because the path length between planes becomes very short. The cube geometry removes this geometric inefficiency, directly addressing the stated 35% large-angle proton fraction.

- *Proton momentum measurement by range:* The median leading-proton momentum is ~450 MeV/c (kinetic energy ~100 MeV, range ~12 cm in polystyrene). A 1 cm cube granularity resolves this range to better than 2%, which translates to a momentum resolution of ~1–2% for stopping protons — far superior to what momentum-by-curvature would give in the modest 0.2 T field for a 10 cm track. The ~6% of protons above 900 MeV/c (range >50 cm) either stop within the ~57 cm depth or exit into the downstream TPCs for momentum-by-curvature.

- *Muon reconstruction at large angles:* The 25% large-angle muon fraction is poorly served by downstream-only spectrometers. The 3D scintillator provides the initial track segment in any direction; the muon then enters the existing dipole volume (TPCs + magnet) where it is momentum-analysed by curvature, or ranges into the instrumented yoke.

- *Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI):* TKI variables (δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T) require both the muon and leading proton 3-momenta. Coplanar reconstruction in the 3D target with ~1 cm position resolution gives angular resolution of order 10–15 mrad on short proton tracks, adequate for resolving the TKI distributions sensitive to nuclear effects. The fine granularity also makes it possible to separate the primary vertex from secondary interactions (re-interactions, neutron conversion) which are the dominant systematic in TKI analyses.

- *Vertex activity and neutron tagging:* The granular topology allows detection of low-energy recoil protons (threshold ~40 MeV kinetic energy, range ~2 cm) that would be invisible in a TPC. This characterises the full hadronic system and reduces model dependence on nuclear final-state interactions.

---

## Upgrade 2: Reinforced SiPM Readout with Increased Dynamic Range and Timing

**Technology:** Replace or supplement the existing SiPM readout on the new target (and optionally the existing scintillator channels interfacing to it) with SiPMs having higher pixel count (~10,000–15,000 microcells per device) and improved timing resolution (~200 ps single-channel), coupled to dedicated ASIC front-end electronics (e.g., a CITIROC or TARGET-C successor) with dual-gain readout.

**Physics motivation:**

- *Proton/pion separation in the active target:* At 450 MeV/c, a proton has β ≈ 0.43 and a pion has β ≈ 0.95. Time-of-flight across 50 cm of target gives a Δt of ~1.4 ns — resolvable at 200 ps resolution at 3σ. This is critical for correctly identifying the leading proton rather than a leading pion, which would corrupt the TKI reconstruction.

- *Saturation avoidance near the vertex:* The hadronic vertex deposits high local light yield that saturates low-pixel-count SiPMs, distorting dE/dx-based particle identification. Higher microcell density extends the linear range from ~200 p.e. to ~2000 p.e., recovering the Bragg-peak identification of stopping protons within 2–3 cm of the vertex.

- *Systematic reduction via in-situ calibration:* The improved timing resolution allows light-propagation corrections along WLS fibres to be measured run-by-run using Michel electrons from stopped cosmic muons, reducing the energy-scale systematic on proton kinetic energy — one of the leading contributions to the current 6% error budget.

---

## Upgrade 3: Thin Upstream Veto and Interaction-Vertex Tagger

**Technology:** Two planes of crossed scintillating-bar hodoscopes (e.g., 1 × 1 cm triangular-profile extruded scintillator bars with WLS fibre + SiPM readout), placed immediately upstream of the new active target, each plane ~2.0 × 1.9 m, total thickness <2 cm.

**Physics motivation:**

- *Sand muon and through-going track rejection:* Muons entering from upstream dirt and rock interactions (so-called "sand muons") create false neutrino-interaction candidates. A coincidence veto on the two hodoscope planes with sub-10 ns timing suppresses these at the trigger level and offline, with an inefficiency <0.1% for genuine neutrino events where no charged particle precedes the vertex.

- *Fiducial volume definition:* An interaction vertex reconstructed in the active target but with a signal in the upstream veto is flagged as likely background. This tightens the effective fiducial volume systematically, reducing the flux-normalisation uncertainty (currently a significant fraction of the 6% budget) by better defining the target mass that is active versus passive.

---

## Upgrade 4: Instrumented Downstream Interface — Thin EM Calorimeter Insert

**Technology:** A single-layer lead-scintillator "pre-shower" panel, ~4 mm Pb (0.7 X₀) followed by one plane of 3 × 3 cm scintillator tiles with SiPM readout, inserted at the downstream face of the new active target, covering the full 2.0 × 1.9 m aperture.

**Physics motivation:**

- *Photon/electron discrimination for NC-π⁰ background:* NC π⁰ events where one photon converts in the active target and mimics an electron track are a known background to νₑ-appearance searches and also contaminate CC-inclusive samples via misidentified vertices. The pre-shower panel identifies electromagnetic showers before they enter the TPC region, allowing these events to be tagged and either removed or treated as a constrained background.

- *Flux systematic reduction:* The photon-tagging function of the removed upstream section must be partially recovered. This thin calorimeter, while not equivalent to the full 16-tonne photon-tagger, provides electromagnetic energy tagging for forward-going photons from the new target at a cost of only a few centimetres of depth — affordable within the 60 cm envelope.

---

## Upgrade 5: Upgraded Trigger and DAQ with Full-Waveform Digitisation

**Technology:** Replace the existing multiplicity-based hardware trigger for the new target region with a software trigger running on FPGA/GPU farm, accepting full-waveform data (12-bit ADC at 250 MHz sampling) from all SiPM channels in the new target, using online reconstruction to select events with two or more reconstructed track stubs.

**Physics motivation:**

- *Low-threshold proton acceptance:* A hardware multiplicity trigger necessarily sets a threshold that eliminates short, low-energy proton tracks. Full-waveform readout with a software vertex-finding trigger can lower the effective proton kinetic energy threshold to ~30–40 MeV (range ~1.5 cm), increasing the reconstructible CC-QE sample by ~15–20% and reducing the model dependence introduced by proton-tracking thresholds.

- *Neutron time-of-flight tagging:* With 250 MHz sampling, neutron interactions in the scintillator cubes can be timed relative to the beam spill with ~4 ns resolution. This enables neutron-energy reconstruction by time-of-flight over 50–150 cm baselines within the target, providing constraints on the multinucleon (2p2h) interaction component — currently poorly constrained and a leading contributor to cross-section systematic uncertainty.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Systematic Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3D scintillator cube active target | Large-angle acceptance, proton ranging, TKI reconstruction |
| 2 | High-pixel SiPM + dual-gain ASIC | Proton/pion PID via ToF, vertex saturation, energy scale |
| 3 | Upstream scintillator hodoscope veto | Sand muon rejection, fiducial mass definition |
| 4 | Thin Pb/scintillator pre-shower panel | NC-π⁰ background, partial photon-tagging recovery |
| 5 | Software trigger + full-waveform DAQ | Proton threshold, neutron ToF, 2p2h constraint |

The combination of upgrades 1 and 2 is the most impactful: the 3D granular target directly solves the large-angle reconstruction deficit that limits the TKI programme, while the improved SiPM timing provides the particle identification needed to trust the proton assignment. Together with the veto (3), these address the dominant sources of the gap between the current 6% and target 4% systematic uncertainty.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Constraints

Before proposing hardware, let me establish what the physics demands:

**Muon reconstruction requirements:**
- ≥25% efficiency at *all* angles including 90° and backward-going
- At 0.7 GeV peak flux, muons carry ~300–500 MeV — they range out in ~tens of cm of plastic scintillator
- Backward-going tracks must be caught before they exit the upstream face
- The existing downstream drift chambers handle forward tracks; the active target must handle the rest

**Proton reconstruction requirements:**
- 60 MeV kinetic energy → range in plastic scintillator ≈ 3–4 mm; in liquid argon ≈ ~5 mm
- This demands *very* fine spatial resolution and low-Z material to maximize range
- All angles means 4π coverage within the target volume

**Hydrogen constraint:**
- H must be ≤2% of target nucleons by number
- Water: H is ~67% of nucleons — ruled out
- Liquid argon: no hydrogen — passes, but reconstruction challenges
- Plastic scintillator (CH₂ₙ): H ≈ ~33% of nucleons — ruled out unless diluted
- Pure carbon target: 0% H — passes trivially but loses fiducial mass
- Scintillator with heavy nucleus doping needed, or non-hydrogenous medium

**Hydrogen fraction calculation for candidate materials:**

| Material | H nucleon fraction |
|---|---|
| CH₂ (polyethylene) | 2/4 = 50% |
| C₈H₈ (polystyrene) | 8/16 = 50% |
| C₅H₄ (approximation for some plastics) | ~44% |
| Pb | 0% |
| Fe | 0% |
| Ar (liquid) | 0% |
| CF₄ gas | 0% |

To reach ≤2% H, one must either use hydrogen-free media or heavily dilute with high-A material. A *layered* approach of thin plastic scintillator interleaved with high-A passive absorber could work: e.g., 1 mm scintillator (C:H ≈ 1:1 by nucleon) + 50 mm iron gives H/(H+Fe+C) ≈ 0.5/(0.5 + ~54 + 6) ≈ **0.8%** — acceptable, but kills the short proton track requirement. This trade-off is the central design tension.

The resolution for 60 MeV protons (range ~3 mm in scintillator) means passive absorber layers cannot exceed ~1–2 mm thickness, which then requires very many layers and the hydrogen fraction climbs. **Therefore the active medium itself must be hydrogen-free or nearly so.**

---

## Proposed Upgrade

### 1. Primary Active Target Medium: Liquid Argon TPC Modules

**Replace the existing target region fill with a segmented liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC) array.**

- Argon (Z=18, A=40) contains **zero hydrogen** — satisfies the ≤2% constraint trivially
- LArTPC provides ~mm-scale 3D reconstruction via ionization imaging
- 60 MeV protons have a range of ~8 mm in LAr — detectable as short tracks with wire pitch ≤3 mm
- Continuous ionization readout captures tracks at all angles without geometric acceptance holes
- The 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume fits a modular LAr system without requiring a monolithic cryostat

**Specific implementation:**

Segment the volume into a **3×2 array of six LArTPC modules**, each approximately 0.85 m (x) × 1.1 m (y) × 0.9 m (z), with:

- **Wire readout planes**: Two induction planes (±60° to vertical) + one collection plane, wire pitch **2.5 mm** in all planes
- **Drift direction**: Horizontal, transverse to beam (x-direction), drift length ≤40 cm per module (half-module drift from central cathode) → keeps drift field practical at ~500 V/cm, HV ≤20 kV
- **Drift field**: 500 V/cm → electron drift velocity ~1.6 mm/μs → maximum drift time ~250 μs
- **Modular cryostats**: Thin-wall (5 mm) stainless steel with foam insulation, each module independently operable
- **Cold electronics**: ASIC-based charge amplifiers mounted inside the cryostat on the wire frames to minimize noise before signal extraction

**Why segmented rather than monolithic:** Allows installation within the existing magnet bore without removing the magnet, staged commissioning, and local HV failure containment.

---

### 2. Scintillation Light Detection System (Essential for Timing and Trigger)

LArTPC alone cannot trigger and cannot resolve the beam spill time-structure without a photon detection system:

- **Install 8× 6-inch cryogenic PMTs (Hamamatsu R5912-MOD or equivalent)** per module (48 total), mounted on the end-caps behind TPB (tetraphenyl butadiene) wavelength-shifting plates that convert 128 nm LAr scintillation to ~430 nm
- Alternatively, **X-ARAPUCA light traps** embedded in the cathode planes — higher photon detection efficiency (~3%), lower profile, no penetrations through the long sides of the cryostat
- Target: ≥0.5 photoelectrons/MeV → sufficient to tag Michel electrons from stopped muons and to provide t₀ for drift coordinate reconstruction
- Timing resolution ~10 ns → resolves beam bunches if applicable, suppresses cosmic backgrounds

---

### 3. Upstream and Downstream Muon Catcher Planes

The existing downstream drift chambers handle forward muons, but **backward-going and large-angle muons** exit the upstream or lateral faces of the active target and must be caught:

**3a. Upstream Muon Catcher Stack**

Install immediately upstream of the active target volume (between target and beam entrance flange):

- **4 layers of 3 cm-thick plastic scintillator bars** (extruded, 3×3 cm² cross-section, Bicron BC-408 or equivalent), alternating x and y orientation
- Each bar read out at both ends by **SiPMs** (3×3 mm² Hamamatsu S13360 or equivalent) — robust in the magnetic field (unlike PMTs at oblique angles to 0.15 T field)
- Total stack depth: ~12 cm → stops muons up to ~180 MeV (sufficient to identify and range backward-going muons from 0.7 GeV interactions, which typically carry 50–200 MeV backward)
- Spatial resolution: 3 cm bar width → adequate for matching to LArTPC tracks
- This stack also serves as a **veto for beam-unrelated entering particles**

**3b. Lateral Muon Tracking Planes**

For 90°-going muons (the most challenging — they exit the 2.3 m-tall side faces):

- Line the four lateral faces (two in y, two in x) of the active target with **2 planes of scintillator strips per face**, strip width 2.5 cm, strips running parallel to the beam axis on one plane and vertically on the other
- SiPM readout at each end
- Provides a 2D hit position on each face for tracks exiting laterally
- These strips are **outside** the cryostat cold volume — no cryogenic requirements — installed between the cryostat outer wall and the magnet coil bore
- Match to the existing downstream drift chambers using a **Kalman-filter track extrapolation** that uses the known 0.15 T dipole field between target exit and drift chamber entrance

---

### 4. Inter-Module Gap Instrumentation

The gaps between LArTPC modules (~1–2 cm) represent dead zones that break track reconstruction for certain angles:

- Fill each inter-module gap with a **1 cm-thick scintillator tile layer** (3×3 cm² tiles, SiPM readout) acting as a **gap tagger and charge injection monitor**
- Tiles provide hit confirmation that a track crossed the gap, allowing the track-stitching algorithm to link segments across modules
- Also used for relative energy-scale cross-calibration between modules using cosmic muons

---

### 5. Beam-Muon Momentum Measurement Cross-Check: Downstream Spectrometer Interface

The existing warm dipole + drift chambers measure forward muon momentum. To extend this to the new active target:

- **No changes to the existing downstream spectrometer hardware** — it already handles forward tracks
- Add a **transition radiation tracker (TRT) or additional drift chamber station** at the downstream face of the active target volume to improve the track-matching efficiency between the LArTPC track stub and the downstream spectrometer
- Specifically: one station of **straw-tube drift chambers**, 4 mm straw diameter, 2 layers × 2 orientations (x,y), covering the full 2.6×2.3 m² face
- This improves muon momentum resolution for tracks that exit downstream but at angles up to ~40° from the beam axis where the existing chambers have reduced efficiency
- The straws are field-tolerant (small diameter, axial field along the straw is acceptable for the 0.15 T transverse dipole field given straw orientation can be chosen appropriately)

---

### 6. Data Acquisition and Trigger

The LArTPC continuous readout generates large data volumes (~100 GB/spill without compression for this volume):

- **Triggered readout**: Use the scintillation light signal (PMTs or X-ARAPUCAs) as the hardware trigger, with ~1 μs coincidence window
- **Trigger threshold**: ≥3 photoelectrons in any module within a 100 ns window → efficient for protons down to 60 MeV (which deposit ~60 MeV, producing ~30 detected photons)
- **Readout window**: Record ±1.5 ms around the light trigger (covering full maximum drift time of 250 μs with margin)
- **Online compression**: Apply lossless Huffman compression + zero-suppression at the FPGA level on the cold ADCs → target ~10:1 compression → manageable bandwidth
- **DAQ backbone**: 10 GbE links from each module to surface DAQ farm; use commodity server hardware with GPU-accelerated online reconstruction for fast feedback

---

| Upgrade | Purpose | Key Specification |
|---|---|---|
| Segmented LArTPC (6 modules) | Active target, all-angle tracking, H-free | 2.5 mm wire pitch, 40 cm max drift, 500 V/cm |
| Cryogenic photon detection (X-ARAPUCAs) | t₀, trigger, Michel tagging | ≥0.5 PE/MeV, ~10 ns timing |
