The **SuperFGD-style 3D scintillator cube** with **time-of-flight** and **high-angle tracking** form the minimum viable upgrade for kinematically complete events. The enhanced proton range detector and neutron tagging are essential for pushing systematics to 4%.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for ND280 Next Phase

## 1. SuperFGD — High-Granularity 3D Scintillator Active Target

**Technology:** ~2 million extruded polystyrene cubes, 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm, each read out in all three orthogonal directions by three wavelength-shifting fibres feeding MPPCs. The cubes interlock into a ~1.8 m × 1.8 m × 0.6 m monolithic block fitting the vacated P0D volume.

**Physics motivation:**

The fundamental problem with the slab-FGD geometry is that tracking is inherently 2D-projection based: a particle must travel several radiation lengths laterally before accumulating enough hits in alternating x/y planes to be reconstructed in 3D. For steeply exiting particles this fails badly. With 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons leaving at more than 50° to the beam, a large fraction of kinematically complete events are lost precisely in the topologies where transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) is most discriminating — the high-angle, high-momentum-transfer regime sensitive to multinucleon correlations and final-state interactions.

A 1 cm³ isotropic voxel gives genuine 3D tracking from the first hit. Any track, regardless of exit angle, immediately produces a resolvable 3D trajectory. The low-momentum proton reconstruction threshold drops to roughly 300 MeV/c (compared to ~500 MeV/c in FGD1) because a proton stopping within only a few cubes still deposits measurable, topologically distinct Bragg-peak light. This directly recovers the bulk of the leading-proton momentum distribution (median ~450 MeV/c) that would otherwise fall below threshold or exit laterally untracked. Particle identification exploits dE/dx cube-by-cube: the Bragg peak shape distinguishes protons from pions from muons on a track-by-track basis without requiring a downstream TPC match, enabling fully contained event selection. Event pile-up confusion is reduced because ghost tracks from ambiguous 2D projection matching are essentially eliminated. The hydrocarbon target composition (polystyrene, CH) is compatible with the stated programme; carbon-to-water comparison is preserved by FGD2 downstream.

---

## 2. High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs) — Six Thin Gas Tracking Chambers Surrounding the SuperFGD

**Technology:** Six rectangular TPCs with resistive Micromegas pads, using the same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ gas mixture as the existing TPCs, arranged as top/bottom/left/right/upstream/downstream faces of a loose box around the SuperFGD. Individual chamber dimensions roughly 2.0 m × 1.9 m in the transverse faces, with ~25 cm drift gap. Readout pads ~1 cm² with ~200 µm position resolution.

**Physics motivation:**

The existing TPCs are downstream-only and cover a limited solid angle. Muons and protons exiting the SuperFGD at large angles currently enter the SMRD or ECal, neither of which provides momentum measurement by curvature. Without a momentum measurement, TKI reconstruction is impossible for these tracks regardless of how well they are found by the SuperFGD.

Surrounding the target on all six faces with thin TPCs allows charged particles to enter the 0.2 T dipole field region and undergo curvature measurement essentially regardless of exit angle. A 25 cm drift in 0.2 T and 2 m lever arm gives momentum resolution δp/p ≈ 10–15% for the typical 300–600 MeV/c protons of interest, sufficient for TKI studies where the relevant momentum-imbalance scale is ~100 MeV/c. For the 6% of protons exceeding 900 MeV/c — which are energetic enough to range out in the ECal otherwise — TPC curvature becomes the primary momentum estimator. Charge-sign determination is maintained, cleanly separating π⁺ from protons and distinguishing μ⁻ from μ⁺ for anti-neutrino beam running. The thin-window design (~5 mm carbon-fibre frames, ~0.5% X₀ per wall) minimises secondary scattering of the very particles being measured.

---

## 3. Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes — Six Faces, 200 ps Resolution

**Technology:** Planes of 2 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm polystyrene scintillator tiles or 2 cm-wide bars with SiPM readout mounted on the inner faces of the HA-TPC frames, providing ~200 ps coincidence-based timing. Total active area ~2 × (2.0 × 1.9) + 4 × (2.0 × 0.6) ≈ 12 m².

**Physics motivation:**

At 300–900 MeV/c, the velocity difference between a proton and a pion of equal momentum is large. At 450 MeV/c (the median proton momentum), β(proton) ≈ 0.43 whereas β(pion) ≈ 0.95: for a 50 cm path the time difference is ~2 ns, trivially resolved at 200 ps. This provides proton/pion separation that is fully independent of the dE/dx-based PID from the SuperFGD and HA-TPCs, constituting a cross-check that is essential for systematic uncertainty reduction. More critically, for tracks that are too short in the TPC to accumulate sufficient dE/dx hits, or for protons that range out before reaching the TPC, ToF is the only available PID. Direction ambiguity (is the particle leaving or entering the SuperFGD?) can also be resolved by ToF when two faces are hit, which is important for identifying neutron-induced backgrounds masquerading as proton recoils. Reducing proton misidentification directly reduces the false-positive rate in kinematically complete event selection, which is the primary driver of the residual 6% systematic uncertainty the upgrade is meant to address.

---

## 4. Thin Lead-Free Electromagnetic Calorimeter Tiles Integrated into HA-TPC Downstream Face

**Technology:** Sampling calorimeter using 2 mm scintillator tiles interleaved with 1 mm tungsten absorber (rather than lead, to reduce weight), embedded as the downstream HA-TPC endcap. Total ~8 X₀, ~40 layers, SiPM readout, ~2.0 m × 1.9 m active area.

**Physics motivation:**

Neutral pions produced in the neutrino interaction vertex decay immediately to two photons. These photons are invisible to tracking detectors and to the ToF/TPC systems, yet they carry away transverse momentum that, if unaccounted for, creates fake TKI signals that mimic multinucleon correlations. The existing ECals subtend only the downstream and lateral faces of the inner detector basket at comparatively large distances; photons from π⁰ decay at the SuperFGD vertex with opening angles of ~30–90° can miss these ECals entirely. A thin integrated calorimeter at the downstream HA-TPC face, closest to the most-forward-going photons, reconstructs these π⁰ with energy resolution δE/E ≈ 10%/√E ⊕ 3%, adequate to constrain the π⁰ transverse momentum vector to ~30 MeV/c accuracy for the dominant sub-500 MeV photons. This allows event-by-event subtraction or vetoing of π⁰ contamination rather than relying on MC-modelled corrections, directly attacking the cross-section model uncertainty component of the 6% residual systematic.

---

## 5. Upgraded MPPC Readout Electronics with ~1 ns Timestamp Resolution

**Technology:** Replace existing AFTER-chip-based front-end ASICs on all scintillator channels (SuperFGD fibres, existing FGD2, ECal, SMRD) with CITIROC or custom SiPM-optimised ASICs providing ~1 ns leading-edge timestamps and 12-bit charge ADC with zero-suppression. Data pushed over GBT optical links to an FPGA-based event builder.

**Physics motivation:**

The J-PARC beam spill is 5 µs long and the interaction rate per spill in the upgraded high-luminosity T2K-II beam (~1.3 × 10²¹ POT/year, roughly 2× present) increases pile-up probability significantly. The existing 50 ns time-bucket resolution of the AFTER chip cannot separate two interactions occurring within the same few-hundred-nanosecond window, causing event mixing that corrupts TKI reconstruction — vectors from two separate vertices are combined into one fake event. With 1 ns timing, the mean interaction separation in the SuperFGD (~few interactions per spill) can be resolved with high efficiency, event-by-event. Additionally, neutron tagging via delayed proton recoils (neutrons from the interaction scattering in neighbouring cubes 10–100 ns later) becomes possible, providing the first direct neutron momentum constraint in this near detector, which is valuable for modelling multinucleon final states where neutrons carry significant momentum. This upgrades the entire detector's physics capability without replacing any active detector element.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Goal |
|---|---|---|
| SuperFGD | 1 cm³ 3D scintillator cubes | Low-threshold isotropic proton tracking; vertex resolution |
| HA-TPCs | 6-face Micromegas TPCs | Momentum measurement at all angles in existing B field |
| ToF planes | SiPM scintillator tiles, 200 ps | p/π PID independent of dE/dx; direction ambiguity resolution |
| Thin W-Ecal endcap | Tungsten-scintillator sampling | π⁰ reconstruction; neutral-particle TKI correction |
| Fast MPPC electronics | CITIROC ASICs, 1 ns timing | Pile-up rejection; neutron tagging in T2K-II intensity |

Together these address the specific failure modes — high-angle track loss, low-momentum proton threshold, π⁰ missing momentum, and pile-up — that collectively constitute the dominant contributions to the residual 6% systematic, with a clear path to the 4% target required for T2K-II.

# Design Review Recommendation for Kestrel Near Detector Active Target

## Executive Summary
I recommend a **high-pressure gaseous hydrogen TPC** with admixed helium or argon, using micromegas or GEM readout. This addresses all critical requirements while maintaining the hydrogen fraction constraint.

## Primary Recommendation: High-Pressure Gas TPC

### Technology Specification
- **Active medium**: H₂:He mixture at 80:20 nucleon ratio (approximately 60:40 by pressure for H₂:⁴He)
- **Pressure**: 10-20 atmospheres
- **Readout**: Micromegas or triple-GEM amplification stages
- **Pad/strip pitch**: 2-3 mm for adequate angular resolution
- **Drift field**: ~400 V/cm with field cage
- **Sampling rate**: ≥40 MHz for 3D track reconstruction

### Justification

**1. Hydrogen Fraction Requirement (≤20% nucleons)**
- 80:20 H:He nucleon ratio remains safely within the 20% limit
- Pure hydrogen would violate this constraint
- Helium provides mass while maintaining low-Z benefits

**2. 4π Angular Coverage**
- Gas TPC provides true 3D tracking with continuous readout
- Backward-going muons traverse sufficient material for reconstruction
- Perpendicular tracks leave ionization trails throughout their path
- No "dead" material or geometric acceptance holes

**3. Low Momentum Proton Detection (60 MeV KE)**
- 60 MeV proton range in 10 atm H₂:He ≈ 15-25 cm (well within 90 cm depth)
- dE/dx measurements enable particle ID
- Full track containment allows calorimetric energy measurement
- Low diffusion in high-pressure gas preserves spatial resolution

**4. Muon Tracking Efficiency**
- Continuous ionization sampling gives >90% efficiency for muons traversing target
- Low multiple scattering in gas allows accurate angle reconstruction
- Even minimum ionizing tracks provide 30-50 primary electrons/cm

**5. Vertex Resolution**
- Expected ~1-2 mm vertex resolution with modern readout
- Critical for separating primary interactions from secondary interactions

## Alternative Readout Options

### Micromegas (Preferred)
- **Advantages**: Proven at high rates (10⁶ Hz/cm²), robust, good ion feedback suppression
- **Examples**: T2K ND280 upgrade, CLAS12
- **Spatial resolution**: ~300 μm demonstrated

### Triple-GEM (Strong Alternative)
- **Advantages**: Excellent gain stability, well-established technology
- **Concern**: Ion feedback at high rates
- **Mitigation**: Optimize voltage configuration

## Essential Supporting Systems

### 1. Field Cage
- Copper rings/strips on PEEK or G10 supports
- Ensures uniform drift field despite magnetic field
- Resistor chain voltage distribution

### 2. Gas System
- Recirculation with purification (O₂, H₂O removal to <1 ppm)
- Pressure regulation to ±0.1%
- Safety systems for hydrogen handling

### 3. Electronics
- Low-noise charge-sensitive preamplifiers on detector
- Flash ADC digitization for full waveform capture
- Zero-suppression with conservative thresholds

### 4. Calibration Systems
- UV laser tracks for drift velocity monitoring
- Cosmic ray tracks (with external trigger counters)
- Possible ⁵⁵Fe or ¹⁰⁶Ru sources for gain calibration

## Risk Mitigation

### High-Pressure Hydrogen Safety
- **Risk**: Flammability, pressure vessel failure
- **Mitigation**: 
  - Pressure vessel certified to appropriate standards (ASME Section VIII)
  - He admixture reduces flammability risk
  - Oxygen monitoring and ventilation
  - Automated shutdown systems

### Rate Capability
- **Risk**: Event pile-up at ~410 m from target
- **Mitigation**: 
  - Fine segmentation (2-3 mm pads)
  - 40+ MHz sampling reduces occupancy per channel
  - Fast ion clearing with Micromegas design

### Magnetic Field Effects
- **Risk**: E×B distortions of drift paths
- **Mitigation**:
  - Orient drift direction parallel to B-field if possible
  - If perpendicular drift needed, correct with detailed field map
  - Consider tilted readout planes

## Implementation Priorities

**Phase 1 (Months 1-12)**: 
- Finalize pressure vessel design and safety reviews
- Prototype 30×30 cm² readout plane with full electronics chain
- Cosmic ray tests in magnetic field

**Phase 2 (Months 13-24)**:
- Full detector construction
- Gas system commissioning
- Integration with existing downstream trackers

**Phase 3 (Months 25-30)**:
- Installation and commissioning
- Calibration campaigns
- Physics data-taking begins

## Cost and Schedule Drivers
- Pressure vessel: ~$200-300K
- Readout planes (full coverage): ~$400-600K
- Electronics: ~$300-500K
- Gas system: ~$150-250K
- **Total estimated cost**: $1.5-2.5M with contingency

## Conclusion

A high-pressure gas TPC with H₂:He mixture optimally satisfies all requirements: hydrogen fraction control, 4π acceptance, low-momentum proton detection, and high muon reconstruction efficiency. This technology is mature, with proven performance in neutrino experiments, and can be implemented on the proposed schedule.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Active Neutrino Target for the Upstream Section

## Executive Summary

The goal is to replace the passive photon-tagging section with an active target that reconstructs kinematically complete charged-current (CC) events — muon plus leading recoil proton — within the available 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m envelope, reducing the residual systematic uncertainty from ~6% to ~4%. The constraints are severe: the box is shallow (0.6 m along beam), ~35% of leading protons exit at >50°, the median proton momentum is ~450 MeV/c (range in plastic ~20 cm), and ~6% exceed 900 MeV/c (range ~90 cm). The detector must therefore simultaneously provide fine-grained vertex finding, large-angle acceptance, and sufficient downstream/lateral containment or ranging capability — all within the existing dipole field (0.2 T).

---

## 1. Constraints and Derived Requirements

### 1.1 Momentum and Range Budget

| Particle | Momentum | Range in CH (ρ ≈ 1.06 g/cm³) |
|---|---|---|
| Proton at 450 MeV/c (median) | ~105 MeV KE | ~9 cm |
| Proton at 700 MeV/c | ~260 MeV KE | ~36 cm |
| Proton at 900 MeV/c | ~430 MeV KE | ~88 cm |
| Muon at 600 MeV/c | ~280 MeV KE | ~110 cm in CH |

The 0.6 m depth along beam contains the median proton comfortably but not the high-momentum tail. Lateral dimensions (2.0 m × 1.9 m) provide real estate for large-angle tracks if the active volume extends transversely.

### 1.2 Angular Acceptance

With 25% of muons and 35% of protons at >50°, reconstruction must not rely on forward projection alone. At 50° a 450 MeV/c proton travels ~14 cm projected radially before stopping — well within the lateral span. The detector architecture must present tracking material in the transverse plane, not just longitudinal samplings.

### 1.3 Systematic Target

Moving from 6% to 4% requires roughly halving the leading uncertainty sources: flux shape, final-state interactions (FSI), and detector acceptance/efficiency. The active target contributes primarily by improving vertex resolution, reducing FSI model dependence through multi-nucleon topology reconstruction, and enabling transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) measurements that are themselves self-calibrating for nuclear effects.

---

## 2. Proposed Architecture: Scintillating-Fibre Straw-Composite Active Target (SF-SCAT)

The core concept is a **3D scintillating-fibre (SciFi) tracker** acting as both neutrino target mass and tracking medium, surrounded on five faces by **thin plastic scintillator ranging walls**, all inside the existing dipole field for muon charge-sign determination, with an **upstream-face veto** and optional **thin liquid-argon or water-layer inserts** for nuclear target tagging.

### 2.1 Why SciFi?

Scintillating-fibre trackers (as demonstrated by LHCb SciFi, and the T2K SFGD concept under development) offer:
- Intrinsic 3D hit reconstruction with ~100–200 μm position resolution per fibre
- Full solid-angle sensitivity — no preferred projection axis, unlike planar strip detectors
- Fast timing (~1 ns) for pile-up rejection
- Low-Z hydrocarbon target (CH close to CH₂; acceptable per problem statement)
- Scalable to the available volume
- SiPM readout compatible with the existing detector infrastructure

---

## 3. Component-by-Component Description

### 3.1 Super-Fine-Grained Detector (SFGD) Core

**Geometry:** 3D array of **1 mm × 1 mm × 1 mm polystyrene scintillator cubes**, each cube threaded in all three orthogonal directions (x, y, z) by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres. This is the Super-Fine-Grained Detector concept, developed for ND280 upgrade; it is proposed here as the primary neutrino target.

**Dimensions within envelope:**
- Instrumented volume: **1.80 m (x) × 1.70 m (y) × 0.56 m (z)**, leaving ~10 cm margins for mechanical supports and fibre routing
- Number of cubes: 1.80 m × 1.70 m × 0.56 m at 1 mm pitch → **~1.71 × 10⁹ cubes** (not all individually read; fibres aggregate hits)
- Each fibre reads out one row of cubes; total fibres: ~2 × (1800 + 1700 + 560) planes — see readout below

**Mass:**
- Polystyrene density ~1.06 g/cm³
- Packing fraction of cubes with fibre holes: ~95% polystyrene by volume
- Mass ≈ 1.80 × 1.70 × 0.56 × 1.06 × 10⁶ g ≈ **1.82 tonnes**
- This is comparable to each existing plastic tracking target (1.1 t), appropriate for statistics

**Fibre layout (3-view readout):**
- X-fibres: 1700 × 560 = 952,000 fibres, bundled end-read in columns → ~1700 × 56 SiPM channels per face = ~95,200 channels per x-face (×2 ends)
- Practically, fibres are grouped: each fibre reads one column of 1800 cubes, so 1700 × 560 = 952,000 fibres in x. With multiplexed SiPM arrays (64-channel arrays as used in T2K SFGD), total channel count is manageable at ~100k channels across all three axes — consistent with the existing SiPM-based readout infrastructure described

**Position resolution:**
- Single-fibre hit: 1 mm / √12 ≈ 290 μm per axis
- With charge sharing between adjacent fibres: ~200 μm 3D vertex resolution
- Vertex resolution of ~1 mm³ voxel size is sufficient to resolve secondary vertices from proton FSI rescattering, pion production near threshold, and neutron elastic scatter

**Why 1 mm cubes rather than the 9.6 mm bars of the existing tracker?**
- The existing 9.6 mm bar design gives ~2.8 mm resolution per view; for a 450 MeV/c proton (~9 cm range), this provides ~32 measurement points but with ~2 cm vertex ambiguity
- 1 mm cubes give ~9 cm range sampled at 90 points with sub-mm vertex, critical for multi-track topologies and for distinguishing genuine TKI from detector smearing

### 3.2 Surrounding Ranging Walls

To contain and range out large-angle protons and to track large-angle muons before they enter the main dipole volume, five thin scintillator planes surround the SFGD:

#### 3.2.1 Lateral Walls (×4: upstream-x, downstream-x, upstream-y, downstream-y)

Each lateral wall is a **2-layer plastic scintillator hodoscope** of 1 cm thick bars with SiPM readout:
- Dimensions: ~1.9 m × 0.6 m per wall (covering the full face of the SFGD)
- Bar orientation: alternating horizontal and vertical for 2D hit position
- Provides exit-point measurement for escaping tracks
- Functions as a **veto** for beam-unrelated backgrounds entering from the side
- Total material: 4 × (1.9 × 0.6 × 0.02 m) × 1.06 g/cm³ ≈ 97 kg — negligible mass perturbation

#### 3.2.2 Downstream Face: Thin ECal Plug

A **3-layer lead-scintillator sandwich** (1 mm Pb + 5 mm scintillator, ×3) on the downstream face:
- Absorbs photons from π⁰ decay that exit downstream
- Provides energy measurement for forward-going photons
- Acts as a preshower detector distinguishing photons from protons
- Thickness: ~1.5 cm total → radiation length ≈ 0.42 X₀ — sufficient for photon tagging
- Does not significantly degrade downstream momentum measurement because the SFGD itself measures track momentum by range/curvature

#### 3.2.3 Upstream Face: Beam-Entrance Veto

A single plane of **3 mm scintillator bars** (x and y views) covering the full 2.0 m × 1.9 m face:
- Tags beam-entering charged particles (cosmics, halo muons, upstream interactions)
- Read out by SiPM; coincidence requirement with SFGD removes ~95% of through-going muon backgrounds
- Thin enough (~3 mm) not to introduce significant interaction probability

### 3.3 Integration with Existing Dipole Field

The SFGD sits within the 0.2 T dipole field. For momentum determination:

**Muons:**
- A 600 MeV/c muon has a sagitta in 0.56 m of field: s = 0.3 × B × L² / (8p) = 0.3 × 0.2 × 0.56² / (8 × 0.6) ≈ **3.9 mm** — measurable at the 1 mm spatial resolution level (~4σ), giving ~25% momentum resolution
- Higher-momentum muons that exit downstream are measured by the existing downstream TPCs with their superior resolution; this is the primary muon momentum measurement
- The SFGD's field measurement provides an independent cross-check and handles muons stopping within the SFGD volume

**Protons:**
- For protons stopping within the SFGD (median range ~9 cm), momentum is determined primarily by **range** with resolution ~2–3% — far better than curvature measurement at these momenta in 0.2 T
- For protons exiting (high-momentum tail, >~700 MeV/c), curvature in the dipole field gives momentum measurement; exiting protons are tracked through the lateral ranging walls and into any downstream/lateral detector material

### 3.4 Optional Water-Layer Inserts (Phase 1b)

To perform direct carbon-to-water comparisons in the same upstream volume (complementing the existing downstream water-layer target):

- Thin **removable polycarbonate bags, 1 cm thick**, can be inserted every 10 cm (i.e., 5–6 layers across the 0.56 m depth)
- Each bag: 1.80 m × 1.70 m × 0.01 m = 30.6 litres of water → ~31 kg per layer
- 6 layers: ~186 kg water on ~1,820 kg polystyrene → water fraction ~9% by mass
- This enables a sample-simultaneous water/CH measurement without moving to the downstream target, reducing systematic uncertainties from time-varying flux conditions
- The SFGD cube density and vertex resolution are sufficient to statistically separate vertices occurring in water bags versus polystyrene, using the z-position distribution

### 3.5 Readout Architecture

Building on the existing SiPM + WLS-fibre + scintillator infrastructure:

**SiPM selection:** 1 mm × 1 mm Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS or equivalent (matching the 1 mm fibre core), operating at ~25°C (no cooling required), Vbr ≈ 65 V, PDE ~40% at 450 nm emission peak of WLS (Y-11 or equivalent)

**Multiplexing:** Each fibre end is read by one SiPM channel. With ~3 × 10⁶ fibres total (1800 × 560 for x-view + 1700 × 560 for y-view + 1800 × 1700 for z-view, times 2 ends), direct readout is impractical. Solution:

- **Fibre bundling with time-of-light position:** Read both ends of each fibre; the time difference (at ~5 ns/m propagation in fibre) gives z-position along the fibre to ~25 cm resolution — supplemented by the orthogonal fibre views for precise 3D reconstruction
- **Effective channel count:** 2 × (1800 × 560 + 1700 × 560 + 1800 × 1700) ≈ 2 × (1,008,000 + 952,000 + 3,060,000) ≈ **10 million fibre ends**
- This is large; practical implementation uses **WAGON (Wavelength-shifting fibres Aggregated for Grid Output in Neutrino detectors)** multiplexing or similar: groups of 64 fibres read on a single 64-channel SiPM array with event-by-event demultiplexing using track pattern recognition
- Reduces electronics channels to ~**160,000** — comparable to the existing ND280 SiPM channel count, manageable with the existing CITIROC/SPIROC-based front-end ASICs already in use for the downstream scintillator channels

**Trigger:** Self-triggering via SiPM threshold; coincidence with beam spill gate (typically 2–10 μs for a narrow-band beam). In-spill cosmic veto via upstream face panel.

**Data rate:** At the nominal beam intensity (~10⁷ POT/spill) and detector mass (~1.82 t), expect ~2–5 CC interactions per spill in the SFGD; with ~200 hit fibres per event and 10 million channels at ~5% occupancy → manageable with existing DAQ architecture extended by additional readout boards

### 4.2 Efficiency for Kinematically Complete CC Events

**Vertex containment:** With 1.80 m × 1.70 m × 0.56 m active volume, fiducial volume (excluding 5 cm from each face) is 1.70 m × 1.60 m × 0.46 m = 1.25 m³ → fiducial mass ~**1.40 tonnes**

**Muon reconstruction efficiency:**
- Forward muons (>50° to beam, ~25% of events): exit laterally, measured by ranging walls + dipole-field curvature → efficiency ~85%
- Forward muons (beam-direction, ~75%): exit downstream into TPCs → efficiency ~95% (existing TPC performance)
- Overall muon reconstruction efficiency: ~92%

**Leading proton reconstruction efficiency:**
- Stopping protons (p < ~600 MeV/c, ~70% of protons): fully contained in SFGD for fiducial vertices → efficiency ~90%
- Large-angle protons (>50°, ~35%): with 85 cm lateral half-span from fiducial edge, most contained → ~88% efficiency
- High-momentum protons (>900 MeV/c, ~6%): exit detector, measured by ranging walls + curvature → ~65% efficiency (momentum resolution degrades)
- Overall proton reconstruction efficiency: **~85%**

**Combined efficiency for kinematically complete events:** ~92% × 85% ≈ **78%** — a substantial improvement over the current upstream section which provides essentially 0% kinematically complete proton reconstruction

### 4.3 TKI Sensitivity

Transverse kinematic imbalance variables (δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T) are constructed from the muon and proton transverse momenta perpendicular to the beam:

- δp_T resolution is dominated by muon and proton p_T resolution
- With the above momentum resolutions, δp_T resolution ≈ **~30 MeV/c** (comparable to the SFGD design benchmark from T2K ND280 upgrade studies)
- This is sufficient to resolve the Fermi-momentum peak (~230 MeV/c) from multi-nucleon correlation tails (~400–600 MeV/c), which is the key measurement for constraining nuclear models and reducing the systematic uncertainty

| Source | Current contribution | With upgrade |

| Flux shape | ~3% | ~2% (TKI self-calibration constrains ν-energy reconstruction) |
| CC-QE vs. 2p2h cross-section | ~2.5% | ~1.5% (δp_T shape separates interaction modes) |
| FSI (pion absorption, proton rescatter) | ~2% | ~1% (secondary vertex resolution identifies FSI events) |

## 6. Cross-Checks and Redundancy

**Range vs. curvature cross-check for protons:** For protons stopping in the SFGD, momentum from range (precise) can be compared to curvature in the 0.2 T field (~20% resolution) on a track-by-track basis, providing an in-situ cross-check of the dE/dx tables and field map

**Upstream-downstream comparison:** Events with vertices near the downstream face of the SFGD that also interact in the existing plastic tracking target provide a direct cross-check of response between the two detectors — essential for systematics control

**Michel electron tagging:** Stopped muons in the SFGD produce Michel electrons (~52 MeV, ~3 cm range in polystyrene); the 1 mm cube granularity resolves these as a distinct topological tag, providing an in-situ efficiency measurement for muon identification and a calibration sample for the energy scale

**Proton-neutron asymmetry:** In TKI measurements, the SFGD's ability to identify secondary protons from neutron elastic scatter (a short, large-angle track appearing displaced from the primary vertex) allows tagging of events with significant neutron FSI — currently a leading systematic uncertainty in water-target far-detector predictions

# Concrete Hardware Upgrades for the Next Phase

## Context and Constraints

The core challenge is replacing the upstream photon-tagger with an active target in a 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box that achieves ~4% systematic uncertainty, while reconstructing kinematically complete CC events including large-angle muons (25% > 50°) and protons with median momentum ~450 MeV/c (6% above 900 MeV/c). The downstream TPCs and tracking targets remain, so the new upstream module must feed cleanly into that spectrometer.

---

## Upgrade 1: High-Granularity Scintillator Target — SuperFGD-Style Plastic Scintillator Cube Array

**Technology:** A 3D array of ~1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each cube read out on three orthogonal axes by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres threaded through holes in x, y, and z, each fibre terminating on a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM). In the available box (~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m) this gives roughly 200 × 190 × 60 cubes ≈ 2.3 million cubes, with fibre count reduced by multiplexing along each axis.

**Physics motivation:**

The fundamental limitation of the existing scintillator-bar targets is 2D readout: bars in alternating x/y planes create ambiguities for multi-track events and give poor tracking for angles beyond ~45° because steeply exiting particles traverse very few layers. A 3D cube geometry eliminates this. Every track segment, regardless of direction, crosses cubes in all three projections simultaneously, giving unambiguous 3D hit association with ~1 cm³ voxel resolution.

This directly addresses the large-angle problem: the 25% of muons and 35% of protons exiting beyond 50° to beam are precisely the kinematic configurations needed for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) measurements, since TKI variables are most sensitive to nuclear effects for events with significant transverse momentum. In the existing bar geometry these tracks are poorly reconstructed or lost; in a cube geometry they are tracked with equal efficiency in all solid angles until they exit into the surrounding TPCs or calorimeter.

The ~1 cm³ granularity gives a track length resolution sufficient to range-out protons. For a proton at the median momentum of 450 MeV/c, the range in polystyrene is approximately 9–10 cm, crossing ~90–100 cubes — enough for clean range-based momentum measurement independent of magnetic bending, which is important because the 0.2 T field gives only modest curvature for low-momentum tracks. Range-based measurement avoids the momentum resolution degradation from multiple Coulomb scattering that afflicts TPCs for sub-500 MeV/c protons. For the 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c, range exceeds ~35 cm and those tracks exit into the downstream TPCs for magnetic momentum analysis.

The hydrocarbon (CH) composition is explicitly acceptable per the requirements. Carbon-to-water comparisons are handled by the downstream water-layer target, so the upstream cube target optimises for statistics and resolution on CH.

The active-target concept also maximises the signal vertex density within the constrained 0.6 m depth: the target is simultaneously the interaction medium and the tracker, unlike the interleaved TPC architecture downstream where dead gas volume dilutes the target mass.

---

## Upgrade 2: Beam-Left and Beam-Right TPC Extensions into Yoke Gaps

**Technology:** Two additional small-format gas TPCs (or resistive-plate-chamber tracking planes) inserted into the return-yoke instrumentation gaps on the lateral faces, supplementing the existing scintillator rangers. Each would be a thin (5–8 cm drift gap) micro-pattern gaseous detector (MICROMEGAS or GEM-based) covering roughly 1.8 × 0.8 m of active area per side, using an Ar:CO₂ or Ar:isobutane mixture compatible with the existing gas infrastructure.

**Physics motivation:**

The existing yoke gaps hold scintillator planes whose purpose is to range out side-going muons — they measure whether a muon stops and at what depth, giving a range-based momentum estimate. However, scintillator planes provide only position along the beam axis and a crude range, not the full momentum vector. For TKI analyses, the muon transverse momentum vector (magnitude and azimuthal direction) must be known precisely, since δp_T and δα_T are formed from the vector sum of muon and proton transverse momenta.

A thin TPC in the yoke gap provides a track trajectory measurement: by observing the curvature of the muon in the 0.2 T dipole field as it traverses the TPC volume, the signed transverse momentum is obtained directly. Even a short lever arm in the gap gives a momentum resolution of order 10–15% for the muons that reach there, which is substantially better than range alone for muons above ~500 MeV/c where range straggling becomes relatively large. Combining the upstream cube target's vertex position with the lateral TPC track vector gives a fully reconstructed muon four-momentum.

The azimuthal coverage improvement is physically significant: the dipole field bends in one plane, so the magnet naturally measures momentum in the bending plane well, but the non-bending plane relies on hit position only. The lateral TPCs are specifically the detectors that see tracks exiting in the direction where the magnetic analysis is weakest (perpendicular to the dominant bending), thereby filling the worst systematic gap.

---

## Upgrade 3: Thin Upstream Time-of-Flight Wall

**Technology:** A plane of fast plastic scintillator paddles (EJ-200 or equivalent), each ~5 × 200 cm, arranged as a grid covering ~2.0 × 1.9 m immediately upstream of the new cube target, read out at both ends by SiPMs with waveform-digitising electronics achieving ~100–150 ps single-channel time resolution, and ~200–300 ps system resolution after time-walk correction.

**Physics motivation:**

The leading-proton momentum below ~600 MeV/c is better determined by range (in the cube target) than by curvature, but above that the proton exits the cube volume and enters the TPC gas, where dE/dx particle identification becomes ambiguous at the pion-proton crossing region (~1 GeV/c). Time-of-flight from the interaction vertex (reconstructed in the cube target using the beam timing reference from the accelerator RF signal) to a downstream scintillator plane separates protons from pions. At 700 MeV/c, the ToF difference between a proton and a charged pion over a 1 m flight path is approximately 1.8 ns — well above the achievable system resolution — providing clean PID through the ambiguous momentum range.

This is directly motivated by the 6% of protons exceeding 900 MeV/c: these are precisely the events where multiple-track final states may include pions (resonance production, multi-nucleon processes), and misidentifying a forward pion as the leading proton would bias the TKI reconstruction systematically. Since TKI variables are designed to cancel Fermi motion and isolate final-state interactions, an asymmetric PID contamination would fake a FSI signal. The ToF wall eliminates this at modest cost, as only one plane is needed upstream of the existing downstream detectors, which themselves provide a downstream ToF reference.

A secondary benefit is that the ToF plane provides an independent beam-interaction trigger with ~ns timing that allows bunch-by-bunch pile-up rejection, which becomes important at the higher beam intensity anticipated in the next phase.

---

## Upgrade 4: SiPM Readout Upgrade and Waveform Digitisation for Existing Downstream Scintillator Channels

**Technology:** Replace the existing SiPM + charge-integrating ASIC readout on the lead-scintillator calorimeter and tracking-target scintillator bars with waveform-sampling ASICs (e.g., DRS4-style or a custom 250 MHz sampling chip) retaining the same SiPM sensors, requiring only back-end electronics board replacement.

**Physics motivation:**

The 6% residual systematic uncertainty has a significant contribution from neutral-current π⁰ backgrounds and from photon conversions that fake electrons or additional protons. The existing calorimeter integrates charge in a gate, losing pulse-shape information. Waveform digitisation gives access to pulse shape discrimination: neutrons and gammas produce different late-light profiles in plastic scintillator (neutrons interact via recoil protons with high dE/dx, producing broader and later pulses than minimum-ionising particles or electromagnetic showers). This distinguishes neutron-induced backgrounds from proton tracks at moderate confidence.

More directly relevant to TKI: neutrons from the final state carry transverse momentum that is currently invisible (neutral, no TPC hit, calorimeter response poorly calibrated for hadronic energy). Waveform digitisation allows the calorimeter to operate in a neutron-tagging mode using time-of-flight from the reconstructed vertex (possible once cube-target vertex resolution is ~few mm) to calorimeter clusters — a ~2 m flight path gives ~15 ns ToF difference between a 300 MeV/c neutron and a prompt photon, well within the resolution of a waveform-digitising system. Including reconstructed neutron momentum in the TKI balance reduces the model dependence introduced by missing final-state particles and thereby reduces the cross-section systematic toward the 4% target.

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Systematic Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| 3D cube scintillator target | ~1 cm³ PS cubes + WLS + SiPM | Large-angle track reconstruction; proton ranging |
| Lateral yoke TPCs | Thin MPGD in return-yoke gaps | Muon p_T vector in non-bending plane |
| Upstream ToF wall | Fast plastic scintillator, ~200 ps resolution | Proton/pion separation above 600 MeV/c |
| Waveform digitiser upgrade | 250 MHz sampling ASIC on existing SiPMs | Neutron tagging; background rejection |

Together these upgrades address the dominant sources of the residual 6% uncertainty — large-angle track inefficiency, transverse momentum vector precision, particle misidentification, and missing neutral hadronic momentum — through hardware changes confined to the upstream region and back-end electronics, without requiring modification of the downstream TPC spectrometer that provides the magnetic momentum measurement and the carbon-to-water comparison capability.

## Key Constraints Analysis

1. **Geometric acceptance**: Need 4π coverage including backward-going tracks
2. **Low-momentum protons**: 60 MeV kinetic energy ≈ 110 MeV/c momentum, range ~2-3 mm in plastic
3. **Muon reconstruction**: 25% efficiency at all angles from ~700 MeV neutrinos
4. **Hydrogen content**: ≤20% of target nucleons
5. **Volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m active target region
6. **Existing infrastructure**: 0.15 T warm dipole, downstream tracking chambers

## Proposed Hardware Upgrade

### **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker**

**Primary detector technology**: Extruded plastic scintillator bars with wavelength-shifting fiber readout and SiPM sensors

**Configuration**:
- **Three orthogonal planes** (XYZ) in repeating super-modules
- **Bar dimensions**: 1.0-1.5 cm × 1.0-1.5 cm × up to 2.6 m length
- **Super-module structure**: X-Y-Z triplet (~4-5 cm thick) repeated ~20-25 times through the 0.9 m depth
- **Effective pitch**: ~1-1.5 cm in all three dimensions

**Material choice**: 
- Low-hydrogen scintillator (e.g., polystyrene-based with reduced hydrogen content)
- Or standard scintillator with careful accounting to stay within 20% H-nucleon limit
- CH formulation provides ~14% hydrogen by nucleon count - acceptable

### **Why This Solution Works**:

1. **Short proton tracks**: 1-1.5 cm granularity provides ~2-3 samples for 60 MeV protons, enabling:
   - Track identification via dE/dx
   - Angular reconstruction
   - Energy measurement via range

2. **4π angular coverage**: Three orthogonal views allow reconstruction of:
   - Forward tracks (measured in XY, confirmed in Z)
   - Perpendicular tracks (full length in at least one view)
   - Backward tracks (visible in all views before exiting upstream)

3. **Muon efficiency**: 
   - High detection efficiency for minimum ionizing particles
   - Multiple scattering in 0.15 T field aids momentum measurement
   - Matching to downstream gas chambers for forward-going muons
   - Standalone momentum from range/scatter for contained/backward muons

4. **Hydrogen constraint**: 
   - Can be met with standard CH scintillator (~14% H-nucleons)
   - Or use deuterated/reduced-H scintillator if needed

### **Readout Architecture**:

- **SiPM arrays** (e.g., Hamamatsu MPPCs) on bar ends
- ~3,500-5,000 channels total
- **Wavelength-shifting fibers** for light collection
- **Front-end electronics**: Multi-channel ASICs with time and charge digitization
- **Timing resolution**: <1-2 ns for event building and cosmic rejection

### **Alternative/Supplementary Options**:

1. **Hybrid design**: Core region with finer granularity (0.5 cm pitch) for better proton measurement

2. **Time projection chamber (TPC)**: 
   - Superior tracking for low-momentum particles
   - Good dE/dx for particle ID
   - **Challenge**: Backward coverage requires complex field cage in magnetic field
   - **Challenge**: Slower readout, possible pileup issues

3. **Straw tube tracker in scintillator matrix**:
   - Add stereo straw tube planes for improved momentum resolution
   - Scintillator provides timing and particle ID

### **DAQ and Trigger**:

- **Self-triggering** on beam spill timing
- Activity threshold in target region
- Cosmic veto using outer scintillator layers
- ~10 μs readout window to contain interaction products

This design balances the competing requirements of fine granularity for short proton tracks, 4π coverage, manageable channel count (~5000 channels vs. ~100,000 for mm-scale options), proven technology, and reasonable cost.

- **Charge-sign separation**: Critical for νμ vs ν̄μ separation, important for beam systematics
- **Systematic reduction**: Field uncertainties propagate directly into cross-section measurements; improved knowledge helps achieve 4% target

---

## 7. **Enhanced Monitoring and Calibration Systems**

**Technology:** Multi-system integration

**Components:**
- **Cosmic ray telescope**: Two crossed scintillator planes above detector for tracker alignment and energy calibration
- **LED pulser system**: Distributed LED network for SiPM gain monitoring and timing calibration (daily/hourly)
- **Radioactive source deployment**: Automated system to position ⁶⁰Co/¹³⁷Cs at fiducial points
- **Laser system**: For TPC E-field monitoring and t₀ calibration
- **Temperature/pressure/humidity sensors**: Dense array for TPC drift corrections and scintillator response stability

**Justification:**
- **Stability**: 3-5 year run requires <1% detector response drift
- **Systematic control**: In-situ calibration validates MC and reduces model uncertainties
- **Cross-checks**: Multiple calibration methods (cosmics, sources, beam data) provide systematic uncertainty reduction pathway to 4%

## 8. **Beamline Instrumentation Upgrades (if in scope)**

**Technology:** Enhanced beam monitoring

**Specifications:**
- Additional beam position monitors (BPMs) near target
- Upgraded horn current monitoring (if applicable to off-axis beam)
- Muon monitors in decay tunnel for flux constraint

**Justification:**
- **Flux uncertainty**: Beam direction/intensity variations contribute significantly to 6% systematic
- **Event-by-event weighting**: Precise beam parameters enable data-driven flux corrections
- **Complementarity**: Near detector data + beam monitoring together achieve 4% target

# Design Review Recommendations: Kestrel Flats Active Target Upgrade

## Executive Summary

The constraints drive toward a fully-active, fine-grained tracking volume with high hydrogen fraction control, capable of reconstructing near-isotropic final states including very short recoil proton tracks. I recommend a **scintillator-based active target** using polystyrene-core extruded plastic scintillator bars in a 3D-crossed geometry, with specific additions detailed below.

---

## Constraint Analysis Before Recommendations

Before naming hardware, the driving constraints deserve explicit unpacking:

**Geometry:** 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m. The short dimension is along the beam (0.9 m), which severely limits longitudinal lever arm and means many muons leave through the transverse faces. This is what makes the ≥25% efficiency at *all angles including backward* hard — backward tracks re-enter upstream material and must still be found.

**60 MeV proton kinetic energy:** A proton at 60 MeV has a range of roughly 3.5 cm in polystyrene (density ~1.05 g/cm³). The granularity must be fine enough to reconstruct a track that may cross only a handful of cells.

**Hydrogen fraction ≤ 20%:** Polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ has a hydrogen mass fraction of about 7.7%, giving a nucleon fraction for hydrogen of ~15.4% by nucleon count — comfortably within the 20% limit. Scintillating water or liquid scintillator would be too hydrogen-rich without dilution. This constraint rules out hydrocarbon liquids and pure water targets.

**Isotropic muon efficiency:** The existing downstream drift chambers handle forward tracks well. The problem is sideward and backward muons, which either leave through the 2.3 m transverse faces or turn around inside the target. The 0.15 T magnet (over 6.5 m) gives a bend of order 0.15 × 6.5 ≈ 0.975 T·m, which is adequate for forward tracks but provides little help for high-angle tracks that spend little path length in the field. The active target itself must therefore provide tracking — not just calorimetry — to seed and match tracks at all angles.

---

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. 3D-Crossed Extruded Polystyrene Scintillator Bar Array (Primary Recommendation)

**Technology:** Extruded polystyrene scintillator bars with embedded wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibre readout, arranged in alternating X, Y, Z (beam-axis) planes — identical in concept to the MINERvA fully-active tracker or the Baby MIND scintillator planes, but with geometry optimised for this volume.

**Specific parameters I recommend:**
- Bar cross-section: **1.5 cm × 1.5 cm** (discussed below)
- Bar orientation: alternating horizontal (X), vertical (Y), and diagonal (U or beam-axis Z) planes, providing 3D point reconstruction without ambiguity
- WLS fibre: **1.2 mm Kuraray Y-11** multi-cladding, routed to **SiPMs** (silicon photomultipliers, 1.3 mm² or 3 mm² Hamamatsu S13360 series or equivalent) at both bar ends for position-along-bar measurement via charge asymmetry
- Light yield target: ≥ 15 photoelectrons per end per minimum-ionising particle per bar, to ensure ≥90% single-bar hit efficiency for a MIP

**Justification of 1.5 cm bar width:**

A 60 MeV proton has a range of ~3.5 cm in polystyrene. At 1.5 cm bar pitch, such a proton crosses at most 2–3 bars in the least favourable (diagonal) orientation before stopping. This is marginal but workable: the stopping bar has enhanced energy deposition (Bragg peak), and the bar immediately prior has measurable ionisation. Studies with MINERvA and T2K's FGD demonstrate that protons down to ~50–55 MeV can be identified by this combination of track stub plus characteristic Bragg deposition in a 1.5–2 cm pitch tracker. Coarser bars (e.g. 3 cm) would render these tracks invisible; finer bars (e.g. 0.5 cm) would multiply channel count by a factor of nine and exceed the realistic budget for this phase.

**Justification for polystyrene (not PVC, not glass, not liquid):**

Polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ: H nucleon fraction ≈ 15.4% — passes the ≤20% constraint with ~5% headroom. The collaboration should formally propagate the systematic uncertainty on hydrogen subtraction as a function of this fraction before finalising, but polystyrene is safe. PVC-based scintillator (as used in NOvA) has lower hydrogen fraction (~8.5% nucleon) and would also pass, but has lower light yield. Liquid scintillator has ~18% hydrogen nucleon fraction — also workable but introduces containment complexity and fire safety requirements incompatible with a warm magnet hall. Plastic is mechanically self-supporting and allows the interlocked-bar geometry needed for 3D tracking.

**Addressing the backward/sideward muon efficiency requirement:**

A muon produced backward (cosθ < 0 in beam frame) or sideward (cosθ ≈ 0) in a 0.9 m deep target will travel at most ~0.9 m before escaping the upstream face, or will immediately escape through the 2.3 m transverse face. The 3D scintillator array reconstructs the vertex and initial track direction purely from ionisation patterns inside the target — no dependence on the downstream spectrometer for the direction measurement. Charge sign and momentum for these tracks require additional measures (see item 2).

---

### 2. Upstream Tracking Planes ("Muon Catcher" Upstream Section)

**Technology:** Four to six additional **scintillator tracking planes identical to the main array**, placed immediately upstream of the active target volume, instrumented identically and read into the same DAQ.

**Justification:**

Backward-going muons exit through the upstream face of the target and enter whatever material sits there. Without instrumented upstream material, these tracks are lost after a few centimetres. The upstream planes — covering at minimum the full 2.6 m × 2.3 m transverse face — catch the backward muon and give it additional measured points from which a momentum-by-range estimate can be made if the muon stops, or a crude direction/curvature if it continues further upstream into existing absorber material.

The collaboration should audit what currently occupies the upstream space (beam window, upstream drift chambers, support structure) and clear or replace it with these planes. Even 60–80 cm of additional instrumented depth upstream gives backward muons 4–6 radiation lengths of tracked path, sufficient for the ≥25% reconstruction efficiency target assuming the vertex is correctly identified.

The 25% efficiency threshold is explicitly "at every angle" — this is a floor, not an average. Backward tracks without upstream instrumentation would have near-zero efficiency and violate this requirement regardless of how well forward tracks are reconstructed.

---

### 3. SiPM Readout with Waveform Digitisation

**Technology:** Replace any PMT-based or simple charge-integrating readout planned for this phase with **waveform-digitising front-end electronics** (e.g. DRS4-based or equivalent ASIC such as TARGET or MUSIC) at 250–500 MHz sampling, coupled to SiPMs as above.

**Justification:**

Three specific requirements drive this:

**(a) Proton/pion separation:** The analysis requires identifying recoil protons. At the momenta of interest (~350–600 MeV/c for protons at 60–200 MeV kinetic energy), pion tracks have similar range to protons but different dE/dx profiles. Waveform digitisation allows pulse-shape discrimination and precise dE/dx-vs-range measurement bar-by-bar, supplementing the tracking information. SiPMs with fast timing (σ_t ~ 1 ns single-photon) provide this.

**(b) Neutron rejection:** Neutrino interactions also produce neutrons that scatter in the target. Waveform timing at the ~1 ns level allows time-of-flight discrimination of neutron-induced recoils from primary vertex protons, reducing the fake short-track rate.

**(c) High-angle track matching:** Matching short track stubs between planes at large angles requires precise hit timing to disambiguate combinatoric background. At the event rates expected near a neutrino beam at 410 m (potentially high beam-related backgrounds), sub-nanosecond timing provides the necessary rejection.

SiPMs are preferred over PMTs here because they operate in the magnetic field without gain degradation (unlike PMTs, which would require mu-metal shielding incompatible with the warm dipole fringe field at the target edges).

---

### 4. Thin Lead or Iron Absorber Planes — Explicitly *Not* Recommended

It is worth stating explicitly what should *not* be added: passive absorber layers interleaved with scintillator (as in a sampling calorimeter). While this would increase the total target mass, it would:

- Raise the nucleon-averaged atomic number, diluting the hydrogen fraction — tightening an already narrow margin
- Increase the minimum detectable proton range (the dense material kills the short proton tracks)
- Destroy the fine-grained tracking needed for backward muon reconstruction

The beam flux peaks at 0.7 GeV; the cross-section on carbon and oxygen is well-studied. There is no physics motivation for adding passive material that the analysis systematics do not require, and several strong reasons not to.

---

### 5. Interface to Existing Drift Chambers: Timing and Track-Matching Firmware

**Technology:** Implement a **hardware-level trigger primitive** that generates a 3D seed vector (position + direction) from the scintillator array and passes it to the existing drift chamber readout within the drift time window (~100–200 ns for a warm gas drift chamber).

**Justification:**

This is a firmware/electronics item rather than a detector item, but it is essential to the stated physics goal. High-angle muons that exit through the transverse faces of the magnet bore may clip the downstream drift chambers at large displacement from beam axis; without an active target seed, these hits would not be associated to a neutrino interaction. The seed vector from the target — available within microseconds from a simple majority trigger on the scintillator — allows the drift chamber reconstruction to search the correct region of its volume, recovering efficiency for near-sideward tracks that would otherwise be lost in pattern recognition.

---

## Summary Table

| Item | Technology | Key Physics Driver |
|------|-----------|-------------------|
| Primary active target | 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm extruded PS scintillator bars, X/Y/Z planes, WLS+SiPM | 60 MeV proton range; H fraction; 3D tracking |
| Upstream muon catcher | Same scintillator planes, 60–80 cm depth upstream of target | Backward muon ≥25% efficiency |
| Front-end electronics | Waveform digitisation, 250–500 MHz, SiPM-coupled | p/π separation; neutron rejection; timing |
| No passive absorber | — | H fraction limit; short proton tracks |
| Trigger primitive to drift chambers | Hardware seed vector, <200 ns latency | High-angle muon efficiency in spectrometer |

---

## Open Questions for the Collaboration

1. **Hydrogen fraction bookkeeping:** The ~15.4% polystyrene nucleon fraction leaves only ~4.6 percentage points of margin. The collaboration should verify that any epoxy, support structure, or WLS fibre material inside the fiducial volume does not push the effective fraction above 20% when mass-averaged. G10/FR4 supports should be minimised inside the fiducial volume precisely for this reason.

2. **Upstream space clearance:** The feasibility of the upstream muon catcher depends on what currently occupies the 60–80 cm upstream of the target position within the magnet bore. This should be the first civil/mechanical check before the design is frozen.

3. **Channel count and DAQ bandwidth:** A 1.5 cm pitch across 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m with X, Y, Z planes at 1.5 cm spacing yields roughly (2600/1.5)×2 + (2300/1.5)×2 + (900/1.5)×2 ≈ 3467 + 3067 + 1200 ≈ 7700 bars and ~15,400 SiPM channels (two per bar). This is well within the range of existing neutrino detector DAQ systems (MINERvA, T2K FGD both handled comparable or larger channel counts) but should be costed explicitly.

# Recommended Hardware Upgrades for Kestrel Flats Near Station

## 1. **3D Tracking Active Target with Fine Granularity**

**Technology:** Time Projection Chamber (TPC) with micropattern readout (MicroMegas or GEM)

**Why:**
- **4π angular acceptance:** TPC's electric field drift naturally enables reconstruction of tracks at all angles, including perpendicular and backward-going trajectories relative to the beam
- **Low threshold for short protons:** Fine ionization sampling (sub-mm resolution) allows reconstruction of 60 MeV protons that stop within ~2-3 cm in appropriate gas mixtures
- **Continuous 3D tracking:** Essential for separating vertices from recoiling protons in the crowded near-detector environment
- **Gas target flexibility:** Allows tuning hydrogen content (see below)

## 2. **Optimized Gas Mixture System**

**Technology:** Gas handling system with mixtures like Ar:CH₄:CF₄ or similar low-hydrogen content

**Why:**
- **Hydrogen constraint:** Need to keep H nucleons <20% of total. Pure hydrocarbons would exceed this; CF₄ or CO₂ admixtures provide carbon/fluorine/oxygen targets while maintaining TPC operation
- **Density control:** Gas pressure regulation (1-10 atm) balances interaction rate versus track resolution
- **Stopping power tuning:** Ensure 60 MeV protons produce measurable tracks before stopping

## 3. **High-Resolution Charge Readout Electronics**

**Technology:** Low-noise front-end ASICs (e.g., AFTER or similar) with <2 fC noise, sampling at 10-50 MHz

**Why:**
- **dE/dx measurement:** Critical for particle ID to distinguish protons from pions/muons
- **Low-energy threshold:** Enables detection of minimum ionizing signals from near-threshold protons
- **Track angle reconstruction:** Fine time sampling necessary for tracks at large angles where projection effects dominate

## 4. **Optical Readout Upgrade**

**Technology:** Light collection system with wavelength-shifting fibers or SiPM arrays covering TPC surfaces

**Why:**
- **t₀ trigger:** Scintillation light provides prompt timing to define event start, crucial for drift time measurement
- **Calorimetric information:** Supplements ionization for energy reconstruction of stopping particles
- **Background rejection:** Fast timing helps reject cosmic rays between beam spills

## 5. **Enhanced Downstream Tracking**

**Technology:** Additional position-sensitive detectors (scintillating fiber planes or silicon strips) immediately downstream of active target

**Why:**
- **Muon matching:** Ensures high-efficiency connection between TPC tracks and momentum-analyzed tracks in the gas drift chambers
- **Forward acceptance:** Critical for maintaining >25% efficiency for forward-going muons that traverse quickly
- **Charge measurement validation:** Redundant charge determination before magnetic deflection

## 6. **DAQ and Computing Upgrade**

**Technology:** High-throughput streaming DAQ with GPU-accelerated online reconstruction

**Why:**
- **Event complexity:** Fine-grained TPC creates ~10⁴-10⁶ channels; near detector sees high interaction rates
- **Real-time processing:** Online track reconstruction and filtering needed to manage data rates
- **Calibration requirements:** Continuous monitoring of gain, drift velocity, and alignment essential for systematic control

## 7. **Target Region Infrastructure**

**Technology:** 
- Field cage with precision HV feedthroughs maintaining <1% uniformity
- Cryogenic/gas system compatible with magnetic field
- Minimal dead material in acceptance

**Why:**
- **Electric field uniformity:** Essential for reliable drift and position reconstruction across 2.6 m × 2.3 m area
- **Magnetic compatibility:** 0.15 T field aids charge sign determination but requires E×B corrections
- **Background minimization:** Target nuclei dominate interactions; structural materials create model-dependent backgrounds

---

## Budget Priorities

1. **Core TPC with readout electronics** (highest priority - enables all physics requirements)
2. **Gas system** (essential for hydrogen constraint)
3. **Enhanced downstream tracking** (necessary for efficiency requirement)
4. **Optical/DAQ systems** (important for performance but can be implemented in phases)

This configuration directly addresses all stated requirements: full angular acceptance through 3D tracking, low-energy proton threshold through fine granularity, and hydrogen content control through gas mixture selection.

# Proposed Upgrade for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Target Region

## Summary

Replace the target region with three subsystems, similar in concept to the T2K ND280 upgrade:

1. **A finely segmented 3D-readout plastic-scintillator target** (1 cm cubes, three orthogonal fibre views). It provides the neutrino target, the vertex and the short proton tracks.
2. **Two thin high-angle TPCs (HA-TPCs)**, one above and one below the target. They measure momentum and charge of tracks at large angles to the beam, which the existing downstream drift chambers cannot see.
3. **A time-of-flight (ToF) envelope** around the whole volume. It separates forward- from backward-going tracks and adds particle identification.

The magnet, its 0.15 T field and the downstream drift chambers stay as they are. The design assumes the field is horizontal and perpendicular to the beam (along x), as in ND280. This must be confirmed: the layout below depends on it.

## 1. Target material and the hydrogen constraint

The target is polystyrene-based scintillator (CH)ₙ.

- Per CH unit there are 13 nucleons, of which 1 is a hydrogen nucleus.
- The hydrogen fraction is therefore 1/13 ≈ **7.7% of target nucleons**, well inside the 20% limit.
- For comparison, water would be 2/18 ≈ 11%, also acceptable. Hydrogen-rich options such as liquid hydrogen or methane would not be.
- Small amounts of extra material are allowed: reflector coating, fibres, mechanics and TPC gas. The total should be checked to stay below roughly 9%.

## 2. Active target: 3D-segmented scintillator cube detector

**Geometry**
- Optically isolated 1 cm³ cubes with a TiO₂-etched reflective surface.
- Each cube has three orthogonal holes carrying 1 mm wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres.
- The array is about 200 (x) × 80 (y) × 80 (z) cubes, i.e. 2.0 × 0.8 × 0.8 m.
- Active mass is about 1.3 t, about 1.3 × 10⁶ cubes.

**Readout**
- Fibres are read on one end by SiPMs (MPPCs). These work in a 0.15 T field, unlike photomultiplier tubes.
- Three 2D projections (xy, xz, yz) need about 200·80 + 200·80 + 80·80 ≈ **38,400 channels**.
- The opposite fibre ends are mirrored.
- Target performance:
  - about 40–60 photoelectrons per MIP per fibre;
  - about 1 ns timing per hit;
  - dE/dx sampled in every cube.

**Why this meets the physics requirements**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Every direction crosses cubes at the same 1 cm pitch, so efficiency does not collapse at 90°. This is unlike planar bar trackers, which are blind to tracks lying in a plane.
- **Low-energy protons.** A 60 MeV proton has a range of about 3 cm in CH, so it crosses about 3 cubes. That is enough for a track, a Bragg-peak dE/dx signature and a direction. The proton threshold should reach about 300 MeV/c.
- **Momentum measurement.**
  - Stopping muons and protons are measured by range.
  - Protons are separated from muons and pions by dE/dx versus range.
- **Neutrons.** Neutron interactions also become accessible through isolated delayed hits with ToF.

## 3. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Geometry**
- Two TPCs, each about 2.0 (x) × 0.6 (y) × 0.9 (z) m, fill the remaining height.
- Total height: 0.8 m target + 2 × about 0.6 m TPCs, plus walls, fits the 2.3 m available.
- The full 0.9 m beam length is used.

**Construction**
- Drift is along x, parallel to B, which minimises transverse diffusion.
- A central cathode gives two drift halves of about 1 m each.
- Field cages are thin composite (low mass, so tracks pass from the target with little scattering).
- Gas is an Ar-based mixture (e.g. Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ as in T2K).
- Readout is resistive (encapsulated-resistor) Micromegas modules with charge spreading. This gives about 0.5–0.8 mm resolution with roughly 1 cm pads.

**Function**
- Muons going up or down, including those at 90° to the beam and backward-going ones, bend in the y-z plane in the x-directed field.
- Expected performance:
  - momentum resolution under about 10% at 1 GeV/c;
  - charge sign;
  - dE/dx with about 8–10% resolution for μ/e separation.
- These tracks are matched to target segments.

## 4. Time-of-flight envelope

**Construction**
- Six faces enclose target plus TPCs.
- Each face uses plastic scintillator bars, about 12 cm wide and 1 cm thick, read at both ends by SiPM arrays.
- Target time resolution is 150 ps or better.

**Function**
- **Direction (forward vs backward).** For about 1 m of path, a relativistic track takes about 3.3 ns, so direction is determined unambiguously. This rejects tracks entering from upstream or outside (sand muons) that would mimic backward muons.
- **Particle ID.** It provides additional particle identification for protons versus muons at low momentum.

## 5. Meeting the "every angle, ≥25% efficiency" muon requirement

| Muon direction | How it is reconstructed |
|---|---|
| Forward | Target track, then the existing downstream drift chambers (as now). |
| Large angle (vertical component) | Target track, then the upper or lower HA-TPC, with ToF. |
| Nearly parallel to B (sideways along x) | Little curvature, so momentum comes from range in the 2 m-long target for stopping tracks. Exiting tracks use multiple-scattering momentum plus ToF; charge comes from Michel-electron tagging (μ⁺ decay vs μ⁻ capture). |
| Backward (exiting the upstream face) | Range/multiple scattering in the target plus ToF for direction. Steeper backward tracks reach the HA-TPCs. |

Detailed simulation should confirm the 25% floor in the worst bins (near ±x and straight backward). If needed, it can be improved by:
- extending the target in x; or
- adding thin TPC or scintillator side modules at the ±x faces where the magnet bore allows.

## 6. Infrastructure and integration

- **Front-end electronics:** about 40k SiPM channels (e.g. CITIROC-based) and about 30–40 Micromegas modules (AFTER/DAQ-type).
- **Mechanics:** a carbon-fibre box for the cube array, with services routed through the magnet gaps.
- **Clock:** a common clock synchronised to beam spills.
- **Calibration:** cosmic and laser/LED calibration, and an Ar gas system with monitoring.
- **Rates:** the event rate at 410 m and 0.7 GeV peak flux is easily handled. Pile-up from out-of-target interactions is controlled by ToF timing and fiducial cuts.

## Expected outcome

- About 1.3 t of CH target with 7.7% hydrogen nucleons, compatible with the hydrogen-subtraction model.
- Near-4π muon acceptance with charge and momentum.
- Proton reconstruction at all angles down to about 60 MeV kinetic energy (about 3 cm range).
- Direction-tagged backward tracks.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Active Neutrino Target for the Upstream Section

## 1. Physics Requirements Analysis

Before specifying hardware, I'll translate the physics goals into engineering constraints.

**Kinematic completeness requires:**
- Muon reconstruction: momentum + sign from magnetic bending or range
- Leading proton reconstruction: momentum from range (most cases) or curvature
- Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI): δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T — these require ~10 mrad angular resolution on both tracks and ~few % momentum resolution

**The geometric challenge in a 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box:**
- 0.6 m depth along beam is severely constrained — insufficient to range out most muons, but adequate for proton ranging at the median momentum
- A 450 MeV/c proton has range ~19 cm in plastic (ρ ≈ 1.05 g/cm³), so ranging is feasible for the bulk of the proton distribution
- The 6% tail above 900 MeV/c (range ~65 cm in plastic) will overflow into the downstream TPCs, which is acceptable since those already exist
- 25% of muons at >50° and 35% of protons at >50° demand good 4π acceptance — the magnet return-yoke scintillator already handles side-going muons; the new target must feed tracks into it cleanly

---

## 2. Proposed Architecture: High-Granularity Scintillator Target (SuperFGD-style)

The natural solution, given the available volume and the need for near-4π proton tracking, is a **fully-active three-dimensional plastic scintillator target** — a large-scale implementation of the "super fine-grained detector" concept demonstrated at T2K ND280 upgrade but adapted to this detector's specific geometry and downstream integration.

### 2.1 Active Target Core

**Geometry:** 2.0 m (x) × 1.9 m (y) × 0.56 m (z)

**Construction:** An array of extruded polystyrene scintillator **cubes**, each **10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm**, with one wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibre threaded through each cube in each of the three orthogonal directions (x, y, z). Each fibre exits the cube array face and is read by a **silicon photomultiplier (SiPM)** at the edge — consistent with the existing detector's readout technology.

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Cube size | 10 × 10 × 10 mm³ |
| Array dimensions | 200 × 190 × 56 cubes |
| Total cubes | ~2.13 × 10⁶ |
| Fibre channels (3 faces × 2 ends, shared per row) | ~3 × (200×190 + 200×56 + 190×56) × 1 readout end | see below |
| Fibre rows in x (through 200 cubes) | 190 × 56 = 10,640 fibres → 10,640 SiPMs |
| Fibre rows in y (through 190 cubes) | 200 × 56 = 11,200 fibres → 11,200 SiPMs |
| Fibre rows in z (through 56 cubes) | 200 × 190 = 38,000 fibres → 38,000 SiPMs |
| **Total SiPM channels** | **~60,000** |
| Total mass (polystyrene, ρ = 1.05 g/cm³) | ~2.13 × 10⁶ × 10⁻³ cm³ × 1000 × 1.05 ≈ **2.24 t** |
| Fiducial mass (excluding 1 cube outer shell) | ~1.9 t |

The cube mass fits comfortably within the structural capacity of the region vacated by the 16.1 t photon-tagging section.

**Why cubes rather than bars?** The existing downstream FGD uses bars alternating in x/y, which gives 2D tracking but has known ambiguities for wide-angle tracks and for short (<3 bar) proton stubs. The 3D-connected cube geometry resolves all three projections simultaneously at each point of energy deposition, eliminating ghost hits and enabling robust reconstruction of:
- Very short proton tracks (threshold ~40 MeV kinetic energy, range ~3 mm → resolved in 3 cubes minimum)
- Tracks at large angles to all three axes
- Michel electrons from stopped pions (important for NC/CC separation and pion background rejection)

**Scintillator specification:** 
- Base material: polystyrene + 1.5% PTP + 0.01% POPOP (standard formulation, same as existing bars downstream — reduces procurement complexity)
- Surface treatment: chemical or mechanical diffuse reflector (TiO₂ coating), no separate reflector film needed if surfaces are roughened, which also simplifies assembly
- Light yield target: >15 photoelectrons per cube for a minimum-ionising particle (MIP) crossing one cube — achievable with this fibre/SiPM combination

**WLS fibres:**
- Kuraray Y-11(200) multi-clad, 1.0 mm diameter — same type as existing detector
- One fibre per row, read out at one end; mirror-coated at the far end to recover ~40% more light
- Fibre-to-cube coupling: fibre passes through a 1.1 mm hole drilled/formed during extrusion; optical coupling compound not strictly required but improves uniformity

**SiPMs:**
- Hamamatsu S13360-1325PE (or equivalent): 1.3 × 1.3 mm active area, 25 µm pixel pitch, ~40% PDE at 520 nm peak, low dark count rate at room temperature
- These are already used elsewhere in the detector — same ASIC-based readout boards can be reused or cloned
- Expected signal: ~20–30 p.e. per MIP per cube (accounting for fibre attenuation over ≤2 m length)

### 2.2 Mechanical Structure

The cube array cannot be self-supporting at this scale. The proposed structure:

**Assembly into "super-layers":**
- Cubes are assembled into slabs of 200 × 190 × 1 cube (one z-layer thick, 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 1 cm), held in an aluminium frame with internal cross-members of 0.5 mm wall thickness (keeping dead material below 0.3% X₀ per layer)
- 56 such slabs are stacked in z and bolted together
- The z-direction fibres pass through all 56 slabs before exiting; care needed to maintain fibre straightness — guided by precision holes in the aluminium frames

**Outer shell:**
- 10 mm aluminium skin on all six faces for structural rigidity and light-tightness
- Total added dead mass: ~15 kg — negligible
- SiPM carrier boards are mounted on the six outer faces; x-fibres exit at ±x faces, y-fibres at ±y faces, z-fibres at ±z faces

**Interface to magnet volume:**
- The assembly slides on rails in the z-direction into the upstream slot vacated by the photon-tagging section
- Alignment survey targets on the outer frame referenced to the existing global coordinate system
- The upstream face sits ~5 cm from the new upstream wall of the instrumented volume, leaving clearance for cabling

### 2.3 Readout Electronics

**Front-end:**
- CITIROC 1A or equivalent 32-channel SiPM readout ASIC: integrates charge in two gains (high/low), provides discriminated trigger output, and time-stamps hits with ~1 ns resolution — adequate for separating the interaction time from delayed Michel electrons (~2.2 µs)
- One ASIC per 32 channels → ~1,900 ASICs total
- ASICs mounted on the outer-face carrier boards, with short (<5 cm) flex-cable connections to SiPMs to minimise capacitance and noise

**Data concentration:**
- FPGAs on mid-level boards aggregate 16 ASICs each (~120 mid-level boards)
- Zero-suppressed hit data (charge + time) transmitted over optical links to the existing DAQ farm — data rate estimated at <500 MB/s at beam intensity, within existing DAQ capacity with minor firmware updates

**Trigger:**
- Self-triggering: any 3D-coincident cluster of ≥3 cubes above threshold within a 100 ns window forms a trigger primitive
- This feeds the global detector trigger already used by the downstream TPCs and calorimeters — no new trigger hardware required at the global level

**Synchronisation:**
- White Rabbit timing node (already deployed in the existing detector) distributes a 10 MHz reference and PPS signal; existing firmware adapted for the new boards

---

## 3. Complementary Upstream Veto / Gamma Catcher

The photon-tagging section being removed had an important secondary function: identifying photons from π⁰ decay to reject NC background. The new target has limited radiation length depth (~0.3 X₀ in 56 cm of polystyrene) so photons will mostly convert downstream. However, to partially restore gamma-rejection capability:

**Proposal:** Instrument the upstream face of the new target with a **2-layer lead-scintillator preshower panel**, 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 2 cm total thickness (1 X₀ of lead + scintillator tiles read by SiPMs). This:
- Tags photons entering from upstream (beam-induced γ, or backscatter)
- Uses the same SiPM type as the main target
- Adds ~200 kg of lead — still well within the structural budget
- Requires ~400 additional scintillator tile channels, trivial compared to the main target

---

## 4. Proton Reconstruction Performance Estimates

| Proton p (MeV/c) | KE (MeV) | Range in CH (cm) | Cubes crossed | Momentum resolution (range method) |
|------------------|----------|------------------|---------------|-------------------------------------|
| 200 | 21 | 0.9 | ~1 | threshold region |
| 300 | 48 | 3.2 | ~3 | ~5% |
| 450 (median) | 109 | 11.3 | ~11 | ~3% |
| 600 | 196 | 22.8 | ~23 | ~2% |
| 900 | 448 | 65 | ~65 | exits; matched to TPC |

The range-momentum relation in polystyrene is well-measured; systematic uncertainty on proton momentum from range is dominated by the cube-size binning (~0.5%) and the energy-loss table uncertainty (~1%), giving combined momentum resolution well below the ~4% systematic target for TKI measurements.

For the 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c that exit the new target, the momentum is reconstructed by curvature in the downstream gas TPCs using the 0.2 T field, with matching of the track stub in the new target providing the entry angle — this combination gives adequate resolution.

---

## 5. Muon Reconstruction

The new target provides the **interaction vertex and initial muon direction** to ~5 mrad. For muons:

- **Stopping muons** (range < 56 cm in CH → p_µ < ~600 MeV/c for forward muons): ranged out in the target itself, with better than 2% momentum resolution
- **Forward-going muons above ~600 MeV/c**: exit through the downstream face into the existing gas TPCs, where momentum is measured by curvature — the existing system is unchanged and already well-characterised
- **Side-going muons** (the 25% at >50°): exit through the x or y faces of the new target into the existing magnet return-yoke scintillator system; the 3D hit pattern in the new target gives the exit angle, and the yoke scintillator ranges out the muon and measures momentum from range (resolution ~10% — adequate for TKI at this level)
- **Backward-going muons**: rare at these energies; the 2-layer preshower panel upstream would provide a first hit, and the cube pattern in the target gives the range

**Charge determination for the muon** relies on the downstream TPCs or yoke system; the new target itself is unmagnetised. This is acceptable because: (a) the magnet field permeates the downstream region where most muons are ranged/bent, and (b) the beam produces essentially pure ν_µ CC, so µ⁻ is the overwhelming species — the charge confusion rate is a small and well-understood systematic.

---

## 6. Impact on Systematic Uncertainty Budget

The 6% → 4% reduction requires roughly halving the dominant flux and cross-section uncertainties. The new target contributes as follows:

**TKI observables:** With kinematically complete CC events (both µ and leading p reconstructed), δp_T in the ~200–600 MeV/c range becomes a direct constraint on nuclear effects (Fermi motion, FSI, 2p2h) independent of flux normalisation. The existing downstream FGD-1/FGD-2 + TPC system already does this for forward tracks; the new target extends acceptance to wide-angle protons and short proton stubs.

**Statistical gain:** Fiducial mass increases from effectively zero (the photon-tagger was passive absorber, not a tracking target) to ~1.9 t of hydrocarbon. Compared to the existing FGD-1 (1.1 t), this roughly doubles the CC event rate available for TKI analysis in a fully-instrumented target, reducing the statistical component of the cross-section extraction uncertainty.

**Cross-section-to-water ratio:** The downstream FGD-2 water layers remain. The new target provides the hydrocarbon reference sample with improved acceptance, directly feeding the C-to-water subtraction that constrains the far-detector (water Cherenkov) prediction.

**Estimated improvement:** Published analyses of TKI systematics suggest that extending proton acceptance from ~40° to ~160° reduces the FSI-driven uncertainty on the CC0π cross section by a factor of ~1.5–2. Combined with the statistical gain and the unchanged downstream detectors, reaching 4% total systematic uncertainty is plausible, though the final number depends on the analysis strategy.

---

## 7. Summary of Proposed Upgrades

| Component | Specification | Purpose |
|-----------|--------------|---------|
| 3D scintillator cube target | 10 mm cubes, 200×190×56 array, ~2.0×1.9×0.56 m, ~2.24 t polystyrene | Active neutrino target, 4π proton tracking, vertex finding |
| WLS fibres | Kuraray Y-11, 1.0 mm, 3 per cube (x,y,z), mirror far end | Light collection |
