| Mechanical frame | Aluminium, rail-mounted for insertion | Structural support, alignment |

The proposal reuses the existing magnet, downstream tracking system, DAQ infrastructure, and SiPM/fibre technology already deployed — minimising risk, cost, and commissioning time — while delivering the kinematic completeness needed to reach the 4% systematic uncertainty target.

# Design Review Recommendations: ND280 Upstream Active Target Upgrade

## Executive Summary

The core challenge is achieving kinematically complete CC event reconstruction in a 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope with a low-Z hydrocarbon target, while maintaining sufficient angular acceptance for the 25–35% of tracks exiting beyond 50° and adequate stopping power for the median 450 MeV/c proton population. I recommend a **SuperFGD-style segmented scintillator cube target** as the primary detector, coupled with **time-projection chamber tracking layers** on the lateral faces, with specific ancillary technology choices justified below.

---

## 1. Primary Target and Tracking: Segmented 3D Scintillator Cube Array (SuperFGD)

### Technology
Extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, nominally **1.0 × 1.0 × 1.0 cm³**, each with three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres (one per axis) read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs, 1.3 × 1.3 mm² MPPC). The cubes are assembled into a monolithic array filling approximately 1.8 × 1.8 × 0.58 m of the available volume, yielding roughly **5.8 × 10⁶ cubes**.

### Justification

**Angular acceptance:** The existing FGD architecture — 2D planar layers with bars oriented perpendicular to the beam — has a geometrical blind spot for large-angle and backward-going tracks. With 1 cm³ isotropic segmentation, every spatial direction is tracked with equal granularity. Tracks at 50–90° deposit hits across multiple cube layers regardless of orientation, directly addressing the 25–35% large-angle leakage fraction. There is no preferred axis.

**Proton tracking threshold:** A proton with momentum 450 MeV/c (kinetic energy ~95 MeV) has a range in polystyrene of approximately 7–8 cm, traversing 7–8 cube lengths with ~10 MeV/cm energy deposition — well above single-cube threshold. Even protons at the low end of the distribution (~200 MeV/c, KE ~20 MeV, range ~2 cm) cross at least 2 cubes, giving a track stub measurable by dE/dx for particle identification. The 6% tail above 900 MeV/c will exit the target volume and be caught by the downstream TPC stack, which remains in place; no modification is needed for that population.

**dE/dx particle identification:** Cube-by-cube charge deposition along the track provides a Bragg peak measurement. The characteristic Bragg curve near track end distinguishes protons from pions at momenta below ~1 GeV/c, which is essential for identifying the leading proton without ambiguity and suppressing pion contamination in the recoil system. This directly enables the transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) measurement.

**Target mass and fiducial volume:** A 1.8 × 1.8 × 0.58 m array of 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes (density 1.05 g/cm³, fill factor ~0.90 accounting for fibre holes and gaps) gives a target mass of approximately **1.75 t**, competitive with the two FGDs combined (~2.2 t), within the available envelope.

**Hydrocarbon composition:** Polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ satisfies the requirement for hydrocarbon interactions. The hydrogen fraction (~7.7% by mass) allows hydrogen subtraction via carbon-only runs, and the downstream FGD2 water layers remain available for the carbon-to-water cross-section ratio programme.

**Technology readiness:** The SuperFGD prototype has been beam-tested at CERN (2017–2019 testbeam campaigns); the full-scale SuperFGD is already under construction for the ND280 upgrade. The collaboration has direct institutional experience with this technology, reducing schedule and technical risk.

---

## 2. Lateral Tracking and Momentum Measurement: Thin-Gap TPCs on Four Faces

### Technology
Four planar **resistive Micromegas TPC modules**, each approximately 1.9 × 0.6 m active area, mounted on the four lateral faces of the cube array (top, bottom, and both transverse sides). Gas: Ar:CF4:iC4H10 95:3:2, identical to the existing ND280 TPCs. Pad pitch 7 × 10 mm, drift gap 10 cm.

### Justification

**Large-angle track momentum:** Tracks leaving the SuperFGD laterally at angles >50° will, in many cases, have insufficient range inside the 58 cm cube depth to determine momentum by range alone (a 450 MeV/c proton ranges out in ~8 cm, so it stops inside; but a 450 MeV/c muon, range ~180 cm in polystyrene, exits laterally). The lateral TPCs measure the curvature of exiting charged particles in the residual 0.2 T dipole field, providing an independent momentum measurement with resolution δp/p ~ 10–15% for tracks with sufficient lever arm.

**Charge sign determination:** The magnet field is essential for distinguishing µ⁻ from µ⁺ in antineutrino-mode running. Tracks exiting the cube array must enter a magnetic volume to have their sign determined; the lateral TPCs within the magnet bore serve this purpose for the large-angle population that would otherwise escape measurement.

**Reuse of existing technology:** The same bulk Micromegas technology, gas system, and front-end electronics (after appropriate scaling) are already deployed and understood in the downstream TPC1–3 modules. This constrains the number of new technology qualifications required.

**Instrumentation of only four faces:** The upstream face is adjacent to the beam entrance and is left un-instrumented to minimise material before the target; the downstream face feeds directly into TPC1 of the existing stack, which provides downstream tracking. This is geometrically consistent with the available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box, where the 0.6 m dimension is along beam and the lateral faces have the largest solid angle coverage for high-angle tracks.

---

## 3. Photon Veto and π⁰ Rejection: Thin Electromagnetic Calorimeter Tiles

### Technology
A single-layer **lead-scintillator sampling calorimeter** (2 mm Pb + 5 mm plastic scintillator tile, SiPM readout) lining the inner face of each lateral TPC module, 4 X₀ total depth, tile segmentation 4 × 4 cm².

### Justification

**π⁰ background:** NC π⁰ production and CC events with an undetected π⁰ can mimic signal. A 4 X₀ preshower layer converts >98% of photons above 50 MeV before they reach the TPC drift volume and cause track-reconstruction confusion. This directly reduces the false-identification rate on the leading recoil system.

**Minimal material budget:** At 4 X₀ ≈ 23 mm Pb-equivalent, this represents only ~0.2 nuclear interaction lengths, adding negligibly to hadronic reinteraction probability for pions and protons crossing into the TPC.

**TKI measurement purity:** The TKI variables (δpT, δαT, δφT) are sensitive to nuclear effects only if the event selection is clean. Photon veto capability at the periphery of the target is essential for controlling the π⁰ contamination that would otherwise systematically bias the missing-momentum inference.

---

## 4. SiPM Selection and Readout: Hamamatsu S13360-1325PE (or equivalent)

### Technology
1.3 × 1.3 mm² MPPCs with 25 µm pixel pitch (~667 pixels), PDE ~40% at 450 nm, dark count rate <90 kcps at 25°C, operating at –30°C to reduce dark noise, multiplexed readout using CITIROC or equivalent ASIC at 64:1 channel multiplexing ratio before digitisation.

### Justification

**Channel count management:** A 5.8 × 10⁶ cube array with three fibres per cube generates up to 17.4 million fibre ends, but each fibre services an entire row of cubes along one axis. For an 180-cube row length, there are approximately 3 × (180 + 180 + 580)/1 ≈ 96,000 readout channels (one SiPM per fibre end, two ends per fibre, with one end read out). This is comparable to the existing FGD channel count (~9,000 per FGD) scaled up by a factor of ~5, manageable with the CITIROC-based multiplexing scheme already proven in the SuperFGD prototype.

**Radiation hardness:** At 280 m from the target, the thermal neutron flux is non-negligible. The 1.3 mm² device has lower total pixel count than larger-area SiPMs, reducing bulk damage dark current increase per unit active area over the T2K-II running period (~10¹¹ n/cm² equivalent over the experiment lifetime).

**Timing resolution:** These devices achieve single-photon timing ~300 ps, enabling time-of-flight discrimination between protons and pions at momenta below ~600 MeV/c over the ~20 cm path length across the SuperFGD — a redundant PID handle supplementing dE/dx.

---

## 5. Mechanical and Integration Considerations

### Structural support
The cube array must be self-supporting and thermally stable. I recommend an **aluminium extrusion cage** with 2 mm wall thickness forming a rectangular frame, with the cube assembly inserted as a pre-assembled module on rails compatible with the existing ND280 magnet-bore tooling. Total mechanical weight of the cube array plus support structure is estimated at ~2.0 t, well within the structural limits of the magnet platform as used by the P0D (13.3–16.1 t).

### Gas containment for TPCs
The lateral TPC modules require a hermetic gas volume. A 5 mm G10 skin on each module face, sealed with standard O-ring flanges, is sufficient. The gas system can be a branch of the existing ND280 TPC gas infrastructure with minor manifold modifications, avoiding a new gas-safety qualification process.

### Upstream material minimisation
The upstream face of the new target should have no additional instrumentation — the beam enters through only the aluminium structural wall (~0.3% X₀). This keeps the event vertex well-defined within the cube array and avoids pre-showering of the neutrino interaction products before they can be tracked.

---

## 6. What Not to Do: Rejected Alternatives

| Alternative | Reason for rejection |
|---|---|
| Liquid argon TPC | Cryogenic infrastructure incompatible with magnet bore; long drift time incompatible with 580 mm constraint along beam; overkill for CC-inclusive programme |
| Water Cherenkov target | No track imaging below Cherenkov threshold (~160 MeV/c for protons); proton PID impossible for the dominant low-momentum population |
| Extending FGD bar geometry | Retains 2D blind spot for large-angle tracks; proven inadequate for TKI at current systematic level; not a new capability |
| Emulsion cloud chamber | Read-out latency incompatible with online trigger; no timing for beam-spill disambiguation |
| Scintillating fibre tracker (SciFi) | Lower target mass per unit volume; proton ranging requires much larger depth than available |

---

## Summary Table

| Component | Technology | Primary Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, WLS fibre + SiPM | 4π tracking, proton ranging, dE/dx PID |
| Lateral tracking | Resistive Micromegas TPC × 4 faces | Momentum by curvature, charge sign for large-angle tracks |
| Photon veto | 4 X₀ Pb-scintillator tile calorimeter | π⁰ rejection, TKI selection purity |
| Photosensors | Hamamatsu S13360-1325PE MPPC | Noise, channel count, radiation hardness |
| Readout ASIC | CITIROC 64-channel multiplexer | Channel-count reduction to manageable DAQ bandwidth |

These changes collectively address the kinematic completeness requirement, reduce the dominant systematic uncertainty from large-angle track loss, and exploit the existing magnet and downstream TPC infrastructure rather than replacing it.

This upgrade transforms the detector from flux-focused to precision exclusive measurement capability, directly addressing the 6% → 4% systematic requirement.

Based on the requirements, I propose a **3D fine-grained scintillator tracker** as the active target. Here's my concrete hardware proposal:

## Core Detection Technology

**Extruded plastic scintillator bars with wavelength-shifting fiber readout**
- Bar dimensions: 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm cross-section

## Geometric Configuration

**Three orthogonal plane orientations:**
- X-measuring planes (vertical bars)
- Y-measuring planes (horizontal bars)

- Hamamatsu MPPC S13360 series or equivalent

**Custom front-end boards:**

## Why This Design Meets Requirements

**Backward and perpendicular tracks:** The quasi-isotropic sampling (bars in 3 orientations) ensures tracks at any angle cross multiple planes with sufficient granularity.

**Short proton tracks (60 MeV):** 60 MeV protons have ~1-2 cm range in plastic scintillator, giving 2-4 bar hits minimum—adequate for reconstruction.

**25% muon efficiency at all angles:** 1 cm granularity provides ~6-10 points for typical muon tracks in any direction through the 90 cm depth.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrade for Kestrel Near Detector Active Target

Given the stringent requirements for angular acceptance, low momentum threshold, and hydrogen content constraints, I propose a **3D fine-grained scintillator tracker** as the primary technology, with the following specific implementation:

## Primary Detector: Extruded Plastic Scintillator Tracker

### Core Technology: **Super-FGD style detector**
- **Scintillator bars**: 1 cm × 1 cm × ~90 cm extruded polystyrene-based scintillator (oriented perpendicular to beam)
- **Optical readout**: Wavelength-shifting fibers embedded in each bar, read out at both ends by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)
- **3D cube configuration**: Three orthogonal orientations (X-Y-Z) in repeating layers
  - Each orientation layer: ~1 cm thick
  - Pattern: XY plane (2 layers) → Z orientation (1 layer), repeated
  - Total: ~90 layers to fill the 0.9 m beam direction

### Specific Implementation Details

**Dimensions and Granularity:**
- Total array: 260 cm × 230 cm × 90 cm
- ~26,000 individual channels (260×230 bars per orientation)
- 1 cm³ voxel resolution for 3D reconstruction

- **SiPMs**: Hamamatsu MPPC S13360-series or equivalent (3×3 mm², ~50 μm pixel pitch)
- **Front-end ASICs**: CITIROC or SPIROC chips for SiPM readout with:
  - Charge integration for energy measurement
  - Time stamping (<1 ns resolution) for track timing
  - High/low gain channels (dynamic range 1-1000 photoelectrons)

**Scintillator Composition:**
- Polystyrene base with 1-2% PPO, 0.03% POPOP wavelength shifters
- **H:C ratio of ~1.1:1** (meeting the <20% hydrogen nucleon requirement: ~14% of nucleons)
- Total mass: ~5.4 tonnes

## Complementary Technologies

### Upstream Veto/Timing Layer
- Two planes of **thin plastic scintillator paddles** (2 cm thick, 20 cm wide strips)

- Provides T0 timing reference (<500 ps resolution)

### Downstream Tracking Transition
- **Three Multi-Wire Proportional Chambers (MWPCs)** immediately downstream of target
- 2 mm wire pitch, X-U-V orientation
- Bridge tracking between active target and existing drift chambers
- Minimal material (argon/CO₂ gas): ~0.003 X₀ per plane

## Performance Justification

**Angular Coverage:**
- Three orthogonal readouts ensure sensitivity to tracks at any angle
- Perpendicular tracks: traverse multiple X or Y layers

**Proton Threshold:**
- 60 MeV protons have range ~2 mm in polystyrene
- 1 cm granularity with dE/dx measurement identifies stopping protons

**Muon Reconstruction:**
- Extended tracks measured through full volume plus drift chambers
- dE/dx + range + magnetic deflection provides momentum

### High-Pressure Gaseous TPC (if budget allows)
- **Ar:CH₄ (90:10) or pure Ar at 10 bar** in the target volume

**Advantages of Super-FGD approach:**

This design prioritizes the critical requirements: full angular acceptance, low proton threshold, and controlled hydrogen content, while using established, reliable technology.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Summary of Constraints Driving the Design

Before proposing hardware, let me be explicit about what the physics demands:

- **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles** including 90° and backward — rules out purely forward-instrumented trackers; requires 4π-ish angular coverage
- **Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** — range ~3.5 mm in liquid argon, ~1.3 cm in polystyrene scintillator; this is very short, demands fine granularity or continuous ionization readout
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of target nucleons** — constrains material choices significantly (pure CH₂ or water are disfavored; more on this below)
- **Volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m** inside an existing warm dipole at 0.15 T
- **410 m from target, ~0.7 GeV peak flux** — quasi-elastic and resonance-dominated interactions, modest multiplicities but low-momentum recoils are common

---

## Hydrogen Fraction Constraint Analysis

This is a non-trivial bookkeeping exercise. For common materials:

| Material | H nucleons / total nucleons |
|---|---|
| Pure CH₂ (polyethylene) | 2/16 = 12.5% |
| Polystyrene (C₈H₈) | 8/104 = 7.7% |
| Water (H₂O) | 2/18 = 11.1% |
| Liquid argon | 0% |
| Iron | 0% |
| Gadolinium | 0% |

This rules out hydrocarbon-dominant targets but permits polystyrene scintillator as a component if diluted with passive or non-hydrogen-bearing material. A purely LAr or iron design would have zero hydrogen but those have their own issues inside a warm magnet. The 20% ceiling gives real design freedom if managed carefully — I will design to ~10% hydrogen by nucleon fraction to give margin.

---

## Proposed Active Target Architecture: Segmented Scintillator + Thin-Gap Trackers + Embedded Absorber Layers

### Core Concept

A **3D-segmented plastic scintillator cube tracker**, interleaved with **thin emulsion cloud chamber (ECC) or low-Z absorber slabs**, read out by **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)**, with **resistive plate chambers (RPCs) or thin-gap RPCs** forming outer tracking planes — all operating inside the existing dipole field.

This is essentially a refinement of the approach used in the NINJA and WAGASCI detectors but scaled to this volume and optimized for the stated constraints.

---

## Component 1: 3D Plastic Scintillator Cube Tracker (Primary Active Target)

**Technology:** 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm polystyrene scintillator cubes, each with two wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers along orthogonal axes (X and Y), read out by **1.3 mm pitch SiPMs** (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS or equivalent).

**Why this cube size:**
- 60 MeV proton has range ~2.5–3 cm in polystyrene → traverses 1–2 cubes; still detectable as a 2-cube cluster with dE/dx above minimum ionizing
- 1.5 cm is the practical lower bound for fiber-in-cube assembly at this scale; going smaller (1 cm) would approximately triple channel count and cost without proportionate physics gain given the ~60 MeV floor
- Comparable to SuperFGD (T2K near detector upgrade), which uses 1 cm cubes — at 60 MeV proton threshold 1.5 cm is marginal but workable given the dE/dx of a ~60 MeV proton is ~5× MIP

**Geometry within 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m:**
- Along beam (Z): 0.9 m / 0.015 m = 60 layers
- Transverse X: 2.6 m / 0.015 m ≈ 173 cubes
- Transverse Y: 2.3 m / 0.015 m ≈ 153 cubes
- Total cubes: ~1.6 million
- Each cube has 2 fibers → readout channels: ~3.2 million SiPM channels (before multiplexing)

**Multiplexing:** Use 64:1 analog multiplexing with time-over-threshold readout to reduce to ~50,000 DAQ channels. Ambiguity resolution exploits the 3D topology — this is well-established from SuperFGD R&D. Alternatively, use the "projective" readout with X-Y fiber crossing as T2K's SuperFGD does, reducing channels to ~2 × (173 + 153) × 60 ≈ 39,000 — much more manageable.

**Hydrogen fraction:** Polystyrene C₈H₈: 7.7% by nucleon — safely under 20%.

**Neutrino interaction rate:** At 410 m with ~0.7 GeV peak flux, typical flux ~10⁷ ν/cm²/spill at this distance; with ~1.5 tonnes of polystyrene (ρ ≈ 1.05 g/cm³, volume = 2.6×2.3×0.9 ≈ 5.4 m³ × fraction filled) expect ~10⁵–10⁶ interactions per year — good statistics.

---

## Component 2: Downstream Muon Catcher / Range Stack

The existing gas drift chambers downstream already provide momentum measurement for forward-going tracks. However, to catch 90° and backward muons, add:

**Technology:** 6 planes of **10 mm-thick aluminum absorber** alternating with **double-sided strip scintillator (DSSS) planes** on each of the four lateral faces of the cube tracker volume (±X and ±Y faces), plus a 2-plane DSSS upstream (−Z face) for backward muons.

Each DSSS plane: 5 mm × 5 mm scintillator strips, two layers at 90° stereo, SiPM readout. This provides X-Y hit coordinates on exiting tracks.

**Lateral face area:** ±X faces each ~2.3 m × 0.9 m = 2.07 m²; ±Y faces each ~2.6 m × 0.9 m = 2.34 m²; upstream face ~2.6 m × 2.3 m = 5.98 m².

For backward muons in a ~0.7 GeV beam, the muon momentum can range from near-zero up to ~600 MeV/c. A 200 MeV/c muon has range ~40 cm in scintillator — it will stop well within or just outside the cube tracker, so the range stack need not be deep (30 cm total depth with alternating absorber/scintillator is sufficient).

**Momentum measurement of sideward/backward muons:** The 0.15 T dipole field acts on sideward tracks. For a 200 MeV/c muon traversing 2 m transversely through the cube tracker, the sagitta is:
s = qBL²/(8p) = (1)(0.15)(2²)/(8 × 0.2 GeV/c × c) → ~28 mm at 200 MeV/c

This is ~19 cube widths — easily measured. The cube tracker itself thus provides momentum for sideward tracks via curvature; the range stack supplements this with range-momentum for stopping tracks.

---

## Component 3: Thin-Gap RPC Planes for Triggering and Muon ID

**Technology:** 6 planes of **single-gap RPCs with 1 cm strip readout** (similar to OPERA RPC design), placed at the upstream and downstream faces and two lateral faces.

Purpose:
- Fast trigger signal (RPC timing ~1 ns) to gate the slower scintillator readout
- Muon/pion discrimination via hit topology
- Veto for interactions originating outside the active target

Strip pitch: 1 cm in one axis, 2 cm in the other (stereo). This is coarser than the cube tracker but adequate for triggering.

**Why RPCs and not additional scintillator:** RPCs are cheap per unit area (~$30/channel including gas system, vs ~$80/channel for SiPM+scintillator). The trigger planes don't need fine granularity for position measurement since the cube tracker handles that.

Gas system: Standard mixture of R-134a (95.2%), isobutane (4.5%), SF₆ (0.3%) at ~1 atm. The gas system for ~40 m² of RPC is a small recirculating unit — well within conventional capabilities.

---

## Component 4: Hydrogen Fraction Control — Thin Lead / Carbon Interleaving

To ensure the hydrogen fraction stays demonstrably under 20%, and to give the hydrogen-subtraction model a well-defined reference, I recommend:

**Every 10th layer (Z-direction) of the cube tracker is replaced by a 2 mm carbon (graphite composite) slab** of the same transverse dimensions. This:
- Reduces effective hydrogen fraction slightly (but polystyrene is already at 7.7%, so this is margin management, not necessity)
- Provides a fiducial layer with known nuclear composition for cross-section ratio measurements
- Acts as a multiplicity buffer helping to separate nearby interaction vertices

Alternatively: interleave one water-target plane per 20 scintillator planes, using a **thin water layer (~3 mm) in a sealed mylar bag**. This enables explicit water-scintillator cross-section subtraction for oxygen-interaction backgrounds. Water has 11.1% H by nucleon, which stays within budget when diluted among many scintillator layers. This is the approach used in T2K's WAGASCI+BabyMIND combination.

---

## Component 5: Upgrade to Existing Downstream Gas Drift Chambers

The existing GDCs measure forward-track momentum. They should be upgraded with:

**Technology:** Replace the innermost wire planes with **micropattern gas detectors (MPGDs)** — specifically **MicroMegas with 400 μm strip pitch**, covering the 2.6 m × 2.3 m downstream face.

Reason: The existing drift chambers likely have ~1–2 mm resolution adequate for forward high-momentum tracks, but adding MicroMegas with ~100 μm spatial resolution improves:
- Low-angle track matching between active target and spectrometer
- dE/dx measurement for particle ID (pion/proton separation at low momentum)
- Efficiency for tracks exiting at angles up to ~40° to beam axis

MicroMegas gas: Ar:CF₄:isobutane (95:3:2) or Ar:CO₂ (70:30) depending on required drift velocity. CF₄ mixtures give faster drift (~8 cm/μs) which is advantageous at the beam repetition rate.

---

## Component 6: Photon Detection Supplement — Lead-Scintillator ECAL Wrapping

For neutrino interaction reconstruction (especially π⁰ → γγ background rejection), add a **thin electromagnetic calorimeter** wrapping the lateral and downstream faces:

**Technology:** 2 mm Pb + 3 mm plastic scintillator sandwiches, 10 layers = 2 radiation lengths total. SiPM readout with 2 cm × 2 cm tiles.

This is not strictly needed for the stated muon/proton physics but is essentially free in terms of volume (it sits outside the cube tracker within the magnet bore) and prevents the analysis being dominated by photon systematics from π⁰ events.

---

## Summary Table

| Component | Technology | Key Specification | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active target | 3D scintillator cubes | 1.5 cm, SiPM+WLS, ~40k channels | ν interaction vertex, proton tracking to 60 MeV |
| Lateral/backward muon catcher | DSSS range stack | 5 mm strips, Al absorber, 6 planes/face | 90° and backward muon reconstruction |
| Trigger/muon ID planes | Single-gap RPCs | 1 cm strips, ~40 m² total | Fast trigger, muon veto |
| Absorber reference layers | 2 mm carbon slabs | Every 10th layer | H-fraction control, nuclear cross-section reference |
| Downstream spectrometer | MicroMegas upgrade | 400 μm strips | Forward track momentum improvement |
| Lateral ECAL | Pb-scintillator sandwich | 2X₀, 2 cm tiles | Photon/π⁰ reconstruction |

---

## Critical Engineering Concerns

**Magnetic field compatibility:** SiPMs operate well in 0.15 T (they are not affected by fields below ~1 T for standard devices). MicroMegas are field-insensitive. RPCs are unaffected. The main concern is WLS fiber routing — keep fibers parallel to B-field lines where possible to avoid Lorentz-angle drift effects in the scintillator readout (though this is a second-order effect for cubes).

**Mass budget:** 1.6 million × (1.5 cm)³ × 1.05 g/cm³ ≈ 1.5 tonnes of scintillator. Plus ~200 kg of absorber slabs, ~300 kg of RPC material, ~400 kg of ECAL. Total ~2.4 tonnes — well within typical floor loading for a near-detector hall.

**Channel count and DAQ:** ~50,000 effective SiPM channels + ~8,000 RPC strips + ~4,000 MicroMegas strips = ~62,000 total readout channels. At ~100 interactions/spill (estimated), this is comfortably handled by modern ATCA-based DAQ systems at ~1 Gb/s aggregate.

**60 MeV proton detection efficiency:** A 60 MeV proton in polystyrene has dE/dx ~20 MeV/cm (Bethe-Bloch, well above Bragg peak). Over one 1.5 cm cube it deposits ~30 MeV, producing ~300 optical photons after scintillation efficiency, of which ~15 reach the SiPM after fiber capture and attenuation. With a typical SiPM PDE of ~40%, this gives ~6 detected photons per cube — above a 2-photon threshold but marginal. **This argues for considering 1 cm cubes for at least the central region** (a 60 MeV proton then traverses 2–3 cubes at high dE/dx), or alternatively a lower detection threshold with careful dark-noise management (SiPM cooling to 0°C approximately halves dark rate).

# ND280 Upgrade Hardware Proposal: Component List

## 1. Active Neutrino Target — SuperFGD

**Technology:** ~2 million optically-isolated polystyrene scintillator cubes, 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm, each read out in three orthogonal directions by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres and silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs/MPPCs)

**Why:** The available volume (2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m) replaces the P0D. The critical physics driver is kinematically complete CC event reconstruction: the muon and the leading recoil proton must both be tracked. The existing planar FGD geometry (2D layers alternating x/y) has poor angular acceptance — with ~25% of muons and ~35% of leading protons leaving at >50° to beam, a substantial fraction of tracks exit through the thin dimension of a planar detector before accumulating enough hits for reconstruction. The 3D cubic geometry provides isotropic tracking with no preferred orientation, recovering the large-angle population. The 1 cm granularity gives sufficient dE/dx sampling for proton–pion separation and for reconstructing the short, low-momentum protons (median ~450 MeV/c corresponds to a range of only ~4–5 cm in plastic scintillator, requiring fine segmentation to contain and measure these tracks). The hydrocarbon (polystyrene, CH) target composition satisfies the stated acceptability criterion and maintains continuity with the existing FGDs. Three-view readout with WLS fibres and SiPMs is proven technology (directly inherited from the existing FGD/ECal readout scheme), is compatible with the 0.2 T magnetic field environment, and minimises dead material compared to wire-based readout.

---

## 2. High-Angle Time Projection Chambers (HA-TPCs)

**Technology:** Two TPCs with resistive Micromegas or resistive bulk-Micromegas readout panels, using an Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ gas mixture (same as existing TPCs), placed upstream and downstream of the SuperFGD — and optionally one on each lateral side — with active volumes extended in the transverse plane relative to the existing TPCs

**Why:** The existing TPCs are optimised for forward-going tracks and sit in fixed interleaved positions downstream. With ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons leaving at >50°, tracks that exit the SuperFGD laterally or at high angle need momentum measurement via curvature in the magnet field. Resistive Micromegas pads (the existing bulk Micromegas technology, already proven in T2K) provide 2D hit position resolution ~300 μm, sufficient for momentum reconstruction. Placing TPCs to intercept large-angle tracks — particularly important for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies that require the full transverse momentum vector of muon and proton — ensures the momentum and sign of both particles are measured. The magnetic field (0.2 T) already exists; the TPCs exploit it. For protons at the high end of the spectrum (6% above 900 MeV/c), range alone in the SuperFGD is insufficient and TPC curvature measurement is required. Resistive readout suppresses the ion backflow and spark rate expected with the higher track density from the more massive active target.

---

## 3. Time-of-Flight Detectors (ToF)

**Technology:** Planes of plastic scintillator bars (or tiles) with SiPM readout on both ends, achieving ~200–300 ps timing resolution, arranged as a barrel around the SuperFGD and HA-TPC assembly on all six faces

**Why:** With a dense 3D scintillator target generating multiple short tracks, track directionality (charge-sign assignment of reconstructed track direction, forward vs. backward) cannot always be resolved from geometry alone, particularly for proton tracks that stop inside the SuperFGD. Time-of-flight between the SuperFGD and an outer ToF plane resolves the direction ambiguity and provides independent particle identification (p/π/μ separation) via velocity measurement. This is especially important for the leading proton reconstruction at momenta below ~600 MeV/c where dE/dx bands from polystyrene alone can be ambiguous for the pion background. ToF also suppresses out-of-fiducial-volume backgrounds by tagging tracks entering from outside. Plastic scintillator with SiPM readout is fast, low-mass, and radiation-tolerant, consistent with existing ND280 readout architecture, minimising new electronics development.

---

## 4. Upgraded Electronics and DAQ

**Technology:** CITIROC or similar SiPM-matched front-end ASICs with ~1 ns time resolution per channel, feeding an FPGA-based data concentrator with continuous (triggerless) readout; synchronised to the J-PARC beam timing system

**Why:** The SuperFGD alone introduces ~1.8–2 million new SiPM channels (three fibres per cube × ~600,000–2,000,000 cubes depending on final design), far exceeding the channel count of the entire existing ND280. The existing TRIP-t based FGD electronics were not designed for this channel density or for the 3D hit-pattern reconstruction needed for multi-track events. Triggerless readout is necessary because the 3D target will record beam-induced neutron interactions, through-going cosmics, and multi-vertex pileup that cannot be pre-selected with a simple trigger. High-precision timing per channel (~1 ns) feeds directly into the ToF system and also allows in-situ characterisation of event timing topology for background rejection. FPGA-based concentrators allow firmware-configurable zero-suppression tuned to the occupancy of each sub-detector.

---

## 5. Retained and Refurbished Downstream Systems

**Technology:** Existing TPC1/TPC2/TPC3 and FGD1/FGD2 retained as-is; existing ECal modules retained; SMRD retained; gas system maintained; FGD2 water layers explicitly retained

**Why explicitly listed:** The proposal must justify that the downstream FGD2 (with water layers) remains in place. The stated physics programme requires carbon-to-water cross-section comparison; FGD2 provides the water target while the SuperFGD provides the hydrocarbon reference in the same flux, so no new water-target hardware is needed. The downstream TPCs provide forward-muon momentum measurement with well-understood systematics, anchoring the new detector's performance. Retaining calibrated existing detectors limits the total systematic re-evaluation burden and reduces cost.

---

## Summary Table

| Component | Technology | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|
| SuperFGD active target | 1 cm³ 3D scintillator cubes, WLS fibre × 3, SiPM | Large-angle proton/muon reconstruction, short-track PID |
| HA-TPCs (×2 or more) | Resistive bulk Micromegas, Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ | Momentum measurement of large-angle tracks, high-p protons |
| Time-of-Flight planes | Plastic scintillator + SiPM, ~200 ps resolution | Track direction, p/π/μ PID below 600 MeV/c, background rejection |
| New FE electronics + DAQ | CITIROC ASICs, triggerless FPGA concentrators | ~2M new SiPM channels, multi-track event reconstruction |
| FGD2 + downstream TPCs | Retained as-is | C-to-water comparison, forward-muon momentum anchor |

# Proposed upgrade: a pixelated liquid-argon TPC active target with high-angle and backward trackers

## 1. Why the target must be argon, not plastic scintillator

The usual choice for this kind of upgrade is a finely segmented plastic-scintillator target, like T2K's SuperFGD. The 2% hydrogen limit rules it out:

- In polystyrene/CH, hydrogen nuclei are about 1 in 13 nucleons, roughly 7.7%.
- Water, at about 11%, is worse.
- Adding passive carbon or metal layers to dilute the hydrogen would remove the uniform, fully active coverage needed for 60 MeV protons at all angles.

Liquid argon has essentially zero hydrogen. It also matches a hydrogen-free far-detector nucleus such as argon, which removes nuclear-model extrapolation between near and far detectors.

The detector should be built so that hydrogen-bearing materials stay outside the fiducial volume. These include:

- G10/FR4 field cages
- printed circuit boards
- wavelength-shifting plastics

Their hydrogen fraction should be budgeted explicitly against the 2% limit. With pure LAr it should come out well below 0.1%.

Gaseous argon TPCs were considered and rejected for the main target. At these dimensions they hold only kilograms of target, too little for useful statistics.

## 2. The active target: modular, pixel-readout LArTPC (ArgonCube / ND-LAr style)

**Envelope**
- Outer size is 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m.
- After a thin cryostat, the active volume is about 2.2 × 1.9 × 0.6 m, roughly 2.5 m³ or 3.5 t of LAr.
- That is ample at 410 m, where several interactions per beam spill are expected.

**Modularity for pile-up**
- Use an array of optically isolated TPC modules, for example 2 × 3 modules with 0.5 × 0.6 m footprints.
- Each module has a central cathode and short drifts of about 30 cm at around 1 kV/cm, giving a maximum drift time of about 200 µs.
- Short drifts limit diffusion and space-charge effects, and avoid long, high-voltage drift requirements.
- Optical segmentation lets each interaction be tied to its own light flash, so overlapping events within a spill can be separated.

**Charge readout**
- Use true 3D pixel readout, such as the LArPix ASIC on pads of about 4 mm pitch, rather than wire planes.
- Pixels give unambiguous 3D reconstruction at high occupancy and for tracks at any angle.
- Wire planes fail for tracks parallel to the wires or to the drift direction.
- This is how the "every angle" requirement is met inside the target itself.

**Proton threshold**
- A 60 MeV proton has a range of about 2.5–3 cm in LAr, so it crosses 6 or more pixels.
- Its dE/dx Bragg peak is then sufficient for identification, with a threshold near 40 MeV kinetic energy.
- This works for any direction, including backward recoils.

**Light readout**
- Use thin dielectric light traps (ArCLight or LCM-type with SiPMs) on the field-cage walls.
- They provide about 1 ns spill timing, t₀ for the drift coordinate, and matching between flashes and charge clusters.

**Cryostat**
- Use a vacuum-insulated, low-mass cryostat with thin walls, for example aluminium or stainless steel of a few mm, or a composite.
- Thin walls keep scattering low for muons exiting into the trackers.
- Field cage, readout boards and cryostat must all fit the 0.9 m beam-direction depth, which is the tightest constraint. Locating the cold electronics on the pixel planes helps here.

## 3. Muon reconstruction at all angles

The existing downstream drift chambers cover only forward tracks. To meet ≥25% efficiency at 90° and backward angles, add:

**High-angle trackers above and below the target, inside the 0.15 T field**
- Use thin-gap gas drift chambers or small resistive-Micromegas TPCs (ND280 HA-TPC style), placed above and below the target.
- In the bending plane they measure the curvature and charge of muons leaving at large angles.
- For a 0.3–0.5 GeV/c muon, the sagitta over about 0.5–0.7 m in 0.15 T is enough for charge-sign determination.

**Side and upstream trackers/scintillator bars**
- Place these on the two lateral faces and on the upstream face to catch backward-going muons.
- The upstream face is critical, because backward tracks do not reach the downstream chambers.

**Momentum for contained and stopping muons**
- Use range in LAr plus multiple-Coulomb-scattering fits inside the TPC.
- At peak energies near 0.7 GeV, many high-angle muons are low-momentum and stop, or nearly stop, in the argon or the surrounding material.

**Time-of-flight**
- Enclose the target and trackers with a ToF shell of plastic-scintillator bars read out by SiPMs, with about 150 ps resolution.
- This plastic is outside the fiducial volume, so it does not count toward the hydrogen budget.
- It sets track direction (forward versus backward), rejects entering background from the magnet and walls, and helps separate muons from protons for exiting tracks.

**Muon identification**
- Combine dE/dx in LAr, ToF, and range.
- Where space in the magnet yoke allows, scintillator planes in the yoke can serve as a muon-range detector.

## 4. Integration notes

- **Field effects:** a 0.15 T field has a negligible effect on LAr drift, since the E×B angle is tiny at these drift velocities. SiPMs are field-tolerant; avoid PMTs.
- **Data acquisition:** use a common triggerless or spill-gated system that time-stamps the LArTPC light, pixels, trackers and ToF with sub-ns clocks.
- **Calibration:**
  - through-going and stopping cosmic and beam muons;
  - UV-laser tracks for drift-field and electron-lifetime maps;
  - ³⁹Ar beta decays for low-energy pixel response.
- **Cryogenics:** argon purification and recirculation must achieve an electron lifetime above about 1 ms. Over a 30 cm drift this is easy to meet.

## Summary

| Component | Choice |
|---|---|
| Active target | About 3.5 t modular LArTPC with 3D pixel charge readout and segmented SiPM light readout, hydrogen-free |
| Large-angle coverage | Gas trackers on all faces inside the magnet (high-angle top/bottom, lateral, upstream) |
| Direction and PID | Full ToF shell |
| Forward tracks | Existing downstream drift chambers |

This combination gives:

- 4π muon reconstruction with charge and momentum;
- proton detection to about 40–60 MeV kinetic energy at all angles;
- an argon target matching a hydrogen-free far detector, with hydrogen contamination far below the 2% limit.

# Proposed Upgrade: A 3D-Granular Scintillator Target Between Two High-Angle TPCs, Enclosed in Time-of-Flight Panels

This is essentially the T2K ND280 upgrade concept. The proposal has three hardware elements in the space freed by removing the photon-tagging section, plus matching electronics.

## Why the current design can't meet the requirements

- **High-angle tracks are lost.** The existing targets use x/y bars perpendicular to the beam, and the TPCs sit only downstream. A track at more than about 60° travels along a single bar layer, so it is poorly reconstructed and never reaches a TPC. That costs about 25% of muons and 35% of protons.
- **Low-momentum protons are missed.** Protons must cross several 1 cm layers in both views. In practice the threshold is about 450–500 MeV/c, which is right at the median of the proton spectrum. Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies need roughly a 300 MeV/c threshold.
- **Proton ranges span the whole box.**

| Proton momentum | Kinetic energy | Range in CH | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~450 MeV/c (median) | ~100 MeV | ~8 cm | Contained in the target |
| ~900 MeV/c | ~360 MeV | ~1 m | Exits the target |

  The target must therefore track short stubs in 3D. The high-momentum tail needs curvature measurement in a TPC, inside the existing 0.2 T field.

## 1. Fine-grained 3D scintillator target ("SuperFGD")

**Structure**
- About 2 million optically isolated polystyrene cubes, 1 × 1 × 1 cm³, arranged 192 (x) × 184 (z, beam) × 56 (y, vertical).
- This gives about 1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m and about 2 t, which fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- Cube material: polystyrene doped with about 1.5% PTP and 0.01% POPOP.
- Each cube has a chemically etched diffuse reflector layer about 50–80 µm thick.
- Each cube has three orthogonal 1.5 mm holes.

**Readout**
- Fibres: 1 mm Kuraray Y-11 wavelength-shifting fibres run along all three axes, giving three 2D projections and true 3D voxels.
- Channel count: about 56,000 fibres, one SiPM each. Each fibre is read at one end, with the far end mirrored or aluminised.
  - 192 × 184 ≈ 35.3k vertical fibres.
  - 192 × 56 ≈ 10.8k fibres along z.
  - 184 × 56 ≈ 10.3k fibres along x.
- Photosensors: 1.3 × 1.3 mm² MPPCs with 25 µm pixels (e.g. Hamamatsu S13360-1325 class), on compact PCB arrays at the box faces.
- Expected performance:
  - About 40–60 photoelectrons per fibre per MIP.
  - Cube-to-cube optical crosstalk of a few percent.
  - About 1 ns time resolution per fibre, or about 0.6 ns per cube using two to three views.

**Physics gains**
- Isotropic 4π acceptance for muons.
- A proton tracking threshold near 300 MeV/c, since about 3 cubes are hit.
- dE/dx particle identification in Bragg peaks to separate protons from pions.
- Neutron tagging: neutron secondaries give isolated cube clusters, and time-of-flight between vertex and cluster gives neutron momentum. This enables antineutrino TKI and more complete event kinematics.

**Mechanics and calibration**
- Cubes are threaded on fishing-line or fibre guides inside a light-tight composite box (CFRP or aluminium honeycomb), with walls thin enough to keep material before the TPCs low.
- An LED/fibre injection system is used for gain calibration.
- Cosmic-ray and through-going muon samples are used for equalisation.

## 2. Two High-Angle TPCs above and below the target

**Purpose:** the vertical space left in the former photon-tagging section (about 2.1–2.4 m) hosts TPCs that capture muons and energetic protons leaving at large angles.

**Geometry**
- Each TPC is about 2.0 m (x) × 0.8 m (y) × 1.8 m (z).
- A central cathode gives about 0.9 m drift along x.
- The field cage is a thin laminated composite (aramid honeycomb with copper-clad Kapton strips). This keeps material to about 1–2% X₀ and the drift field near 275 V/cm.

**Gas**
- The existing T2K mixture Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ (95/3/2), which gives low diffusion and fast drift.

**Readout: encapsulated resistive Micromegas (ERAM)**
- About 8 modules per endplate, 32 modules in total.
- About 1 × 1.1 cm² pads.
- A DLC resistive layer spreads the charge over neighbouring pads. This yields:
  - better than 0.6 mm spatial resolution with large pads,
  - lower channel count,
  - spark protection.
- Front-end electronics use AFTER/ASIC-based cards derived from the existing TPC electronics.

**Targets**
- About 8–10% dE/dx resolution for e/μ/p separation.
- About 10% momentum resolution at 1 GeV/c in 0.2 T.
- Charge-sign identification.

## 3. Time-of-Flight envelope

**Layout:** six panels enclose the target and the high-angle TPCs.

**Construction**
- Each panel uses plastic scintillator bars about 12 cm wide, 1 cm thick and up to 2.3 m long.
- Each bar is read out at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs (e.g. eight 6 × 6 mm² devices per end, summed).
- Readout is waveform or TDC based.

**Performance:** about 150 ps time resolution.

**Functions**
- Track direction: distinguishes forward from backward and inward from outward tracks. This rejects out-of-fiducial-volume and magnet-originated backgrounds and recovers backward muons.
- Particle identification by time-of-flight for protons above about 900 MeV/c, where TPC dE/dx crosses the MIP band.
- Cosmic-ray triggering for calibration.

## 4. Electronics, DAQ and integration

**Scintillator front-end**
- New front-end boards using the CITIROC ASIC, which provides dual-gain charge plus timing.
- 256 channels per board, giving about 220 boards in total.
- They are mounted on the magnet frame, outside the light-tight box.
- Board-level timestamping is synchronised to the beam spill clock.

**Integration**
- A common global DAQ integrates with the existing detector.
- Cooling and stabilisation keep SiPM gain under control.

**Unchanged components:** the existing downstream tracker (three TPCs plus the two plastic targets, including the water-layer one), the calorimeters and the side muon detectors remain in place. Events with a SuperFGD vertex therefore have high-angle coverage from the high-angle TPCs and forward coverage from the existing TPCs. The carbon-to-water comparison is preserved.

## Expected impact

- Near-4π acceptance for muons and protons.
- A proton threshold of about 300 MeV/c.
- 3D vertex activity measurement.
- Neutron kinematics.
- A similar or larger fiducial mass on CH.

Together these sharpen constraints on nuclear effects (TKI, 2p2h, final-state interactions) and on flux and cross-section parameters. This is the route to reducing the systematic uncertainty from about 6% toward the required 4%.

# ND280 Upgrade Proposal: Hardware for a High-Angle, Kinematically Complete Target Region

## Why the current detector falls short

- **High-angle muons are lost.** The TPCs sit only downstream of the FGDs. Muons leaving FGD1 at more than about 50° (≈25% of the sample), or going backward, either miss the TPCs or cross very few hits. They then get no momentum or charge measurement, only crude ECal information.
- **The FGD bar geometry suits forward tracks only.** All FGD bars are perpendicular to the beam and give 2D projections in alternating layers. Tracks nearly parallel to the layers (high angle) cross few planes and reconstruct poorly. Short tracks have no 3D view.
- **Protons have a high tracking threshold.** A proton must cross several FGD layers to be tracked, so the threshold is roughly 450 MeV/c, which is right at the median of the leading-proton spectrum. That cuts away about half the protons needed for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI). About 35% of protons are also at high angle.
- **The P0D is now less important.** It is a passive-heavy π⁰ detector whose physics role is largely replaced by water-layer FGD2 comparisons. Its volume can host a better target.

Goals: 4π acceptance for the muon, a low proton threshold (~300 MeV/c), and full 3D reconstruction. Neutron detection would be a bonus. Together these should bring the systematic uncertainty from ~6% toward 4%.

## 1. Super-Fine-Grained Detector (SuperFGD): a 3D-segmented active target

**Technology**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, with reflective chemical-etched surfaces.
- Arranged as roughly 192 × 182 × 56 cubes, filling the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box with about 2 t of CH target.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibres along x, y and z, giving about 56,000 readout channels.
- Each fibre is read at one end by a compact MPPC (e.g. Hamamatsu S13360-1325-type), with a mirrored far end.
- Front-end electronics use CITIROC-based boards for charge and ~ns timing.

**Physics motivation**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three orthogonal views give genuine 3D hits. Tracks are reconstructed equally well at any angle, including backward and at 90°, which recovers the high-angle muons and protons.
- **Low proton threshold.** Protons can be tracked from about 300 MeV/c, since only a few centimetres of range is needed with 1 cm granularity. This recovers most of the leading-proton spectrum below the 450 MeV/c median.
- **Momentum by range and calorimetry.** Stopping protons and pions get momentum from range and dE/dx. Bragg-peak particle ID separates p, π and μ, and improves Michel-electron tagging.
- **Neutron detection.** Neutron-induced proton recoils in isolated cube clusters, combined with ~1 ns per-channel timing, give a time-of-flight neutron energy. This allows full TKI in antineutrino CC events (μ⁺ + n), probing nuclear effects, 2p2h and the energy carried by neutrons.
- **Electron/γ separation and fiducial mass.** 3D granularity improves e/γ separation for νₑ studies. The fiducial mass doubles relative to FGD1.
- **Carbon versus water.** Hydrocarbon is acceptable here. FGD2 stays for the C/H₂O comparison.

## 2. Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs) above and below SuperFGD

**Technology**
- Two new TPCs, each about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m, in the remaining space of the former P0D region inside the magnet.
- Same T2K gas (Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2) and 0.2 T field.
- Lightweight field cage of composite/aramid-honeycomb laminate with a Kapton strip foil. This keeps the material thin, so tracks pass from SuperFGD into the gas with little scattering, and limits dead space.
- Readout by **resistive (encapsulated) bulk Micromegas** (ERAM). A resistive DLC/Kapton layer spreads charge over neighbouring pads, giving better than ~600 µm spatial resolution with larger pads and fewer channels. It also gives spark protection.
- Electronics use AFTER/AGET-ASIC-based front-ends.

**Physics motivation**
- **Muon measurement at high angle.** Muons and the >900 MeV/c protons (≈6%) that exit the target at high angle get momentum and charge from curvature (δp/p ≲ 10% at 1 GeV/c). They also get dE/dx particle ID (<10% resolution). Escaping high-angle tracks therefore receive the same quality of measurement that forward tracks get in the existing TPCs.
- **Wrong-sign separation.** Charge measurement separates wrong-sign backgrounds in antineutrino mode.
- **e/μ identification at high angle.** dE/dx separates electrons from muons at high angle, important for the νₑ contamination measurement.
- **Better match to Super-K.** Super-K has 4π acceptance. A near-detector phase space covering the full angular range reduces model extrapolation from forward-only data, which drives the flux×cross-section systematic.

## 3. Time-of-Flight (ToF) envelope

**Technology**
- Six panels surrounding the SuperFGD + HA-TPC system.
- Each panel is made of 2.2 m × 12 cm × 1 cm plastic scintillator bars read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Waveform/TDC digitisation gives about 150 ps time resolution.

**Physics motivation**
- **Track direction.** Timing resolves whether a track goes upstream or downstream (in or out). This rejects out-of-fiducial-volume and external backgrounds, such as interactions in the magnet or ECal faking backward tracks.
- **Particle ID.** Combining ToF with TPC momentum separates p, π and e where dE/dx bands cross, around 1 GeV/c.
- **Neutron timing.** ToF provides the event T₀ reference for SuperFGD neutron time-of-flight.
- **Trigger.** ToF can supply a cosmic trigger for calibration.

## 4. Supporting upgrades

- **Electronics, DAQ, calibration and SMRD/ECal.**
  - A common new DAQ and clock distribution is needed for about 60k new channels, with a timing reference below 1 ns for neutron and ToF measurements.
  - MPPC gain is monitored with an LED calibration system, and SuperFGD cube response is calibrated with cosmics.
  - Existing SMRD and ECal readout should be refurbished where MPPCs or electronics have aged.
- **Beam-power readiness.** J-PARC's power increase toward 1.3 MW raises pile-up. Faster electronics and per-bunch time separation in SuperFGD (~ns) maintain clean event isolation.

## Expected outcome

The upgraded detector would provide:
- near-4π muon acceptance;
- proton reconstruction down to about 300 MeV/c, with 3D TKI including neutrons;
- improved PID and charge measurement at all angles;
- doubled target mass.

Together these give direct constraints on nuclear effects (Fermi motion, 2p2h, FSI) and on the flux. That is what is needed to push the ND280-propagated systematic from about 6% to the ~4% required for T2K-II CP-violation sensitivity, and it serves as a prototype for Hyper-K near detectors.

Based on the detector description and physics requirements, here are concrete hardware upgrade proposals:

## 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Cube (SuperFGD-style target)**

**Technology:** Replace the upstream photon-tagging section with a ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m active target consisting of 1 cm³ optically-isolated polystyrene scintillator cubes, each read out by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres coupled to SiPMs (~2 million cubes, ~6 million readout channels).

**Physics motivation:** 
- **True 3D tracking** enables reconstruction of large-angle tracks (>50°) in all directions, critical for the 25% of muons and 35% of protons at high angles
- **Low momentum threshold** (~200 MeV/c for protons) captures the median 450 MeV/c leading-proton population
- **Vertex resolution** <1 cm enables clean separation of primary vertices from secondary interactions
- **dE/dx measurement** distinguishes protons from pions for particle ID
- **4π acceptance** within the active volume maximizes kinematically-complete event fraction

## 2. **Thin High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC Insert**

**Technology:** Insert a thin (10-15 cm) high-pressure (10 bar) argon gas TPC with GridPix or Topmetal micro-pattern readout immediately downstream of the scintillator target, within the available 60 cm depth budget.

**Physics motivation:**
- **Argon target** provides direct nuclear-target match to far detector (critical for flux/cross-section systematics)
- **High pressure** achieves ~10% of LAr density, providing sufficient interaction rate in compact volume
- **Excellent energy resolution** for stopping protons enables calorimetric reconstruction of nuclear recoil energy
- **Low material budget** (~3% X₀) minimizes multiple scattering for forward-going particles
- **Continuous 3D tracking** with ~100 μm resolution improves transverse momentum reconstruction

## 3. **Time-of-Flight System**

**Technology:** Two planes of fast plastic scintillator (BC-418 or EJ-228) with SiPM readout at the upstream and downstream faces of the new target volume, achieving ~200 ps timing resolution.

**Physics motivation:**
- **Proton/pion separation** via TOF over ~1 m baseline for momenta 300-900 MeV/c where dE/dx becomes ambiguous
- **Event timing** for beam-related background rejection
- **Neutron detection** via TOF of scattered protons from surrounding materials (crucial for missing transverse momentum corrections)
- **Trigger information** for selecting vertex-containing events

## 4. **Enhanced Electromagnetic Calorimeter Upgrade**

**Technology:** Replace surrounding lead-scintillator with a compact lead-glass or crystal (BGO/LYSO) electromagnetic calorimeter with 2-3 cm granularity in the barrel region flanking the new target.

**Physics motivation:**
- **Photon detection** from π⁰ decay is essential for correcting transverse kinematic imbalance measurements
- **Better angular resolution** distinguishes photons from high-angle charged particles
- **Energy resolution** ~5%/√E improves π⁰ mass reconstruction, separating signal from background
- **Neutron sensitivity** via capture gammas provides additional handle on final-state nucleons

## 5. **Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) Tracking Layers**

**Technology:** Insert 4-6 thin (~1 cm) glass RPC planes with 1 cm strip readout between the scintillator target and downstream detectors.

**Physics motivation:**
- **High time resolution** (~1 ns) provides additional TOF measurement point
- **Low mass** (~1% X₀ per plane) preserves momentum measurement
- **Excellent position resolution** improves track matching between target and TPCs
- **Trigger capability** enables self-triggering on target-originating events
- **Cost-effective** large-area coverage for escaping high-angle tracks

## Integrated System Impact

This combination addresses the 6%→4% systematic uncertainty goal by:
- Increasing kinematically-complete event fraction from ~40% to >70% via 4π acceptance
- Reducing proton reconstruction threshold, capturing more of the recoil momentum distribution
- Providing multiple complementary PID methods (dE/dx, TOF, calorimetry)
- Enabling direct argon-target measurements to reduce far-detector extrapolation uncertainties
- Improving transverse kinematic imbalance measurements through photon detection and neutron tagging

The **primary recommendation** is the **3D scintillator cube + thin HPG-Ar TPC combination**, which maximizes physics reach within the space constraint while maintaining hydrocarbon compatibility and adding crucial argon-target capability.

Based on the constraints and physics requirements, I propose a **3D fine-grained scintillator tracker (3DST)** as the new active target:

## Core Design: SuperFGD-style Detector

**Configuration:**
- ~2 million extruded polystyrene cubes, **1.0 × 1.0 × 1.0 cm³** each
- Arranged in a ~200 × 190 × 60 cm³ active volume
- Each cube has **three orthogonal through-holes** (1.5 mm diameter)
- Three **wavelength-shifting fibers** (Kuraray Y11 or equivalent) thread through each cube in X, Y, and Z
- Total mass: ~4.5 tonnes of polystyrene (comparable to existing targets)

## Readout Technology

**Front-end:**
- **Multi-Pixel Photon Counters (MPPCs/SiPMs)** on all fiber ends

**Electronics:**

- Time-to-digital conversion for <1 ns timing resolution
- Enables multi-event pile-up rejection at the few-hundred-meter near site

## Why This Satisfies Requirements

**Large-angle acceptance:**
- True 3D readout with 1 cm granularity captures tracks at all angles
- No "blind" projections from 2D bar geometries
- Critical for the 25%/35% of leptons/protons >50° to beam

**Proton reconstruction:**
- 1 cm voxels provide ~5% momentum resolution for stopping protons via range

- Handles 450 MeV/c median protons (range ~60 cm in polystyrene)

## Alternative Considered

A **high-pressure argon gas TPC** (10-20 bar) was considered but rejected because:

# Recommended Hardware Upgrades for Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## 1. **Three-Dimensional Tracking Active Target Technology**

**Technology:** Time Projection Chamber (TPC) with resistive micromegas or resistive pad readout

**Why:**
- **Full 4π angular coverage:** TPC provides continuous 3D tracking throughout the volume, essential for reconstructing muons at all angles including perpendicular and backward-going tracks relative to the beam
- **Low-Z material:** Minimizes multiple scattering and allows detection of low-momentum recoil protons (60 MeV kinetic energy ≈ 110 MeV/c momentum)
- **dE/dx measurement:** Enables particle identification to distinguish protons from other hadrons
- **Fine spatial resolution:** ~1 mm or better allows reconstruction of short proton tracks (60 MeV protons have ~2-3 cm range in suitable gas)

**Alternative consideration:** Fine-grained scintillator detector (3D grid of scintillating bars with SiPM readout) could work but would have higher effective Z and more mass.

## 2. **Low-Z, Hydrogen-Rich Target Medium**

**Technology:** Hydrocarbon gas mixture (e.g., CH₄-based) at 1-3 bar, or pure hydrogen with argon/CF₄ admixture

**Why:**
- **Hydrogen content requirement:** Need substantial hydrogen (but <20% of nucleons) for model-dependent subtraction
- **CH₄ or similar:** Provides ~25% hydrogen by nucleon count (4H + 12C = 4/16 nucleons), meeting the constraint while maintaining reasonable density
- **Gas medium advantages:** 
  - Uniform, well-characterized target
  - Compatible with TPC drift requirements
  - Low density reduces secondary interactions
  - Tunable via pressure to optimize event rate vs. pattern recognition

**Pressure optimization:** Higher pressure (2-3 bar) increases interaction rate while maintaining good tracking.

## 3. **High-Granularity Readout Electronics**

**Technology:** Multi-channel ASICs with continuous sampling (e.g., AGET, AFTER chips) at 10-25 MHz

**Why:**
- **Track separation:** At 410 m from target with ~0.7 GeV beam, expect significant neutrino event rate; need time resolution to separate interactions
- **Multiple track reconstruction:** Complex final states require fine segmentation
- **Charge measurement:** For dE/dx-based particle ID and energy reconstruction of stopping particles
- **Dead-time minimization:** Continuous sampling ensures 25% efficiency requirement is met uniformly across angles

**Scale:** For 2.6 m × 2.3 m readout plane with ~1 cm pad pitch: ~60,000 channels required

## 4. **Field Cage and HV System**

**Technology:** Field cage with resistive strip/chain voltage dividers, stable HV supply (20-50 kV)

**Why:**
- **Uniform drift field:** Essential for accurate 3D reconstruction across 90 cm drift distance
- **E/p ratio optimization:** Typically 400-1000 V/cm in gas TPC for good drift properties
- **Compatibility with magnetic field:** 0.15 T B-field perpendicular to drift requires careful E×B optimization

## 5. **Upgraded DAQ and Computing Infrastructure**

**Technology:** High-bandwidth DAQ (>10 GB/s), GPU-based online reconstruction, expanded storage

**Why:**
- **Data volume:** 60,000 channels × 25 MHz × continuous running generates TB/day
- **Online processing:** Pattern recognition in 3D with multiple tracks requires significant computing
- **Calibration data:** Need extensive monitoring of gas properties, E-field uniformity, electronics response

## 6. **Gas Handling System**

**Technology:** Recirculation system with purification (O₂, H₂O removal to <ppm levels)

**Why:**
- **Electronegative impurities:** Must maintain electron drift over 90 cm; O₂ and H₂O dramatically reduce electron lifetime
- **Cost efficiency:** Recirculation essential for expensive gas mixtures
- **Safety:** For hydrocarbon gases, need leak detection and ventilation

## 7. **Calibration Systems**

**Technology:** 
- Laser calibration system for drift velocity mapping
- Cosmic ray trigger system
- Radioactive source deployment system

**Why:**
- **Drift velocity monitoring:** Must track time-dependent variations in gas properties
- **Spatial calibration:** Verify field uniformity and reconstruction algorithms
- **Energy scale:** Cosmic muons provide minimum-ionizing reference; sources calibrate low-energy response for 60 MeV protons

## Budget Considerations

The proposal should emphasize that the TPC technology provides the **only realistic path** to meeting the simultaneous requirements of:
- 4π angular acceptance (backward/perpendicular tracks)
- Low-Z for short proton tracks
- Sufficient hydrogen content
- 25% efficiency uniformly across angles

The ~60,000-channel readout represents the dominant cost driver.

This is a fascinating detector upgrade challenge. Let me analyze the constraints and propose a solution.

## Key Requirements Analysis

1. **Active target volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (beam direction)
2. **Track reconstruction needs**:
   - Muons at all angles (including backward) with ≥25% efficiency
   - Protons down to ~60 MeV KE at all angles
   - Short, stopping tracks must be measurable
3. **Composition constraint**: ≤2% hydrogen by nucleon count
4. **Environment**: 0.15 T field, existing gas chambers downstream

## Critical Physics Considerations

- **60 MeV protons** have ranges of ~10-20 mm in typical materials
- **Backward/perpendicular muons** need 3D tracking without relying on downstream chambers
- **Low hydrogen fraction** rules out liquid scintillator, plastic scintillator, or hydrocarbon-based TPCs
- Need **dE/dx** for particle ID to separate protons from pions

## Proposed Solution: **High-Pressure Argon TPC with Resistive Micromegas Readout**

### Core Design

**Time Projection Chamber with:**
- **Gas mixture**: Ar + 1% CH₄ (provides <1% H by nucleon count while ensuring stable operation)
- **Pressure**: 5-10 bar (increases stopping power, contains 60 MeV protons in ~5-10 cm)
- **Drift direction**: Perpendicular to beam (horizontal drift to avoid track distortion in B-field along beam)
- **Maximum drift distance**: 1.15-1.3 m (half the width)

### Readout System

**Resistive Micromegas on both sides** (±1.3 m):
- **Pixel pitch**: 3 mm × 3 mm (provides adequate spatial resolution)
- **Readout planes**: 2.6 m × 0.9 m each side
- **Total channels**: ~500,000 per side (manageable with modern ASICs)
- **Time sampling**: 20-40 MHz (provides ~2 mm z-resolution at typical drift velocities)

### Why This Works

1. **Low hydrogen**: Ar-based with minimal CH₄ gives ~0.5-1% H by nucleon
2. **Short proton tracks**: High pressure + pixel readout captures 60 MeV protons in measurable tracks
3. **All-angle coverage**: True 3D reconstruction doesn't rely on downstream chambers
4. **Particle ID**: Excellent dE/dx resolution in TPC (5-10%) separates p/π/μ
5. **Backward tracks**: Horizontal drift means backward tracks project fully onto readout planes

### Additional Hardware

**Field cage**:
- Resistive strips or chains (Kapton-based) on inner surfaces
- 250-500 V/cm drift field (perpendicular to 0.15 T B-field)

**Cathode plane**: 
- Central high-voltage plane at maximum drift distance

**Calibration systems**:
- UV laser tracks for drift velocity monitoring
- Radioactive source deployment (e.g., ²²²Rn injection)

**DAQ upgrades**:
- Self-triggering electronics (existing ND280 or ProtoDUNE-style)
- ~1 million channels total
- 10 kHz trigger rate capability

### Alternative If Space/Cost Constrained

**3D segmented scintillator cubes** (1-2 cm³) with SiPM readout:
- Polystyrene-based (minimizes H, ~8% by nucleon - marginal)
- Full 3D reconstruction with timing
- Simpler but worse particle ID and borderline on H-content

## Recommendation

The **high-pressure argon TPC** is optimal because it uniquely satisfies the strict hydrogen constraint while providing excellent 3D tracking, particle ID, and containment for low-energy protons at all angles. The technology is proven (ALICE, T2K ND280 upgrade concepts, DUNE) and scalable to this volume.

# Recommendation: Replace the P0D with a 3D-Granular Scintillator Target, High-Angle TPCs and a Time-of-Flight Envelope

## 1. Why the present design cannot meet the goal

The FGDs and the forward TPC stack were optimised for forward-going muons. Two features limit them:

- **Orientation.** FGD bars are perpendicular to the beam and arranged in alternating x/y layers. Each layer is a single 2D projection, so the detector gives no true 3D view.
- **Acceptance gaps.** A track at more than about 60–70° crosses many bars within one layer and few layers. Such tracks are short, ambiguous in reconstruction and miss the downstream TPCs.

With about 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons above 50°, this geometric hole becomes a model-dependent acceptance correction. Low-momentum protons give only a few hits in two views, which degrades the vertex activity needed for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI).

Reaching about 4% systematic uncertainty therefore needs three things: near-4π muon acceptance, a low proton threshold, and isotropic tracking.

## 2. Recommended hardware

### A. Active target: "SuperFGD", a 3D matrix of 1 cm scintillator cubes

**Design**
- About 192 × 184 × 56 extruded polystyrene cubes (1 × 1 × 1 cm³), each with a reflective chemically etched surface.
- Each cube carries three orthogonal 1.5 mm holes threaded with Y-11 WLS fibres.
- The array is about 1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m, which fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box with room for the support frame and light-tight box.
- Mass is about 2 t of CH, roughly double FGD1 + FGD2. This gives higher statistics, and hydrocarbon is acceptable for this programme.
- Readout is about 56,000 channels (192·184 + 192·56 + 184·56). Each fibre has one end on a 1.3 mm MPPC (Hamamatsu S13360-class) and the other end mirrored.

**Justification**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three orthogonal projections give an unambiguous 3D image with the same response at any angle. This includes the 25% of muons and 35% of protons above 50°.
- **Low proton threshold.** A 300 MeV/c proton (kinetic energy about 47 MeV) ranges about 2 cm in plastic, so it crosses 2–3 cubes and is reconstructable. The median 450 MeV/c proton (about 100 MeV) ranges about 8 cm. That is many cubes, giving good range-based momentum and dE/dx particle ID.
  - By contrast, FGD-style 2D layering effectively loses protons below about 450 MeV/c, roughly half the sample.
- **Light yield.** About 40–60 photoelectrons per fibre per MIP gives high hit efficiency and dE/dx particle ID for p/π/μ separation.
- **Timing.** Sub-ns timing per cube (about 1 ns per fibre, better when combined) allows neutron detection by time-of-flight between the vertex and a secondary-interaction cube. This enables full TKI in antineutrino CC events (μ⁺ + n).
- **Readout compatibility.** The same WLS + MPPC technology already used throughout ND280 keeps the calibration and DAQ heritage, read out with CITIROC-based front-end boards.

**Alternatives rejected**
- *Bar-based FGD extension:* has the high-angle gap described above.
- *Liquid argon:* cryogenics are impractical inside the magnet and the target nucleus changes.
- *Water-based liquid scintillator:* insufficient granularity. Carbon–water comparison is in any case kept by FGD2.

### B. Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs) above and below the new target

**Design**
- Each HA-TPC is about 2.0 m (along beam) × 0.8 m × 1.8 m.
- Gas: the same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2 as the existing TPCs.
- Thin, light composite field cages (aramid/honeycomb laminate) to minimise multiple scattering and conversions.
- Readout uses **resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive-anode, "ERAM")** modules.

**Justification**
- **Momentum and charge for high-angle tracks.** The SuperFGD alone can only range out stopping tracks. High-angle muons, and the roughly 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c (kinetic energy about 360 MeV, range well beyond 1 m, often re-interacting), escape vertically. They need curvature measurement in the 0.2 T field and dE/dx particle ID.
- **Resolution targets.** About 10% momentum resolution near 1 GeV/c and about 10% dE/dx resolution, matching the existing TPCs, so e/μ/p separation stays consistent across the detector.
- **Why resistive Micromegas.** The resistive layer spreads the avalanche charge over neighbouring pads. This gives:
  - better than 0.8 mm spatial resolution with larger pads (about 1 × 1 cm²), which cuts the channel count and cost;
  - spark protection without complex protection circuitry.
- **Reuse.** Gas, slow control and analysis tools can be reused from the existing TPCs.

### C. Time-of-Flight (ToF) envelope around the new target and HA-TPCs

**Design**
- Six planes enclosing the new upstream assembly.
- Each plane is made of plastic scintillator bars (about 220 × 12 × 1 cm³), read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Target time resolution is about 150 ps.

**Justification**
- **Track direction.** Distinguishes inward from outward tracks, rejecting backgrounds from interactions in the magnet, ECal and other out-of-fiducial material, which are significant for high-angle selections.
- **Particle ID.** Adds a timing measurement that improves PID for exiting tracks, especially p/μ separation and e/μ separation at momenta where dE/dx bands cross.
- **Calibration and triggering.** Provides a cosmic trigger and a precise t₀ for the TPCs and SuperFGD.

### D. Supporting changes

- **Removal.** Fully remove the P0D (with its water, brass and lead). Retain or refurbish the P0D-region ECal where possible to keep photon and electron containment.
- **Front-end electronics.** Common upgraded electronics for the SuperFGD and ToF.
- **DAQ integration.** HA-TPC readout integrated into the existing global DAQ and clock distribution.
- **Calibration.** In-situ systems:
  - LED or laser light injection for the MPPCs;
  - cosmic-ray and through-going muon calibration;
  - a laser or photoelectric calibration of the HA-TPC drift.
- **Unchanged downstream.** Keep the downstream TPC–FGD1–TPC–FGD2–TPC tracker unchanged. FGD2's water layers continue to provide the carbon-to-water comparison, and the overlap between old and new systems allows cross-calibration.

## 3. Expected impact

| Requirement | Present ND280 | With upgrade |
|---|---|---|
| Muon acceptance | Mostly forward | Near-4π (SuperFGD + HA-TPCs + ToF) |
| Proton threshold | ~450 MeV/c | ~300 MeV/c, isotropic |
| High-momentum protons (>900 MeV/c) | Poorly measured | Curvature in HA-TPCs |
| Neutrons | None | ToF within SuperFGD |
| CH target mass | ~2.2 t (FGD1 + FGD2) | +~2 t |
| Kinematic completeness for TKI | Partial | μ + p (ν) and μ⁺ + n (ν̄) |

The combination yields kinematically complete CC events with a phase space matched to Super-Kamiokande's 4π acceptance. This reduces the model dependence of the flux and cross-section extrapolation, which is the dominant route from about 6% to the about 4% systematic uncertainty required for T2K-II.

## 4. Key risks to track

- **Cube production and assembly.** Dimensional tolerance (about ±30 µm) is needed so that fibres can be threaded through about 2 million cubes.
- **Light crosstalk between cubes.** Mitigate with reflector quality control and calibrate it.
- **HA-TPC field-cage uniformity and gas tightness** with thin composite walls.
- **SiPM and MPPC noise and timing calibration** across about 60,000 channels.

Prototype beam tests should precede full construction to verify light yield, timing, crosstalk, and Micromegas resolution.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrade for ND280: SuperFGD

Given the stringent requirements for kinematically complete charged-current event reconstruction with large-angle particles, I propose replacing the P0D with a **3D-segmented plastic scintillator cube detector** with the following specifications:

## Core Technology: SuperFGD-style 3D Scintillator Cube

### Basic Configuration
