## Physics Justification for Key Choices

The 1 cm cube granularity is the central choice and deserves explicit justification. A **450 MeV/c proton** has a range in polystyrene of approximately 9 cm (from Bethe-Bloch, stopping power ~40 MeV·cm²/g at this momentum), giving a 9-cube track — sufficient for direction reconstruction and range-based momentum measurement to ~5–10%. A **200 MeV/c proton** (range ~2 cm) gives a 2-cube stub, which with 3D coincidence is still reconstructible as a short track rather than a point deposit, distinguishing it from a neutron scatter. This is the threshold below which the TKI programme accepts some inefficiency. The 1 cm scale also means that at the 0.6 GeV beam peak, the typical CC interaction produces a vertex resolvable from the muon and proton tracks — there is no ambiguity about which particle is the leading proton that would arise in a coarser detector. The 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c will exit the cube array (~85 cm range), but their direction is well-measured in the cube array and they enter the downstream TPCs, providing momentum measurement by curvature in the 0.2 T field — the two systems are complementary.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Kestrel Flats Near Station Active Target

## Physics-Driven Requirements Summary

Before proposing hardware, let me extract the hard constraints:

| Requirement | Implication |
|---|---|
| Muon efficiency ≥25% at **all** angles including 90° and backward | Cannot rely on forward-going track topology; need 4π-sensitive tracking |
| Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy | Range ~3.5 cm in water; need fine-grained, low-density OR high-resolution dE/dx |
| H fraction ≤20% of target nucleons | Limits how hydrogen-rich the active material can be |
| Fit inside 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m | Tight transverse envelope, shallow along beam |
| Existing downstream drift chambers + 0.15 T dipole for muon momentum | Active target must be compatible with tracks exiting into existing spectrometer |

---

## Proposed Upgrades

### 1. Plastic Scintillator 3D-Granular Core ("SuperCube" array)

**What:** Replace the passive target material with a fully-active array of extruded polystyrene scintillator **cubes**, 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm, read out on three orthogonal faces by **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers** routed to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs).

**Why this geometry:**

- Three-view fiber readout (X, Y, Z projections) gives unambiguous 3D hit reconstruction without requiring stereo wire planes—critical for the high-multiplicity, isotropic topology.
- 1.5 cm cube pitch → ~3 cm³ voxel. A 60 MeV proton has a range of ~3–4 cm in polystyrene (density ~1.05 g/cm³), giving 2–3 hit cubes: reconstructable as a stub track with dE/dx identification.
- A 90° or backward muon that travels even one cube-length deposits a measurable, isolated hit pattern distinguishable from nuclear fragments by dE/dx (Birks-saturated light yield separates pions, protons, muons cleanly).
- Polystyrene is ~92% carbon, ~8% hydrogen **by mass**. By nucleon count: CH ratio gives H/(C+H) ≈ 8/(96+8) ≈ **~8% hydrogen nucleons** — comfortably under the 20% ceiling, leaving margin for structural material.

**Scale:** Filling 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m³ with 1.5 cm cubes gives roughly **170 × 153 × 60 ≈ 1.56 million cubes**. This is large but precedented (the technology is directly derived from the NINJA/WA105 and especially the **SuperFGD** built for T2K, whose 2×1.8×0.6 m³ module contains ~2 million 1 cm cubes).

**Readout:** Three WLS fibers per cube face (X, Y, Z), one SiPM per fiber end (or per fiber with mirrored far end). Total SiPM channel count ~3 × (N_X + N_Y + N_Z) fibers; with fiber multiplexing along rows this is manageable at ~200k–300k channels. Use SiPMs with 1 mm² active area, ~35% PDE at 450 nm (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK NUV-HD).

---

### 2. Thin Beam-Perpendicular Scintillating-Fiber Planes at the Upstream Face and Downstream Face

**What:** Two planes of **0.5 mm diameter scintillating fibers** (e.g., Kuraray SCSF-78) arranged in X–Y doublets, one plane at the upstream face of the cube array (z = 0) and one at the downstream face (z = 0.9 m), each ~2.6 m × 2.3 m.

**Why:**

- Provides a high-resolution entrance/exit veto and trigger seed. Fibers at 0.5 mm pitch give ~150 μm position resolution in the transverse plane.
- Backward-going muons that re-enter the upstream face are tagged with their exit point before entering the upstream beam infrastructure—prevents misidentification as beam halo.
- The downstream plane gives a precision handoff point for tracks entering the drift-chamber spectrometer, reducing lever-arm extrapolation errors from the coarser cube granularity.

---

### 3. Upgrade of the Surrounding Magnet Yoke Inner Wall with Thin Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) or Thin-Gap Chambers (TGCs)

**What:** Line the four non-beam faces of the active target volume (top, bottom, left, right walls) with **single-gap glass RPCs**, 2–3 mm gas gap, strip readout at 1 cm pitch in both coordinates, operated in avalanche mode.

**Why:**

- A truly 90°-going muon (perpendicular to beam) exits through one of these lateral walls. The RPC layer catches it and provides a precise exit hit for momentum measurement via curvature in the existing dipole field (which bends tracks horizontally—so at least the horizontal component of a sideways track is measured).
- RPCs are thin (~8 mm per layer including electrodes and gas gap), low-mass, and large-area—ideal for lining a magnet yoke interior without occupying significant fiducial volume.
- Two RPC layers separated by ~5 cm on each wall give a local track direction at the boundary, constraining the angle for the momentum handoff.
- Efficiency >95% per layer at standard avalanche operating point; two layers give redundancy.

**Note on backward muons:** A backward-going muon exits through the upstream face of the cube array and then travels back through the beam line infrastructure. The scintillating-fiber plane at the upstream face tags this exit. Such tracks are inherently short in the near-station geometry; their momentum will be poorly measured by the downstream spectrometer (they never enter it), but can be estimated from range within the cube array + possible additional instrumentation upstream. See item 5.

---

### 4. Thin Radiator / Converter Layers Interleaved Every ~15 cm Along z (Optional Upgrade for γ Reconstruction)

**What:** Thin (3 mm) lead sheets interleaved at every ~10 cube layers along the beam direction, with associated scintillating fiber sandwich planes.

**Why (optional):** π⁰ → γγ reconstruction benefits from early photon conversion. However, this adds material and raises average nuclear A, so it should be considered only if the physics program explicitly needs π⁰ kinematics. At 0.7 GeV peak flux, quasi-elastic interactions dominate and π⁰ production is secondary. **Recommend deferring this sub-upgrade** unless the oscillation analysis later requires NC π⁰ background characterization—the cube array's light yield already allows rough γ-ray shower tagging.

---

### 5. Upstream Mini-Spectrometer for Backward-Going Tracks

**What:** Immediately upstream of the active target (in existing beam-line space, within ~50 cm), install **two stations of drift tubes or straw tubes** (4 mm diameter, two X–Y planes each station) sandwiched around a **thin permanent magnet slab** (e.g., a 10 cm thick, 0.5 T samarium-cobalt or ferrite block, 2.6 m × 2.3 m effective aperture — tiled from smaller magnets).

**Why:**

- Backward muons that exit through the upstream face must have their momentum measured *somewhere*. The existing downstream dipole does not see them.
- A short baseline (two stations ~20–30 cm apart) with even a modest field integral (B·L ~ 0.05 T·m) gives momentum resolution σ_p/p ~ 20–30% for muons of a few hundred MeV — adequate for a cross-section measurement.
- Straw tubes are radiation-hard and low-mass per unit area; a two-station system adds ~1–2% X₀ to the upstream material budget.
- **This is the single most important addition** for the backward-track efficiency requirement, since no existing hardware serves this role.

---

### 6. Trigger and DAQ Upgrades

**What:** 
- Replace any existing NIM/CAMAC trigger logic with a **fully-pipelined SiPM readout ASIC** system (e.g., CITIROC or TARGET ASICs), with zero-suppressed readout and ~10 ns timestamp resolution.
- Implement a **hardware-level cluster trigger**: fire on any pattern of ≥3 adjacent cubes above threshold within a 100 ns window, in any orientation—this is topology-agnostic and fires on 90° tracks and backward tracks without bias toward forward-going multiplicity.
- For the RPCs and straw tubes: use TDC-based readout (e.g., CAEN V1290N or equivalent) synchronized to the SiPM system via a common White Rabbit timing network to maintain <5 ns synchronization across sub-detectors.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Addresses | Key Parameter |
|---|---|---|
| SuperFGD-style 1.5 cm scintillator cubes + SiPM/WLS | Short proton tracks; 4π muon tracking; H fraction control | 1.5 cm pitch; ρ~1.05 g/cm³; H~8% of nucleons |
| Upstream + downstream sciFi planes | Backward-track tagging; spectrometer handoff | 0.5 mm fiber, ~150 μm resolution |
| Lateral RPC lining on magnet yoke inner walls | 90°-going muon exit detection | 1 cm strip pitch, 2 layers/wall |
| Upstream mini-spectrometer (straw tubes + thin magnet) | Backward muon momentum measurement | σ_p/p ~20–30%, B·L ~ 0.05 T·m |
| Pipelined, topology-agnostic trigger | Unbiased efficiency at all angles | ≥3-cube cluster, 100 ns window |

---

## Cross-Check Against Requirements

**Muon ≥25% efficiency at all angles:**
- Forward muons → cube array + downstream drift chambers (existing). ✓
- 90° muons → cube array tracks + RPC exit hit. Even a 10 cm lateral track in cubes (7 cubes) with an RPC hit is reconstructable. ✓
- Backward muons → upstream SciFi tags exit, upstream mini-spectrometer measures momentum. ✓

**Protons to 60 MeV KE:**
- Range in polystyrene at 60 MeV ≈ 3.3 cm → ~2 cubes minimum. dE/dx in those cubes (~10–15 MeV/cm in scintillator) gives saturated but nonzero Birks response, distinguishable from minimum-ionizing particles. ✓

**Hydrogen ≤20% of nucleons:**
- Polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ: H nucleons/(total nucleons) = 8/(8+48+8) = 8/64 ≈ **12.5%** ✓ (margin remains for WLS fiber material, SiPM encapsulants, structural carbon-fiber supports)

**Compatibility with existing spectrometer:**
- Downstream SciFi plane provides clean track seeds for drift chamber matching; no structural modification to the magnet or drift chambers required. ✓

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for Kestrel Near Detector

## 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker with SiPM Readout**

**Technology:** Extruded polystyrene scintillator bars (1-1.5 cm² cross-section) arranged in alternating X-Y-Z orientations with multi-pixel silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readout at both ends.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Full angular acceptance**: The 25% efficiency requirement for perpendicular and backward-going muons is extremely challenging. Fine 3D segmentation ensures tracks at all angles cross multiple detector planes
- **Low proton threshold**: 60 MeV kinetic protons have ~3 cm range in scintillator. Fine granularity captures these short tracks with sufficient points for reconstruction
- **Timing resolution**: SiPMs provide ~1 ns timing, enabling position resolution along bars via time-difference and separating interaction vertices in the active volume
- **Hydrogen content**: Polystyrene (CH) provides ~7.7% hydrogen by mass of nucleons, safely below the 20% constraint while maintaining reasonable statistics

## 2. **Time Projection Chamber (TPC) with Resistive Micromegas Readout**

**Technology:** Gaseous TPC using Ar:CH₄ (90:10) or similar gas mixture with 2D resistive Micromegas charge readout (3 mm pitch) and continuous sampling.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **True 3D tracking**: TPCs provide complete trajectory information with no blind angles—critical for backward and perpendicular tracks
- **dE/dx particle identification**: Continuous ionization measurement distinguishes protons from pions/muons, essential for identifying recoil protons and reducing systematic uncertainties
- **Low material budget**: Minimizes secondary interactions and multiple scattering, preserving proton momentum information even for low-energy recoils
- **Hydrogen tuning**: CH₄ fraction directly controls hydrogen content (can adjust 5-15% to optimize statistics vs. modeling systematics)
- **Vertex resolution**: ~1 mm³ vertexing capability separates primary vertices from secondary interactions

## 3. **High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC (HPgTPC)**

**Technology:** Time projection chamber filled with argon gas at 10 bar pressure, with charge and scintillation light readout.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Pure argon target**: Zero hydrogen content matches far detector composition, eliminating need for hydrogen subtraction modeling entirely
- **Scalable volume**: High pressure increases interaction rate 10× versus atmospheric pressure while maintaining gaseous detector advantages
- **Dual readout**: Simultaneous charge (tracking) and scintillation light (fast timing, calorimetry) provide complementary information
- **Low threshold**: Excellent sensitivity to low-energy protons through combined dE/dx and range measurement
- **Uniform response**: No passive support structures or dead regions throughout the active volume

## 4. **Straw Tube Tracker (STT) in Active Target Region**

**Technology:** Dense array of 1 cm diameter straw tubes filled with Xe:CO₂:O₂ gas mixture, read out at both ends.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Minimal material**: Each tube is ~20 µm aluminized mylar, reducing multiple scattering of low-momentum protons
- **Excellent angular coverage**: Tubes can be arranged in multiple stereo angles to provide hit positions for tracks at any angle
- **Fast timing**: <5 ns resolution enables event pile-up rejection in high-intensity beam
- **Transition radiation**: Addition of radiator foils between tube layers provides e/π separation, reducing backgrounds
- **Low hydrogen**: Xe-based gas mixtures can achieve <5% hydrogen content

## 5. **Fine-Grained Graphite Target with Embedded Scintillating Fibers**

**Technology:** Graphite plates (2-3 mm thick) interleaved with planes of 1 mm diameter scintillating fibers read by SiPMs, oriented in orthogonal views.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Zero hydrogen**: Pure carbon target completely eliminates hydrogen modeling uncertainties
- **Nuclear target matching**: Carbon provides nuclear effects (FSI, binding) more similar to argon far detector than hydrogen
- **High granularity**: Fiber spacing of 1-2 mm provides adequate sampling for 60 MeV protons (~25 cm range in graphite)
- **Timing capability**: Fast scintillator response enables multi-interaction vertex separation
- **Cost-effective scaling**: Mature scintillating fiber technology can instrument large volumes affordably

## 6. **Hybrid Design: CH₂/Carbon Replaceable Target Modules**

**Technology:** Modular target system with removable cassettes containing either CH₂ (polyethylene) or pure carbon targets, each with embedded wavelength-shifting fiber readout.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Direct hydrogen subtraction**: Taking data with both CH₂ and C targets enables empirical subtraction (H = CH₂ - C) without relying entirely on modeling
- **Systematic control**: Direct measurement of hydrogen interaction rate validates/constrains nuclear models
- **Flexible operation**: Can tune hydrogen fraction by adjusting CH₂/C module ratio
- **Model validation**: Different target configurations test nuclear model dependencies affecting far detector extrapolation

## **Recommended Configuration**

For optimal performance, I recommend the **gaseous TPC option (#2)** with the following implementation:

- **Central TPC volume**: 2.0 m × 2.0 m × 0.9 m with 400 V/cm drift field
- **Gas mixture**: Ar:CH₄ (92:8) giving ~12% hydrogen by nucleon
- **Readout**: 3 mm pitch Micromegas on both ends (drift distance 1.0 m each direction)
- **Supplemental**: Thin scintillator planes at upstream and downstream ends for timing

This provides complete angular coverage, excellent proton detection down to threshold, tunable hydrogen content, and particle identification through dE/dx—addressing all the analysis requirements within the physical and systematic constraints.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Continuous 3D tracking:** TPCs provide true 3D space points along particle trajectories without discrete layers
- **dE/dx particle identification:** Energy loss measurements distinguish protons from charged pions at all angles—critical for modeling nuclear effects
- **Low material budget:** Minimal multiple scattering preserves momentum resolution for tracks entering the downstream spectrometer
- **Short proton tracks:** Excellent position resolution enables reconstruction of 1-2 cm tracks from threshold protons
- **Zero hydrogen:** Pure argon or P10 gas contains no hydrogen, eliminating systematic uncertainties from hydrogen subtraction

## 3. **Straw Tube Tracker in Dipole Volume**

**Technology:** Close-packed straw tubes (4-5 mm diameter) with X-Y orientations filling the magnetic volume, operated with Ar-CO₂ gas.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Enhanced momentum resolution:** Multiplying measurement points in the 0.15 T field improves σ(p)/p, particularly for the critical 0.3-1.5 GeV/c muon range
- **Charge-sign determination:** Better curvature measurement for tracks at large angles to the beam where path length in the field is limited
- **Backward track measurement:** Captures muons exiting upstream that the downstream chambers miss entirely
- **Low mass:** Straw tubes add minimal material before the existing drift chambers

## 4. **Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECAL) Surrounding Target**

**Technology:** Lead-scintillator sampling calorimeter or plastic scintillator planes at target boundaries.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Photon detection from π⁰ decay:** Distinguishes neutral-current from charged-current events; π⁰ production is a major background and nuclear physics observable
- **Containment:** Identifies events where particles escape the tracking volume, flagging incomplete energy reconstruction
- **Neutron detection:** Time-of-flight and energy deposition patterns identify neutrons from nuclear breakup
- **Electron identification:** Separates electron neutrino events from muon neutrino events for beam contamination studies

## 5. **High-Angle Muon Ranger (HAMR) Panels**

**Technology:** Planes of plastic scintillator with steel absorber plates positioned upstream and radially around the target, outside the magnet bore.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Range-based momentum for perpendicular/backward muons:** These tracks don't traverse the magnetic spectrometer; range-energy tables provide momentum measurement
- **Meeting the 25% efficiency requirement:** Without this, backward-going muons are completely lost, making the physics requirement impossible to meet
- **Low-energy muon measurement:** Muons below ~0.5 GeV often don't reach the downstream chambers; ranging recovers them

## 6. **Precision Optical Alignment and B-Field Mapping System**

**Technology:** Laser alignment grid and Hall probe array for field mapping to <1 mT precision.

**Physics Motivation:**
- **Systematic uncertainty reduction:** Momentum scale uncertainties directly propagate to neutrino energy reconstruction
- **Track matching:** Precise survey enables reliable linking between active target tracks and downstream spectrometer measurements
- **Time-dependent corrections:** Monitors field stability and detector movements over multi-year running

---

## Recommended Configuration

**Primary recommendation:** **Option 1 (Fine-grained scintillator tracker)** best balances all requirements:
- Meets angular acceptance requirement
- Achieves low-energy proton threshold
- Respects hydrogen constraint  
- Proven technology at appropriate scale (similar to MINERvA, T2K ND280)

**Enhanced option:** Combine scintillator tracker with **partial TPC** in central region for optimal dE/dx PID, with scintillator providing surrounding veto and proton detection.

# Proposed Upgrade for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Target Region

## 1. What the requirements rule out

The hydrogen limit decides the target material.

| Candidate active target | Fraction of target nucleons that are hydrogen |
|---|---|
| Polystyrene scintillator (CH)n | ~7.7% |
| Water | ~11% |
| Argon (liquid or gas) | ~0% |

- Any plastic-scintillator target exceeds the 2% limit by about a factor of 4. That includes a SuperFGD-style 3D cube array, which would otherwise be the obvious choice for 4π coverage and low-threshold protons.
- Since the far detector contains no hydrogen, a noble-element target is the natural fit. Argon is the assumed choice here: it matches an argon far detector, and the same reasoning would apply to any hydrogen-free far-detector nucleus.

**Core proposal:** replace the target region with a liquid-argon TPC using pixel readout. A high-pressure gas argon TPC is the fallback (Section 7).

## 2. Active target: modular pixelated LArTPC (ArgonCube / ND-LAr style)

**Volume and mass**
- The space is 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m³, about 5.4 m³ gross.
- After the cryostat and insulation, roughly 2.3 × 2.0 × 0.65 m³ of active LAr remains, about 4 tonnes.
- This gives a high event rate even with timing-based pile-up handling.

**Modules**
- Use a 2 × 2 array of optically isolated modules.
- Each has a central cathode and short drifts of about 30–50 cm.
- Short drifts keep the drift time near 200–300 µs, reduce the space-charge build-up that matters in a high-intensity near beam, and lower the high voltage needed to roughly 25–50 kV.
- The drift field should be about 500 V/cm.

**Charge readout**
- Native 3D pixel readout (LArPix-type ASICs) with about 4 mm pixel pitch.
- Wire planes are a poor choice here. Several interactions occur per spill, and tracks at high and backward angles create the classic wire-ambiguity problems. True 3D pixels remove both.

**Light readout**
- Segmented thin-panel detectors (ArCLight / LCM-type with wavelength-shifting light traps and SiPMs) lining the module walls.
- They provide ns-scale t₀ for each interaction and match flashes to charge clusters, which handles pile-up.

**How it meets the proton requirement**
- A 60 MeV proton travels about 3 cm in LAr.
- That is 7 or more pixel hits, so the track is resolved at any angle.
- dE/dx particle ID and range-based kinetic energy are available down to roughly 30–40 MeV.

**How it meets the muon angular requirement**
- The pixel TPC is intrinsically isotropic, so reconstruction efficiency does not collapse at 90° or for backward tracks the way it does for planar trackers.

## 3. Cryostat compatible with the warm magnet

- Use a non-magnetic, thin-walled vessel: a membrane or aluminium/composite inner vessel with vacuum or foam insulation.
- Keep the walls to a few percent of X₀ on the downstream face and on the top and bottom faces, so exiting muons reach the trackers without heavy multiple scattering.
- Run cryogenic and purification lines (recirculation pumps, O₂/H₂O filters, purity monitors) through the magnet gaps. Place the cryoplant outside the magnet.
- In the 0.15 T field, the readout electronics and HV feedthroughs must be validated for force and field effects. The field also produces a small, acceptable E×B drift correction, so a field-aligned layout is preferred.

## 4. Momentum and charge for muons in every direction

At about 0.65 m along the beam, the target cannot contain most muons. Muon momentum therefore has to come from several detectors working together.

**Forward muons**
- Use the existing downstream gas drift chambers, which already measure curvature and charge.

**High-angle muons (around 90°)**
- Add two high-angle TPCs directly above and below the target, inside the magnet, similar to the T2K ND280 HA-TPCs.
- Construction: resistive Micromegas readout, gas mixture Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ (T2K mix), thin composite field cages.
- These measure curvature in the bending plane.
- Orientation must match the field: if the dipole field is horizontal and transverse to the beam, put the HA-TPCs on top and bottom; for a vertical field, put them on the sides.

**Backward muons**
- Add an upstream tracker plane: a thin TPC, or scintillator-bar or Micromegas planes.
- Combine it with multiple-Coulomb-scattering momentum from the LAr track and range in the LAr.

**Muons that stop**
- Measure momentum by range in the LAr.
- The pixel TPC also gives an MCS estimate for partially contained tracks.

**Time of flight**
- Surround the target and tracker assembly with time-of-flight panels: plastic scintillator bars with SiPM readout, about 150 ps resolution.
- Their uses:
  - Determine forward versus backward direction, which resolves the backward-muon ambiguity.
  - Reject particles entering from outside.
  - Help separate muons from pions.
- These panels contain hydrogen, but they lie outside the fiducial target. Selecting vertices inside the LAr keeps hydrogen-target interactions far below the 2% budget.

**Outer layer (optional)**
- Retain or refurbish the side muon-range detectors in the magnet yoke to tag wide-angle muons.

## 5. Expected performance against the requirements

| Requirement | How it is met |
|---|---|
| Muon efficiency ≥25% at all angles | Isotropic 3D LAr reconstruction, plus HA-TPC, upstream tracker and ToF coverage. Combined efficiency should be well above 25% even at 90° and backward. |
| Protons at all angles down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy | ~3 cm tracks, 4 mm pixels, dE/dx particle ID, no angular dead zones. |
| Hydrogen ≤2% of target nucleons | Argon target contains essentially 0%. Hydrogenous material is placed only outside the fiducial volume. |
| Matching the far-detector nucleus | Argon on argon, which minimises nuclear-model extrapolation. |

## 6. Supporting systems

- **DAQ:** triggerless pixel readout synchronised to the beam spill. Use a White-Rabbit-type timing distribution shared with the ToF and TPCs.
- **Calibration:** cosmic rays, a UV laser for drift-field and space-charge mapping, and charge-injection pulsers on the pixel ASICs.

## 7. Fallback: high-pressure gas argon TPC

- About 10 bar argon with a low-hydrogen quencher (Ar/CO₂ or a few % CH₄, which keeps hydrogen at roughly 0.3% or less of nucleons).
- Read out with Micromegas or GEMs.
- Advantages: very low proton threshold, with 60 MeV protons travelling about 1 m; full 4π acceptance; curvature measured in the magnetic field.
- Drawback: only about 90 kg of target, which is roughly 40 times fewer events than LAr.
- Best role: a complementary low-threshold detector rather than the main target.

# Proposed Upgrade for the Kestrel Flats Near Station

## Recommendation in brief

Fill the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m target region with a **modular liquid-argon TPC using 3D pixel readout**, built in the ArgonCube / ND-LAr style. Add three supporting systems:

- thin tracking and time-of-flight (ToF) panels on the sides and upstream face,
- a low-mass cryostat engineered to fit inside the warm dipole,
- light-detection, purity and DAQ systems sized for near-detector pileup.

The hydrogen limit decides the target material. Plastic scintillator, the usual choice (a SuperFGD-type cube detector), is CH, so about 1 in 13 nucleons (~7.7%) is hydrogen. Water is ~11%. Both are well over the 2% limit. Argon has no hydrogen. It also matches a hydrogen-free far detector, most plausibly argon, so the nuclear target is identical near and far. This helps cancel nuclear-effect uncertainties.

## 1. Active target: pixelated LAr TPC

**Mass and layout**
- The volume holds about 5.4 m³ of LAr, roughly 7.5 t. At 410 m and 0.7 GeV this gives a high event rate.
- Split it into about 4–6 optically isolated modules. Each would be roughly 0.9 m deep along the beam, with a central cathode and two short drift regions of about 30–45 cm each.
- Short drifts reduce the requirements on electron lifetime, diffusion, and space-charge effects.
- Modularity confines each interaction's light to one module, which is essential for associating light and charge under pileup.

**Charge readout**
- Use LArPix-style cold pixel ASICs with roughly 3–4 mm pitch, giving true 3D imaging with no wire ambiguities.
- This matters for the angular requirement. Wire planes lose efficiency for tracks parallel to the wires or perpendicular to the drift; pixels do not have that weakness, so tracks at 90° and backward tracks are imaged as well as forward ones.

**Low-energy protons**
- A 60 MeV kinetic-energy proton ranges out in roughly 2.5–3 cm of LAr, about 8 pixels.
- That is enough for dE/dx-versus-residual-range identification and direction from the Bragg peak.
- A threshold of order 20–30 MeV kinetic energy is realistic, comfortably meeting the 60 MeV requirement at all angles.

**Light detection**
- Mount thin, large-area light traps on the field-cage walls, either ArCLight or LCM-style wavelength-shifting tiles read by SiPMs.
- These give nanosecond timing for spill sub-structure, t₀ for drift-coordinate assignment, and separation of pileup interactions.

**Field cage**
- Use a resistive-film field cage on thin substrates rather than bulky G10 or plastic rings, to minimise passive and hydrogenous material at the boundaries.

## 2. Keeping hydrogen below 2%

**Inside the fiducial volume:** only argon, so the hydrogen fraction there is zero.

**Near the fiducial volume:** some hydrogen is unavoidable in pixel PCBs, light-detector substrates, cables and field-cage supports. It must still be controlled:
- Choose low-hydrogen alternatives where possible, such as ceramic or Kapton-minimised boards and metal or quartz light-detector structures.
- Apply a fiducial cut of a few cm from these surfaces, since vertex resolution is about mm.
- Keep a material inventory showing that the effective hydrogen contamination of selected vertices is well under 2%. Out-of-fiducial vertices are rejected by the 3D vertex position.

**Cryostat:** use vacuum insulation with thin aluminium or stainless walls, not polyurethane foam. Foam is hydrogenous, and its bulk would also degrade tracking of exiting tracks.

## 3. Cryostat inside the warm magnet

- The 0.15 T field is compatible with the TPC. The Lorentz angle for electrons drifting in LAr is negligible, and pixel ASICs and SiPMs are unaffected.
- Make the cryostat walls as thin as possible, particularly on the downstream and side faces, so exiting muons reach the trackers with little scattering.
- Route cryogenic lines and recirculation and purification (getter/filter loop, purity monitors) through the magnet's existing openings, keeping clear of the downstream drift-chamber acceptance.

## 4. Meeting the all-angle muon requirement

The existing downstream drift chambers only cover forward muons. With only 0.9 m along the beam, high-angle and backward muons leave through the sides, top/bottom or upstream face. Three measures cover them:

**Momentum inside the LAr**
- Contained muons get momentum from range.
- Exiting muons get momentum from multiple Coulomb scattering along the imaged track. A 90° muon can traverse up to about 2.6 m of LAr, giving roughly 10–20% resolution.
- This alone should provide well above 25% efficiency at high angles.

**New side and upstream trackers**
- Fit thin gas TPC or drift-chamber panels on the four sides and the upstream face, between the cryostat and the magnet yoke.
- One option is resistive-Micromegas readout like the ND280 upgrade HA-TPCs. Another is compact multi-layer drift-tube or straw planes.
- These measure exit-point curvature in the 0.15 T field to give charge sign for high-angle and backward muons.
- They can use hydrogenous gas or materials freely, because they lie outside the target.

**ToF panels**
- Surround the cryostat with plastic-scintillator bars read by SiPMs, with about 100–150 ps resolution. They are outside the target, so hydrogen there is irrelevant.
- They resolve forward-versus-backward direction ambiguity for exiting tracks.
- They also reject entering backgrounds: cosmics and "rock"/magnet-iron muons.
- They provide additional particle-ID information.

## 5. DAQ and pileup

- A few interactions per spill are likely in about 7 t at this baseline, plus entering particles from upstream material.
- Pixel readout is natively 3D and self-triggering, and segmented light detection gives an independent t₀ per module. Together they separate overlapping interactions.
- Run the TPC, ToF, side trackers and existing drift chambers on a common clock with beam-spill timing, so tracks can be matched across subsystems.

## What this delivers against the requirements

| Requirement | How it is met |
|---|---|
| Hydrogen ≤ 2% of target nucleons | Argon target (0% H in the fiducial volume); low-hydrogen boundary materials and a fiducial cut |
| Muon efficiency ≥ 25% at all angles | Isotropic 3D pixel imaging; range/MCS momentum in LAr; side and upstream trackers for charge; ToF for direction |
| Protons at all angles down to ~60 MeV | Mm-scale 3D pixels with dE/dx PID; threshold ~20–30 MeV |
| Same nucleus as the far detector | Argon, assuming the hydrogen-free far detector is argon |

**Fallback:** if cryogenics inside the magnet proves impractical, a high-pressure gaseous-argon TPC (~10 bar) in the same volume also has no hydrogen. It gives an even lower proton threshold and excellent angular coverage, but only about 40 kg of target, so the statistics would be much lower. The LAr option is the primary recommendation.

# Proposed Upgrade: A 3D-Granular Target with High-Angle TPCs and a Time-of-Flight Envelope

## 1. Why the current detector falls short

The existing tracker planes (the plastic targets and the three TPCs) are all perpendicular to the beam. This geometry causes three problems.

- **High-angle tracks are lost.** Tracks above about 50–60° run nearly parallel to the bar layers and the TPC readout planes. They are poorly reconstructed or missed. That affects about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons, so the acceptance is forward-biased. This drives model dependence when extrapolating to a 4π water far detector.
- **The proton threshold is too high.** A 1 cm bar with alternating x/y views needs a proton to cross several layers before it forms a 3D track. This puts the threshold at about 450–500 MeV/c, roughly the median of the leading-proton spectrum. About half the protons, the low-momentum ones most sensitive to nuclear effects, are lost.
- **Neutrons and timing are absent.** Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) is cleaner when the final-state neutron in antineutrino CC events can be measured. Track direction (forward/backward) and out-of-fiducial-volume (OOFV) backgrounds also need better timing.

The upgrade therefore has to deliver 4π acceptance, a low proton threshold, neutron tagging and good timing.

## 2. Proposed configuration (the photon-tagging volume is replaced)

### (a) Central target: a 3D-segmented scintillator detector (fine-grained cube detector)

- **Geometry:** about 192 × 182 × 56 cubes of 1 × 1 × 1 cm³.
  - That is about 2 million optically isolated polystyrene cubes, about 2 t of target. This is a mass gain of roughly 2× over a single existing target.
  - The cubes fill the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box. The 0.6 m dimension is vertical, with the beam along the 1.9 m axis, which leaves room for TPCs above and below.
- **Cube construction:**
  - Extruded scintillator cubes with a chemical-etch reflective (TiO₂) skin.
  - Three orthogonal 1.0 mm holes per cube, each holding a 1 mm wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibre.
  - The fibres give three 2D projections (XY, XZ, YZ) that are combined into a true 3D image.
- **Readout:**
  - About 56,000 channels, one silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) per fibre.
  - This reuses the proven fibre-plus-SiPM technology and front-end board style of the existing detector.
  - Reading out one end of each fibre, with a mirror on the far end, keeps the channel count manageable.
- **Performance targets:**
  - About 40 photoelectrons (p.e.) per cube per fibre for a minimum-ionizing particle (MIP).
  - About 1 ns time resolution per channel, and about 0.6 ns per cube when channels are combined.
  - Isotropic acceptance, because there is no preferred plane orientation.
  - A proton tracking threshold of about 300 MeV/c, since a proton needs only about 2–3 cubes. This recovers most of the leading-proton spectrum below the 450 MeV/c median.
  - Calorimetric dE/dx for proton/pion/muon identification.
  - Separation of γ → e⁺e⁻ conversions.
  - Neutron detection from the delayed, displaced isolated hits of neutron re-scatters, with energy measured by time of flight (ToF) between vertex and hit over tens of cm.
- **Higher-momentum particles:** protons above about 900 MeV/c (about 6%) and most muons exit the cube detector. They are momentum-analysed by the TPCs, while range and curvature in the cubes cover stopping tracks.
- **Mechanics:**
  - A low-mass carbon-fibre/composite box with tensioned fishing-line or fibre alignment during assembly.
  - Cube position tolerance of about 0.2 mm across 2 m.
  - Cube faces are kept free of glue so the WLS fibres can be threaded through.
- **Calibration:** a light-injection system plus cosmic and through-going muons.
- **Target material:** the target is hydrocarbon (CH), which is acceptable. The downstream water-layer target remains for the C/O comparison.

### (b) Two high-angle TPCs (HA-TPCs), above and below the cube target

- **Geometry:**
  - Each is about 2.0 m (along the beam) × 2.0 m × 0.8 m.
  - The drift is horizontal, perpendicular to the beam, with a central cathode and readout on both side walls.
- **Field cage:** a thin, light composite (aramid honeycomb/kevlar) cage. This minimises dead material between the target and the TPC gas, which matters for low-momentum protons and for electron/γ separation.
- **Gas:** the existing argon-based mixture, e.g. Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ (95/3/2), for continuity of systematics.
- **Readout:** resistive Micromegas, with charge spreading through a resistive DLC layer.
  - Pad size of about 1 × 1 cm, giving about 10 mm × 11 mm pads with charge sharing for sub-mm spatial resolution.
  - About 8 modules per readout plane and 16 per TPC.
  - The resistive layer also suppresses sparks.
- **Performance:**
  - Momentum resolution better than 10% at 1 GeV/c in the 0.2 T field.
  - dE/dx resolution better than 10% for μ/e separation and proton ID.
  - These TPCs give momentum and charge for high-angle muons and for protons above about 900 MeV/c that leave the cube volume.
- **Electronics:** a reused AFTER/AGET-type chip, with front-ends mounted on the module back to save space.

### (c) Time-of-flight envelope

- **Layout:** six ToF panels enclose the cube detector and HA-TPC assembly (top, bottom, upstream, downstream and two sides).
- **Construction:**
  - Each panel uses plastic scintillator bars about 2.2 m × 12 cm × 1 cm.
  - Each bar is read out at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
  - The bars are read out directly, with no WLS fibre, to preserve timing.
- **Performance and uses:**
  - Time resolution of about 150 ps per bar.
  - Distinguishes inward-going from outward-going tracks.
  - Rejects OOFV backgrounds such as interactions in the magnet, the electromagnetic calorimeter (ECal) or the sand.
  - Provides track timing for neutron ToF and supports particle ID alongside the TPC dE/dx.

### (d) Integration and supporting changes

- **Basket mounting:** the cube detector, HA-TPCs and ToF panels mount in the existing upstream basket region. Cables route through the yoke gaps.
- **Shared timing:** a common clock and trigger distribution synchronises the new subsystems with the existing TPCs, fine-grained detectors (FGDs), ECal and the scintillator planes in the yoke gaps.
- **Data acquisition:** a modest DAQ upgrade to handle about 60,000 new SiPM channels plus about 100,000 TPC pads.
- **Rate check:** per-spill pile-up in about 2 t of target at a few hundred metres is acceptable given 3D imaging and nanosecond timing. Bunch-by-bunch separation, at roughly 580 ns spacing, is retained.
- **Upstream side:** the upstream barrel ECal is kept, or retrofitted where the photon-tagging section's ECal was, to contain photons from π⁰ decays in the new target.

## 3. Expected physics gain

- **Acceptance:** near-4π for muons, matching far-detector phase space and removing the forward-angle extrapolation.
- **Protons:** threshold lowered from about 450 to about 300 MeV/c. This gives TKI variables (δpT, δαT, δφT) with both the muon and the leading proton fully reconstructed in most CC0π events.
- **Neutrons:** event-by-event detection with ToF-based kinematics in ν̄ CC events, giving fully closed kinematics for ν̄ₘ p → μ⁺ n.
- **Electron/photon separation:** improved, for the νₑ background constraint.
- **Statistics:** roughly double the fiducial target mass in the upstream region.

Together, better flux×cross-section modelling (nuclear effects, two-particle-two-hole contributions, removal energy) and the acceptance match should reduce the extrapolated systematic from about 6% toward the roughly 4% required.

# Recommendation: Hardware Changes for the Near-Detector Upgrade

## 1. What the current detector cannot do

The present tracker was optimised for forward-going muons. Three features limit it.

- **Bar orientation.** The target bars are all perpendicular to the beam, in alternating x/y layers. A track near 90° runs within one or two layers, so its 3D trajectory and its energy loss per unit length (dE/dx) are poorly measured.
- **TPC placement.** The gas TPCs sit downstream of the targets. Tracks above about 50–60° never reach them, so they get no momentum or dE/dx measurement.
- **Proton threshold.** A proton must cross several 1 cm layers to be tracked. This sets a threshold near 450 MeV/c, which is roughly the median of the leading-proton spectrum, so about half the protons are lost.

The consequences for the physics programme:

- About 25% of muons and 35% of protons exit above 50°.
- Most low-momentum protons are lost.
- The near detector therefore samples a different region of phase space than the 4π water far detector. Extrapolating between them leans on the cross-section model, which is a large part of the residual 6%.
- Reaching 4% requires near-4π, low-threshold, kinematically complete events. That is also exactly what transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) needs.

## 2. New active target: a 3D-readout, finely segmented scintillator-cube detector

This follows the "SuperFGD" concept.

**Construction**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes.
- Each cube has a chemically etched reflective surface and three orthogonal 1.5 mm holes.
- A 1 mm Kuraray Y11 wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibre runs through each hole, along x, y and z.

**Geometry**
- 192 × 56 × 182 cubes, about 1.92 m (x) × 0.56 m (y, vertical) × 1.82 m (z, beam).
- This fills the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box with mechanical clearance.
- Target mass is about 2 t of CH, roughly double the existing first target.

**Readout**
- One end of each fibre goes to a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), for example a Hamamatsu S13360-series 1.3 mm device.
- Channel count: 182·56 + 192·56 + 192·182 ≈ **56,000 channels**.
- Front-end: CITIROC-based boards, matching the existing SiPM experience in the collaboration.

**Justification**

- **Isotropic acceptance.** Every cube gives three orthogonal 2D projections, so a track is reconstructed equally well at any angle. This directly recovers the 25% of muons and 35% of protons above 50°, including tracks perpendicular to the beam.
- **Low proton threshold.**
  - A 300 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 47 MeV and travels about 2 cm in plastic, crossing 2–3 cubes. That is enough for tracking and for particle identification from the Bragg peak.
  - The threshold falls from about 450 to about 300 MeV/c, recovering most of the spectrum below the median.
  - The median 450 MeV/c proton (kinetic energy about 100 MeV, range about 8 cm) is fully contained and measured by range to a few percent.
- **Fine calorimetry and timing.**
  - Light yield is about 40 photoelectrons per channel for a minimum-ionising particle, giving good dE/dx for separating protons from pions and muons.
  - Time resolution is about 1 ns per channel, and below 1 ns per cube when combining fibres. This allows neutron detection via secondary-proton hits and time of flight. Neutrons complete TKI for antineutrino events, a bonus beyond the stated requirement.
- **Matched target material.** Hydrocarbon is accepted for this programme. The downstream water-layer target remains in place for carbon/water ratios.

**Design risks to control**
- Optical crosstalk between cubes, about 3%. Specify the reflector quality and require crosstalk-aware hit unfolding.
- Assembly tolerance of the cube matrix. A fishing-line or rod assembly method, with fibres inserted after alignment, is the proven approach.

## 3. Two High-Angle TPCs above and below the new target

This follows the "HA-TPC" concept.

**Layout**
- The target uses only about 0.6 m of the roughly 2.2 m height of the removed photon-tagging volume.
- Place one horizontal gas TPC above and one below the cube detector. Each is about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m, with the drift running perpendicular to the cathode.

**Construction**
- **Gas:** the same argon-based mixture as the existing TPCs (Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2), so the gas system and calibration are shared.
- **Field cage:** thin, low-mass composite walls (about 4% of a radiation length). This keeps tracks entering from the target from multiple-scattering or showering in the wall.
- **Readout:** resistive (encapsulated-anode) bulk Micromegas, "ERAM".
  - The resistive layer spreads the charge over neighbouring pads. This gives spatial resolution below 0.6 mm with roughly 1 cm pads, so fewer channels are needed.
  - It also intrinsically protects against sparks.
- **Electronics:** compact AGET-based front-ends mounted on the modules.

**Justification**

- **High-momentum protons.**
  - About 6% of protons exceed 900 MeV/c, corresponding to a kinetic energy of about 370 MeV and a range of about 80 cm.
  - These escape the 0.56 m-tall target vertically, so range cannot measure them. Magnetic curvature in the 0.2 T field can, at about 10% resolution near 1 GeV/c.
- **Momentum and PID for high-angle muons.**
  - High-angle muons leaving up or down are measured by curvature, with charge sign and dE/dx identification (about 10% dE/dx resolution separates electrons, muons and protons).
  - This complements range measurement inside the target, and gives the angle-independent muon reconstruction the far-detector extrapolation needs.
- **Full solid-angle coverage.** Together with the existing downstream TPCs (forward tracks) and the side ECal and yoke-gap scintillator (side-going tracks), every exit direction of the cube detector is spectrometer-instrumented.

## 4. Time-of-Flight shell around the new target and HA-TPCs

**Construction**
- Six planes enclosing the target and HA-TPC module.
- Each plane is made of plastic scintillator bars, about 2.2 m × 12 cm × 1 cm.
- Bars are read out at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs with fast sampling electronics.
- Time resolution: about 100–150 ps per bar.

**Justification**

- **Direction of travel.** Timing gives an unambiguous direction (sense) for each track. This rejects backward-entering particles from interactions in the magnet, coil and calorimeter, which matters much more once high-angle and backward tracks are accepted.
- **Extra PID.** Time of flight over about 1 m separates protons from muons and pions around 1 GeV/c. This is where TPC dE/dx bands cross, which helps the high-momentum proton tail.
- **Trigger and cosmics.** It provides a fast cosmic-ray trigger and calibration source.
- **Neutron energy.** It sharpens the neutron time-of-flight reference.

## 5. What to keep unchanged

- **Magnet and side-muon range detector.** Keep the 0.2 T magnet and the yoke-gap scintillators (side-muon ranging for very high-angle muons).
- **Downstream modules.** Keep the three existing TPCs and the two plastic targets, including the water-layer target, unchanged. This provides:
  - continuity with existing datasets;
  - the carbon-to-water comparison.
- **Surrounding calorimeters.** Keep the lead-scintillator calorimeters.
  - Their upstream section may need rearrangement for cable routing of about 56k new channels plus HA-TPC services.
  - Plan for the fibre/SiPM heat load and service paths through the magnet early.

## 6. Expected impact on systematics

- **Phase-space coverage.** Near-detector angular acceptance becomes approximately 4π, matching the water far detector. This removes model-dependent extrapolation into unmeasured high-angle regions.
- **Better final-state constraints.** Lower proton thresholds plus complete muon/proton (and neutron) kinematics enable TKI variables such as δp_T, δα_T and δφ_T. These separate nuclear effects (Fermi motion, multinucleon/2p2h interactions, final-state interactions) and constrain the cross-section model directly.
- **Larger, cleaner sample.** Doubling the active target mass, with a more uniform efficiency, cuts statistical and detector-efficiency uncertainties.

Together, these changes are the most direct route from roughly 6% to roughly 4% on the far-detector prediction.

## Summary of recommended hardware

| Component | Technology | Key number |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | 1 cm³ scintillator cubes, 3D WLS fibre + SiPM readout | ~2 M cubes, ~2 t, ~56k channels; proton threshold ~300 MeV/c |
| High-angle tracking | 2 HA-TPCs, resistive Micromegas, light composite field cage | dE/dx ~10%; p resolution ~10% at 1 GeV/c |
| Timing and veto | 6-plane scintillator ToF shell, double-ended SiPM readout | ~100–150 ps |

Based on the constraints and physics requirements, I propose a **3D fine-grained scintillator tracker (3DST)** as the replacement target. Here's the specific hardware design:

## Core Target Design: SuperFGD-style 3D Scintillator Cube

**Technology**: Optically-isolated cubic scintillator cells with three-axis readout
- **10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm polystyrene cubes** (compatible with existing bar cross-section)
- Each cube wrapped in reflective coating (ESR film or TiO₂-loaded coating)
- **Three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres** threaded through each cube (one per axis)

- **CITIROC or SPIROC ASICs** (proven in CALICE, used in similar detectors)

**Muon reconstruction**:
- 10 mm granularity gives **~5° angular resolution**

- Multiple scattering momentum for exiting tracks
- High acceptance for >50° tracks via 4π readout

**Proton reconstruction**:
- **dE/dx discrimination** via multi-cube energy deposits

If water target is strongly preferred for direct far-detector matching:

## Recommended Solution: Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker

### Primary Technology: Extruded Plastic Scintillator Bar Array

**Specific Implementation:**
- **1 cm × 1 cm × 2.6 m extruded polystyrene scintillator bars** (similar to MINERvA, T2K ND280)
- Three orientations (X, U, V at 0°, +60°, -60°) in alternating planes
- **5 mm bar spacing** to achieve required spatial resolution
- **Wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber readout** embedded in each bar

**Justification:**

1. **Hydrogen fraction control**: Polystyrene (CH) provides ~7.4% hydrogen by nucleon count, well below 20% limit
   
2. **60 MeV proton detection**: 
   - 60 MeV protons have ~3 mm range in polystyrene
   - 1 cm granularity with 5 mm effective resolution captures these tracks
   - High sampling frequency ensures multiple hits even for short tracks

3. **4π angular acceptance**:
   - Three orientations provide 3D tracking
   - Upstream/downstream planes capture forward/backward tracks
   - Short radiation length (X₀ ~43 cm) minimizes scattering for backward reconstruction

4. **Muon efficiency >25% at all angles**:
   - Fine granularity enables pattern recognition even for complex topologies
   - Multiple scattering in thin planes aids low-momentum reconstruction
   - dE/dx provides particle identification

5. **Magnetic field compatibility**: SiPMs unaffected by 0.15 T field (unlike PMTs)

### Supplementary Technology: Precision Tracking Planes

**Specific Implementation:**
- **Thin plastic scintillator planes with silicon photomultiplier arrays** at 3-4 locations within volume
- OR **Micromegas chambers** (2-3 layers) for improved angular resolution

**Justification:**
- Enhances vertex resolution to ~2-3 mm for improved proton/pion separation
- Better angle measurement for tracks entering drift chambers
- Minimal mass addition (~0.5% X₀ per layer for Micromegas)

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near-Detector Target Region

The 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m region should become a combined system. A fine-grained, fully 3D scintillator target sits in the middle. Thin gas TPCs sit above and below it, and fast timing planes enclose the assembly. Each element addresses a specific requirement.

## 1. Active target: 3D-segmented plastic scintillator ("SuperFGD"-type)

**Technology**
- Roughly 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each with a reflective (chemically etched) surface.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibers.
- Each fiber is read out at one end by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM/MPPC).
- The volume is a central slab spanning the full width and beam length. It is about 0.6–0.8 m tall, leaving room above and below for the TPCs.
- Mass: roughly 1.5–2 t.
- Scale: on the order of 2 million cubes but only about 60,000 readout channels, because readout is by fiber, not by cube.

**Why**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three orthogonal projections give true 3D reconstruction for tracks at any angle. This is unlike bar or plane trackers, which lose tracks running parallel to the planes, which is exactly the high-angle and perpendicular case.
- **Low proton threshold.** A 60 MeV proton travels only about 3 cm in plastic. That is about 3 cubes, enough to reconstruct and identify it by dE/dx near the Bragg peak. Coarser segmentation (2.5 cm bars or more) cannot do this.
- **Hydrogen fraction within limits.** In polystyrene (CH)ₙ, hydrogen is 1 of 13 nucleons, about 7.7%. This is comfortably under the 20% ceiling, so the hydrogen-subtraction model remains valid. The fiber, glue and coating materials are also CH-based and do not change this.
- **Timing.** Sub-ns timing per channel supports time-of-flight measurements across the cube volume. It also supports neutron detection via delayed or displaced isolated hits.
- **Momentum by range.** In a weak 0.15 T field, range in the target gives the momentum of stopping muons and protons.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Two thin gas TPCs fill the remaining height of the region (on the order of 0.7–0.8 m each) and span the full 2.6 m × 0.9 m footprint.
- Each has a central cathode and a lightweight composite (low-mass) field cage.
- Gas is a T2K-type argon mixture, e.g. Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2. Its hydrogen content and mass are negligible.
- Readout is by resistive Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode). Charge spreading gives about 0.5 mm resolution with about 1 cm pads, at modest channel count.

**Why**
- **Coverage of high-angle tracks.** Tracks at large angles, including those perpendicular to the beam, leave the target upward or downward. They never reach the downstream drift chambers, so without these TPCs they are lost.
- **Charge and momentum.** The TPCs measure charge sign and momentum from curvature in the 0.15 T field.
- **Particle identification.** dE/dx separates μ, π, p and e, which keeps the muon efficiency at or above 25% at all angles.
- **Low material.** The low-mass field cage minimizes multiple scattering before the momentum measurement.
- **Field orientation.** The TPCs should be oriented so that the bending plane is measured, given the field direction. Side-going tracks that run nearly parallel to the field get little curvature. Those rely on range in the target plus the timing planes.

## 3. Time-of-flight envelope around the target and TPCs

**Technology**
- Planes of plastic scintillator bars enclosing all six faces of the target region.
- Each bar is read out at both ends with arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Target timing resolution is about 150 ps or better.

**Why**
- **Track direction.** Backward-going muons are the hard case. Timing between the target and the TOF planes identifies inward versus outward going tracks, and rejects tracks entering from outside, such as cosmics or interactions in the magnet and surrounding material.
- **Particle identification.** Combining TOF with momentum improves μ/p and e/μ separation at low momentum.
- **Trigger and calibration.** The planes provide a cosmic trigger and a timing reference for calibration.

## 4. Supporting systems (budget line items)

- **Electronics.** Front-end and DAQ electronics for about 60,000 SiPM channels and the Micromegas pads. These must be integrated into the existing drift-chamber DAQ with common timing to the beam spill.
- **Mechanics.** A mechanical support "basket" sized to the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m envelope. It should be low-mass where tracks exit, and made of non-magnetic material inside the dipole.
- **Calibration.** An LED/light-injection system for SiPM gain monitoring, a TPC laser calibration system, and temperature control.
- **Gas.** A gas system for the new TPCs.

## How the requirements are met

| Requirement | Provided by |
|---|---|
| Muon efficiency ≥25% at all angles, including perpendicular | 3D cubes (isotropic) + top/bottom TPCs + TOF |
| Backward-going muons | 3D cubes (isotropic) + top/bottom TPCs + TOF (direction by timing) |
| 60 MeV protons at all angles | 1 cm³ 3D segmentation, range and dE/dx |
| Charge and momentum of escaping tracks | High-angle TPCs + existing downstream chambers in 0.15 T |
| Hydrogen ≤20% of target nucleons | Polystyrene target (~7.7% H); gas TPCs negligible mass |

# Recommendation: Re-equipping the Kestrel Flats Near-Station Target Region

## Summary

Replace the target region with three systems:

1. **A finely segmented 3D plastic-scintillator cube target** (SuperFGD-style).
2. **Two high-angle TPCs** above and below it, read out with resistive Micromegas.
3. **A hermetic time-of-flight shell** around the assembly.

This follows the logic of the T2K ND280 upgrade, scaled to a box that is only 0.9 m deep along the beam. It meets the angular-acceptance, proton-threshold and hydrogen-fraction requirements at once.

## 1. Active target: 3D-readout scintillator cubes

**Technology**
- About 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres.
- Each fibre is read at one end by a silicon photomultiplier (MPPC/SiPM).
- Front-end electronics with about 1 ns hit timing.

**Indicative size:** about 2.0 m (x) × 1.0 m (vertical, y) × 0.75 m (along beam, z). That is roughly 1.5 million cubes, 1.5 t, and about 4.5 × 10⁴ channels.

**Justification**

- **Hydrogen constraint.** In polystyrene (CH)ₙ, hydrogen supplies 1 of 13 nucleons per CH unit, about 7.7%. Fibres, reflective coating and glue keep the total below about 9%, well inside the 20% limit.
  - Water (2 of 18, about 11%) would also pass, but it is passive and needs separate tracking planes.
  - A gas or liquid-argon TPC target would push mass, cryogenics or space beyond this box.
- **Isotropic acceptance.** The three orthogonal projections reconstruct tracks equally well at any polar angle, including 90° and backward.
  - Bar-layer detectors such as FGD or MINERvA planes lose tracks lying in a plane.
  - The cubes therefore remove the angular hole that prevents ≥25% muon efficiency near 90°.
- **Low-energy protons.** A 60 MeV proton has a CSDA range of about 3 cm in polystyrene, so it crosses about 3 cubes with high dE/dx.
  - At 1 cm granularity this gives a reconstructable short track, with particle identification from dE/dx and range.
  - Coarser segmentation (2–3 cm bars) would lose these protons. Finer than 1 cm multiplies channel count without much gain at this energy.
- **Neutrons and timing.** The detector is fully active and sub-ns timed. This adds neutron detection by time of flight as a bonus and helps separate pile-up from the magnet walls.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Two TPCs, each about 2.0 m × 0.6 m tall × 0.75–0.9 m deep.
- Low-mass composite field cages.
- Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ (T2K) gas mixture.
- Read out by **resistive (encapsulated-resistive-anode) Micromegas**.

**Justification**
- The existing downstream drift chambers only see forward-going tracks. High-angle muons, with polar angle around 50–130°, leave the target vertically and need their own momentum and charge measurement.
- The warm dipole field is horizontal and transverse to the beam, so tracks heading up or down curve in the measured plane.
- At 0.15 T, a 500 MeV/c muon has a radius of about 11 m. Only a gas tracker with a lever arm of tens of cm can measure that sagitta with useful precision (around 10% at 1 GeV/c).
- Resistive Micromegas spread charge over pads, which gives:
  - better spatial resolution with fewer, larger pads, controlling cost;
  - spark protection;
  - dE/dx for muon/electron/proton separation.
- With 1.0 m of cubes plus 2 × 0.6 m of TPCs, the vertical stack is 2.2 m, leaving about 10 cm for the ToF and services.

## 3. Time-of-flight shell

**Technology**
- Planes of about 2 cm-thick plastic-scintillator bars on all six faces.
- Read out at both ends with SiPM arrays.
- Target timing resolution of about 150 ps.

**Justification**
- **Track direction.** A 1 m path gives about a 3.3 ns flight time, so a resolution of about 150 ps unambiguously distinguishes:
  - a backward-going muon from the vertex;
  - a forward-going particle entering from upstream material such as the magnet or sand.
- Without this, backward tracks are lost or mis-identified, which breaks the "all angles" requirement.
- **Veto and PID.** The shell vetoes externally produced backgrounds and adds β-based particle identification for low-momentum tracks.

## How the muon-efficiency requirement is met at each angle

| Muon direction | Measurement |
|---|---|
| Forward (θ < ~40°) | Existing downstream drift chambers in the 0.15 T field. |
| High-angle, up or down | The new TPCs give momentum and charge from curvature. |
| Near 90°, sideways (along the field) | Little bending, because the track runs nearly parallel to B. The cubes give momentum by range for contained tracks, and the ToF tags exiting tracks. |
| Backward | Cubes, then the upstream ToF or high-angle TPCs; ToF timing fixes the direction. |

The sideways region along the field is only a slice of azimuth at each polar angle. Averaged over azimuth, efficiency at θ ≈ 90° stays comfortably above 25%.

## Ancillary items

- Calibration is by cosmic muons, a light-injection system and per-channel SiPM gain and temperature monitoring.
- Electronics and SiPM readout must tolerate the 0.15 T fringe field. SiPMs are insensitive to it, which is a further reason to choose them over PMTs.
- A support frame and mechanics must place the cube assembly within the existing inner volume. Leave about 5 cm clearance for routing fibre and readout cables out of the magnet.

# Hardware upgrades for the Kestrel Flats near detector active target

## 1. Choice of target material: argon

The 2% hydrogen limit decides the target technology before anything else.

- **Plastic scintillator is ruled out.** Scintillator is CH, so hydrogen is 1 of every 13 nucleons, about 7.7%. That is roughly four times over the limit. This excludes scintillator-cube or bar detectors (SuperFGD-style) as the target, even though they are the usual choice for 4π proton tracking.
- **Water is also ruled out.** Hydrogen is 2 of every 18 nucleons, about 11%.
- **Argon is the natural choice.** It contains no hydrogen. It also matches a hydrogen-free far detector, which is very likely argon, so nuclear effects largely cancel between near and far.

## 2. Primary upgrade: modular liquid-argon TPC with pixel readout

**What it is:** an optically segmented LAr TPC, in the style of ArgonCube or the DUNE ND-LAr modules, filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region. That volume holds about 5.4 m³, or roughly 7.5 t of LAr.

**Why each design feature is needed:**

- **Pixel (3D) charge readout instead of wire planes.**
  - At 410 m from the target, each spill contains many interactions.
  - Pixels give true 3D space points, which avoids the ambiguities wire planes create under this pile-up.
  - Native 3D also makes reconstruction equally good at every angle, including tracks perpendicular to the beam.
- **Small pixel pitch (about 3–4 mm) and short drift (about 30–50 cm per module).**
  - A 60 MeV proton travels only about 3 cm in LAr.
  - This pitch gives roughly ten or more samples along such a track, enough to reconstruct it and identify it as a proton from dE/dx and its Bragg peak.
  - Short drifts keep diffusion, space-charge distortion and argon purity requirements manageable.
- **Optically isolated modules with fast light readout** (ArCLight / LCM-type light-collection tiles):
  - assign each charge cluster to the correct interaction in the spill (t₀ determination);
  - provide timing for the trigger.
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Protons at all angles, including backward, are reconstructed with no geometric hole. A scintillator bar or layer geometry would leave one.
- **Low-mass walls and an oriented drift direction.** Use thin cryostat walls and choose the drift direction so that cathodes and other dead material between modules stay small. Tracks then cross between modules and leave the target with little energy loss.

**Gaseous-argon alternative:** a high-pressure gaseous argon TPC also meets the hydrogen limit, provided the quencher is chosen carefully.

- Ar/CH₄ at 90/10 gives about 1.1% hydrogen by nucleon count.
- The T2K mixture Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ at 95/3/2 gives about 0.5%.
- However, it would hold only about 100 kg of target at roughly 10 bar, compared with about 7.5 t of LAr.

LAr is therefore the baseline for statistics. Whichever is chosen, the proposal should require that the full hydrogen content inside the fiducial volume be budgeted against the 2% limit. That includes quench gas and any plastic or G10 structures.

## 3. Large-angle and backward muon tracking around the target

**The problem:** the existing drift chambers are downstream, so they only see forward-going tracks. Muons near 90° leave through the sides, and backward muons leave through the upstream face. A muon of about 0.7 GeV has a range of about 3 m in LAr, so many of these muons are not contained in a 2.3–2.6 m wide volume.

**The upgrade:** thin, low-mass gas TPC or tracker panels inside the 0.15 T field, in the style of the ND280 high-angle TPCs with resistive Micromegas readout.

- Place panels above and below the target, and on the sides where the magnet geometry permits.
- Extend coverage to the upstream face for backward tracks.

**What they provide:**

- momentum and charge sign from curvature for tracks that exit at high angle;
- sustained muon efficiency of at least 25% at every angle, together with:
  - range-based momentum for muons contained in the LAr;
  - multiple-scattering momentum for partially contained muons.

## 4. Time-of-flight layer enclosing the target and trackers

**What it is:** thin, fast plastic-scintillator ToF panels surrounding the target and tracker assembly, with sub-nanosecond timing (about 100–150 ps, read out by SiPMs).

**Why it is needed:**

- It distinguishes backward-going muons from forward-going tracks that enter from outside. At these angles the curvature alone gives a direction ambiguity.
- It rejects interactions in the magnet and walls that send particles into the target.
- It provides timing for the spill.

**Hydrogen check:** the panels are outside the argon fiducial volume, so they do not count against the 2% hydrogen budget.

## 5. Supporting infrastructure

- **Cryostat** that fits inside the warm magnet. It needs:
  - thin, low-Z entrance and side walls to minimise dead material for exiting muons and backgrounds;
  - argon purification and recirculation to maintain electron lifetime over the drift.
- **Upstream veto** (thin scintillator or ToF panels) to tag rock and magnet muons entering the volume.
- **Triggerless, high-rate DAQ** that combines pixel charge, light and ToF data.
- **Calibration systems:**
  - laser or radioactive sources for drift-field and purity monitoring;
  - cosmic-ray running for alignment with the downstream drift chambers.

## Summary

| Upgrade | Technology | Driving requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | Modular pixel-readout LAr TPC with optical segmentation (~7.5 t) | ≤2% hydrogen; argon match to far detector; 60 MeV protons (~3 cm tracks) at all angles; pile-up at 410 m |
| High-angle and backward trackers | Low-mass gas TPCs (resistive Micromegas) in the 0.15 T field | Muon efficiency of at least 25% at 90° and backward |
| ToF enclosure | Fast scintillator with SiPMs, ~100–150 ps | Track direction (backward vs. entering); background rejection |
| Cryostat, veto, DAQ, calibration | Thin-wall cryostat, scintillator veto, triggerless DAQ, laser/source calibration | Low dead material; reliable operation |
